title: Prompt-Based Cognitive Scaffolding
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
bf7bc1447e7ed3caf087f04fb77606d4e98c71c2.abstract: <jats:p>While research on AI literacy, prompt engineering, and prompt literacy has expanded rapidly, an integrated framework explaining prompt-mediated learning remains underdeveloped. We introduce the Prompt-Based Cognitive Scaffolding (PBCS) model, which conceptualizes prompts as regulatory mechanisms that coordinate cognitive, epistemic, and metacognitive processes during human–AI interaction. Building on cognitive scaffolding, distributed cognition, epistemic cognition, and prompt literacy, PBCS explains learning as a recursive coordination process in which human reasoning and AI-generated outputs are continuously refined. The model is operationalized through three interacting scaffolding dimensions and a functional prompt typology. Its explanatory scope is demonstrated across seminar-based learning, academic writing, collaborative learning, and research-oriented inquiry. We provide a theoretical foundation for understanding recursive human–AI knowledge construction.</jats:p>

title: Prompt Engineering as Distributed Cognition and Epistemic Infrastructure in Higher Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
d3ce7c75e5f8d37877d734c90b6dc48c96bd1c5b.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter theorizes prompt literacy as epistemic infrastructure in higher education, conceptualizing prompting as distributed cognition across learners, generative systems, artifacts, and disciplinary genres. It models prompting as a regulated workflow of specification, constraint-synthesis, iterative diagnosis, triangulated verification, uncertainty labelling, and accountable disclosure, reframing authorship as auditable process rather than polished output. Integrating mediated action, activity-system contradictions, pragmatics, genre theory, and epistemic cognition, the chapter translates construct logic into scalable pedagogies, evidence-centred assessment architectures, and integrity-by-design governance. It foregrounds equity as a capability condition, embedding culturally responsive prompting, multilingual burden reduction, accessibility-by-design, and privacy-security postures within institutional quality assurance. The result is a tool-agnostic blueprint for future-ready universities that stabilizes validity, trust, and learning under platform volatility.</jats:p>

title: Prompting for Academic Writing and Research
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
a33a6033f3bf398f73b26ab21bb6cfa211ed34c1.abstract: <jats:p>The chapter examines the role of prompt literacy as a structured academic competence in AI-supported writing and research within higher education. It develops and empirically tests a conceptual framework linking prompt quality to academic writing and research performance through the mediating role of cognitive engagement and the moderating influence of institutional academic integrity orientation. Drawing on cognitive, academic literacy, metacognitive, and socio-technical perspectives, the chapter demonstrates that effective prompting is not merely technical but central to scholarly practice. Findings indicate that high-quality prompts enhance analytical depth, coherence, and methodological clarity, particularly when users actively engage with AI outputs. Furthermore, institutional integrity environments strengthen responsible AI use and amplify performance outcomes. The chapter contributes theoretical, pedagogical, and policy insights by positioning prompt literacy as essential for sustaining academic rigor in AI-mediated scholarship.</jats:p>

title: Experiment-specific memory and relaxation structure in graphene transport: a kernel-first state-trajectory analysis
container-title: Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter
7c1703c29eb0feff11158cec1c151106c260aa26.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Graphene transport experiments probe relaxation through different observables, timescales and measurement domains, making direct comparison of reported relaxation parameters difficult. Here we develop a kernel-first, provenance-constrained methodology for determining what aspects of relaxation structure can be identified from heterogeneous transport measurements before assigning them a common physical interpretation. The approach distinguishes measured, processed, fitted and theoretically derived quantities, and separates response magnitude, kernel sensitivity and experimentally observed state evolution. The method is applied to three complementary graphene experiments. Frequency-resolved complex conductivity provides identifiable spectral relaxation descriptors and, where an admissible parametrisation is supported, permits explicit kernel-sensitivity and state-trajectory analysis. Ultrafast electronic heat spreading constrains an additional short-time response relative to an independently determined momentum-relaxation interval, but does not identify a unique kernel time. DC electrical and thermal measurements constrain integrated response weights, geometry dependence and a relative relaxation hierarchy without uniquely determining temporal kernel shape. The three experiments therefore occupy different levels of dynamical identifiability rather than providing interchangeable relaxation times. A localized change in an effective-kernel trajectory is not by itself interpreted as a triggered process. The stronger test requires such a change to reproducibly predict an independently measured dynamical response. We propose a same–device, cross-domain experiment implementing this criterion across controlled state trajectories. The principal contribution is a general analysis methodology for determining what relaxation information heterogeneous measurements support and what additional evidence is required before state-dependent response is promoted to a physical mechanism.</jats:p>

title: Excavating History, Mobilizing Memory
container-title: Moving Memories
83cde5932e9b6a0af93491eec4d035fc0c326670.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter examines two ambulatory, site-specific performances that transformed memorial spaces into sites of remembrance, intercultural dialogue, and historical excavation. These pieces mobilized memories through embodied enactments deeply rooted in the politics of place. The chapter first analyzes Tamar Rogoff’s nostalgic and haunting The Ivye Project (1994), which was performed by a transnational cast of actors, dancers, musicians, and community members in Ivye, Belarus. The immersive piece led audiences through a forest surrounding a mass gravesite, reanimating the town’s Jewish past and commemorating a history suppressed through years of Sovietization. It then discusses Spring in Warsaw by the Israeli collective Public Movement, which reimagined Holocaust tourism and civic ritual through a participatory walk through the Warsaw Ghetto. The chapter argues that site-specific Holocaust performance conjures bodies of the past through the activation of bodies in the present, involving performers and spectators in collective acts of excavation and mourning, accountability and healing.</jats:p>

title: Entangled Histories
container-title: Moving Memories
830a0b79b464393ddf530372769d7faf676dac82.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter discusses two dances by prominent, Black choreographers—Robert Battle and Donald Byrd—set to the music of Erwin Schulhoff, an avant-garde, Jewish composer who perished in a Bavarian labor camp. It considers the composer’s fusion of Black and European aesthetics in relation to modern-dance history and Black-Jewish power dynamics. The chapter analyzes Battle’s No Longer Silent and Donald Byrd’s The Theater of Needless Talents as enactments of multidirectional memory—a concept articulated by Michael Rothberg that rejects competitive approaches to transgenerational trauma by reflecting on the Holocaust in tandem with anti-Black racism and global legacies of colonialism. Battle and Byrd, both of whom identified with Schulhoff’s artistry and marginalization, responded to the Holocaust multidirectionally by using choreographic layering and movement motifs to speak to issues of degradation, persecution, and resistance. The chapter shows how these dances commemorate the Holocaust while encouraging diverse audiences to contemplate ongoing violence toward Black bodies in the United States, as well as other genocides worldwide.</jats:p>

title: Boundary memory in ultrafast field emission: a two-time quantum statistical theory
container-title: Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter
368097744d015db6eba80fbc322d096bfc8ac859.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ultrafast field emission is usually modelled by evaluating the stationary tunnelling current at the instantaneous driving field. We show that this fails whenever the emitting surface has electronic structure near the Fermi level: the vacuum escape channel reacts back on the occupied boundary spectrum that feeds it, and because that spectrum relaxes on a finite timescale the emitted current carries memory of the field’s recent history. Formulating the driven emission problem on the Keldysh contour and propagating the boundary Green functions with a material specific surface spectrum, we find two distinct kinds of memory: a traversal memory that filters and delays the carrier when the driving frequency approaches the tunnelling rate, and a spectral relaxation memory that suppresses and reshapes the current when a pulse drives a thin barrier emitter through the stationary overcoupling turnover. The second can dominate even when the barrier traversal is quasistatic, and predicts a current that falls while the instantaneous transparency still rises. Which memory governs a surface is set by its barrier thickness and its coupling to the vacuum, so the ultrafast waveform distinguishes emitters that the instantaneous theory treats alike.</jats:p>

title: Assistive Monitoring and Support Quality in Cognitive Disability Care
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Advancing Disability Inclusion Through AI
db5a35fb0006e94c20dd6e10396daf586441ad4d.abstract: <jats:p>Disability support organisations must maintain safety while supporting independence for people with cognitive disabilities. Traditional supervision relies on routine observation, manual documentation, and reactive intervention, which often creates workload pressure and inconsistent outcomes. Intelligent monitoring systems provide continuous behavioural observation and automated alerts. Many organisations fail to achieve measurable improvement because monitoring data is not integrated into staff workflows, response responsibility, and performance evaluation. This chapter examines monitoring as an organisational decision integration challenge using implementation science, socio-technical theory, and technology adoption theory, explains how monitoring signals influence staff decisions, workflow coordination, and service performance. Introduces the Institutional Integration Framework, which translates monitoring signals into structured workforce response and measurable performance outcomes</jats:p>

title: Comparison of ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot Performance in Answering Questions About the Structure of Atoms
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
f648170227a2dcf14c457db8406cc2d4610f0113.abstract: <jats:p>In fields with a high concentration of abstract concepts, such as science education, large language models (LLMs) are attracting attention for their potential to provide explanatory and personalized content. This study aims to compare the performance of LLMs ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot in explaining the topic of “The Structure of the Atom” in the context of science education, based on criteria such as scientific accuracy, clarity, pedagogical appropriateness, and misconception risk. Ten questions appropriate for the middle school level were prepared with expert opinion to evaluate the models' response generation capacity and analyzed using rubric-based scoring. The study utilized descriptive statistics, the Friedman test, and the technique for order preference by similarity to ideal solution to determine the models' overall performance levels. The findings indicate that ChatGPT demonstrated consistent and superior performance. The findings guide in terms of science concept teaching, misconception prevention strategies, and scientific accuracy.</jats:p>

title: Quantifying multitime memory in sequential measurement statistics through violations of the quantum regression theorem
container-title: Physical Review A
bd52eccaf16122ebc58103451c3400c4cd32c0d9.abstract: <jats:p>We investigate the presence of memory in the sequential measurement statistics of an open quantum system, as witnessed by the departure from the quantum regression theorem (QRT), that is, the possibility to predict multitime probabilities from one-time reduced dynamical maps. For factorized initial states, we identify an exact decomposition of the two-time propagator into a QRT-like contribution, fully determined by the reduced dynamical map, and a memory term encoding system-environment correlations across the intervention. In the weak-coupling regime, the memory term yields an explicit second-order correction expressed in terms of the reduced map and bath correlation functions. Furthermore, we introduce an operational quantifier of QRT violations based on the distance between exact and QRT-predicted joint probabilities. Benchmarking the framework on a spin-boson model and using a pseudomode embedding as nonperturbative reference, we comprehensively analyze the impact of spectral-density parameters, environmental temperature, and measurement protocols on the non-Markovianity of the multitime statistics. Comparison with a one-time witness shows that reduced-state non-Markovianity and multitime memory are related but inequivalent: the latter, as probed through sequential statistics, is intrinsically protocol dependent and can become visible at higher temporal orders even when lower-order statistics remain compatible with QRT predictions.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive correlates of diffusion tensor imaging analysis along the perivascular space index in amnestic mild cognitive impairment: a preliminary study

1e1bf996cda945b0527e40176b2aa62fdc1d4c7d.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The diffusion tensor imaging analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index is an imaging-derived metric related to perivascular water diffusion and has been reported to correlate with global cognitive performance in dementia. However, its associations with specific cognitive functions in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) remain underexplored. This study aimed to characterize the cognitive correlates of the DTI-ALPS index in individuals with amnestic MCI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this cross-sectional study, 57 participants with amnestic MCI underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging and a neuropsychological assessment battery. Correlations between the DTI-ALPS index and performance across the assessed cognitive measures were examined before and after adjustment for age, sex, education, and Fazekas score.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Prior to adjustment, the DTI-ALPS index showed significant positive correlations with global cognitive measures, episodic memory retrieval, and semantic verbal fluency. After controlling for potential confounders, only the correlations with episodic memory and semantic verbal fluency remained significant.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The DTI-ALPS index remained significantly associated with episodic memory retrieval and semantic verbal fluency in amnestic MCI after adjustment, suggesting a possible link with frontotemporal network-related cognitive functions. Further studies incorporating multimodal imaging and disease-specific biomarkers are warranted to clarify the biological significance of the DTI-ALPS index and its potential clinical relevance in early cognitive impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Order-tunable chaotic dynamics, memory-state-dependent coexistence, and reservoir computing in a fractional memfractor-based oscillator
container-title: Physica Scripta
30db02e5d4f782c8c14eeaabc050144f35a705ce.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    In this paper, an autonomous oscillator utilizing a memfractor with fractional-order elements is presented and analyzed with regard to its order-dependent chaotic behavior, memory state-dependent coexistence, and reservoir computing properties. The design includes a Lorenz-like nonlinear element and a memfractor branch where the effective input is generated using the memory state along with a fractional-order accumulation state. The memfractor is first analyzed on an elemental basis through frequency-dependent pinched
                    <jats:italic>v–i</jats:italic>
                    hysteresis loops, which confirm the expected fading-memory signature. Thereafter, the generated oscillator is analyzed using equilibria, stability metrics, phase planes, bifurcations, finite-time Lyapunov analysis, and initial-condition scans. For the default parameter set, nine equilibrium points are detected, including two locally stable equilibria and seven unstable equilibria. Under the same parameters, the system exhibits coexistence between stable equilibrium convergence and bounded chaotic oscillations, mainly selected by the initial memfractor memory state. The memfractor coupling strength controls the transition toward chaos, while the fractional orders tune the intensity of memory-induced divergence. The numerical credibility of the reported regimes is supported by Grünwald–Letnikov and predict–evaluate–correct–evaluate / Adams–Bashforth–Moulton solver cross-validation, together with time-step, simulation-length, and memory-length sensitivity tests. Finally, the oscillator is evaluated as a memory-tunable reservoir on NARMA10 and NARMA20 tasks. In the reservoir-computing tests, the full fractional memfractor configuration gives the lowest representative NARMA10 and NARMA20 prediction errors. The ablation results further indicate that fractional dynamics and memfractor feedback contribute differently to temporal retention and nonlinear prediction. These results show that the fractional memfractor provides a compact mechanism for memory-controlled chaos, coexistence, and reservoir-performance tuning.
                  </jats:p>

title: Cognitive-affective functions, neighborhood opportunity, and social functioning in youth with neurofibromatosis type 1

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study evaluated associations between social functioning and cognitive-affective functions (CAF), including executive function, face processing, and theory of mind, and neighborhood opportunity, in youth with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Youth with NF1 (n = 37), ages 8–14 (M = 11.8 years), with no prior autism diagnosis, completed assessments of CAF and peer relationships. Parents completed questionnaires on executive function skills, social impairments, and peer relationships. The Childhood Opportunity Index national composite score quantified neighborhood opportunity. Correlation and hierarchical linear regression analyses evaluated associations between social functioning, CAF, and neighborhood opportunity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Executive functioning and neighborhood opportunity were significantly associated with parent reports of social impairments and peer relationships. Executive functioning and facial expression recognition were correlated with self-reported peer relationships, but were not significant in regression models. Facial identity recognition was significantly correlated with social impairments and parent-rated peer relationships. Theory of mind was not associated with any outcome.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings underscore the interplay between CAF, neighborhood opportunity, and social functioning in children with NF1. Case conceptualizations should integrate social determinants of health with measures of cognition and behavior. Longitudinal research is needed to understand mechanisms driving variability in social outcomes and inform equitable care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Parental scaffolding and cognitive development in early childhood: Insights from a dynamic systems perspective
container-title: Child Development
958b98b1626b048c7804b6008b090f93e5b57b23.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Grounded in dynamic systems theory, which conceptualizes parent–child interactions as evolving systems of reciprocal influence over time, the main objective of this study was to examine which patterns of parent–child scaffolding in a problem-solving situation were associated with children's early cognitive development and to explore whether these patterns were influenced by prior child characteristics. A total of 193 mother–child dyads (109 girls) were observed during a number–image association task at 48 months. Children were predominantly White (95%) and of Canadian or European ethnic background. Three scaffolding phases were examined using the State Space Grid (SSG): modeling (problem-solving strategies are demonstrated by parents), guidance (characterized by shared participation in task execution), and fading (support is gradually withdrawn and greater initiative is shown by children). Only the fading phase was found to be associated with higher complex executive functioning (β = 0.30) and number knowledge (β = 0.42) 1 year later, at 60 months, controlling for prior child cognitive abilities. Furthermore, higher socioeconomic status, receptive vocabulary, and cognitive flexibility at 42 months were positively associated with fading. These findings highlight the importance of interactional processes that promote children's active participation in problem- solving for subsequent cognitive development.</jats:p>

title: Large language models in geospatial science
container-title: Global Knowledge, Memory and Communication
e20d6a7d2d4c9dba958b9f01bf132d87fe48b90a.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Large language models are opening new ways to work with geospatial data, from asking questions about places to building analytical workflows. This study aims to examine how these applications fit together and what they suggest about the developing role of LLMs in geospatial science.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic review of 55 studies was conducted, covering GIScience and related spatial applications. Dictionary-based coding, supported by manual review, was combined with term frequency–inverse document frequency analysis and non-negative matrix factorisation to examine research roles, tasks and themes. Comparisons between core GIScience and adjacent fields helped place the overall patterns in context.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Benchmarking was the most common research role (41.8%), followed by multimodal interpretation (20.0%). Across the literature, two complementary directions emerge: using language models to organise geospatial operations and using vision-language models to interpret spatial observations. The abstracts place particular emphasis on methods, while the thematic analysis connects general GIS evaluation with code generation, remote sensing and applied spatial reasoning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The synthesis points to the value of combining flexible language interfaces with established GIS computation. Practical evaluation should consider how a system turns a request into a verified spatial result, including the time and expert involvement needed to complete that process.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By bringing GIScience and adjacent spatial research into one analytical framework, the review shows how model capabilities, data representations and external tools contribute to geospatial workflows. This perspective offers a basis for comparing systems and identifying productive connections between research communities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Digital literacy competencies among library professionals: a systematic literature review
container-title: Global Knowledge, Memory and Communication
dbcbc3e8a445c7ba8f3b2a1c5fbdf1881528cedb.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to assess the digital literacy proficiency, identify gaps in digital literacy and challenges encountered by library professionals in acquisition and application of digital literacy skills.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic literature review was carried out by using PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The databases used in this study includes Scopus, Web of Science, Emerald, Taylor and Francis. Articles published from 2020 to 2024 were included in this study. Initially, a total of 561 articles were identified from the selected databases, and after applying the criteria of inclusion and exclusion, 18 articles were selected for detailed analysis. The included studies were conducted across various countries, which indicates a broad geographical coverage of this study.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings of this study indicated that most of the library professionals were well-versed in basic digital literacy skills, while a gap was observed in advanced level of digital literacy skills. The major challenges faced by them were lack of funds or budget allocation, followed by lack of digital infrastructure and lack of support from the authorities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This systematic review examines digital literacy competencies among library professionals to identify key competency areas, gaps and challenges faced by them. Existing literature lacks a comprehensive review focusing on current level of digital literacy competencies among library professionals. Therefore, this research work contributes to better understanding of digital literacy competencies among library professionals. The findings will also help inform future strategies, training programmes and initiatives aimed at strengthening digital literacy within the library profession.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Application of long short-term memory and convolutional neural networks for real-time bridge pier scour prediction
container-title: Machine Learning and Data Science in Geotechnics
bea5a7a04efb44510e1434f62058289956ad8e7e.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Scour around bridge piers poses a major threat to structural safety, yet existing empirical and machine learning approaches are limited in accuracy, generalisation and real-time applicability. This paper aims to evaluate the effectiveness, efficiency and generalisability of deep learning models for real-time bridge pier scour forecasting.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study formulates scour forecasting as a multivariate time-series prediction problem using real-world sensor data from monitored bridges in Alaska and Oregon (2006–2021). Multiple variants of long short-term memory (LSTM) and temporal convolutional neural network (CNN) models are designed and systematically evaluated. Random-search heuristics and sequential evaluation are used to optimise hyperparameters, improve robustness and assess computational efficiency.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Results show that LSTM models achieve high predictive accuracy for larger data sets, with a mean absolute error as low as 0.024 m for one-week-ahead forecasts. Fully convolutional networks deliver comparable accuracy with substantially lower training and inference times. Feature analyses indicate that historical scour time series dominate predictive performance, with flow-related features contributing only marginal or site-specific improvements.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Model performance depends on data availability, noise levels and site-specific scour behaviour, particularly for smaller data sets. Future work should explore broader geographic validation and hybrid or physics-informed extensions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The proposed models enable efficient real-time scour forecasting, supporting early-warning systems and improved decision-making for bridge monitoring and infrastructure risk management.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper presents one of the first systematic comparisons of LSTM and CNN models for real-time scour prediction using long-term field data, highlighting accuracy–efficiency trade-offs for operational deployment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Research on the impact of vertical fiscal imbalance on the supply of basic public services from the perspective of tax effort
container-title: China and World Business Review
37e5c2413ae3dbe31528e21ce7b76e3dad5f9488.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper investigates the impact of vertical fiscal imbalance (VFI) on local public service provision and environmental pollution, and examines the moderating role of fiscal transfers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using panel data from Chinese prefecture-level cities, we construct econometric models with a VFI index as the key independent variable. Dependent variables include basic public service supply and pollution emissions. Two-way fixed effects and instrumental variable methods are applied.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>VFI significantly reduces the level of local public services, especially in fiscally weak regions. It also aggravates industrial pollution, suggesting that fiscal pressure may relax environmental regulation. General-purpose transfers mitigate the negative service effect, but earmarked transfers do not.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study extends VFI research to public service and environmental outcomes, provides new empirical evidence from China, and reveals differentiated roles of transfer types, offering policy implications for fiscal reform.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Optimising sleep regularity during shiftwork is important for cognitive performance, sleepiness and mood
container-title: SLEEP Advances
1feb0e7d2cb9f318c1cf9eac264b69994eea234b.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Sleep regularity is important for performance and wellbeing. Sleep regularity is underexplored in shiftworkers, a population that may struggle to maintain regular sleep timing due to unstable work hours. It is important to understand how sleep regularity relates to wellbeing and performance outcomes for shiftworkers. Using the sleep regularity index (SRI), we assessed the relationship of sleep regularity to performance and wellbeing in maritime watchstanding shiftworkers who worked two different schedules (known as “watchbills”). Active-duty sailors (N = 23, aged 25.96 ± 3.13 years, [mean ± standard deviation]) wore an actiwatch for ~14 days while underway on the 5-hrs on/10-hrs off watchbill, and four months later for ~10 days while on the 3-hrs on/9-hrs off watchbill. The psychomotor vigilance task (PVT) was administered 2 to 4 times daily during both underway periods; the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and Profile of Mood States (POMS) were administered at the end of both data collection periods. High variability in SRI score was observed for shiftworkers on the same shift of the same schedule. Higher SRI scores were associated with faster reaction times (Spearman’s rho [ρ] = -0.73, p = .019) and better cognitive performance on seven other PVT metrics (all p &lt; .05), and reduced daytime sleepiness (ρ = -0.512, p = .013) and total mood disturbance (ρ = -0.634, p = .005). The study found that sleep regularity is an important dimension of sleep to optimise during shiftwork to improve cognitive performance and reduce daytime sleepiness and mood disturbance.</jats:p>

Thermal properties were determined using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), while magnetic behavior was assessed with a physical property measurement system (PPMS). XRD results indicated that Fe
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                    nanoparticles were homogeneously distributed in the matrix, with an increased contribution from the magnetic crystal phase. FTIR indicated that the additive was integrated into the structure via physical interactions, without establishing chemical bonds with the polymer chains. Based on SEM and AFM images, the fiber diameters have grown significantly as the Fe
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                    content has increased. TGA analyses indicate that the thermal stability of nanocomposites has increased, while DSC results demonstrate that as the filler amount increases, the degree of polymer crystallization decreases. title: When adaptation has no endpoint: cognitive flexibility under prolonged organizational strain
container-title: International Journal of Organization Theory & Behavior
92698333062c10aa1921da14210cc39e769836e4.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper examines how cognition operates under conditions of prolonged organizational strain where demands persist, interpretations do not converge and disengagement does not occur. It challenges the dominant assumption in organizational behavior that cognitive processes under strain are inherently directional and oriented toward resolution, coherence or withdrawal.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper develops a conceptual framework through integrative analysis of stress and coping, sensemaking and burnout literatures. It identifies a shared directional assumption across these perspectives and demonstrates its limitations under conditions of sustained and indeterminate strain. A new construct is introduced and formalized through a set of theoretical propositions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis shows that individuals may sustain cognitive engagement without reducing demands, achieving interpretive coherence or disengaging. To account for this pattern, the paper introduces cognitive flexibility under prolonged organizational strain, defined as a mode of functioning characterized by interpretive openness, non-directional engagement and ongoing meaning adjustment without convergence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper contributes by identifying prolonged organizational strain as a distinct condition and re-specifying adaptation as sustained cognitive functioning without directional progression. It extends organizational behavior theory by explaining how cognition operates when resolution, coherence and disengagement do not structure activity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Cognitive styles and resource orchestration capability: pathways to innovation and competitive advantage under environmental dynamism in hotels
container-title: Journal of Hospitality and Tourism Insights
01822006967d988fa49d250e9e8c6efe4d862551.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study examines how hotel management uses cognitive styles to optimize resource allocation and gain competitive advantage amid rapid technological advances, changing customer needs, and intensified market competition. The study focuses on how the three cognitive styles-creating, planning, and knowing-influence organizational agility and resource orchestration capability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The research used a quantitative survey design. The researchers collected survey data from 325 hotel managers and used structural equation modelling to test the proposed theoretical framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results are in line with the framework suggested. The three cognitive styles have positive effects on both organizational agility and resource orchestration capability. The relationship between these capabilities and competitive advantage as well as organizational growth is mediated by organizational innovation. Environmental dynamism reinforces the effects of organizational agility and resource orchestration capability on innovation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results give hotel leaders practical information about innovation that suggests that workforce development strategies and managerial practices should be in line with the latest market trends. It shows that managerial cognitive styles are central to developing dynamic capabilities, and that leadership training, recruitment, and strategic planning have implications to develop the creating, planning, and knowing styles to increase the agility of the organization, its resource management, and ability to innovate.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper combines the Dynamic Capabilities Theory and the Resource Orchestration Theory in explaining how hotels gain competitive advantage as a result of innovation in an environment of market instability. It also determines managerial cognitive styles to be the core microfoundations of dynamic capability development and provides a new understanding of how organizations develop strategic flexibility and economic value in the hospitality industry.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Ambivalent close ties and cognitive functioning: Does coping play a role?
container-title: Innovation in Aging
419f0d405dbcdc84839382b903d619de51c8a365.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Close relationships that are characterized by both positive and negative qualities (i.e., ambivalent ties) are common in later life and often give rise to interpersonal tensions with deleterious consequences for well-being. However, little is known about their effect on cognitive health. These effects may depend on seldom-studied interpersonal coping strategies that may either stimulate or deplete cognitive resources. This study tested whether ambivalent ties relate to lower cognitive functioning among older adults, and whether interpersonal coping strategies moderate these associations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As part of the Daily Experiences and Well-being Study (DEWS), participants (N = 271, ages 65-89) completed an in-person baseline interview assessing positive and negative qualities of their close social relationships and overall cognitive functioning (composite of four tests), followed by a self-administered questionnaire assessing three interpersonal coping strategies (engaged, avoidant, destructive).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Linear regression models revealed that a greater proportion of ambivalent ties was associated with worse overall cognitive functioning, but this association was not moderated by any interpersonal coping strategy. Sensitivity analyses of the separate cognitive tests revealed, unexpectedly, that greater use of engaged coping strengthened the association between ambivalent ties and worse executive functioning performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A greater proportion of ambivalent ties in one’s social network is associated with lower cognitive functioning among older adults, a link that may not easily be buffered through coping. Results suggest that ambivalent ties are an understudied important potential risk factor for adverse cognitive outcomes in later life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Elite basketball athletes at rest: enhanced sensorimotor activity and reduced cognitive load
container-title: Brain Communications
a867f1111467f16d2068d87c0420c2f94da66236.abstract:
<jats:p>Long-term sports training is associated with experience-dependent brain plasticity, but the core functional architecture of open-skill athletes remains unclear. As a representative open-skill sport, basketball requires rapid sensorimotor integration in dynamic settings. This study examined resting-state functional characteristics in elite basketball athletes, focusing on interactions between sensorimotor and advanced cognitive systems. Fifty-seven national first-class basketball athletes (mean age 20.17 ± 1.87 years, twenty-three males) and sixty-one healthy controls (mean age 20.33 ± 1.89 years, twenty-five males) underwent resting-state functional MRI. Fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF) and degree centrality (DC) were used to evaluate regional spontaneous activity and overall brain network integration, respectively. Group comparisons controlled for age, sex and head motion. Athletes showed a dual pattern of functional differences. First, athletes showed changed sensorimotor processing: significantly higher fALFF and DC in the superior temporal gyrus, cerebellum (anterior and posterior), parahippocampal gyrus, cuneus, and lingual gyrus, indicating stronger neural substrates for visuospatial integration and motor coordination. Second, athletes showed greater neural efficiency: lower fALFF and DC in the middle frontal gyrus, cingulate cortex, medial prefrontal cortex, and precuneus (parts of the default mode network), which may reflect enhanced cognitive control and reduced cognitive load. Notably, the insula and midbrain showed a distinct pattern (increased fALFF but decreased DC), indicating a specialized "high-readiness and low-redundancy" state for salience monitoring. Long-term basketball training is associated with distinct patterns of functional brain characteristics, marked by improved sensorimotor processing and greater neural efficiency within cognitive control networks. These training-related neural patterns may serve as biomarkers for athlete evaluation and selection.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Abbreviated summary</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Wang et al. report that elite basketball athletes exhibit distinct resting-state functional brain characteristics, including enhanced sensorimotor-related activity and altered cognitive control network organization. These findings suggest that basketball expertise is associated with specialized neural organization supporting the demands of open-skill sports.</jats:p>

title: Joint associations of handgrip strength and chair-stand performance with motoric cognitive risk syndrome in older adults
container-title: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
7a38c90b286ffa04131bcbafb5ff6cbfb6a0faf0.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Motor dysfunction is associated with cognitive vulnerability, but whether impairments across body regions jointly contribute to motoric cognitive risk syndrome (MCR) remains unclear. We examined the independent and joint associations of handgrip strength and chair-stand test (CST) with MCR.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional study included 6258 dementia-free older adults (mean age 71.5 ± 6.6 years; 63.1% women) from a community-based cohort. Handgrip strength and CST performance were used to define upper- and lower-extremity motor impairment. Participants were classified as normal, handgrip weakness only, CST impairment only, or combined motor impairment. Multivariable logistic regression was performed with adjustment for demographic, socioeconomic, lifestyle, and clinical factors. Additive and multiplicative interactions were assessed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>MCR was present in 10.4% of participants. Using the A/B CST cutoff as the primary definition, adjusted odds ratios (95% confidence intervals) for MCR, compared with normal function, were 1.84 (1.14–2.97) for handgrip weakness only, 4.17 (2.97–5.85) for CST impairment only, and 9.17 (6.56–12.81) for combined motor impairment. Associations were directionally consistent across alternative CST cutoffs. A positive additive interaction was observed at the A/B CST cutoff (relative excess risk due to interaction = 3.48; attributable proportion = 0.40; and synergy index = 1.83), whereas multiplicative interaction was not positive.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Combined handgrip weakness and poorer CST performance were strongly associated with prevalent MCR. A positive additive interaction at the primary CST cutoff suggests that joint motor impairment may help characterize MCR-related vulnerability in older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Objective Pre-Shift Cognitive Readiness as a Human Factors Barrier: Field Evidence from Offshore Operations
container-title: ADIPEC
cd7a65cb092fe5f60c57cfac271e71bc3cf677e2.abstract:
<jats:p>Offshore operations depend on reliable performance in safety-critical functions, and the industry's human performance framework treats that performance as shaped by the conditions under which work is done, among them workload, sleep opportunity, rotation design, and supervision (IOGP 2026). When these conditions degrade, the effect reaches the operation as well as the safety record: in the deployments described in this paper, events whose investigations recorded reduced human performance among the contributing factors also carried production cost, in interrupted operations and deferred output. The controls that address these conditions, from fatigue risk management to competence assurance, primarily operate at the level of the schedule and the job category, and do not ordinarily provide a standardized, individual-referenced signal before the shift. In current practice, that space is covered by the supervisor's judgment and the pre-shift conversation. A standardized signal would give that judgment an instrument: an indication of when to offer support, and when to review the day's risk controls before critical work begins.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The barrier literature offers a test for what a daily process built around such a signal would need to do. Sklet (2006) describes active safety barriers as realizing a sequence of functions: detect a deviation, decide on a response, and carry the response out. In the barrier models the industry applies across many domains, bowtie analysis among them, degraded human performance appears as one of several escalation factors that can erode the performance of other barriers, together with technical and organizational degradation. The controls that address the contributing conditions are set in advance and calibrated for groups: rosters, hours-of-service limits, training cycles. The growing use of leading indicators in operational safety follows a logic that applies here as well: monitor conditions relevant to barrier performance before the barrier is called on, instead of counting the events it failed to stop (IOGP 2023). A daily, individual-referenced readiness signal has not been routinely integrated with this set of controls, a gap discussed at greater length in the field study that precedes this paper.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>That field study showed the signal can be produced under routine offshore conditions. Before the shift, each operator in a safety-critical function completes a short cognitive task of under three minutes, delivered as a standardized digital application with the format of a game and the function of an instrument: the result is derived from measured performance on the task, not from a questionnaire. The task is calibrated to each function through an onboard neuroergonomic assessment, the application of neuroscience methods to the study of work (Parasuraman and Wilson 2008), which characterizes the cognitive demands the activity places on whoever performs it. The result is read against the operator's own accumulated baseline together with the cognitive demands of the function, so a deviation records a change in test performance relative to that combined reference, and it enters the day's risk assessment as an individual-referenced input, read much as a wind limit is read before work at height: the value is compared with a reference range, and an out-of-range reading changes how the task is conducted and which controls apply. A green result, within the operator's normal range, requires no further step. A yellow result opens a support conversation between operator and supervisor and activates predefined, graded, non-punitive risk controls, co-designed with the asset team, before critical work begins; the result is not a diagnosis and is not used for appraisal or discipline, and activation is used in this sense throughout the paper. Over a 22-month evaluation at one asset, the program was associated with a sustained reduction in events whose investigations recorded reduced human performance among the contributing factors, and in the production downtime attributed to those events (Baldassim et al. 2026, in press).</jats:p>

title: Red Palm Oil Administration in Undernourished Wistar Rats: Effects on Cognitive, Gastrointestinal, Skeletal, and Organ Parameters
container-title: An Idea Health Journal
e0f104d2a2eaedbeac3776f2088ad73e7d068247.abstract:
<jats:p>Background: Malnutrition affects multiple physiological systems, including cognitive, gastrointestinal, skeletal, and organ functions. Red palm oil (RPO) contains bioactive compounds that may influence physiological responses to malnutrition. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of RPO on biomedical parameters in undernourished Wistar rats.
Methods: This experimental laboratory study integrated several sub-studies using post-test-only and pretest-posttest control group designs. Male Wistar rats aged 3–4 weeks underwent 50% feed restriction for 14 days, followed by RPO administration at doses of 2, 4, or 6 mL/kgBW for 28 days. Groups included normal, negative, and selected positive vitamin A controls. Sample sizes varied across sub-studies. Data were analyzed using ANOVA, Kruskal– Wallis, post hoc tests, and correlation analyses, with p < 0.05 considered significant.
Result: Significant differences were observed in Y-maze cognitive performance (p = 0.031), intestinal weight (p = 0.003), femur weight (ANOVA p = 0.037; Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.048), and heart (p = 0.010), liver (p = 0.002), and kidney (p = 0.004) indices. Femur length differed significantly using Kruskal–Wallis (p = 0.042), but not ANOVA (p = 0.052). No significant differences were observed in hemoglobin levels (p = 0.494),motor performance (p = 0.120), lung (p = 0.070), or spleen (p = 0.120) indices.
Contribution for Practice: RPO administration produced variable responses across biomedical parameters, providing preliminary preclinical evidence for further nutritional research. However, inconsistent dose-response patterns and the absence of significant effects on several outcomes limit its clinical applicability. Further mechanistic and clinical studies are required before RPO can be recommended for nutritional rehabilitation.</jats:p>

title: Selective Memory Operations Shape History-Dependent Population Representations and Choice under Sensory Ambiguity: A Hippocampal-Inspired Dynamic Gating Model
6cdecb36295b30a492b011930036e32926ed9cfc.abstract: How does past experience continue to shape behavior? The hippocampal–entorhinal system supports memory-guided behavior, yet how selective memory operations shape population activity and history-dependent choice remains unclear. We introduce a hippocampal-inspired dynamic gating model (HDGM) that integrates predictive recurrence, online associative memory, and feedback-dependent regulation to examine how past experience shapes population representations and subsequent choice under sensory ambiguity. HDGM exhibited distinct history-conditioned population states despite identical current sensory input. Selective disruptions of encoding and associative processing altered subsequent population activity and impaired history-dependent choice. Output-gain modulation increased linear decoding accuracy for task-relevant classes, whereas cross-trial gate reassignment reduced delay-state separation with little change in mean choice performance. Across complementary tasks, population organization, linear information accessibility, and behavioral choice showed distinct responses to selective memory operations. Together, these findings provide a computational framework for investigating how selective memory operations shape the expression of past experience and its relationship to subsequent choice.

title: The impact of sensorimotor and cognitive capacity on the kinematic performance of instrumental activities of daily living across the lifespan
986366547da9aacf1c54bd93a739860c106c8f9b.abstract: Background With advancing adult age, sensorimotor and cognitive capacity (e.g., muscular strength) are declining and limitations in instrumental activities of daily living (iADL) are frequently reported. The translation of individual capacity to iADL performance represents a significant research object not only to better understand everyday life behavior but also to apply preventive measures in time. Due to the submaximal nature of iADL, we aimed to identify transition points, beyond which associations between capacity and performance appear, i.e., iADL stop to be submaximal. Methods A set of sensorimotor and cognitive capacity tests and kinematic analyses of hand movements in different complex kitchen tasks were conducted in a sample of 95 healthy adults with an age span of 18 to 93a. An iADL score was derived from the kinematics using a principal component analysis. Transition point segmented regression analyses were applied to examine the association of capacity and the iADL score. Results Most tests reacted to ageing and (negative) outlier frequencies in capacity and, to a weaker extent, in kinematics increased with advancing age. Transition points were identified in most tests and confirmed our hypothesis but were generally high. The best iADL performance was observed in persons between 42 and 58a despite decreased capacity. Discussion It appeared that iADL can be limited by impaired capacity, but profit from experience that can compensate capacity losses to a certain degree. The high transition points point towards the need for early interventions long before subtle alterations in iADL performance become subjectively observable.

title: Reading–Writing Integration Through ChatGPT-Supported Feedback: Growth, Associations, and Mediated Pathways of Student Engagement in Chinese Classrooms
160b16f92b37d381fb94d058e2607c75228ade64.abstract: Although reading–writing integration has been increasingly advocated in Chinese language education, limited empirical evidence explains how reading, writing, and student engagement become integrated, particularly under AI-supported feedback. To address this issue, this study examined whether ChatGPT-supported feedback improved reading outcomes, writing outcomes, and student engagement, while investigating their interrelationships, the mediating role of student engagement, and the corresponding pathways in reading–writing integration. A total of 400 middle school students from eight intact classes in Shenzhen participated, with 200 students receiving ChatGPT-supported feedback and 200 receiving human-generated feedback. Using a quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design, data were analyzed within a quantitative longitudinal framework integrating baseline equivalence tests, 2 × 2 mixed-design ANOVAs, factor-level correlation analyses, and multi-group cross-lagged path analysis to examine changes and temporal relationships among reading, student engagement, and writing across two groups (N = 400). Despite comparable pretest scores, findings showed that Group 1 demonstrated significantly greater pretest–posttest gains in reading, student engagement, and writing, with significant Time × Group interactions and large effects. Correlations further indicated stronger posttest associations among engagement, reading, and writing in Group 1, whereas these relationships remained weak in Group 2. Longitudinal analyses revealed stronger T2 within-time direct and mediating pathways in Group 1, alongside several significant cross-lagged effects, but cross-lagged mediating effects were generally nonsignificant in both groups. The findings theoretically highlight student engagement as a potentially time-sensitive mechanism through which AI-supported learning may strengthen the integration of reading and writing. Practically, they suggest the pedagogical value of AI-supported learning environments for fostering engagement and connecting literacy processes, while emphasizing sustained instructional exposure to consolidate these relationships over time.

title: Brain Tissue Proportionality and General Cognitive Ability Across Three Adult Cohorts
c22391ea400307f1b2e7328843950bfa5df04104.abstract: General cognitive ability may relate to the proportional allocation of brain tissue beyond overall tissue volume. We examined five FreeSurfer compartments using compositional data analysis: cortical gray matter, cerebral white matter, subcortical gray matter, total cerebellum, and brainstem. Human Connectome Project Young Adult data (HCP-YA; N = 1,101) provided discovery estimates; the Dallas Lifespan Brain Study (DLBS; N = 418) and Amsterdam Open MRI Collection ID1000 (AOMIC; N = 926) provided independent cohort tests. Four isometric log-ratio coordinates represented composition, with age, sex, and log total analyzed tissue volume included separately. Composition explained additional cognitive variance in DLBS (partial R² = 4.20%, p = .00154) and AOMIC (partial R² = 1.35%, p = .014). The total-cerebellum-to-cerebral-white-matter contrast selected in HCP was positive in both replication cohorts: standardized β = 0.162 (heteroskedasticity-robust 95% confidence interval 0.072–0.252) in DLBS and 0.097 (0.024–0.170) in AOMIC. Participant-pairs bootstrap intervals supported both associations. Replacing total tissue volume with estimated intracranial volume attenuated the AOMIC association, whereas including both preserved it. Relative macroanatomical allocation is associated with broad cognitive ability conditional on analyzed tissue volume, with differing effect magnitudes across cohorts. These cross-sectional findings do not establish causal tissue trade-offs.

title: Predicting teachers’ intentions to implement bring your own device and take-home student device programs: a cognitive-affective-behavior framework with sem-ann analysis
container-title: BMC Psychology
c03cb4c92fc7e96303b83387a72c67dfcfe4fb00.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Limited attention has been given to teachers’ intentions to implement Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) and Take-Home Student Device (THSD) as an integrated digital learning initiative, particularly from a psychological perspective. Accordingly, this study examines K-12 teachers’ behavioral intention to implement BYOD​ and ​THSD​ programs using the Cognitive–Affective–Behavior (CAB) framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A survey was conducted with 176 K-12 teachers in Taiwan. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), Artificial Neural Network (ANN) analysis, and Importance-Performance Map Analysis (IPMA).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Understanding, ability, and self-confidence were positively associated with behavioral intention. Self-confidence mediated the relationships between the two cognitive factors and behavioral intention. In addition, the IPMA results showed that ability had the highest importance value, followed by self-confidence, whereas understanding showed the highest performance but the lowest importance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings suggest that teachers’ readiness to implement BYOD and THSD depends not only on their understanding of the programs but also on their perceived ability and confidence to manage the demands of implementation. The study extends CAB-based research on educational technology implementation and provides implications for teacher preparation and digital education policy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Postoperative Behavioural, Cognitive, And Psychological Changes Following General Versus Regional Anaesthesia: A Narrative Review
container-title: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
0837caae74ea0092c1a28aa77142bc487df3c443.abstract: <jats:p>Postoperative behavioural, cognitive, and psychological changes represent an important spectrum of recovery-related complications after surgery and anaesthesia. This narrative review examines the available evidence comparing general anaesthesia with regional anaesthesia, with particular attention to postoperative delirium, delayed neurocognitive recovery, postoperative neurocognitive disorder, behavioural changes, and psychological outcomes. The available literature suggests that these outcomes are multifactorial and are influenced by patient vulnerability, surgical stress, inflammation, pain, sleep disturbance, medications, haemodynamic and respiratory changes, and anaesthetic exposure. Comparative evidence has not consistently demonstrated superiority of regional over general anaesthesia for prevention of postoperative delirium or cognitive dysfunction. Regional techniques may reduce exposure to general anaesthetic agents and postoperative opioid requirements in selected settings, but sedation and other perioperative factors can confound comparisons. Preoperative risk assessment, appropriate anaesthetic depth, effective analgesia, physiological optimisation, and multimodal postoperative care remain important components of prevention. Further well-designed studies using standardised definitions, baseline cognitive assessment, validated outcome measures, and adequate follow-up are needed.</jats:p>

title: Regional and Hormone-Associated Adaptations of Tissue-Resident Memory T cells across the Human Female Reproductive Tract.
5f40b39be962f7c69763c5aaeb6a41eb4864ebd0.abstract: Tissue-resident memory T cells (TRM) are essential components of mucosal immunity, yet their organization and regulation across the human female reproductive tract (FRT) remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated TRM across the FRT from donors with diverse hormonal profiles and identified regional and lineage-specific differences in phenotype, transcriptional programming, and abundance. CD8 T cells displayed greater enrichment of canonical TRM signatures and extensive T cell receptor clonal sharing across tissues, suggesting a common antigenic immune history. Despite these differences, resident CD4 and CD8 T cells shared CCR5 protein expression and TSC22D3 transcript enrichment, highlighting potentially distinctive features of FRT TRM. Single-cell transcriptomics revealed compartmental differences in metabolic, stress- and hormone-response pathways. Progesterone and testosterone levels were associated with differences in cervical T cell composition and CD8 TRM abundance. Together, these findings describe regional specialization by resident T cell immunity across the FRT and show that hormonal cues contribute to their homeostasis, offering new insight into factors that shape immune surveillance at mucosal sites of urogenital pathogen exposure.

title: Association between serum ferritin levels and mild cognitive impairment risk in middle-aged and older adults: evidence from the health and retirement study
container-title: Frontiers in Neurology
cb7d1944920c651db99c40c50b6068f82baafa33.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ferritin serves as the main iron-storage form in the human body. Iron ions are critical for numerous brain-related physiological processes. This study aimed to explore the association between serum ferritin levels and the risk of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in middle-aged and older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants aged 50 years and above with available cognitive function assessments were selected from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS) database. Baseline data for this retrospective cohort study were collected in 2016, and MCI occurrence was recorded through 2022. Cognitive function was assessed using tests of episodic memory and executive function. The primary MCI outcome was based on an operational cognitive-score definition rather than a clinical MCI diagnosis: the cognitive function score was at least one standard deviation (SD) below the age-specific normative value. Cox regression models were employed to explore the association between serum ferritin [tertiles: &lt;76 μg/L, 76-151 μg/L (reference group), ≥151 μg/L] and MCI risk, as well as impairments in episodic memory and executive function.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A total of 6,572 participants were enrolled in the analytical cohort. Of these, 1,435 (21.84%) participants developed MCI, while 5,137 (78.16%) were free of MCI events. Individuals with serum ferritin ≥151 μg/L were related to a higher risk of MCI [HR = 1.15 (95%CI: 1.01–1.31)] compared to those with serum ferritin 76-151 μg/L, but no association was found in those with serum ferritin &lt;76 μg/L [HR = 1.04 (95%CI: 0.91–1.19)]. Serum ferritin levels showed a significant U-shaped non-linear association with MCI risk (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>non-linear</jats:sub>
                       = 0.03). Moreover, individuals with serum ferritin ≥151 μg/L were associated with a higher risk of episodic memory impairment [HR = 1.15 (95%CI: 1.01–1.30)] versus those with serum ferritin 76–151 μg/L. No significant associations were found between serum ferritin and executive dysfunction [HR = 0.99 (95%CI: 0.90–1.10)].
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>High serum ferritin levels were associated with an increased risk of MCI among middle-aged and older adults, especially episodic memory impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Integrative approaches to acupuncture therapies for post-stroke mild cognitive impairment: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
container-title: Frontiers in Neurology
a56db80e45958d437dd76d9d5f41eaf1b67fc933.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Post-stroke mild cognitive impairment (PSMCI) frequently occurs after stroke and substantially restricts patients’ functional restoration and overall quality of life. Acupuncture has been widely adopted as an adjunctive intervention; however, the relative efficacy and safety profiles among different acupuncture modalities for PSMCI have not been clearly established.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To assess the comparative effectiveness and safety of multiple acupuncture therapies for treating PSMCI via network meta-analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>RCTs on acupuncture for PSMCI published from their inception to October 2025 were retrieved from nine databases and four clinical trial registries. Study quality was assessed via the Cochrane risk of bias tool. Meta-analysis was performed with ReviewManager and Stata software.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In total, 47 RCTs featuring 3,680 participants and 15 types of acupuncture-related interventions were included. Electroacupuncture combined with Moxibustion showed the highest efficacy in improving both MoCA score [MD = 5.42, 95%CI (2.10, 8.74)] and total effective rate. Electroacupuncture plus HBOT [MD = 8.00, 95%CI (5.19, 10.82)] and manual acupuncture plus rTMS [MD = 3.42, 95%CI (0.87, 5.97)] were most effective in improving MMSE. Manual acupuncture plus donepezil [MD = 8.67, 95%CI (5.47, 11.88)] and Electroacupuncture plus cognitive training [MD = −8.09, 95%CI (−10.56, −5.62)] achieved the greatest improvement in Barthel index. Moreover, the adverse events of these interventions were acceptable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study suggested that acupuncture was effective and safe for PSMCI treatment. However, the poor methodological quality and uneven evidence quality of existing studies warrant further rigorously designed trials to confirm our findings.</jats:p>

title:
Projected Disc-type Phase-change Memory for Analog In-Memory
Computing
bf295d493f1e62a5102a034dbdec66323d25418b.abstract: Resistive memory technologies offer a compelling advantage for in-memory computing. However, realizing a device architecture that simultaneously achieves high computational precision, efficiency, and density has remained elusive due to inherent trade-offs among these performance metrics. Here, we introduce a compact phase-change memory device architecture that combines an ultra-confined active switching volume for enhanced electro-thermal efficiency with a non-insulating thin film that suppresses temporal conductance fluctuations. We analytically model and back-end integrate these devices into crossbar arrays. Even with conventional, undoped phase-change materials, the device architecture enables a computational precision approaching 6 bits, low conductance values below 50 μS with an adequate conductance window, and a viable pathway toward sub-100 μA programming currents under nominal operating voltages.
