title: Formoterol attenuates lipopolysaccharide-induced mnemonic impairment in the delayed nonmatch to position task in rats
container-title: Behavioural Pharmacology
9adcd82abcb06b852806b8cbd1b0bba248d4e406.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title/>
                    <jats:p>
                      The delayed nonmatch to position (DNMTP) task is an instrumental learning paradigm applied to assess higher executive functions including attention and working memory in rats. In this study, the effect of systemic challenge with the acute inflammatory stimulus [lipopolysaccharide (LPS) 0.25 mg/kg, intraperitoneally] was assessed in Wistar rats on performance in the DNMTP task. By means of validation, the effect of treatment with the muscarinic receptor antagonist scopolamine [0.02 mg/kg, subcutaneously (s.c.)], known to disrupt performance in the task, and its reversal by coadministration of the cognitive-enhancing agent and acetylcholinesterase inhibitor donepezil (0.3 mg/kg, s.c.) were confirmed. Sex differences emerged between males’ and females’ mnemonic response to LPS 24-h postadministration with males showing reduced performance in the DNMTP task at higher working memory loads compared with females. Noradrenaline is an endogenous neurotransmitter with innate anti-inflammatory properties. The impact of targeting the noradrenergic system with the β
                      <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                      -adrenoceptor agonist Formoterol was further assessed on LPS-induced cognitive impairment in the DNMTP task. Coadministration of Formoterol (0.5 mg/kg, s.c.) attenuated LPS-driven mnemonic impairments in males but not females. Overall, the results show the DNMTP task is a paradigm sensitive to acute systemic inflammation and indicate that Formoterol may have useful anti-inflammatory properties in mitigating inflammatory-associated cognitive impairment.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: AI, Democracy, and the Transformation of Legal Norms
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics

title: Foundations of AI Governance
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI, Democracy, and the Transformation of Legal Norms
9f630b63700f2df7c972c28e264e05e6ceddde77.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence governance has emerged as a critical imperative in contemporary digital societies, demanding comprehensive frameworks that balance innovation with accountability, human rights, and democratic values. This chapter examines the foundational principles, institutional mechanisms, regulatory approaches, and ethical considerations that constitute effective AI governance systems. Through analysis of global governance frameworks including the EU AI Act, risk-based regulatory models, and international cooperation mechanisms, the chapter explores how legal norms are being transformed to address AI's unique challenges. Key governance dimensions examined include algorithmic accountability, transparency requirements, human rights safeguards, and the integration of democratic oversight into AI systems. The chapter provides empirical insights from recent governance initiatives across jurisdictions, analyzing both regulatory successes and persistent governance gaps.</jats:p>

title: AI Governance Foundations
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI, Democracy, and the Transformation of Legal Norms
2b28db33bf306c935f211bfca2b70402877fdf38.abstract: <jats:p>Government Artificial intelligence altering the governmental systems and substituting the traditional e-government models with the more algorithmic system of governance, where the decisions are increasingly mediated by the automated systems and processes based on the data. This has created challenging legal, ethical, and regulatory challenges of responsibility, accountability, transparency and fairness. The governance principles of AI involve the establishment of legal definitions, framework and standards to define responsibilities, scope and rights of AI usage in government and civil service. System regulation, risk reduction and protection of the right of the citizens demands definite legal definitions of AI, automated decision-making, and algorithmic accountability. Efficiencies can be opened up by making e-government, centered around digital service delivery, to become algorithmic governance, with incorporation of AI tools to analyze policies to distribute resources, predictive services, and make administrative judgments.</jats:p>

title: Generative AI and Foundation Models
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI, Democracy, and the Transformation of Legal Norms
c1f53c26084dcc82007fb1323a246abfe7791ac5.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence and foundation models represent a paradigm shift in computational capabilities, raising unprecedented governance challenges. This chapter examines the intersection of these technologies with democratic institutions, legal frameworks, and ethical norms. It analyzes emerging regulatory approaches including the EU AI Act and OECD principles, explores algorithmic bias and accountability mechanisms, and investigates tensions between innovation and rights protection. Through systematic review of recent scholarship and policy developments, the chapter identifies critical challenges in transparency, intellectual property, and algorithmic decision-making legitimacy.</jats:p>

title: The New Social Contract
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI, Democracy, and the Transformation of Legal Norms
22bdcab34bf4ce9285fa937f0a7ef9efba76e478.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter explores the transformation of democratic accountability in the age of artificial intelligence through legal, institutional, and political analysis. It examines how algorithmic decision-making reconfigures authority and responsibility, emphasizing the need for a new social contract integrating AI within constitutional frameworks. Focusing on India, the chapter proposes participatory, rights-based, and accountable governance models to align technological innovation with democratic legitimacy and public trust.</jats:p>

title: The Role of Constitutional Law in Structuring AI Governance
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI, Democracy, and the Transformation of Legal Norms
4b4b0de7a68d19261bb75753772840e30a18eec7.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the foundational role of constitutional law in structuring artificial intelligence governance frameworks. As AI systems increasingly influence democratic processes, individual rights, and societal structures, constitutional principles provide essential constraints and guidance for regulatory design. The analysis explores how fundamental rights doctrines, separation of powers, democratic accountability mechanisms, and rule of law principles shape AI governance approaches across jurisdictions. Drawing on comparative constitutional frameworks, including the EU AI Act and emerging international instruments, the chapter demonstrates how constitutional law bridges normative values and technical regulation. Key challenges include algorithmic accountability, automated decision-making impacts on fundamental rights, and the tension between innovation and constitutional safeguards.</jats:p>

title: A Conceptual Shift in Governance
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI, Democracy, and the Transformation of Legal Norms
ab477729de01bf724d4e82f352be4fc70e322edf.abstract: <jats:p>Today, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is an integral part of governance. This chapter examines the paradigm shift that is necessary for the governance of AI, which includes four key components: legality, transparency, accountability, and respect for human rights. By referring to global instruments like the European Union AI Act and the UNESCO's Ethics of AI as well as the respective national laws, it is proposed that the governance of AI should not only be about the technical but rather the rethinking of public law in light of human rights. The chapter conducts a conceptual analysis of the gaps between the regulatory framework and the actual implementation of AI in practice, particularly in high-risk industries. An Integrated Governance Framework (IGF) is proposed, in which all four pillars are interrelated.</jats:p>

title: Principles of Good Governance in the Age of AI
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI, Democracy, and the Transformation of Legal Norms
f1bf41b5e570221d1d030fc576b518faa6ad2712.abstract: <jats:p>The concept of artificial intelligence is becoming a part of the governance, artificial administration, and even the decision-making process in legal administration, which prompts serious questions about the quality of democracy and institutional control. With the impacts of algorithmic systems becoming a regulatory enforcer and in policy outputs, the opportunities of risks linked to transparency, discrimination, and lack of accountability escalate. This chapter discusses the ways in which the rule of law and democratic practices should be supported by relying on the principles of legality, transparency, and accountability in governing AI. It examines issues like black box problem, diffusion of responsibility and algorithmic discretion and suggests a normative model entailing the combination of legal protection, oversight and transparency norms to guarantee responsible and trustworthy AI usage.</jats:p>

title: Adaptive Regulation, Sandboxes, and Experimentalist Approaches
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI, Democracy, and the Transformation of Legal Norms
7e11bfc9418f4605cdb5f5a63e9b3f499236e89e.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence technologies presents unprecedented challenges to traditional regulatory frameworks and democratic governance structures. This chapter examines how adaptive regulation, regulatory sandboxes, and experimentalist governance approaches are reshaping the social contract between citizens, governments, and technology corporations in the AI era. Through comprehensive analysis of emerging regulatory models across multiple jurisdictions, this study demonstrates how experimentalist approaches enable responsive governance while maintaining democratic accountability. The chapter evaluates the effectiveness of regulatory sandboxes in balancing innovation with risk management, explores the theoretical foundations of adaptive regulation in complex technological environments, and proposes a reconceptualized framework for the social contract that accommodates algorithmic decision-making while preserving fundamental rights.</jats:p>

title: Legal Ontologies as Semantic Infrastructure for Normative Governance
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI, Democracy, and the Transformation of Legal Norms
f174114117b770c5b4a90db645fc80ad53f70442.abstract: <jats:p>The future challenge in AI & Law is not merely computational performance or post-hoc interpretability, but the translation of legal meaning into forms that computational systems can process without downgrading the normative structure of the Law into statistical correlations. This chapter introduces the philosophical argument that legal ontologies should be treated as semantic infrastructure for normative governance, that is, a mediating layer between legal texts, institutional practice, and AI-based decision support. Legal ontologies as computational artefacts that encode legal knowledge in a machine-understandable way, make explicit the conceptual commitments that enable systems to qualify facts in legally relevant terms, align conclusions to rules, exceptions, and principles, and generate explanations that simulate legal justification. Synthesizing the literature on legal ontologies (i.e., scope, engineering methodology, applications), this chapter focuses on developing a theoretical description of legal ontologies as semantic infrastructure for accountable AI in legal domains.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence, Economic Development, and Human Rights
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI, Democracy, and the Transformation of Legal Norms
4ee6296fcf5b904bf56fa2f91c3f8be35f78cd19.abstract: <jats:p>Over the last century, the world witnessed unprecedented technological advancements and economic growth. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been a major technological breakthrough, decisively transforming economic interactions in various sectors. With their unique characteristics of speed, accuracy, and efficiency, AI-enabled systems enhanced innovation, increased productivity, and advanced economic growth. However, current experience affirms that the benefits of AI-empowered economic development are not equitably shared. It results in rising poverty, economic inequality, and human insecurity worldwide. Developing countries experience them most severely due to the increased digital divide. The human rights of millions of people are directly or indirectly denied on account of the biased interplay between AI and economic development that primarily favors advanced countries. From this perspective, this chapter, using the qualitative methodology's narrative synthesis and critical analysis tools, examines the correlation between AI and economic development through the lens of human rights.</jats:p>

title: Algorithmic Accountability and Protection of Fair Procedure Rights in AI-Driven Public Administration
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI, Democracy, and the Transformation of Legal Norms
a83d8cfd752d0d873913a4e386493a38c0794f36.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter analyzes the paradigm shift from human-based bureaucracy to data-based governance and the tensions between algorithmic logic and fair procedure rights. The authors argue that automated decision-making in public administration triggers algorithmic procedural erosion, where traditional legal protections fail to address “black box” opacity. By identifying research gaps in how administrative law handles algorithmic discretion, this chapter explores the realignment of state power from officials to code developers. The authors propose reconstructing legal norms through an “Accountability by Design” framework, integrating procedural rights such as notification, intelligible explanation, and human intervention directly into AI architecture. Furthermore, this chapter advocates for independent algorithmic audits as legal evidence in judicial reviews to bridge information asymmetry. Finally, the authors conclude that normative redesign is essential to ensure digitalization strengthens democratic sovereignty and the rule of law, rather than creating an unaccountable technocracy.</jats:p>

title: The “Legitimate Interest Trap” in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI, Democracy, and the Transformation of Legal Norms
2e9944fcddef72768c2ae829a9e0e2ec444ccbc0.abstract: <jats:p>As organizations accelerate the deployment of AI systems, many default to the “legitimate interest” lawful basis for processing personal data. This move appears attractive because it avoids consent friction and accommodates broad operational goals such as security, fraud prevention, or service optimization. In practice, however, AI amplifies the evidentiary and governance burden embedded in legitimate interest, namely controllers must show a specific legitimate purpose, prove necessity (no equally effective, less intrusive alternative), and demonstrate that the interest is not overridden by individuals' rights and freedoms. Drawing on the European Data Protection Board's Guidelines 1/2024 on Article 6(1)(f) and the EDPB's Opinion 28/2024 on AI models, this chapter argues that “legitimate interest” becomes a trap when treated as a rhetorical justification rather than a structured test that must be operationalized through technical and organizational safeguards. The chapter proposes an “LIA-by-design” approach, that aligns privacy assessments under the EU AI Act.</jats:p>

title: Algorithmic Governance and Due Process in India
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI, Democracy, and the Transformation of Legal Norms
588dcb96d6cae7a2831ce0b99703c07178f2e3ab.abstract: <jats:p>The expansion of digital governance in India has embedded algorithmic systems within welfare administration, particularly in identity verification, eligibility determination, and benefit delivery. While these systems are justified on grounds of efficiency and scalability, they raise significant concerns for due process and administrative fairness. This chapter examines how core procedural safeguards notice, hearing, and reasoned decisions are affected by automated decision-making frameworks. It argues that algorithmic governance introduces opacity, limits avenues for contestation, and weakens accountability. The integration of digital identity further conditions access to welfare on technological compliance, increasing risks of exclusion. The chapter concludes that algorithmic systems fundamentally reshape state citizen relations and require recalibrated legal safeguards.</jats:p>

title: Digital Sovereignty and Legal Pluralism
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI, Democracy, and the Transformation of Legal Norms
0e1ac7826c5e0fc071b7288b1558bb3f5df99b2a.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the evolving concept of digital sovereignty through a comparative analysis of the European Union, the United States, and India within conditions of legal pluralism. It explores how democratic systems negotiate authority, rights, and regulation across overlapping legal, technological, and market domains. The European Union's rights-based constitutionalism, the United States' market-oriented digital order, and India's developmental-democratic model reveal diverse strategies for governing data, platforms, and infrastructure. Drawing on secondary data from 2020–2025, the chapter analyzes regulatory frameworks such as the GDPR, DPDP Act 2023, and the U.S. FTC's enforcement regime. It identifies convergences in recognizing data as a strategic resource and divergences in institutional design, enforcement capacity, and global influence.</jats:p>

title: The Adoption of International Artificial Intelligence Frameworks in Latin America
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI, Democracy, and the Transformation of Legal Norms
4701fb43814a97a05be3830c6acecafd8a990cf2.abstract: <jats:p>This article examines emerging AI regulation in Latin America through qualitative comparison of countries participating in the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on AI—Argentina, Mexico, Uruguay (Group 1)—versus influential non-participants—Brazil, Chile, Colombia (Group 2). It contrasts international soft law with the first global binding treaty, highlighting its universal openness and risk-based approach. Group 1 shows proactive adherence (Uruguay pioneering signatory, Mexico active observer) through ethical yet fragmented national strategies, while Group 2 prioritizes sovereignty via advanced risk-based legislative projects, indirectly aligned with Council of Europe standards through EU AI Act and UNESCO guidelines. The study concludes that the globalist-national dichotomy is converging toward risk-based governance and proposes the OAS as a strategic forum for an Inter-American AI Declaration to harmonize both groups, standardize supervisory mechanisms, and catalyze Council of Europe adherence, strategically positioning Latin America within global AI governance frameworks.</jats:p>

title: Digital Illiteracy and Accounting Compliance
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI, Democracy, and the Transformation of Legal Norms
5efe409d16d9b3864a79a51144be26f5f26411d2.abstract: <jats:p>This study investigates how digital illiteracy affects accounting compliance during the transition to mandatory e-invoicing in Greece. A quantitative approach was employed using data from 220 enterprises located in the Prefecture of Eastern Macedonia and Thrace. A structured questionnaire measured digital skills, awareness of e-invoicing procedures, and perceptions of state support. The results reveal that educational level and gender significantly influence the effective implementation of e-invoicing tools, while age has no significant impact. Despite gradual improvements in digital competence, digital illiteracy remains a key barrier to full compliance, especially among SMEs. The findings highlight the need for targeted digital training programs, simplified e-invoicing platforms, and policy incentives aimed at strengthening SMEs' technological capacity. This research empirically links digital literacy to compliance behavior in an emerging economy context, offering actionable insights for policymakers, tax authorities, and accounting practitioners.</jats:p>

title: Educating Citizens in the Algorithmic State
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI, Democracy, and the Transformation of Legal Norms
c36db21603c573e6fb9e8bf58f69f40ba2fba2e3.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines ethical AI awareness as a necessary form of civic competence in the algorithmic state. As AI systems increasingly shape public administration, healthcare, welfare, education, local governance, public safety, and democratic communication, citizens need more than basic digital skills. They require the capacity to understand how AI may affect rights, equality, transparency, accountability, inclusion. The chapter presents a curriculum for ethical AI awareness designed to educate AI-aware citizens and stakeholders on the ethical foundations of AI, bias and discrimination, sources of algorithmic harm, mitigation strategies, ethical frameworks, transparency, accountability, policy advocacy, and collaborative problem-solving. It argues that such education should be accessible, interdisciplinary, participatory, and inclusive, addressing not only citizens but also public officials, policymakers, educators, developers, civil society actors, and professionals.</jats:p>

title: Smart Resilience
container-title: Strategic Planning and Adaptation of Resilient Agri-Food Systems in a Changing World
1daef2626367c084bc117f883f6ea817c3e58afb.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can be integrated with strategies for adapting to climate change in the planning of the agricultural and food sectors. The goal is to make food systems more resilient and ensure long-term food security in the country. As climate change, resource shortages, and social and economic inequalities exert increasing pressure on global food systems, the utilization of data and flexible planning methods presents new opportunities for change. This chapter demonstrates how AI tools, such as machine learning, predictive analysis, and geospatial data, can facilitate climate-smart farming by enabling better decision-making, mitigating risks, and enhancing productivity. Examples from India, the Netherlands, and Kenya show how AI has been successfully used to build climate resilience worldwide. The chapter also introduces a new framework, the Data-Driven Strategic Planning Matrix (DSPM), to help match new technologies with fairness and sustainability objectives.</jats:p>

title: AI- and IoT-Driven Sustainable Smart Farming Through Modernizing Traditional Rice Machinery
container-title: Strategic Planning and Adaptation of Resilient Agri-Food Systems in a Changing World
1d19d443915e719ae530b58cbd9a0addd601cbb2.abstract: <jats:p>The combination of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) into the established works in rice farming is a radical change in the direction of sustainable and climatically adapted agriculture. By retrofitting traditional machinery with modular sensors, microcontrollers and edge/cloud AI, real-time data on soil moisture, temperature, crop health and nutrients is available. Intelligent irrigation, intelligent fertilizer prescriptions, and intelligent pest control maximize inputs, minimize labor, fuel, and chemical expenditures, and improve productivity. The chapter relies on secondary data and theoretical analysis, which limits its scope for empirical study. Bangladesh, Indian and Chinese case studies show that real efficiency, cost savings and yield stabilization are achieved. Adoption requires digital literacy, inclusiveness of services, and favorable policies; future research activities must focus on multi-season testing, interoperable systems, and gender-sensitive and sustainable deployment.</jats:p>

title: Explainable AI and ESG-Driven Decision Intelligence for Strategic Leadership in the Creative Economy
container-title: Reengineering Strategic Leadership for the Creative Economy in the ESG-Digital Nexus
d8b4eafefe49e40a437d889529cb8c99644dca1c.abstract: <jats:p>As ESG principles and cutting-edge digital innovations intersect in the creative economy, strategic leadership is changing in ways never before imaginable. This chapter discusses the role of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in supporting ESG-driven decision intelligence by allowing a leader to make transparent, accountable, and data-informed decisions. Based on the Resource Based View and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, the chapter advances a conceptual framework that combines explainability, ESG performance measures, and strategic leadership capabilities. The conversation focuses on the benefits of explainable AI for governance, stakeholders' trust, sustainability, and organizational resilience in the creative sector. The chapter also provides future research directions in the context of responsible human-centric AI leaders in the changing digital and sustainability landscapes.</jats:p>

title: Navigating India's ESG–Digital Nexus Through AI-Driven Ethical Transformation
container-title: Reengineering Strategic Leadership for the Creative Economy in the ESG-Digital Nexus
22f3457abdf2fffb7ebe5401b54c2f7bc15f8c5c.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how India's creative economy might navigate the ESG–Digital Nexus via an AI-driven ethical shift, not just tech for tech's sake. It draws on Dynamic Capabilities Theory and Stakeholder Theory, and basically looks at how AI-Driven Digital Capability, Big Data and IoT Integration, Ethical Digital Transformation, Strategic Leadership Agility, ESG Performance, and Sustainable Creative Economy Development connect together. The study uses survey data from 412 professionals, and it then analyses the whole thing with PLS-SEM. The outcome of the study is that AI capabilities and digital integration really do improve ESG performance, but they do it through ethical digital transformation. Strategic leadership agility tends to reinforce these effects, while ESG performance in turn supports sustainable creative economy development. Overall, the chapter stresses that technological experimentation has to be matched with ethical governance and sustainability objectives if India wants long-term competitiveness and responsible digital expansion.</jats:p>

title: Human-Centered Leadership in the Age of AI and Automation
container-title: Evolving Societies and Contemporary Workplace Issues
80fd311f525faf8dbdb5cda66118e610c171be8c.abstract: <jats:p>In the age of AI and automation, organizations need leadership that combines technological advancement with humanity. Human-centered leadership emphasizes empathy, ethics, and inclusiveness to ensure that innovation enriches and does not undermine the human experience at the workplace. As digital systems further impose decision-making, leaders will need to navigate complex ethical dilemmas, facilitate workforce development, and drive trust, culture, flexibility, and psychological safety. This approach requires open communication, equal access to opportunities, and anticipatory action in response to algorithmic discrimination and digital exclusion. This paper, based on international case studies and cross-cutting expertise, considers how leaders across the public, private, and nonprofit sectors are evolving their practices in response to the challenges of digitally reshaping workplaces. This study ends with actionable frameworks, policy guidance, and research directions.</jats:p>

title: Assessing the Quality of AI Explanations of Atrial Fibrillation: Comparative Analysis of ChatGPT and Google Gemini
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
598e2fa6d5c1d1ee8bb1eebc101a66353744cb13.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Atrial fibrillation (AF) is one of the most common arrhythmias and is associated with multiple risk factors, including stroke and heart failure. Therefore, it is important that accurate and comprehensive educational resources on AF are available. Artificial intelligence (AI) platforms such as Google Gemini and ChatGPT are emerging tools for medical education. To our knowledge, this is the first study to assess the quality of these platforms for AF education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This pilot study aimed to (1) assess the quality of ChatGPT and Google Gemini explanations of AF and its treatment, (2) compare responses from both platforms, and (3) analyze differences in interpretation between cardiologists and nonmedical professionals.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The prompt “Explain atrial fibrillation and how to treat it to a patient” was entered into both ChatGPT and Google Gemini. The responses, along with a survey created in Google Forms, were sent out to potential participants between September and October 2024. The survey questions were derived from the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials and DISCERN criteria. Each survey question was multiple choice and rated on a 5-point Likert scale, where 1 indicated strong disagreement and 5 indicated strong agreement. Averages of each answer from the survey were calculated and compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The survey was completed by 28 participants, including cardiologists and cardiology fellows and 17 nonmedical professionals (college graduates not employed in the medical field). No significant overall quality differences were observed between ChatGPT and Google Gemini. When comparing participant groups, cardiologists rated AI-generated responses higher than nonmedical professionals for perceived bias (mean 3.82 vs mean 4.33; P=.04) and for explaining consequences of no treatment (mean 2.85 vs mean 1.86; P=.005). In contrast, nonmedical professionals rated structural and organizational features more favorably than cardiologists, including visual cues (mean 3.97 vs mean 2.48; P<.001), informative headers (mean 4.77 vs mean 3.95; P=.001), concise sections (mean 4.71 vs mean 4.29; P=.04), identifiable patient actions (mean 4.21 vs mean 3.19; P=.04), and references to additional resources (mean 2.65 vs mean 1.71; P=.006).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The comparable quality of ChatGPT and Google Gemini suggests that both are viable for AF education. Differences in ratings of organizational features versus perceptions of bias and consequences of no treatment highlight a disconnect between cardiologists and nonmedical professionals. To optimize clinical application, cardiologists should evaluate both comprehensiveness and clarity of AI-generated responses. This serves as a pilot study, and future research should focus on longitudinal studies of AI-generated responses and their effects on clinical outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery, Endobariatrics, and AI - How AI is Contributing to Surgery and Endoscopy
Towards Realistic Project-Level Code Generation via Multi-Agent Collaboration and Semantic Architecture Modeling
container-title: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
2e98affb75fe6b1c9fa0a80bf39cb6bb48af6b14.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in automated code generation. In real-world software engineering, the growing demand for rapid iteration and continuous delivery underscores the importance of project-level code generation, where LLMs are expected to generate complete software projects directly from complex user requirements. This task, however, presents greater challenges due to larger input scales, multi-modal information, and the need for holistic architectural reasoning. Although existing studies have made initial explorations, they still face key limitations, including unrealistic datasets and unreliable evaluation metrics that fail to reflect real-world complexity, the semantic gap between human-written requirements and machine-interpretable structures, and difficulties in managing hierarchical dependencies and maintaining quality throughout the generation process. To address these limitations, we first introduce
                    <jats:sc>CodeProjectEval</jats:sc>
                    , a project-level code generation dataset built from 18 real-world repositories with 12.7 files and 2,388.6 lines of code per task on average, supplemented with documentation and executable test cases for automatic evaluation. We further propose
                    <jats:sc>ProjectGen</jats:sc>
                    , a multi-agent framework that decomposes projects into architecture design, skeleton generation, and code filling stages with iterative refinement and memory-based context management. Within this framework, we introduce the Semantic Software Architecture Tree, a structured and semantically rich representation that effectively bridges user requirements and source code implementation. Experiments show that
                    <jats:sc>ProjectGen</jats:sc>
                    achieves state-of-the-art performance, passing 52/124 test cases on the small-scale project-level code generation dataset DevBench, a 57% improvement over the baseline approaches, and 310 test cases on
                    <jats:sc>CodeProjectEval</jats:sc>
                    , representing an improvement of roughly tenfold compared to the baselines.
                  </jats:p>

title: AI-Generated Exposure Hierarchies for Body Dysmorphic Disorder: Proof-of-Concept Study
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
475970c23de59b336f5f102fda0e80aa46b47e4e.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is a chronic, impairing condition for which cognitive behavioral therapy, including exposure and response prevention (ERP), is the first-line treatment, but few clinicians are trained in BDD-specific ERP. Constructing personalized exposure hierarchies is time-intensive and requires clinical expertise, particularly for patients with absent insight who may hold appearance beliefs with delusional conviction. Generative AI (GenAI)–powered chatbots, such as ChatGPT, have shown utility for clinical content, but their capacity to produce safe, appropriate ERP hierarchies for BDD has not been examined.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study evaluated the feasibility of using ChatGPT (GPT-5) to generate ERP hierarchies for BDD, assessed the influence of clinical and demographic characteristics on output quality, benchmarked AI-generated hierarchies against those created by doctoral-level BDD specialists, and tested whether blinded experts could distinguish AI-generated from expert-generated hierarchies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GPT-5 generated 10-item graded exposure hierarchies for 72 simulated vignettes that varied by body area, insight level (good, limited, or absent), symptom specificity, age, and gender. Expert clinicians independently generated hierarchies for a subset of 18 vignettes. Two researchers rated all GPT-5 hierarchies for task completion and information integration. Three BDD expert clinicians, blinded to the hierarchy source (expert vs GPT-5), rated all 90 hierarchies for relevance, specificity, variability, safety, and overall quality. After unblinding, raters attempted to identify the AI-generated hierarchy in the 18 matched pairs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      GPT-5 generated complete hierarchies for 69 of 72 (95.8%) vignettes. Blinded experts rated GPT-5 hierarchies highly across all dimensions (mean scores ranging from 4.39, SD 0.26 to 4.90, SD 0.16 out of 5), with no significant differences from expert-generated hierarchies except for variability, where experts scored modestly higher (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.02;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.24). After unblinding, raters correctly identified AI-generated hierarchies only 31.5% (17/54) of the time, significantly below chance (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.009); this below-chance result was mostly due to one rater, and no rater performed above chance. Insight level was the most consistent predictor of quality: absent-insight hierarchies received significantly lower safety (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.73) and overall quality ratings (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.01;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.43). This pattern was not unique to GPT-5; safety ratings for expert-generated hierarchies also declined significantly by insight level (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03). Miscalibration of exposure difficulty, particularly for low- and absent-insight cases, was the most common rater concern (30/43, 69.8% comments), disproportionately directed at GPT-5 hierarchies.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GPT-5 generated ERP hierarchies for BDD that blinded experts rated as comparable to clinician-created hierarchies and could not reliably distinguish them from clinician-created hierarchies. However, hierarchies for patients with absent insight received lower safety and quality ratings from both AI and expert sources, and qualitative comments suggested AI-generated hierarchies were less well calibrated to delusional-level presentations. GenAI thus shows promise as a clinician-facing aid for ERP hierarchy generation, but these findings underscore the need for clinician oversight, especially for patients with delusional conviction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: SAI: Virtualizing Shared Memory of GPU for AI workload acceleration
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
c8fa29b0323351e1659db262fc936958ed20d580.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    AI workloads increasingly demand high parallelism and efficient on-chip memory utilization on modern GPUs. However, the limited capacity of shared memory often constrains thread-level parallelism, while portions of the L2 cache remain underutilized. In this work, we propose
                    <jats:bold>SAI</jats:bold>
                    , a mechanism that virtualizes shared memory into the L2 cache to improve GPU performance for AI applications. SAI dynamically activates virtualization based on runtime resource usage, enabling additional CTAs with minimal architectural modifications. We further introduce an L2 cache management strategy that integrates associativity-based virtual page allocation and a replacement information table, reducing page-swapping overhead while preserving L2 cache performance. Experimental results demonstrate that SAI achieves an 18.6% performance improvement over the baseline design and outperforms SMILE-opt, our reproduced state-of-the-art baseline, by 8.8%. Moreover, SAI captures 60.2% of the performance gain delivered by the idealized Double SMEM design while reducing energy consumption to 87.7% of the baseline. These results highlight the effectiveness of SAI in enhancing thread-level parallelism and optimizing on-chip memory for AI workloads.
                  </jats:p>

title: AI-Enabled Early Detection of Epidemic Threats in a Resource-Constrained Health System: Implementation Research from Lebanon
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
94bf395e649f9c13344c021277ab854ad6c98be5.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Global South countries face heightened infectious disease risks compounded by fragmented surveillance systems and resource constraints. Lebanon’s health system crisis and recurrent outbreaks highlight the urgent need for new approaches to epidemic and pandemic preparedness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To describe the design, implementation process, and early implementation findings of an artificial intelligence (AI)–enabled early warning system (AI-EWS) that automates detection of epidemiologically relevant events using laboratory data in Lebanon, with emphasis on feasibility, workflow integration, stakeholder engagement, and implementation learnings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We applied an implementation research approach to co-design and validate an AI-EWS prototype integrated within a university hospital laboratory. The system incorporates a hybrid statistical and machine learning analytic pipeline and a real-time dashboard for detecting epidemic events across multiple pathogens using routine laboratory information systems (LIS) data. The system was developed in collaboration with the Ministry of Public Health (MoPH) to support future national adoption.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The project produced a structured framework for pathogen selection, rule development, dataset creation, and platform co-design with clinical and epidemiological experts, medical informatics professionals, MoPH experts, and technical specialists. Early implementation observations indicate operational feasibility within existing infrastructure, strong stakeholder engagement, and trust-building around AI-enabled surveillance through participatory design and responsible-AI governance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI-enabled laboratory surveillance is a viable and scalable approach to strengthening epidemic preparedness in low-resource health systems when grounded in implementation science and responsible AI, and when explicitly aligned with local workflows and national policy priorities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Bayesian Forecasting as the Analytical Core of an AI-Assisted Early Warning System for Dengue Outbreaks during the 2023 Epidemic: Implementation and Emergency Management in a Dominican Pediatric Hospital
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
056417fa3dbad64347775b6e5020ffb82cf01df1.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Dengue remains a major cause of pediatric morbidity in the Dominican Republic, with increasingly intense epidemic cycles. Advances in statistical modeling, probabilistic forecasting, and AI-assisted digital health systems offer new opportunities to enhance early warning capabilities and strengthen hospital preparedness. This study evaluated a Bayesian negative binomial regression forecasting model as the analytical core of an AI-assisted early warning system (EWS) for predicting weekly dengue cases nationwide, using strict out-of-sample validation during the 2023 epidemic and applying its outputs operationally in a high-demand pediatric hospital. National surveillance data (PLISA/PAHO), hospital records from the Dr. Hugo Mendoza Pediatric Hospital (HPHM), and climatic and satellite indicators (NOAA, MODIS) for 2014–2024 were integrated. The model incorporated climatically plausible lags, harmonic seasonality, two vegetation indices (NDVI_lag4 and EVI_lag4), a long-term spline trend, and weakly informative priors, achieving excellent convergence (Rhat = 1.00). Climatic and environmental predictors exhibited small and uncertain effects, whereas the temporal spline accounted for most long-term epidemic variability. In the 2023 national validation, the model captured the broad epidemic trajectory and improved RMSE and MAE compared with the historical seasonal baseline (RMSE = 783.3; MAE = 423.4; MAPE = 80.2%), although proportional accuracy remained limited during abrupt epidemic acceleration. The national model also captured ascending-phase signals that were temporally aligned with the HPHM hospital outbreak, including its sharp rise during epidemiological weeks 36–40. These outputs were used alongside routine surveillance and hospital indicators to support operational situational awareness, capacity planning, patient-flow reorganization, strengthened triage, and emergency preparedness during the epidemic. The model demonstrated temporal signal detection and operational relevance, positioning Bayesian probabilistic forecasting, embedded within an AI-assisted digital health workflow, as a useful analytical component for epidemic monitoring and hospital preparedness, subject to limitations in peak magnitude calibration and proportional accuracy.</jats:p>

title: Toward Human-Centered Pedagogy in the Age of Generative AI Among Higher Education Educators: Qualitative Phenomenological Study
container-title: JMIR Medical Education
46248c918f688c3c5f2cc8bb261f150c45f4e9cf.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Generative AI (GenAI) expands possibilities for content generation, feedback, personalization, and instructional support in higher education. Its growing use also challenges established assumptions about teaching, assessment, professional expertise, academic integrity, and educational responsibility. Although research has examined technology adoption and AI competencies, less is known about how educators experience and interpret the pedagogical transformation associated with GenAI in everyday teaching.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study explored how higher education educators experience GenAI-mediated pedagogical transformation, focusing on pedagogical practices, professional roles and expertise, educator agency, human-AI relationships, and associated opportunities and tensions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A qualitative phenomenological inquiry involved 23 educators from 3 Palestinian universities. Purposive maximum-variation sampling sought variation in academic rank, discipline, teaching experience, and experience with AI tools. Individual semistructured, in-depth interviews were conducted from March to April 2026, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and returned to participants for review. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis informed by phenomenology. Initial coding was inductive and grounded in participants’ accounts; human-centered AI and sociomateriality subsequently informed interpretation as sensitizing concepts. Themes were developed through iterative comparison of transcripts, analytic memos, and alternative interpretations. Informational sufficiency was observed after approximately 20 interviews, with 3 additional interviews used to examine the developing thematic structure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis generated 8 interconnected themes. Educators described a shift from content transmission toward mediation, inquiry, reflective learning, creative exploration, and process-oriented assessment. Professional expertise increasingly centered on facilitation, pedagogical design, contextual interpretation, ethical guidance, and evaluation of AI-generated content. Human-AI collaboration involved bounded and integrated configurations, with humans retaining responsibility for judgment and educational consequences. Educator agency appeared through decisions about AI participation, independent student reasoning, and the boundaries of human expertise. Credibility, bias, authorship, authenticity, and academic integrity became embedded as pedagogical concerns. Participants valued opportunities for creativity, personalization, flexibility, and instructional support while expressing concerns about dependence, reduced intellectual effort, and weakened human connection.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GenAI-mediated pedagogical transformation depends on educators’ alignment of AI use with learning purposes, the allocation of responsibilities, and the preservation of ethical accountability and meaningful relationships. The resulting human-centered pedagogy framework positions pedagogical intentionality, contextual judgment, negotiated agency, and relational presence as central to responsible integration. Universities should complement technical training and institutional policies with support for pedagogical design, critical evaluation, process-oriented assessment, and ethical reasoning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: AI and Machine Learning in Broadcast Media
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Machine Learning in Broadcast Media
0cea04df1f33891ac6e61332b69e78c30652b6e1.abstract: <jats:p>News gathering, production, verification, and distribution have been reshaped—sometimes profoundly, sometimes quietly—by the growing presence of artificial intelligence and machine learning in broadcast operations. This chapter surveys the main areas where these technologies operate: automated news production, deepfake detection, audience analytics, recommender systems, and voice synthesis. It also examines ethical questions emerging in each domain. Drawing on recent scholarship across journalism studies, computer science, media ethics, and communication research, the chapter explores tensions between operational efficiency and journalistic integrity, between personalization and information diversity, and between AI-assisted verification and its vulnerability to synthetic content. A key theme is that productivity gains, though real, are not self-sustaining. Responsible deployment requires editorial oversight, effective governance, and transparent disclosure to audiences. The chapter concludes by outlining a research agenda for an information environment increasingly shaped by AI.</jats:p>

title: The Digital Transformation of Television Broadcasting Supported by Artificial Intelligence
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Machine Learning in Broadcast Media
35b7dc9c798c6869d6eeb6921fd0c44c284f95bc.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines the digital transformation brought about by artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies in television broadcasting within a conceptual and critical framework. It discusses how processes such as content production, automation, scheduling, audience measurement and personalisation have been reorganised through data-driven systems. Furthermore, by assessing the impacts of algorithmicisation on editorial independence, public accountability, transparency, privacy and accountability, the study argues that the future of television broadcasting is shaped not only by technical innovation but also by institutional and ethical choices.</jats:p>

title: The Future of Television
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Machine Learning in Broadcast Media
bff6f50e054390e2c139c80e7fb45824d6ff514a.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) and automation are transforming the television and broadcast media industry by reshaping production workflows, distribution models, and audience engagement strategies. Intelligent systems are increasingly applied in automated content creation, smart studio operations, personalized recommendation services, and predictive audience analytics. These innovations enhance efficiency, reduce operational costs, and enable broadcasters to deliver more adaptive and customized viewing experiences across digital platforms. However, the growing integration of AI also raises important challenges related to ethical accountability, algorithmic bias, transparency, and workforce transformation. Human creativity, editorial judgment, and trust remain essential elements in ensuring responsible media practices. The future of television will depend on balancing technological innovation with human-centered values to build sustainable and socially meaningful broadcast ecosystems.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence in Digital Television Platforms
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Machine Learning in Broadcast Media
054cd1bab132b082e3e6a31810c1cc1a1ff38db7.abstract: <jats:p>This study investigates how artificial intelligence–driven algorithms on digital television platforms transform the processes of cultural production, distribution, and consumption within the media ecosystem. Focusing on Netflix as a case study, it analyzes how algorithmic recommendation systems structure content visibility, shape user preferences, and reorganize audience behavior through data-driven mechanisms. Drawing on sociological theories of power and cultural production, the study conceptualizes algorithms not merely as technical tools but as socio-technical actors that establish new regimes of visibility and control. In this context, the notion of the “algorithmic field” is proposed to explain how platform-based systems redefine power relations, mediate cultural hierarchies, and reproduce structural inequalities. The findings suggest that digital platforms operate as influential intermediaries that both organize and govern cultural circulation in contemporary media environments.</jats:p>

title: From Broadcast to Platform Power
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Machine Learning in Broadcast Media
0039e4646b5f12e04840a5816064712c21fdb48a.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the transformation of Turkish television from a broadcast-centered system into a platform-based, datafied media ecology shaped by Netflix, BluTV, Exxen, and related streaming services. It argues that streaming in Turkey cannot be understood as a simple technological shift, because platforms entered a media system already defined by dizi exports, RTÜK regulation, broadcast scarcity, censorship pressures, and audience dissatisfaction with long-form television. Through case studies of The Protector, Ethos, BluTV, and Exxen, the chapter analyzes how platform commissioning, personalization, metadata, recommendation systems, and AI-assisted workflows reshape cultural visibility, editorial authority, and creative labor. The chapter also considers how state regulation and media capture complicate platform governance in Turkey. It concludes that Turkish television's future depends on balancing algorithmic efficiency, cultural specificity, regulatory pressure, and editorial responsibility.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence, Local Broadcasting, and the Logic of Innovation From the Periphery
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Machine Learning in Broadcast Media
993d09fe2a97e708c317641849a351071457e373.abstract: <jats:p>Drawing on a qualitative case study of Radio Kepulauan Seribu, this chapter examines how these tensions unfold within Indonesia's small-island broadcasting context. Rather than framing AI as a disruptive force that automates editorial work, the chapter advances the concept of guided augmentation, in which AI supports preparatory cognitive tasks while ethical judgment, contextual interpretation, and public responsibility remain human-centered. Through interviews and non-participant observation, the study demonstrates how AI adoption emerges from structural constraints, limited resources, and public service mandates rather than technological ambition. The findings challenge dominant, Global North–centric narratives of AI-driven media transformation by presenting small islands as sites of adaptive innovation and relational accountability. By reframing hybrid broadcasting as a stable, context-sensitive media configuration, the chapter contributes to broader debates on AI, ethics, and the future of broadcasting in community-oriented media ecosystems.</jats:p>

title: Algorithmic Television
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Machine Learning in Broadcast Media
857bae5718eff00351eeae246d5c2a40314cac99.abstract: <jats:p>With the process of digitalization, television broadcasting has evolved into a data-driven, algorithmic structure through digital platform services. In this context, the use of artificial intelligence is regarded as a tool that increases efficiency in television broadcasting. However, gaining competitive advantage through algorithmic infrastructures and the commodification of viewer data create forms of algorithmic management. This study examines the transformation created by artificial intelligence in the field of television broadcasting through platformization shaped by data ownership, the reshaping of labor processes through automation, and algorithmic governmentality as the outcome of these processes. The fact that artificial intelligence produces transformations in relation to capital accumulation, labor regimes, data ownership, and ideological control makes it necessary to evaluate television broadcasting from a political-economic perspective.</jats:p>

title: Algorithmic Curatorial Shift
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Machine Learning in Broadcast Media
1559be582d93ad91c2a432d936327ea610496ff5.abstract: <jats:p>Television program scheduling has long been an exercise in editorial authority: decisions regarding which programs to air, when, and in what order have shaped viewer behavior, structured the revenue logic of commercial broadcasting, and reproduced the broader ideological and economic conditions of the broadcasting system. The integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning into broadcasting operations is restructuring this framework. Algorithmic tools are increasingly shaping audience forecasting, ad placement, content performance evaluation, and recommendation systems. Drawing on Raymond Williams' flow theory, gatekeeping theory, and platform capitalism, this chapter examines this transformation through the concept of algorithmic curatorial shift, the redistribution of editorial authority from human planning experts to algorithmic systems.</jats:p>

title: Personalized Broadcasting and Algorithmic Recommender Systems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Machine Learning in Broadcast Media
45211ebcedbc6bad1d33a282df18d35a0dac1227.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines the digital transformation of television broadcasting through personalized broadcasting and algorithmic recommender systems. It aims to explain how television has evolved from a linear medium into a data driven, platform centered, and algorithmically organized environment. The study discusses the conceptual foundations of personalized broadcasting and the main types of recommender systems, including content based, collaborative, and hybrid models. The findings show that these systems are not merely technical tools for content discovery, but socio technical mechanisms that shape audience experience, engagement, content visibility, and cultural circulation. The Netflix case further demonstrates that algorithmic personalization has become a strategic force that restructures media economies, influences user preferences, and redefines contemporary broadcasting practices.</jats:p>

title: Watching What You Want
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Machine Learning in Broadcast Media
d1ff86b30e4ee238eb295d1fbf660002d7278fc2.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how algorithmic recommendation systems have become central to television broadcasting. Drawing on critical media theory, platform studies, and research, it argues artificial intelligence and machine learning reshaped relationships between broadcasters and audiences by shifting curation from human programmers to automated systems. It situates collaborative filtering, content-based filtering, and deep learning within debates on filter bubbles, cultural fragmentation, editorial responsibility, and the political economy of digital media. Treating recommendation as a categorical transformation, it addresses ethics, including transparency, bias, and viewer autonomy, reviews regulatory and self-governance frameworks, and outlines future trends such as emotion-aware AI and cross-platform personalization.</jats:p>

title: AI, Television News, and the Future of Democratic Gatekeeping
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Machine Learning in Broadcast Media
3ee3b8c7e6d4280704c4999714e0509349e034cd.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is increasingly shaping television news production by influencing how stories are selected, prioritized, and targeted to audiences. While AI offers efficiency and data-driven decision-making, it also raises concerns about democratic gatekeeping in broadcast journalism by challenging traditional ideas of editorial judgment, accountability, transparency, and pluralism. This chapter examines how AI reshapes gatekeeping in television news by shifting decisions from human editors to hybrid human-AI systems. Drawing on gatekeeping theory and journalism studies, it explores issues such as algorithmic opacity, automation bias, and reduced diversity in news coverage. The chapter argues that without proper governance, AI-assisted gatekeeping may weaken the democratic role of television news. To address these concerns, it proposes a framework for democratic gatekeeping in AI-assisted television news based on transparency, human oversight, editorial responsibility, and pluralism, offering guidance for integrating AI into news workflows.</jats:p>

title: The Transformation of News Discourse in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Machine Learning in Broadcast Media
8e94f02ed0fdcf254c98a1451e802610a07e5039.abstract: <jats:p>In the digital media ecosystem, AI-based text generation systems, particularly large language models, have become increasingly influential in news production processes. These systems are viewed not only as technical tools but also as new mechanisms of discourse production that reshape how news content is created. This development has made the comparative examination of human-produced and AI-generated news texts increasingly important. In this context, the study comparatively analyzes news texts selected from international news organizations such as Al Jazeera and Reuters alongside texts generated by ChatGPT. The research focuses on military interventions and violent incidents in Palestine. Using document analysis as a qualitative research method, the study evaluates the texts through Teun A. van Dijk's Critical Discourse Analysis approach and identifies major differences between human-produced and AI-generated news texts in terms of discourse structure, framing strategies, linguistic choices, and meaning production practices.</jats:p>
