title: Polycentrism in the Digital Geoeconomic Order
container-title: Rethinking Authority and Legitimacy in Global Politics
711935f459dab859b4d3505b506126d69c84de7d.abstract: <jats:p>The twenty-first century is marked by the paradox of global interdependence alongside deepening fragmentation, as digital infrastructures and data regimes reshape economic and geopolitical dynamics. This chapter critiques the limits of monocentric governance models and advances polycentric governance as a more adaptive framework for a complex digital era. Drawing on Ostrom, it conceptualizes polycentrism as a multi-level, networked mode of governance suited to distributed authority and uncertainty. Through cases such as COVID-19 governance failures, data sovereignty disputes, and digital inequality in the Global South, it shows how overlapping governance systems can enhance resilience and legitimacy. Compared to hierarchical models, polycentric systems enable flexibility, innovation, and coordination across diverse actors. The chapter argues that polycentric governance is both theoretically robust and empirically necessary for sustaining cooperation in the evolving digital geoeconomic order.</jats:p>

title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
Digital Transformation of Accounting and Financial Management Through Emerging Technologies
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
072ee30c1139742aaee5825be31b3e984571eca4.abstract: <jats:p>Digital transformation has created an opportunity for accountants and financial managers to create new efficiencies, add transparency to their work, and develop better strategies for decision-making. This chapter looks at how artificial intelligence, automation, big data analytics, and cloud-based financial management are changing how accountants use technology, as well as how those technologies are changing the practices and processes that accountants follow when doing their jobs. It also describes how the digital transformation of Finance will cause a dramatic shift in the way financial services are delivered to customers from being reactive to value-driven. By integrating intelligent systems into forecasting, performance management, risk assessment, and real-time reporting functions, the ability to make informed decisions is enhanced. The chapter identifies the organizational, regulatory, and ethical challenges that digital finance poses, including data privacy, cybersecurity, and governance risks.</jats:p>

title: The Importance of the Mastering of Technological Skills and Profile of Professional Accounting
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
50dd51a7264e3966f834e8645c738ce22d306e48.abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to assess whether the importance given to information and communication technologies by accounting professionals is conditioned by age, gender, and the type of company where they work. It also intends to assess the relationship between the skills under study, determining which one is most important. The main results obtained allow us to affirm that the variables age and gender do not condition the importance given to information and communication technologies by accounting professionals, while for the type of company there are differences of opinion, constituting the main innovative contribution of this article to academic knowledge, given the scarcity of studies on this topic. We also conclude that “specific accounting technological skills” are the strongest manifestation in the construct of “technological skills”. This study aims to contribute to the reflection of Professional Orders and Higher Education Institutions on the importance of information and communication technologies for accounting professionals.</jats:p>

title: Preparing Finance Professionals for the Digital Age
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
a93fe9bb395867eb78859ec32fbdad9bef6d3cb5.abstract: <jats:p>Emerging digital technologies—AI, big data, RPA, blockchain, and cloud computing—are rapidly transforming the financial sector, shifting finance professionals from traditional record-keepers to strategic digital advisors. Using a qualitative approach grounded in academic literature and institutional reports, this study identifies critical technical competencies including data analytics, financial modeling, cybersecurity awareness, and digital literacy, alongside essential soft skills such as strategic thinking, communication, adaptability, and emotional intelligence. A significant gap is revealed between current educational and corporate training systems versus industry expectations. To bridge this divide, the study proposes a comprehensive competency model integrating digital proficiency, behavioral skills, and financial expertise. The findings underscore the necessity of continuous learning and digital resilience, ensuring sustained professional relevance in an increasingly technology-driven financial landscape.</jats:p>

title: Education and Curriculum Design for Future Finance Professionals
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
688a834c57266bfb9c64b3f458ee9b94b666529f.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid digital transformation of global financial systems has created an urgent need to redesign finance education and curriculum frameworks for future professionals. Traditional finance curricula remain largely theory-oriented and often fail to address emerging competencies related to artificial intelligence, FinTech, blockchain, data analytics, sustainability, and ethical governance. This chapter proposes the Future Finance Curriculum Framework (FFCF Model), an integrated and competency-based framework designed to bridge the gap between academic learning and evolving industry expectations. Drawing upon theories of competency-based education, outcome-based learning, and experiential learning, the study emphasizes interdisciplinary approaches, industry collaboration, technology integration, and continuous curriculum upgradation. The chapter also highlights the growing importance of analytical, digital ethical, and soft skills in preparing adaptive finance professionals for a globally connected financial environment and society too.</jats:p>

title: The Accounting Professional in the Fourth Industrial Revolution
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
09542450f279522e6869f1c9442864fdbc2fe620.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how the digital transformation of accounting is reflected in labour-market demand in Spain. Using a quantitative content analysis of 803 accounting-related job advertisements published on InfoJobs, the study identifies the digital competencies explicitly required by employers and analyses the factors associated with more digitally intensive vacancies. A Digital Demand Index is constructed from four technological dimensions: Excel and data processing, data visualisation and business intelligence, ERP and management systems, and artificial intelligence (AI). The results show that digital demand is mainly concentrated around established tools, particularly Excel and ERP systems, while business intelligence and AI remain much less visible in recruitment requirements. The regression analysis indicates that higher salaries, junior profiles, large firms, and higher education requirements are associated with stronger digital competence demand.</jats:p>

title: Digital Skills and Professional Judgment in AI-Driven Financial Decision-Making
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
fa94d39fbd808cc46e56a32eb78b60762c9d5124.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping financial decision-making by altering how information is analyzed, interpreted, and translated into professional judgment. This chapter examines the role of digital skills in determining whether AI strengthens or undermines the quality and accountability of financial decisions. Drawing on interdisciplinary literature, the chapter conceptualizes digital skills as cognitive–governance capabilities that extend beyond technical proficiency to include critical interpretation, calibrated reliance on AI, explainability, professional skepticism, and ethical judgment. Particular attention is given to automation bias, accountability risks, and the organizational conditions that shape human–AI interaction. The chapter concludes that responsible AI-enabled financial decision-making depends not on algorithmic capability alone, but on the alignment of digital competence, professional judgment, and effective governance.</jats:p>

title: Agricultural Water Management for Rice Production: A Comprehensive Analysis
container-title: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF AGRICULTURE AND EARTH SCIENCE
c92167c10c493f951b9b5f61be37cf4bfb12167e.abstract:
<jats:p>The identified problem revolves around establishing the water requirements for rice seeding,
growth, and maturity in hot climatic conditions. This study reviews the net water requirement
for rice growth or production under various climatic conditions in the Cross River Basin. It
was observed that the water requirement from seeding to harvest varies from location to
location, maintaining a FAO range, as postulated by Brouwer et al., 1986, ultimately falling
between 450mm to 700mm for hot weather.The methodology used for investigating the Net
Irrigation Water Requirements for rice growth to maturity involves the application of
New_Clim Location and CropWater software. These tools were utilized to compute Reference
Evapotranspiration (ETo) and Crop Water Requirements (CWR) for the net irrigation water
requirements of rice, respectively. The data were obtained from meteorological stations within
the Cross River Basin. In rainfed conditions, no water stress is practically observed throughout
the entire crop cycle, affirming that no irrigation system is needed in such a specific climate.
This study uses data generated through New_LocClim as input into CropWat, which, among
other factors, determines the net water requirement for rice growth and production.
Consequently, the results obtained from the use of the CropWat model in determining rice
water requirements for Obudu, Nkari, Ikom, and Ijegu-Yala were 633.7 mm, 397.9 mm, 303.0
mm, and 548.4 mm, respectively. The water requirement of only two locations, Obudu and
Ijegu-Yala, fell within the FAO-suggested range of 450 mm to 700 mm (Brouwer et al., 1986)
for hot climates, while Nkari and Ikom LGAs did not comply with Brower et al., 1986
postulation due to their location in a relatively less hot climate.</jats:p>

title: Decentralized Finance and Digital Assets: A New Perspective on Financial Management and Risk
container-title: Lex localis - Journal of Local Self-Government
13b14090a5c64d7c3224b43ae85f72408e707dbf.abstract: <jats:p>Financial services are being transformed, how they are designed, accessed, and managed, by the rise of decentralized finance (DeFi) and digital assets. These innovations via blockchain networks, smart contracts, and tokenization offer alternatives to existing models for payments, lending, investment, and asset exchange. But the economic, institutional and operating risks of financial intermediation are not eroded when transactions are automated. In this conceptual study, the impact of DeFi and digital assets on financial management is explored, including capital allocation, treasury operations, risk management, and the governance of digital assets. It assesses what could be gained from this technology, alongside its potential technological vulnerabilities, market instability, regulatory uncertainty and inability to provide meaningful financial inclusion. An analysis approach is built to present a managerial perspective, which considers digital financial arrangements from an economic function, dependency and accountability standpoint. It points out that sustainable adoption requires coordination of technology with financial management, strong rights, organizational efficiency and appropriate governance. DeFi is therefore a reorganization of financial management and not the automatic replacement of existing financial institutions.</jats:p>

title: Blockchain Technology in Management: Opportunities, Risks and Governance Challenges
container-title: Lex localis - Journal of Local Self-Government
37cc95f3465e4e0fb32f40a5e9c5644d70c42fdc.abstract: <jats:p>The idea of using blockchain seems to be gaining support as a way to facilitate transactions between organizations which don't have a shared database or administration. The importance of its management, however, is subject to debate. This article provides a critical assessment of the opportunities, risks and governance issues of organizations taking up blockchain technology. Research is synthesized into a focused narrative organized by three themes—Organizational Value, Implementation Constraints and Institutional Governance Responsibilities—that are grounded in the foundational research, further developed by management and information-systems scholarship, and then extended by institutional guidance. Several potential benefits are suggested in the literature: record reconciliation, traceability of the supply chain, auditing and rule-based transaction processing. This is only achievable by partner willingness to share, the validity of the source information and the appropriateness of blockchain over traditional databases. Potential gains might be offset by technical risks, privacy issues, organizational challenges, and uncertainties regarding regulations. In arguing this, the article does not suggest that you can forgo identifiable decision responsibilities, human responsibility or good dispute resolution when you decentralize record validation. Strategic fit, network design, accountability, information stewardship and performance review are the elements of an integrated governance framework. The paper provides an action-oriented consideration of blockchain adoption, considering benefits not as inherent properties of blockchain but rather possibilities that are likely to occur when blockchain is adopted.</jats:p>

title: Assessing the Quality of AI Explanations of Atrial Fibrillation: Comparative Analysis of ChatGPT and Google Gemini
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
598e2fa6d5c1d1ee8bb1eebc101a66353744cb13.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Atrial fibrillation (AF) is one of the most common arrhythmias and is associated with multiple risk factors, including stroke and heart failure. Therefore, it is important that accurate and comprehensive educational resources on AF are available. Artificial intelligence (AI) platforms such as Google Gemini and ChatGPT are emerging tools for medical education. To our knowledge, this is the first study to assess the quality of these platforms for AF education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This pilot study aimed to (1) assess the quality of ChatGPT and Google Gemini explanations of AF and its treatment, (2) compare responses from both platforms, and (3) analyze differences in interpretation between cardiologists and nonmedical professionals.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The prompt “Explain atrial fibrillation and how to treat it to a patient” was entered into both ChatGPT and Google Gemini. The responses, along with a survey created in Google Forms, were sent out to potential participants between September and October 2024. The survey questions were derived from the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials and DISCERN criteria. Each survey question was multiple choice and rated on a 5-point Likert scale, where 1 indicated strong disagreement and 5 indicated strong agreement. Averages of each answer from the survey were calculated and compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The survey was completed by 28 participants, including cardiologists and cardiology fellows and 17 nonmedical professionals (college graduates not employed in the medical field). No significant overall quality differences were observed between ChatGPT and Google Gemini. When comparing participant groups, cardiologists rated AI-generated responses higher than nonmedical professionals for perceived bias (mean 3.82 vs mean 4.33; P=.04) and for explaining consequences of no treatment (mean 2.85 vs mean 1.86; P=.005). In contrast, nonmedical professionals rated structural and organizational features more favorably than cardiologists, including visual cues (mean 3.97 vs mean 2.48; P<.001), informative headers (mean 4.77 vs mean 3.95; P=.001), concise sections (mean 4.71 vs mean 4.29; P=.04), identifiable patient actions (mean 4.21 vs mean 3.19; P=.04), and references to additional resources (mean 2.65 vs mean 1.71; P=.006).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The comparable quality of ChatGPT and Google Gemini suggests that both are viable for AF education. Differences in ratings of organizational features versus perceptions of bias and consequences of no treatment highlight a disconnect between cardiologists and nonmedical professionals. To optimize clinical application, cardiologists should evaluate both comprehensiveness and clarity of AI-generated responses. This serves as a pilot study, and future research should focus on longitudinal studies of AI-generated responses and their effects on clinical outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Expectation-driven gain modulation of preparatory spatial attention
container-title: eLife
42e0bff514a13e990dde6d5376170bcb87804ae4.abstract: <jats:p>The visual system can flexibly adjust attentional deployment to match task demands, but whether observers can proactively modulate the spatial scope of attention based on expectations about upcoming search difficulty remains unclear. According to the zoom lens model, attention can narrow or broaden its spatial extent, with narrower focus enhancing processing efficiency, a mechanism that would benefit target discrimination in crowded displays. We tested whether observers adjust attentional scope when expecting sparse versus dense search arrays by combining spatial cueing with block-wise manipulations of display density expectations. Participants performed a visual search task in which endogenous cues predicted target location, while blocks predominantly contained either sparse (1 target, 3 distractors) or dense (1 target, 7 distractors) displays. We applied inverted encoding models to broadband EEG data to reconstruct spatial channel tuning functions, enabling precise characterization of both the locus and breadth of attentional deployment. Behaviorally, expecting difficult searches selectively improved accuracy at cued locations without costs elsewhere. Consistent with this selective benefit, neural measurements revealed that expectancy enhanced the amplitude of spatially selective responses at the attended location but did not alter tuning width. These findings demonstrate that expectations about search difficulty modulate attention through gain-based signal enhancement rather than adjustments to spatial scope, revealing that preparatory attentional control operates via amplitude modulation within a stable spatial focus. This mechanism complements reactive attentional adjustments and provides an efficient means for the visual system to optimize processing under predictable task demands.</jats:p>

title: Assessing the Effectiveness, Engagement, and Acceptability of a Smartwatch Healthy Lifestyle Intervention for Cognitive Enhancement in Healthy Adults: Mixed Methods Electroencephalography Protocol
container-title: JMIR Research Protocols
7e6b65fd0eceaed8ad891218da9c81d3f193d863.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Wearable technologies are rapidly transforming the health care landscape by enabling the tracking of real-time physiological and behavioral data used in healthy lifestyle interventions. Despite their widespread adoption in the consumer market, scientific validation of their impact on the brain remains limited, and factors influencing effects on cognition and adherence are not fully understood. This gap is critical, as consumers, health care providers, and researchers depend on these data to unlock the potential of wearables for cognitive support.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We aim to assess the effectiveness, engagement, and acceptability of a commercially available smartwatch healthy lifestyle intervention on cognitive enhancement in healthy adults, using a convergent parallel mixed methods design. We seek to provide a comprehensive, replicable methodological framework to evaluate wearable technology interventions targeting cognitive enhancement in healthy adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Healthy adults aged 18 to 40 years with a sedentary lifestyle (N=72) interested in participating in a healthy lifestyle intervention will be recruited in the Vancouver Metropolitan Area, BC, Canada. Participants will be randomly assigned into an intervention group using an Apple Watch or a control group following standard physical activity guidelines without an Apple Watch for a period of 4 weeks. Effectiveness will be evaluated through (1) cognitive function (primary outcome)—executive function, specifically inhibitory control, via electroencephalogram-based event-related potentials (N2/P3) during a go/no-go task; (2) resting-state brain activity via electroencephalogram spectral power; (3) behavioral performance (reaction time and accuracy); (4) perceived health (36-item Short Form Health Survey); and (5) qualitative analysis of factors affecting the intervention’s effectiveness. Engagement will be assessed through goal completion metrics and qualitative analysis of barriers, facilitators, and usage patterns. Acceptability will be assessed through System Usability Scale scores and qualitative analysis of factors affecting usability, satisfaction, and user preferences. This design integrates assessments before, during, and after intervention. Qualitative assessments will include weekly check-ins and semistructured interviews to obtain a comprehensive understanding of factors influencing the effectiveness, engagement, and acceptability of the intervention. Exploratory outcomes include descriptions of possible interactions between the 3 constructs and comparison of smartwatch-tracked vs self-reported goal completion.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study received funding from the AGE-WELL Network Centres of Excellence (April 2020-March 2023) and was approved by the Simon Fraser University Research Ethics Board. Enrollment for the study is ongoing. As of October 2026, data have been collected from 48 participants and are currently being processed and analyzed. The first results are expected to be published in 2027.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study outlines a foundational framework for evaluating the effectiveness, engagement, and acceptability of wearable health interventions targeting cognitive enhancement in healthy adults. Furthermore, our mixed methods approach with randomized controlled comparison is expected to inform the design and development of effective, engaging, and friendly wearable brain health technologies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Trading-Off Performance and Sustainability in Internet of Things: An Uncertainty-Aware Hierarchical Energy Management Approach
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
fd3d451e23529f6c37adeff5a792d90cc52faa50.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Internet of things (IoT) devices have been heralded as a key technology to enable several high-impact applications, such as healthcare, remote environmental monitoring, and digital agriculture. However, they suffer from energy sustainability challenges due to small form-factor and batteries. Recent research has proposed to integrate energy harvesting (EH) technologies into IoT devices. However, ambient sources are highly stochastic in nature, which introduces new challenges in IoT energy management (EM) since the decisions must account for the associated uncertainty. To this end, this article presents a multi-target conformal prediction algorithm to provide
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">provably correct uncertainty estimation</jats:italic>
                    of future energy prediction for multiple future time steps. Prediction of energy alone is not sufficient since we must use the predictions along with uncertainty estimates in an energy management algorithm to make energy consumption decisions. A common approach in IoT devices is to follow energy-neutral operation (ENO), whereby the energy consumed in a given period is equal to the harvested energy. However, this may lead to low performance in cases where the energy harvest is insufficient. To resolve this, we propose to design a suite of policies that can tradeoff performance and energy sustainability. Moreover, the proposed approach includes a charging management policy that aims to introduce additional energy into the system when the energy harvest is low to maintain system performance. Evaluations with two real-world datasets show that the proposed conformal prediction algorithm achieves the desired coverage level of 90% for all users. The energy management policies achieve performance that is within 10% of an optimal Oracle that has the knowledge of future energy harvest. Moreover, evaluation of the charging management policy shows that it provides additional energy only when EH values are low. Finally, measurements on an IoT device show that the proposed algorithms are light-weight and consume less than 10 mJ per decision.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p/>

title: Towards Realistic Project-Level Code Generation via Multi-Agent Collaboration and Semantic Architecture Modeling
container-title: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
2e98affb75fe6b1c9fa0a80bf39cb6bb48af6b14.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in automated code generation. In real-world software engineering, the growing demand for rapid iteration and continuous delivery underscores the importance of project-level code generation, where LLMs are expected to generate complete software projects directly from complex user requirements. This task, however, presents greater challenges due to larger input scales, multi-modal information, and the need for holistic architectural reasoning. Although existing studies have made initial explorations, they still face key limitations, including unrealistic datasets and unreliable evaluation metrics that fail to reflect real-world complexity, the semantic gap between human-written requirements and machine-interpretable structures, and difficulties in managing hierarchical dependencies and maintaining quality throughout the generation process. To address these limitations, we first introduce
                    <jats:sc>CodeProjectEval</jats:sc>
                    , a project-level code generation dataset built from 18 real-world repositories with 12.7 files and 2,388.6 lines of code per task on average, supplemented with documentation and executable test cases for automatic evaluation. We further propose
                    <jats:sc>ProjectGen</jats:sc>
                    , a multi-agent framework that decomposes projects into architecture design, skeleton generation, and code filling stages with iterative refinement and memory-based context management. Within this framework, we introduce the Semantic Software Architecture Tree, a structured and semantically rich representation that effectively bridges user requirements and source code implementation. Experiments show that
                    <jats:sc>ProjectGen</jats:sc>
                    achieves state-of-the-art performance, passing 52/124 test cases on the small-scale project-level code generation dataset DevBench, a 57% improvement over the baseline approaches, and 310 test cases on
                    <jats:sc>CodeProjectEval</jats:sc>
                    , representing an improvement of roughly tenfold compared to the baselines.
                  </jats:p>

title: Cancer therapy-induced intestinal injury: Mechanisms, clinical manifestations, and management strategies
container-title: World Journal of Gastroenterology
d1d689a4bbcfb3aeb71042a5a37c1821dbf157df.abstract: <jats:p>As cancer treatment advances in recent years, people with cancer are living longer, but the side effects of these treatments on normal tissues remain a major challenge, particularly the intestines. Intestinal injury induced by chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and surgical intervention represents an important factor that limits the effectiveness of cancer treatment. The common symptoms are diarrhea, abdominal pain and malabsorption, which can substantially impair the patients’ quality of life and may lead to severe complications. At present, the clinical strategies for the prevention and treatment of therapy-induced intestinal injury are still relatively scarce. In this minireview, we focus on the mechanisms underlying cancer therapy-induced intestinal injury, including oxidative stress, inflammation, apoptosis, and gut microbiota imbalance, and discuss targeted therapeutic strategies aimed at reducing morbidity, improving patient outcomes, and fostering a better quality of life.</jats:p>

title: Beautiful Particulars
c6fe3d0377956ff06d423eb5e3d727284e365eac.abstract:
<jats:p>A fresh and eye-opening new explanation of AI—and how its focus on specifics is changing our ideas about ourselves and our world.From a Harvard researcher, philosopher, entrepreneur, former comedy writer, and bestselling author.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Amid the clamor about AI, Beautiful Particulars poses a unique question: Not how does our use of AI change what we do, but how is the idea of AI already subtly yet fundamentally reshaping how we think about ourselves and our world?</jats:p>
                  <jats:p/>
                  <jats:p>In clear, engaging, and even humorous prose, David Weinberger offers a new perspective on how machine learning works and how it may already be changing our basic and deepest ideas. Through lively examples, he shows that AI’s success—with all its risks and dangers—is taking us past our millennia of reliance on laws and principles by revealing what morality, free will, creativity, causality knowledge, and even reality itself look like now that we’re able to let the particulars speak their tiny truths.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p/>
                  <jats:p>The author poses questions not usually asked: What does a coin look like to AI? When AI gives you evidence that the earth is round, why are its own reasons for saying that so different? Why does an AI image generator create a “selfie” of ancient Aztec warriors with broad smiles that it “believes” are historically unlikely? If AI becomes conscious but bodiless, could it still make good moral decisions? Why is the world so much better at being causal than AI could ever “understand”? How does AI show us that genuine creativity is not about a “spark” but about moments that feel right? And how can you take the temperature of a joke?</jats:p>
                  <jats:p/>
                  <jats:p>Beautiful Particulars offers a new—and hopeful—perspective on how machine learning works, and how that’s already changing how we understand what it means to be human in the age of AI.</jats:p>

title: Optimal Capital and Asset Structure under Compositional Constraints: A Dual-Outcome Modeling Approach Linking Financial Ratios to Profitability and Cash Conversion Efficiency
container-title: Global Journal of Management and Business Research
1464691b024e5cb1d1d5fd5389ffcacd470d1491.abstract:
<jats:p>This paper develops an integrated econometric and optimization framework to examine how capital structure and asset composition jointly influence firm performance through both profitability and liquidity dimensions. Unlike traditional compositional approaches, the model allows financial structure variables to vary independently without summation constraints, enabling more flexible and realistic estimation.
Using a system of three profitability equations (ROA, ROE, ROI) and a liquidity equation based on the Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC), the study identifies structural trade-offs between performance dimensions. Empirical results reveal that receivables and inventory significantly enhance profitability but simultaneously deteriorate liquidity efficiency by extending the cash conversion cycle. Conversely, short-term liabilities reduce liquidity pressure by financing working capital externally.
A multi-objective optimization function is constructed to jointly maximize profitability and minimize liquidity inefficiency. The results identify an optimal financial structure corridor characterized by moderate leverage, balanced working capital components, and controlled liquidity exposure.
The findings contribute to financial management literature by introducing a dual-outcome modeling approach combined with non-compositional structural analysis and multi-objective optimization.</jats:p>

title: Financial Performance Metrics and Basic Earnings per Share: A Panel Data Analysis of Japanese Automobile Companies
container-title: Global Journal of Management and Business Research
0d151ba72a54b2888c443c2cf6a6ff6100473935.abstract:
<jats:p>Over the past decade, the importance of financial performance evaluation has grown substantially amid intensifying competition in global markets. Among the key indicators of corporate performance, Basic Earnings per Share (EPS) remains one of the most significant measures of shareholder profitability. EPS indicates the amount of net income attributable to each outstanding common share and serves as a fundamental benchmark of financial stability, operational efficiency, and investment attractiveness.
Financial ratios such as Gross Margin, Pre-tax Profit Margin, Return on Assets (ROA), and Long-term Debt to Capital Ratio are widely used to assess a company’s financial condition and investment potential. These indicators capture essential aspects of profitability, efficiency, and capital structure, and may also function as determinants of shareholder returns reflected through EPS. Understanding the extent to which these financial metrics influence EPS is crucial for both theoretical development and practical financial decision-making.
The Japanese automotive industry, known for its advanced technological capabilities, strong export orientation, and highly competitive global position, offers a particularly relevant context for such analysis. Nevertheless, financial performance volatility within the sector may significantly affect shareholder returns. Identifying the most influential financial drivers of Basic EPS is therefore of considerable importance.
This study aims to evaluate the impact of selected financial ratios on Basic EPS, determine the strength and direction of their relationships, and analyze their contribution to shareholder profitability in Japanese automotive companies. The research contributes by proposing a structured analytical framework for examining the linkage between financial indicators and Basic EPS, providing valuable insights for investors, financial analysts, and corporate managers.</jats:p>

title: AI-Generated Exposure Hierarchies for Body Dysmorphic Disorder: Proof-of-Concept Study
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
475970c23de59b336f5f102fda0e80aa46b47e4e.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is a chronic, impairing condition for which cognitive behavioral therapy, including exposure and response prevention (ERP), is the first-line treatment, but few clinicians are trained in BDD-specific ERP. Constructing personalized exposure hierarchies is time-intensive and requires clinical expertise, particularly for patients with absent insight who may hold appearance beliefs with delusional conviction. Generative AI (GenAI)–powered chatbots, such as ChatGPT, have shown utility for clinical content, but their capacity to produce safe, appropriate ERP hierarchies for BDD has not been examined.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study evaluated the feasibility of using ChatGPT (GPT-5) to generate ERP hierarchies for BDD, assessed the influence of clinical and demographic characteristics on output quality, benchmarked AI-generated hierarchies against those created by doctoral-level BDD specialists, and tested whether blinded experts could distinguish AI-generated from expert-generated hierarchies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GPT-5 generated 10-item graded exposure hierarchies for 72 simulated vignettes that varied by body area, insight level (good, limited, or absent), symptom specificity, age, and gender. Expert clinicians independently generated hierarchies for a subset of 18 vignettes. Two researchers rated all GPT-5 hierarchies for task completion and information integration. Three BDD expert clinicians, blinded to the hierarchy source (expert vs GPT-5), rated all 90 hierarchies for relevance, specificity, variability, safety, and overall quality. After unblinding, raters attempted to identify the AI-generated hierarchy in the 18 matched pairs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      GPT-5 generated complete hierarchies for 69 of 72 (95.8%) vignettes. Blinded experts rated GPT-5 hierarchies highly across all dimensions (mean scores ranging from 4.39, SD 0.26 to 4.90, SD 0.16 out of 5), with no significant differences from expert-generated hierarchies except for variability, where experts scored modestly higher (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.02;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.24). After unblinding, raters correctly identified AI-generated hierarchies only 31.5% (17/54) of the time, significantly below chance (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.009); this below-chance result was mostly due to one rater, and no rater performed above chance. Insight level was the most consistent predictor of quality: absent-insight hierarchies received significantly lower safety (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.73) and overall quality ratings (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.01;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.43). This pattern was not unique to GPT-5; safety ratings for expert-generated hierarchies also declined significantly by insight level (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03). Miscalibration of exposure difficulty, particularly for low- and absent-insight cases, was the most common rater concern (30/43, 69.8% comments), disproportionately directed at GPT-5 hierarchies.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GPT-5 generated ERP hierarchies for BDD that blinded experts rated as comparable to clinician-created hierarchies and could not reliably distinguish them from clinician-created hierarchies. However, hierarchies for patients with absent insight received lower safety and quality ratings from both AI and expert sources, and qualitative comments suggested AI-generated hierarchies were less well calibrated to delusional-level presentations. GenAI thus shows promise as a clinician-facing aid for ERP hierarchy generation, but these findings underscore the need for clinician oversight, especially for patients with delusional conviction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Leveraging Electronic Patient-Reported Symptoms to Optimize Family Caregivers’ Symptom Support for Patients With Cancer: Qualitative Formative Evaluation of the FamilyAWARE Intervention Concept
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
77a46eb0bb30e09a8143711ec91383c2587a92c6.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Each year, family caregivers help the 2 million patients newly diagnosed with cancer manage their symptoms; however, few interventions have been developed and proven efficacious to enhance their symptom-support role. The recent expansion of electronic patient-reported outcomes (ePROs), including remote symptom monitoring, presents an opportunity to explore novel approaches to supporting caregiver symptom management by leveraging patient ePRO data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The objective of this study was to elicit feedback on a theory-based intervention concept, called FamilyAWARE, consisting of one-on-one coaching on providing effective symptom support to patients and access to a web-based dashboard reporting summaries of their care recipient’s most recent ePRO symptom reports and tailored recommendations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This was a qualitative formative evaluation study (National Institutes of Health stage IA) where family caregivers (n=20), patients with stage I to IV cancer (n=20), and oncology clinicians (n=25) were recruited from a comprehensive cancer center in the US South and participated in semistructured, one-on-one interviews (January 2025-July 2025). Participants were shown an outline of the FamilyAWARE intervention concept and asked open-ended questions about the proposed content, format, and delivery of the intervention. Professionally transcribed interviews were analyzed using a thematic analysis approach.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Analysis yielded 4 primary themes. The first theme was first impressions and relevance. Participants’ initial impressions of FamilyAWARE were generally positive, with caregivers viewing it as highly relevant and potentially beneficial. Patients and clinicians expressed more cautious optimism, shaped by considerations of relevance and minimizing burden. The second theme was key factors for acceptability and engagement. Caregivers showed strong interest in the intervention’s potential to increase confidence in symptom support; however, engagement was seen as contingent on the perceived value, minimal burden, and flexible delivery of the intervention, particularly given time and technology constraints. The third theme was coaching content and delivery. The proposed format was widely viewed as feasible. Participants emphasized content that helps caregivers balance supporting patients with promoting patient independence while also guiding them in deciding when to seek additional help and providing proactive symptom management strategies. Opinions on delivery by phone, in person, or videoconference varied. The fourth theme was dashboard design and information access. Participants emphasized the importance of a simple, mobile-friendly dashboard designed for low digital literacy, with plain language and visual cues. Caregiver access to patient symptom data was broadly supported if patient permission was obtained.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings highlight strong interest and insights into designing a caregiver-focused intervention that integrates one-on-one coaching with ePRO patient symptom reports and tailored recommendations. Participant insights from this study will directly inform refinement of the intervention’s content, format, and delivery, with the goal of advancing it to pilot testing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial Registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>N/A</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Recurrence and mortality after non-operative management of acute gallstone disease: nationwide registry study
container-title: BJS Open
e0ea5e140719c734b5a926befb66c61ca606eaf3.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Non-operative management of gallstone complications (acute cholecystitis, cholangitis, and biliary pancreatitis) carries a significant risk of recurrence. Nevertheless, definitive surgery is often deferred in co-morbid patients due to their perceived short life expectancy. This study assessed the prevalence of non-operative management, and its associated mortality and recurrence risk, accounting for the competing risk of death due to other causes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A nationwide cohort of patients admitted with gallstone complications and treated with non-operative management between 2006 and 2019 was identified in the Swedish National Patient Register. Competing risk and Cox proportional hazards models were used to evaluate recurrence and mortality risks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Overall, 82 101 patients were included (median age 68 years, 48% female), of whom 41 283 (50.3%) experienced cholecystitis, 10 272 (12.5%) experienced cholangitis, and 30 546 (37.2%) experienced pancreatitis. Patients with cholangitis were older and had more co-morbidities than those with cholecystitis or pancreatitis. The cumulative recurrence risk at 1 year was 16.0% for cholecystitis, cholangitis, and pancreatitis. At 3 years, the risk was 19.8% for cholecystitis and 23.0% for cholangitis and 22.5% for pancreatitis. In patients aged ≥ 80 years, 3-year mortality was 41.2%, and 17.0% of deaths were gallstone related. In competing risk analyses, cholangitis and pancreatitis were associated with a higher recurrence risk than cholecystitis in alive patients, with hazard ratio (HRs) of 1.22 (95% confidence interval (c.i.) 1.16 to 1.28) and 1.28 (95% c.i. 1.24 to 1.32), respectively, whereas female sex was associated with a lower recurrence risk (HR 0.92; 95% c.i. 0.89 to 0.94). Increasing age (HR 1.08; 95% c.i. 1.08 to 1.09), co-morbidities (HR 1.17; 95% c.i. 1.16 to 1.17), and cholangitis (HR 1.31; 95% c.i. 1.26 to 1.36) were associated with an increased risk of mortality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The risk of recurrent gallstone complications remains clinically important, even among older and co-morbid patients, despite their higher competing risk of death. These findings support consideration of early cholecystectomy in patients with an acceptable operative risk, with the aim of reducing subsequent morbidity and recurrence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Perioperative pulmonary embolus: diagnosis, classification and management
container-title: Advances in Perioperative Care
c89b4dc5c1827287a31c7565d6c6621b70bf59d8.abstract: <jats:p>Post-surgical patients are vulnerable to the development of pulmonary emboli, a condition associated with significant mortality and morbidity. This review discusses the diagnosis, classification and treatment modalities available for pulmonary emboli. A pulmonary embolus is diagnosed by amalgamating clinical symptoms, signs, blood tests and imaging results. The European Society of Cardiology schema is commonly used to risk stratify patients with a pulmonary embolus. The treatments available are medical (oral anticoagulation and systemic thrombolysis), interventional (catheter-directed treatments) and surgical (embolectomy). This review aims to discuss these domains with a perioperative focus, acknowledging the uncertainty associated with decision-making surrounding bleeding risk with perioperative anticoagulation.</jats:p>

title: Transformation of Human Resource Management in Islamic Education: Problems, Global Challenges, and Future Prospects
container-title: AL GHAZALI: Jurnal Pendidikan dan Pemikiran Islam
d8f6091cae373aac54479dbe68a21392e1fc2bfe.abstract: <jats:p>Human resource management in Islamic education has become a strategic issue in improving the quality, competitiveness, and sustainability of educational institutions in the modern era. This article aims to analyze the transformation of human resource management in Islamic education by focusing on major problems, global challenges, and future development prospects. This study employs a qualitative approach using library research methods through the collection of books, scientific journals, academic articles, and relevant documents related to Islamic educational management and human resource development. Data were analyzed using content analysis techniques to identify important themes and concepts associated with the transformation of human resource management in Islamic education. The findings indicate that Islamic educational institutions continue to face several major problems, including limited teacher professionalism, inadequate digital competence, weak organizational leadership, and insufficient welfare systems for educators. Global challenges such as digital transformation, educational competition, technological disruption, and changing student characteristics have intensified the need for strategic reform in educational management. However, Islamic education also possesses strong future prospects through the integration of Islamic values, digital innovation, continuous professional development, and transformational leadership models. The novelty of this study lies in its integrative analysis that combines the dimensions of organizational transformation, global educational challenges, and value-based human resource development within the context of twenty-first-century Islamic education</jats:p>

title: SAI: Virtualizing Shared Memory of GPU for AI workload acceleration
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
c8fa29b0323351e1659db262fc936958ed20d580.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    AI workloads increasingly demand high parallelism and efficient on-chip memory utilization on modern GPUs. However, the limited capacity of shared memory often constrains thread-level parallelism, while portions of the L2 cache remain underutilized. In this work, we propose
                    <jats:bold>SAI</jats:bold>
                    , a mechanism that virtualizes shared memory into the L2 cache to improve GPU performance for AI applications. SAI dynamically activates virtualization based on runtime resource usage, enabling additional CTAs with minimal architectural modifications. We further introduce an L2 cache management strategy that integrates associativity-based virtual page allocation and a replacement information table, reducing page-swapping overhead while preserving L2 cache performance. Experimental results demonstrate that SAI achieves an 18.6% performance improvement over the baseline design and outperforms SMILE-opt, our reproduced state-of-the-art baseline, by 8.8%. Moreover, SAI captures 60.2% of the performance gain delivered by the idealized Double SMEM design while reducing energy consumption to 87.7% of the baseline. These results highlight the effectiveness of SAI in enhancing thread-level parallelism and optimizing on-chip memory for AI workloads.
                  </jats:p>

title: Graphene/SiC nanowire heterointerfaces in wood-derived carbon scaffolds for integrated electromagnetic attenuation and phase-change thermal management
container-title: Nano Research
329b646dd266bdebd3d47ffdb69358b81386426b.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The progressive miniaturization and high power density of modern electronic devices have created an urgent demand for multifunctional materials that can simultaneously address electromagnetic interference (EMI) and thermal dissipation challenges. Herein, a wood-derived carbon (WDC) scaffold was sequentially modified with SiC nanowires (SiCnws) and graphene (GE) nanosheets via sol–gel/carbothermal reduction and chemical vapor deposition, followed by paraffin wax (PW) infiltration, to fabricate a multifunctional WDC-SiCnws-GE-PW phase change composite. The synergistic incorporation of SiCnws and GE constructed abundant heterointerfaces and a continuous conductive network within the hierarchically porous WDC skeleton. The WDC-SiCnws-GE absorber delivered a minimum reflection loss of −54 dB and an effective absorption bandwidth of 3.1 GHz at an ultrathin thickness of 2.1 mm. Cole–Cole analysis, together with microstructural and compositional evidence, suggested that the enhanced absorption performance is associated with a synergistic dielectric loss mechanism involving interfacial polarization at multiple heterointerfaces such as SiCnws-GE, WDC-GE, and WDC-SiCnws, dipole polarization from SiCnws stacking faults and GE edge functional groups, and conduction loss from the interconnected GE network. After PW infiltration, the resulting WDC-SiCnws-GE-PW composite exhibited outstanding thermal management performance, including a high axial thermal conductivity of 1.35 W/(m·K) (419% enhancement over WDC-PW), high melting and crystallization enthalpies (149.53 and 138.50 J/g), an energy storage efficiency of 99.35%, and rapid thermal response. This work provides a promising strategy for constructing lightweight, high-performance, multifunctional biomass-derived carbon-based composites for integrated EMW absorption and thermal management applications.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Co-Designed Text Messaging Intervention for Parents of Children With Early Childhood Caries: Randomized Controlled Trial
container-title: JMIR mHealth and uHealth
a6850389fd0c78a00994c29313541824776e2e31.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Early childhood caries (ECC) is a prevalent yet preventable disease that significantly impacts young children’s health and quality of life. The World Health Organization’s
                      <jats:italic>Global Strategy and Action Plan on Oral Health 2023–2030</jats:italic>
                      highlights the potential of mobile health programs to enhance engagement and support sustained oral health behavior change.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The aim of this study was to assess the effectiveness of the SmilesUp 12-week SMS text messaging–based education and support program to improve parents’ management of their children’s oral health behaviors compared to standard clinical care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a multisite, assessor-blinded, parallel-design randomized controlled trial among parents of children aged 0 to 6 years who had an ECC diagnosis and attended 1 of 6 public dental clinics in metropolitan, regional, and rural New South Wales, Australia. Participants were randomly assigned to either an intervention group receiving the fully automated 12-week SmilesUp program (3 SMS text messages weekly) or a control group. Both groups continued to receive usual standard dental clinical treatment. The primary behavioral outcome was parent-reported twice-daily toothbrushing with fluoride toothpaste. Secondary outcomes included adherence to oral health–promoting bedtime routines and child consumption of sugar-sweetened foods and beverages. Oral health self-efficacy was measured using 6 behavioral theory–mapped items across oral hygiene, diet, and bedtime routines.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A total of 154 participants were enrolled and randomized (n=78, 50.6% in the control group; n=76, 49.4% in the intervention group) across 6 sites, with 80.5% (124/154) completing the follow-up assessment. High program adherence was observed, with 96.1% (73/76) of intervention participants completing the program. At 12 weeks, a greater proportion of SmilesUp participants reported brushing their children’s teeth twice daily (45/61, 73.8% vs 42/63, 66.7%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.45, 95% CI 0.95-6.74;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.07), though this difference was not statistically significant. Significant improvements were observed in adherence to bedtime routines (54/61, 88.5% vs 45/63, 71.4%; aOR 3.25, 95% CI 1.15-10.18;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03) as well as oral health knowledge on toothbrushing (46/50, 92.0% vs 41/52, 78.8%; aOR 5.47, 95% CI 1.48-25.19;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.02). No statistically significant differences were found in sugar-sweetened food (10/61, 16.4% vs 4/63, 6.3%; aOR 3.72, 95% CI 1.02-17.14;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.06) or beverage (25/61, 41.0% vs. 27/63, 42.9%; aOR 1.08, 95% CI 0.49-2.30;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.85) consumption.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that co-designed SMS text messaging–based programs show promise and may represent a feasible strategy for oral health behavior change. However, larger-scale and longer-term studies are needed to confirm sustained effectiveness using clinical outcomes. Future research should also explore ways mobile health can be scaled and cost-effectively embedded into comprehensive, interdisciplinary primary models of care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: AI-Enabled Early Detection of Epidemic Threats in a Resource-Constrained Health System: Implementation Research from Lebanon
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
94bf395e649f9c13344c021277ab854ad6c98be5.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Global South countries face heightened infectious disease risks compounded by fragmented surveillance systems and resource constraints. Lebanon’s health system crisis and recurrent outbreaks highlight the urgent need for new approaches to epidemic and pandemic preparedness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To describe the design, implementation process, and early implementation findings of an artificial intelligence (AI)–enabled early warning system (AI-EWS) that automates detection of epidemiologically relevant events using laboratory data in Lebanon, with emphasis on feasibility, workflow integration, stakeholder engagement, and implementation learnings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We applied an implementation research approach to co-design and validate an AI-EWS prototype integrated within a university hospital laboratory. The system incorporates a hybrid statistical and machine learning analytic pipeline and a real-time dashboard for detecting epidemic events across multiple pathogens using routine laboratory information systems (LIS) data. The system was developed in collaboration with the Ministry of Public Health (MoPH) to support future national adoption.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The project produced a structured framework for pathogen selection, rule development, dataset creation, and platform co-design with clinical and epidemiological experts, medical informatics professionals, MoPH experts, and technical specialists. Early implementation observations indicate operational feasibility within existing infrastructure, strong stakeholder engagement, and trust-building around AI-enabled surveillance through participatory design and responsible-AI governance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI-enabled laboratory surveillance is a viable and scalable approach to strengthening epidemic preparedness in low-resource health systems when grounded in implementation science and responsible AI, and when explicitly aligned with local workflows and national policy priorities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Bayesian Forecasting as the Analytical Core of an AI-Assisted Early Warning System for Dengue Outbreaks during the 2023 Epidemic: Implementation and Emergency Management in a Dominican Pediatric Hospital
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
056417fa3dbad64347775b6e5020ffb82cf01df1.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Dengue remains a major cause of pediatric morbidity in the Dominican Republic, with increasingly intense epidemic cycles. Advances in statistical modeling, probabilistic forecasting, and AI-assisted digital health systems offer new opportunities to enhance early warning capabilities and strengthen hospital preparedness. This study evaluated a Bayesian negative binomial regression forecasting model as the analytical core of an AI-assisted early warning system (EWS) for predicting weekly dengue cases nationwide, using strict out-of-sample validation during the 2023 epidemic and applying its outputs operationally in a high-demand pediatric hospital. National surveillance data (PLISA/PAHO), hospital records from the Dr. Hugo Mendoza Pediatric Hospital (HPHM), and climatic and satellite indicators (NOAA, MODIS) for 2014–2024 were integrated. The model incorporated climatically plausible lags, harmonic seasonality, two vegetation indices (NDVI_lag4 and EVI_lag4), a long-term spline trend, and weakly informative priors, achieving excellent convergence (Rhat = 1.00). Climatic and environmental predictors exhibited small and uncertain effects, whereas the temporal spline accounted for most long-term epidemic variability. In the 2023 national validation, the model captured the broad epidemic trajectory and improved RMSE and MAE compared with the historical seasonal baseline (RMSE = 783.3; MAE = 423.4; MAPE = 80.2%), although proportional accuracy remained limited during abrupt epidemic acceleration. The national model also captured ascending-phase signals that were temporally aligned with the HPHM hospital outbreak, including its sharp rise during epidemiological weeks 36–40. These outputs were used alongside routine surveillance and hospital indicators to support operational situational awareness, capacity planning, patient-flow reorganization, strengthened triage, and emergency preparedness during the epidemic. The model demonstrated temporal signal detection and operational relevance, positioning Bayesian probabilistic forecasting, embedded within an AI-assisted digital health workflow, as a useful analytical component for epidemic monitoring and hospital preparedness, subject to limitations in peak magnitude calibration and proportional accuracy.</jats:p>

title: Toward Human-Centered Pedagogy in the Age of Generative AI Among Higher Education Educators: Qualitative Phenomenological Study
container-title: JMIR Medical Education
46248c918f688c3c5f2cc8bb261f150c45f4e9cf.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Generative AI (GenAI) expands possibilities for content generation, feedback, personalization, and instructional support in higher education. Its growing use also challenges established assumptions about teaching, assessment, professional expertise, academic integrity, and educational responsibility. Although research has examined technology adoption and AI competencies, less is known about how educators experience and interpret the pedagogical transformation associated with GenAI in everyday teaching.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study explored how higher education educators experience GenAI-mediated pedagogical transformation, focusing on pedagogical practices, professional roles and expertise, educator agency, human-AI relationships, and associated opportunities and tensions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A qualitative phenomenological inquiry involved 23 educators from 3 Palestinian universities. Purposive maximum-variation sampling sought variation in academic rank, discipline, teaching experience, and experience with AI tools. Individual semistructured, in-depth interviews were conducted from March to April 2026, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and returned to participants for review. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis informed by phenomenology. Initial coding was inductive and grounded in participants’ accounts; human-centered AI and sociomateriality subsequently informed interpretation as sensitizing concepts. Themes were developed through iterative comparison of transcripts, analytic memos, and alternative interpretations. Informational sufficiency was observed after approximately 20 interviews, with 3 additional interviews used to examine the developing thematic structure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis generated 8 interconnected themes. Educators described a shift from content transmission toward mediation, inquiry, reflective learning, creative exploration, and process-oriented assessment. Professional expertise increasingly centered on facilitation, pedagogical design, contextual interpretation, ethical guidance, and evaluation of AI-generated content. Human-AI collaboration involved bounded and integrated configurations, with humans retaining responsibility for judgment and educational consequences. Educator agency appeared through decisions about AI participation, independent student reasoning, and the boundaries of human expertise. Credibility, bias, authorship, authenticity, and academic integrity became embedded as pedagogical concerns. Participants valued opportunities for creativity, personalization, flexibility, and instructional support while expressing concerns about dependence, reduced intellectual effort, and weakened human connection.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GenAI-mediated pedagogical transformation depends on educators’ alignment of AI use with learning purposes, the allocation of responsibilities, and the preservation of ethical accountability and meaningful relationships. The resulting human-centered pedagogy framework positions pedagogical intentionality, contextual judgment, negotiated agency, and relational presence as central to responsible integration. Universities should complement technical training and institutional policies with support for pedagogical design, critical evaluation, process-oriented assessment, and ethical reasoning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Digital Augmentation of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 for Obesity Management: Retrospective Study
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
0c23ca513d5b5a47aa7bd9ddcc81c35d4082df21.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), including semaglutide and tirzepatide, are highly effective for weight management; however, long-term outcomes depend on sustained behavioral engagement. Digital health tools may enhance these behavioral components, but evidence regarding their real-world benefit alongside pharmacotherapy remains limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to evaluate whether augmenting a direct-to-consumer GLP-1 RA program with a behavioral support smartphone app improves weight-loss outcomes compared with medication alone, and to identify which app features are associated with weight loss over time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A retrospective observational cohort study was conducted using data from 6113 adults (older than 18 years) in Australia who self-enrolled into the Mosh direct-to-consumer weight-loss program between July 1, 2024, and August 13, 2025, with their weight data recorded at baseline and at least 1 other timepoint. Participants received semaglutide or tirzepatide, with optional access to a smartphone app and clinician support. Logistic regression models examined achievement of ≥5%, ≥10%, and ≥15% weight-loss thresholds at 60, 120, and 180 days. Linear mixed-effects models interacting with app feature use, with linear and quadratic time terms, assessed the association of different features with percentage weight loss trajectories over time. Both models adjusted for medication type, gender, ethnicity, age, and baseline BMI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Participants using the program plus medication had higher odds of achieving clinically significant weight loss than those using medication only. Adjusted odds ratio point estimates for day 60, 120, and 180 (±10) days indicated they were 1.38 (95% CI 1.09-1.75) times to 2.22 (95% CI 1.40-3.45) times more likely to achieve ≥5% weight loss across timepoints, 1.67 (95% CI 1.33-2.10) times to 1.97 (95% CI 1.35-2.90) times more likely to achieve ≥10% weight loss by day 120 and 180, and 1.99 (95% CI 1.26-3.29) times more likely to achieve ≥15% weight loss by 180 days. Mixed-effects modeling demonstrated that progress logging was associated with more rapid weight loss over time (β=.26 percentage-point additional weight lost per 30 days, SE 0.06;
                      <jats:italic>t</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>4336</jats:sub>
                      =4.46; 95% CI 0.14-0.38;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001). No other app features were consistently associated with changes in weight-loss trajectories.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Augmenting GLP-1 RA treatment with a behavioral smartphone app was associated with a higher likelihood of achieving clinically significant weight loss, although differences in overall weight-loss trajectories were modest. Progress logging emerged as the primary behavioral predictor of improved outcomes. While not causal effects, these findings are consistent with the positive value of integrating digital tools with pharmacotherapy for weight loss.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Bridging the Gap: Student Perceptions of Instructor Engagement in Pandemic-Era Online Learning
container-title: The Journal  of Technology, Management, and Applied Engineering
452b4dd3c76ef236fdfaa05cc15c934e6b286cde.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines student perceptions of instructor engagement in online learning environments during the initial onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, with particular attention to differences between students with prior online learning experience and those transitioning from traditional face-to-face instruction. Grounded in Moore’s transactional distance theory, the research explores how sudden shifts in instructional modality influenced students’ perceptions of instructor engagement and identifies strategies that may reduce perceived distance in online learning contexts. Survey data were collected during the summer of 2020 from students enrolled at a regional comprehensive university in the mid-South following the emergency transition to remote instruction. A comparative analysis was conducted across course modalities, focusing on seven survey items related to academic engagement, changes in instructor interaction, and student preferences for engagement. Findings indicate that students with prior experience in online courses perceived less disruption in instructor engagement following the transition, while students who had been enrolled primarily in face-to-face courses reported more noticeable declines. These differences suggest that familiarity with online learning environments may buffer students against perceived losses in engagement during periods of instructional disruption. Overall, this study contributes to the growing body of research on online learning during the COVID-19 pandemic by emphasizing how instructional practices and student experience intersect to influence motivation, engagement, and perceived learning success in online environments.</jats:p>
