title: Toward Human-Centered Pedagogy in the Age of Generative AI Among Higher Education Educators: Qualitative Phenomenological Study
container-title: JMIR Medical Education
46248c918f688c3c5f2cc8bb261f150c45f4e9cf.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Generative AI (GenAI) expands possibilities for content generation, feedback, personalization, and instructional support in higher education. Its growing use also challenges established assumptions about teaching, assessment, professional expertise, academic integrity, and educational responsibility. Although research has examined technology adoption and AI competencies, less is known about how educators experience and interpret the pedagogical transformation associated with GenAI in everyday teaching.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study explored how higher education educators experience GenAI-mediated pedagogical transformation, focusing on pedagogical practices, professional roles and expertise, educator agency, human-AI relationships, and associated opportunities and tensions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A qualitative phenomenological inquiry involved 23 educators from 3 Palestinian universities. Purposive maximum-variation sampling sought variation in academic rank, discipline, teaching experience, and experience with AI tools. Individual semistructured, in-depth interviews were conducted from March to April 2026, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and returned to participants for review. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis informed by phenomenology. Initial coding was inductive and grounded in participants’ accounts; human-centered AI and sociomateriality subsequently informed interpretation as sensitizing concepts. Themes were developed through iterative comparison of transcripts, analytic memos, and alternative interpretations. Informational sufficiency was observed after approximately 20 interviews, with 3 additional interviews used to examine the developing thematic structure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis generated 8 interconnected themes. Educators described a shift from content transmission toward mediation, inquiry, reflective learning, creative exploration, and process-oriented assessment. Professional expertise increasingly centered on facilitation, pedagogical design, contextual interpretation, ethical guidance, and evaluation of AI-generated content. Human-AI collaboration involved bounded and integrated configurations, with humans retaining responsibility for judgment and educational consequences. Educator agency appeared through decisions about AI participation, independent student reasoning, and the boundaries of human expertise. Credibility, bias, authorship, authenticity, and academic integrity became embedded as pedagogical concerns. Participants valued opportunities for creativity, personalization, flexibility, and instructional support while expressing concerns about dependence, reduced intellectual effort, and weakened human connection.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GenAI-mediated pedagogical transformation depends on educators’ alignment of AI use with learning purposes, the allocation of responsibilities, and the preservation of ethical accountability and meaningful relationships. The resulting human-centered pedagogy framework positions pedagogical intentionality, contextual judgment, negotiated agency, and relational presence as central to responsible integration. Universities should complement technical training and institutional policies with support for pedagogical design, critical evaluation, process-oriented assessment, and ethical reasoning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: AI-Enabled Quality Assurance in Higher Education
container-title: Harnessing Digital Platforms for Quality Assurance and Monitoring in Higher Education
fb5843c135ec13caf51a5f619643fd47db8d0fec.abstract: <jats:p>In today's dynamic landscape of higher education, institutions must prove to society the societal benefits of their teaching, learning, and research. Many organizations are embracing AI-enabled quality assurance (QA) to foster a mindset of constant growth and outstanding performance inside their institutions. This approach aims to enhance education, cater to the requirements of students and communities, and ultimately help them stay competitive. The complex quality assurance system is open to multiple interpretations and potential improvements due to the interconnected nature of technology in higher education. Excellence requires continuous institutional growth. It is common for stakeholders to see quality assurance as too bureaucratic. To prioritize institutional change and ongoing improvement, modern QA frameworks should use organic and dynamic operating methods.</jats:p>

title: AI-Enabled Digital Platforms for Learning-Centred Quality Assurance in Higher Education
container-title: Harnessing Digital Platforms for Quality Assurance and Monitoring in Higher Education
2e6b9dfed2d61a7b891e8850e05ec19839ab8002.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter theorises AI-enabled digital platforms as socio-technical quality infrastructures that orchestrate learning, accountability, and equity in higher education. It fuses constructs from quality theory, learning sciences, organisational studies, and critical datafication to recast quality as holistic capability formation rather than performance compliance. The chapter outlines competing quality lenses, sketches platform typologies and algorithmic logics, and shows how governance architectures and stakeholder attitudes co-produce datafied regimes of merit and risk. It then advances design principles for learning-centred, justice-responsive AI ecosystems that foreground equity-sensitive analytics, participatory governance, and reflexive professional judgment. The chapter contends that AI must be treated as pedagogical and civic infrastructure, with human actors retaining epistemic primacy in steering quality work toward rigorous, inclusive higher education.</jats:p>

title: Next-Generation AI Architectures for ECG Arrhythmia Detection
container-title: Harnessing Digital Platforms for Quality Assurance and Monitoring in Higher Education
c06f20ff59b2a1a32fbb1574e77b84f20954089e.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) has revolutionized cardiac healthcare by enabling rapid, accurate, and automated arrhythmia detection using electrocardiogram (ECG) signals. This chapter explores advanced AI-driven arrhythmia classification techniques that integrate deep learning (DL), preprocessing, and explainable model interpretation. Emphasis is placed on convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent networks, and hybrid architectures capable of learning morphological and temporal ECG features. The proposed framework covers data acquisition, filtering, segmentation, feature extraction, model training, and validation. Ethical challenges, interpretability, and clinical deployment frameworks are discussed. By bridging computational intelligence with clinical expertise, AI systems have demonstrated near-cardiologist-level diagnostic accuracy, making them vital in next-generation cardiac care.</jats:p>

title: Governing AI-Driven Universities in Cambodia
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Responsible AI Governance in Higher Education Management for Creative Public Sector Innovation
1c876c30e971c0906955347a760678450910f5f3.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter focuses on Cambodian higher education institutions to explain the pillars of Trust-Centred AI Governance for responsible AI and how AI can support services and functions currently burdened by demand and under-resourced in the Cambodian higher education sector, which is rapidly growing and flexible in enrollment. Without governance, the Threats to Educational Equity caused by algorithmic bias, Data Breaches, Digital Exclusion, and Breaches of Trust will dangerously flourish. This chapter presents a Trust-Centred AI Governance Framework built around seven principles: ethical leadership, transparency, and data privacy. It is supported by core ideas such as algorithmic accountability, inclusive access, human oversight, and public-sector innovation, and guides partner institutions on fostering ethical innovation ecosystems. It presents, through analyses and the implementation of proposed strategies, case studies, and policy frameworks, a model that balances technological efficiency with human-centred principles, empowering global competence and leadership in the south.</jats:p>

title: Responsible AI Governance Frameworks for Intelligent Higher Education Management and Creative Public Sector Innovation
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Responsible AI Governance in Higher Education Management for Creative Public Sector Innovation
99d99fa7c05bdbaa0acde5b32467be06597babd5.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines responsible AI governance for intelligent higher education management and public-sector innovation. It highlights the importance of ethical AI, governance transparency, institutional readiness, stakeholder AI literacy, and sustainability-oriented governance in AI-enabled ecosystems. The study proposes a conceptual governance framework integrating ethical oversight, intelligent decision-support systems, governance interoperability, and adaptive governance mechanisms. The chapter also discusses governance challenges associated with generative AI, including algorithmic bias, explainability, misinformation, and compliance risks. The findings emphasize that responsible AI governance supports sustainable institutional transformation, public trust, accountability, and human-centred innovation across higher education and public-sector environments.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive Adaptation and Leadership in AI-Augmented Higher Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Responsible AI Governance in Higher Education Management for Creative Public Sector Innovation
a5612c037c0c5391ee895bba1a4fc5ae65f530b1.abstract: <jats:p>Generative AI poses pressing governance challenges regarding the future of human-AI interaction and how it enhances or diminishes the cognitive capabilities, professional role, and leadership of academic professionals. Three cognitive adaptation patterns emerge from the analysis of the qualitative data (retrieved from the interviews) and the quantitative data (PLS-SEM survey): AI Augmentation, AI Dependency, and AI Co-construction. The positive relationship between adaptation outcomes and AI trust is supported by PLS-SEM, with the cognitive load change as a mediator and the organisational learning orientation as a moderator, the most significant institutional factor influencing adaptation outcomes. The chapter suggests embedding metacognition and AI literacy in workforce governance, institutional reflection in HR and L&D processes, and complementarity guardrails. For practical governance tools for adopting responsible AI in higher education, a validated diagnostic instrument and a Human-AI Capability Convergence Model are provided.</jats:p>

title: Transforming Academic Governance in the AI Era
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Responsible AI Governance in Higher Education Management for Creative Public Sector Innovation
e49d653e589a416eb7de0e2ea2a3cdd823c5f09a.abstract: <jats:p>Generative AI (GAI) has rapidly become an integral part of higher education, significantly reshaping the teaching, learning, assessment, and research experiences of institutions around the globe, thereby creating unprecedented moral, legal, and governance dilemmas. Academic honesty and honour codes, which typically aimed to combat cheating and plagiarism in human-powered settings, are no longer adequate to deal with the challenges of AI-enabled environments. The study critically reviews the current paradigm of academic governance in the context of the emergence of generative AI and addresses the interplay of institutional honour codes, ethical responsibility, accountability systems, and regulatory compliance in higher education institutions. The research is done by a doctrinal, interdisciplinary and policy-oriented approach, analysing new institutional polices on AI, international ethical guidelines, university governance frameworks, data protection laws, and current academic discussions on responsible use of AI in academia.</jats:p>

title: AI Governance in Academia
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Responsible AI Governance in Higher Education Management for Creative Public Sector Innovation
82978771df486b7a50f02bfe7e3688784c7559c6.abstract: <jats:p>The ability to add artificial intelligence (AI) to higher education institutions in the entire public sector has opened up never-before opportunities to personalised learning, administrative efficiency and evidence-based policy-making. However, such opportunities are kept in company with serious governance issues that relate to transparency, fairness and institutional accountability. The chapter examines ethical strains that are inherent in utilisation of AI systems in the evaluation of students, collection of admission details, and distribution of resources, and argues that without the presence of robust governance architectures these systems have a risk of entrenching the existing inequalities and also eroding democratic educational values. The chapter is based on a multi-layered governance model which incorporates regulatory compliance, stakeholder participation, algorithmic auditing, and continuous ethics oversight.</jats:p>

title: Agentic AI as a Catalyst for Intelligent Transformation in Higher Education Administration
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
666d4eec1099228678f9ba6af74a13a32a982a4f.abstract: <jats:p>The growing complexity of higher education administration has exposed the limitations of fragmented, rule-based systems that struggle to support timely and data-driven decision-making. This chapter examines agentic artificial intelligence (AI) as a catalyst for transforming administrative ecosystems into adaptive, intelligent, and coordinated systems. Moving beyond traditional automation, agentic AI introduces autonomy, context-awareness, and continuous learning, enabling real-time data integration, predictive–prescriptive analytics, and workflow orchestration across core domains. Drawing on frameworks such as multi-agent systems, decision intelligence, and socio-technical systems, the chapter analyzes how agentic AI reshapes institutional processes and decision structures. It also highlights key challenges, including data silos, governance complexities, and ethical concerns. Ultimately, the chapter argues that effective implementation requires systemic integration, robust governance, and strong human–AI collaboration.</jats:p>

title: Decision Intelligence for AI-Enabled University Governance and Data-Driven Administrative Transformation
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
1ea21bd12f81b110514bb8aff08dc36ff1204ee4.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming governance and administrative processes in higher education institutions. Traditional systems relying on manual operations and fragmented data are increasingly inadequate. This chapter proposes an AI-driven decision intelligence framework for efficient, data-driven, and policy-aligned governance. The framework integrates data collection, preprocessing, feature selection, and predictive analytics within a unified architecture, where institutional data from student, financial, and human resource systems are analyzed using machine learning models to generate insights. These are refined through policy-based decision mechanisms to ensure transparency and compliance. Results show improved decision accuracy, operational efficiency, and reduced processing time, supported by dashboards for real-time monitoring. Ethical concerns such as data privacy and bias are also addressed. A case study from Tamil Nadu demonstrates the framework's applicability as a scalable model for AI-enabled governance.</jats:p>

title: Agentic AI as a Governance Partner in Higher Education Leadership
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
57435d97d2fd69fae64c511686c94b37c80641ef.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter advances the argument that agentic artificial intelligence should be theorized as a governance partner in higher education leadership rather than as a mere administrative tool. As universities operate within intensifying accountability, datafication, and audit regimes, agentic systems increasingly participate in enrollment, budgeting, accreditation, and research decisions, reshaping institutional decision architectures. To address this shift, this chapter proposes the Strategic Agentic Governance Framework, a feedback-driven model linking data intelligence, normative framing, decision orchestration, accountability, and adaptive institutional learning. Drawing on distributed leadership, institutional agency, algorithmic governance, and socio-technical systems theory, the framework reconceptualizes leadership as meta-governance, the deliberate design of hybrid human and machine decision systems. The chapter also examines accountability diffusion, algorithmic bias, and data sovereignty, and offers testable propositions and a maturity continuum for future research.</jats:p>

title: Digital Catalytic Leadership for Governing Agentic AI
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
a7a2f25db22c009ea70fb3c60ff8c7c5966288e7.abstract: <jats:p>The evolution of agentic AI is transforming higher education administration beyond simple automation. This chapter examines the governance challenges of AI integration in universities and proposes Digital Catalytic Leadership (DCL) as an adaptive governance framework. The study finds that while agentic AI can improve administrative effectiveness, it also creates challenges related to accountability, data security, and human–AI relations. This chapter argues that DCL is important for building adaptive, ethical, and human-centered higher education governance in the AI era.</jats:p>

title: Intelligent Budget Allocation and Predictive Financial Analytics Using AI in Higher Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
811b776505e2e740c926ee67de48c35b2159227e.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter considers the potential use of an agentic AI in changing the face of financial planning and budgeting in higher education organizations characterized by uncertain funding, unpredictable enrollments, and increasing accountability. This chapter criticizes the conventional approach to incremental budgeting and advances a governance-centered model in which AI functions as an agent for enhancing collaboration in financial decision-making rather than taking control from people's hands. Informed by Dynamic Capabilities theory, the contribution illustrates the role of AI in improving the capabilities for sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring at institutions for adaptive management. This chapter further develops the concept of a four-step RACT model for implementing AI in responsible ways. The contribution is enriched through institutional case illustrations with emphasis on the advantages gained through AI adoption. The challenges associated with the application of AI in financial management are discussed, alongside mitigation approaches. Research gaps are clearly stated.</jats:p>

title: Administrative System Transformation Through Agentic AI in Enrollment and Admissions Management
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
19d4c9a3cbac21418f82ad721e79494df8fa79eb.abstract: <jats:p>Administrative challenges are increasing in higher education establishments in light of the rising enrollment pressures, changing student needs, and heightened demands for accountability. Agentic AI, with its capacity to self-directly perceive, plan, act, and learn, opens up avenues for a novel way to revolutionize enrollment and admissions management. This chapter provides an overview of the ways in which agentic AI is transforming the enrollment cycle, including the engagement of students, admission applications, prediction and planning, decision-making, and yield management. Based on the recent research and practical experience of various educational establishments, the potential, as well as possible difficulties associated with automation, ethical issues, privacy concerns, workforce transformation, among other issues, are discussed.</jats:p>

title: Agentic AI in Enrollment and Admissions Management
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
00d998159a5393674028a10b076cd1fb8a858ea4.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the role of agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) in transforming enrollment and admissions management within higher education institutions. The chapter discusses the evolution of admissions systems from traditional manual structures to intelligent, data-driven administrative ecosystems supported by predictive analytics, workflow automation, applicant screening, and conversational AI. The study highlights how AI-enabled systems improve enrollment forecasting, communication responsiveness, institutional coordination, and operational efficiency while reducing administrative delays and inconsistencies. Empirical findings from multi-institutional analysis demonstrate measurable improvements in applicant engagement, screening accuracy, workflow synchronization, and fairness in admissions processes. The chapter further explores governance, ethical considerations, explainability, and human-AI collaboration frameworks necessary for responsible implementation of intelligent admissions systems in higher education.</jats:p>

title: Agentic AI in Higher Education Administration
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
cf8cf6f3740adc256c5ee8a80e0a1c1edcb0aaeb.abstract: <jats:p>Higher education institutions are increasingly transitioning from traditional rule-based automation toward autonomous, goal-directed agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems within administrative environments. Unlike conventional automation tools, agentic AI systems can interpret context, plan actions, utilize external tools, and adapt dynamically to changing conditions. This chapter examines the opportunities and risks associated with these systems in student support services. It discusses benefits such as improved responsiveness, continuous service availability, and reduced administrative workload, while also evaluating risks including algorithmic bias, data privacy concerns, decision opacity, and the potential reduction of human-centered support. The chapter further proposes a governance framework based on Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) and Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL) oversight models to support responsible and transparent AI deployment in higher education administration</jats:p>

title: Typologies and Competencies of Prompt Literacy in Generative Artificial Intelligence
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
013ea58d255cd2cb20230cf35206aa2e5da0de6b.abstract: <jats:p>This scoping review summarizes findings on an emergent area, “prompt literacy,” in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). It specifically maps key types identified in prompt literacy, including the competencies associated with each. Using a systematic approach to analyze recent literature on the types of prompts (e.g., instruction, exploration, iteration, and evaluation) used throughout GenAI's development provides insight into how they have shaped users' experiences and interactions with new AI-based systems. Additionally, this report provides a list of basic competencies to support effective development of prompt literacy skills, including linguistic accuracy/precision, context awareness, ethical reasoning, and iterative problem-solving—all of which help individuals become successful with their digital and information literacy skills but offer new challenges when people work with AI systems. In conclusion, this review revealed that prompt literacy is a technical/cognitive skill set that encompasses (but isn't limited to) flexibility and critical thinking at all levels.</jats:p>

title: Generative AI in Fashion Design Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
63247d82c461a4523c3e4a79b2e2ae1f0fd715d7.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter covers the transformative role of artificial intelligence in fashion design education, with particular attention to the creation of a framework for prompt literacy utilizing generative AI technologies, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Midjourney, and Newarc AI. This chapter also examines how second-year students in Amity University Kolkata's fashion design and fashion communication department generate virtual rapid clothing prototypes of their designs and develop print motifs using AI-powered tools, especially generative AI, which ultimately enhances the significance of these tools for the changing fashion landscape. Participants have created artwork in a variety of mediums, including Mahbubani art, terracotta, ceramics, and print motifs inspired by seashells, insect using mandalas art, Persian carpets, and other subjects like “Joy in Simplicity” and “The Harmony of Nature and Feminine Grace”. The AI-Augmented Fashion Design Education Framework (AI-AFDEF) was emphasized in this book chapter's discussion of traditional versus tech-driven approaches.</jats:p>

title: Assessing Prompt Literacy Without Rewarding AI Dependence
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
87efe6b64abb52ecb3ebc29c6cb22b3f5ea3063e.abstract: <jats:p>Generative AI has made a visible educational skill, yet many assessments still reward polished final outputs more than genuine understanding. This creates a perverse incentive: students who outsource the most thinking often appear the most competent. This chapter argues that prompt literacy must be assessed in ways that do not reward AI dependence. It reframes prompt literacy as evaluative and disciplinary judgement, demonstrated when students frame tasks, set constraints, iterate purposefully, verify outputs, document tool use, and decide when to limit or refuse AI support. The proposed approach rests on three ideas: rubrics that value judgement over polish, authentic tasks that make process and transfer visible, and academic integrity by design. Supported by seven tables and five figures, the chapter offers practical tools and concludes that the real challenge is designing assessment that promotes accountable thinking, calibrated trust, and durable learning rather than automated text production.</jats:p>

title: AI as a Tool for Inclusive Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
2008fbfe45df9c72649fb888472056d12c0aa3be.abstract: <jats:p>There is an increasing presence of artificial intelligence (AI) in the classroom, but our conversation on how it can serve inclusive education (in both face-to-face and online settings) is inconsistent and often underdeveloped. Much of the discourse around AI celebrates that it can finally address large, structural inequalities in education, but this is not truly the case. When put into practice, AI tools tend to widen or narrow the gap based on how they are integrated into institutional practice. This chapter introduces AI as a practical, and sometimes suboptimal, means to serve diverse needs of learners in both online and offline contexts. The focus is on learners who have frequently been marginalized in instructional design, including those with disabilities, non-native learners, students who are first generation, and those in low-resource settings. AI-powered applications such as speech-to-text systems, intelligent reading platforms, automatic translation, and personalized feedback engines will be explored in realistic classroom scenarios.</jats:p>

title: AI-Driven Assessment Systems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
3b1af0102e45438b02902d5aaef2200558af7377.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence rapid integration into educational assessments is reshaping monitoring, measurement and support of learning across diverse educational contexts worldwide. Artificial Intelligence powered tools present unprecedented opportunities for efficiency, personalization and scalability while simultaneously raising complex ethical, equity-related and pedagogical challenges. This book chapter therefore critically examines transformative potential of Artificial Intelligence driven assessments, situating it at the intersection of inclusivity, innovation and integrity. Drawing from multiple theories, the chapter develops a model balancing automation and human oversight for transparency, fairness, and well-being. It examines applications and explores policy, governance, bias, privacy, and readiness, guiding responsible adoption. This chapter concludes with implications for practice, policy, and research, emphasizing AI as a human-centered tool for learning, innovation, and equity, and presents a framework for ethical, adaptive AI assessment.</jats:p>

title: AI-Driven Educational Innovation
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
0304897651337a7bb39664e76309ee3a7ff3c822.abstract: <jats:p>The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) has revolutionized modern education, changing the way teaching and learning are designed, delivered, and experienced. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping the landscape of modern education by reimagining the instructional design and development, personalization of learning, and engagement in learning through adaptive and data-driven systems of education. This chapter explores how AI can be applied to curriculum innovation, interactive learning environments, intelligent tutoring systems, and pedagogies that focus on the learner. It also examines the ways in which AI-powered tools enhance accessibility, motivation, and immediate feedback and aid teachers in planning and assessing instruction. The chapter also assesses critically ethical, social, and pedagogical issues such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, and digital inequality. Last but not least, it identifies future directions and strategic implications for the sustainable integration of AI in the education sector.</jats:p>

title: Behavioural Laboratories and Smart Games for AI-Driven Educational Innovation
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
2388769aa5f39ba722184caad912298e0d1014b5.abstract: <jats:p>This Chapter examines the integration of behavioral laboratories and Artificial Intelligence enabled smart games as complementary infrastructures for advancing educational innovation. It establishes the purpose of grounding AI-driven systems in robust empirical evidence, theoretical frameworks, and ethical considerations to enhance instructional design and decision making. Behavioral laboratories are presented as controlled environments for generating high quality data on learner cognition, motivation, and behavior while smart games operationalize these insights though adaptive learning, real time feedback and learning analytics. Drawing on Self Determination Theory, Constructive Learning Theory and Behavioral Learning Theory, this Chapter proposes a multi-layered framework linking experimental research, computational modelling and institutional implementation. Applications across teacher professional development, early childhood education, vocational training, and resource constrained contexts are examined.</jats:p>

title: Designing Meaningful Learning in the AI Era
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
3c25d7c0f40619104554425c39194f433f48c95f.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education is prompting teacher education programs to reconsider their pedagogical foundations. Many current approaches, however, equate technological adoption with meaningful learning, overlooking deeper epistemological and instructional challenges. This chapter presents the Meaningful AI-Integrated Learning Framework (MAILF), a theoretically grounded model designed for teacher education. Drawing on constructivism, Meaningful Learning Theory, and the TPACK model, MAILF defines four interconnected dimensions: conceptual grounding, critical AI literacy, reflective pedagogical design, and ethical agency. It argues that effective AI integration depends less on technical skills and more on developing educators' critical, reflective, and ethical capacities. The framework positions AI as a cognitive partner that enhances learning. Implications for curriculum design, faculty development, and institutional policy are also discussed.</jats:p>

title: Enhancing Writer Identity Through Generative AI
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
020e0600325ece480d5771e7e3d50a13da2cbdfb.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid integration of generative AI tools has transformed writing instruction, raising questions about authorship, agency, and academic integrity in teacher education. Unlike search engines, generative AI produces synthesized text that supports brainstorming, drafting, revising, and feedback. While these tools can reduce cognitive load and enhance higher-order thinking, they may also weaken productive struggle, writer identity, and promote overreliance without intentional instructional design. These issues are especially relevant for preservice teachers who must learn to use AI both ethically and instructionally. Grounded in self-regulation, self-efficacy, metacognitive theory, and the cognitive process model of writing, this study frames AI as metacognitive scaffolding for writing development. The framework highlights a gap between preservice teachers' frequent use of AI and their limited readiness to teach with it. The article argues that intentional, theory-driven integration can support planning, monitoring, and reflection while preserving student voice and autonomy. I</jats:p>

title: Examining K-2 Educators' Perceptions of Project Read AI in Developing Instructional Materials
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
29c4149b0dd803e30bf4a61cd3842b2b95796a1a.abstract: <jats:p>This qualitative study examined K-2 early childhood educators' perceptions of Project Read AI, an artificial intelligence platform designed specifically to support phonics-based instruction aligned with the Science of Reading. Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model, the study investigated both the perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness of the platform among six kindergarten through second-grade teachers at a suburban New York elementary school. Findings indicated that educators perceived the platform as generally user-friendly and expressed strong intentions to integrate it into their practice. Evaluations of instructional materials yielded mixed results: the Decodable Game was viewed as a highly effective engagement tool, the Lola Science of Reading chatbot produced lesson frameworks valued as supplemental resources, and the Decodable Text Generator showed instructional promise but required improvements. Implications are given for educator practice, professional development, and future research on AI-powered literacy tools in early childhood education.</jats:p>

title: Institutionalizing AI Literacy in Teacher Preparation
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
64c8459cd7f2dfb824514d9f0d3651ac28aff692.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is reshaping teaching, learning, assessment, and professional judgment across P–16 education. This chapter presents a competency-based microcredential framework designed to prepare teacher candidates for responsible AI use before clinical practice. The framework positions AI literacy as a professional competency grounded in instructional design, ethical stewardship, data privacy, equitable access, human–AI collaboration, and reflective judgment. It moves from foundational understanding to applied classroom implementation through modules focused on responsible AI adoption, AI fluency, prompt literacy, AI limitations and risks, instructional design in AI-rich environments, classroom guardrails, and a culminating AI Integrity Statement. Drawing on literature synthesis, stakeholder feedback, policy analysis, and professional standards, including TPACK and UDL-informed approaches, the chapter offers an adaptable framework for guiding responsible implementation across educator preparation contexts.</jats:p>

title: Integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence in Flipped Classrooms
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
1e4670d3841466f96a03163cc6c1855c53c8ffb3.abstract: <jats:p>This study explores the impact of integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into a flipped classroom in higher education. Using a quantitative approach with complementary qualitative data, the research involved 136 management students, yielding 77 valid responses. Data were analysed via IBM SPSS 29.0, employing descriptive, inferential, and Exploratory Factorial Analysis. Findings indicate that GenAI integration enhances student engagement and promotes a deeper understanding of AI tools. Students reported increased awareness of GenAI's capabilities and limitations, and improved critical evaluation skills. Class size emerged as a significant factor influencing participation and organizational effectiveness. Overall, results provide empirical evidence of the educational benefits of GenAI in flipped settings, supporting teaching and learning. The study contributes to discussions on fostering critical GenAI use and offers practical implications for AI-driven pedagogical strategies.</jats:p>

title: Positioning AI as a Tool to Revitalise Kenya's Higher Education Sector
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
ef7bb52bc1b22a095002589d4c1959c4788e780a.abstract: <jats:p>The Kenyan education system is undergoing reform through the Competency-Based Education (CBE) and through the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI). In the higher education sector, both educators and students are embracing AI as a powerful tool in the learning process. Students, many of whom are more techno-savvy than their teachers, have embraced AI excitedly. This chapter employed a qualitative methodology to analyse selected AI policies applied in Kenya to interrogate how the adoption of the technology is harnessed in the higher education sector. Findings indicate that some of the selected AI policies do not adequately address Kenya's higher education issues. The study further established that a huge segment of the higher education sector has not yet institutionalised AI adoption into policy. The chapter argues that Kenya's higher education sector must actively participate in the AI policy and regulation discussion to ensure that the innovation is embraced in the ongoing education reforms.</jats:p>

title: Strategic AI Integration in Higher Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
da3558bb98cb0ef90363674494624fdfcfde03c2.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of artificial intelligence in higher education is occurring at a rapid pace and institutions are still playing catch-up with piecemeal strategies. This chapter presents a governance model that integrates artificial intelligence into curricula, teaching practices, ethical considerations and student learning outcomes. The work is informed by recent research on adaptive learning systems, algorithmic accountability, and outcome-based education (OBE). The model places emphasis on four key elements: curriculum design, faculty training, student data management and institutional governance, outlining roles and decision-making processes. The argument is clear. The incorporation of AI is not a technical issue The framework presented here is grounded in current literature from 2020 to 2024 and incorporates evidence from global pilot programmes in the US, United Kingdom, Australia and India. The chapter concludes that sustainable AI integration depends not on the sophistication of the tools deployed but on the quality of the human decisions made around them.</jats:p>

title: Ethical AI and Responsible Data Use in Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
0ca0030d0a293ae102a203b25f3dbc50eda12d8c.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter introduces the concept of personalised learning, learning analytics, automated assessment, and the emergence of generative AI in transforming education, while also highlighting the ethical, privacy, governance and cybersecurity dilemmas that arise with implementation of Artificial Intelligence in the education sector. The chapter gives an overview of ethical and responsible use of AI in education, starting with an examination of the educational AI ecosystem, followed by a discussion of data lifecycle in education, and concluding with an exploration of algorithmic bias, transparency, informed consent, data ownership, surveillance and risks posed by generative AI. It outlines the principles of responsible data governance, privacy-by-design, privacy-preserving methods and other international frameworks like GDPR AI Ethics and OECD Principles. The topics of AI-driven cybersecurity, key practice insights for both educators and institutions, developers and policymakers, and future research areas for AI are also discussed.</jats:p>

title: Protecting Student Data in AI-Driven Education Privacy, Consent, Ownership, and Ethical Use
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
1adcff266d66b42b3bb260619da2d8a4f2415ffe.abstract: <jats:p>Through technologies like intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics, adaptive learning platforms, and generative AI, artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming education by making learning more efficient, personalized, and interactive. Large volumes of student data are necessary for these technologies to comprehend learning trends, deliver prompt feedback, and aid in educational decision making. While AI has many advantages for educators, institutions, and students, it also brings up significant issues regarding the gathering, storing, sharing, and security of student data. As educational institutions implement AI-enabled systems, concerns about privacy, informed consent, data ownership, transparency, fairness, and ethical use have grown in significance. The main obstacles to safeguarding student data in AI-driven education are examined in this chapter, including concerns about surveillance, algorithmic bias, cybersecurity threats, and unauthorized access.</jats:p>

title: Information Governance of Student Data in AI-Powered Educational Systems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
9ebb5c39ff6576139082e5f69c7ac01d59c0f7b9.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter presents a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) examining student data cybersecurity and information governance within AI-powered educational systems. Adhering to PRISMA 2020 guidelines, the review systematically screens 237 published documents to ensure a transparent, replicable, and unbiased synthesis of the intersecting legal, technical, and pedagogical challenges in EdTech. The technical analysis is structured around the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (CSF 2.0), evaluating the literature across its six core pillars: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover. Furthermore, the study anchors its regulatory analysis within FERPA and the GDPR, with a specific focus on how the GDPR's strict lawful-basis and data-minimization principles govern complex, cross-border educational data flows. Ultimately, this review bridges theory and compliance to offer a comprehensive framework for securing student data in the AI era.</jats:p>

title: Secure Design Principles for AI-Driven Learning Platforms
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
32bea6d3eaecbb0e62a89d791d1f4072a5b07d66.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into educational tools such as learning management systems, analytics dashboards, adaptive assessment services, and generative AI assistants. These platforms support personalized learning and institutional decision-making, but they create risks linked to digital identity, learner profiling, data misuse, model leakage, prompt injection, and weak governance. This chapter analyzes cybersecurity governance in AI-driven learning platforms from the perspective of identity security and data privacy. It examines AI-specific privacy threats and safeguards such as zero trust, decentralized identifiers, verifiable credentials, encryption, federated learning, differential privacy, secure aggregation, and accountable oversight. The chapter proposes a layered cybersecurity framework integrating identity assurance, privacy-preserving processing, AI model protection, secure platform operations, institutional governance, and continuous risk monitoring. The contribution supports trustworthy, privacy-aware, and secure AI-enabled education ecosystems.</jats:p>

title: Cybersecurity Awareness and Digital Literacy for Students and Educators Strengthening Data Privacy with AI-Powered Cybersecurity
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
30cafb06bf9daabec321a6848bf1479377de9a8e.abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to investigate the significance of cybersecurity awareness, digital literacy, and artificial intelligence in fostering data privacy protection for students and teachers in North India. The study was an exploratory descriptive study with a cross-sectional quantitative design, based on primary data gathered from a structured questionnaire with 620 respondents. The methods used were descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression. The correlation was positive for all of the variables, and the highest was between the AI-driven cybersecurity and data privacy protection (r = .741, p < .001). The results of the regression showed that artificial intelligence cybersecurity, digital literacy and cyber security awareness had significant predicting power for data privacy protection, accounting for 66.3% of its variance. The results highlight the need for a holistic approach to integrating AI into education, fostering digital literacy, and raising cybersecurity awareness to ensure safer and privacy-conscious learning spaces.</jats:p>

title: AI-Enabled Financial Phishing and the Digital Literacy Deficit Protecting Student and Young Learner Data
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
65ab6f5f760fd3d653bfc26c66ada7b9512e9487.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence has structurally transformed financial phishing, collapsing the cost of personalised attacks; India recorded 135,173 financial phishing attacks in H1 2024, a 175% rise over 2023. This chapter examines the convergence of AI-enabled phishing, student data vulnerability, and digital literacy deficits in India's skill-based educational institutions (ITIs, polytechnics, skill universities), a population absent from existing cybersecurity literature despite holding data regulated under the DPDP Act, 2023. Drawing on Routine Activity Theory, Protection Motivation Theory, the Digital Literacy Continuum, and Institutional Theory, it develops the Protection Gap construct and a Four-Layer Institutional Defence Model. A primary survey (N = 96, seven states) finds 66.7% encountered suspected phishing, mostly via WhatsApp; only 25.0% identified a genuine message; 59.4% were unaware of the DPDP Act; and 43.8% reported no explicit consent for Aadhaar/bank data. The chapter closes with recommendations for MeitY, AICTE, NSDC, and the Data Protection Board of India.</jats:p>

title: AI-Generated Deepfakes and Trust in Digital Communication in Namibia
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
9ae33c567c1e3c1be30b3c19886f0820b1ea2ad9.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has accelerated the development of deepfake technology, enabling the creation of highly realistic fabricated audio, video, and visual content that closely resembles authentic media. A mixed-method approach was employed, combining an online survey of 47 Namibian internet users and a total of 12 key informants were interviewed. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics, while qualitative data were subjected to thematic analysis. The findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge on deepfake technologies by providing empirical evidence from Namibia and offering practical recommendations for enhancing digital literacy, strengthening regulatory frameworks, and improving institutional preparedness.</jats:p>

title: Reassessing Faith and Facts in AI-Augmented Modern Higher Education
container-title: Negotiating Faith, Fact, and the Future of Higher Education
7acbc3cc08e83ccb86f74983a4af53870891720e.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into modern higher education has produced a dual impact: while AI has opened new opportunities for innovation in teaching, learning, and research, it has also introduced significant challenges for academic practice. This paper explores how AI reshapes epistemic boundaries by challenging traditional notions and examines how confidence in institutional traditions and technological promise intersects with empirical data and algorithmic reasoning, and the ethical implications for transparent decision-making frameworks. By combining theoretical perspectives with practical examples, this paper highlights how AI is redefining epistemological foundations by the need to strengthen the relationship between faith and facts. The paper argues for a human-centred approach that promotes adaptive learning cultures. It concludes by proposing a forward-looking framework to help modern universities remain grounded in an AI-intensive future.</jats:p>

title: Integrasi AI dalam Kurikulum Akuntansi Pendidikan Pesantren: Tinjauan Literatur Sistematis tentang Kesiapan Teknologi, Pemahaman AI, dan Karakteristik Siswa
container-title: Business and Accounting Education Journal
e0f60edd89c8c829c91e27e2720ae59dca61591c.abstract: <jats:p>Perkembangan Artificial Intelligence (AI) telah mendorong transformasi pendidikan akuntansi dan menuntut penyesuaian kurikulum agar sesuai dengan kebutuhan dunia kerja digital. Namun, adopsi AI dalam kurikulum akuntansi masih dipengaruhi oleh berbagai faktor, khususnya pada konteks pendidikan pesantren yang memiliki karakteristik unik. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis pengaruh kesiapan teknologi, pemahaman AI, dan karakteristik siswa terhadap adopsi AI dalam kurikulum akuntansi serta mengidentifikasi faktor yang paling dominan. Penelitian menggunakan metode Systematic Literature Review (SLR) dengan pedoman PRISMA 2020. Data diperoleh dari 38 artikel ilmiah terindeks Scopus yang dipublikasikan pada periode 2015-2026 dan dianalisis menggunakan sintesis tematik. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa kesiapan teknologi merupakan faktor yang paling dominan dalam mendorong adopsi AI, diikuti oleh pemahaman AI dan karakteristik siswa. Ketiga faktor tersebut saling melengkapi dalam meningkatkan penerimaan dan pemanfaatan AI dalam pembelajaran akuntansi. Temuan ini berkontribusi pada pengembangan model adopsi teknologi pendidikan serta menjadi dasar pengembangan kurikulum akuntansi berbasis AI di lingkungan pesantren.</jats:p>

title: Bridging or Widening the Gap? AI Policies and Social Justice in Education
container-title: Social Justice in Education
038583ab9446f69693d78ffd45b815c6af816060.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is widely promoted as a means to improve educational quality, efficiency, and equity. However, when introduced into systems already shaped by inequality, AI risks reproducing rather than reducing social injustice. This chapter examines whether AI policies in education bridge or widen existing gaps, drawing on Nancy Fraser's framework of redistribution, recognition, and representation. Through a comparative analysis of supranational frameworks and national strategies in the United States, China, India, and Türkiye, the chapter identifies persistent tensions between innovation-driven agendas and justice-oriented goals. The findings suggest that equity is often framed in technocratic terms, while issues of power, participation, and accountability remain marginal. The chapter concludes by proposing a justice-centered policy evaluation framework that emphasizes democratic governance, cultural responsiveness, and the right to contest or refuse harmful AI systems.</jats:p>

title: Facilitating generative mentoring in higher education: a systematic review and measurement framework for mentoring, generativity, and the minority tax
container-title: International Journal of Mentoring and Coaching in Education
287d779db5963bc4e348125285588dc8efc6ffb4.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The purpose of this study is to synthesise how faculty mentoring in higher education has been evaluated in relation to mentor generativity and equity-related pressures (including the minority tax) and to propose a minimum measurement framework for valid evaluation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020-guided systematic review was registered on the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD42025647836). The review question was developed using a Sample, Phenomenon of Interest, Design, Evaluation, Research-informed approach appropriate to the inclusion of both quantitative and qualitative evidence. Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect and EBSCOhost were searched from database inception to June 2025. Two reviewers independently screened and extracted data, study quality was appraised using design-appropriate tools, and findings were narratively synthesised.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Eight studies met the inclusion criteria (six quantitative, two qualitative), with most of the evidence from the USA. No study directly measured mentor generativity using validated generativity instruments; instead, studies relied on proxy outcomes (e.g. satisfaction, productivity, promotion). This limits conclusions about the construct validity of generativity and may obscure costs when mentoring demands are high and recognition is low, especially for historically marginalised faculty.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The evidence base was small (eight studies), predominantly U.S.-based, methodologically heterogeneous, and reliant on proxy outcomes rather than validated measures of mentor generativity. These limitations precluded meta-analysis and causal inference. Future research should directly measure generativity alongside mentoring load, institutional recognition, strain, and equity-related indicators across more diverse regions, disciplines, and institutional contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework provides institutions and researchers with a concise set of indicators to evaluate mentoring programmes, inform workload crediting and promotion criteria, and monitor equity in the distribution and recognition of mentoring labour.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This review reframes the evaluation of faculty mentoring as a construct-measurement problem and proposes a minimum measurement framework that distinguishes direct generativity from commonly used proxy outcomes. By integrating mentoring load, institutional recognition, strain, and equity considerations, the framework also provides a basis for empirically testing the proposed “generativity paradox”, the conditions under which mentoring may be experienced as renewing, burdensome, or both.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: University students' disciplinary perspectives on generative AI after two years of its widespread use
container-title: Journal of Applied Research in Higher Education
5cfc2677f2ff083e2ccefb422d4ee92c351ab20c.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study explores how university students use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) across various disciplines, including STEM, Business, Education Futures, Clinical & Health Sciences (CHS), Creative and Allied Health & Human Performance (AHHP). It aims to identify discipline-based perspectives, perceived benefits, ethical boundaries and the support needs required for responsible use of GenAI tools.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A survey was conducted approximately two years after the widespread use of GenAI, by which time participants were expected to be familiar with its use. Students were categorised based on their discipline, English fluency, mode of learning and level of study. Their responses were analysed to compare usage patterns, satisfaction levels and ethical considerations across disciplines.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results highlight that student perspectives on GenAI tools are discipline-dependent. STEM and Education Futures showed the highest acceptance, while CHS and Business students were more cautious and sceptical about accuracy and ethical issues. Non-native English speakers rated GenAI tools more favourably as aids for writing and comprehension. Novice users expressed enthusiasm, while expert users showed dissatisfaction due to errors and false information.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study relied on self-reported perceptions and represents a single institutional context. Broader investigations are recommended, with a particular focus on equity groups such as students with disabilities, low-SES students and remote learners.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Different approaches were suggested for integrating GenAI into learning. STEM students favoured comparative tasks; CHS recommended support for diagnostic reasoning; Allied Health preferred role-playing simulations; Education Futures highlighted lesson planning; and Business students suggested case-based and productivity uses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study provides cross-disciplinary analyses of GenAI use by students and proposes approaches for ethical and discipline-specific integration into university curricula.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Construction and Case Study of a Quality Evaluation Model for Intelligent Information Systems in a Generative Artificial Intelligence Environment: The Case of Bilibili
container-title: Computers and Artificial Intelligence
c7d63252644539de3df39bb8cce6761d736c89be.abstract: <jats:p>After generative artificial intelligence (AI) was embedded in search, content generation, and user interaction, traditional information system quality evaluation faced new boundaries. Based on the DeLone and McLean (D&M) Information Systems Success Model, this study adopts literature research and a single-case study, takes Bilibili as the case, and constructs and applies a six-dimensional evaluation framework based on public materials, observations of platform functions, and publicly available user feedback. The findings show that system quality, information quality, and service quality can still explain basic platform operation, information output, and service support, but they cannot fully cover AI’s semantic understanding and task completion, the trustworthiness of generated results, and continuous human-computer interaction. Therefore, this study introduces AI intelligence quality, trustworthiness quality, and interaction quality on the basis of the three traditional dimensions and clarifies the boundary of each dimension. The Bilibili case shows that the framework can identify both basic capabilities and AI-specific quality, thereby helping to avoid conflating technical performance, content quality, intelligent capability, and trust issues. The study provides a structured analytical framework for evaluating the quality of intelligent information systems in a generative AI environment and a reference for platforms to optimize AI functions and governance mechanisms.</jats:p>

title: DIGITAL LABOUR AND EPISTEMIC ERASURE: A SEMIOTIC ANALYSIS OF INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE AND AI INFRASTRUCTURES IN HUMANS IN THE LOOP
container-title: Interdisciplinary Perspectives of Education
1590acb16f54ed93cfb734fd74f1156ff456f6f0.abstract:
<jats:p>This paper explores how artificial intelligence (AI) and digital labour affect marginalised identities, using the 2025 Netflix film Humans in the Loop (directed by Aranya Sahay). Research follows the female protagonist of the film, named Nehma, an Indigenous (Adivasi) woman who works as a data labeller. Her deep, traditional knowledge about nature is ignored because of the way AI categorisation systems use a rigid, one-size-fits-all sorting method and act as epistemic hierarchies that erase Indigenous ways of living and thinking. Using a social semiotic approach, the research identifies a disconnection between local ecological knowledge and the rigid binary logic of machine-learning infrastructures.
The article argues that digital frameworks mirror power dynamics inside educational institutions, where underrepresented students often have their cultural identity and cultural expressions erased or misrepresented. By analysing the lived experiences of marginalised communities, the study critiques techno-solutionist solutions and proposes solutions grounded in epistemic justice, cultural agency and equity and recommends that equitable AI systems require moving away from extractive labour practices to recognise the intellectual and cultural contributions of the Global South.</jats:p>

title: FROM DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION TO AI-ENABLED EDUCATION: A CRITICAL REVIEW OF EMERGING TRENDS, OPPORTUNITIES, AND CHALLENGES
container-title: Interdisciplinary Perspectives of Education
8cda0a5f9293b593d4351c19c874a8fba3d6b9cc.abstract: <jats:p>The higher education sector has seen the emergence of several technological advancements over the past two decades. These include learning management systems, massive open online courses, and the latest on the market: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI). This paper aims to make a critical review of the shift from Digital Transformation to AI-driven education as a whole. The paper particularly emphasizes the shift of the digital transformation from being an administrative phenomenon to being more of a central feature in education. The paper summarises the literature on the concepts of digital transformation, the implementation of generative AI, and adaptive learning and AI ethics in the teaching and learning process, based on peer-reviewed papers that were mainly published in Scopus and Web of Science from 2019 to 2026. There are three themes that are repeated in the literature. First, AI in education is a further step towards digital transformation in which capacity building processes are substituted with independent decision making. Second, personalisation, accessibility and efficiency are opportunities, not equally accessible or equally taken up, nor equally realised; and these opportunities go first to the best resourced institutions.</jats:p>

title: FROM FINANCIAL LITERACY TO AI LITERACY: PREPARING COMMERCE STUDENTS FOR ALGORITHM-DRIVEN FINANCIAL DECISION-MAKING
container-title: Interdisciplinary Perspectives of Education
5a17ee01335a01b44902b57e48596ccad344f33b.abstract:
<jats:p>Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly visible in everyday financial activities. Students and consumers now encounter automated financial recommendations, digital investment platforms, personalised financial information and AI-based tools when making or evaluating financial choices. This changing environment raises an important question for Commerce education: is conventional financial literacy sufficient when financial information is increasingly mediated by algorithms?
The present study examines financial literacy, AI literacy and awareness of ethical issues associated with AI-supported financial applications among Commerce students, and investigates their relationship with algorithmic financial decision quality. The study follows a descriptive and analytical research design and considers 250 student observations. Data were examined using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple linear regression. Four major constructs were considered in the analysis: financial literacy, AI literacy, ethical awareness and algorithmic financial decision quality. The findings show that financial literacy recorded the highest mean score (M = 3.56), while AI literacy recorded a comparatively lower mean score (M = 3.33). AI literacy demonstrated the strongest correlation with algorithmic financial decision quality (r = .705, p ≤ .01), followed by financial literacy (r = .623, p ≤ .01) and ethical awareness (r = .605, p ≤ .01). The regression model explained 67.2% of the variation in algorithmic financial decision quality. AI literacy emerged as the strongest predictor (β = .443), followed by financial literacy (β = .376) and ethical awareness (β = .199), with all three predictors statistically significant at p ≤ .001.
The findings suggest that financial knowledge remains essential, but it needs to be complemented by the ability to understand, question and evaluate AI-generated financial information. Commerce education therefore needs to move towards an integrated approach in which financial literacy, AI competence and ethical awareness support independent and responsible financial judgement.</jats:p>

title: THE ROLE OF AI-POWERED DUOLINGO AND ELSA SPEAK APPS IN REDUCING SPEAKING ANXIETY AMONG ENGLISH LEARNERS IN PRIVATE UNIVERSITIES OF DHAKA, BANGLADESH
container-title: Interdisciplinary Perspectives of Education
01004d9d938d57121213e543fe3b6316ae463c99.abstract: <jats:p>This study has explored the influence of speaking anxiety as a major obstacle for English as foreign language learners (EFL) in their non-native environment like in the private universities in Dhaka, Bangladesh. With the up rise of Artificial Intelligence, English language learning applications have incorporated AI-based features to enhance the learning experience. This finding examined how AI-supported speaking apps, in this instance, Duolingo and ELSA Speak, reduce speaking anxiety and increase learners' confidence, fluency and speaking skills through AI-driven personalized feedback, gamified interaction and adaptive learning. This research used mixed-method approach, which included qualitative and quantitative methods to provide comprehensive insights and understanding. The results of the study pointed to the effectiveness of AI-based language learning apps in creating a supportive language-learning atmosphere, enhancing the learning process and reducing stress levels when practicing oral communication. The results of this study could contribute to the understanding of how AI-based app-based learning can be incorporated in the university curriculum and evidence-based recommendations for teachers, educational technology designers and policy makers.</jats:p>

title: Evaluating the Validity of AI-Generated Writing Feedback for Students With Learning Disabilities
container-title: Journal of Special Education Technology
948e28e353237873e163e223dcbad1abba57bdb6.abstract: <jats:p>Students with learning disabilities need clear, direct, and useful writing feedback. However, teachers often find it hard to provide this consistently because of time and workload pressures. New developments in generative artificial intelligence (AI) might help improve both the frequency and quality of feedback for students. Still, we know very little about whether AI-generated comments are valid or useful for struggling writers. This qualitative study looked at teachers' views on writing feedback from the AI-SCORE automated writing evaluation tool. Nine upper elementary and middle school teachers took part in two focus groups. They reviewed AI-generated feedback on student informational writing. They also discussed its clarity, teaching value, and suitability for students with disabilities. Thematic analysis revealed several areas for improving AI-generated feedback. Teachers want more guidance on specific revisions, language that suits students’ development, a consistent tone, and alignment with writing goals. They shared cautious optimism, noting that AI feedback could enhance teaching capacity and provide more practice opportunities for students, if it meets their needs. The findings stress the importance of teacher involvement, the potential benefits of AI for writing instruction, and key factors for creating AI tools that effectively support students with learning disabilities.</jats:p>

title: Ethical Implications of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) Use Among Library and Information Science (LIS) Students: A Narrative Review
container-title: Education for Information
134409bd05e521d5a6bc11cc9a5957b37d242bf9.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly being used by students and is reshaping the way information is accessed, processed, and utilised for academic work and everyday purposes. As the use of AI technologies continues to expand, there is a growing need to discuss the ethical implications associated with the use of generative AI among LIS students. This study employed a narrative review method to analyse and synthesise evidence from existing scholarly literature obtained through various library resources and online databases on the Internet. The study identified several ethical implications regarding the use of generative AI among LIS students, which include breaches of academic integrity, plagiarism risks, misinformation, output bias, privacy and security concerns, reduced critical engagement with learning materials, overdependence on AI systems, fabricated references, and so on. The findings revealed that ethical use of generative AI requires LIS students to critically evaluate AI-generated content, acknowledge AI assistance where necessary, and maintain responsibility for the accuracy and originality of their academic work. The study showed areas for future research directions in ethical concerns of generative AI use among LIS students for responsible AI use in academic practices.</jats:p>

9cbcf754d1f035894fda3592ea4c7a94d12fb539.abstract: <jats:p>Dual mandate - the federal College of Education act 2023 signed by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu legally and officially empowered these institutions to award education degrees while the NCE programmes continues. The Nigerian curriculum for biology at the senior secondary school level is designed to help students develop a range of skills which include understanding biological concepts and principles, application of the knowledge to solve real-life situations, problem solving skills and ability to communicate biological ideas and concepts effectively. Problem based learning is a pedagogical approach that involves students learning through the experience of solving real world problems. It is a student centered approach that encourages critical and creative thinking, collaboration, active learning and application of skills to solve real world problems. Problem based learning can be effectively integrated with STEM subjects; science, technology, education and mathematics. Problem based learning is grounded in several theories like constructivist, social constructivism posits by Vygotsky 1978. Artificial Intelligence has the potential to make up for the shortcomings of traditional problem based learning by giving full account of students reports in the project, timely feedback and helps teachers to monitor students learning outcome. AI tools used in education/science include machine learning algorithms; natural language processing techniques which are used to create personalized learning; AI powered VR or AR are also used.  AI driven PBL used include Khammigo or custom GPT, Google Docs, Padlet AI, Gradescope, Google sheets etc. The global AI in education market size was estimated at USD 5.88 billion in 2024 is projected to grow at Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 31.2% from 2025 to 2030. However, with PBL, the teachers have to provide students with necessary resources e.g. learning materials, tools and technological support as well as guidance. One of the opportunities of integrating AI in education include personalized learning, creating more interactive and immersive learning experiences, games and simulations that boost students confidence, motivation and persistence leading to improved academic achievement.</jats:p>

title: Why Do University Students Use AI: Drivers and Barriers?
container-title: Journal of Higher Education Theory and Practice
4b33af4066ce0da2b4fe8fc20cd5464539c791bf.abstract: <jats:p>As generative artificial intelligence becomes integrated into academic life, understanding what drives student adoption is essential for informed institutional policy. This study examines AI engagement among 672 students at a public midsize southern university, integrating the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) to evaluate eight constructs: perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, perceived trust, perceived risk, social influence, self-efficacy, anxiousness, and affection. Survey data show students frequently use AI for information retrieval and writing assistance, while specialized applications such as graphic and video generation remain underutilized. Regression analysis shows perceived usefulness, affection, and trust are the primary positive predictors of adoption, whereas anxiety and perceived risk are significant deterrents. Notably, affection, the emotional enjoyment of technology, emerged as one of the most consistent motivators across academic tasks, from research to creative ideation. These results suggest emotional and trust-based factors are as critical as functional utility in shaping student behavior. Universities should prioritize emotional comfort and ethical trust alongside technical training to foster responsible, confident AI integration..</jats:p>

title: Enhancing Students' Critical Evaluation of AI Versus Human-Generated Literature Reviews: Deliberative Pedagogy
