title: A CDIO-Based Reform of Advanced Separation Engineering: AI-Supported Curriculum Innovation and Practice
container-title: Education Sciences
b012bd00a96421009e1d2ce45919d420e9788fd9.abstract: <jats:p>Advanced Separation Engineering requires graduate students to connect separation principles with process design and engineering decision-making. Using action research, this study developed and refined a reform based on the Conceive–Design–Implement–Operate (CDIO) framework across four annual offerings from 2022 to 2025. The reform integrated authentic engineering projects, AI-supported learning resources, digital process simulation, collaborative inquiry, and continuous assessment. Course evaluations from the 2021 pre-reform historical cohort (n = 46) were compared with those from the pooled reform cohorts (n = 254), supplemented by open-ended responses and interviews. The reform cohorts reported higher ratings on all five common course-evaluation items, with differences remaining statistically significant after Holm adjustment and Hedges’ g ranging from 1.29 to 2.11. Overall satisfaction averaged 3.41 in the historical cohort and 4.58 in the reform cohorts. On supplementary single-item self-report questions, 91.7% considered the CDIO reform helpful for developing comprehensive engineering competence, and 76.4% reported that AI-supported resources and digital simulation helped them understand complex separation processes. Student feedback identified software learning demands, group coordination, verification of AI outputs, and inconsistent industry-expert participation as continuing challenges. This four-year action research study provides a practice-informed reference for integrating CDIO projects and technological support in graduate engineering courses, based on students’ reported experiences.</jats:p>

title: AI Adoption at Higher Education Institutions: A Call for Designated AI Management
container-title: Education Sciences
d8d7be8d30b7824aa8c81b83b178ad1441b2e5ba.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is transforming teaching, learning and administration in higher education institutions (HEIs), yet responsibility for its governance is rarely assigned. This article develops and empirically tests the profile of an AI Manager for HEIs proposed by the Erasmus+ project FORCE AI. A literature-based definition and nine-area competence profile were examined in a sequential mixed-methods study, a survey of 387 students and staff from 13 countries and five nominal-group focus groups in Germany, Latvia, the Netherlands, and Türkiye in 2025, which tested the elements stakeholders can rate: competences, responsibilities, placement, and qualifications. Only 17% of respondents knew of a designated AI-management responsibility at their institution; of the remainder, 71% considered one necessary and 76% expected an AI Manager to improve their experience. The expected mandate comprised training, ethical oversight, data security and strategy; preferences were split between a dedicated position and a shared cross-functional function. Survey respondents portrayed the role as a compliance-oriented technical specialist, whereas staff-dominated focus groups, rating the same competencies, prioritised leadership, change and project management, and communication alongside AI expertise and ethics; this contrast between methods and samples persists for staff respondents alone. The revised definition and profile position designated AI management, a dedicated AI Manager or a team with an accountable lead, as change leadership with technical credibility and give HEIs a tested basis for establishing this role.</jats:p>

title: Research on the Teaching Practice of AI Teaching Assistants in C Language Programming Courses
container-title: Journal of Education and Educational Research
7f63b566761c25e282747abfd51e236fa5772e2b.abstract: <jats:p>Under the traditional teaching model, C language programming has long faced practical pain points such as high entry barriers for beginners, delayed feedback on programming practice, insufficient supply of tiered teaching, and excessive teaching burden on frontline teachers. This study, with the core support of the human-machine collaborative education concept, explores the normalized implementation path of deeply embedding AI teaching assistants into the entire process of programming classes, and constructs a ternary collaborative teaching framework of "teacher guidance, AI teaching assistance, and student subjectivity". The study simultaneously sorts out practical issues existing in current AI teaching applications, such as superficial problem-solving, excessive dependence of students on technical tools, and insufficient adaptability to curriculum scenarios, and proposes targeted optimization strategies accordingly. Practice has shown that this teaching model can effectively compensate for the shortcomings of traditional classrooms, providing a practical reference for improving the intelligent teaching quality of computer programming courses in universities.</jats:p>

title: The Impact of AI Assistance on the Academic Writing Self-Efficacy of Undergraduates with Different Writing Abilities
container-title: Journal of Education and Educational Research
1f64a67f212a7b328cb7a8f7b29132196170c4ea.abstract: <jats:p>Against digital education background, generative AI has become common writing assistance for undergraduates. Existing studies mainly focus on second-language writing and ignore stratified comparisons across learners, while the dual effects of AI on academic writing self-efficacy remain understudied. Based on self-efficacy theory, this paper distributes questionnaires and divides respondents into three proficiency groups by CET-4 scores. Descriptive statistics, group difference tests and correlation analysis are adopted for empirical analysis. The results reveal prevalent AI over-dependence despite its polishing functions. Participants’ writing self-efficacy stays at medium-upper level yet hampered by writing anxiety. AI delivers short-term confidence promotion but impairs independent writing competence in the long run, with stronger influences on low-proficiency students. This stratified dual-path framework offers empirical references for standardized AI application in university writing teaching.</jats:p>

title: Reimagining adolescent education with ephegogy: generative AI and active learning in practice
container-title: Artificial Intelligence in Education
220e444d9a9e452e785384a5a44dda5c4c02db1e.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper introduces ephegogy, a theory addressing the gap between traditional educational models and adolescents' developmental needs in artificial intelligence (AI)-augmented societies. Blending constructivism, connectivism and generativism, it explores how integrating generative AI (GenAI) and active learning can scaffold motivation, autonomy, and relevance for adolescent learners.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A mixed-methods case study conducted in a single secondary-school geography course during 2024–2025. Quantitative data came from matched pre- and post-intervention surveys measuring motivation and self-efficacy (N = 17; N = 11 for the self-efficacy composite) and locus of control (N = 12), using instruments adapted for an under-14, predominantly English-as-an-additional-language cohort. A separate matched engagement survey (N = 24) and an end-of-course co-creation survey (N = 33) provided further data. Qualitative data comprised 74 individual student reflections analysed thematically using the cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) framework, alongside open-text survey responses from 74 students. The study was designed using three frameworks (self-determination theory, ephegogy and CHAT).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings are associational and exploratory, specific to this pilot. Composite motivation increased significantly (p = 0.043, d = 0.53), led by a significant rise in school enjoyment (p = 0.028). On a separate instrument, confidence in using AI tools showed the largest single increase (p = 0.016) and motivation relative to traditional courses also rose (p = 0.040); as several items were examined, these are treated as exploratory. Self-efficacy and locus of control showed no reliable change. Qualitatively, choice, the learning contract, and resource autonomy were dominant themes; most students disclosed and reflected on their AI use, and the modal student experience was ambivalent, valuing autonomy while finding it demanding.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As a single pilot case study with small, matched samples, no control group and a single teacher-researcher as sole coder, findings are context-specific and cannot support causal claims. Future research should evaluate the framework with larger samples, control conditions, and across diverse cultural contexts and disciplines.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ephegogy provides actionable strategies for scaffolding student autonomy and ethical AI use within project-based learning. Tools such as the Student-Author Voice (SAV) rubric support metacognitive reflection and responsible co-creation, assessing authored voice rather than relying on AI detection.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ephegogy provides actionable strategies for scaffolding student autonomy and ethical AI use within project-based learning. Tools such as the SAV rubric support metacognitive reflection and responsible co-creation, assessing authored voice rather than relying on AI detection.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ephegogy reconceptualises adolescent education for the AI era as a distinct developmental stage requiring its own framework, operationalised through gradual immersion and the assessment of authored voice. This paper reports an initial classroom pilot offering preliminary, transferable insights rather than confirmatory evidence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: From Promise to Peril: generative artificial intelligence's potential to deepen educational inequalities in geographically diverse contexts
container-title: Artificial Intelligence in Education
a8d1eef8843dd8135aaec6dcc6aee4026960d314.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study critically examines how van Dijk's Digital Divide Theory applies to generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) access in regional, remote and rural (RRR) educational contexts. It interrogates whether a framework designed for standardised digital tools adequately captures GenAI-specific barriers, while mapping where existing research concentrates and where significant gaps remain across van Dijk's four dimensions of access.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A scoping review was conducted using the Population, Concept, Context (PCC) framework across four academic databases, with AI-assisted Boolean search development validated through pilot testing and supervisory oversight. Strict inclusion criteria focused on peer-reviewed publications examining GenAI in RRR educational settings. Twenty-nine articles were analysed using van Dijk's four-dimensional framework: material access, skills access, usage access and motivational access.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Material and skills access emerged as the most researched dimensions, with material access representing a necessary but insufficient condition for equitable GenAI engagement and skills access requiring interventions across student, educator and policy levels simultaneously. Usage patterns cannot be assumed to follow naturally from material and skills access, requiring sustained time investment, pedagogical framing and institutional support. Motivational access remained critically under-researched, with only one study explicitly examining this dimension. The synthesis suggests sequential relationships across the four dimensions, where foundational precursors in material, skills and usage shape the conditions under which motivational engagement develops. This sequential pattern is presented as a provisional theoretical proposition warranting targeted empirical investigation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The interconnected nature of access barriers creates systemic constraints extending beyond van Dijk's original conceptualisation. The synthesis suggests that sequential relationships between dimensions help explain why motivational access remains under-researched, with GenAI lacking foundational precursors necessary for widespread motivational engagement in RRR communities. Evidence-based policy addressing material and skills dimensions becomes essential for preventing systematic exclusion from GenAI's transformative educational potential.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research reveals that GenAI introduces a less visible form of digital exclusion in regional, remote and rural (RRR) educational contexts. Unlike previous digital divides characterised by observable access deficits, GenAI enables superficially sophisticated outputs from shallow engagement. This produces performative usage, defined here as the production of well-formed GenAI outputs that mask shallow understanding of subject content. Students in RRR communities may appear to use GenAI productively while developing neither subject mastery nor critical evaluation skills. Educational institutions serving RRR populations must therefore develop context-specific assessment frameworks capable of distinguishing between performative and meaningful GenAI engagement, ensuring that technology deployment addresses rather than obscures the educational disadvantages these communities already experience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research highlights that motivational disengagement from GenAI in regional, remote and rural (RRR) communities emerges not from technology rejection but from cascading structural barriers. When infrastructure deficits create skills gaps and repeated failure diminishes perceived effort-to-benefit ratios, self-reinforcing cycles of technological disengagement develop that persist even when access improves. Motivational access remains the least researched dimension of GenAI's digital divide, despite being central to the conditions under which other access dimensions translate into sustained engagement. Policymakers and educational institutions serving RRR communities must recognise that addressing material and skills barriers alone proves insufficient without concurrent attention to how these compounding disadvantages shape willingness and aspiration to engage with GenAI technologies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study provides the first application of van Dijk's Digital Divide Theory as an analytical framework for examining generative artificial intelligence education research in regional, remote and rural (RRR) contexts. Theoretically, it proposes a provisional reconceptualisation of van Dijk's sequential dimensions, suggesting that material access supports skills development, which supports usage patterns, which subsequently shape motivational engagement. This proposition offers a coherent explanation for why motivational access remains critically under-researched in RRR communities, namely that foundational precursors necessary for motivational engagement are themselves absent. title: Ethnic AI instructor: when a minority professor uses AI voice-over tools
container-title: Quarterly Review of Distance Education
f3233122ad1d540d56f1b49985d9ee1a78ea64d6.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Student evaluations of teaching influence faculty promotion and tenure decisions, yet research demonstrates these evaluations systematically reflect instructor demographic characteristics independent of teaching quality. As online education expands and instructors increasingly adopt AI technologies like text-to-speech voice narration, questions arise about whether racial bias and AI skepticism interact to create compounded disadvantages for minority instructors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using a 2×2 experimental design (Instructor race: White vs. Asian × Voice type: Human vs AI-generated), 172 undergraduate students evaluated identical online lecture content. Instructors were identified through photographs and names.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Results showed significant racial bias with the White instructor rated higher than the Asian instructor across evaluation dimensions. Students also rated the AI-voiced lecture significantly worse than the human-voiced lecture across all evaluation dimensions. While voice type did not moderate the race effect statistically, simple effects analyses revealed that racial bias was manifested within the AI voice condition. Perceived social presence mediated voice type effects on evaluations. Students' comfort with AI technology moderated voice type effects, with the AI discount effect weakening among high-comfort students.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Racial bias in student evaluations persists regardless of voice types, while AI-generated voices substantially reduce evaluations through decreased social presence. These findings have practical implications for equitable faculty assessment as institutions adopt AI technologies and for instructors from racial minority groups who face evaluation penalties independent of teaching quality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study is among the first to examine how racial bias and AI voice technology intersect in student evaluations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title:
When
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    Anxiety Coexists With Capability:
                    <scp>ICT</scp>
                    Self‐Efficacy and Institutional Support in Preservice Teacher Education
container-title: European Journal of Education
8023ff8220c7abd1981190c02480790dc714cdd7.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Preparing preservice teachers for AI‐enabled teaching requires understanding anxiety alongside perceived capability and self‐regulated learning (SRL). Drawing on data from 12,147 third‐year preservice teachers across 17 Chinese institutions, this study combined structural equation modelling, observed‐score moderation, and latent profile analysis. Four profiles emerged: the Moderate Profile, the Lower‐Efficacy, Lower‐SRL Profile, the Low‐Anxiety, Higher‐SRL Profile, and the High‐Anxiety, Higher‐SRL Profile. The two higher‐SRL profiles shared high ICT self‐efficacy despite contrasting anxiety levels. AI anxiety was positively associated with ICT self‐efficacy, which was strongly associated with SRL. Perceived institutional ICT support strengthened the anxiety–efficacy association. These complementary findings identify perceived capability as a key differentiator of regulated learning across anxiety levels. Teacher‐education programmes can assess anxiety, efficacy, and SRL together and provide practice opportunities and institutional resources that support learning.</jats:p>

title: Digital borders, algorithmic governance and civic digital literacy: examining the educational implications of AI-driven immigration management in post-apartheid South Africa
container-title: Frontiers in Education
75c979d57f44775da1be193368ae35484957aa5e.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>South Africa is moving towards AI-based digital border management, including biometric screening, drone-supported aerial surveillance and the Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) system. This paper explores the educational consequences of that shift, with a special focus on the civic digital literacy that algorithmic immigration governance requires of citizens, policymakers and educators.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study takes a qualitative, interpretive approach, drawing on critical digital pedagogy, algorithmic accountability theory and postcolonial education studies. It synthesises peer-reviewed scholarly works, policy documents and grey literature on the Border Management Authority's use of biometric surveillance, drone technology and the ETA system. A corpus of 53 sources was screened through an adapted PRISMA-style procedure and analysed through a three-phase thematic synthesis that produced five descriptive and three analytical themes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI-based border governance exposes a pressing and largely ignored digital literacy gap. The communities most affected by algorithmic immigration decisions are those without the conceptual tools to engage with, debate or take part in the governance of the AI systems that regulate their lives and rights. Standard digital literacy programmes are not sufficient to equip learners with the knowledge to participate in the governance of algorithmically driven systems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Geography and social sciences education has a special role in equipping learners with the skills needed for critical AI citizenship. The study proposes that algorithmic governance be incorporated into the school curriculum, that community-facing digital civic education programmes be developed, and that participatory AI accountability structures be established in border management. The study advances digital learning innovation by theorising civic AI literacy as a new educational priority in the Global South and by showing that algorithmic governance necessitates a fundamental redefinition of digital citizenship education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Teacher competence and institutional governance for learner data privacy in AI mediated education
container-title: Frontiers in Education
fc8047ffcdeed230dceddf5aa7850917318e1c06.abstract: <jats:p>Teachers can recognise a privacy problem yet lack the authority or resources needed to act on that judgement. Conversely, institutions can provide technically safeguarded services while teachers disclose unnecessary information or accept unsupported inferences. This Hypothesis and Theory article develops the Learner Data Protection Competence and Governance Framework to explain these two failures. A purposive conceptual synthesis connects contextual integrity with distinctions between demonstrated competence, confidence, perceived control and actual institutional provision. The framework relates risk recognition, defensible decisions, institutional enablement and accountable review. Its central prediction distinguishes support that complements professional judgement in discretionary tasks from safeguards that substitute for particular skills in constrained tasks. A second central prediction separates access to reporting, implementation of corrective action and subsequent recurrence. Three supporting propositions address recognition, confidence calibration and purpose-specific authorisation. Each proposition specifies separate measures, rival explanations and conditions for disconfirmation. Two hypothetical cases illustrate competing educational and privacy considerations and show why institutional approval is insufficient to establish ethical justification. A bounded application to teacher education and school placements in Zambia identifies context-informed predictions concerning divided authority, advice latency, language and connectivity. The framework offers an explanatory model with normative criteria and assessment implications. Neither the reviewed evidence nor the worked cases validate its causal relationships or demonstrate reduced privacy harm; the contribution is a more discriminating and testable account of how professional judgement interacts with institutional arrangements.</jats:p>

title: Generative AI Use and Critical Thinking among University Students
container-title: Lecture Notes in Education Psychology and Public Media
821cfb063f1211d21187ef0c214f37fa5504cfe5.abstract: <jats:p>How students use artificial intelligence and what they learn from it cannot be ignored. According to how often people use AI tools, the groups were divided, and then descriptive statistics, Welch's ANOVA test and independent-sample t-tests were carried out to compare the critical-thinking scores of these groups. Based on the above description, the mean critical-thinking scores of the four groups using AI are relatively high. However, Welch's ANOVA showed that there were no significant differences among the four groups (F(3, 24.71) = 1.586, p = .218). The two groups were divided into regular and non-regular AI users; the mean critical-thinking scores of the regular-use group (50.06) and the non-regular-use group (45.42) were significantly higher for the regular-use group; t(100) = 2.948, p = .004, and Cohen's d = .750. Based on the above results, the impact of AI on students' critical thinking ability is not straightforward; it may vary according to how they use AI. AI can help students learn better by learning to think independently; however, if they rely on AI too much, they may not develop their own thinking skills. Given the small sample size, uneven distribution of groups, self-reported data, cross-sectional design, etc., only associations can be concluded from the results and not cause-and-effect relationships.</jats:p>

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Language Learning: Cognitive Mechanisms, Theoretical Tensions, and Ethical Governance
container-title: Lecture Notes in Education Psychology and Public Media
0796b58d89d60973e3d08c8cbd763f0b2a7a0bac.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the environment of language learning, but its theoretical basis and ethical boundaries have not been fully explored. This paper builds a multi-level analytical system for AI-assisted language learning based on cognitive load theory, the zone of proximal development, generative linguistics and the technology acceptance model. AI can help students learn better by reducing extraneous cognitive load and providing easy-to-access support and instant correction; however, due to technological limitations, it may also reduce students' sense of ability and self-management. Generative linguistics and generative AI are not in opposition; rather, the former advocates for data frugality and innate mechanisms, while the latter is characterized by data maximalism and statistical learning; they are in harmony at the level of third factors and the Minimalist Program. According to the above research, chatbots have shown a modest positive effect on language learning; this degree varies depending on the learner's level, interface Design, interaction characteristics, etc. Based on the above, this paper introduces a "Smart Chinese" collaborative learning plugin that integrates ChatGPT with special scaffolding tools for assessment, planning, practice, feedback and community support. Finally, it presents the ethical problems of algorithmic bias, data privacy, over-reliance, and educational gaps, and proposes a multi-level governance system at the institutional, technological and pedagogical levels.</jats:p>

title: Future Faculty Development in the Age of AI: University Teachers’ Roles, Needs, and Institutional Support
container-title: Frontiers of Digital Education
badf99c98fa48d62567058c9a1da8fbd985e698a.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>AI is reshaping higher education in ways that extend beyond the adoption of new tools, challenging established assumptions about assessment, curriculum, ethics, graduate preparation, and the work of university teachers. Drawing on insights from the Teacher Panel at the International Conference on GenAI and Pedagogical Innovations held in Hong Kong in May 2026, this commentary argues that faculty development in the AI era must move beyond generic technology training towards a more role-based, discipline-sensitive, future-oriented, and ecosystemic approach. The commentary identifies four key insights from the panel discussion: AI use is already widespread and assessment has become an immediate pressure point; AI literacy is necessary but insufficient without disciplinary, professional, ethical, and human-centred dimensions; universities must connect learning more explicitly with the authentic world beyond campus while renewing the role of the campus as a site of experimentation and futures literacy; and institutions need stronger capacity for evidence-informed, forward-looking AI governance. Building on these insights, the commentary proposes seven emerging roles for university teachers: human-centred educator; disciplinary and professional expert; learning architect and intellectual guide; assessment (re)designer; technically competent and critically informed professional; ethical steward; and educational experimenter and evidence-based practitioner. Corresponding faculty development needs are then discussed, including support for human-centred education, curriculum renewal, world-connected learning, assessment redesign, technical-pedagogical AI capability, ethical stewardship, AI policy literacy, and scholarship-informed educational improvement. The commentary concludes with a preliminary role-based framework for faculty development. It emphasises that these roles need not be performed by a single individual teacher. Rather, as educational design and delivery become more complex in the age of AI, university education should increasingly be understood as a collective endeavour involving academic staff, educational developers, technology specialists, professional staff, students, external partners, employers, and community organisations.</jats:p>

title: Teachers’ self-reported AI literacy across educational levels in Greece: Awareness without conceptual depth?
container-title: International Journal of Research Studies in Education
71fccc939e629043e8b58d2572a3d9d8ae16f21d.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is increasingly recognized as an essential teacher competence, yet evidence concerning its dimensional structure and variation across educational sectors remains limited. This study investigated self-reported AI literacy among 1,173 in-service teachers in primary, secondary, and higher education in Greece, examining its empirical structure, overall levels, and associations with prior AI-related training and teaching level, while accounting for academic qualifications. Data were collected through a researcher-developed questionnaire and analyzed using exploratory factor analysis, descriptive statistics, and general linear models. Two dimensions emerged: Conceptual–Technical AI Literacy and Critical–Ethical AI Literacy, while Practical AI Use was retained as a separate indicator. Overall self-reported AI literacy was relatively low, with substantially higher scores on critical–ethical indicators than on conceptual–technical indicators, suggesting a profile of perceived awareness without corresponding conceptual depth. Prior AI-related training was positively associated with all AI-literacy outcomes across educational sectors. However, significant teaching-level × training interactions revealed particularly strong associations in higher education, especially for Conceptual–Technical AI Literacy. These findings highlight the multidimensional and context-sensitive nature of teachers’ self-reported AI literacy and the importance of distinguishing perceived confidence from demonstrated competence. They underscore the need for differentiated, pedagogically grounded professional development that integrates conceptual understanding, practical AI applications, critical evaluation, and ethical judgment across educational sectors.</jats:p>

title: Educational Pathways for AI-Empowered General Education: A Case Study of "Introduction to Artificial Intelligence"
container-title: Education Insights
b09e63fa5059c587eb5980dca64552886e091666.abstract: <jats:p>General education-a critical arena for cultivating interdisciplinary and innovative talents in higher education-faces structural dilemmas such as outdated content, undiversified pathways, and disconnection from industry demands. Taking tourism colleges as the empirical setting, this study draws on the theories of competency-based education (CBE) and outcome-based education (OBE) to explore educational pathways for AI-empowered general education courses. A three-tier progressive competency map spanning cognition, application, and creation was constructed; a modular curriculum system driven by the dual engines of OBE and project-based learning (PBL) was designed; and a spiral action research mechanism was introduced for empirical validation in teaching practice. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed pathway effectively addresses such challenges as the lack of vehicles for cultivating AI literacy among non-computer-science students and the mismatch between curriculum provision and industry demands, thereby achieving a value leap of general education from "inward talent cultivation" to "outward empowerment." The closed-loop paradigm of "demand insight–curriculum reconstruction–practical validation–outcome transformation" proposed in this study offers a replicable model for the digital-intelligent reform of general education in application-oriented universities.</jats:p>

title: Green AI-Driven Synthetic Data Generation for Improved Industrial Metal Surface Defect Detection
container-title: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF COMPUTERS  COMMUNICATIONS & CONTROL
7cb4bdcba33492ba6826438a8e4421a4967bef1a.abstract:
<jats:p>Defect detection of industrial metal surfaces is often limited by the scarcity of annotated data and the high cost of manual labeling, which limits the performance of data-driven inspection systems. This paper presents a Green AI-driven framework for synthetic data generation that efficiently augments industrial defect datasets while minimizing computational and annotation costs. The proposed approach employs a deterministic procedural pipeline to generate synthetic defect images together with aligned segmentation masks at the pixel-level, providing accurate supervision without the computational overhead of deep generative models. The framework is evaluated on the Kolektor Surface-Defect Dataset 2 (KSDD2), which is extended into a hybrid dataset through synthetic augmentation followed by human-in-the-loop validation, to ensure the realism and reliability of the generated samples and annotations. A lightweight state-of-the-art anomaly detection model, SuperSimpleNet, is trained under controlled ablation settings on both the original and hybrid datasets using identical test splits for fair comparison.
Performance is evaluated using both image-level and pixel-level metrics, including AUROC and average precision. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid dataset consistently improves defect detection and localization performance while substantially reducing the need for costly data acquisition and manual annotation. Unlike computationally intensive generative approaches based on GANs or diffusion models, the proposed procedural framework synthesizes defects directly within predefined regions, enabling automatic generation of pixel-accurate ground-truth annotations without human intervention. The resulting hybrid dataset improves all evaluation metrics, achieving the largest gain in anomaly localization performance, with AP-loc increasing by 5.3%, while image-level AUROC increases from 0.9840 to 0.9907. By combining efficient synthetic data generation with precise automatic annotation, the proposed approach provides a resource-efficient solution that aligns with Green AI principles.</jats:p>

title: The Role of Integrated TPACK in Empowering Pre-Service Teachers and Shaping Their Attitudes Toward Generative AI in Teaching
container-title: Education Sciences
35854f9e2231ff6ce271a65b4859a8e4227ea547.abstract: <jats:p>This study examined whether pre-service teachers’ Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) integrated with generative AI is associated with their attitudes toward generative AI. Using a cross-sectional questionnaire, data were collected from a convenience sample of 988 pre-service teachers in Egypt and Oman. A 33-item instrument measured Technological Knowledge (TK), Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (TPK), Technological Content Knowledge (TCK), integrated TPACK, and, with a single item, attitudes toward generative AI. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses and structural equation modeling (SEM) were conducted. The four-factor model showed acceptable fit and convergent validity, but discriminant validity was not supported (HTMT = 0.92–0.99), and the predictors were highly collinear (VIF up to 10.42). TCK (β = 0.67, p < 0.001) and TPK (β = 0.41, p = 0.025) predicted integrated TPACK, whereas TK did not (β = −0.10, p = 0.066); given the overlap among constructs, these individual paths are tentative. Integrated TPACK was strongly associated with the single-item attitude measure (β = 0.75, p < 0.001; R2 = 0.563). Gender differences did not survive Holm correction, and academic-year differences were medium in size. Teacher preparation programs may benefit from integrating AI with pedagogy and content, and future work should use performance-based measures and multi-item attitude scales.</jats:p>

title: Exploring Faculty Readiness for Generative AI Integration in UAE Higher Education
container-title: Education Sciences
75720d048015cfc6320500c4012b0aadcff97299.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid emergence of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has reshaped higher education by extending AI use beyond specialized applications into broader academic practices. Although student adoption has occurred rapidly, effective integration of generative AI in teaching and learning depends largely on faculty readiness and institutional support. This study conducted a preliminary examination of self-reported faculty AI readiness and adoption among 144 faculty members who responded to a cross-sectional quantitative survey distributed across higher education institutions in the United Arab Emirates. Exploratory factor analysis identified five dimensions of faculty AI engagement: AI Awareness and Literacy, AI Teaching Use, Perceived AI Benefits, Institutional Support, and Personal Readiness. The findings indicate that respondents reported high self-perceived AI Awareness and Literacy and comparatively lower AI Teaching Use. However, Spearman correlations showed that AI Teaching Use was positively associated with both AI Awareness and Literacy and Perceived AI Benefits, with a stronger association observed for Perceived AI Benefits. Individual faculty characteristics, including academic rank, discipline, and teaching experience, were not significantly associated with differences in AI engagement, whereas institutional context was associated with variation in perceived support and benefits. These findings suggest that strengthening faculty AI adoption requires universities to move beyond awareness-building toward providing clear pedagogical guidance, appropriate infrastructure, and targeted professional development opportunities.</jats:p>

title: Association of Preexamination AI Virtual-Patient Trainer Scores With Scores on a Local Single-Station History-Taking Objective Structured Clinical Examination: Observational Cohort Study
container-title: JMIR Medical Education
7ccc0fe5a5c60bed5908dcbb21009564b4d40558.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Large language model–based virtual-patient systems score history-taking practice, but whether scores correspond to independently scored examination performance remains untested. Existing evaluations emphasize internal platform metrics or simulated-patient fidelity, leaving criterion-related evidence limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study tests whether mean preexamination AI-trainer practice scores were associated with performance on 1 local objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) history-taking station, whether the association depended on the complaint-matched training case, and whether a model including the trainer score retained predictive performance in held-out students.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>At 1 medical school, second-year students received a required 6-case assignment on the AI-Powered Medical History-Taking Training and Evaluation System (AMTES) and completed an end-of-course OSCE. Each student completed 1 station rated by 1 examiner; interrater and cross-station reliability could not be estimated. The 4 OSCE diagnoses differed from the training diagnoses: 3 shared a presenting-complaint category with an AMTES case, whereas 1 OSCE case had no presenting-complaint match. Platform-to-OSCE record linkage was 474 out of 480 (98.8%); 473 students with analyzable preexamination practice formed the analytic sample. The primary predictor was the mean of normalized scores across practice records time-stamped before each student’s examination-day cut-off. Analyses used Spearman correlations, OSCE-case fixed-effects regression, and repeated 5-fold cross-validation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>OSCE scores (mean 81.5, SD 6.7) were associated with platform practice scores (Spearman ρ=0.388; P<.001). With OSCE-case fixed effects, each 1SD increase in the platform score corresponded to a 2.83-point increase in the OSCE score (95% CI 2.26-3.39). The association was observed in the AMTES-unmatched low back/flank pain stratum (Spearman ρ=0.370; n=108) and with a leave-matched-case-out score (Spearman ρ=0.398 vs 0.370 for the full mean among the same 339 students). Under a single cohort-wide cut-off at the first examination day, the association attenuated but persisted among the same 469 students (Spearman ρ decreased from 0.385 to 0.346; paired difference −0.040, 95% CI −0.065 to −0.018; regression coefficient decreased from 2.83 to 2.68 points per SD). In repeated 5-fold cross-validation (n=471), the platform-only model achieved Spearman ρ=0.374 and R2=0.176. Adding the platform score to the 2 prior physical-examination course scores increased cross-validated R2 from 0.141 to 0.236 (ΔR2=0.096; 95% CI 0.053-0.142). Adding practice volume and case breadth did not improve performance (ΔR2=−0.002).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By linking required curricular practice scores to the score on 1 independently scored local OSCE history-taking station, this observational study provides criterion-related evidence for interpreting AMTES scores. The association did not depend on including the complaint-matched training-case score. The scores also added predictive information beyond the 2 prior physical-examination course scores in internal cross-validation. These findings establish neither causal effects of practice nor within-student transfer, and residual confounding by prior ability cannot be excluded. They support further evaluation of AMTES analytics as a candidate low-stakes formative signal, with independent external validation required before operational use.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Exploration of Precise Teaching Pathways for Integrating Ideological and Political Education into University Economics and Management Courses via AI Technology
container-title: Academic Journal of Education
01d95a78b7ca43af16daddd814ee513f30df34ed.abstract: <jats:p>The deepening implementation of educational digitalization strategies, coupled with the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, has opened up new possibilities for achieving precision-oriented ideological and political education in economics and management courses. Currently, such education faces three practical challenges: value disconnection, fragmented competency development, and a lack of feedback mechanisms; consequently, traditional teaching approaches often fail to organically integrate value guidance, knowledge transmission, and competency cultivation. Building upon a rigorous definition of "precision-oriented teaching," this study constructs a three-stage integration model— "value–knowledge–competency" —and employs a data chain to vertically connect the value guidance layer, the knowledge construction layer, and the competency cultivation layer, thereby establishing a closed-loop, interconnected educational system. On this foundation, the study systematically designs AI-driven implementation pathways for precision-oriented teaching across three instructional phases—pre-class, in-class, and post-class—supported by a collaborative learning community comprising "teacher–student–AI" and corresponding safeguard mechanisms. This research demonstrates that AI technology serves as a pivotal variable in transitioning course-based ideological and political education from an "experience-driven" paradigm to a "data-evidenced" approach, and from a "linear additive" model to a "spiral symbiotic" framework. Furthermore, AI can provide systematic pathway references to overcome the three key difficulties in integrating such education into economics and management curricula: integration challenges, evaluation challenges, and coherence challenges.</jats:p>

title: <b>Enhancing EFL students’ reading comprehension through AI-assisted tools: Evidence from Islamic higher education institutions</b>
container-title: Englisia: Journal of Language, Education, and Humanities
1579b62aac4019c1bbd57abf702ea1f61015ac6c.abstract: <jats:p>The study examined the use of AI-assisted reading teaching to improve EFL students’ reading comprehension and the students’ perception of the use of AI in conducting Extensive Reading exercises in an Islamic higher education setting. A quasi-experimental pre-test-post-test control group design was employed with 32 fourth-semester English education students. In the experimental group, 17 pupils used Google Gemini for reading tasks and 15 students in the control group received standard instruction. The intervention was four weeks long. Reading comprehension was measured using 20 item essay test . Students’ impression was measured using five point likert scale questionnaire . The experimental group’s mean score rose from 63.94 on the pretest to 82.65 on the posttest, whereas the control group’s score rose from 68.87 to 74.27. The gain scores differed significantly between the two groups (t(30) = 13.90, p <.001). ANCOVA revealed that after accounting for pre-test scores, the groups differed significantly in post-test performance (F(1,29) = 145.36, p <.001, partial η 2 =.834). Students also had positive Attitudes toward AI assisted reading with an overall mean of 4.39; the highest evaluations were for engagement (M=4.50) and usefulness (M=4.40). These results suggest that generative artificial intelligence may be a focused cognitive support in conjunction with active reading, critical evaluation, and student responsibility for their own learning. The study emphasizes the necessity of incorporating cognitive support, technology acceptance and learner autonomy in the application of AI in EFL reading education.</jats:p>

title: Digital learning anxiety and UTAUT predictors of university students’ intention to use generative artificial intelligence in Ghana
container-title: Frontiers in Education
f04d8588d14cdb97b2f469dc54b96c7f9bc72af4.abstract: <jats:p>This study investigates the factors associated with university students’ intention to use Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in Ghana, with particular attention to the role of psychological barriers in shaping technology use intention. This study extends the UTAUT model by incorporating the concept of digital learning anxiety in understanding the psychological dimension of students using generative AI. The study employed a quantitative approach using a cross-sectional survey design, with data analyzed through covariance-based structural equation modeling (CB-SEM). The sample consisted of 350 university students in Ghana. Structural equation modeling and a bias-corrected percentile bootstrapping method were conducted in AMOS (v 23) to estimate the path coefficients. The results showed that performance expectancy and effort expectancy were positively associated with students’ intention to use GenAI. Additionally, a significant but small indirect association was found between effort expectancy and behavioral intention through digital learning anxiety. However, the findings indicate the insignificant influence of social influence. This study contributes to the literature by providing context-specific evidence from Ghanaian higher education on the role of Digital Learning Anxiety in students’ intention to use GenAI. However, because the study used cross-sectional data, this indirect relationship should be interpreted as an association rather than evidence of a causal mechanism. The findings suggest that students’ intention to use GenAI is associated with both their perceptions of the technology and their psychological responses to its use. These findings provide context-specific evidence on GenAI acceptance among the students surveyed.</jats:p>

title: Disciplinary thinking and AI perception: a case study of undergraduate students’ evaluation of an AI music quiz
container-title: Frontiers in Education
52cdec1a1c2fed1b1ea3e1b4cb57b1774a6bbed2.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Artificial intelligence in the form of Large Language Models is increasingly being incorporated into music education, yet much of the existing literature concentrates on composition, performance, assessment, creativity, and teacher adoption rather than music humanities education. This article examines student responses to Mystic Melodies, a gamified adaptive-difficulty AI quiz used in a compulsory first-year musicology unit at the Sydney Conservatorium of Music.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Students attended a one-hour lecture and then completed the quiz based on the lecture content during a one-hour tutorial. The quiz used short answer questions, adaptive difficulty, hints, immediate feedback, explanatory teaching points, and a quest narrative in which correct responses generated gifts while incorrect responses withheld them.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thirty-four post-activity surveys comprising five-point Likert items and open-ended questions were received. The quantitative data show that students felt positive about how well they understood the topic, but were divided about all other aspects of their app experience. The qualitative data suggests an explanation for this pattern. Several critical comments point to concerns about humanities learning, expert teaching, independent thinking, meaningful feedback, and the limits of correct-incorrect quiz logic.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This intervention highlighted a design problem: in music humanities education, AI-supported activities may be accepted as useful review or feedback tools, but they risk resistance when students perceive them as replacing expert-led, interpretive, or dialogic forms of learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Good questions, sound measurement? Item-writing quality, psychometric functioning, and competence-level alignment of AI-generated multiple-choice assessments in chemistry education
container-title: Frontiers in Education
de42925ef649e5b0368565ce87dd340d73215762.abstract: <jats:p>Generative AI is increasingly used in education, yet evidence on the quality and validity of AI-generated assessments in science remains limited. This study examines whether large language models can support the development of high-quality multiple-choice tests in secondary-school chemistry. Using GPT-4, we generated an electrochemistry test from the curriculum and evaluated item quality against established item-writing criteria. The instrument was administered to 95 students at the end of an electrochemistry unit. Psychometric functioning was examined with Rasch modelling, and competence-level alignment was investigated through scale anchoring. The AI-generated items generally satisfied item-writing standards, with strengths in curricular alignment, alongside recurrent weaknesses in specialized language and option-length balance. Rasch analyses indicated acceptable fit and a stable item hierarchy, with measurement precision concentrated in the mid-ability range and distractor quality varying across items. Alignment between intended competence levels and empirical levels was weak, indicating that competence-level claims cannot be inferred from empirical difficulty alone. This study is, to our knowledge, the first in chemistry to generate a curriculum-anchored multiple-choice test with an LLM and evaluate it with mixed methods. Taken together, AI-generated items can serve as an initial draft requiring human oversight, with expert review and model-based checks before any consequential use.</jats:p>

title: From competency to conscientization: a Freirean critical AI literacy framework for post-secondary education
container-title: Frontiers in Education
2e4ea1b29cf3b6e254001dc56174969048acf42b.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) literacy frameworks in post-secondary education has generated a substantial body of competency-based scholarship focused on technical understanding, applied use, evaluation of AI outputs, and ethical awareness. These contributions are necessary, yet competency specification can leave under-theorized the pedagogical process through which learners move from critical evaluation toward conscientization and transformative action. To that extent, competency-oriented AI literacy risks functioning as a domesticating rather than a liberating educational practice. Drawing on Paulo Freire's theory of conscientization, generative themes, problem-posing education, and praxis, this conceptual paper proposes the Freirean Critical AI Literacy (FCAIL) framework. The paper makes three contributions. Theoretically, FCAIL derives its architecture from specific Freirean educational concepts rather than using Freirean vocabulary to support conclusions reached by other means. Architecturally, FCAIL organizes AI literacy around four interrelated dimensions, each pairing a learner capacity with the educational conditions that enable or constrain it: AI World-Reading, the capacity to read AI as socially and historically produced; Contradiction Naming, the capacity to articulate lived AI-mediated tensions as objects of structural inquiry; Critical Praxis, the capacity to connect critical analysis with action; and Solidary Conscientization, the capacity for shared analysis and collective claim-making. Integratively, FCAIL places Freirean critical pedagogy and decolonial AI scholarship in structural relationship: Freirean theory specifies educational conditions for developing critical consciousness, while decolonial AI scholarship identifies the epistemological stakes for marginalized communities. The decolonial dimension is constitutive across the framework because critical AI literacy remains theoretically incomplete if it does not engage the colonial knowledge hierarchies embedded in AI systems. The paper develops implications for pedagogy, curriculum design, assessment, and institutional governance, positions FCAIL as a complement to competency frameworks, and identifies priorities for empirical research.</jats:p>

title: Awareness of Generative AI Limitations and Students’ Intention to Use ChatGPT: A Moderated Mediation Analysis
container-title: Journal of Advanced Research in Education
2b83fad3d16665e8e1efb29889de46a07511e57c.abstract: <jats:p>This research examined the importance of understanding generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) limitations in predicting college students’ likelihood of using ChatGPT, based on a modified Technology Acceptance Model. It treated awareness, perceived usefulness, and perceived anxiety about skills deterioration related to GenAI as independent variables, with intention to use ChatGPT as the dependent variable. The first-stage moderated mediation model was applied to analyze participants’ responses, with cooperation from 931 college students from different fields of study at a private higher education institution in the Philippines. The findings revealed that the awareness of GenAI limitations exerted a positive impact on the intention of college students to use ChatGPT, in particular, both its direct positive effect (c’ = 0.169, p < .001) and an indirect effect through the mediation of perceived usefulness. Conditional process analysis confirmed that skill-erosion concern moderated the relationship between awareness and perceived usefulness (moderated mediation index = -0.075, 95% CI [-0.107, -0.046]). Although perceived usefulness remained a significant mediator of the relationship between awareness and intention, the indirect effect diminished as skill-erosion concern increased, dropping from 0.233 for students with low-little concern to 0.105 for students with great concern. The collinearity analysis confirmed that the predictors were empirically distinguishable. The findings show that beliefs about risks regulate the technology acceptance process, and that AI-literacy training can be pursued alongside measured caution about dependency rather than treating these goals as alternatives.</jats:p>

title: From Computational Literacy to Algorithmic Agency: Re-Envisioning Researcher Preparation in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence
container-title: Frontiers of Digital Education
13463932f07152ed999f9dcaabfdd4e63902716d.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) systems has fundamentally altered the epistemological conditions under which educational research is conducted, rendering existing faculty preparation frameworks necessary but insufficient. Building on a call for a computational mindset and subsequent work on educational data literacy, this article proposes a three-stage developmental progression culminating in algorithmic agency, which is the capacity to critically co-construct scientific knowledge with large language models and automated analytical pipelines while maintaining methodological rigor and preserving human epistemic authority. Unlike prior frameworks, which conceive of artificial intelligence as an analytical instrument under human direction, algorithmic agency addresses the qualitatively distinct challenge posed by GenAI systems that function as epistemic participants capable of synthesizing literature, constructing arguments, and producing knowledge claims that enter scholarly discourse alongside human-authored work. To operationalize this progression, we propose the Co-Intelligent Academic Practice (CAP) framework, a theoretically grounded developmental architecture comprising four cumulative competency domains organized across three developmental stages. A methodology integrating design and systems thinking provides the developmental process through which faculty build and sustain these competencies. We further argue that individual competency development is insufficient without commensurate institutional enablement, including governed infrastructure, value-aligned policy, scholarly recognition, community-based developmental support, and equitable global participation. The article concludes by identifying empirical validation of the CAP staging model as the field’s most urgent methodological priority and arguing that faculty development is the primary institutional lever through which epistemic norms for the co-intelligent era are established or abandoned.</jats:p>

title: Secure Edge-AI Sensing on an FPGA SoC: Lightweight ASCON Authentication of Model Updates and Interface-Bound Inference for Bearing-Fault Detection
container-title: Computers
303d4ba538744ba35fa73581feb18063f5c07d26.abstract: <jats:p>Vibration monitoring increasingly classifies on the sensing node. We ask where the cost of running and securely updating a small classifier on an FPGA system-on-chip node lies. One Q4.12 multilayer perceptron for bearing-fault detection, trained on 40 CWRU recordings over four loads and three severities, is deployed bit-exactly on an ESP32-S3, a Cortex-A53 and a custom AXI4-Lite accelerator of the same Zynq UltraScale+ device (Kria KV260), checked on all 2132 windows. The fabric computes one inference in 36 cycles (0.36 µs), yet the latency under the PYNQ driver is 133.2 µs; a native-C driver reduces it to 3.59 µs, placing 95–97% of the per-transaction cost in the host software stack. Moving the update decision into the fabric, with the ASCON-AEAD128 tag check, version freshness and staging enforced in hardware, rejects every tested forgery, replay and direct write, and cuts a 608-byte authenticated update from 148.7 to 66.0 µs in native C. The full chain runs in real time, with no deadline miss over 552 windows (worst case 1.8% of the 171 ms window), and feature extraction dominates its cost. The model reaches 98.2% on unseen segments but generalizes poorly to unseen fault severities and to real damage of unseen Paderborn bearings, which makes field updates a requirement.</jats:p>

title: Edge AI Imitation of Event-Triggered Model Predictive Control for an Inverted Pendulum
container-title: Computers
05938ee211a2e0d7b4b9a7b07cb4c17bb8bcfd63.abstract: <jats:p>Event-triggered model predictive control (MPC) updates the control input only when needed, but it still solves an optimization problem at every event, which on the studied cart–pole can exceed its 10 ms control period. We propose a compact multi-task neural network that replaces the whole scheme: it decides when to update the input and which value to apply, using only online measurements. It is trained on 500 physical recordings, adapted to a simulated teacher and refined with DAgger. Feeding it the held input produces a copycat policy that is accurate in open loop but sluggish in closed loop; in a matched comparison over four training seeds, removing that input raises full-episode success from three to 39 of 40 episodes. In simulation, at the default sensor noise, the final network completes all swing-up and tracking episodes, with time to upright and tracking error close to the teacher’s, whereas on the simulated teacher, tree ensembles have 1.4–1.6 times its open-loop error. In an open-loop replay on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller, a step takes under 40% of the period. In tracking and full episodes, it updates the input 33–39% more often than the teacher, mainly because it does not learn the rule’s sparsity.</jats:p>

title: Explainable Machine Learning for Analyzing AI Adoption and Teachers’ Professional Development Needs: Evidence from TALIS 2024 in Kazakhstan
container-title: Computers
d995276851023c13b6f90d18faa245a7956a09a2.abstract: <jats:p>The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in education highlights the need to distinguish teachers’ AI adoption from their professional development needs. This study examined these outcomes as separate predictive tasks using OECD TALIS 2024 data for 7360 teachers in Kazakhstan at ISCED level 2. After excluding invalid outcome records, the analytical samples comprised 2430 teachers for AI adoption and 4868 for professional development needs. Population estimates and confidence intervals were calculated using teacher weights and 100 Fay-BRR replicate weights, while predictive performance was assessed using out-of-fold predictions and school-grouped validation. The weighted prevalence of AI adoption was 59.0% (95% CI: 56.1–61.9). Logistic Regression and CatBoost demonstrated comparable discrimination (ROC-AUC = 0.754 and 0.753, respectively), with no clear performance advantage for CatBoost. SHAP analysis identified prior AI-related professional learning, uncertainty regarding AI attitudes, and perceived AI benefits as prominent predictive factors. Moderate or high professional development need was estimated at 80.3% (95% CI: 78.7–81.9). However, individual prediction was weak, with balanced accuracy of 0.268 and a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.082. These findings indicate that TALIS variables provide a moderate predictive signal for AI adoption but are insufficient for reliable, individualized professional development decisions.</jats:p>

title: From Shadow IT to Shadow AI: A Scoping Review of How Embedded AI and Employee Use Increase Cybersecurity and Data Privacy Risk
container-title: Journal of Cybersecurity Education, Research and Practice
3805a82bfed81dbc127e741fe1c526c220ff0684.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into enterprise software has introduced a critical governance challenge: Shadow AI, the unmanaged and often invisible adoption of AI tools and features by employees outside formal IT oversight. Unlike traditional Shadow IT, which centers on unauthorized data storage and infrastructure, Shadow AI operates at the knowledge and decision-making layer, introducing probabilistic risks including data leakage, agentic misalignment, and indirect prompt injection that existing security frameworks are ill-equipped to address. This paper presents a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) synthesizing 38 peer-reviewed and industry sources to investigate three research questions: how organizational visibility gaps into embedded and employee-used AI increase cybersecurity and data privacy risk; what cybersecurity incident types are most commonly associated with ungoverned AI-enabled applications; and what risks employee interactions with AI pose to sensitive, proprietary, and regulated data. The analysis identifies a critical visibility deficit created by AI capabilities embedded within vendor-managed platforms, the semantic opacity of large language model interactions, and employees' utilitarian bypass of security policies. A taxonomy of six AI-specific incident types is presented, encompassing data leakage, prompt injection, credential compromise, agentic misuse, phishing augmentation, and insecure plugin exploitation. Findings demonstrate that existing governance mechanisms, including data loss prevention systems, identity and access management frameworks, and static risk assessments, are structurally misaligned with the dynamic nature of generative AI. The paper recommends a transition to dynamic, risk-based governance integrating continuous monitoring, cross-functional oversight, and AI TRiSM frameworks.</jats:p>

title: An AI-Integrated Constructivist Learning Environment Framework for Thai as a Second Language in Higher Education: Design and Expert Review
container-title: Higher Education Studies
5b84317555b53bc0e68cbff36996349ce2167909.abstract: <jats:p>Digital technology is now central to higher education, yet learner engagement is usually measured as an outcome after instruction rather than designed into the learning environment. This study designs an AI-integrated constructivist learning environment (CLE) framework for promoting learning engagement and creative writing, referred to here as the CLE-EW framework, for Chinese university learners of Thai as a second language. The study followed design and development research (DDR). It combined an integrative literature synthesis, a contextual analysis, a theory-driven design synthesis, and expert review. The contextual analysis took place at two universities in Yunnan Province, China, with 120 third-year Thai majors, their two writing instructors, and four support staff. The framework has seven interrelated centers: Problem Base, Learning Resources, Cognitive Tools, Collaboration, Promoting Learning Engagement and Creative Writing, Scaffolding, and Coaching. AI is used in five centers in three bounded forms (rule-based formative feedback, a retrieval-based answer system, and an external generative tool used to seek, collect, organize, and integrate information), while the Collaboration and Coaching Centers are human-led. The rule-based and retrieval-based forms run in the learner&rsquo;s browser and send no learner writing to an external service. Five experts rated the framework in two rounds: the theoretical framework, the design framework and the model, and then the learning environment as built. They rated all items of all five forms as relevant, and every form met the content validity criteria. The theoretical framework was revised in response to expert comments. The contribution is twofold: engagement is specified as a designed structural component, and AI is given defined forms and limits alongside instructor and peer mediation.</jats:p>

title: AI-Supported Programming Environments and Pair Programming Role Strategies in Secondary School: An Exploratory Study
container-title: Education Sciences
730a90690436e7cd6a55e00cab261143155f1b65.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into programming education has accelerated rapidly in recent years. Yet, existing research has largely focused on individual learning or human–AI interaction, with limited attention to human–human–AI collaboration and pair programming role strategies. This study conducted an exploratory comparison of learning outcomes across four classroom conditions combining AI support (with/without) and role strategy (fixed/rotating). Participants were 198 eighth-grade students from four intact classes in a public junior secondary school in Xi’an, China, who participated in an eight-week programming course. Linear mixed-effects models were used to examine programming performance, computational thinking, cognitive load, and programming anxiety. Programming performance differed by classroom condition (p = 0.023) and session (p = 0.014), with a significant classroom-condition-by-session interaction (p = 0.010). Tukey-adjusted comparisons showed higher estimated means in the AI-supported/rotating-role classroom than in the non-AI/fixed-role classroom in Session 1 and the AI-supported/fixed-role classroom in Session 2. Computational thinking did not differ significantly across conditions. The non-AI/fixed-role classroom showed higher cognitive load than the non-AI/rotating-role and AI-supported/rotating-role classrooms, and higher programming anxiety than the other three classrooms. Overall, this study offers exploratory insights into AI-supported programming and pair-programming roles in secondary education.</jats:p>

title: Exploring Generative AI Adoption Among Community College Faculty and Staff: Practices, Perceptions, and Challenges
container-title: Journal of Education, Humanities, and Social Research
e1a94a627bdf3109bc7f74c75ed41f14a46056fe.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) presents new opportunities for teaching, learning, and professional productivity in higher education. However, evidence on its adoption among community college faculty and staff remains limited. This descriptive, exploratory study examined GenAI practices, perceptions, and institutional support needs using aggregated findings from a 2026 institutional survey conducted at a U.S. community college. Results indicated that 84.8% of respondents reported previous experience with AI technologies, although comfort levels and perceived understanding varied. GenAI was more frequently reported for writing, professional communication, and general workplace tasks than for learning management system course design and student support. Respondents also expressed interest in hands-on professional development and clearer institutional guidelines, alongside concerns about academic integrity, information accuracy, and data privacy. Drawing on conceptual perspectives related to self-efficacy, perceived usefulness, and facilitating conditions, the study highlights the importance of examining professional applications, employee perceptions, and institutional support needs together. These findings provide descriptive insights that may inform professional development and responsible GenAI integration in community college settings.</jats:p>
