title: AI Policing in Nigeria: A Review on Feasibility, Legality, and Legitimacy in an Era of Trust Deficit
container-title: SocioEdu: Sociological Education
ade3e6464d7ec5532e316c0dbdc2325fc850fa34.abstract: <jats:p>The implementation of AI policing in Nigeria presents both potential benefits and significant challenges. Key advantages must be weighed against risks such as algorithmic bias and privacy infringements that mainly affect marginalized communities. The Nigeria Police Force contends with severe issues, including low public trust, insufficient funding, and a poor officer-to-citizen ratio (1:650), which is far below UN standards. Additional systemic barriers include out-dated paper records and the absence of a national biometric database. Legal and ethical concerns spotlight historical biases inadequately addressed by current regulations. Notably, the Nigeria Data Protection Act lacks mandatory bias evaluations, further eroding public confidence. Practical challenges arise from poor infrastructure, low data quality, and a skilled workforce deficit. To navigate these complexities, a comprehensive framework for AI deployment is proposed, which emphasizes legal protections, community engagement, and welfare improvements. This study advocates for a gradual AI adoption strategy using frameworks like the Technology-Organization-Environment model, emphasizing training and audits to uphold ethical standards and rebuild trust.</jats:p>

title: Mind the AI policy gap: a policy analysis across global funding bodies
container-title: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
80a01c8444044c3d3d44ddf81b0fdf46993960c5.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Research funding bodies have significant influence on what research is prioritised, how it is conducted, and what standards are enforced. While a number of global frameworks provide normative guidance on AI ethics, there is a clear gap in understanding how these principles are implemented at the funding-body level. This study aims to examine the current AI policies and guidelines of research funding bodies across different geographical regions. Inductive thematic analysis was adopted to analyse 56 AI-related policies from 46 funding agencies across the US, the UK, Europe, Australia, Singapore, Mainland China, and Hong Kong. The analysis revealed five common themes: human-centredness, safeguarding, embeddedness, governance, and AI readiness. It was also found that current funding-specific policies lack explicit guidelines on how broad principles and macro-level regulations can be interpreted and applied in AI-enabled research funding processes. The findings underscore the important role of funding agencies as key actors in defining responsible AI use in research processes. Finally, the practical implications of this study for regulators, funding bodies, and researchers are discussed, highlighting the value of policy document analysis in shaping ethical, transparent, and responsible AI frameworks.</jats:p>

title: Reform and Practice of Modern Cryptography Courses in Integrated Undergraduate–Graduate Cybersecurity Education: Science–Education Integration and AI as Dual Drivers
container-title: Journal of Education, Teaching and Social Studies
5bd449ff48492ec92f1db4a48ef127a0c86d70c6.abstract: <jats:p>In order to tackle the problems that exist in integrated undergraduate–graduate cybersecurity education at provincial universities with significant differences in the level of student preparedness, lack of coherence between undergraduate and graduate programs, inability to transform the results of faculty research into instructional resources, and disjointed use of artificial intelligence, the given study uses the Modern Cryptography course which is provided to the undergraduate students, the academic master’s students and the professional master’s students in Cybersecurity at Heilongjiang University as a case study. Design-based action research methodology was employed in order to form a three-level curriculum chain of undergraduate foundations, undergraduate–graduate articulation, and advanced graduate-level research training. Moreover, a four-step mechanism for transforming research outputs into teaching resources was devised, consisting of selecting the research outcome, pedagogical adaptation, implementation in the classroom, and iterative feedback. AI-based learning diagnostics, literature assistance, and learning behavior recording were incorporated in the entire process of instruction. Five dimensions of process-oriented assessment were developed, namely: theoretical knowledge, practical skill, research-focused reading and participation in tasks, innovation capacity, and learning behavior. The initial pilot implementation involved using process documentation, laboratory reports, observation in the classroom and formative feedback as the main sources of evidence to determine the viability of the reform plan, the viability of collecting evidence and the completeness of the assessment chain. This paper has important practical implications to promote integrated undergraduate-graduate cryptography education and enhance the research-education integration reform in provincial universities.</jats:p>

title: Cultural and Digital Readiness for AI-Integrated Higher Education: A C-TAM-Informed Curriculum Design Framework
container-title: Advances in Curriculum Design&Education
17b44f0dea25eae53e8d9d505d096a49a7584ffa.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) requires higher education institutions to redesign curricula, assessments, and student support rather than merely authorize or prohibit a new tool. This article develops a Cultural-Technology Acceptance Model (C-TAM) as a theory-building curriculum framework. It integrates current studies of university students’ GenAI use with established technology-acceptance research, cross-cultural scholarship, AI-literacy frameworks, backward design, constructive alignment, and assessment reform. The revision explicitly limits the role of pre-GenAI evidence. Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2018 and World Values Survey (WVS) Wave 7 indicators are treated as contextual evidence about the digital and cultural readiness pipeline entering higher education; they are not treated as measures of GenAI acceptance, and no cross-national structural equation model is estimated from them. The synthesis identifies five mechanisms that curriculum designers should anticipate: perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use and AI competence, attitudes shaped by trust and ethical risk, social and institutional norms, and culturally patterned expectations about uncertainty and authority. These mechanisms are translated through backward design into aligned learning outcomes, assessment evidence, pedagogy, and support. An AI-Ready Curriculum Reconstruction Matrix specifies adaptations for students who combine high uncertainty avoidance with high power-distance expectations, including explicit permissions, low-stakes rehearsal, modelled verification, multiple participation routes, process evidence, and equitable access. The article contributes a bounded and testable framework for culturally responsive AI integration while providing a transparent protocol for future direct, multilevel, cross-cultural validation.</jats:p>

title: Preparing students for AI-integrated workplaces: a programme-level process framework for digital capability development and graduate career readiness
container-title: Frontiers in Education
b2dbd1be3792984c582f5107757d40e55164ac7c.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into workplaces is changing the capabilities expected of graduates, while higher-education curricula often adapt more slowly to labour-market developments. This article addresses the need for a structured, accountable process through which academic programmes can respond to AI-integrated work.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study uses a purposive conceptual synthesis of literature on digital capability, labour-market information, constructive alignment, human capital, stakeholder participation, socio-technical systems, and responsible AI governance. Kenya is used as an illustrative context rather than as a site of empirical validation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The synthesis produces a programme-level process framework comprising six stages: sensing, validation, diagnosis, redesign, implementation, and outcome review. These stages are supported by cross-cutting conditions involving data infrastructure, stakeholder participation, faculty capability, ethical governance, and academic authority. AI is positioned as a decision-support resource for interpreting labour-market signals and identifying potential competency gaps. However, stakeholder validation, academic prioritisation, formal authorisation, curriculum decisions, and outcome review remain subject to human and institutional accountability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework integrates previously separate strands of research into an evidence-to-model process with explicit decision gates and traceability requirements. It offers propositions for empirical testing and provides a basis for programme-level curriculum review and renewal. The framework does not establish that AI-enabled curriculum processes improve graduate employability; such effects must be evaluated through programme-level pilots and longitudinal studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Reimagining built environment education in Malaysia: an AI-enhanced BIM teaching and learning framework
container-title: Frontiers in Education
9c670b39c0246853768acbc90406868036fe6c22.abstract: <jats:p>Building Information Modelling (BIM), with growing links to artificial intelligence (AI), is creating new requirements for built environment education. However, BIM curriculum integration remains uneven internationally and in Malaysia, with implementation shaped by staff capability, infrastructure, institutional support and industry engagement. This conceptual study proposes the Digital Built Environment Education Framework (DBEEF) for integrating BIM and AI within built environment programmes. The framework was developed through a structured supplementary literature search and interpretive synthesis of 78 studies, supported by policy analysis and an illustrative institutional analysis of Tunku Abdul Rahman University of Management and Technology (TAR UMT). DBEEF comprises five pillars: Adaptive Learning and Personalisation, Intelligent Content Delivery, Collaboration and Communication Enhancement, Ethics and Governance in AI Use, and Curriculum Alignment and Industry Relevance. The included evidence was concentrated on curriculum alignment, collaborative learning and technology-supported delivery, while evidence relating to AI-enabled personalisation and comprehensive AI ethics and governance was comparatively limited and indirect. The TAR UMT analysis indicates that existing curricula, infrastructure and industry relationships may support pilot implementation, while gaps remain in AI-enabled pedagogy, governance, staff capability and outcome assessment. The institutional analysis does not validate DBEEF or demonstrate improvements in student or graduate competencies. DBEEF provides an evidence-informed basis for pilot implementation and empirical evaluation of integrated BIM–AI education in Malaysia.</jats:p>

title: Exploring Postgraduate Students' Generative AI Use in English Academic Writing: Practices, Challenges and Pedagogical Implications
container-title: Asian Journal of Education and Social Studies
583bed3643a68eefce1ca655005d2e56fcdc7217.abstract:
<jats:p>Aims: This study investigated the use of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) by postgraduate students in English as a foreign language (EFL) thesis introduction writing, focusing on their interaction practices, rhetorical and functional writing difficulties, and relationships between these difficulties and observable GAI use.
Study Design: An exploratory, classroom-embedded study combining qualitative analysis with descriptive statistics.
Place and Duration of Study: A postgraduate thesis writing course at a Chinese university, September–December 2025, with data drawn primarily from the first five weeks.
Methodology: The study analysed 35 students' thesis introduction drafts and corresponding GAI interaction records, supplemented by stimulated-recall interviews with three participants. GAI-use practices were examined in terms of interaction patterns, task focus, and text-generation responsibility. The drafts were analysed with reference to the Create a Research Space model and functional adequacy, followed by a cross-source analysis.
Results: Students used GAI for diverse writing tasks and differed in their allocation of text-generation responsibility, but sustained interaction around individual writing problems was limited. Although most drafts contained recognisable rhetorical moves, difficulties persisted in literature synthesis, research-gap construction, and argumentative coherence. Cross-source analysis further revealed difficulties in identifying genre-specific writing problems, formulating targeted GAI requests, and evaluating generated content against relevant evidence and rhetorical expectations.
Conclusion: Meaningful GAI-assisted academic writing requires more than frequent interaction or control over text generation. Genre-specific diagnostic criteria and process-oriented support are needed to promote purposeful GAI use and evidence-based authorial judgement.</jats:p>

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Ethics in Language Education: Evidence from a Systematic Review and Thematic Synthesis of Research in Türkiye (2022–2026)
container-title: HAYEF: Journal of Education
acea99cf8d4a2444ee1fae7b0111d87f5168b97e.abstract:
<jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence has entered language education faster than frameworks and policy guidance for teacher educators and teachers. This focused systematic review synthesizes empirical evidence on the ethical dimensions of generative artificial intelligence use in language education in Türkiye. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines, a systematic literature review was carried out, and nine studies obtained from the Web of Science and Scopus databases were included in the analysis. Thematic synthesis revealed four themes: (1) contested academic integrity, authorship, and originality; (2) overreliance and erosion of human cognitive and authorial control; (3) ethics–competence gap in artificial intelligence literacy; and (4) responsible use as mediated and institutionally governed practice. The results showed that ethical competence appeared comparatively weaker than other artificial intelligence–related competencies as ethical awareness ranked lower than both artificial intelligence literacy and pedagogical integration among teachers, and plagiarism attitudes were not significantly associated with artificial intelligence literacy. Within the four artificial intelligence literacy dimensions, ethics was the weakest predictor of teachers’ technology acceptance, although it remained statistically significant. Teachers embraced artificial intelligence as a supplementary tool, provided that human authorship and judgment were not compromised, and those who used artificial intelligence selectively retained stronger authorial control. They positioned artificial intelligence as a conditional participant on teacher-defined terms, while institutional support, infrastructure, and policy alignment were linked to ethical practice alongside individual competence. The reviewed literature mostly included perceptual, self-reported, and cross-sectional studies and lacked interventions, underscoring the need for longitudinal, experimental, and intervention research.
Cite this article as: Işıklıgil, N. C. C., & Gülbak, G. M. (2026). Generative artificial intelligence ethics in language education: evidence from a systematic review and thematic synthesis of research in Türkiye (2022–2026). HAYEF: Journal of Education, 23, 0097, doi: 10.5152/hayef.2026.26097.</jats:p>

title: Generative AI in Mathematics Learning: A Bibliometric Analysis and Narrative Review
container-title: International Journal of Humanities, Education, and Social Sciences
05363bef4dfdea2e1e67ff8e2353ed59e5fd08f4.abstract: <jats:p>Since late 2022, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has expanded rapidly in mathematics education, yet the research field remains insufficiently mapped, and evidence of its effects on learning is inconsistent. This study mapped the development, structure, and emerging topics of research on GenAI in mathematics learning and synthesized evidence on its uses, effects, and challenges. Bibliometric analysis was combined with a narrative review. Searches for records published between 2022 and 2026 in OpenAlex, ERIC, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, and Garuda yielded 1,480 records, with 1,206 unique records retained after cleaning. Descriptive and text-mining analyses examined the full corpus, while citation and keyword co-occurrence analyses were conducted in VOSviewer using 758 OpenAlex records. The findings show that 95.2% of records were published from 2024 onward, 48.6% mentioned ChatGPT, and 29.5% explicitly addressed primary or secondary education. The keyword network comprised five clusters, with AI literacy, academic integrity, and self-regulation emerging as the newest topics. The narrative synthesis indicates that GenAI can support learning when integrated into scaffolded instruction with safeguards, whereas unrestricted use as an answer source can undermine learning. These findings highlight instructional design as central to the educational value of GenAI and inform the extension of scaffolding perspectives to AI-mediated mathematics learning. The study identifies school-level experimental research and teacher preparation as priorities for advancing evidence and guiding GenAI integration.</jats:p>

title: Teaching in the Age of AI: Exploring Faculty Perceptions and Practices
container-title: AI in Education
83f84abad6e24fb2b9a7e9daf963be9fa00c85b9.abstract: <jats:p>As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into higher education, understanding how faculty perspectives change over time is essential to supporting responsible adoption. Because much existing research captures faculty views at a single point in time, this two-wave longitudinal qualitative study examined how perceptions and practices related to AI changed over approximately one year at a large public research university in the Southeastern United States. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 22 full-time faculty members from a college of education in Fall 2024, and 12 completed follow-up interviews in Fall 2025. These paired interviews were compared within participants to identify changes and continuities across the two time points. Findings suggested predominant shifts from conceptual exploration to practical integration, from cautious curiosity to conditional confidence, and from monitoring AI use to guiding responsible AI use, although some participants became more critical of AI. By 2025, many participants recognized AI’s permanence and articulated more concrete needs for institutional policies and professional development. Concerns about academic integrity, ethical implications, and human oversight remained consistent across both time points. These findings suggest the value of examining faculty AI adoption over time and highlight the importance of continued institutional support as faculty engagement with AI evolves.</jats:p>

title: Social Presence Literacy in the Age of AI: A Framework for Human-Centered Teaching
container-title: Education Sciences
4d24c0454a9a39ec7e4fb9b567d186251633d32c.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming online higher education by increasing efficiency in instructional design, feedback, and communication. However, its integration raises important questions about preserving social presence and meaningful human connection in digitally mediated learning environments. This conceptual, practice-informed interdisciplinary synthesis examines the relationship between technological efficiency and relational engagement in asynchronous online education. Drawing upon Social Presence Theory, the Community of Inquiry framework, the Social Presence Model, social development theory, and research on human-centered pedagogy, the manuscript extends the Social Presence Literacy Framework) to AI-mediated instructional decision-making. The synthesis identifies three potential relational challenges associated with unintentional AI integration: the displacement of meaningful engagement through task automation, diminished opportunities for empathy and emotional attunement, and the erosion of human-centered teaching practices. In response, a five-step decision-making framework is proposed, connecting the SPLF dimensions of Knowledge, Application, Evaluation, and Creation to evaluating, identifying gaps, adjusting, testing, and refining AI-supported instructional practices. Although the proposed framework has not been empirically validated, it offers educators a practical approach to balancing technological efficiency with relational intentionality. The manuscript concludes by emphasizing the importance of reflective instructional judgment, student experiences, and institutional support in sustaining human-centered AI integration.</jats:p>

title: Digital and AI-Supported Learning Together for Pre-Service Mathematics Teachers’ Statistics Education: An Intact-Class Study
container-title: Higher Education Studies
cd60e97cffeba5ae29ceeb5187bebbbc24a59d3a.abstract: <jats:p>Pre-service mathematics teachers need opportunities to interpret evidence, explain statistical reasoning, and communicate conclusions, providing a rationale for examining structured cooperative approaches in undergraduate statistics. This study compared statistics achievement in two intact classes after one class received Learning Together (LT) with digital and artificial intelligence-supported resources and the other received conventional instruction. A pretest-posttest comparison involved 54 second-year pre-service mathematics teachers (27 per class) at a Thai Rajabhat University. The two classes were allocated to conditions by drawing lots. Both classes studied the same content with the same instructor and completed the same 30-item test. ANCOVA compared posttest scores while adjusting for pretest achievement. The LT-based class had a higher adjusted posttest mean (20.22, 95% CI [19.11, 21.33]) than the comparison class (17.37, 95% CI [16.27, 18.48]), F(1, 51) = 13.34, p &lt; .001, partial &eta;&sup2; = .207; the adjusted difference was 2.85 points (95% CI [1.28, 4.41]). The integrated condition was associated with higher achievement; because each condition was represented by one class, the result is exploratory and cannot separate the contributions of LT, digital tools, AI-supported resources, and class membership. The findings suggest that university teacher-preparation courses can combine structured cooperative tasks with guided verification of AI-supported materials as a practical design for undergraduate statistics.</jats:p>

title: An educational activity tailored for undergraduate students on AI-driven nanobody design for targeted antiviral therapeutics
container-title: Journal of Microbiology & Biology Education
c9a01ee34315bd1026ca9ce0d511190d21767b6d.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title/>
                    <jats:p>
                      Protein-based biologics are converging at an unprecedented pace as generative artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes early-stage drug discovery. Nanobodies, single-domain antibody fragments derived from camelid heavy chain-only immunoglobulins, are an emerging class of antiviral biologics prized for their small size, stability, and access to cryptic viral epitopes. Traditional nanobody discovery relies on animal immunization and phage display screening, a process that can take 6 to 12 months and is entirely inaccessible within a standard undergraduate laboratory session. Here, we describe a succinct,

                      -based laboratory activity that uses a generative AI protein design server, GeoFlow-V3 (
                      <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="https://prot.design/" xlink:type="simple">https://prot.design/</jats:ext-link>
                      ), to allow undergraduate students to design a novel antiviral nanobody against the influenza A virus (IAV) hemagglutinin (HA) protein. This activity builds on our group’s prior use of generative AI for undergraduate siRNA design teaching and extends the same pedagogical model to structural protein engineering. To our knowledge, this is the first use of a generative AI protein design platform for teaching nanobody design at the undergraduate level.

title: A Study on the Coupling Relationship Between AI Personalization and Long-Context Management
container-title: Computers and Artificial Intelligence
49889832b6f70b95f1a638c748d37b18136de351.abstract: <jats:p>With the large-scale deployment of large language models (LLMs) in various intelligent assistants and agent systems, homogenized outputs and the loss of user preferences across sessions have become key bottlenecks restricting improvements in user experience. Personalization technology aims to adapt LLMs to the language habits, thinking patterns, and subjective preferences of different users, while long-context and agent memory management addresses the underlying technical problems of storing, filtering, and reusing temporal information for LLMs. Current academic research mostly treats the two directions as independent fields, and systematic reviews of their internal coupling relationship are relatively scarce. This study first defines the core concepts of LLM personalization and long-context memory management and systematically reviews the technical principles, advantages, and existing limitations of four personalization paradigms: prompt-engineering personalization, lightweight parameter fine-tuning, user-preference alignment, and dynamic user profiling. It then divides long-context and agent-memory technologies into five routes: native-window expansion, context pruning and compression, adaptive context extraction, hierarchical memory architectures, and external retrieval-augmented memory, and analyzes the applicable scenarios and technical shortcomings of each route. On this basis, this study reviews progress in four intersecting directions: preference-aware memory updating, structured persona-memory representation, long-horizon personalization evaluation benchmarks, and training-free collaborative control at inference time. It further analyzes the internal coupling mechanism through which the two directions empower each other and summarizes three core conflicts: the capacity-accuracy trade-off, the conflict between general governance rules and personalized characteristics, and the conflict between computational cost and personalization stability. The study also summarizes five research challenges: difficulty in adapting to the dynamic evolution of user preferences, failure to recall implicit preferences, memory errors and preference drift, fragmented evaluation systems, and difficulty balancing engineering implementation costs. It proposes subsequent research paths in six dimensions: cognitively inspired memory architectures, preference-aware context compression algorithms, multimode hybrid indexing and retrieval, unified long-horizon personalization evaluation protocols, memory-error verification mechanisms, and multimodal long-term personalization. The findings indicate that long-term personalized intelligent systems cannot optimize the personalization module or memory module in isolation. Their coupling relationship should serve as the underlying design logic to promote the iterative upgrading of LLMs toward adaptation to individual user characteristics and to provide a reference for the theoretical research and engineering development of long-term agents and personalized dialogue assistants.</jats:p>

title: Chemistry teachers’ research competence following AI-supported professional development: a mixed-methods pre–post study

                    <jats:p>Developing teachers' research competence is a strategic priority in contemporary education, where artificial intelligence can support educational data analysis and evidence-informed pedagogical decision-making. Data were collected from 105 chemistry teachers using closed-ended questionnaire scales and two open-ended questions administered before and after a six-week professional development program. Descriptive statistics, Pearson's correlation analysis, paired-samples t-tests, Cohen's dz, and qualitative content analysis were used.</jats:p>

title: Case Study—AdWords to AdWards: AI as a Coding Partner in Teaching Online Optimization Algorithms
container-title: INFORMS Transactions on Education
acadf24affb4d897a0e7adef93390843a564f5e9.abstract:
<jats:p>This case illustrates teaching online optimization algorithms for sequential decision making using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as an assistant, making complex concepts in algorithm design, implementation, and evaluation accessible even to nontechnical student audiences. Students are asked to translate an unfamiliar healthcare setting into the Google AdWords problem. The well-known structure of the Google AdWords problem both facilitates students’ conceptual learning and makes it easier for GenAI tools to assist with algorithm implementation. However, the complexity of the healthcare environment makes the mapping difficult, requires discussions with “experts” with domain knowledge and various stakeholders in the process, and raises ethical questions. The case is based on an actual process improvement project aimed at maximizing the use of a hospital’s capacity. The main character, Dr. Kelly, heads an observation unit and had tried a predictive model for patient assignments to her unit versus the hospital wards, which, however, can sometimes lead to inefficient bed capacity management. She is looking to improve patient allocation decisions made in real time. The case empowers students to (1) identify situations in which sequential decision-making models and online algorithms are appropriate and preferable to predictive models, (2) discover the concept of inventory balancing, (3) map its application in an unfamiliar setting (healthcare) to a well-studied setting (advertising) through inquiry and stakeholder analysis, and (4) embrace GenAI as a partner in algorithm implementation and testing. Realistic data, code, and models are provided. The rich context of the case makes it appropriate for use in courses in operations management, business analytics, marketing, machine learning, and operations research, both at the advanced undergraduate level and at the masters/MBA level.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Supplemental Material: The Teaching Note is available at https://www.informs.org/Publications/Subscribe/Access-Restricted-Materials .</jats:p>

title: Budget-Aware Adaptive Test-Time Compute with Hierarchical Self-Verification for Semantic ID Generative Recommendation
container-title: Computers
ad812a7a10cc5144461b6cebf5c51d87590389d3.abstract: <jats:p>Semantic identifier (SID) generative recommenders cast retrieval as autoregressive decoding over short sequences of residual-quantized codewords. Most published SID recommenders decode all requests with one fixed beam width, which is optimal only if the marginal utility of compute is constant across requests. We find that it is not; additional search changes little for users with consistent histories, but improves accuracy substantially for cold start, interest-drifting, and long-tail users. The main methodological contribution of this paper is request-level allocation of decoding compute, in which a router predicts the accuracy gain of each configuration in a finite decoding menu over the cheapest configuration and selects the configuration with the largest gain net of a priced cost. The selection rule follows from standard Lagrangian arguments, which we use as tools; what is specific to this work is the use of this per-configuration gain as the routing target for SID decoding instead of a difficulty or uncertainty score. The resulting framework, called Bastion, combines the router with a hierarchical process verifier over the quantization levels, a listwise terminal verifier, codeword consistency voting, and budget-constrained group relative policy optimization. On five benchmarks built from Amazon Reviews 2023, MovieLens, and MicroLens, Bastion improves NDCG@10 by 5.7% to 8.7% over the strongest baseline. Its mean latency on Amazon-Beauty is 14.5 ms, against 14.6 ms for a beam-20 TIGER decoder, while its median and 99th-percentile latencies are higher by 0.9 ms and 7.0 ms. At every evaluated budget, its accuracy exceeds that of all baselines on the three datasets for which accuracy versus latency frontiers was measured.</jats:p>

title: Polish and Ukrainian Future and Early-Career Educators’ Perspectives on AI Competencies and Curriculum Priorities in Primary Computer Science Education
container-title: Education Sciences
4ae1f6b975cf27d08d28d42c2ec83988378c0234.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is becoming an important component of primary Computer Science education, creating new expectations for both pupil competencies and teacher preparation. This study examined how Polish and Ukrainian future and early-career educators perceive curriculum priorities, AI-related competencies for primary school pupils, professional-development needs, and directions for curriculum innovation in teacher education. A cross-sectional comparative mixed-methods design was applied to data from 64 respondents from Poland and Ukraine (32 per country). Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics and Mann–Whitney U tests, with Holm adjustment for multiple comparisons and rank-biserial correlations as effect-size measures, while open-ended responses were examined through qualitative thematic analysis. Across both national samples, critical evaluation of AI-generated content and understanding AI-related risks were among the highest-rated AI competencies, whereas prompt engineering and AI-project creation were comparatively less emphasised. Although Ukrainian respondents rated prompt development more highly than Polish respondents in the unadjusted analysis (U = 294.5, p = 0.007), this difference did not remain statistically significant after Holm adjustment (adjusted p = 0.056). Ukrainian respondents also tended to report stronger professional-development needs; after adjustment for multiple comparisons, statistically significant differences remained only for robotics and STEAM education. Overall, the findings indicate broadly similar descriptive priorities across the two samples rather than evidence of cross-national equivalence. The results support a human-centred, competency-based approach to teacher education integrating AI foundations, critical evaluation, ethical and responsible use, practical applications, and context-sensitive professional learning.</jats:p>

title: Comparing Use of Human-Created to AI-Generated Instructional Materials to Teach Science Vocabulary: A Randomized Controlled Trial
container-title: Journal of Special Education Technology
f8a30a9cae1bf2d1c9e31ca8da903ef2faa513a2.abstract: <jats:p>Evidence-based vocabulary instruction is essential for literacy and content learning, yet many educators face barriers, such as lack of training and time constraints, to implementing it. Content Acquisition Podcasts (CAPs) are multimedia instruction that incorporate evidence-based practice to teach vocabulary yet can be arduous to create. This randomized controlled trial (RCT) examined whether generative AI-created Content Acquisition Podcasts–Student (CAP-S) produced vocabulary outcomes comparable to researcher-created CAP-S and whether cognitive load predicted performance. Participants included 116 fifth- and sixth-grade students, including students with disabilities (SWD), randomly assigned to AI-generated or researcher-created CAP-S across three science vocabulary lessons. No statistically significant differences in vocabulary outcomes were found between conditions at any assessment point in the study. Results also showed that perceived cognitive load significantly predicted performance, while instructional condition did not. Findings suggest AI-generated CAP-S may provide a scalable approach, that also mitigates workload burdens of educators, without compromising instructional effectiveness.</jats:p>

title: <b>From anxiety to empowerment: AI-supported speaking practice for low-literacy EFL university students</b>
container-title: Englisia: Journal of Language, Education, and Humanities
420d49c63ddb7c90f5a8504d607c01fe35d61b02.abstract: <jats:p>This study explored oral proficiency, attitudes toward AI-assisted speaking practice and empowerment in low-literacy EFL university students. This study adopted mixed methods involving 120 first-year students of Universitas Muhammadiyah Purworejo, Indonesia and Universiti Teknologi MARA Cawangan Pahang, Malaysia. These students were purposefully selected on the basis of their performance in the university English proficiency assessments. Data were gathered using a post-speaking performance assessment, survey, and semi-structured interviews. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and qualitative data using thematic analysis. The results indicated that students achieved a good level of speaking proficiency, with comprehension being the strongest area of speaking. The survey results showed positive perceptions of AI-assisted speaking practice, particularly regarding its usefulness, accessibility, motivational effect, and the increase in speaking confidence. The interview results revealed that AI-assisted speaking practice improved learner empowerment by reducing speaking anxiety, increasing speaking confidence, promoting learner independence, and strengthening students’ belief in their ability to communicate in English. The results demonstrate that AI-assisted speaking exercises are capable of promoting the linguistic and psychological development of low-literate university students learning EFL.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The rapid spread of generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) technologies into various aspects of second/foreign language (L2) education has recently attracted increasing scholarly attention. However, the way GenAI literacy may be associated with English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers' emotional state has received insufficient attention. To address this gap, the present quantitative study drew on control‐value theory (CVT) and the broaden‐and‐build theory (BBT) in examining the role of GenAI literacy and emotional literacy in EFL teachers' teaching enjoyment in the context of AI‐mediated instruction. Three questionnaires were completed by 679 Chinese EFL teachers. The results revealed positive pairwise correlations among GenAI literacy, emotional literacy and teaching enjoyment. Moreover, structural equation modelling showed that both GenAI literacy and emotional literacy were positively associated with teaching enjoyment when modelled simultaneously. The study offers practical implications for EFL teachers and teacher educators, inviting them to pay more attention to the emotional aspects of AI‐integration, fostering more enjoyable L2 instruction.</jats:p>

title: Generative AI literacy and administrative staff's innovative work behavior: the context of vocational colleges in Northeastern China

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Generative AI is increasingly incorporated into higher education administration, yet limited attention has been paid to how administrative staff members' generative AI literacy relates to their innovative work behavior. This study examined the associations between five dimensions of generative AI literacy and innovative work behavior, the indirect associations through perceived dynamic capabilities and AI knowledge-sharing participation, and the moderating role of organizational structure.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cross-sectional questionnaire survey collected 765 valid responses from administrative staff at vocational colleges in Liaoning, Jilin, and Heilongjiang, China. Structural equation modeling (SEM) was employed to examine direct and indirect associations, while hierarchical regression analysis was conducted to test the moderating effects of organizational structure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>All five dimensions of generative AI literacy were positively associated with innovative work behavior. Significant indirect associations were identified through perceived dynamic capabilities and AI knowledge-sharing participation. Organizational structure positively moderated all five literacy–behavior associations in a separate composite-score analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>

title: Pedagogical practices and generative AI integration across the spectrum of learning theories: a systematic review

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Contemporary technological interventions in the pedagogical system have created substantial learning opportunities across educational communities. Learning theories provide a framework for effective learning practices.                   <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>

The data were visualised and interpreted through bibliometric analysis using the Biblioshiny application integrated with RStudio. For the content analysis, 163 articles were screened through a systematic review process.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>

title:

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To evaluate whether dental professionals can distinguish human‐authored from generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)‐generated dental research abstracts under blinded conditions and to explore differences in detectability across contemporary large language models (LLMs).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this exploratory blinded cross‐sectional study, 23 dental professionals (10 general dentists, 7 specialists, 6 dental students) evaluated 60 abstracts derived from 15 published dental research articles: the 15 published abstracts and 45 GenAI‐generated abstracts produced from the main text of the same articles by Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT‐5.4 and Gemini 3. Participants classified each abstract as human‐authored, AI‐generated or ‘Unsure’ and rated confidence, quality and credibility on five‐point scales. Discrimination was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, balanced accuracy and signal‐detection measures, with a probit mixed‐effects model accounting for variability between participants, abstracts and source articles.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Of 1377 classifications, 10.0% were ‘Unsure’. Balanced accuracy was 56.0% (95% CI 49.6%–62.4%) and did not differ significantly from chance (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.070). In the mixed‐effects model, discrimination was weak and not statistically significant (
                      <jats:italic>d</jats:italic>
                      ' = 0.39, 95% CI −0.08–0.86) and participants showed no systematic response bias. Detectability did not differ between LLMs (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.157) or expertise groups (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.99). Confidence was not calibrated to accuracy (mean 3.58 for correct vs. 3.61 for incorrect classifications,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.75) and GenAI‐generated abstracts were not rated lower than human‐authored abstracts in quality or credibility. Findings were consistent across sensitivity analyses.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Dental professionals showed limited ability to distinguish human‐authored from fully GenAI‐generated dental research abstracts, regardless of expertise or LLM and their confidence did not reflect their accuracy. title: ‘Hey, I See You. Do You Need Help?’: Understanding the Algorithmic Gaze of AI-Driven Student Surveillance
container-title: Postdigital Science and Education
8e9b4a6f235ec14362293cf8011d35029317ea4e.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven surveillance systems in educational settings is becoming increasingly common as policymakers, school leaders, and educators seek to enhance student safety and wellbeing. Understanding what student data are collected, how monitoring occurs, and what assumptions are embedded within these systems is therefore essential to informing ethical approaches to educational technology governance. This exploratory paper investigates the potential implications of AI-driven surveillance in Australian K-12 schools. Using a qualitative case study design, it examines three surveillance tools through the conceptual lens of the algorithmic gaze. The impacts of the algorithmic gaze are particularly concerning in educational settings where AI technologies are increasingly used to monitor students’ behaviour and mental health, often without students fully understanding how their actions, opportunities, and experiences may be mediated by code. To reveal how this process operates, the study undertakes a thematic analysis of product website discourses, including product marketing pages, customer story blogs, and support documentation. More specifically, the paper examines the learning, psychological, and equity harms that might arise from this form of surveillance in schools.</jats:p>

title: <b>How AI shapes learner agency in English language learning: A qualitative study of first-year undergraduate EFL students in west Kalimantan</b>
container-title: Englisia: Journal of Language, Education, and Humanities
585310083fe68474a88e55e1dca6728f594b2181.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing the way we learn English by providing instant access to information, personalized feedback, and flexible learning support. Previous studies have mostly looked at students' perception of AI and its impact on language learning, but the impact of AI on learner autonomy has been little researched.  This study investigates how first-year EFL students exercise learner agency via AI in their English learning. The study employed qualitative exploratory design with 18 first-year undergraduate students of English Education at a private university in West Kalimantan, Indonesia. The participants were purposefully selected based on their experience with AI-based apps like ChatGPT, Gemini, Grammarly and the like. Data was collected by semi-structured interviews and analyzed by reflexive thematic analysis. Three themes emerged: AI as a driver of informed educational decisions, self-directed learning strategies in AI-augmented education, and pros and cons of AI utilization. These findings suggest that students were able to steer their learning in a successful way by selecting appropriate AI tools, critically assessing AI-generated responses, refining prompts, and combining AI with other learning resources. Attendees worried about the accuracy of information, too much dependence on AI and ethical questions in academia. The findings highlight learner autonomy as an essential factor in maximizing the pedagogical promise of AI, contributing to the body of knowledge on AI-assisted language learning in higher education.</jats:p>

title: A program evaluation for teaching AI prompt engineering for evidence-based medicine to fourth year medical students
container-title: BMC Medical Education
2d24dcf603ee893f9e4f9c89476289caf34592aa.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Prompt engineering is an emerging competency in medical education, essential for applying large language models (LLMs) to evidence-based medicine (EBM). This study evaluates an instructional approach designed to introduce medical students to two prompt engineering frameworks using a closed AI-assisted interdisciplinary database to answer clinical questions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Nineteen fourth-year medical students participated in three 45-minute, one-on-one individualized sessions facilitated by faculty. Students were trained to construct AI prompts using PICO (Patient, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) and CLEAR (Concise, Logical, Explicit, Adaptive, Reflective) frameworks within Scopus AI. Effectiveness was measured through weekly evaluations and end-of-program structured group interviews.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>All students completed the 3-part program. Mean confidence in prompt generation was high throughout the program: 1.16 for week one, 1.32 week two, and 1.05 week three (1 = Strongly Agree, 4 = Strongly Disagree). Students preferred the PICO framework for clinical use, finding it more straightforward and applicable for quick searches than CLEAR. Scopus AI was specifically valued for providing credible, verifiable, and peer-reviewed references compared to other open general AI tools such as ChatGPT.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Brief, individualized instruction is perceived as an effective model for teaching AI literacy and prompt engineering, though scaling requires balancing faculty time with educational value. Utilizing a closed AI system helps mitigate inaccuracies while enhancing student confidence in EBM application. This 3-part one-on-one curriculum provided a viable framework for integrating prompt engineering into fourth-year medical student clinical rotations to support evidence-based, point-of-care clinical decisions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Assessing Self-Perceived Critical Thinking in AI-Mediated Academic Tasks: Development and Initial Psychometric Evidence for the Critical Thinking with AI Scale for Students (CTAI-S)
container-title: Education Sciences
354600dbb593f593a6db155facc9a3df7bc34da1.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is commonly used in university academic work, yet existing instruments mainly assess AI literacy, readiness, or levels of permitted use rather than the critical-thinking processes students activate when working with AI. This study developed the Critical Thinking with AI Scale for Students (CTAI-S) and provided initial psychometric evidence for its use. An initial 15-item questionnaire was administered to 271 university students, and one item was removed after item analysis. Parallel analysis favored one predominant factor (KMO = 0.927), and a theory-guided three-factor representation was also examined. Ordinal confirmatory factor analyses (WLSMV; n = 257) yielded scaled CFI = 0.964 and RMSEA = 0.072 for the one-factor model, and CFI = 0.977 and RMSEA = 0.059 for the equivalent correlated-three-factor and second-order models; robust indices were less favorable, and latent correlations were very high (0.85–0.88). Total-score reliability was high (ω = 0.898), whereas the third grouping showed low reliability (ω = 0.557). Mean responses were above the scale midpoint (M = 3.97), with Reflective Judgment and Self-Regulation being highest (M = 4.07). The CTAI-S is best interpreted as a global self-report measure of critical thinking in AI-mediated academic tasks; independent validation is needed before dimensional or diagnostic applications.</jats:p>

title: Generative AI Use in Indonesian Language Learning: A Descriptive Survey of University Students
container-title: International Journal of Humanities, Education, and Social Sciences
c69b4ba6eaa5297e26cd468d7acd89b6ab38cfdc.abstract: <jats:p>Despite considerable research attention to generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education, empirical evidence on its use in Indonesian language courses remains limited, particularly studies integrating usage, perceptions, opportunities, challenges, AI literacy, and ethics. This study aimed to describe these six dimensions among first-year university students. A quantitative descriptive survey involved 69 students from two parallel classes. Data were collected using a 30-item questionnaire (Cronbach’s α = .752–.873) and analyzed using descriptive statistics, categorical interpretation, and supplementary nonparametric comparisons. The findings showed that 87.0% of students had used GenAI, primarily Gemini and ChatGPT. Perceptions (M = 3.79), opportunities (M = 3.70), and ethical awareness (M = 3.82) were high, whereas challenges (M = 3.37), AI literacy (M = 3.27), and usage intensity (M = 2.88) were moderate. Users scored higher than non-users on perceptions, opportunities, and AI literacy; however, among users, AI literacy was not associated with frequency or duration of use. These findings suggest that students’ acceptance of GenAI exceeds their AI literacy, identifying a potential acceptance–competence gap in GenAI adoption. The study contributes a conceptual perspective on this gap and highlights the need for lecturers and institutions to integrate structured AI literacy and ethics instruction into Indonesian language courses. Further research should examine this gap using larger samples and performance-based measures.</jats:p>

title: Generative AI in Gamified Learning: A Systematic Literature Review on Student Motivation
container-title: Research in Education, Technology, and Multiculture
96476196bfcfd1c9cf2c5a871d3b5fbc8b73ae94.abstract: <jats:p>This Systematic Literature Review (SLR) synthesizes how Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) is implemented in learning environments, with and without gamification, and what studies report about students’ motivation and engagement. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, structured searches in Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and ScienceDirect identified 792 records, and 116 full-text reports were assessed. Sixty-nine peer-reviewed journal articles were included: 21 on AI-supported gamified or game-based learning and 48 on Generative AI and motivation or engagement without gamification. In the gamified subset, four implementation forms appear (AI characters and role-play partners, LLM feedback and adaptive difficulty, AI-generated assessment items, and Generative AI as a game design tool), and all eight comparison studies reported higher or favorable motivation, engagement, or related outcomes. Across the whole corpus, two meta-analyses and one systematic review report positive overall effects of ChatGPT and Generative AI on engagement or motivation, with moderators and mixed emotional evidence. Individual studies are not uniformly positive: one found that videos outperformed a Generative AI assistant on knowledge gains and curiosity, one found no significant effect on behavioral engagement, and one found that Generative AI use may reduce active learning and motivation. The evidence is concentrated in higher education (48 of 69 articles) and in 2025 (52 of 69); the most frequently stated limitations are small or single-context samples (20 articles) and short interventions with novelty effects (12), and the most frequent recommendations are longer studies (18) and larger and more diverse samples (17). Future research should isolate the AI component's contribution and test it over time. Keywords: Generative AI, Gamification, Gamified learning, Student motivation, Systematic review of literature.</jats:p>

title: Can AI Help Students Explain “Recursion”? A Platform-Based Intervention for Developing Explanatory Competence
container-title: Education Sciences
fc817ef282d10c70d85e65a7d1e8f682fc56c6bd.abstract: <jats:p>English for Academic Purposes (EAP) has traditionally focused on helping students enter disciplinary discourse communities yet has largely overlooked explanatory competence. This gap is particularly pronounced at cross-disciplinary universities where students must articulate specialized concepts across diverse audiences. This study investigated the role of AI-mediated dialogue in helping EAP students enhance their explanatory competence, as manifested in their metaphor refinement across three dimensions: clarity, accuracy, and audience adaptation. A three-week intervention was conducted with 41 first-year undergraduate EAP students at a cross-disciplinary university in Guangzhou, China. Students refined their metaphorical explanations of the term ‘recursion’ under two conditions: Group A (n = 26) engaged in AI-mediated dialogue via ParallelX.cn, an AI-powered educational platform, featuring branching conversation prompts and peer feedback, while Group B (n = 15) refined independently. Results showed that both groups reported positive gains in perceived explanatory competence. In comparison, however, Group A scored slightly higher than Group B in perceived clarity, accuracy, and audience adaptation, while also rating higher AI’s capacity to balance simplicity with accuracy though this difference did not reach statistical significance. Group B valued independent reflection but also expressed a desire for additional support. By contrast, Group A registered slightly higher scores in their belief that AI-mediated dialogue facilitated their deep thinking and metaphorical clarity. Qualitative analysis of AI dialogue logs further suggested iterative refinement and increased technical precision, consistent with the survey findings. These findings suggest that AI-mediated refinement can support the development of metaphor-mediated explanatory competence, with implications for EAP pedagogy and AI-enhanced language learning.</jats:p>

title: Innovator 5.0: Integrating Design Thinking and Responsible Innovation into AI and Robotics Research Environments for Industry 5.0 and Society 5.0
container-title: Education Sciences
86d29795e15a2d3a865a66faee23509a3fa65f80.abstract: <jats:p>Industry 5.0 and Society 5.0 call for a shift in AI and robotics development from a primary focus on automation and technical sophistication to holistic solutions that address human needs, social contexts, stakeholder perspectives, and broader societal impacts. Preparing future engineers for this shift requires educational approaches that connect technical development with design thinking and responsible innovation. To address this need, this study introduces Innovator 5.0, an educational framework that extends the Science–Engineering–Design (SED) model by incorporating responsibility (R + SED) within a design-thinking process. The proposed framework was implemented through seven embedded workshops during a five- to six-month international research internship involving nine undergraduate students across six AI and robotics projects. An exploratory post-programme evaluation examined participants’ design-oriented practices, perceived capability development, and experiences within the research environment. Participants reported high ratings across several evaluated dimensions, particularly for challenging problem statements before solution development (M = 6.78/7), systems thinking (M = 6.67/7), creative innovation (M = 6.56/7), contextual awareness (M = 6.33/7), and iterative revision (M = 6.11/7). They also highlighted project autonomy and facilitative mentoring as valued features, while limited direct stakeholder access was identified as an important implementation constraint. Together, these findings provide practical guidance for preparing engineers to consider the purpose, societal implications, and value of AI and robotics innovations alongside their technical feasibility, supporting people-centric and responsible engineering innovation.</jats:p>

title: Theorising Algorithmic Colonialism: Generative AI and the Threat to Indigenous Knowledge Systems in African Higher Education
container-title: Trends in Higher Education
68e0238dc9916d34b72f6ced9b1a291d7cb954ec.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence in higher education has precipitated a new crisis of legitimacy for Indigenous Knowledge Systems. While the utility of large language models is widely touted, this paper critically interrogates the epistemological architecture of these tools, theorising algorithmic colonialism as a curricular mechanism of epistemic erasure in post-#FeesMustFall South African universities. Designed as a conceptual paper, the article extends the boundaries of knowledge by theorising peer-reviewed literature and policy frameworks between 2020 and 2025 to understand the specific threat Generative AI poses to Indigenous Knowledge Systems within African curricula. The principal analytical findings reveal that Large Language Models rely on data extractivism and linguistic hegemony, mechanisms that systematically marginalise Indigenous Knowledge Systems in favour of Western cognitive models. Drawing on decoloniality and critical digital pedagogy, the paper argues that the uncritical integration of these tools into African university curricula risks entrenching a monoculture of the mind where machine-generated consensus displaces localised, context-specific wisdom. The analysis explores the specific mechanisms through which algorithmic bias reinforces historical inequities. Consequently, the paper proposes a robust, operational framework for AI sovereignty within African higher education grounded in data trusts, Reinforcement Learning from African Feedback (RLAF), and algorithmic literacy as counter-conduct. The paper concludes that for the Fourth Industrial Revolution to be emancipatory rather than recolonising, the curriculum must explicitly teach students to audit the colonial logic embedded within the code itself.</jats:p>

title:
ChemMindLab:
An Intelligent Web-Based Platform for
the Integrated Development of Computational and AI Thinking
container-title: Journal of Chemical Education
7da285ee294c5514355d8982d268f86cd5e26439.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>AI for Science (AI4S) education has become an important direction in chemistry education as artificial intelligence increasingly shapes the formulation, screening, and validation of molecular and materials problems. ChemMindLab was developed as a web-based instructional platform that uses AI4S-oriented molecular candidate-screening activities to cultivate interdisciplinary learners with both computational and AI thinking. Through two representative instructional activities, the platform introduces students to research practices resembling authentic AI4S materials discovery: comparison of quantum mechanical (QM) calculations with machine-learning-potential (MLP) predictions for a molecular structure, followed by extension to isomeric candidate-set screening. A context-aware large language model (LLM) assistant supports explanation, operational guidance, and troubleshooting. Preliminary classroom use with undergraduate and graduate chemistry students suggests that ChemMindLab can support guided activities based on the two instructional workflows.</jats:p>

title: Governing AI-Supported Decisions: A Maqasid-Shura Decision-Escalation Model for Madrasahs
container-title: At Tadbir: Islamic Education Management Journal
862360e0fa17df03ba1de15554df29ef79083643.abstract: <jats:p>This study analyses the use and role of artificial intelligence (AI) in managerial decision-making at madrasahs and formulates governance mechanisms to determine the circumstances under which AI-assisted decisions require human review and more in-depth ethical consideration. This study employs a qualitative approach using a case study design at MAN 1 Bojonegoro, East Java, involving 15 participants comprising the headteacher, teachers, academic coordinators and system operators. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, non-participant observation and document analysis, and were subsequently analysed thematically through triangulation and member checking. The findings indicate that AI enhances administrative efficiency, real-time reporting, learning analytics and early warning functions; however, decision-making authority remains with human actors based on the level of consequences of the decision. Islamic values, particularly amanah and shura, serve as governing principles through responsible data management, consultation and ethical consideration. Based on these findings, this study developed the Maqasid-Shura Decision-Escalation (MSDE) analytical model, formulated on the basis of empirical findings and comprising five stages: AI-assisted evidence, human verification, consequence classification, Maqasid-Shura escalation, and accountable authorisation and feedback. This research contributes to the management of Islamic education by offering a testable governance proposition to integrate AI, human accountability and Islamic ethical principles into decision-making in madrasahs. However, the model still requires further validation in contexts beyond this single case study.</jats:p>

title: An Analysis of Paths for Integrating AI Assessment in English Teaching Scenarios
container-title: Academic Journal of Education
11a51f8871a14498c562be658bf4e79d7a06e911.abstract: <jats:p>This paper studies practical paths for applying artificial intelligence in assessment in English language teaching. AI-based assessment is defined here as the supervised application of automated scoring, speech or text analysis, adaptive task delivery, and generative feedback to support evidence collection and pedagogical decisions. AI will be used to build the assessment system; it will not function independently as an examiner. It is a staged path that begins with the construction of definitions and low-stakes formative uses, continues to teacher moderation and learner dialogue, and develops into institutionally regulated implementation with validation, privacy protection, fairness review, and appeal mechanisms. Examples of writing, speaking, reading, listening and classroom feedback are provided. The paper is theoretical and practical, and there are no original learners, datasets, experiments, scores or statistical results. Therefore, it is not expected that AI will improve accuracy, achievement, efficiency and fairness. At its core, the educational goals are to learn by example, to think independently, and to be accountable.</jats:p>

title: Research and Practice on Developing Teaching Teams for AI General Education in Higher Vocational Colleges
container-title: Academic Journal of Education
8f48a384f99a5d585fd1ea8a7791857fdf13e4dd.abstract: <jats:p> This study examines how teaching teams can develop the complementary capabilities in technology application, industry understanding, and translation of expertise into teaching required for AI general education in higher vocational colleges. Taking Jiangsu Maritime Institute as a case, it explores pathways for team development and mechanisms for teaching delivery. Within the “1+M+N” curriculum framework, shared platforms bring together faculty from different disciplines, research–teaching integration converts projects supporting industrial digital and intelligent transformation into teaching resources, and a three-setting professional development initiative strengthens teachers’ capabilities. Collaboration between general education and disciplinary faculty, structured mentoring, and human–AI collaboration supports the division of teaching responsibilities, knowledge sharing, and classroom improvement. The resulting approach connects team development with teaching practice and offers a reference for industry-oriented vocational colleges developing AI general education teaching teams.</jats:p>

title: Transitional challenges in integrating AI into the curriculum: The case of higher education in the Philippines as a developing country
container-title: International Journal of Education and Practice
fbfd1f9377ea4caaaa4453fb40c042afadf7034e.abstract: <jats:p>Despite the rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education worldwide, existing studies are predominantly focused on the opportunities and technological benefits of AI adoption, while paying limited attention to the transitional challenges experienced by higher education institutions in developing-country contexts, such as the Philippines. This gap is problematic because uneven institutional readiness, technological inequality, faculty adaptation struggles, and ethical uncertainties may hinder sustainable and equitable AI integration within higher education systems. Understanding these transitional realities is essential for developing context-sensitive educational policies and institutional strategies that support responsible and inclusive AI-driven transformation. This study employed a qualitative exploratory narrative design involving selected higher education educators and academic personnel from institutions in Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao in the Philippines. Data were gathered through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using thematic narrative analysis. The findings revealed that institutional unpreparedness, curriculum disruption, technological limitations, faculty adaptation struggles, ethical tensions, and unequal institutional capacity shape AI integration. Educators likewise perceived AI as an inevitable educational shift while expressing concerns regarding declining critical thinking, loss of human connection, and unequal readiness for future AI integration. The study highlights the need for responsive policies, faculty development initiatives, ethical AI governance, and sustainable educational planning for developing-country higher education systems. </jats:p>

title: Reconceptualizing student teachers’ AI literacy in the Global South: Towards a teacher AI-readiness mapping framework
container-title: Journal of Education and e-Learning Research
21d1b1f99bf1c1cae765740df5e90c7a8560eff5.abstract: <jats:p>The responsible use of AI in the classroom begins with teachers’ knowledge and skills needed to integrate AI into the educational context. This study used a qualitative single-case study design to examine AI literacy and readiness among pre-service teachers in the Global South. Grounded in a conceptual framework combining AI literacy and technology acceptance, the study explores how pre-service teachers perceive, use, evaluate, and envision AI as their professional roles evolve. Data were generated from open-ended questionnaire responses from 197 first-year Bachelor of Education students enrolled at the University of South Africa, an open distance e-learning institution. Through iterative engagement with the data, six interrelated themes emerged: AI knowledge, AI skills, AI ethics, AI confidence, AI critical reflection, and AI pedagogical imagination. The findings indicate that AI readiness extends beyond technical competence or familiarity with tools. It is developmental, uneven, and shaped by contextual conditions such as access, language, and institutional guidance. Based on these insights, a framework is proposed to map teacher AI readiness and identify readiness gaps. The findings emphasise that teacher education programmes should go beyond tool training to include ethical clarity, policy guidance, confidence, critical thinking, pedagogical design, and equitable access.</jats:p>

title: Micro-Credentials as an Institutional Response to AI: Early Implementation in Pre-Service Teacher Education at a Chinese Normal University
container-title: Education Sciences
535d842bf5d98d31e185c83cc3c579fbd08fb297.abstract: <jats:p>Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are unsettling established ways of preparing teachers, pressuring higher education institutions to reform curricula faster than conventional degree structures allow. This study examines how one Chinese normal university initiated and implemented an AI-focused micro-credential program for pre-service teachers as an institutional response to these pressures. Drawing on Institutional Theory and Activity Theory, the case study combines document analysis, semi-structured interviews, a student satisfaction questionnaire, and comparative analysis of pre- and post-course lesson plans. Findings show that the program emerged from coercive, normative, and mimetic pressures emanating from national policy, professional communities, and peer institutions, and was implemented through cross-faculty collaboration, university–industry–school partnerships, and a phased curriculum progressing from technical application to pedagogical integration. Students reported high satisfaction, and their revised lesson plans showed stronger relative associations among AI-related technological, pedagogical, and content codes; however, the program encountered challenges including academic workload, learner heterogeneity, and limited hands-on practice. The study contributes to understanding early institutional adoption and organizational adaptation by examining how one university established an AI-focused initiative and adjusted its implementation arrangements during the first semester. Whether these arrangements become enduring institutional practices or similar dynamics arise in other national contexts requires longitudinal and comparative research. These insights offer change agents—teacher educators, university leaders, and policymakers—a case-based account of an initial institutional response to technological and policy pressure.</jats:p>

title: From Code-Centric to Intent-Centric Software Engineering: A Reflexive Thematic Analysis of Generative AI, Agentic Systems, and Engineering Accountability
container-title: Computers
b8b475504b37ed3bec01880f6991e5586b1ec8f1.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and agentic systems are shifting software engineering from code-centric production toward intent-centric human-agent work, in which natural language, repository context, tools, tests, and governance shape delivery. Prior studies examine code generation, AI pair programming, and software engineering agents, but less is known about how public technical discourse and peer-reviewed evidence jointly frame the profession’s near-term transition. This study addresses that gap through a reflexive thematic analysis (RTA) of public-discourse and document analysis. The corpus combines peer-reviewed software engineering and AI literature, technical benchmarks, public talks and interviews, essays, product-facing technical announcements, and X-originated discourse. The corpus contains 49 unique artifacts across three evidentiary layers: 28 peer-reviewed sources, 6 technical preprints/benchmarks, and 15 public discourse artifacts. Sources were organized using a corpus register, codebook, coding matrix, theme-to-source traceability table, DOI/reference audit, and reproducibility protocol. The analysis indicates that GenAI lowers the cost of producing plausible code while increasing the importance of intent specification, context curation, architecture knowledge, verification, security, provenance, governance, and accountable human judgment. Software engineering is consequently becoming less about isolated code authorship and more about supervising, validating, and governing socio-technical systems of humans, agents, tools, and evidence gates. Bounded autonomy can preserve quality, security, maintainability, and trust while limiting hidden technical debt and accountability gaps.</jats:p>
