title: Known by the Machine: Building Relational Presence with AI NPCs for Stigma-Free Mental Health Literacy in Games
container-title: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
4c9c9964378a64482a43967764b54ff15bb6fa76.abstract: <jats:p>Mental Health (MH) remains a global priority, yet low literacy and stigma frequently limit open discussion and help-seeking behaviors. While game-based education has shown promise in supporting stigma reduction and literacy improvement, the potential for Large Language Models (LLMs) to support non-judgmental, playful exploration of sensitive topics remains underexplored, specifically, the role of conversational memory to support trust-building in MH discussions. We conducted a four-session, longitudinal mixed-methods study to evaluate how the relational presence of AI characters, powered by GPT-4o-mini with varied memory designs, relates to player experience and learning. Moving beyond an evaluation of learning, we examine how the perception of being known by an AI NPC is associated with engagement with stigmatized content. Results indicate that while participants achieved significant and sustained gains in Mental Health Literacy (MHL), these improvements did not differ by memory condition. Instead, memory appeared to operate as a relational design feature that shaped participants’ perceptions of social presence, with many describing conversational NPCs as supportive companions. We also identify interactional risks, such as algorithmic vagueness and privacy-induced hesitation, that participants described as reducing their comfort during conversations. We conclude by offering design recommendations for leveraging LLM memory to create more relational and stigma-sensitive environments for MH education.</jats:p>

title: Guards & Wards: The Creative Labour of GMs and Considerations for Designing with AI
container-title: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
97f59e27090381539a8186baf42b7de0cca1bb39.abstract: <jats:p>Tabletop role-playing games (TTRPGs) provide a complicated environment for creativity. Game masters (GMs) co-create a story along with their players and many choose to complete significant labour both prior to and during a gaming session. However, the boundaries that GMs may have about generative artificial intelligence (AI) being used in this creative hobby have not been examined. We examine the perceptions of GMs on the use of AI for creativity support in TTRPGs. We conducted a survey of GMs to discover the labour they completed in preparation for and play of TTRPG sessions, the existing creativity support tools (CSTs) that they use for this labour, and their opinions on the use of AI in TTRPGs. We performed both qualitative and quantitative analysis to examine survey data. We contrasted our results across two participant groups: those who have or have not been paid to GM a gaming session, and those who have or have not used AI as GMs. From our data, we created twelve distinct orientation groups encompassing the opinions of participants on AI for use in TTRPGs. We propose thirteen design considerations in the form of questions AI tool developers should ask when creating AI-based CSTs for TTRPG use.</jats:p>

title: Age Matters: Age-Differentiated Playtesting for AI Educational Games
container-title: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
51c2ffec725312491c89a2f2140899598712ae8b.abstract: <jats:p>Playtesting is widely employed in educational game design as a post-hoc method for game design validation within the age groups that the learning goals target. For domains such as AI literacy, age-targeted educational games testing may be limiting, as AI learning goals are relevant and frequently misunderstood by children, adolescents and young adults. Designing educational games that teach AI to a wider audience of ages requires playtesting with players of different ages to better interpret gameplay and narrative appropriateness of AI in AI educational games. In this study, we playtested four AI educational games with middle, high school, and college aged students, and analyzed playtesting data, including verbal discourse, in-game behaviors, and post-playtesting reflections. Our findings demonstrate that playtesting can serve as an asset-based practice which reveals how players of different age groups make sense of educational games during play. We provide critical reflections from multi-age playtesting of AI educational games that inform design, and recommendations for engaging AI educational game design.</jats:p>

title: Does Trust Spill Over?: Exploring Asymmetric Trust Dynamics Between Teammate AI and Guide AI in Cooperative Games
container-title: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
aa082ec48f7a3ea66734c5c6aa6b23a8c21c5b8a.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Cooperative games increasingly feature multiple AI agents serving distinct roles, yet how players form and transfer trust across such agents remains unclear. We investigated trust spillover between a task-executing Teammate AI and an advisory Guide AI in a web-based cooperative cooking game (within-subjects, N = 23). Teammate AI ability (high vs. low) and Guide AI accuracy (high vs. low/absent) were experimentally manipulated. Results revealed a directional asymmetry in trust spillover. Teammate AI ability significantly influenced trust in the Guide AI (
                    <jats:inline-formula content-type="math/tex">
                      <jats:tex-math notation="LaTeX" version="MathJax">\(\eta _p^2 =.220\)</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ), whereas Guide AI accuracy and presence had no effect on trust in the Teammate AI (
                    <jats:inline-formula content-type="math/tex">
                      <jats:tex-math notation="LaTeX" version="MathJax">\(\eta _p^2 =.002\)</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ). This suggests that, under cognitive constraints, trust propagates from high-salience task agents to lower-salience advisory agents, but not vice versa. Additionally, the presence of the Guide AI improved performance and perceived control independent of advice accuracy, suggesting an attentional cueing effect. Finally, congruent agent quality levels enhanced perceived relatedness, highlighting the importance of system-level coherence. These findings demonstrate asymmetric trust spillover in cooperative games with role-differentiated AI, where execution-focused agents anchor system-wide trust formation, with implications for multi-agent AI systems in which agents serve distinct functional roles.
                  </jats:p>

title: Player Perceptions of Generative AI in Games: A Steam Review Analysis
container-title: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
08911279f04c0994a25c0ab11145fcff09c60790.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid adoption of generative AI in game development has created large discussions among players, yet little empirical work has examined how players actually perceive AI-generated content. Employing quantitative methods, we study the adoption of generative AI in games in the Steam marketplace, using procedural content generation (PCG) as a baseline of a generative technology that was successfully integrated into games over several decades. Furthermore, using qualitative methods, we study player reception of generative AI by analyzing 508,192 English-language reviews. We found that games disclosing generative AI use receive lower recommendation rates and more negative overall sentiment than PCG games. Thematic analysis of 600 reviews shows that players perceive the use of generative AI in games as low developer investment in the game. Drawing on human-centered AI frameworks, we argue that successful generative AI adoption requires deploying generative AI for what players need, not for what makes development cheaper.</jats:p>

title: Meritocracy and generative AI in higher education: institutional pathways and use–response alignment across four systems
container-title: Advances in Social Behavior Research
1d18258e5287d5117654b68c5dc746e92d867f48.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines how higher education systems respond to the rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) under different institutional conditions, asking how meritocratic competition is translated into assessment and credential pressure and how student GenAI use aligns with institutional responses. Using a comparative qualitative case-study design, the study analyzes secondary evidence from China, the United Kingdom, the United States, and Germany through two a priori frozen indicator frameworks. The first framework traces how meritocratic competition is institutionalized through admissions, grading, and credential differentiation; the second maps student GenAI use patterns against institutional responses in teaching, assessment, and support. Strong credential differentiation and education–labour-market linkage emerge in all four systems, but through distinct pathways: state-coordinated in China, marketized in the United Kingdom, decentralized and market-oriented in the United States, and state–professional in Germany. Partial use–response alignment is the cross-system norm; systems differ mainly in pedagogical integration, regulatory adaptation, and institutional support. AI literacy and support provision lag behind student adoption in all four cases, making institutional capacity the most persistent source of misalignment, while limited comparable measurement of equity alignment and of guarded and compensatory use shows that monitoring capacity is itself part of governance. GenAI governance therefore converges less on common rules than on common capability gaps. The findings suggest that governing GenAI in meritocratic systems depends less on uniform rules than on sustained investment in institutional monitoring and support capacity.</jats:p>

title: Generative AI-enabled writing feedback in primary school English instruction: application landscape, practical dilemmas, and a teacher-led collaborative framework
container-title: Advances in Social Behavior Research
46a2a0e62e833b05feb28298ad275d5b27608889.abstract: <jats:p>Writing feedback is a pivotal yet chronically constrained component of primary school English writing instruction, squeezed by large class sizes, low marking frequency, and homogeneous comments. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), with its immediacy, personalization, and dialogic interaction, opens new possibilities for reconstructing writing feedback. Drawing on a narrative synthesis of 52 Chinese and international sources, and addressing a literature in which research on AI writing feedback concentrates on higher education and on the learner side, this paper maps the application landscape of GenAI-enabled writing feedback in primary school English, consolidates and examines five practical dilemmas concerning accuracy, appropriateness, teacher literacy, ethics, and evaluation orientation, and proposes a Teacher-led, AI-assisted, Student-centered Collaborative Feedback Framework (TAC-F). The framework assigns teachers responsibility for goal setting, affective support, and feedback verification, positions GenAI as an initial assessor and material provider, and treats students as reflective revisers within a pre-writing, while-writing, and post-writing closed loop, supported by prompt-template libraries, feedback-verification routines, school-based teacher AI literacy development, and ethical data norms. Preliminary multi-tool observations, together with a six-dimension observation framework and a same-prompt pilot protocol, are developed to help teachers screen AI-generated feedback; the observations suggest that current tools are reliable on explicit errors but unstable at the discourse level. Six implementation suggestions are advanced to inform the digital transformation of primary school English writing instruction.</jats:p>

title: Visual Sexual Health Communication Assisted by AI: The Case of Synthetic Menstruation Images
container-title: Archives of Sexual Behavior
08fb882f77177fa29f70584626a13ad9137367d1.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Public communication about sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) relies on both text and images. A recent development is the proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) image generators, which enable rapid, cost-effective, and highly customizable images with appealing aesthetics based on textual requests (prompts). To examine the opportunities and challenges of AI-generated images in SRHR communication, we used the topic of menstruation and developed six research questions (RQs) anchored in the current state of research on AI-supported visual health communication. These questions addressed key areas of concern, such as unsuccessful image creation (RQ1), objective image flaws (RQ2), lack of diversity of human representation (RQ3), stereotypical portrayals of women (RQ4), use of visual symbols (RQ5), and image valence (RQ6). Our study applied 15 AI image generators, 2 user accounts per generator, 5 menstruation-related prompts, 2 prompt languages, and 2 images per prompt, resulting in a sample of
                    <jats:italic>N</jats:italic>
                     = 600 AI outputs generated in Autumn 2025. All outputs were manually coded using a reliability-tested codebook developed through both deductive and inductive approaches. In 20.0% of cases, menstruation prompts did not produce the requested image but only text output (RQ1). When images were generated, they often (78.1%) exhibited visual and/or textual flaws (RQ2). The images showed a lack of diversity in some human attributes (e.g., body type) but not in others (e.g., skin tone; RQ3). Stereotypical depictions of women were observed but not predominant (RQ4). Common menstruation-related visual symbols (e.g., blood, pain) were identified (RQ5), but most images did not convey a negative portrayal and instead a neutral or positive portrayal of menstruation (RQ6). While results show that initial outputs from AI image generators are often not directly suitable for visual sexual health communication, they might work with targeted refinement. Further research is required to examine the production, characteristics, consumption, and effects of AI-generated images in SRHR communication.
                  </jats:p>

title: Secure Edge-AI Sensing on an FPGA SoC: Lightweight ASCON Authentication of Model Updates and Interface-Bound Inference for Bearing-Fault Detection
container-title: Computers
303d4ba538744ba35fa73581feb18063f5c07d26.abstract: <jats:p>Vibration monitoring increasingly classifies on the sensing node. We ask where the cost of running and securely updating a small classifier on an FPGA system-on-chip node lies. One Q4.12 multilayer perceptron for bearing-fault detection, trained on 40 CWRU recordings over four loads and three severities, is deployed bit-exactly on an ESP32-S3, a Cortex-A53 and a custom AXI4-Lite accelerator of the same Zynq UltraScale+ device (Kria KV260), checked on all 2132 windows. The fabric computes one inference in 36 cycles (0.36 µs), yet the latency under the PYNQ driver is 133.2 µs; a native-C driver reduces it to 3.59 µs, placing 95–97% of the per-transaction cost in the host software stack. Moving the update decision into the fabric, with the ASCON-AEAD128 tag check, version freshness and staging enforced in hardware, rejects every tested forgery, replay and direct write, and cuts a 608-byte authenticated update from 148.7 to 66.0 µs in native C. The full chain runs in real time, with no deadline miss over 552 windows (worst case 1.8% of the 171 ms window), and feature extraction dominates its cost. The model reaches 98.2% on unseen segments but generalizes poorly to unseen fault severities and to real damage of unseen Paderborn bearings, which makes field updates a requirement.</jats:p>

title: Edge AI Imitation of Event-Triggered Model Predictive Control for an Inverted Pendulum
container-title: Computers
05938ee211a2e0d7b4b9a7b07cb4c17bb8bcfd63.abstract: <jats:p>Event-triggered model predictive control (MPC) updates the control input only when needed, but it still solves an optimization problem at every event, which on the studied cart–pole can exceed its 10 ms control period. We propose a compact multi-task neural network that replaces the whole scheme: it decides when to update the input and which value to apply, using only online measurements. It is trained on 500 physical recordings, adapted to a simulated teacher and refined with DAgger. Feeding it the held input produces a copycat policy that is accurate in open loop but sluggish in closed loop; in a matched comparison over four training seeds, removing that input raises full-episode success from three to 39 of 40 episodes. In simulation, at the default sensor noise, the final network completes all swing-up and tracking episodes, with time to upright and tracking error close to the teacher’s, whereas on the simulated teacher, tree ensembles have 1.4–1.6 times its open-loop error. In an open-loop replay on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller, a step takes under 40% of the period. In tracking and full episodes, it updates the input 33–39% more often than the teacher, mainly because it does not learn the rule’s sparsity.</jats:p>

title: Explainable Machine Learning for Analyzing AI Adoption and Teachers’ Professional Development Needs: Evidence from TALIS 2024 in Kazakhstan
container-title: Computers
d995276851023c13b6f90d18faa245a7956a09a2.abstract: <jats:p>The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in education highlights the need to distinguish teachers’ AI adoption from their professional development needs. This study examined these outcomes as separate predictive tasks using OECD TALIS 2024 data for 7360 teachers in Kazakhstan at ISCED level 2. After excluding invalid outcome records, the analytical samples comprised 2430 teachers for AI adoption and 4868 for professional development needs. Population estimates and confidence intervals were calculated using teacher weights and 100 Fay-BRR replicate weights, while predictive performance was assessed using out-of-fold predictions and school-grouped validation. The weighted prevalence of AI adoption was 59.0% (95% CI: 56.1–61.9). Logistic Regression and CatBoost demonstrated comparable discrimination (ROC-AUC = 0.754 and 0.753, respectively), with no clear performance advantage for CatBoost. SHAP analysis identified prior AI-related professional learning, uncertainty regarding AI attitudes, and perceived AI benefits as prominent predictive factors. Moderate or high professional development need was estimated at 80.3% (95% CI: 78.7–81.9). However, individual prediction was weak, with balanced accuracy of 0.268 and a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.082. These findings indicate that TALIS variables provide a moderate predictive signal for AI adoption but are insufficient for reliable, individualized professional development decisions.</jats:p>

title: Generative AI in English Language Teaching: A Systematic Review of Its Impact on Teaching Practices and Learning Outcomes
container-title: International Journal of Social Science and Human Research
8fb433a0a2295e097a0eab7db1db828dcf5bf252.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are now common in English classrooms, but the research on them is spread thinly across different tools, settings and skills, and most of it records what people think rather than what learners actually gained. This review looks at how GenAI is changing the way English is taught and what learners gain from it. Using the PRISMA procedure, the review drew on Web of Science, Scopus, ScienceDirect and Springer, selecting peer-reviewed journal papers from 2024 to 2026; 28 studies were analysed in full. In most studies GenAI served as a helper for teachers in lesson planning, materials, feedback and classroom activities, but how far it was taken up varied with teachers’ own attitudes, self-assurance and preparation. Assessment was the area most challenged, prompting teachers to rethink task design and academic integrity. In terms of learning, GenAI is associated with perceived improvements in writing, grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation, motivation, confidence, and autonomy, but most evidence is perception-based rather than measured. The review concludes that GenAI is best used as a supplement to teacher-guided instruction, with teachers checking its output and guiding learners towards critical use. Future research should adopt longitudinal and controlled designs that measure language outcomes directly.</jats:p>

title: A Study on the Coupling Relationship Between AI Personalization and Long-Context Management
container-title: Computers and Artificial Intelligence
49889832b6f70b95f1a638c748d37b18136de351.abstract: <jats:p>With the large-scale deployment of large language models (LLMs) in various intelligent assistants and agent systems, homogenized outputs and the loss of user preferences across sessions have become key bottlenecks restricting improvements in user experience. Personalization technology aims to adapt LLMs to the language habits, thinking patterns, and subjective preferences of different users, while long-context and agent memory management addresses the underlying technical problems of storing, filtering, and reusing temporal information for LLMs. Current academic research mostly treats the two directions as independent fields, and systematic reviews of their internal coupling relationship are relatively scarce. This study first defines the core concepts of LLM personalization and long-context memory management and systematically reviews the technical principles, advantages, and existing limitations of four personalization paradigms: prompt-engineering personalization, lightweight parameter fine-tuning, user-preference alignment, and dynamic user profiling. It then divides long-context and agent-memory technologies into five routes: native-window expansion, context pruning and compression, adaptive context extraction, hierarchical memory architectures, and external retrieval-augmented memory, and analyzes the applicable scenarios and technical shortcomings of each route. On this basis, this study reviews progress in four intersecting directions: preference-aware memory updating, structured persona-memory representation, long-horizon personalization evaluation benchmarks, and training-free collaborative control at inference time. It further analyzes the internal coupling mechanism through which the two directions empower each other and summarizes three core conflicts: the capacity-accuracy trade-off, the conflict between general governance rules and personalized characteristics, and the conflict between computational cost and personalization stability. The study also summarizes five research challenges: difficulty in adapting to the dynamic evolution of user preferences, failure to recall implicit preferences, memory errors and preference drift, fragmented evaluation systems, and difficulty balancing engineering implementation costs. It proposes subsequent research paths in six dimensions: cognitively inspired memory architectures, preference-aware context compression algorithms, multimode hybrid indexing and retrieval, unified long-horizon personalization evaluation protocols, memory-error verification mechanisms, and multimodal long-term personalization. The findings indicate that long-term personalized intelligent systems cannot optimize the personalization module or memory module in isolation. Their coupling relationship should serve as the underlying design logic to promote the iterative upgrading of LLMs toward adaptation to individual user characteristics and to provide a reference for the theoretical research and engineering development of long-term agents and personalized dialogue assistants.</jats:p>

title: Budget-Aware Adaptive Test-Time Compute with Hierarchical Self-Verification for Semantic ID Generative Recommendation
container-title: Computers
ad812a7a10cc5144461b6cebf5c51d87590389d3.abstract: <jats:p>Semantic identifier (SID) generative recommenders cast retrieval as autoregressive decoding over short sequences of residual-quantized codewords. Most published SID recommenders decode all requests with one fixed beam width, which is optimal only if the marginal utility of compute is constant across requests. We find that it is not; additional search changes little for users with consistent histories, but improves accuracy substantially for cold start, interest-drifting, and long-tail users. The main methodological contribution of this paper is request-level allocation of decoding compute, in which a router predicts the accuracy gain of each configuration in a finite decoding menu over the cheapest configuration and selects the configuration with the largest gain net of a priced cost. The selection rule follows from standard Lagrangian arguments, which we use as tools; what is specific to this work is the use of this per-configuration gain as the routing target for SID decoding instead of a difficulty or uncertainty score. The resulting framework, called Bastion, combines the router with a hierarchical process verifier over the quantization levels, a listwise terminal verifier, codeword consistency voting, and budget-constrained group relative policy optimization. On five benchmarks built from Amazon Reviews 2023, MovieLens, and MicroLens, Bastion improves NDCG@10 by 5.7% to 8.7% over the strongest baseline. Its mean latency on Amazon-Beauty is 14.5 ms, against 14.6 ms for a beam-20 TIGER decoder, while its median and 99th-percentile latencies are higher by 0.9 ms and 7.0 ms. At every evaluated budget, its accuracy exceeds that of all baselines on the three datasets for which accuracy versus latency frontiers was measured.</jats:p>

title: Offloading Thoughts to the Bots: How Generative AI Access Influences Cognitive Reflection
container-title: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
89abf0f54d025ddf7e06b07b896cddba60561ff9.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly used to support reasoning and decision-making, raising questions about how AI influences reflective cognition and trust. This study examined how AI pedigree and reliability influenced cognitive reflection performance, cognitive load, trust, and performance overestimation during a verbal Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT-V). Participants (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">N</jats:italic>
                     = 148) were assigned to a no-AI control condition, a low-pedigree AI condition, or a high-pedigree AI condition. Participants in the high-pedigree AI condition demonstrated significantly greater trust and CRT performance than participants in both other conditions while also exhibiting lower performance overestimation. AI access did not significantly reduce perceived cognitive load, although greater cognitive load predicted poorer CRT performance overall. Importantly, trust interacted with AI condition such that greater trust predicted lower CRT performance in the low-pedigree AI condition but not in the high-pedigree AI condition. These findings support theories of calibrated reliance rather than indiscriminate cognitive offloading.
                  </jats:p>

title: A Study on AI Digital Competency and the Perceived Need for AI Utilization Education among Physical Therapy Students
container-title: Journal of Clinical Movement Science in Human
f8b52f591df875ac1c2019dd4f4b18ce9752e66d.abstract: <jats:p>Purpose This study aimed to examine AI digital competency and the perceived need for AI utilization education among physical therapy students and to analyze the relationship between the two variables. Methods This crosssectional correlational survey was conducted with 232 physical therapy students at S University using an online survey. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Pearson correlation analysis. Results The mean score for AI digital competency was 3.48±0.57, with communication and collaboration showing the highest score at 3.84±0.62 and digital content creation showing the lowest score at 3.03±0.71. The mean score for the perceived need for AI utilization education was 3.91±0.71. AI digital competency was positively correlated with the perceived need for AI utilization education (r=0.320, p<.001). Conclusion These results suggest the need for systematic educational support to help physical therapy students effectively use AI in majorrelated learning and clinical problemsolving.</jats:p>

title: From Code-Centric to Intent-Centric Software Engineering: A Reflexive Thematic Analysis of Generative AI, Agentic Systems, and Engineering Accountability
container-title: Computers
b8b475504b37ed3bec01880f6991e5586b1ec8f1.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and agentic systems are shifting software engineering from code-centric production toward intent-centric human-agent work, in which natural language, repository context, tools, tests, and governance shape delivery. Prior studies examine code generation, AI pair programming, and software engineering agents, but less is known about how public technical discourse and peer-reviewed evidence jointly frame the profession’s near-term transition. This study addresses that gap through a reflexive thematic analysis (RTA) of public-discourse and document analysis. The corpus combines peer-reviewed software engineering and AI literature, technical benchmarks, public talks and interviews, essays, product-facing technical announcements, and X-originated discourse. The corpus contains 49 unique artifacts across three evidentiary layers: 28 peer-reviewed sources, 6 technical preprints/benchmarks, and 15 public discourse artifacts. Sources were organized using a corpus register, codebook, coding matrix, theme-to-source traceability table, DOI/reference audit, and reproducibility protocol. The analysis indicates that GenAI lowers the cost of producing plausible code while increasing the importance of intent specification, context curation, architecture knowledge, verification, security, provenance, governance, and accountable human judgment. Software engineering is consequently becoming less about isolated code authorship and more about supervising, validating, and governing socio-technical systems of humans, agents, tools, and evidence gates. Bounded autonomy can preserve quality, security, maintainability, and trust while limiting hidden technical debt and accountability gaps.</jats:p>

title: Quantum-secure and AI-driven UAV-enabled 6G networks: a unified architecture for communication, intelligence, efficiency, and resilience
container-title: The Computer Journal
2706b267c202c5d2b4e0d881162c56dccf975efc.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The sixth generation (6G) of wireless networks is expected to meet stringent requirements such as ultra-low latency, massive connectivity, global coverage, and intrinsic security. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are emerging as key enablers of space–air–ground integrated networks, providing flexible and on-demand communication support for beyond-5G and 6G applications. In parallel, advances in quantum communication introduce new opportunities for achieving information-theoretic security against postquantum threats. This paper proposes a unified framework for quantum-secure and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven UAV-enabled 6G networks, integrating communication, intelligence, energy efficiency, and resilience into a coherent architecture. Beyond the design perspective, the paper evaluates network performance through Quality of Service and Grade of Service metrics, comparing 5G and 6G systems with and without AI and quantum-security capabilities. A ranking-based analysis is developed to assess the impact of these technologies on latency, reliability, scalability, and overall service performance. The results highlight the performance gains enabled by AI-driven optimization and quantum-secure communication, while also revealing trade-offs related to energy consumption, system complexity, and deployment constraints. Key challenges such as interoperability, hardware limitations, and scalability are discussed, along with design directions for realizing efficient, secure, and resilient UAV-enabled 6G networks.</jats:p>

title: Revisiting the diffusion of innovations theory: artificial intelligence adoption in social media

449a974a4bc897e7abdf866fa890c855a1b3ed29.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec id="j_omgc-2026-0013_abs_001">
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The present study aims at revisiting the applicability of Rogers’ diffusion of innovations theory in the digital era, particularly in relation to recent advancements in Artificial Intelligence and their use in social media. It further explores the role of generational differences in shaping AI adoption patterns.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_omgc-2026-0013_abs_002">
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drawing on rich qualitative data, the researchers adopt a multi-method approach comprising eighteen interviews with academic and professional experts across different countries, and four focus group discussions among different generations to collect first-hand insights on GenAI adoption. AI was itself used during qualitative data analysis following our AI-Assisted Data Analysis Procedure (ADAP), including generating and categorizing codes, themes, and excerpts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_omgc-2026-0013_abs_003">
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings provide updated insights into the elements of the diffusion process, establishing potential grounds for modernizing the theory in light of AI-driven innovations. Shifts in innovation attributes, decision-making processes, and generational influences are identified, revealing how AI adoption transforms communication practices within digitally networked environments that increasingly shape contemporary global communication. The study further highlights patterns of resistance and reasons for non-AI adoption.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_omgc-2026-0013_abs_004">
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study offers insights for communication professionals, platform designers, policymakers, and technology developers seeking to design and implement AI tools in social media environments in ways that account for generational differences in adoption patterns and decision-making processes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_omgc-2026-0013_abs_005">
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By examining GenAI adoption within digitally mediated societies, the study contributes to broader discussions about technological change, generational divides, societal consequences of GenAI integration, and the evolving diffusion of AI-driven innovations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_omgc-2026-0013_abs_006">
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study advances diffusion scholarship by empirically reassessing Rogers’ framework in the context of global AI-mediated communication and by proposing ADAP as a methodological contribution to qualitative communication research.</jats:p>

title: Trustworthy Federated Clinical Intelligence with Homomorphic Encryption and  Explainable AI
container-title: International Journal on Advanced Computer Engineering and Communication Technology
52dc2d5fa5cc8d54dabc189da8b019169d1f9138.abstract: <jats:p>Cross-institutional clinical artificial intelligence is constrained by fragmented patient data, non-identically distributed (non-IID) populations, leakage from shared model updates, and limited interpretability. Federated learning (FL) preserves data locality, but ordinary FL neither makes model updates confidential nor guarantees stable optimization under heterogeneous clients. This paper proposes a defense-in-depth framework that coordinates Federated Proximal (FedProx) optimization, record-level differential privacy (DP), Cheon–Kim–Kim–Song (CKKS) approximate homomorphic encryption, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). FedProx limits local model drift; DP-SGD bounds the influence of an individual training record; and CKKS permits weighted aggregation while client updates remain encrypted. A key-separated design keeps the aggregation server from being provisioned with the secret key used to reveal individual contributions; only the aggregate is released for global-model construction. Grad-CAM and SHAP/LIME provide clinician-facing explanations, while an audit dashboard reports convergence, privacy-accounting inputs, encryption status, and systems overhead. We formalize the learning objective, privacy mechanism, encrypted aggregation, threat model, numerical approximation error, communication footprint, and an evaluation protocol spanning IID and controlled non-IID partitions. The contribution is a reproducible system-level co-design and evaluation framework rather than a new cryptographic primitive or optimization algorithm.</jats:p>

title: Assessment of Taraba Broadcast Journalists Knowledge, Adoption and Usage of Artificial Intelligence in Journalistic Practices

3d595057b3e03ea8fa7b358699deebe39aca77a9.abstract:
<jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become an essential tool in various fields, including journalism.
However, the extent to which broadcast journalists in Taraba State, Nigeria embraced and utilized
AI in their practices remains a subject of debate. It is on the above premise that this research
examined Taraba State broadcast journalists' knowledge and usage of AI in journalistic practices.
The paper was built on the technology acceptance model, diffusion of innovation theory, and social
learning theory. The study adopted a qualitative approach where in-depth interviews were used.
The in-depth interviews were conducted until the results reached saturation point. Findings of the
study revealed that in journalists in Taraba State, Nigeria are slowly beginning to embrace AI for
journalistic practice. However, there knowledge of AI usage for journalistic practices is low hence
there is a significant knowledge gap that needs to be bridged. Therefore, the study recommends
among other things that journalists in Taraba State need to gain more knowledge about AI and its
potential applications in journalistic practices. The paper concludes that with proper training and
guidance, journalists in Taraba State can harness the power of this AI technology to improve their
reporting practices while ensuring ethical standards are upheld.</jats:p>

title: Health Information-Seeking Behaviour Using Artificial Intelligence Applications in Mobile Phones Among University Undergraduates in Anambra State
container-title: RESEARCH JOURNAL OF MASS COMMUNICATION AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY
fd09e6681e6192c0ba32d60c1070cf2cc3b130b9.abstract:
<jats:p>Seeking health information is a common practice that helps individuals understand health
conditions and manage illnesses. Among young people, this behaviour has increased due to the
rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, improved mobile phone capabilities, and
widespread internet access. However, despite the speed and convenience AI applications provide,
there is a risk of inaccurate or misleading information, especially when users’ health conditions
differ from the data on which the AI systems were trained. This study assessed the use of AI
applications on mobile phones for health information-seeking among university undergraduates
in Anambra State. The main objective was to examine undergraduates’ health information-seeking
behaviour in relation to their utilization of AI mobile applications. The study was anchored on the
Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Diffusion of Innovation theory. A quantitative
survey design was adopted, using a structured Likert-scale questionnaire for data collection. From
a population of 60,903 students, a sample size of 358 was determined using the Krejcie and
Morgan formula. Data were analysed using mean scores, with 3.0 as the decision benchmark:
items with mean scores below 3.0 were rejected, while those above 3.0 were accepted. Findings
indicated that most respondents use AI applications on their mobile phones to seek health
information, largely due to accessibility, convenience, and ease of interaction. The study concludes
that although AI health information tools are useful, there is a need for greater caution and
guidance regarding the quality of information accessed. It recommends the development and
enforcement of stricter regulations on AI health information tools and the implementation of
institutional educational programmes to improve students’ understanding of responsible AI use.</jats:p>

title: Public Awareness of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Utilisation in Healthcare Institutions in Anambra State
container-title: RESEARCH JOURNAL OF MASS COMMUNICATION AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY
b95afc8cfcf288eee154d73cf330cab3e4fc70d8.abstract:
<jats:p>Given the growing adoption of AI-driven diagnostic and treatment tools across health systems,
understanding community awareness is crucial for effective integration and health
communication. Applying the survey design, data were collected from 384 adult residents selected
from across six Local Government Areas of Anambra State, Nigeria, using multistage and
proportionate sampling techniques. Findings revealed a moderately high level of awareness of AI
utilisation, with respondents expressing the strongest familiarity with AI-powered tools such as
automated diagnostics and virtual assistants. Social media emerged as the dominant source of AI
information, followed by traditional media, while healthcare providers contributed minimally to
public knowledge. Respondents also recognised significant benefits of AI, including improved
diagnostic accuracy, enhanced service delivery, and overall healthcare quality. However, concerns
were evident regarding potential medical errors, privacy concerns, and job displacement of
healthcare workers. These findings align with national and international studies showing high
exposure but limited depth of understanding among the public and health workers. Guided by the
Diffusion of Innovations and Agenda-Setting theories, the study concludes that public awareness
is largely media-driven and remains at an early diffusion stage, underscoring the need for
deliberate institutional communication, ethical safeguards, and structured public sensitisation.
The study recommends strengthening health communication strategies, promoting data protection
frameworks, and enhancing healthcare worker involvement in public AI education.</jats:p>

title: Artificial intelligence in science communication: emerging practices, credibility, and public trust
container-title: Frontiers in Communication
a42bacc09eb8293068a9cea69e6f02bab9a6f30f.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence has spread rapidly through the infrastructure of science communication. However, its implications for how the public accesses, evaluates, and trusts science remain uncertain. This mini-review brings together current conceptual, experimental, and survey-based research. The aim is to develop an integrated framework that positions generative AI as an epistemic intermediary. The framework connects three areas: emerging communication practices, the credibility of AI-enhanced messages, and public trust in science. The literature on practices shows that large language models can enhance understanding through simplification, translation, and dialogue, and may even reduce skepticism toward science. However, these tools carry risks of inaccuracy and bias. Credibility studies attribute a small but consistent penalty to visible AI authorship. However, this effect is strongly context-dependent; findings regarding both pro-human bias and the lack of impact from labeling remain controversial. Trust studies, meanwhile, reveal that the public's trust in generative AI remains limited. Furthermore, the disclosure of AI use, even by researchers, can reduce perceived legitimacy and thereby diminish trust. Across these three areas, transparency design, AI literacy, prior trust in science, and the controversial nature of the topic emerge as key moderating factors.</jats:p>

7f9682e3b2249ce09af819a20d7a1833adfea108.abstract: <jats:p>The detection involves correctly categorizing the smishing message and delivering the warning clearly to facilitate mobile cybersecurity decision making. In this study, an explainable machine-learning pipeline is evaluated on a public dataset of 5,971 legitimate, spam and smishing messages. After removing conflicting labels and repeated messages, the number of records to be used in the training, validation and test sets was 5,797. Multiple classifiers were used to assess word and character TF-IDF representations with structural attributes. The logistic regression model trained with text-only data, selected by training cross-validation, had an accuracy of 97.36% and an F1 score of 0.9156 (macro average). When a warning threshold of 0.45 was used, precision and recall for smishing were 93.42% and 89.87% respectively. The mean maximum predicted-class probability reduction using token-deletion analysis for 30 messages was 0.0942, and four changes in classification occurred. The experimental environment had a median prediction latency of 1.22 milliseconds. The conclusions are relevant to efficient and inspectable SMS screening, and for operational effectiveness and the usefulness of explanations, external validation, probability calibration, and SMS testing with smartphones are still required.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Women Entrepreneurship in the IT Sector: Emerging Opportunities and Entrepreneurial Challenges
container-title: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
57468ea9c09dfbf28e329fedbc923e46969e52db.abstract: <jats:p>The Information Technology (IT) industry is undergoing significant changes as Artificial Intelligence (AI) launches new areas for innovation, business expansion and entrepreneurship. Women entrepreneurs are increasingly embracing AI technologies to set up startups, to enhance their business operations. To increase productivity and take part more in domestic and international markets. In the present study, the role of Artificial Intelligence in the future of women entrepreneurship in the IT sector was discussed, with a special focus on emerging opportunities and challenges for the entrepreneurs. It brings to the forefront the potential of leveraging AI-powered tools, automation, machine learning, data analytics, and digital platforms for business planning, decision-making, customer relationship management, and resource optimization, particularly for women entrepreneurs. The research also pinpoints the major challenges such as limited access to finance, gender inequality, technical knowledge, digital skills gap, cyber security threats, and lack of institutional support. Particular emphasis is placed on the Indian context and how government’s initiatives, digital transformation and entrepreneurship development programmes are providing new opportunities for women entrepreneurs. The research method used in the study is descriptive and analytical descriptive method using secondary data or secondary sources of information. It seeks to grasp the potential of AI in fostering inclusive entrepreneurship, enhancing the role of women in the IT sector, and supporting sustainable economic growth.</jats:p>

title: Privacy-Aware Adaptive Mental State Intelligence for AI-Assisted Decision-Making in Digital Mental Health Systems: Architecture and Empirical Evaluation
container-title: Computer and Decision Making: An International Journal
9a40c2f17e45e936b135acb9748f1677c7ab5896.abstract: <jats:p>Opportunities to anticipate changes in depressive symptoms are provided by longitudinal digital mental-health records, but the usefulness of algorithmic recommendations and the preservation of model utility under privacy protections cannot be established from predictive accuracy alone. A Privacy-Aware Adaptive Mental State Intelligence (PA-AMSI) architecture was specified and evaluated using the Corona Health smartphone dataset. Historical Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) assessments were used to predict five symptom-severity categories 14–30 days ahead. Following duplicate-origin correction and participant-disjoint partitioning, 6,314 forecasting samples from 903 participants were retained; 5,025 samples from 722 participants were allocated to development, and 1,289 samples from 181 participants were reserved for a single locked-test evaluation. Persistence, centralized classifiers, simulated federated averaging, and participant-clipped Gaussian-noised training were compared. On the locked test, the highest macro-F1 (0.6541) was obtained with persistence, whereas the highest accuracy (0.7168) was obtained with Random Forest. A macro-F1 of 0.2743 was obtained with the Gaussian-noised model, and none of the 46 severe-class assessments was detected. Under a predefined illustrative loss matrix, a lower mean simulated decision cost was obtained with the questionnaire-only policy (0.5531) than with Random Forest-assisted (0.6175) and privacy-noised (0.6594) policies. Higher costs for the AI-assisted policies were supported by participant-cluster bootstrap intervals. It is therefore shown that privacy assumptions, class-specific reliability, and decision consequences must be assessed together before digital mental-health prediction systems are considered for clinical evaluation.</jats:p>

title: An Assessment of the Familiarity of Undergraduates with the  Application of Artificial Intelligence Programs in Project Writing  and Development in Polytechnics in Nigeria
container-title: International Journal of Computer Science and Mathematical Theory
ce073cbba2236ec8c523b5b4bd7dcee50b6b1033.abstract:
<jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) programs have progressively permeated the academic ecosystem, 
altering the manner in which students conceive, research, write, and defend project reports. This 
study assessed the familiarity of undergraduates with the application of artificial intelligence 
programs in project writing and development in polytechnics in Nigeria. The study was anchored 
on the Technology Acceptance Model (Davis, 1989) and the Diffusion of Innovation Theory 
(Rogers, 2003), both of which provided a theoretical lens for interpreting how perceived 
usefulness, perceived ease of use, and innovation attributes shape students' adoption of AI-driven 
tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, QuillBot, the Turnitin AI detector, and Google Gemini. A 
descriptive survey design was adopted, and a multi-stage random sampling technique was used to 
select six federal and state polytechnics spanning the six geopolitical zones of Nigeria, namely 
Federal Polytechnic Nasarawa, Yaba College of Technology, Kaduna Polytechnic, Akanu Ibiam 
Federal Polytechnic Unwana, Rivers State Polytechnic, and Federal Polytechnic Bauchi. A 
structured questionnaire was administered to 300 final-year and penultimate-year Higher 
National Diploma (HND) and National Diploma (ND) students, out of which 268 copies (89.3%) 
were validly completed and returned. Data were analysed using frequency counts, simple 
percentages, mean scores, and chi-square statistics at the 0.05 level of significance. Findings 
revealed that undergraduates in Nigerian polytechnics possess a moderately high level of 
familiarity with generic AI programs such as ChatGPT (86%) and Grammarly (71%), but 
comparatively low familiarity with more specialised tools such as Jasper/Copy.ai (11%) and 
Perplexity AI (22%). AI programs were most frequently applied at the proofreading, grammar
checking, and literature-search stages of project writing, while application at the data-analysis 
stage remained the least explored. Unstable electricity and internet connectivity, inadequate 
digital literacy training, the cost of premium subscriptions, and the fear of being accused of 
academic malpractice emerged as the most prominent challenges limiting deeper engagement with 
these tools. The chi-square analysis indicated a statistically significant relationship between 
students' level of familiarity and their institutional location (urban versus semi-urban campuses). 
The study concluded that although AI literacy is gradually taking root among polytechnic 
undergraduates, its application remains uneven, superficial in places, and insufficiently guided by 
institutional policy. It was recommended, among other things, that polytechnic management 
should integrate AI literacy modules into general studies curricula, provide subsidised access to premium AI tools, and develop clear ethical guidelines that distinguish permissible assistive use 
of AI from outright academic misconduct.</jats:p>

container-title: International Conference on Wireless, Optical Communication, and Information Engineering (WOCIE 2026)
3dce4b94762af4295ccc55331c5abd2af8b304b5.abstract: <jats:p>The purpose of this article is to discuss the construction of international sports communication curriculum system and the assessment of instructional effect with the assistance of artificial intelligence (AI). Under the background of globalization, the importance of international sports communication is increasingly prominent, and the rapid development of AI technology provides new opportunities for the optimization of curriculum system and the improvement of instructional effect. This article first defines the goal and orientation of the international sports communication course, and then designs a comprehensive curriculum system covering theoretical knowledge, practical skills and cultural literacy. On this basis, AI technology is introduced and intelligent learning support and services are provided. In order to scientifically assess the instructional effect, this article constructs a instructional effect assessment model based on deep learning (DL), and carries out experimental verification. The results show that the model has the advantages of fast convergence and small prediction error, and can accurately reflect the learning effect of students and the instructional effect of teachers. AI-assisted international sports communication course system construction and instructional effect assessment have obvious advantages, which provides new ideas for the innovation and development of international sports communication education.</jats:p>

title: Edge intelligence drives multiscale anomaly detection network for heterogeneous IoT traffic
container-title: International Conference on Wireless, Optical Communication, and Information Engineering (WOCIE 2026)
3fa3bcfb6aaffc7a22496a380913b0ef41e0ce25.abstract: <jats:p>When edge nodes undertake the task of near-source traffic monitoring in the Internet of Things (iot), limited computing resources and the difference of abnormal behavior time span are easy to cause local mutation and insufficient information representation of continuous attack. To solve this problem, this paper constructs a multi-scale anomaly detection network for heterogeneous traffic driven by edge intelligence. The traffic information is extracted at the edge side, and the communication changes of different persistence ranges are depicted through short, medium and long time scale coding, and the dynamic fusion is performed according to the scale contribution to realize the identification of normal communication and multi-class abnormal traffic. Experiments were carried out based on the CICIoT2023 dataset. The detection accuracy of DDoS, DoS, Recon, Web, Brute Force, Spoofing and Mirai traffic in our network reaches 99.2%, 98.9%, 97.8%, 96.4%, 96.9%, 98.1% and 99.0%, respectively. The accuracy is 97.88% when the traffic scale is 90000, and the average detection delay is 18.6 ms when the proportion of available computing resources of edge nodes is 20%. The results show that the constructed network can balance the accuracy of heterogeneous traffic anomaly detection, the stability of scale change and the real-time performance of edge deployment, which can provide technical support for the edge side anomaly communication monitoring of iot.</jats:p>

4846ee45d9ccb49cd3a949b62abb95032a2dfb03.abstract: <jats:p>Financial distress prediction for corporations demands analytical systems that not only discriminate well, but also are sufficiently transparent to allow for responsible management actions. This work proposes an explainable AI system to automate the analysis of accounting-based financial indicators to support strategic bankruptcy-risk decision-making. A leakage-resistant development – validation – locked-test design was used to analyze the Taiwanese Bankruptcy Prediction dataset of 6,819 firms and 95 financial variables. Stratified cross-validation was used for tuning Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Extra Trees and Histogram Gradient Boosting with precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) serving as the main selection criterion due to the low proportion of bankrupt firms (3.23% of observations). Extra Trees had the perfect validation profile with a locked-test PR-AUC of 0.4567, ROC-AUC of 0.9422 and Brier of 0.0227. Validation based risk bands focused 87.88% of bankruptcies in the locked test in the High and Critical categories and the permutation importance identified borrowing dependency, interest-bearing debt cost and financial leverage. It shows how explainable and calibrated financial-risk analytics can be used for an automated accounting-based screening process while maintaining interpretable evidence for corporate decision making.</jats:p>

title: Journalists' trends towards employing artificial intelligence tools in media content production
container-title: Middle East Journal of Communication Studies
fb7c48b19f55b8a88cebedd28f9b96110e897e88.abstract: <jats:p>This study aimed to identify Jordanian journalists’ attitudes toward employing artificial intelligence tools in media content production, examine the extent to which these tools are used, identify the main factors limiting their adoption, and explore the perceived benefits and concerns associated with their use in journalistic work. The study adopted a descriptive-analytical approach and employed a questionnaire administered to a random sample of 306 Jordanian journalists who are members of the Jordan Press Association. The findings showed that 57.9% of the respondents did not use artificial intelligence tools in producing media content, compared with 41.8% who reported using them. The main factors limiting the use of these tools were the lack of accuracy in verifying references and the origins of the information and data obtained, with a mean of 3.89, followed by variations in the quality of information and data generated through artificial intelligence tools, with a mean of 3.88. The findings also indicated that the most prominent uses of artificial intelligence tools involved extracting quantitative information and data, with a mean of 3.92, followed by analyzing digital data, with a mean of 3.79. Furthermore, 71.9% of the journalists considered the use of artificial intelligence tools a current necessity in light of ongoing technological developments. The main perceived benefits included saving time and effort, analyzing large datasets, and improving efficiency and productivity. The main concerns included information security and privacy, potential restrictions on expression and creativity, and ethical concerns related to information credibility. The study also found a statistically significant relationship between the use of artificial intelligence tools and media content production.</jats:p>

title: Awareness of Media Students in Jordan Regarding the Ethical Dimensions of Employing Artificial Intelligence Tools in University Education
container-title: Middle East Journal of Communication Studies
2bcb39fa9bbeb11328358f7c277d5dd7788d4b51.abstract: <jats:p>This study examined the level of awareness among media students in Jordan regarding the ethical dimensions of employing artificial intelligence tools in university education. The study explored students’ patterns of AI usage and measured their cognitive, emotional, and behavioral awareness associated with the ethical and academic use of artificial intelligence. The growing use of artificial intelligence tools in university education has raised ethical and academic concerns related to academic integrity, proper documentation, and responsible use of AI-generated content. It also aimed to identify the extent to which students adhere to academic integrity and proper documentation practices when using AI tools in their university assignments. The study adopted the descriptive approach using the survey method. A questionnaire was administered to a sample of 573 male and female students from media faculties in private Jordanian universities. The findings revealed that the level of AI tool usage among students was moderate, whereas the levels of cognitive, emotional, and behavioral awareness were high. The results further showed that the most common uses of AI tools were searching for information and generating media ideas, while the use of AI in advanced technical and production-related fields, such as audio-visual editing and voice-over generation, was low. In addition, students demonstrated a high awareness of the ethical risks associated with artificial intelligence, alongside a relatively low level of commitment to documenting the use of AI tools in academic assignments.</jats:p>

title: Design of an edge-intelligence-supported image processing and real-time control system
container-title: International Conference on Communication, Sensing, and Intelligent Computing (CSIC 2026)
9d103c656a72ec2e85a55600059bdc80ae097c4e.abstract: <jats:p>Cloud-centered visual control systems are constrained by uplink bandwidth, network jitter, and the separation of perception and actuation. This paper designs an edge-intelligence-assisted image processing and real-time control system in which image acquisition, target detection, state estimation, command generation, and task scheduling are carried out on the edge hot path, and the supervisory computer receives compressed semantic results and selected diagnostic frames. EdgeVisionNet is a relatively small detector that improves the target representation under scale variation, blur, and partial occlusion by adding depthwise separable convolutions, cross-scale feature aggregation, and channel attention. Detection confidence and bounding-box centres are then converted into a motion state by Kalman filtering, and a confidence-adaptive controller closes the loop between visual perception and actuator motion. A high-priority scheduler manages sensing, inference, control, and status-reporting tasks within a bounded-latency budget. A reproducible software-in-the-loop prototype was tested on 1,820 procedurally generated industrial scenes and a 360-frame dynamic control sequence. EdgeVisionNet has an F1 score of 0.6848 and a mean intersection-over-union of 0.5574 with 49,285 parameters; its CPU inference p95 is 0.640ms. The full edge closed-loop required 8.34ms and was about 6.1 times faster than the 51.12ms cloud-centered path; semantic reporting reduced the uplink rate to 23.04kbps from 55.296Mbps. The proposed estimator-controller reduced the image-plane control RMSE from 13.40pixels to 4.03pixels under delay and observation loss.</jats:p>
