title: An Explainable Hybrid AI Framework for Real-Time Cyber Threat Detection, Predictive Intelligence and Adversarially Robust Defense
container-title: Computer and Decision Making: An International Journal
a38980a80ac5f2deb7c9aab67155632592108768.abstract:
<jats:p>Artificial-intelligence-based intrusion detection must simultaneously address detection accuracy, early warning, adversarial robustness, interpretability, and operational latency. This study presents an explainable hybrid AI framework that combines supervised classifiers with unsupervised anomaly detection for near-real-time cyber threat detection and predictive intelligence. The controlled experiment contains 18,000 observations described by 16 network and host-behavior features, partitioned into 10,800 training, 3,600 validation, and 3,600 held-out test records. The proposed hybrid detector achieved 92.25% accuracy, 89.40% precision, 82.93% recall, 86.04% F1-score, 96.02% specificity, ROC-AUC 0.948, and PR-AUC 0.922 at a validation-selected threshold of 0.58. The confusion matrix contained 860 true positives, 2,461 true negatives, 102 false positives, and 177 false negatives. Five-fold validation produced a mean F1-score of 85.29%, while bootstrap analysis yielded a 95% F1 interval of 84.34-87.59%. The predictive module detected 89.23% of attack episodes with a median warning lead of 6.0 s and ROC-AUC of 0.989. Under the strongest bounded evasion test (epsilon=0.40), adversarial augmentation retained 92.57% recall compared with 73.58% under standard training. SHAP and LIME analyses identified destination-port count, failed logins, process-spawn rate, and connection rate as influential indicators. Median single-record inference was 124.83 ms and batch throughput reached 11,029 records/s. These results demonstrate a promising integrated approach, while the findings remain controlled-simulation results pending external validation on public and enterprise traffic.
 
 
 </jats:p>

title: Artificial intelligence and managerial decision-making: strategies to improve productivity and efficiency in organisations
container-title: Computer and Decision Making: An International Journal
969e596e19f3e8b6b9a9ac1888192f0ab8c3d3ab.abstract: <jats:p>In the world of administrative transformation and improved decision-making in organisations, artificial intelligence (AI) has made its mark as a strategic tool. This article aims to explore the impact of AI on managerial decision-making and to pinpoint methods that can help enhance productivity and organisational efficiency. The research is carried out using a qualitative, documentary, and descriptive approach, which is enhanced by the review of recent scientific articles related to artificial intelligence, business management, decision-making, and productivity. The applications of AI in data analysis, automation of processes, generation of information for decision-making, the optimisation of resources and the anticipation of business scenarios are analysed. The results enable us to conclude that the strategic use of these technologies can have a positive impact on more timely and informed decision-making, on the time spent on some administrative tasks and on the use of resources. But there are problems with their implementation in terms of data quality, digital skills, ethics, information security, and the need for human supervision. The AI tools can, therefore, be utilised as a complementary management tool provided they are implemented in accordance with the goals of the organisations and a combination of human abilities and responsible principles of their use</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence in Classical Homoeopathy: A Cross-Sectional Observational Study on Clinical Utility, Repertorial Accuracy, and Therapeutic Outcome
container-title: Computer and Decision Making: An International Journal
a077acb9c4926c3f75e6921b357e3a8948b87ae1.abstract: <jats:p>Use of artificial intelligence in classical homoeopathic repertories can help in improving the computational decision making, information retrieval and evidence traceability. But comparative study between lexical, semantic and hierarchy aware retrieval approaches is still not well explored. In this study, an explainable AI-assisted repertorial retrieval and remedy ranking framework was developed and evaluated by combining BM25, sentence embedding using Sentence-BERT, RRF, hierarchical reranking, and evidence-traceable remedy aggregation. There were 74,513 hierarchical rubrics and 507,179 of rubric–remedy occurrences in the Kent Repertory. 300 source-derived queries were used to test seven retrieval configurations. Recall at position K, Mean Reciprocal Rank at position 10 and Normalised Discounted Cumulative Gain at position 10 were used to evaluate the performance of the proposed system, along with paired statistical testing, ablation analysis and robustness evaluation. The BM25–Sentence-BERT hybrid obtained the best NDCG@10 score of 0.9951 and MRR@10 score of 0.9933, which are better than the proposed QHNS-RDS V4 framework (0.9656 and 0.9536, respectively). The result of the statistical comparison showed that the ranking effectiveness of the proposed configuration was significantly low. For NDCG@10, removing hierarchical reranking resulted in a significant improvement of 0.9946, indicating that the fixed structural weighting hurt retrieval performance. All models were negatively affected by severe query truncation, while semantic embeddings made a positive contribution. However, the framework produced remedy ranking results that provided interpretable information using supporting rubric identifiers, hierarchical paths, and source references, and allowed for clear review of computational remedy rankings. These findings prove the feasibility of evidence-traceable repertorial decision support but not necessarily the improvement of clinical decision-making or therapeutic effectiveness. Limitations in generalisability include source-derived benchmarking, OCR uncertainties and inactive uncertainty weighting. The next steps would be to use separately annotated queries, expert verified associations, adaptive-hierarchical scoring and human-centred evaluation for future research prior to practical clinical use.</jats:p>

title: An Explainable Hybrid Artificial Intelligence Framework for Predictive Analytics and Intelligent Decision-Making in Complex Information Systems
container-title: Computer and Decision Making: An International Journal
6bcdc4191ae8bf2a6bbd32050209c3d607d6d5c4.abstract:
<jats:p>The growing complexity of modern information systems has increased the need for intelligent predictive frameworks that can identify operational failures while providing transparent, actionable decision support. Preprocessing, handling class imbalance, baseline machine-learning algorithms, a stacking-based hybrid ensemble, SHAP explainability, and a risk-oriented decision-support layer were used in a quantitative computational design. The predictive models used were Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, XGBoost and Artificial Neural Network, and the hybrid framework involved the combination of predictions from the Random Forest, XGBoost and ANN models. Random Forest outpaced all the other models in terms of accuracy, precision, specificity, F1-score and Matthews correlation coefficient, whereas the hybrid stacking model had the highest ROC-AUC (0.9762) and PR-AUC (0.8056) with 89.71% recall. In the hybrid model, 61 machine failures were correctly identified, and 7 were missed. The most important factors determining the risk of failure were identified by the SHAP analysis as: torque, wear of the tool, rotational speed and air temperature. Overall, the proposed framework showed that a framework that integrates predictive performance, interpretability and risk-based decision support can improve intelligent maintenance systems that are transparently useful and operationally effective. The framework also provided a translation of predicted failure probabilities into maintenance-priority categories, aiding the monitoring, preventive action, and human-centred operational decision-making in industrial settings.
 </jats:p>

title: Selective attention or inattention? Enabling efficient perception in embodied intelligence agents
container-title: Frontiers of Computer Science
977d66ee308835bba303da319eacf6e914bcb2b1.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>As embodied intelligence increasingly operates in the physical world, perception efficiency, robustness, and adaptability become central bottlenecks separating artificial agents from biological organisms. Unlike conventional perception pipelines, biological perception is inherently selective and resource-aware: attention amplifies task-relevant information, while inattention suppresses distraction and redundancy. This survey investigates attention-driven adaptive perception as a promising mechanism for improving embodied systems. We consolidate interdisciplinary findings from neuroscience, cognitive science, robotics, and machine learning to clarify the distinct yet complementary roles of selective attention and inattention in optimizing perceptual processing. Building on these insights, we introduce the Unified Selective Attention and Inattention Model (U-SAIM) and extend it into a three-tier architectural framework that maps biological principles to embodied perception systems. Guided by this structure, we review existing implementations across robotics, multimodal fusion, lightweight perception, and attention modulation strategies, extracting design patterns and performance implications. Moreover, we discuss the challenges and opportunities for future development. Together, these perspectives chart a unified theoretical and practical roadmap toward attentional embodied perception—agents capable of perceiving, reasoning, and acting with the adaptive intelligence, efficiency, and flexibility that define human perception.</jats:p>

title: Green AI for Sustainable Agriculture: An Explainable-AI (XAI) Perspective on Energy-Efficient Crop Intelligence
container-title: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
88212f3988da8ca8d548c2cfd044d37d838996f1.abstract: <jats:p>In modern agriculture precision forecast crop yields, diagnose plant disease and schedule irrigation systems rely on machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL). Cost of training and deploying these models is weighed their accuracy. Two research threads have far developed largely in parallel. Green AI, which treats computational and energy efficiency as a first-class evaluation criterion alongside accuracy and Explainable AI(XAI) uses technology like Shapley additive explanations(SHAP), LIME and Grad-CAM to open the “black box” models so that farmers , and policymakers can act on their predictions.This paper synthesises recent literature (2017–2026) at the intersection of these threads as they apply to agriculture, covering crop-yield prediction, plant-disease detection, and soil- and irrigation-modelling studies that report either energy-efficiency measures or explainability analyses, or both. The synthesis identifies a specific and consistent gap: while explainability is now common in high-performing agricultural ML studies, almost none of them report the energy or carbon cost of training the underlying models, and the one purpose-built Green-AI agriculture framework identified in the review explicitly leaves explainability as future work rather than integrating it. Building on this synthesis, the paper proposes a unified Green-XAI methodological framework for agricultural ML that couples resource-appropriate model families – tree-based ensembles such as Random Forest, XGBoost and LightGBM, alongside a compact CNN architecture for imagery – with SHAP-based interpretability and continuous energy/carbon instrumentation across the training and inference lifecycle. The paper details the proposed dataset scope, the governing model equations, the SHAP computation, and an accuracy-versus-energy evaluation protocol, and positions the framework against a comparative synthesis of the performance figures reported by prior studies</jats:p>

title: Workforce knowledge and operational skills in cyber threat intelligence
container-title: Information & Computer Security
bdba6e891c9ad065316c2eca2c9d132f9ed332a3.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to explore the knowledge and skills practitioners consider important for cyber threat intelligence (CTI) practice in organizations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Semi-structured interviews with 14 CTI practitioners and cybersecurity leaders were analyzed using deductive qualitative analysis. Socio-technical systems theory informed interpretation, while the NICE Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity supplied organizing categories. Interview excerpts were coded for knowledge, skills, tasks and work roles and tagged to collection, processing, analysis and dissemination. The mapping was refined through member checking with four original participants selected for complementary areas of expertise.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis identifies four knowledge areas: cybersecurity and IT domain knowledge, intelligence tradecraft knowledge, situational awareness and business context knowledge. Eleven operational skills encompass technical, analytical, communicative and interpersonal capabilities. Reported competency associations vary across lifecycle activities, with some spanning all four stages. Two practitioner profiles emerged: technical-operational and intelligence-analytical.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The competencies and mapping provide a starting point for recruitment, training, mentoring and team design, subject to contextual adaptation and further evaluation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study contextualizes established CTI competencies through practitioner accounts and connects reported knowledge and skills to lifecycle activities. It offers an exploratory mapping rather than evidence of effects on intelligence quality or organizational performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: A Configurational Approach to Investigating the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Self‐Regulated Learning From Needs Satisfaction, Learning Environments and Perceived Affordances
container-title: Journal of Computer Assisted Learning
4797e107590ea3351ab21b6456696ccbfe0a6972.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) tools into self‐regulated learning (SRL) is complex and multifaceted. Configurational approaches are based on the concept that combinations (or configurations) of causally relevant factors should be connected to the desired outcome.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Self‐determination theory (SDT), the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) and perceived affordances focus on basic needs, technology adoptions and technological designs, respectively. Taking a configurational approach, this study investigates how the combinations of SDT, UTAUT and perceived affordances affect SRL with AI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We employed fuzzy‐set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to uncover the complex interplay of factors that facilitate effective SRL. Data from 248 students reveal that a combination of autonomy satisfaction, relatedness satisfaction and performance expectancy is the most influential factor affecting the use of AI in SRL.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our results suggest that both innate psychological needs and external learning environments should be considered together for understanding the adoption of AI in SRL. They also further highlight the critical role of perceived affordances as mediators and moderators, enhancing the relationships between innate psychological needs and external learning environments. This integrative approach provides valuable insights into the design and implementation of AI‐supported SRL environments. We recommend designing the environments to foster autonomy and relatedness while also ensuring ease of use for learners.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Intelligent Medical Decision-Making Through Artificial Intelligence, Predictive Modeling, and Advanced Healthcare Analytics
container-title: Computer and Decision Making: An International Journal
d161349547e7ed96d211be321fc28b010b171437.abstract: <jats:p>AI and ML are becoming more common for supporting decisions in diagnostics, but the evaluation needs to be leakage safe, evidence needs to be interpretable, and there needs to be careful distinction between benchmark performance and claimable deployable clinical performance. The objective of this study was to create an AI based medical-intelligence framework for diagnosis of breast-cancer based on Wisconsin Breast Cancer (Diagnostic) dataset. Five hundred sixty-nine observations and 30 quantitative morphological predictors obtained from fine-needle aspirate images were analyzed. Logistic regression, radial-basis-function support vector machine (RBF SVM), random forest and histogram gradient boosting were compared by using a stratified 70/15/15 train-validation-locked-test design. The RBF SVM had the best cross-validated ROC-AUC of 0.9925 and after tuning, 0.9950. It correctly classified all 86 locked-test cases, with a threshold of 0.320 derived from validation that resulted in ROC-AUC and PR-AUC values of 1.000. The morphological separation was the largest for concave points, perimeter, radius, area and measures of concavity. The framework illustrates how predictive analytics and interpretation of models can be used to prioritize diagnostics, and highlights the importance of external validation for clinical use.</jats:p>

title: An Explainable Artificial Intelligence Framework for Predicting Green Entrepreneurial Intention Through Policy Support, Higher Education, and Entrepreneurial Self-Efficacy
container-title: Computer and Decision Making: An International Journal
37ed617cf002a1d96a42a0976397ed39892e498c.abstract: <jats:p>Green entrepreneurship is increasingly recognized as a pathway toward sustainable economic development, yet the predictive contributions of institutional, educational, and psychological factors remain insufficiently understood. This study evaluated an explainable artificial intelligence framework for predicting green entrepreneurial intention through government policy support, higher education exposure, and entrepreneurial self-efficacy. Questionnaire data from 1,046 respondents across Nigeria, Ghana, and South Africa were examined using descriptive statistics, reliability assessment, correlation analysis, exploratory factor analysis, and machine learning. Predictive performance was assessed through five-fold cross-validation using Elastic Net, Random Forest, Histogram Gradient Boosting, and Support Vector Regression. Although green entrepreneurial intention exhibited the highest mean score (3.8713), internal consistency was inadequate across all constructs, with Cronbach's alpha ranging from −0.1092 to 0.0503. Factorability diagnostics revealed weak sampling adequacy (KMO = 0.5088) and a nonsignificant Bartlett's test (p = 0.8399). All predictive models produced negative cross-validated R² values, indicating no improvement over baseline prediction. Cross-country validation further demonstrated limited generalizability. These findings underscore the importance of establishing measurement validity before applying explainable artificial intelligence to entrepreneurial behavior. Future research should prioritize validated instruments, cross-national measurement equivalence, and external predictive validation to support reliable, interpretable, and evidence-based green entrepreneurship decision-making.</jats:p>

title: Explainable and Fairness-Aware Artificial Intelligence in Strategic Human Resource Management: A Dual-Module Machine-Learning Framework for Employee Retention and Promotion Decisions
container-title: Computer and Decision Making: An International Journal
4e9d312779c46929419ee3dbd99e5713dc610633.abstract: <jats:p>AI has a lot of promise in the field of HRM, but relying on predictive outcomes isn't enough to make HR decisions. Two complementary open workforce datasets were used to create a machine learning dual-modules approach for employee attrition and promotion oriented to the governance. We used stratified benchmarking, nested cross-validation, paired out-of-fold classifiers, probability calibration and one-time untouched holdout testing to evaluate the conventional and advanced classifiers. Precision-recall discrimination, calibration, threshold performance, explainability, demographic fairness, proxy detection, review-capacity evaluation, and demographic fairness were all assessed using a model. The best holdout PR-AUC, ROC-AUC, precision and Matthews correlation coefficient for attrition were obtained with a sigmoid-calibrated linear support vector machine, with values of 0.6025, 0.7944, 0.7000 and 0.4968, respectively. The CatBoost model with an isotonic calibration was chosen for promotion and has the following metrics: PR-AUC of 0.5503, ROC-AUC of 0.8193, precision of 0.8734 and Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.5516. Explainability analysis found stable workforce predictors and subgroup and proxy audits showed that removing sensitive attributes from the workforce did not remove any demographic information or disparity risks. Positive net benefit and large lift over random review suggested that there is potential decision utility under constrained review capacity. The results endorse calibrated machine learning as an augmentative decision-support system, which is subject to global thresholds, fairness, contextual evaluation, and compulsory human supervision and not automated hiring choices.</jats:p>

title: Emotional Intelligence and Academic Achievement of High School Students: A Data-Driven Decision Support and Predictive Analysis Framework
container-title: Computer and Decision Making: An International Journal
bafdbd3725a99eefd4098bc15d7a2641abce2c61.abstract: <jats:p>Emotional intelligence (EI) has grown in importance for educational decision making in the recent past because it involves emotional and self-regulatory skills that could be useful in addition to traditional academic measures. This study creates an interpretable predictive framework to analyze the relationship between EI and academic achievement of high-school student profiles. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, multiple linear regression, ridge regression, k-nearest-neighbours regression, held-out validation, permutation importance and support-priority grouping were combined in the analysis. EI showed a moderate positive association with academic achievement (r = 0.578). Ridge regression had the highest generalization with a five-fold cross validation RMSE of 6.49 and held-out RMSE of 5.98 with 49.4% of the variance in achievement explained. Based on the results of the permutation analysis, EI was the most important predictor, followed by study hours, parental support, stress and attendance. The decision-support layer also divided profiles into three groups of priority: high-support, monitoring, and low-support, each having its own achievement and EI pattern. Results show how this interpretable predictive workflow can transform emotional and educational markers to academic-support priorities without superseding professional judgment.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Decision Support for Biotechnology Engineering: Integrating Computational Intelligence with Strategic Management
container-title: Computer and Decision Making: An International Journal
a47d78c976002b2b0a294d0c2e00c440054815f2.abstract:
<jats:p>Artificial intelligence offers new opportunities to improve biotechnology engineering by converting complex process data into predictive and strategically useful information. This study developed an AI-driven decision-support framework integrating computational intelligence, explainable modelling, and multi-objective strategic analysis. Biomass concentration, substrate concentration, dissolved oxygen, process temperature, energy consumption, and operating cost were evaluated as predictors of product yield. Six modelling approaches were compared using R², RMSE, MAE, and MAPE. The proposed hybrid AI model achieved the strongest predictive performance, with an R² of 0.967, RMSE of 2.18, MAE of 1.64, and MAPE of 2.09%. SHAP analysis identified biomass concentration (27.8%), dissolved oxygen (21.6%), and substrate concentration (18.9%) as the most influential predictors. Multi-objective analysis demonstrated that maximizing productivity alone increased economic and energy requirements, whereas the AI-balanced strategy provided a more favorable compromise. This strategy achieved a predicted yield of 90.2%, reduced operating cost by 10.2% and energy demand by 20.3%, and improved resource efficiency from 71.2% to 87.4% compared with conventional operation. The findings demonstrate how predictive accuracy, model interpretability, and strategic optimization can be integrated to support balanced biotechnology engineering decisions involving technical, economic, resource, and operational considerations.
 </jats:p>

title: Academic performance of students in Relation to Emotional Intelligence and mental health
container-title: Computer and Decision Making: An International Journal
ccd0ce8bcf62aaa9223aee17cf82f816754d67a2.abstract:
<jats:p>Emotional competences and psychological functioning have been found to affect academic achievement, but their unique explanatory and predictive power is unclear. The current study aimed at analyzing the personality trait of emotional intelligence (EI), mental health related emotional well-being and academic achievement of secondary school students in an integrated statistical and machine-learning approach. Secondary cross-sectional data of 96 students aged 15–18 years was analyzed using Pearson and Spearman correlation, hierarchical regression (HC3 robust inference), sensitivity analysis, and Elastic Net regression (nested five-fold outer cross-validation and three-fold inner cross-validation). There was no significant bivariate correlation between achievement and either EI, r = 0.192, p = 0.121 (after Holm adjustment), or emotional well-being, r = 0.179, p = 0.121, but EI was a significant correlate of emotional well-being, r = 0.438, p < 0.001. Well-being did not add much in terms of explanatory power and the explanatory power of demographic controls increased by adding EI, from 0.1658 to 0.2275. Adding EI and well-being increased held-out R² from 0.0804 to 0.1345; the broader psychological model achieved R² = 0.2187, MAE = 0.8043, and RMSE = 1.0069. An eight-predictor EI-branch model (MAE = 0.8012) was found to be preferred by ablation; repeated validation showed partition sensitivity. Small sample sizes and the lack of external validation make claims of deployment impossible and psychological measures provide only modest incremental information.
 </jats:p>

title: Federated Machine Learning for Privacy-Preserving Predictive Analytics and Distributed Decision Intelligence
container-title: Computer and Decision Making: An International Journal
74c7ab20cc7330b5d68ac8bad4e267b29f684fdd.abstract: <jats:p>In distributed and heterogeneous computing environments, federated machine learning has proven to be a viable approach to privacy-preserving predictive analytics. This study introduced a federated system for anomaly detection to aid in collaborative learning and distributed decision intelligence, without aggregating raw network data on the central server. An unsupervised federated autoencoder was applied to learn traffic representations across decentralized clients, and Federated Averaging was applied to collect locally trained model parameters into a global model. To assess the model performance, reconstruction loss, accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1 score, and ROC AUC were calculated. The federated model shows that the mean reconstruction loss gradually decreases with the number of communication rounds, indicating convergence, and the loss in the 10th communication round is 0.6754, which is approximately a 32.14% decrease from the loss in the 1st communication round. With respect to recognition of benign traffic, the model attained accuracy rate of 70.44% and specificity of 91.96% which is good. The attack recall was however, limited to 6.36%, F1-score of 9.76% and ROC-AUC of 0.365, which showed that the system discriminated poorly between malicious and non-malicious observations. The results indicate that convergence from a federated perspective does not always result in intrusion detection success. The study also highlights the importance of adaptive aggregation.</jats:p>

title: Collaborative Intelligence for Group Decision Problems Under Conflicting Preferences and Uncertainty
container-title: Computer and Decision Making: An International Journal
b3ede5775c87af9c40fc3f6e2371cf20edb4e440.abstract:
<jats:p>Group decision making problems in complex socio-technical areas are characterized by conflicting preferences among stakeholders and significant uncertainty. These dimensions are usually tackled in isolation by the existing decision support approaches. This study proposes a collaborative intelligence framework that combines probabilistic linguistic term set encoding, conflict-derived influence weighting, TOPSIS based on expected probabilistic-linguistic indices, and preference revision. The reported experiment executes the deterministic pipeline and does not exercise the recommendation component. The probabilistic encoding rule converts each linguistic judgment into a probability-weighted term set. The framework measures pairwise divergence with a normalized Manhattan distance. The influence allocation adjusts expert contribution under equal prior credibility. The TOPSIS procedure based on expected probabilistic-linguistic indices ranks the weighted assessments. The framework is assessed on the APOLLO dataset of ten experts, twenty-five risks, and four criteria. The proposed framework reaches a consensus of 0.9455 after 19 feedback iterations, compared with 0.8793 for the equal-weight common-metric baseline on the same metric. The configured stopping threshold of 0.95 is not reached within the allowed iteration horizon. The run terminates at the iteration cap. The ranking agreement with the equal-weight common-metric baseline equals 0.9892 under the Spearman correlation. The preference revision loop executes 19 feedback cycles because the initial consensus falls below the configured threshold. No LLM call occurs in the reported run. The consensus improvement thus denotes the deterministic pipeline and not any of the recommendation elements. This attribution is supported by the ablation study. The results confirm the reproducibility of the deterministic pipeline.
 </jats:p>

title: A Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Framework for Explainable and Trustworthy Decision Support Systems: Driver-Support System for Work-Zone Hazards
container-title: Computer and Decision Making: An International Journal
f82812c0171142caee0f67012d2bf548b8d2a92b.abstract:
<jats:p>Background: Work-zone warning systems are required to identify hazardous encounters with sufficient time for human reaction, but false classifications can mask ineffective warnings.Objective: Assess explainable vehicle–worker warning models in the context of an updated physics-based pre-onset endpoint. Methods: There were two sessions in October 2018 that gave 29,273 synchronised observations, of which 7,101 were suitable for being modelled over 2 seconds. However, six models were evaluated – including weighted and unweighted XGBoost models – and compared to chronological validation and a later-session test with seven proxy events. The factors of calibration, explanation stability and sensor sensitivity and warning burden were analysed.Results: Unweighted XGBoost identified 5 out of 7 test events and generated 300 false episode warning events, while weighted XGBoost identified 4 events, and missed 3 and generated 7 false episode warning events. The mean lead times for detected events were 0.749 and 0.655 seconds, respectively. A warning was not issued for at least 1.5 seconds prior to onset for none of the seven test events, with a maximum of 1.178 seconds before onset.Opinion: Physics derived proxy onsets are not sufficient evidence for the quality of actionable warnings. The limited diversity of events, short lead times recorded and response delays that are not measured do not allow for conclusions of deployment readiness. For external safety evaluation the additional continuous recording and independent event annotations are required.
 </jats:p>

title: Knowledge-enhanced named entity recognition for cyber threat intelligence: a multi-stage classification and retrieval framework
container-title: Journal of Computer Virology and Hacking Techniques
687ca3e6ee3796ccbf4f8c2627e7bc818b49c862.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) increasingly appears as unstructured text across social media and open-source security reports, yet its volume and noise make timely, accurate extraction a persistent bottleneck for defenders. We present a multi-stage CTI processing framework that couples domain-specific classification with knowledge-enhanced Named Entity Recognition (NER). A classifier fine-tuned from SecureBERT, a cybersecurity-specific language model, first filters threat-relevant content, achieving 92.41% accuracy and a 93.36% F1-score on a public CTI classification corpus and achieving the highest observed performance for Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), and the larger general-domain DeBERTa-Large baselines trained under matched conditions. A knowledge retrieval module then augments candidate text with external context drawn from Wikipedia and Wikidata using three Best Matching 25 (BM25) strategies: sparse Wikipedia retrieval, sparse Wikidata retrieval, and Wikidata entity-attribute lookup. Evaluated on the DNRTI benchmark with a SecureBERT encoder coupled to a Conditional Random Field (CRF) layer, knowledge augmentation raises entity-level F1 from 87.16% (no retrieval) to 93.01%, attaining the highest recall (93.44%) and F1-score among reported methods; the gains are most pronounced for proper-noun entity types such as hacker organisations and affected geographic areas, where external descriptions resolve aliases and ambiguity. We analyse each retrieval strategy, report category-level results, and candidly delineate the framework’s limitations, including the report-versus-tweet domain gap, English-only coverage, and the absence of statistical significance testing. Overall, the study shows that pairing a domain-adapted encoder with lightweight external knowledge retrieval is an effective and computationally economical route to improving CTI extraction.</jats:p>

title: Finlet AI: An Evidence-Driven Multi-Agent Financial Intelligence Platform Using Model Context Protocol and Deterministic Risk Governance
container-title: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
27dad0acee8d55eb44e2d11a6bed4fb2d73d8d08.abstract: <jats:p>Standalone conversational language models struggle to satisfy audit and compliance standards in institutional equity research. When an equity analyst prompts an ungrounded model to evaluate a listed company, three operational defects appear almost immediately: the model quotes outdated share prices from its pre-training cutoff, invents page or footnote numbers when summarizing regulatory filings, and produces inconsistent numerical risk ratings when executed repeatedly on identical inputs. This paper presents Finlet AI, a twelve-layer multi-agent financial intelligence platform that decouples quantitative market arithmetic and primary-source retrieval from neural text synthesis. Once an analytical query is submitted through our asynchronous FastAPI gateway, a stateful LangGraph supervisor triggers concurrent parallel fan-out across three specialized domain workers covering historical price series, live financial news feeds, and statutory annual reports isolated behind standardized Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool interfaces. Technical price action, 20-day volume momentum ratios, and 30-day annualized volatility (σ	) are computed directly from three-month 30d Open-High-Low-Close-Volume (OHLCV) series fetched via Yahoo Finance. Real-time news catalysts are gathered through Google News RSS syndication and sanitized of HTML markup, while balance-sheet debt and liquidity disclosures are extracted page by page from SEC Form 10-K and Indian annual reports indexed locally in ChromaDB using 384-dimensional all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings. Rather than delegating risk scoring to subjective prompt completion, our Risk & Governance module evaluates a bounded mathematical index weighting volatility (45% weight), news sentiment risk (35% weight), and filing flags (20% weight). Live validation on Reliance Industries (RELIANCE.NS) demonstrates real-time tracking at ₹1,184.50 (−2.03%), 23.1% annualized volatility, 1.0x volume momentum, and a deterministic risk score of 0.365 (LOW), while high-risk runs (≥ 0.65) pause at a persistent SQLite Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) checkpoint before compiling the final ReportLab PDF dossier..</jats:p>

title: An Intelligent Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Automated Dental Image Analysis and Clinical Decision Support Using Explainable Artificial Intelligence
container-title: Computer and Decision Making: An International Journal
136b5560ea35cc929b4fa1de6f2c5891b5b8661f.abstract:
<jats:p>Anatomical overlap, heterogeneous abnormalities, class imbalance, and prediction interpretability are still challenges in automated dental radiographic analysis. This research proposes a hybrid deep learning model combining EfficientNetV2-S and Swin Transformer-T with Lesion-Aware Gated Attention Fusion (LAGAF) for the detection of dental objects and reporting for clinical decision support in multicategory. It involved multiscale Feature Pyramid Network aggregation, localization with Faster R-CNN, visual attribution, confidence calibration and rule-constrained reporting. For experiments, OralXrays-9 was used, which contains 12,688 panoramic images in 9 annotated categories, of which 2,688 images are held out and used for independent evaluation. Compared to independent CNN and Transformer baselines in terms of COCO detection metrics, fusion ablations, computational benchmarking, and 2,000 paired image-level bootstrap resamples. Hybrid-A2 got the best held out mAP@0.50:0.95 (0.5843), precision (0.8253), and F1-score (0.8790), while decreasing false-positive detections by 31.2% and 36.4% compared to CNN and Swin-T, respectively. But, there was a decrease in recall of 0.9401, pointing towards lesser detection power. The improvement over CNN was confirmed by bootstrap analysis, while the improvement over Swin-T was not clear. During development, there was a slight improvement in the results of the fixed-gate fusion methods, suggesting that learned gating did not consistently lead to improved performance with added complexity. Without independently establishing attribution faithfulness, calibration improvement and clinical effectiveness, explainability and confidence-aware reporting were implemented. These findings demonstrate the computational feasibility of hybrid dental detection and highlight the need for improvements in pathological sensitivity, external validation and clinician-supervised evaluation to facilitate clinical deployment.
 </jats:p>

title: MediDocker: An AI-Enabled Healthcare Intelligence Ecosystem Integrating Clinical Decision Support, Predictive Analytics, and Emergency Response
container-title: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
d04969a768c3b17a9f37083acda948b7e5571bb5.abstract: <jats:p>Patients keep their health information in places that do not talk to each other: handwritten prescriptions, PDF blood reports, appointment cards and paper bills, and in an emergency nobody can quickly see their blood group or allergies. This paper presents MediDocker, a web platform that keeps these records in one secure place and explains them in plain language. A vision-language model (Qwen2.5-VL, run locally) only copies what a prescription says; every medicine is then verified against RxNorm, an Indian brand dictionary and a hand-checked drug table, and its purpose and warnings come from verified sources, never from the model. Blood (CBC) reports are encrypted, read with a PDF text layer or PaddleOCR, checked by seven plausibility rules, and followed across reports with reference change values, a personal set point and Theil–Sen projection. A LightGBM model trained on 14,134 laboratory-confirmed NHANES participants screens for iron deficiency from the CBC alone and answers only when it is confident, otherwise advising a serum ferritin test. On 1,945 unseen participants from 2021 onwards it reached an AUROC of 0.836 (95% CI 0.816–0.857) and 94.2% accuracy on the 10.6% of cases it decides, with sensitivity 99.6% and specificity 99.3% at its two cut-offs. A record-aware assistant detects emergencies with rules before any language model is used, and an Ed25519-signed emergency QR code can be verified offline by anyone, without login</jats:p>

title:
Research Trends of Artificial Intelligence‐Facilitated Computational Thinking in K‐12
                    <scp>STEM</scp>
                    : A Systematic Review Through the Lens of Activity Theory
container-title: Journal of Computer Assisted Learning
50a7c557e85930f55486025b6c3e3d6739b9afa8.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), research in the cross‐disciplinary field of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education has increasingly focused on how to leverage AI to foster computational thinking (CT) among K‐12 students, given that CT, recognized as a core 21st‐century competency, plays a pivotal role in cultivating students’ literacy and equipping them with the ability to tackle complex problems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Grounded in activity theory, this study seeks to identify the key factors shaping K‐12 students’ CT development in AI‐enhanced STEM education. It systematically analyzes: (a) the subjects involved and the types and roles of AI tools employed, (b) the purposes, periods, and CT dimensions within the object, (c) the methods, strategies, and evaluation performance applied within rules, (d) the learning domains within communities and the interactions within the division of labor, and (e) the developmental trends in outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study employed the PRISMA framework to systematically review 57 SSCI journal publications published between 2017 and 2025. In addition, Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) was utilized to examine the current state of CT evaluation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings indicate that: (1) the primary subjects of the studies were elementary school students; expert systems and robotics were the most prevalent types of AI, which were frequently employed as learning tools; (2) the primary objective was to evaluate the effectiveness of AI in CT–K12–STEM, with periods typically ranging from 2 to 6 months, focusing on conceptual knowledge and practical skills; (3) the rules focused on exploratory learning and gamification strategies, employing quantitative research methods; (4) communities spanned cross‐disciplinary domains, with division of labor tending towards mixed interaction types; and (5) outcomes focused on the learning cognitive perspective, encompassing aspects such as learning performance and problem solving. Based on the research results, practical recommendations are provided for educational researchers and policymakers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Sustainable Marketing: A Systematic Literature Review Between Products and Social Media
container-title: Journal of Digital Marketing and Communication
d2640a57d9f5497db7a9d15e649ec2396144445e.abstract: <jats:p>The increasing adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in digital marketing has transformed conventional message automation into interactive communication between consumers and intelligent agents. However, the prevalence of greenwashing on social media and limited transparency in AI-driven communication have intensified consumer skepticism toward sustainability claims. This study aims to examine the role of AI as a communication agent in sustainable marketing and develop a conceptual framework for strengthening consumer trust through Meta-Authenticity. A qualitative research approach was employed using a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) guided by the PRISMA 2020 framework. The review examined 21 peer-reviewed journal articles, five theoretical textbooks, supplemented by four methodological references. The selected literature was analyzed using thematic analysis and systematic coding to identify recurring patterns, conceptual relationships, and emerging challenges. The findings indicate that AI-driven communication can enhance the perceived credibility of sustainable products by providing consistent, evidence-based, and technically objective information. However, excessive algorithmic personalization may contribute to sustainable filter bubbles, selective information exposure, and algorithmic greenwashing, potentially undermining consumer trust. This study concludes that effective AI-driven sustainable marketing requires more than technological efficiency and personalized communication. Consumer trust depends on algorithmic transparency, data accountability, and ethical consistency in human–machine interactions. By integrating Human–Machine Communication (HMC) theory and Platform Political Economy, the proposed Meta-Authenticity framework offers a conceptual foundation for developing transparent, accountable, and trustworthy AI-mediated sustainability communication.</jats:p>
