title: Assessing the Quality of AI Explanations of Atrial Fibrillation: Comparative Analysis of ChatGPT and Google Gemini
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
598e2fa6d5c1d1ee8bb1eebc101a66353744cb13.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Atrial fibrillation (AF) is one of the most common arrhythmias and is associated with multiple risk factors, including stroke and heart failure. Therefore, it is important that accurate and comprehensive educational resources on AF are available. Artificial intelligence (AI) platforms such as Google Gemini and ChatGPT are emerging tools for medical education. To our knowledge, this is the first study to assess the quality of these platforms for AF education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This pilot study aimed to (1) assess the quality of ChatGPT and Google Gemini explanations of AF and its treatment, (2) compare responses from both platforms, and (3) analyze differences in interpretation between cardiologists and nonmedical professionals.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The prompt “Explain atrial fibrillation and how to treat it to a patient” was entered into both ChatGPT and Google Gemini. The responses, along with a survey created in Google Forms, were sent out to potential participants between September and October 2024. The survey questions were derived from the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials and DISCERN criteria. Each survey question was multiple choice and rated on a 5-point Likert scale, where 1 indicated strong disagreement and 5 indicated strong agreement. Averages of each answer from the survey were calculated and compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The survey was completed by 28 participants, including cardiologists and cardiology fellows and 17 nonmedical professionals (college graduates not employed in the medical field). No significant overall quality differences were observed between ChatGPT and Google Gemini. When comparing participant groups, cardiologists rated AI-generated responses higher than nonmedical professionals for perceived bias (mean 3.82 vs mean 4.33; P=.04) and for explaining consequences of no treatment (mean 2.85 vs mean 1.86; P=.005). In contrast, nonmedical professionals rated structural and organizational features more favorably than cardiologists, including visual cues (mean 3.97 vs mean 2.48; P<.001), informative headers (mean 4.77 vs mean 3.95; P=.001), concise sections (mean 4.71 vs mean 4.29; P=.04), identifiable patient actions (mean 4.21 vs mean 3.19; P=.04), and references to additional resources (mean 2.65 vs mean 1.71; P=.006).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The comparable quality of ChatGPT and Google Gemini suggests that both are viable for AF education. Differences in ratings of organizational features versus perceptions of bias and consequences of no treatment highlight a disconnect between cardiologists and nonmedical professionals. To optimize clinical application, cardiologists should evaluate both comprehensiveness and clarity of AI-generated responses. This serves as a pilot study, and future research should focus on longitudinal studies of AI-generated responses and their effects on clinical outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: AI-Generated Exposure Hierarchies for Body Dysmorphic Disorder: Proof-of-Concept Study
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
475970c23de59b336f5f102fda0e80aa46b47e4e.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is a chronic, impairing condition for which cognitive behavioral therapy, including exposure and response prevention (ERP), is the first-line treatment, but few clinicians are trained in BDD-specific ERP. Constructing personalized exposure hierarchies is time-intensive and requires clinical expertise, particularly for patients with absent insight who may hold appearance beliefs with delusional conviction. Generative AI (GenAI)–powered chatbots, such as ChatGPT, have shown utility for clinical content, but their capacity to produce safe, appropriate ERP hierarchies for BDD has not been examined.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study evaluated the feasibility of using ChatGPT (GPT-5) to generate ERP hierarchies for BDD, assessed the influence of clinical and demographic characteristics on output quality, benchmarked AI-generated hierarchies against those created by doctoral-level BDD specialists, and tested whether blinded experts could distinguish AI-generated from expert-generated hierarchies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GPT-5 generated 10-item graded exposure hierarchies for 72 simulated vignettes that varied by body area, insight level (good, limited, or absent), symptom specificity, age, and gender. Expert clinicians independently generated hierarchies for a subset of 18 vignettes. Two researchers rated all GPT-5 hierarchies for task completion and information integration. Three BDD expert clinicians, blinded to the hierarchy source (expert vs GPT-5), rated all 90 hierarchies for relevance, specificity, variability, safety, and overall quality. After unblinding, raters attempted to identify the AI-generated hierarchy in the 18 matched pairs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      GPT-5 generated complete hierarchies for 69 of 72 (95.8%) vignettes. Blinded experts rated GPT-5 hierarchies highly across all dimensions (mean scores ranging from 4.39, SD 0.26 to 4.90, SD 0.16 out of 5), with no significant differences from expert-generated hierarchies except for variability, where experts scored modestly higher (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.02;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.24). After unblinding, raters correctly identified AI-generated hierarchies only 31.5% (17/54) of the time, significantly below chance (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.009); this below-chance result was mostly due to one rater, and no rater performed above chance. Insight level was the most consistent predictor of quality: absent-insight hierarchies received significantly lower safety (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.73) and overall quality ratings (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.01;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.43). This pattern was not unique to GPT-5; safety ratings for expert-generated hierarchies also declined significantly by insight level (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03). Miscalibration of exposure difficulty, particularly for low- and absent-insight cases, was the most common rater concern (30/43, 69.8% comments), disproportionately directed at GPT-5 hierarchies.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GPT-5 generated ERP hierarchies for BDD that blinded experts rated as comparable to clinician-created hierarchies and could not reliably distinguish them from clinician-created hierarchies. However, hierarchies for patients with absent insight received lower safety and quality ratings from both AI and expert sources, and qualitative comments suggested AI-generated hierarchies were less well calibrated to delusional-level presentations. GenAI thus shows promise as a clinician-facing aid for ERP hierarchy generation, but these findings underscore the need for clinician oversight, especially for patients with delusional conviction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Human Socialization (and Dis-Socialization) by AI and Robotic Companions in Educational Ecosystems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Robotic Companions for Human Socialization
21e354c94bb2573462d54359bd698db08de31a01.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter interrogates how AI chatbots, social robots, and ambient agents function as companion technologies that reconfigure human socialization and dis-socialization in educational ecosystems. Drawing on socialization theory, ecological systems, sociocultural mediation, sociomaterial assemblages, and posthuman subjectivity, it constructs a multi-level lens spanning micro interactional dynamics, meso institutional architectures, and macro political economies. The chapter develops typologies of companion configurations, maps learner needs to companion affordances, and analyses interactional quality through constructs such as social presence, parasociality, and epistemic justice. It then articulates normative, rights-based, and governance frameworks that distribute responsibilities across learners, educators, institutions, vendors, regulators, and civil society. The chapter positions humane companionable education as an agenda that seeks to harness machine companionship for inclusion and flourishing while resisting surveillance, stratification, and civic erosion.</jats:p>

title: Emotional and Social Intelligence in AI Systems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Robotic Companions for Human Socialization
6a2e01dfa5708795013bf97dce0351890b7ec891.abstract: <jats:p>As artificial intelligence increasingly engages emotional and social dimensions of human life, its ability to recognize and respond to emotion raises important ethical and philosophical concerns. This chapter examines the development of emotional and social intelligence in AI, highlighting the shift from rational computation toward affective interaction. Drawing on cognitive psychology, affective computing, and moral philosophy, it explores whether machine empathy reflects genuine understanding or performative simulation. The discussion addresses risks such as emotional surveillance, manipulation, dependency, and cultural misrecognition, while acknowledging benefits of emotionally responsive AI in education, healthcare, and assistive contexts. To address ethical gaps, the chapter proposes a Computational Compassion Framework (CCF) integrating moral intentionality, transparency, human oversight, and contextual sensitivity into AI design. It argues that the future of emotional AI lies not in humanizing machines, but in embedding ethical responsibility within technological systems.</jats:p>

title: Unlocking Profits in Generative AI: The Impact of AI Adaptive Learning on Freemium Strategy
container-title: Information Systems Research
1e71b78eb99b705782120789109bb4b568ed47eb.abstract: <jats:p>Generative AI firms increasingly rely on freemium strategies, offering a basic service at no charge while charging for a more capable version. Unlike conventional digital products, generative AI systems can improve through user interactions, making free users a potential source of valuable learning data. Using an analytical model, this study shows that freemium is not always the most profitable strategy. Free access can expand the user base and accelerate AI adaptive learning, but it can also cannibalize paid demand and create substantial service costs. More effective adaptive learning does not necessarily make freemium more attractive; under some conditions, the firm earns more by offering only a paid version at a lower price. When freemium is used, a moderate capability gap between free and premium versions can be more profitable than making the free tier either too limited or too close to the premium product. Managers should evaluate learning benefits alongside service costs, market coverage, and premium cannibalization. Policymakers should also avoid assuming that free access automatically improves consumer welfare, because capability gains may allow firms to raise premium prices.</jats:p>

title: Attention, Obligation, and the Rootedness of Human Identity in the AI Renaissance
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Reconfiguring Human Identity and Social Contracts in the AI Renaissance
e4417ce1339c12cc05dc70011ea7ae674c983fe8.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how the AI renaissance is reconfiguring fundamental anthropological conditions of human existence and how Simone Weil's ethics of attention, obligation, and rootedness can provide a normative framework for understanding these transformations. Methodologically, the analysis combines conceptual reconstruction, philosophical-hermeneutic updating, and critically reflected conceptual engineering to translate Weil's categories into contemporary AI contexts. The analysis identifies three interconnected transformations: AI-mediated environments can reshape the conditions for sustained attention; distributed human-machine agency can create responsibility and obligation gaps; and digital infrastructures can weaken the conditions for social, economic, and political rootedness. The chapter develops a Weilian governance framework that deepens human-centered AI by identifying the anthropological conditions that underlie rights, human oversight, accountability, and participation.</jats:p>

title: Human Rights in the AI Renaissance
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Reconfiguring Human Identity and Social Contracts in the AI Renaissance
b6cc6cdaede90b65d88551af1e19e431b12e7088.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is an innovation that is fast changing society, economy, and government structures. Although it is extremely advantageous, it also triggers the issue of human rights, fairness, and accountability. This chapter focuses on the discussion of the manner in which human rights will be protected in the ascendancy of AI. It raises the red flag over perilous algorithms, the absence of transparency and surveillance technologies proliferation. Legal frameworks and considerations that can be used to steer innovation towards dignity, equality, and justice are also addressed. Healthcare, employment, policing case studies gives an example of how AI affects the basic freedom. The chapter proposes a right based regulation of AI, stating that innovation should be moderated and should not harm people and society. It concludes with the policy suggestions that can make AI advocacy to social justice and maintain human freedoms.</jats:p>

title: Exploring ChatGPT-Assisted Qualitative Data: Comparing Human and AI-Assisted Coding Using Braun and Clarke’s Thematic Analysis
container-title: American Journal of Qualitative Research
d1da3462e4a00cf9a9e2a1ed853867d5195ec143.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en"><i>The use of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models such as ChatGPT, has significantly expanded across academia and research in recent years. Of growing interest is AI’s potential role in qualitative research, especially in expediting tasks such as literature review and synthesis, data management and coding, and manuscript preparation, all while striving to maintain the rigor expected of qualitative inquiry. This paper explores the degree of alignment between AI-generated thematic analysis and a traditional, manual approach to analyzing focus group data and potential uses of AI in qualitative research. Using Braun and Clarke’s thematic analysis framework, a publicly available focus group dataset was analyzed in three stages: (1) Data Familiarization, (2) Human-Led Thematic Analysis, and (3) AI-Generated Analysis using ChatGPT. The human coders followed all six phases of the framework prior to engaging with the AI, to prevent influence from AI-generated output. The comparison revealed partial overlap between the human and AI-generated categories, particularly at the level of broader categories and themes. However, ChatGPT’s analysis tended to reflect a more superficial reading of the data, lacking the interpretive depth and nuance demonstrated by the human coders. While AI tools like ChatGPT show potential for supporting certain aspects of qualitative analysis, this study highlights key limitations in their ability to fully replicate the complexity and contextual understanding that human-led analysis provides. Further exploration is needed to define appropriate and ethical roles for AI in qualitative research workflows.</i></jats:p>

title: Evaluating an AI-Powered Patient Simulator for Communication Skills Training: One-Year Randomized Controlled Trial
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
95a62b89e12f29ec2d10ee4b3bff78918b9670c6.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Clinical communication skills are a core yet complex competency in medical education and practice. However, early-stage medical students often struggle to apply communication frameworks in practice due to limited opportunities for structured simulation training. Generative AI (GenAI)–supported training has the potential to offer a scalable and innovative approach for clinical communication skills training.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examined the longitudinal development of medical students’ clinical communication skills over 1 academic year and investigated whether AI-powered simulation contributed to differential improvement relative to conventional training. In addition, the study explored motivational, behavioral, and affective mechanisms associated with communication skills development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A nonblinded randomized controlled design was used at a medical school in the United Kingdom, with students assigned either to the control group (n=28, 56%) or to the AI group (n=22, 44%), who practiced with SimPatient, a patient-simulator chatbot accessed through a web browser. Communication skills performance was assessed using standardized objective structured clinical examinations (OSCE) scores relative to the pass marks to enable comparison across time points. Paired t tests and difference-in-differences (DID) analyses were conducted between groups and over time to examine changes in communication skills. Latent change score modeling was used to identify predictors of communication skills change. Sentiment analysis was conducted on 6120 comments from AI-student conversations. Finally, a system quality survey was used to assess participants’ feedback on the AI-powered simulator.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Latent change score modeling showed that gains in intrinsic motivation and behavioral learning were significant predictors of students’ communication skills change. The AI group showed a greater descriptive increase in communication skills than the control group, yet the between-group difference was not statistically significant. Within the AI group, consultations whose lexical tone trended more strongly toward resolution (consultation tone) were descriptively associated with communication skills improvement; given the small subsample (n=17), this finding is reported as exploratory. The AI group’s confidence level in AI use was negatively associated with communication skills improvement, while the group nevertheless reported a generally high level of satisfaction with the system.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this study, medical students’ clinical communication skills increased over the academic year, with this development most strongly associated with their motivation and behavioral engagement; the AI-supported group did not differ significantly from conventional training. The simulator responded appropriately and provided a usable environment for practicing foundational communication behaviors but was limited in capturing the affective complexity, vulnerability, and narrative unpredictability of real clinical encounters. In conclusion, this study suggests that GenAI holds promise for supporting foundational clinical communication training and providing positive practice environments, thereby fostering motivation and behavioral engagement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Emotional Intelligence and Mental Well-Being in AI-Driven Hospitality
container-title: Experience Economy Insights on Human-Centric Hospitality 5.0
53a8b9399dccecdf1d6c3cc1543b58d05b5ccf4c.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, and digital service systems within the hospitality sector has ushered in an era known as Hospitality 5.0. While these advancements enhance efficiency, personalization, and guest satisfaction, they also increase emotional labor, psychological strain, and occupational stress among employees. This chapter analyzes, using major theories and frameworks, how emotional intelligence and mental well-being mediate sustainable workforce outcomes in AI-intensive hospitality. An original conceptual model, the Emotionally Sustainable Hospitality Workforce Model (ESHWM), is introduced, highlighting sustainable HRM as critical for maintaining emotional and psychological health amid digital disruption. The chapter summarizes empirical evidence linking AI adoption to increased workplace stress and shows how high emotional intelligence protects and boosts frontline hospitality worker performance. Practical implications are offered for managers, HR practitioners, and policymakers, aligning with UN SDGs 3, 8, and 9.</jats:p>

title: AI-Newton: A concept-driven physical law discovery system without prior physical knowledge
container-title: Physical Review Research
ea8da7c32b2a591d9ac52aeb9a7ee781fb421226.abstract: <jats:p>While current artificial intelligence (AI)-driven methods excel at deriving empirical models from individual experiments, a significant challenge remains in uncovering the common fundamental physics that underlie these models—a task at which human physicists are adept. To bridge this gap, we introduce AI-Newton, a framework for concept-driven scientific discovery. Our system autonomously derives general physical laws directly from raw, multiexperiment data, operating without supervision or prior physical knowledge. Its core innovations are twofold: (1) proposing interpretable physical concepts to construct laws and (2) progressively generalizing these laws to broader domains. Applied to a large, noisy dataset of mechanics experiments, AI-Newton successfully rediscovers foundational and universal laws, such as Newton's second law, the conservation of energy, and the universal gravitation. This work represents a proof-of-concept step toward autonomous, humanlike scientific discovery.</jats:p>

title: PlantVirDisConDB: an integrated resource linking plant virus sequence records with hosts, phenotypes, targets, antiviral evidence, and AI-assisted prioritization
container-title: Nucleic Acids Research
94e3d3d5856ce7833815016738df99245ff17364.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Research on plant viruses depends on taxonomy, nucleic acid sequences, host and disease records, molecular targets, and antiviral assays. These data are distributed across separate resources, making integrated retrieval and comparison difficult. PlantVirDisConDB (https://dpai.ccnu.edu.cn/PVDCDB) is freely accessible without login or registration and links these data through curated plant virus records. At the July 2026 reporting date, it comprised, in round numbers, 5000 virus and subviral agent records and 38 000 sequence accessions. It also included approximately1900 hosts, 9000 virus–host associations, 4800 disease names, 5000 structure records, and 25 000 small molecules. Direct assay records for plant viruses are distinguished from general antiviral background data; experimental and predicted structures, and measured activities and model outputs, are also labelled separately. Linked record pages support retrieval across these data types, access to individual sequence records, target searches, and molecular similarity searches. An activity prediction module ranks candidate molecule–virus pairs with applicability warnings and does not imply experimental or field efficacy. PlantVirDisConDB links viral nucleic acid entities to hosts, phenotypes, targets, and antiviral information and is updated through continuing curation and user feedback.</jats:p>

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Practice: How Should Rheumatologists Evaluate and Monitor Emerging Tools?
container-title: Arthritis Care & Research
3f160ed41d422ffb9dd3b8b7e40c689996ef000c.abstract:
<jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in rheumatology practice, to assist with tasks such as documentation, record summarization, and clinical decision support. Rheumatologists need a practical approach to determining what evidence and oversight each application requires. This narrative review proposes a framework based on two dimensions: contextual complexity and influence on patient care. Greater contextual complexity can make errors harder to detect, whereas greater influence on care increases the potential consequences of an undetected error. We examine evidence for workflow benefits and clinical effectiveness within this framework and consider safety, equity, privacy, governance, and implementation. Existing evidence on the benefits, accuracy, and reliability of AI applications remains mixed. For example, studies of ambient AI scribes suggest reduced documentation burden, but evidence of improved patient outcomes from applications supporting clinical decisions is more limited. For applications with limited clinical influence, evaluation has initially focused on workflow, usability, and documentation quality. Tools that synthesize longitudinal information require additional assessment of completeness and source traceability. Those influencing diagnosis or treatment require prospective evaluation of clinical benefit and safety. Relevant vendor evidence should be assessed alongside proportionate local testing and ongoing monitoring. Safeguards should address risks such as hallucinations, automation bias, and propagating documentation errors, with attention to performance across patient groups. Changes in functionality or clinical use should prompt reassessment. The framework provides a structured basis for adoption decisions and identifies priorities for research on patient outcomes and feasible oversight in routine rheumatology care.</jats:p>

title: AI adoption in purchasing and supply management: how institutional voids rewire the UTAUT framework
container-title: Modern Supply Chain Research and Applications
fd976dc156551128de71dc829f70972275c8141d.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigates how institutional voids and behavioral factors jointly drive artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in purchasing and supply management (PSM) within emerging economies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Survey data from 200 PSM professionals in Morocco were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to test an integrated UTAUT–institutional theory framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Performance expectancy (PE) (ß = 0.530) and social influence (ß = 0.453) primarily drive behavioral intention (BI), while coercive pressure is non-significant (ß = 0.050, p = 0.260). Facilitating conditions (FC) (ß = 0.472) and (BI) (ß = 0.497) exert near-equal direct effects on actual use, confirming an “infrastructure imperative”. Post-hoc multi-group analysis reveals that PE dominates predictive AI adoption, whereas effort expectancy dominates Generative AI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Organizations in emerging economies must pair AI software procurement with dedicated infrastructure, data governance and peer-led change management rather than relying on unsupported mandates.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study demonstrates that institutional voids modify the UTAUT nomological network by elevating FC to a primary co-determinant of technology use, proving infrastructure readiness equals user intention in driving adoption.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: University students' disciplinary perspectives on generative AI after two years of its widespread use
container-title: Journal of Applied Research in Higher Education
5cfc2677f2ff083e2ccefb422d4ee92c351ab20c.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study explores how university students use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) across various disciplines, including STEM, Business, Education Futures, Clinical & Health Sciences (CHS), Creative and Allied Health & Human Performance (AHHP). It aims to identify discipline-based perspectives, perceived benefits, ethical boundaries and the support needs required for responsible use of GenAI tools.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A survey was conducted approximately two years after the widespread use of GenAI, by which time participants were expected to be familiar with its use. Students were categorised based on their discipline, English fluency, mode of learning and level of study. Their responses were analysed to compare usage patterns, satisfaction levels and ethical considerations across disciplines.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results highlight that student perspectives on GenAI tools are discipline-dependent. STEM and Education Futures showed the highest acceptance, while CHS and Business students were more cautious and sceptical about accuracy and ethical issues. Non-native English speakers rated GenAI tools more favourably as aids for writing and comprehension. Novice users expressed enthusiasm, while expert users showed dissatisfaction due to errors and false information.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study relied on self-reported perceptions and represents a single institutional context. Broader investigations are recommended, with a particular focus on equity groups such as students with disabilities, low-SES students and remote learners.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Different approaches were suggested for integrating GenAI into learning. STEM students favoured comparative tasks; CHS recommended support for diagnostic reasoning; Allied Health preferred role-playing simulations; Education Futures highlighted lesson planning; and Business students suggested case-based and productivity uses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study provides cross-disciplinary analyses of GenAI use by students and proposes approaches for ethical and discipline-specific integration into university curricula.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Human-AI Collaboration in Urban Digital Transformation: Balancing Efficiency and Human Values in Shanghai’s AI-Enabled Talent Recruitment
container-title: Digital Technologies Research and Applications
9846cab94a199e2bda9d30d406a36d92a6eb9deb.abstract: <jats:p>In the context of the urban digital revolution, recruitment through AI technologies has become common practice to address competition in the labor market. However, it is still unclear how the effectiveness of such recruitment is connected with humanistic values. For this research, an exploratory qualitative research design was used, involving semi-structured interviews with eight human resource professionals in Shanghai. Based on the results, the use of AI in recruitment led to increased efficiency mainly when screening candidates through high-volume, standardized processes, although the promised efficiency was not delivered in practice because the introduction of the AI system increased the workload. Patterns of human-machine cooperation were observed in different companies: tech companies and foreign companies are inclined to adopt interactive adjustment approaches, while state-owned enterprises retain human-dominated decision-making. Transparency of algorithms was still lacking in numerous instances, and there was an asymmetry in the accountability framework of algorithms, wherein disobeying algorithms carries more personal consequences than obeying them. The more experienced professionals became more autonomous in their work, while the less experienced professionals depended more on the algorithm. Issues like management support, information accuracy, and departmental integration have a major impact on implementation. This study contributes to the theory of human-machine collaboration by proposing the concept of asymmetric algorithmic accountability, which captures the uneven distribution of organizational consequences for following versus overriding AI recommendations and shapes practitioner behavior in ways that extend beyond individual trust or algorithmic transparency.</jats:p>

title: Editorial: generative AI and the small business frontier – charting pathways toward meaningful social impact
container-title: Journal of Social Impact in Business Research
8f33d12dc321c5cdc4af11947e236ec5f5d588ae.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to examine how small and medium-sized enterprises can leverage generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to create social impact, by developing a multidimensional framework linking GenAI adoption with social-value creation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This editorial adopts a conceptual synthesis approach, that integrates insights from the special-issue papers with emerging research and identifies principal domains of social impact.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Social impact is not a property of GenAI but a contingent outcome of how it is applied and adopted. While firms may have similar GenAI potentialities across various impact domains, success is dependent on human, organisational, sectoral and institutional contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This editorial provides a framework for assessing where GenAI can support social-value creation whilst managing ethical, organisational and workforce risks. Impact accrues through organisational processes rather than through adoption itself.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The social impact of GenAI is extended beyond productivity and efficiency and positioned as a multidimensional and contingent outcome of technology adoption. A four-element framework links GenAI capability, organisational mechanisms, enabling and constraining conditions and stakeholder outcomes, which then informs a research agenda.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Trustworthy Federated Clinical Intelligence with Homomorphic Encryption and  Explainable AI
container-title: International Journal on Advanced Computer Engineering and Communication Technology
52dc2d5fa5cc8d54dabc189da8b019169d1f9138.abstract: <jats:p>Cross-institutional clinical artificial intelligence is constrained by fragmented patient data, non-identically distributed (non-IID) populations, leakage from shared model updates, and limited interpretability. Federated learning (FL) preserves data locality, but ordinary FL neither makes model updates confidential nor guarantees stable optimization under heterogeneous clients. This paper proposes a defense-in-depth framework that coordinates Federated Proximal (FedProx) optimization, record-level differential privacy (DP), Cheon–Kim–Kim–Song (CKKS) approximate homomorphic encryption, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). FedProx limits local model drift; DP-SGD bounds the influence of an individual training record; and CKKS permits weighted aggregation while client updates remain encrypted. A key-separated design keeps the aggregation server from being provisioned with the secret key used to reveal individual contributions; only the aggregate is released for global-model construction. Grad-CAM and SHAP/LIME provide clinician-facing explanations, while an audit dashboard reports convergence, privacy-accounting inputs, encryption status, and systems overhead. We formalize the learning objective, privacy mechanism, encrypted aggregation, threat model, numerical approximation error, communication footprint, and an evaluation protocol spanning IID and controlled non-IID partitions. The contribution is a reproducible system-level co-design and evaluation framework rather than a new cryptographic primitive or optimization algorithm.</jats:p>

title: TECHNOLOGICAL EMPOWERMENT AND VALUE BALANCE: DUAL PATHWAYS IN CHINA’S TECHNOLOGY GOVERNANCE POLICIES FOR THE AI ERA
container-title: Trends in Social Sciences and Humanities Research
970345be14784ec01aa2dabb94b086731cf1daa2.abstract: <jats:p>The deep embedding of artificial intelligence (AI) technology is reshaping global governance. The tension between “technological empowerment” and “value balance” has become a common governance challenge for countries worldwide. Based on a dual-pathway framework of “technology-driven modernization of state governance” and “technology-embedded multi-actor social co-governance,” this paper systematically analyzes the internal logic and operational mechanisms of technology governance in China in the AI era. The study finds that China’s technology governance is not a single efficiency-oriented application of technology; rather, through the coordinated operation of dual pathways, it comprehensively achieves four major governance functions: efficiency improvement, equity promotion, security assurance, and institutional reconstruction. In terms of model characteristics, China has developed a distinctive paradigm centered on “enabling governance”-one that takes state capacity as its foundation, institutional flexibility as its safeguard, and plural public values as its goals. This paradigm transcends the single efficiency-oriented governance logic of the West and offers a non-Western pathway with both theoretical inspiration and practical reference for global digital governance. This paper argues that the core of “enabling governance” lies in resolving the tension between technological empowerment and value balance through institutional design, and that the transferability of its experience depends on the conditions of fit in specific institutional contexts.</jats:p>

title: tModBase v2.0: an expanded database of tRNA modifications with an AI-powered assistant
container-title: Nucleic Acids Research
be1c00314cb8dff0cfa4d3051d7c0b9d755da68a.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Chemical modifications of transfer RNAs (tRNAs) are crucial for tRNA stability, codon decoding, translational fidelity, and tRNA-derived small RNA (tsRNA) biogenesis. Changes in these modifications are associated with stress responses, physiological regulation, and human disease, underscoring the need to integrate modification information with experimental evidence and biological context. We previously established tModBase, a web resource to organize and explore tRNA modification-related data. Its first release integrated modification sites, high-throughput sequencing-derived signals, and condition-dependent changes. Since then, tRNA profiling has expanded through modification-specific and direct RNA sequencing strategies, with rapidly growing datasets across species and conditions. Here, we present tModBase v2.0 (http://www.tmodbase2.com/), containing 528 datasets across 23 species, 40 sequencing and library-preparation methods, and 42 modification types. It includes 68 third-generation and 210 modification-specific sequencing datasets, extending coverage of direct-RNA and modification-specific approaches. tModBase v2.0 further integrates sequencing-derived signals, condition-dependent information, and biological annotations linking modifications with enzymes, genetic variants, tsRNAs, diseases, and expression profiles. The LLM- and retrieval-augmented generation-powered assistant tModBot enables natural-language exploration across database modules while grounding responses in retrieved tModBase evidence. tModBase v2.0 therefore provides an expanded resource for investigating the diversity, dynamics, and biological context of tRNA modifications.</jats:p>

title: An Application of the Self-Determination Theory Model for AI-Enhanced, Digital Psychosocial Interventions for Pediatric Disabilities
container-title: Western Journal of Nursing Research
c620cf1b4f812518b0ef9e1f32165cf0b13e2621.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Youth with developmental disabilities (DDs) experience elevated psychosocial challenges, including difficulties with emotion regulation, self-concept, and access to timely mental health support. Pediatric nurses are well-positioned to address these needs; however, time constraints, limited training, and restricted access to specialty services often impede the provision of consistent psychosocial care. Digitally delivered psychosocial interventions enhanced by artificial intelligence (AI) offer new opportunities for individualized, accessible support, but these approaches frequently lack a clear theoretical foundation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper applied Self-Determination Theory (SDT), specifically Basic Psychological Needs Theory, to guide pediatric nurses’ use of AI-enhanced, digital psychosocial interventions for DDs in practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A theory-driven synthesis mapped SDT needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness) to AI-enabled intervention features: conversational agents, neuro/adaptive feedback, and emotion-recognition tailoring.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework specifies how these features can promote volitional engagement, optimal challenge with timely feedback, and supportive interactions for youth with DDs. It also notes evidence gaps (small, heterogeneous samples; limited comparisons and follow-up) and barriers involving payment/workload, equity and access, and data protection, transparency, and bias.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions/Implications:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>SDT offers a coherent, testable foundation for designing, evaluating, and integrating AI-enhanced psychosocial supports for pediatric DDs. Nurses can screen for support, coach families, monitor risks, and advocate for ethical deployment and rigorous research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: AI-Powered Global Expansion: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Adoption on Firms’ Outward Foreign Direct Investment
container-title: Journal of Academic Research and Advances
2a05bfef34581f00a29abb04125f82b362ae925e.abstract:
<jats:p>Against the backdrop of profound shifts in the global economic landscape and rapid advances in digital technologies, artificial intelligence (AI) offers firms new opportunities to expand into international markets and improve the allocation of resources across borders. Drawing on a sample of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2009 to 2024, this study empirically examines the relationship between AI adoption and outward foreign direct investment (OFDI), with particular attention to the mechanisms underlying this relationship.
The findings indicate that AI adoption is positively and significantly associated with firms’ OFDI activities. This result remains robust across a range of alternative specifications, including different measures of AI adoption, adjustments to fixed effects and standard-error clustering, and the exclusion of selected observations. Heterogeneity analyses suggest that the positive relationship is more pronounced among technology-intensive firms and larger enterprises. Further analysis identifies two potential channels through which AI adoption may facilitate OFDI: technological innovation and the alleviation of financial constraints. Together, these mechanisms may strengthen firms’ technological capabilities and improve their access to the financial resources required for international expansion.
By examining OFDI through the lens of firm-level AI adoption, this study extends the literature on the determinants of international investment and provides further insight into how AI may shape firms’ internationalization strategies. The findings also offer empirical evidence relevant to the integration of AI into the real economy, the enhancement of firms’ international competitiveness, and China’s efforts to pursue higher-standard economic opening-up.</jats:p>

title: Measuring the geometric parameters of woven fabrics with AI chatbots: a benchmark and three paths to higher accuracy
container-title: Research Journal of Textile and Apparel
3ffaff0ae17f162fded7c0bb0202aa1d6f53d2f8.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Publicly available multimodal chatbots could make fabric geometry measurement accessible in low-resource settings, yet their accuracy for this task has never been systematically evaluated. This study aims to benchmark six such chatbots and investigates whether protocol-level improvements can raise measurement accuracy without model fine-tuning, unavailable to end users.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>One hundred woven fabrics were scanned and their ground-truth values – weave type, thread count, cover factor, twist direction and twist angle – were measured according to ISO/ASTM. Six chatbots were tested with five runs per fabric, yielding 3,000 tests. Three improvement paths were examined: intra-system averaging, prompt enrichment with known fabric data and inter-system aggregation. Errors were quantified via misclassification rate (MCR) and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Baseline accuracy was far below metrological requirements (MCR = 15–46%, MAPE = 9–34%). Three repeated runs indicated variability of ± 2–4 percentage points. Intra-system averaging and prompt refinement produced small, heterogeneous changes within this variability. Inter-system aggregation reduced five errors: weave MCR 32% to 21%, thread count MAPE 14% to 7%, cover factor MAPE 12% to 7%, twist direction MCR 32% to 20% and twist angle MAPE 28% to 18%. Paired tests showed significant differences between Path 3 and matched conditions after correction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Aggregating heterogeneous, non-specialised chatbot outputs reduced fabric-geometry measurement error without model training. The resulting applicability matrices illustrate the potential operational range of each parameter, providing a parameter-by-parameter framework for interpreting the trade-off between accuracy and accessibility in low-infrastructure textile screening.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: AI INVESTMENT AND THE UK STARTUP ECOSYSTEM: COMPETING WITH SILICON VALLEY IN THE AGE OF GENERATIVE AI
container-title: International Journal of Financial Research and Business Development
f3cbb5c8ad7299bb52973b4cdbae65b0f77adeb8.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines the evolution and competitive positioning of the United Kingdom's AI startup ecosystem amid the rise of generative AI. Using a qualitative desk-research design based on secondary investment data, policy documents, and academic literature from 2015-2026, the study analyzes how the UK has transitioned from a research-driven niche to a globally recognized hub, leveraging world-class universities, dense financial and healthcare markets, and a principle-based regulatory framework. Growth has been propelled by a robust spinout cycle from anchor institutions and accessible early-stage capital. Despite these strengths, structural constraints threaten long-term scale, including a persistent late-stage funding gap, infrastructure bottlenecks in compute access and energy costs, and intensifying global competition for talent. The study finds the UK is best positioned to capture value in autonomous enterprise agents, AI for scientific discovery, and multimodal systems. Sustaining global competitiveness will require expanding domestic growth capital, ensuring reliable compute access, and maintaining regulatory clarity without stifling agility.</jats:p>

title: Prediction of Grape Disease using Deep Learning based on MobileNetV2 and Explainable AI with Grad-CAM for Disease Management
container-title: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
976d8ee6eea9aa8cebb950869ad418aad2ddc182.abstract:
<jats:p>The grapes production can be affected by diseases that cause changes to the look and state of the leaves and may reduce the quality of the crop if the disease are not detected in time. Even though visual diagnosis is of some help, it depends on the operator's experience and can become difficult when different diseases show similar symptoms.
The study presents an image-based approach for predicting and Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) for providing a visual explanation. The System can detect four kinds of disease: Black Measles, Black Rot, Healthy, and Isariopsis Leaf Spot. The model produces a distribution of class probabilities and Grad-CAM is used to highlight the parts of the image that are related to the predicted class.
A general module based on knowledge then provides information regarding the symptoms, advice on how to manage the disease, and preventive measures for the disease which has been predicted. Having been tested on 903 images, the system achieved 886 correct predictions and 17 incorrect ones, giving an accuracy of 98.12%, a weighted precision of 98.13%,a weighted recall of 98.12%, and a weighted F1-score of 98.12%. The errors that were seen were mostly between Black Measles and Black Rot. The study therefore incorporates prediction, visual explanation, and disease-management information into one workflow, while at the same time recognizing the need for further validation with a wider variety of field images..</jats:p>

title: Green Software Tracker for Web Applications Using AI
container-title: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
32cd4198505bdadb721d420dbc77bc155c5606f7.abstract: <jats:p>Web applications consume computing resources such as CPU, memory, and network bandwidth during request processing. High resource consumption can increase energy usage and contribute to carbon emissions. This research proposes a Green Software Tracker for Web Applications Using AI to monitor resource utilization and estimate the environmental impact of web applications. The proposed system uses Python and the psutil library to collect process-level CPU and memory data at defined intervals. It aims to estimate energy consumption using a documented estimation method and calculate associated carbon emissions using an appropriate electricity emission factor. A dashboard is planned to display resource usage, estimated emissions, a Green Score, and recommendations for improving software efficiency. The current recommendation approach is rule-based. Further implementation and experimental evaluation are required to validate the estimation method and assess the system's performance</jats:p>

title: Dissolve What Extracts: AI, Wellbeing, and the Composition of Economic Life (A Compositional Theory of the AI Wellbeing Dividend, with a Constructive Policy Triad)
container-title: Wellbeing Futures: Innovation, Policy and Research
1865837f0b74f04993f06567454229f396e00120.abstract: <jats:p>AI's most important wellbeing dividend may not come from producing more output, but from changing the composition of economic life. By reducing the administrative, cognitive, financial, and procedural burdens that absorb human capacity without building capability, AI can dissolve forms of extractive friction. But unless the resulting gains are protected from rent migration and redirected into formative infrastructure, extraction will not disappear; it will reappear in AI-native form. This paper develops a compositional theory of AI and wellbeing, distinguishing the philosophical hinge between extractive friction (burdens that drain capacity without building it) and formative friction (difficulty that develops judgment, skill, relationship, and responsibility). The wellbeing dividend is mapped across four BANI channels, with Brittleness treated explicitly as a hypothesis-generating channel rather than an established mechanism. The paper distinguishes theory from prescription. The prescription is a triadic policy mechanism: dissolution compresses extractive friction; anti-recapture prevents migrated rents from forming a new layer of extraction (taxation is its principal fiscal instance, alongside interoperability mandates, fiduciary duties, antitrust scrutiny, and public AI provision); and formation funding directs released capacity into relational and developmental infrastructure. The triad is operationalised through a five-test evaluative toolkit (Capability, Proportionality, Distribution, Migration, Formation) designed to assess whether any AI deployment or proposed policy actually advances compositional change rather than merely automating the existing equilibrium.</jats:p>

title: Should there be a teacher in-the-loop? A study of generative AI-personalized tasks middle school
container-title: Educational technology research and development
3d9a8256df0161cc1e4abba7e65cb1cef7d87775.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Large language models can be used to design instructional tasks to align to students’ needs. These generative AI models can create tasks that correspond to students’ out-of-school interests in areas like sports or music, which may enhance students’ interest in learning. However, little is known about teachers’ processes for creating or modifying tasks with generative AI, despite commercial AI companies’ claims that they will save teachers time. In the present study, 7 middle school mathematics teachers used ChatGPT to create personalized versions of problems in their curriculum to correspond to their students’ interests. The prompting moves teachers made and their students’ open-ended feedback on personalized problems were examined through thematic analysis. Teachers’ efficiency when creating problems and the ratings of their 7th grade students who received personalized assignments were examined. Results from this sample suggest that having a teacher-in-the-loop may result in generative AI-enhanced personalization being enacted at a broad grain size, whereas students often expressed preference for a smaller grain-size where they receive specific popular culture references that interest them. Teachers used prompting to adjust popular culture references and address issues with the depth, ethics, or realism of the problems generated, in some cases showing epistemic agency. The article closes with an exploratory, design-focused look at scalability trade-offs with teacher-facing personalization, patterns of teacher prompting practices, and opportunities for teachers to exercise epistemic and ethical monitoring of personalization outputs.</jats:p>

title: Where Do We Look? Visual Attention Competition Between Hyper-Salient Objects and AI-Generated Virtual Endorsers in Generative Artificial Intelligence Advertising
container-title: Journal of Eye Movement Research
498fcba14c2a3120971f1b6fed27c097dac981bd.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (AI) advertising, defined as advertising content created or substantially assisted by generative AI systems (AIGC), has introduced new visual features that combine algorithmically generated objects with human-like representations. Hyper-salient objects, defined by exaggerated perceptual prominence and semantic incongruity, and AI-generated virtual endorsers, represented by human-like AI-created figures, have become increasingly common in such advertisements. However, little is known about how these distinct visual cues compete for consumers’ limited attentional resources when presented together. Drawing on visual attention and scene perception perspectives, this study investigated how hyper-salient objects and AI-generated virtual endorsers influence visual attention allocation in AI-generated advertising. A 2 (hyper-salient object: present vs. absent) × 2 (AI endorser: present vs. absent) between-subjects eye-tracking experiment was conducted with 160 participants in a controlled laboratory setting using static AI-generated advertisements. Eye movements were recorded, and memory was assessed using signal detection measures (d′) from a recognition task involving target and distractor advertisements. Advertising attitude and product trust were measured using established scales. Results from linear and generalized linear mixed-effects models showed that hyper-salient objects increased early fixation probability and attracted a larger dwell time proportion, demonstrating strong attentional capture. AI-generated endorsers also attracted attention when presented alone, but their proportional attention share decreased when hyper-salient objects were simultaneously present. The effects of these visual elements on memory and product trust were conditional on their co-occurrence rather than uniform across conditions. Within the specific set of experimentally constructed stimuli and four sampled product categories, this research contributes to AIGC advertising literature by developing a visual competition perspective on how multiple AI-generated visual cues interact under limited attentional capacity, offering implications for designing effective generative AI advertisements.</jats:p>

title: Evaluating the AI-predictive potential of the PIC database for pediatric ICU mortality
container-title: Pediatric Research
26145527ca2a0920ee7bcbfa5626a9721be47cf7.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Reliable Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in healthcare depend on both data quality and model design. However, the predictive integrity of datasets is rarely assessed. Publicly available resources for critically ill children remain scarce. The Pediatric Intensive Care (PIC) database remains, to the best of current knowledge, the only open-access resource focused on pediatric critical care research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study evaluates the predictive potential of the PIC database. After applying strict cohort selection and data preprocessing, mortality risk was analyzed using statistical analysis through univariate Odds Ratio (OR) to measure associations, and machine learning (ML) models interpreted through SHAP values to assess feature importance and model behavior.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>ML experiments showed moderate but limited predictive performance for mortality. CatBoost performed best, with an AUC of 0.8521 (0.8414–0.8627) on the hold-out test set, but low sensitivity (42%) limited its ability to identify non-survivors. These findings suggest dataset-related constraints that reduce clinical reliability. Most relevant variables were minimum lactate, maximum lactate, mean respiratory rate, maximum hematocrit, and minimum urea.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Analysis showed that PIC lacks essential physiological data, highlighting the limits of current pediatric databases and the need for richer multicenter datasets to enable more robust, clinically applicable AI models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Impact</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      <jats:list list-type="bullet">
                        <jats:list-item>
                          <jats:p>Provides the first comprehensive evaluation of the PIC database, assessing its suitability for machine learning-based predictive modeling.</jats:p>
                        </jats:list-item>
                        <jats:list-item>
                          <jats:p>Identifies key clinical variables and data gaps that influence the reliability of AI–based mortality prediction and model performance.</jats:p>
                        </jats:list-item>
                        <jats:list-item>
                          <jats:p>Underscores the need for richer, multicenter pediatric ICU databases for research that incorporate essential physiological and neurological indicators.</jats:p>
                        </jats:list-item>
                        <jats:list-item>
                          <jats:p>Demonstrates the value of combining statistical association and AI interpretability methods to assess the predictive integrity of clinical datasets.</jats:p>
                        </jats:list-item>
                      </jats:list>
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Technical Evaluations in the Field of AI Music Composition
container-title: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
d684b84b17df63518ef57781a746fe12e8de09ce.abstract: <jats:p>AI-based music composition has progressed from symbolic melody generation to systems that produce audio from natural-language prompts, melodic references, or combinations of both. However, the perceived usefulness of a generated track cannot be captured by audio realism alone. A system may sound convincing yet ignore the requested mood, lose musical structure over time, offer little editing control, or provide insufficient information about the provenance of its training data. This paper develops a practical, multidimensional framework for evaluating AI music composition systems. The framework organizes evaluation into five dimensions: audio and musical quality, prompt and structure alignment, controllability and editability, workflow usefulness, and responsible-use transparency. It proposes a staged evaluation protocol combining listening tests, task-based assessment, technical checks, and documentation review. The framework is a conceptual synthesis informed by published work on text-to-music generation, controllable music models, synthetic-music detection, and the supplied systematic review of AI music composition. No new experimental dataset or performance results are claimed. The paper's contribution is an evaluation blueprint that researchers, developers, educators, and music practitioners can adapt before conducting empirical validation</jats:p>
