title: Public Awareness of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Utilisation in Healthcare Institutions in Anambra State
container-title: RESEARCH JOURNAL OF MASS COMMUNICATION AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY
b95afc8cfcf288eee154d73cf330cab3e4fc70d8.abstract:
<jats:p>Given the growing adoption of AI-driven diagnostic and treatment tools across health systems,
understanding community awareness is crucial for effective integration and health
communication. Applying the survey design, data were collected from 384 adult residents selected
from across six Local Government Areas of Anambra State, Nigeria, using multistage and
proportionate sampling techniques. Findings revealed a moderately high level of awareness of AI
utilisation, with respondents expressing the strongest familiarity with AI-powered tools such as
automated diagnostics and virtual assistants. Social media emerged as the dominant source of AI
information, followed by traditional media, while healthcare providers contributed minimally to
public knowledge. Respondents also recognised significant benefits of AI, including improved
diagnostic accuracy, enhanced service delivery, and overall healthcare quality. However, concerns
were evident regarding potential medical errors, privacy concerns, and job displacement of
healthcare workers. These findings align with national and international studies showing high
exposure but limited depth of understanding among the public and health workers. Guided by the
Diffusion of Innovations and Agenda-Setting theories, the study concludes that public awareness
is largely media-driven and remains at an early diffusion stage, underscoring the need for
deliberate institutional communication, ethical safeguards, and structured public sensitisation.
The study recommends strengthening health communication strategies, promoting data protection
frameworks, and enhancing healthcare worker involvement in public AI education.</jats:p>

title: Med Intel: An AI-Based Healthcare Pharmacy Management System with Intelligent Prescription Recognition and Drug Safety Verification
container-title: International Journal of Scientific Research in Engineering & Technology
7ba7fd98e9124ed3b3a1fccd44a69fa3e2e086f5.abstract: <jats:p>The manual processing of handwritten prescriptions and the lack of automated drug safety verification in pharmacy management systems pose significant risks to patient safety and operational efficiency. This paper presents MedIntel, an AI-based healthcare pharmacy management system that integrates intelligent prescription recognition and comprehensive drug interaction detection. The prescription recognition module employs a dual-engine optical character recognition (OCR) pipeline combining EasyOCR with Tesseract as a fallback, enhanced by four image preprocessing strategies: grayscale conversion, contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE), median filtering denoising, and Otsu binary thresholding. Extracted text undergoes a multi-stage natural language processing pipeline that splits recognized text into individual word candidates, filters noise using stop-word elimination and alphabetic character ratio thresholds, and matches each candidate against the medicine database using prefix-based SQL ILIKE queries augmented by RapidFuzz token-based fuzzy matching. The drug interaction detection system performs real-time pairwise checking of all cart items against a pre-populated DrugInteraction database using bidirectional ILIKE fuzzy matching, presenting warnings categorized by four severity levels: critical, severe, moderate, and mild, each accompanied by clinical descriptions and actionable recommendations. The system is developed using Python with Flask framework on the backend and Bootstrap 5.3 on the frontend, with SQLite for persistent storage. Evaluation of the medicine name recognition module achieves a token-level accuracy of 99.19% with an entity-level F1-score of 0.971 across 140 annotated prescription sentences, and the drug interaction database covers 15 clinically validated interaction pairs across four severity categories. The system demonstrates the feasibility of deploying lightweight, database-driven AI approaches for enhancing pharmacy safety in resource-constrained healthcare environments.</jats:p>

title: AI-Based Smart Traffic Monitoring System
container-title: International Journal of Scientific Research in Engineering & Technology
c3b99836cce9ad2dbbea106a68666770420653a2.abstract: <jats:p>Manual enforcement of traffic rules in Indian cities is slow, inconsistent and difficult to scale, and most automated systems treat every offence identically regardless of the offender’s history. This paper presents the design and prototype implementation of the AI-Based Smart Traffic Monitoring System, built with Flask and OpenCV. The system registers five classes of camera-detectable violations (illegal parking, red-light jumping, riding without a helmet, wrong-way driving and triple riding) from simulated multi-camera feeds, uploaded images or video, and browser camera snapshots; stores evidence with each complaint; resolves owner details through a simulated RTO lookup; and uses a rule-based Violation Predictor to compute a Rule Breach Rate (15–98%) from prior violations and violation severity. The predictor then decides automatically between an official Warning for first-time offenders and a Direct E-Challan whose fine is escalated by 25% (third offence) and 50% (fourth and later offences), removing operator ambiguity at the review stage. A browser-side offline queue with idempotent retry prevents loss of evidence during server outages. Testing of the prototype showed that the decision logic behaves deterministically across all nine supported violation types, that image analysis takes 3–30 ms per 800×420 image on a CPU, and that the live scene renderer sustains the 45 ms stream interval comfortably. The detection layer is simulated and has not been validated on real CCTV data; this limitation, together with a weakness we found in the thumbnail-based demo matcher, is discussed along with the steps required for real deployment.</jats:p>

title: AI-Assisted Analysis of Spontaneous Affective Facial Responses for Cognitive Status Assessment in Older Adults: Exploratory Feasibility Study
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
97a7c39fc651c92b0504e2c164b26bd1dedf8810.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As Taiwan enters a super-aged society, the prevalence of dementia continues to rise, highlighting the need for scalable, noninvasive approaches to identify behavioral alterations associated with cognitive decline. AI-based analysis of spontaneous affective facial responses has emerged as a potential digital phenotyping tool, but its feasibility for assessing cognitive performance remains underexplored.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to examine the feasibility of using AI-derived spontaneous affective facial response metrics, including affective expression congruency and onset latency, to characterize differences across cognitive performance levels in older adults with healthy cognition (HC), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), or dementia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 60 participants (HC, MCI, and dementia; 20 per group) were presented with positive and negative emotion-eliciting videos and completed Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) recall and calculation tasks. Facial expressions were video-recorded and analyzed using a convolutional neural network–based AI system. AI-derived metrics included affective expression congruency, categorized as congruent, neutral, or incongruent according to the detected facial response, and affective expression onset latency, defined as the time from stimulus presentation to the emergence of a nonneutral facial expression detected by the AI model. Group differences were analyzed using 1-way ANOVA, Pearson chi-square or Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact tests, Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise post hoc comparisons, analysis of covariance adjusting for age and education, and exploratory receiver operating characteristic analyses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Affectively congruent responses were generally less frequent among participants with lower cognitive performance. During the 14-second positive stimulus, congruent positive expressions were observed in 65% (13/20) of HC participants, 20% (4/20) of MCI participants, and 0% (0/20) of participants with dementia. During the 48-second negative stimulus, congruent negative expressions were observed in 60% (12/20) of HC participants compared with 5% (1/20) of both MCI and dementia participants. Onset latency differed significantly across groups for the 14-second positive stimulus (F2,57=19.63; P<.001; η2=0.41), 52-second positive stimulus (F2,57=4.25; P=.02; η2=0.13), 48-second negative stimulus (F2,57=15.61; P<.001; η2=0.35), and MMSE-based cognitive-task condition (F2,57=11.28; P<.001; η2=0.28). After adjustment for age and education, the group effect remained significant for all latency outcomes (F2,55=3.89-10.68; all P≤.03; partial η2=0.12-0.28). Exploratory receiver operating characteristic analyses showed stronger separation in several HC vs MCI and HC vs dementia comparisons, whereas MCI vs dementia comparisons showed limited separability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI-assisted analysis of spontaneous affective facial responses revealed differences in expression congruency and onset latency across cognitive performance levels. These preliminary findings suggest that AI-derived facial behavioral metrics may serve as noninvasive adjunctive features for observational cognitive assessment. However, the findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the exploratory design, modest sample size, and absence of internal or external validation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Institutional Approval Is Not Public Authorization: Legitimacy as a Governance Requirement for Clinical AI
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
45db74e8ff47b10e8d34e165c3b3348988fad886.abstract: <jats:p>Clinical AI governance has advanced rapidly in technical validation, regulatory compliance, risk management, human oversight, and postdeployment monitoring. Yet a more fundamental question often remains implicit: under what conditions are health institutions justified in exercising consequential authority through AI over patients, clinicians, and communities? In this Viewpoint, we argue that legitimacy should be recognized as an independent governance requirement, distinct from technical assurance, legal and ethical compliance, trust, acceptance, and institutional approval. Our aim is to distinguish institutional approval from public authorization and to propose a normative framework for authorizing consequential clinical AI deployments. We address health system leaders, clinical AI governance and procurement teams, frontline clinicians, and patient and community representatives. Drawing on theories of legitimacy and public value and published clinical AI governance research, we make the following contributions: (1) the concept of the unclaimed decision, defined as a consequential choice about purpose, threshold, population, or priority for which no actor clearly assumes responsibility for public justification; (2) a tripartite framework comprising procedural authorization, substantive justification, and relational renewal; and (3) practical governance tools to support public justification, contestation, and renewal. These tools include 3 minimum auditable conditions: visibility of deployment; affected-party input before governing conditions are fixed; and conditional reviewability, which requires a predefined trigger that can be invoked by a named actor outside the deploying team. A 5-question public authorization test examines purpose, distribution, exclusion, meaningful choice and contestability, and renewal. Governance intensity should increase with clinical consequence; distributive reach; difficulty of reversal; and the absence of genuine, informed choice. For smaller health care organizations, we propose ways to perform the same core governance functions through existing advisory bodies, targeted interviews, shared regional resources, and standardized documentation. We also outline a heuristic for identifying affected publics, procedures for specifying participation authority and resolving disagreement, and procurement provisions that preserve reviewability across vendor boundaries. These are normative proposals requiring evaluation. Public authorization requires continuing substantive justification; it cannot be inferred from compliance, popularity, or completion of an audit checklist.</jats:p>

title: Investigating Patient Trust and Intention to Act in AI-Supported Clinical Decisions: Cross-Sectional Survey
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
2aa6f72e378267fb7b8566a58fb1730bb5db7964.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In health systems, AI is increasingly being implemented as a form of clinical decision support (CDS). Research on patient perspectives, however, lags behind clinician-focused studies. Before the introduction of AI-based tools, clinicians often used and continue to use rule-based guidelines and risk calculators (RCs) to inform decision-making. Prior research has shown that RCs for CDS have mixed effects on patient adherence to treatment recommendations, whereas for AI-based tools, the effect is still not clear.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to assess differences in patients’ behavioral intentions, trust, and preferences for clinical recommendations provided by doctors alone, doctors supported by RCs, and doctors supported by AI-based risk predictions. We also evaluate how sociodemographic characteristics affect these perceptions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We surveyed 1185 US-based adults. Participants rated their likelihood of taking recommended clinical actions (behavioral intentions) across 6 clinical scenarios, where they were randomized to a different recommendation source (doctor, doctor + RC, and doctor + AI). Participants also rated their trust in the recommendation, indicated their preferred source for recommendations, and provided qualitative feedback.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Behavioral intentions differed by recommendation source such that the doctor + RC condition had greater odds of behavioral intention than the doctor + AI condition. Behavioral intentions were also affected by the clinical condition. Participants had greater odds of trusting doctors alone over doctor + RC, and both doctors alone and doctor + RC had greater trust than doctor + AI. However, a plurality of participants ultimately preferred a doctor using an RC for making recommendations. Several sociodemographic differences were detected, namely, participants with higher subjective numeracy and literacy had higher odds of taking clinical action and higher trust across decision-support sources. We detected qualitative themes in the following categories: decision quality and reliability; trust and perceptions; patient-centeredness and autonomy; fairness, transparency, and ethics. Across categories, participants reported skepticism toward all decision sources and potential misunderstanding of AI’s ability to personalize risk predictions. Some participants also stated that they had no additional concerns or were uncertain regarding their feelings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings reveal novel, nuanced patient preferences shaped by task and context, offering guidance for aligning AI-supported care with patient values. Patients were not aligned on the recommendation source across intentions, trust, and preferences. Taken together, our results indicate that patients prefer doctors working with easy-to-understand, explainable support but are still learning to trust these tools. Our findings also highlight the continued importance of the clinical context and its interaction with computer-assisted decision support. Future work should evaluate how we can transparently convey to patients the use of AI in clinical decision-making, embedded within the given clinical context. This may present an opportunity to bolster, rather than erode, patient trust.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Do AI-Based Ensembles Improve Typhoon Inland Extreme Rainfall Prediction through Better Representation of Physical Processes? A Case Study of Typhoon GAEMI (2024)
container-title: Environmental Research Communications
b744c2de93f8684071b917637e5b9be5934472af.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>AI-based ensemble weather prediction is emerging as a new paradigm for probabilistic forecasting, yet its ability to represent the key physical processes that govern high-impact extreme rainfall remains unclear. Here, we compare an AI-based ensemble system (AIFS-CRPS) with a conventional physics-based ensemble (IFS-ENS) in relation to the July 2024 extreme rainfall event in Hunan, China, associated with the remnants of Typhoon GAEMI. Both systems captured the large-scale process chain linking the western Pacific subtropical high (WPSH), remnant-vortex evolution, moisture transport, and inland convergence, but differed in their representation of the steering environment. In this event, AIFS-CRPS members were more concentrated around the rainfall-producing regime, whereas IFS-ENS sampled a broader range of circulation states. These case-specific results illustrate how the organization of large-scale ensemble uncertainty can influence rainfall placement and provide a process-oriented framework for interpreting ensemble forecasts. Broader multi-event evaluation is needed to determine whether this relationship is systematic across high-impact rainfall events.</jats:p>

title: Research on the Teaching Practice of AI Teaching Assistants in C Language Programming Courses
container-title: Journal of Education and Educational Research
7f63b566761c25e282747abfd51e236fa5772e2b.abstract: <jats:p>Under the traditional teaching model, C language programming has long faced practical pain points such as high entry barriers for beginners, delayed feedback on programming practice, insufficient supply of tiered teaching, and excessive teaching burden on frontline teachers. This study, with the core support of the human-machine collaborative education concept, explores the normalized implementation path of deeply embedding AI teaching assistants into the entire process of programming classes, and constructs a ternary collaborative teaching framework of "teacher guidance, AI teaching assistance, and student subjectivity". The study simultaneously sorts out practical issues existing in current AI teaching applications, such as superficial problem-solving, excessive dependence of students on technical tools, and insufficient adaptability to curriculum scenarios, and proposes targeted optimization strategies accordingly. Practice has shown that this teaching model can effectively compensate for the shortcomings of traditional classrooms, providing a practical reference for improving the intelligent teaching quality of computer programming courses in universities.</jats:p>

title: The Impact of AI Assistance on the Academic Writing Self-Efficacy of Undergraduates with Different Writing Abilities
container-title: Journal of Education and Educational Research
1f64a67f212a7b328cb7a8f7b29132196170c4ea.abstract: <jats:p>Against digital education background, generative AI has become common writing assistance for undergraduates. Existing studies mainly focus on second-language writing and ignore stratified comparisons across learners, while the dual effects of AI on academic writing self-efficacy remain understudied. Based on self-efficacy theory, this paper distributes questionnaires and divides respondents into three proficiency groups by CET-4 scores. Descriptive statistics, group difference tests and correlation analysis are adopted for empirical analysis. The results reveal prevalent AI over-dependence despite its polishing functions. Participants’ writing self-efficacy stays at medium-upper level yet hampered by writing anxiety. AI delivers short-term confidence promotion but impairs independent writing competence in the long run, with stronger influences on low-proficiency students. This stratified dual-path framework offers empirical references for standardized AI application in university writing teaching.</jats:p>

title: L’adoption et l’utilisation de l’IA dans l’économie sociale et l’action communautaire
The Adoption and Use of AI in the Social Economy and Community Action
container-title: Canadian Journal of Nonprofit and Social Economy Research
4a97dd034b468d523b6ce16bd683b645570b4068.abstract: <jats:p>Despite AI’s potential to significantly improve how organizations involved in the social economy and community action (ÉSAC, from the French économie sociale et action communautaire) use their limited resources to carry out their important mission, their adoption of AI has been slow because of the constraints they face. This article analyzes the use of AI in Quebec’s ÉSAC sector, which comprises cooperatives, membership organizations, nonprofits, and community action organizations. We conducted 27 semi-structured interviews with three distinct groups of professionals: managers, counsellors, and trainers. Of these participants, 25 work for ÉSAC organizations, and two are external IT trainers who intervened in ÉSAC entities. Drawing on a research framework based on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) adapted to AI, we used thematic analysis to identify the factors influencing the adoption and use of AI within the participating organizations. We grouped the identified factors under the four dimensions of the SWOT strategic analysis tool: strengths and weaknesses within the organization, opportunities for improvement, and potential threats to be mitigated.</jats:p>

title: Exploration of the mechanism by which quorum sensing signals AI-2 and AIP enhance ethanol tolerance of Lacticaseibacillus paracasei 5
container-title: Food Science and Human Wellness
dcc785851cee11e3f907af2e094a4b78d8d567f7.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Lacticaseibacillus paracasei (L. paracasei) plays an indispensable role in food fermentation and probiotic formulations. Nonetheless, its industrial utilization is frequently limited by its low tolerance to ethanol. Given that biofilm formation constitutes a critical survival mechanism for bacteria under stress conditions, this study sought to examine the impact of exogenous autoinducer-2 (AI-2) and autoinducing peptides (AIP) on the biofilm formation of L. paracasei in the presence of ethanol stress. The findings revealed that both AI-2 and AIP substantially enhanced biofilm formation, increased membrane fluidity, and augmented exopolysaccharide (EPS) production under ethanol stress conditions. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed distinct regulatory mechanisms: AI-2 primarily upregulated genes encoding ABC transporters (e.g., potABCD, phnCDE, oppABCDF), which support ATP-driven uptake of compounds essential for cellular homeostasis under ethanol stress. In contrast, AIP mainly activated genes involved in the phosphotransferase system (PTS) (e.g., BglF, MtlA, CelB, CelC), facilitating carbohydrate uptake and central carbon metabolism to meet the biosynthetic demands of EPS and biofilm matrix assembly. This work would provide important insights into the stress adaptation mechanisms mediated by quorum sensing (QS) in L. paracasei 5.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: AI-based Efficient Hallway Attendance Monitoring using Confidence-driven Face Recognition
container-title: Journal of ICT Research and Applications
c4177f8c45cfa79ef662338cf767dfacf467bc1d.abstract: <jats:p>Attendance monitoring deployed at entrance areas offers reliable tracking for institutional environments. We propose an efficient face-recognition-based framework combining YOLOv11-based face detection, motion-based tracking, and FaceNet-based recognition. Our key contribution is a confidence-driven face selection method that collects multiple face images per track and selects the highest-quality image for recognition. Experiments on real-world 60-second hallway footage (1,800 frames at 30 FPS) demonstrated up to 77.7% improvement in processing speed (79.36 FPS vs. 44.66 FPS baseline) while maintaining equivalent recognition accuracy. Collection windows of 5 to 7 images provide optimal balance between latency and throughput (73.67–75.86 FPS), demonstrating that strategic recognition frequency reduction enables real-time attendance monitoring suitable for resource-constrained environments</jats:p>

title: Multi Objective Optimization of Distribution in Supply Chains using Green AI via an Enhanced Hippopotamus Algorithm
container-title: Journal of ICT Research and Applications
d1ed91f0a8ed48bf35917913d418ccb42db0e284.abstract: <jats:p>Modern supply chains require innovative, sustainable, and computationally efficient solutions for physical distribution. This paper proposes the Enhanced Hippo Optimization (EHO) algorithm, a novel, nature-inspired metaheuristic designed to solve the Multi-Objective Vehicle Routing Problem (MO-CVRP). The (EHO) algorithm mathematically models three key hippo herd behaviors: exploration (herd positioning), defensive coordination, and strategic withdrawal, to achieve a dynamic balance between global exploration and local exploitation. By integrating real-world geospatial data from the Google Maps Directions API and customer demand modeling via a Zipf distribution (α = 0.9), (EHO) simultaneously reduces total distance, delivery time, operating costs, and CO2 emissions. The algorithm was evaluated under twenty scenarios across a network of nineteen cities in Egypt, outperforming six advanced algorithms Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), Genetic Algorithm (GA), Ant Colony Optimization (ACO), RUN, Artemisinin Optimizer (AO), and Fata Morgana in eighteen cases. The framework achieved an average reduction of 26.9% in distance and emissions, with total computational runtime ranging from 12.77 to 25.1 seconds depending on the scenario. Visual analyses, including optimized route maps and radar performance charts, confirmed the robustness, scalability, and practical effectiveness of the EHO system in transforming logistics into a driver of economic and environmental sustainability.</jats:p>

title: Embedded Edge Ai-Based Smart Dam and Bridge Structural Health Monitoring with Predictive Flood Analytics and Iot System
container-title: International Research Journal on Advanced Engineering Hub (IRJAEH)
6776e16fbd6ed420e267aa171394b330d702e57f.abstract: <jats:p>Dams and bridges require continuous monitoring to ensure safety and long-term performance, yet conventional inspection relies on periodic manual measurements that can delay the detection of abnormal behavior. This paper presents an embedded Edge AI-based smart dam and bridge structural health monitoring system with predictive flood analytics and IoT connectivity. ESP32-based monitoring units acquire temperature, humidity, rainfall, water level, load, vibration, acceleration, gyroscope, strain and tilt-related parameters from prototype dam and bridge models, while an ESP32-CAM provides live visual surveillance. Feed-forward artificial neural networks developed with TensorFlow/Keras, using 17 input features for the dam and 15 for the bridge with StandardScaler normalization, classify each structure as NORMAL, WARNING or CRITICAL; the dam model is converted to TensorFlow Lite for edge deployment. A Flask backend connects the units to a web dashboard, and critical conditions trigger LED, buzzer and siren alerts, an automated motor/gate response and e-mail notification. Dashboard outputs, logged sensor records and time-wise event analyses from the prototype demonstrate continuous, low-cost and real-time condition assessment that reduces dependence on manual inspection.</jats:p>

title: Who Shapes AI? Technology, Institutions, and Power in the Development of Artificial Intelligence
container-title: Communications in Humanities Research
1c4f3b07d5aa2ed98414c236a298d3ddc1f04493.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is usually mainly explained through technological breakthroughs, such as larger models, improved algorithms, stronger computing power and expanded datasets. This article challenges this interpretation by viewing artificial intelligence as a sociotechnical system whose development and consequences are constantly influenced by social institutions. Based on research of the history of the Internet and human-computer interaction, institutional development, automated responsibility, and algorithmic labor, this paper compares early computing systems with contemporary artificial intelligence. Analysis shows that technical capabilities themselves cannot determine how a technology develops or how it affects society. Governments, universities, companies, markets, legal systems, workers and users all influence the way artificial intelligence is funded, deployed, regulated and understood. Meanwhile, these actors do not have equal power. Cases such as moral collapse zones and algorithmic wage discrimination demonstrate how automation unevenly redistributes responsibility, information and economic benefits. Therefore, this article holds that the future of artificial intelligence is not determined by the technology itself, but rather by the institutional structure and power relations in which the technology is developed and utilized.</jats:p>

title: Technological Empowerment and Subject Integrity: Fostering Originality and Constructing Ethical Norms in AI-Assisted Dance Choreography Pedagogy
container-title: Communications in Humanities Research
a9a5836766437daf6f68a2615600e0b5e72fc463.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is deeply involved in dance choreography, and it has impacted the traditional logic of creation and brought about problems such as the dissolution of student subjectivity, originality problems, and ethical anomie. This study aims to explore how to hold on to creative subjectivity under technological empowerment, to cultivate original ability, and to construct ethical norms. The study uses a method that combines literature review, classroom observation, and action research; it defines the boundaries of concepts, diagnoses the typical problems of AI involvement in teaching, and revises the teaching plan through pilot iteration. The results show that although AI has expanded the boundaries of creation, it has also led to "prompt-first," the homogenization of works, and integrity risks. On this basis, this study proposes three results: first, reconstructing the "three-stage progressive" teaching model and establishing the order of bodily experience first, AI placed later, and reverse verification; second, designing a "four-node" embedded ethics module that covers the key links of the whole creation process; third, building a process-based evaluation system in which the human-machine division of labor is visible, and bringing the personal character of body vocabulary and the critical handling of AI output into scoring. The conclusion holds that the core issue lies in "how to use" rather than "whether to use." Only when technology and the subject constrain each other can compound choreography talents be cultivated. The course system proposed in this paper can provide a promotable model for the "AI+" teaching reform of the dance major.</jats:p>

title: Visualizing Subculture: Symbolism, Storytelling and Media Behavior in AI Videos — A Case Study of The Era of Smart Guardian?
container-title: Communications in Humanities Research
afca65cf7154179463eedcceccee29b83987979e.abstract: <jats:p>In the era of rapid development in the AI industry, AI can accurately answer the meanings and connotations of many concepts, including subcultures. However, some people question whether AI generated videos can fully reflect its understanding of the subcultures being represented. This study examines how subcultural elements are represented in AI-generated advertising videos, using the case study of a Chinese commercial The Era of Smart Guardian. The investigation analyzes from three dimensions, which are visual symbols, storytelling and media behaviors. The advertisement mainly incorporates three subcultural elements: "cyberpunk", "pop art", and "surrealism". The overall research has found that the synergistic effect of these three dimensions forms a phenomenon, which is "hollowed representation", where subcultures retain high visual recognizability, whereas they lost their contextual meaning and critical potential, becoming mere aesthetic commodities for commercial consumption.</jats:p>

title: Ethical Controversies in AI-Driven Risk Control and Content Moderation on Social Platforms—A Case Study of Xiaohongshu
container-title: Communications in Humanities Research
502d8f6c8abdb749dc7baccfccf5ec0e787b02f5.abstract: <jats:p>The use of artificial intelligence (AI) to identify and manage content risks on social platforms is growing. It raises ethical questions about uncertain classifications, proportionate intervention and opportunities to challenge decisions. This paper examines Xiaohongshu through a qualitative documentary case study comprising a technical publication, a regulatory document and three original news reports. The analysis distinguishes source identification, harmfulness assessment and moderation action, and examines the relationship between internal explanations and user-facing remedies. The selected documents separately describe evidence for reviewers, information for audiences and appeal access, leaving their integration unevaluated. This study argues that technical explanations alone do not establish user-facing procedural protection, understandable reasons and accessible correction are also necessary. Source labels can provide transparency without establishing harm, while stronger restrictions require an additional justification appropriate to their consequences. Differentiated review, bounded disclosure and traceable appeals are proposed as design requirements whose effectiveness remains to be evaluated. The contribution emphasizes linking content-safety objectives with user protections in platform governance.</jats:p>

title: Language-Mediated Frenchness: Cultural Representation and Distributed Authorship in Multilingual Generative AI Narratives
container-title: Communications in Humanities Research
834ee9816db2807d8cb65e132202f72ecdbaa428.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence is gradually expanding beyond information retrieval and text-assistance tools into storytelling, literary production, and cultural expression. For multilingual AI, language not only serves an informational function but may also be associated with different training data, forms of cultural knowledge, and narrative conventions. Consequently, the same narrative task may yield cultural expressions that are not entirely identical when generated in different linguistic contexts. Taking "a French child leaving home for the first time" as a common narrative theme, this study compares three stories generated by ChatGPT from equivalent prompts in French, English, and Chinese. Using comparative textual analysis, the three texts are coded across multiple dimensions. The findings show that although the texts share a common narrative structure, they differ markedly in their cultural expressions and representational choices. These linguistic differences should not be interpreted as evidence that language directly determines culture. Rather, language can be understood as a cultural interface and cue that prompts the model to activate different language–culture associations, which in turn shape the characters, spaces, values, and narrative forms of the stories.</jats:p>

title: Teachers’ self-reported AI literacy across educational levels in Greece: Awareness without conceptual depth?
container-title: International Journal of Research Studies in Education
71fccc939e629043e8b58d2572a3d9d8ae16f21d.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is increasingly recognized as an essential teacher competence, yet evidence concerning its dimensional structure and variation across educational sectors remains limited. This study investigated self-reported AI literacy among 1,173 in-service teachers in primary, secondary, and higher education in Greece, examining its empirical structure, overall levels, and associations with prior AI-related training and teaching level, while accounting for academic qualifications. Data were collected through a researcher-developed questionnaire and analyzed using exploratory factor analysis, descriptive statistics, and general linear models. Two dimensions emerged: Conceptual–Technical AI Literacy and Critical–Ethical AI Literacy, while Practical AI Use was retained as a separate indicator. Overall self-reported AI literacy was relatively low, with substantially higher scores on critical–ethical indicators than on conceptual–technical indicators, suggesting a profile of perceived awareness without corresponding conceptual depth. Prior AI-related training was positively associated with all AI-literacy outcomes across educational sectors. However, significant teaching-level × training interactions revealed particularly strong associations in higher education, especially for Conceptual–Technical AI Literacy. These findings highlight the multidimensional and context-sensitive nature of teachers’ self-reported AI literacy and the importance of distinguishing perceived confidence from demonstrated competence. They underscore the need for differentiated, pedagogically grounded professional development that integrates conceptual understanding, practical AI applications, critical evaluation, and ethical judgment across educational sectors.</jats:p>

title: Pemanfaatan Fitur AI Text-to-Image pada Canva untuk Meningkatkan Kreativitas Desain Antarmuka Siswa SMP
container-title: Journal of Authentic Research
a142fac353f2b423b90c767539e9abfe829d594f.abstract:
<jats:p>Kreativitas siswa dalam merancang antarmuka digital dapat terhambat ketika pembelajaran terlalu bergantung pada template siap pakai. Penelitian ini bertujuan membandingkan kreativitas desain antarmuka siswa yang belajar dengan fitur AI Text-to-Image pada Canva dan siswa yang menggunakan fitur standar Canva, mengukur peningkatan kreativitas, serta menjelaskan pengalaman siswa selama ko-kreasi dengan AI. Penelitian menggunakan metode campuran dengan desain sekuensial eksplanatori. Tahap kuantitatif menerapkan kuasi-eksperimen nonequivalent control group pada 61 siswa kelas VIII SMP Negeri 2 Sijunjung, terdiri atas 30 siswa kelompok eksperimen dan 31 siswa kelompok kontrol. Kreativitas dinilai melalui tes unjuk kerja berdasarkan kelancaran, keluwesan, orisinalitas, dan elaborasi; tahap kualitatif menggunakan wawancara reflektif terhadap enam siswa kelompok eksperimen. Analisis tanpa penyesuaian skor awal menunjukkan rata-rata posttest kelompok eksperimen (12,80) lebih tinggi daripada kelompok kontrol (9,20), t(59) = 8,712, p < 0,001, Cohen’s d = 2,23, 95% CI [1,58, 2,87]. Secara deskriptif, N-Gain kelompok eksperimen sebesar 0,66 dan kelompok kontrol 0,29, dengan selisih indikator terbesar pada orisinalitas. Wawancara menunjukkan bahwa siswa terbantu memunculkan ide visual, merevisi prompt secara iteratif, dan merefleksikan tanggung jawab etis. Temuan ini menunjukkan hasil yang menjanjikan bagi integrasi AI Text-to-Image melalui prompt engineering terstruktur, tetapi interpretasi kausal perlu dibatasi karena penugasan kelas tidak dilakukan secara acak.
Students’ creativity in digital interface design can be constrained when learning relies heavily on ready-made templates. This study compared interface-design creativity between students learning with Canva’s AI Text-to-Image feature and those using standard Canva features, quantified improvement, and explored students’ experiences during human–AI co-creation. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed. The quantitative phase used a nonequivalent control group quasi-experiment involving 61 eighth-grade students at SMP Negeri 2 Sijunjung, with 30 students in the experimental group and 31 in the control group. Creativity was assessed through a performance task covering fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration; the qualitative phase used reflective interviews with six experimental-group students. The unadjusted posttest comparison showed a higher mean for the experimental group (12.80) than the control group (9.20), t(59) = 8.712, p < .001, Cohen’s d = 2.23, 95% CI [1.58, 2.87]. Descriptively, normalized gain was 0.66 in the experimental group and 0.29 in the control group, with the largest indicator-level difference in originality. Interviews indicated that students generated visual ideas more easily, revised prompts iteratively, and reflected on ethical responsibility. These findings suggest promising educational value for structured prompt-engineering activities with text-to-image AI, while causal claims should remain cautious because class assignment was nonrandom.
 </jats:p>

A multi-database search was conducted to locate 846 records, and 17 primary studies yielding 36 effect sizes were included in this meta-analysis after deduplication, screening and full-text eligibility assessment. Aggregated results show that AI use has a large average impact on English learner engagement (

title: Democratizing Optimization with Generative AI
container-title: Operations Research
1fc4ae59952488eb9cfb8a74999dcdf8dc183494.abstract: <jats:p>Recent breakthroughs in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have captured the public imagination, whereas mathematical optimization remains little recognized beyond specialists. In this article, we argue that GenAI can bridge the persistent gap between optimization's technical capabilities and its limited real-world uptake. We present the 4I framework (Insight, Interpretability, Interactivity, Improvisation) as a set of design principles for combining GenAI with mathematical optimization. Insight establishes a trusted, up-to-date view of current operations; Interpretability explains model logic and trade-offs; Interactivity enables conversational what-if analysis; Improvisation supports model updates and event-driven re-optimization. By making optimization tools more intuitive, explainable, interactive, and adaptable, we envision a future in which frontline decision-makers can base their choices on rigorous, iterative analysis. We discuss how GenAI complements, rather than replaces, optimization: GenAI lowers barriers to modeling and interpretation; mathematical optimization reliably enforces the business goals, rules, and hard constraints encoded in the model. We also address emerging concerns, from hallucinations to the risk of over-reliance, and outline research directions for integrating GenAI and optimization responsibly. The GenAI boom gives the optimization community an opportunity to expand its impact by making optimization more accessible and trustworthy to a wider audience.</jats:p>

title: Beyond Explainability: User Agency, Operational Control, and Interaction Design in Human–AI Systems: A  Critical Narrative Review
container-title: Journal of Engineering Research and Reports
be7baafb58e5696d5f879329c16067f56bae5685.abstract: <jats:p>Human–artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly influence decisions, workflows and creative production, yet the presence of explanations or a nominal human approval step does not establish that people can direct, question or meaningfully correct an AI-mediated outcome. This critical narrative review examines how user agency is constituted, constrained and evaluated through the interaction design of contemporary human–AI systems. A targeted, multidisciplinary examination of peer-reviewed research published from 1999 to 24 August 2026, supplemented by earlier foundational work where conceptually necessary, integrates human–computer interaction, automation psychology, decision science, organisational research and sociotechnical governance. The synthesis distinguishes explanation, comprehension, calibrated reliance, operational control and contestability rather than treating them as interchangeable manifestations of human-centred design. Experimental studies show that explanations may improve performance where their claims can be checked against task evidence, but may also amplify misplaced reliance, impose cognitive demands or fail to improve complementary human–AI performance. Studies of mixed-initiative interfaces, adjustable recommendations and co-creative tools demonstrate that users' opportunities to select, revise, refuse and renegotiate AI contributions are consequential, while perceived ownership or nominal choice does not necessarily entail consequential authority. Research in clinical, organisational and public-decision settings further indicates that time constraints, institutional rules and unequal access to appeals can determine whether interface controls are usable in practice. An integrative, explicitly provisional framework is advanced in which agency depends jointly on information, feasible action, consequential feedback, accountable recourse and distributional accessibility. The most pressing research needs concern longitudinal, ecologically valid and comparative evaluation of effective override, decision quality, learning, procedural fairness and unintended burdens. Explainability remains useful, but should be assessed as one component within a broader architecture of meaningful participation and control rather than as its proxy.</jats:p>

title: AI-Based Sign Language Recognition and Translation System
container-title: International Journal of Scientific Research in Engineering & Technology
20be4a02183dfedc7169ef8517386207f13bbb5b.abstract: <jats:p>The AI-Based Sign Language Recognition and Translation System is a computer vision-based application designed to facilitate communication between individuals with hearing and speech impairments and people who do not understand sign language. The system captures hand gestures through a webcam and uses OpenCV and MediaPipe to extract hand landmarks for gesture recognition. A machine learning model processes the extracted features to identify corresponding English alphabet signs and display the recognized letters as text through a Streamlit-based user interface. The system supports both single-hand and two-hand gesture recognition based on the trained datasets. Text-to-speech technology is used to convert recognized text into audible speech, while speech recognition enables spoken input to be converted into text for reverse communication. The system also incorporates multilingual translation and an Emergency Mode to support communication in different situations. Python serves as the primary programming language, while OpenCV, MediaPipe, NumPy, and Joblib support image processing, landmark extraction, and model prediction. The proposed system aims to reduce communication barriers and provide an accessible platform for sign language-based interaction. However, recognition performance depends on lighting conditions, camera quality, hand positioning, and variations in gestures. Further testing with diverse users and real-world conditions is required to evaluate the system's generalization and reliability.</jats:p>

title: Role Radar: An AI-Based Resume Intelligence and Skill Gap Analysis System
container-title: International Journal of Scientific Research in Engineering & Technology
9d2e83fdca6d967c999174c04ac4bc9c28b0e577.abstract: <jats:p>Job seekers face two linked problems: finding postings that are genuinely open and suitable, and presenting their experience to automated screening without exaggeration. General-purpose language-model resume writers aggravate the second problem because they can invent skills, metrics, and seniority. This paper presents RoleRadar, a full-stack career platform built on one rule: deterministic code decides what is true, and the language model only rephrases it. A geometry-based parser turns an uploaded resume into atomic, provenance-tagged evidence units. Job requirements are mapped to that evidence on an eight-level support scale, and a category-aware six-factor model yields an explainable match score and a readiness verdict. A rule-based Truth Guard compares every tailored bullet with its source and reverts fabricated technologies, unsupported metrics, inflated titles, and broken sentences before one-page export. Supporting modules provide a taxonomy of 119 roles, prerequisite-ordered learning roadmaps, verified job ingestion from direct employer feeds, and an assistant restricted to the signed-in user’s data. A regression suite of 1,268 test cases, internal validation harnesses, and an end-to-end acceptance run indicate that the pipeline is consistent and auditable. The system has not yet been evaluated with recruiters or in a controlled user study.</jats:p>

title: Anti-Money Laundering Tracker Using Graph-AI
container-title: International Journal of Scientific Research in Engineering & Technology
1506097a26b2241025df874d902c5af1ea7f89d4.abstract: <jats:p>Money laundering schemes can involve transfers through several connected accounts, so suspicious activity may be difficult to recognize by examining each transaction separately. This paper presents an Anti-Money Laundering (AML) Tracker that combines graph-pattern analysis with graph representation and machine-learning methods to support the examination of potentially suspicious transaction networks. Accounts are represented as nodes and transfers as directed relationships in Neo4j. The project uses the IBM AMLSim synthetic dataset, with approximately 9,945 accounts and 68,289 transactions reported in the project materials. Following data validation and preprocessing, account and transaction records are loaded into the graph database. Cypher queries are used to explore circular transfers, layering-like chains, fan-in and fan-out structures, and multi-hop paths. The described graph-AI pipeline includes FastRP embeddings, Random Forest classification, and GraphSAGE-based neighbourhood learning. Graph visualization helps users inspect connected accounts and candidate suspicious paths. The functional checks documented for the project show that selected graph operations and pattern queries produced their expected outputs. These checks do not demonstrate predictive accuracy; no verified numerical model-evaluation results are available for reporting. The system is intended to assist investigators, not to determine criminal activity automatically. Future evaluation should document model settings, use held-out data, measure false positives, and assess whether findings from synthetic data generalize to real financial transactions.</jats:p>

title: AI-Based Cyber Threat Detection System: A Hybrid Machine Learning and AI Reasoning Approach for Real-Time Malicious URL Detection
container-title: International Journal of Scientific Research in Engineering & Technology
52cc922520941e3a05826897eb100f7e62c117f4.abstract: <jats:p>Phishing and malicious URLs remain a common cybersecurity problem because attackers can create new links faster than static blocklists can be updated. This paper presents CyberShield, a real-time URL detection system that combines a calibrated machine-learning ensemble with a separate AI reasoning layer. Random Forest and XGBoost use 11 structural URL features to produce a confidence score. For URLs that are not covered by the trusted-domain whitelist, Google Gemini provides an additional assessment and a plain-English explanation. The system is integrated with a Chrome extension, a FastAPI backend, a React dashboard, email alerts, and a human-reviewed learning process. The evaluated dataset contains 641,119 URLs and is divided into training, calibration, and test subsets. On the held-out test set, the ML ensemble achieved 94.32% accuracy, 91.45% precision, 91.47% recall, a 91.46% F1-score, and a 98.46% AUC-ROC. These metrics describe the ML ensemble, not a separate quantitative evaluation of the complete Gemini-assisted application. Functional tests also checked URL scanning, warning display, and fallback to ML results when the AI service was unavailable. The results show the potential of combining URL-based machine learning with AI explanations, although broader end-to-end testing is needed.</jats:p>

title: AI-Based Image Forgery Detection System Using EfficientNet-B0 and Grad-CAM Explanations with a Web-Based Interface
container-title: International Journal of Scientific Research in Engineering & Technology
1237433e1f0163fe9aa538dd8cfe03c5ba8cb50f.abstract: <jats:p>Digital photographs are now routinely used as evidence in news reporting, courts, insurance claims and identity checks, yet inexpensive editing software and generative models make it easy to alter them without visible traces. Manual inspection by experts does not scale, and many classical detectors fail once an image has been recompressed or resized. This paper presents the design and prototype implementation of an AI-based image forgery detection system that labels an uploaded picture as genuine or forged, reports a confidence value, and shows a Grad-CAM heat map of the regions that most influenced the decision. The system couples a Streamlit front end with a Flask back-end service. Uploaded images are resized to 224×224 pixels, smoothed with a Gaussian filter (σ = 0.5), normalised in the manner expected by EfficientNet, and passed to an EfficientNet-B0 classifier. A history page and a downloadable PDF report are provided for registered users. The prototype was exercised on sample inputs, and the captured screens show end-to-end operation, including a low-margin decision (56.43 % confidence) whose Grad-CAM map illustrates why a confidence score alone is not sufficient for forensic use. A quantitative evaluation protocol on public tampering benchmarks is specified as the next phase of the work.</jats:p>

title: Consumer Agency and Decision Quality in AI-Assisted Augmented-Reality Commerce
container-title: Journal of Theoretical and Applied Electronic Commerce Research
be2ca1c2f326c95be83b53b34cb37d0e9405df66.abstract: <jats:p>AI assistance and augmented reality (AR) can make shopping easier without necessarily improving the resulting decision. This conceptual article develops a model of when consumers can inspect, redirect, or reject assistance and when those opportunities may fail. A targeted literature synthesis connects marketing research on autonomy and algorithm overdependence with human–AI reliance studies. The model separates effective decision authority from perceived agency, and distinguishes confidence in advice before acceptance from confidence in the final choice. Three central predictions concern cosmetic controls, checking versus delegation, and persuasive presentation that encourages reliance on inferior advice. Shopping-specific extensions examine whether corrected requirements propagate across a product shortlist, conversation, and AR display, and whether repeated claims from one source are mistaken for independent verification. Decision quality is evaluated only where independent product facts and defensible preference benchmarks permit comparison with an initial unaided choice. A staged preference-review protocol identifies ambiguous cases rather than assigning them arbitrary correctness labels. The evidence table records access depth, and the research agenda specifies results that would count against the central predictions. Practical and governance implications are proposals to evaluate. The model is unvalidated and makes no claim to demonstrate consumer-welfare effects.</jats:p>

title: Legal protection of Omani folklore (popular heritage) in the AI-driven virtual world: Preserving identity
container-title: International Journal of Law Research and Studies
efdf3c33f6b77ca94e9affc3cece4779b06b916b.abstract: <jats:p>Folklore and intangible cultural heritage reflect the folk traditions and identity of a specific society. States intervene to protect such heritage—both domestically and internationally—a practice adopted by the Sultanate of Oman through various legislative frameworks. These include laws concerning copyright and related rights, regulations governing cultural heritage, and penal provisions. Such heritage is considered state-owned intangible property; its distortion or commercial exploitation without official authorization from the competent authorities is prohibited and subject to specific legal penalties and enforcement measures. This study underscores the significance of cultural heritage and its intrinsic link to national identity, while highlighting the need to address legal gaps in intellectual property protection to keep pace with digital transformation and support the digital cultural economy. The study aims to identify the digital risks posed to folklore in the virtual realm—exacerbated by the widespread use of artificial intelligence—and to evaluate the adequacy of existing laws in addressing challenges related to digital platforms and AI. Ultimately, it seeks to propose legal and technical solutions that safeguard heritage and preserve identity by integrating digitalization and modern technologies, all in alignment with the "Oman Vision 2040."</jats:p>

title: Known by the Machine: Building Relational Presence with AI NPCs for Stigma-Free Mental Health Literacy in Games
container-title: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
4c9c9964378a64482a43967764b54ff15bb6fa76.abstract: <jats:p>Mental Health (MH) remains a global priority, yet low literacy and stigma frequently limit open discussion and help-seeking behaviors. While game-based education has shown promise in supporting stigma reduction and literacy improvement, the potential for Large Language Models (LLMs) to support non-judgmental, playful exploration of sensitive topics remains underexplored, specifically, the role of conversational memory to support trust-building in MH discussions. We conducted a four-session, longitudinal mixed-methods study to evaluate how the relational presence of AI characters, powered by GPT-4o-mini with varied memory designs, relates to player experience and learning. Moving beyond an evaluation of learning, we examine how the perception of being known by an AI NPC is associated with engagement with stigmatized content. Results indicate that while participants achieved significant and sustained gains in Mental Health Literacy (MHL), these improvements did not differ by memory condition. Instead, memory appeared to operate as a relational design feature that shaped participants’ perceptions of social presence, with many describing conversational NPCs as supportive companions. We also identify interactional risks, such as algorithmic vagueness and privacy-induced hesitation, that participants described as reducing their comfort during conversations. We conclude by offering design recommendations for leveraging LLM memory to create more relational and stigma-sensitive environments for MH education.</jats:p>

title: Guards & Wards: The Creative Labour of GMs and Considerations for Designing with AI
container-title: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
97f59e27090381539a8186baf42b7de0cca1bb39.abstract: <jats:p>Tabletop role-playing games (TTRPGs) provide a complicated environment for creativity. Game masters (GMs) co-create a story along with their players and many choose to complete significant labour both prior to and during a gaming session. However, the boundaries that GMs may have about generative artificial intelligence (AI) being used in this creative hobby have not been examined. We examine the perceptions of GMs on the use of AI for creativity support in TTRPGs. We conducted a survey of GMs to discover the labour they completed in preparation for and play of TTRPG sessions, the existing creativity support tools (CSTs) that they use for this labour, and their opinions on the use of AI in TTRPGs. We performed both qualitative and quantitative analysis to examine survey data. We contrasted our results across two participant groups: those who have or have not been paid to GM a gaming session, and those who have or have not used AI as GMs. From our data, we created twelve distinct orientation groups encompassing the opinions of participants on AI for use in TTRPGs. We propose thirteen design considerations in the form of questions AI tool developers should ask when creating AI-based CSTs for TTRPG use.</jats:p>

title: Age Matters: Age-Differentiated Playtesting for AI Educational Games
container-title: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
51c2ffec725312491c89a2f2140899598712ae8b.abstract: <jats:p>Playtesting is widely employed in educational game design as a post-hoc method for game design validation within the age groups that the learning goals target. For domains such as AI literacy, age-targeted educational games testing may be limiting, as AI learning goals are relevant and frequently misunderstood by children, adolescents and young adults. Designing educational games that teach AI to a wider audience of ages requires playtesting with players of different ages to better interpret gameplay and narrative appropriateness of AI in AI educational games. In this study, we playtested four AI educational games with middle, high school, and college aged students, and analyzed playtesting data, including verbal discourse, in-game behaviors, and post-playtesting reflections. Our findings demonstrate that playtesting can serve as an asset-based practice which reveals how players of different age groups make sense of educational games during play. We provide critical reflections from multi-age playtesting of AI educational games that inform design, and recommendations for engaging AI educational game design.</jats:p>

title: Does Trust Spill Over?: Exploring Asymmetric Trust Dynamics Between Teammate AI and Guide AI in Cooperative Games
container-title: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
aa082ec48f7a3ea66734c5c6aa6b23a8c21c5b8a.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Cooperative games increasingly feature multiple AI agents serving distinct roles, yet how players form and transfer trust across such agents remains unclear. We investigated trust spillover between a task-executing Teammate AI and an advisory Guide AI in a web-based cooperative cooking game (within-subjects, N = 23). Teammate AI ability (high vs. low) and Guide AI accuracy (high vs. low/absent) were experimentally manipulated. Results revealed a directional asymmetry in trust spillover. Teammate AI ability significantly influenced trust in the Guide AI (
                    <jats:inline-formula content-type="math/tex">
                      <jats:tex-math notation="LaTeX" version="MathJax">\(\eta _p^2 =.220\)</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ), whereas Guide AI accuracy and presence had no effect on trust in the Teammate AI (
                    <jats:inline-formula content-type="math/tex">
                      <jats:tex-math notation="LaTeX" version="MathJax">\(\eta _p^2 =.002\)</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ). This suggests that, under cognitive constraints, trust propagates from high-salience task agents to lower-salience advisory agents, but not vice versa. Additionally, the presence of the Guide AI improved performance and perceived control independent of advice accuracy, suggesting an attentional cueing effect. Finally, congruent agent quality levels enhanced perceived relatedness, highlighting the importance of system-level coherence. These findings demonstrate asymmetric trust spillover in cooperative games with role-differentiated AI, where execution-focused agents anchor system-wide trust formation, with implications for multi-agent AI systems in which agents serve distinct functional roles.
                  </jats:p>

title: Player Perceptions of Generative AI in Games: A Steam Review Analysis
container-title: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
08911279f04c0994a25c0ab11145fcff09c60790.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid adoption of generative AI in game development has created large discussions among players, yet little empirical work has examined how players actually perceive AI-generated content. Employing quantitative methods, we study the adoption of generative AI in games in the Steam marketplace, using procedural content generation (PCG) as a baseline of a generative technology that was successfully integrated into games over several decades. Furthermore, using qualitative methods, we study player reception of generative AI by analyzing 508,192 English-language reviews. We found that games disclosing generative AI use receive lower recommendation rates and more negative overall sentiment than PCG games. Thematic analysis of 600 reviews shows that players perceive the use of generative AI in games as low developer investment in the game. Drawing on human-centered AI frameworks, we argue that successful generative AI adoption requires deploying generative AI for what players need, not for what makes development cheaper.</jats:p>
