title: GROUND: An Actionable Model for Overcoming Challenges in Grounded Theory
container-title: American Journal of Qualitative Research
a123b5fff08ae65d3fc25b5cd84710409f30dc25.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en"><i>Grounded Theory (GT) is widely used in Information Systems (IS) research, yet there are many challenges in following the methodology, particularly for novice researchers. While prior work has extensively described challenges, concrete and practice-oriented solutions remain underdeveloped. This study addresses this gap by conducting a structured literature review and an in-depth qualitative analysis of two empirical GT projects that encountered significant methodological difficulties. Using a combined approach of Directed and Conventional Content Analysis, we identified eight interrelated themes spanning the phases of open coding, axial coding, and selective coding. For each theme, we developed problem–solution pairings to address issues such as: navigating large volumes of collected data, transitioning from specific details to abstract concepts, interpreting qualitative data, relating categories to construct logical theoretical explanations, determining when categories are sufficiently related, finding an appropriate generalization level, coaching and guiding single GT researchers, and choosing a GT approach These themes are integrated into a coherent model, MAPS, that reveals their causal relationships. Our study provides micro-level methodological guidance for GT practice and complements existing GT literature by offering empirically grounded and actionable solutions rather than high-level principles.</i></jats:p>

title: Craniofacial Education in Accredited Graduate Speech-Language Pathology Programs: National Patterns in Coursework and Clinical Training
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
bc0e92d0c5aff0bf24744b6e8155547207dce3c8.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study provides an updated national examination of craniofacial education across accredited graduate speech-language pathology programs in the United States.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A survey was distributed to 289 accredited graduate speech-language pathology programs. Ninety-nine programs completed all or part of the survey. Publicly available curricular materials were reviewed for nonresponding programs, and brief follow-up correspondence was conducted when necessary. The final data set included 281 programs. Data were analyzed descriptively to characterize coursework structure and clinical training opportunities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among the 281 programs analyzed, 19.9% offered a dedicated and required craniofacial course and 11.4% offered a dedicated elective course. The majority of programs (68.7%) reported covering craniofacial content exclusively through embedded instruction. Sixty-three percent of programs reported offering clinical experiences involving individuals with craniofacial conditions, although most indicated that fewer than 25% of students engaged in these experiences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although craniofacial content remains present within graduate curricula, dedicated coursework and consistent clinical exposure are limited. These findings extend previous national reports and highlight continued variability in specialty preparation within graduate speech-language pathology programs. Ongoing examination of curricular structures is warranted to better understand factors influencing preparation in this specialty area.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Screening Beyond First Words: A Scoping Review of Speech and Language Screening Tools and Approaches for 2- and 3-Year-Olds
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
323c47a85fce4b4d8e150b65993400e68ec2d2c8.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The task of being able to accurately and efficiently identify children in the early years at risk of future speech sound and/or language disorders remains elusive. To progress toward more accurate identification, the breadth of skills examined in current screening tools and approaches needs to be determined. Our purpose was to (a) understand the key characteristics of screening tools and approaches for children aged 2–3 years, (b) determine the psychometric quality of screening tools and approaches, and (c) identify the early years health and education professionals who screen toddlers' speech and language skills.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A scoping review was conducted following Arksey and O'Malley's (2005) methodological framework and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension guidelines. A systematic search of the literature was conducted, and the data were described through data extraction, quality appraisal, percentage and frequency counts, and a narrative synthesis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There were 101 studies that met the inclusion criteria, with screening more commonly occurring with 2-year-olds. Of the 114 unique tools and approaches identified, most screened expressive language, particularly vocabulary and/or word combinations. When speech skills were screened, intelligibility was the primary skill examined. Across these tools, indirect measures were most common. There was low reporting on the psychometric quality of tools and the professional completing the screening, which impacted the conclusions that could be drawn.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This review highlights the diversity of tools available for screening speech and/or language development between the ages of 2;0 and 3;11 (years; months), as well as the need to consider the child's age at the time of administration and the content of the tools being used when screening beyond first words.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: ND-LDM: An enhanced latent diffusion model for data augmentation in industrial surface defect detection
container-title: Measurement Science and Technology
78c4ba38df472e3443a371634108d4c2f23ada18.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>To address the common bottleneck of insufficient labeled samples and class imbalance that restricts the measurement accuracy and robustness of industrial visual surface inspection systems, this paper focuses on the bearing surface defect detection scenario and proposes an enhanced latent diffusion model (LDM)-based data augmentation method termed ND-LDM. ND-LDM introduces three complementary components: an Adaptive Min-SNR weighting strategy for balancing optimization across diffusion timesteps, a Spatial-Frequency Gated Fusion module for joint spatial-frequency feature modeling, and a Solver-Aware Adaptive Guidance mechanism for dynamically regulating conditional guidance during sampling. Experiments on a real industrial bearing defect dataset show that ND-LDM achieves an Fréchet Inception Distance of 87.6 and an structural similarity index measure of 0.6829, outperforming the evaluated Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model and LDM baselines. Component and subcomponent ablations confirm the contribution of each design. When ND-LDM-generated samples are added to the RT-DETR training set, mAP(50) increases from 0.948 ± 0.003–0.957 ± 0.001, mAP(50:95) from 0.594 ± 0.004–0.595 ± 0.008, and Recall from 0.922 ± 0.015–0.939 ± 0.003, with larger gains for minority defect categories. These results demonstrate that ND-LDM can generate high-fidelity defect samples with reliable metrological consistency, which effectively improves the detection and measurement performance of downstream visual models under limited-data conditions. The proposed framework provides a generalizable data augmentation solution for small-sample industrial visual measurement tasks and has broad application prospects in surface quality metrology.</jats:p>

title: <b>Analysis of Sociology Literature on the  Novel “5 cm”Written by Dhonny Dhirgantoro</b>
container-title: Journal of Literature Language and Academic Studies
ede575223a4d88dd992dc292f7cb6341b0d64037.abstract:
<jats:p>Purpose – This study aims to describe the theory of sociology of literature, focusing on the mimetic approach in Donny Dhirgantoro’s novel 5 cm, as well as the relationship between the author and his work. 
Methodology – This study employs a qualitative method. The aspects analyzed are the sociological aspects represented in the novel “5 cm” through a mimetic approach. The data include characterizations, social status, attitudes toward life, daily behavior of the characters, and events. 
Findings – The main character in the novel is Genta, with Arial, Zafran, Riani, and Ian as additional characters. The social status depicted in the novel is influenced by economic, cultural, and psychological factors. The attitudes toward life represented in the novel include affection among fellow human beings, affection between parents and children, and responsibility between individuals. 
Novelty – The novelty of this study lies in examining the sociological aspects of “5 cm” through a mimetic approach by connecting characterizations, social status, attitudes toward life, daily behavior, and events with the relationship between the author and his work.
Significance – This study contributes to the understanding of sociology of literature by showing how social realities and human attitudes are represented through the characters and events in “5 cm”.
 </jats:p>

title: Macroeconomic Planning
container-title: Planned Economies
f624e4109f30acccb5ec0ab04ed872c55840d968.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter analyzes a macroeconomic planning model and its critiques. The core of the model is the “Soviet model” prepared by Feldman. Mahalanobis provided the algebraic proof of Feldman’s hypothesis. This chapter also discusses the evolution of the macroeconomic planning model from Leotief’s model to the optimal control model applied in the Soviet Union and India. The industrialization strategy articulated by Mahalanobis remained influential in India until at least 1992. The frameworks established by Feldman in 1928 and Mahalanobis in 1952 were fundamentally informed by the theoretical underpinnings proposed by Marx and Engels. Their seminal works, notably The Reproduction Scheme and The Expanded Reproduction Scheme, constitute essential components for the formulation of a national economic strategy. This chapter analyzes these issues in a systematic way and suggests a planning model.</jats:p>

title: Macroeconomic Development Strategy
container-title: Planned Economies
e6daff364ec6dad254d94758dc25cbd02f5920b4.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter analyses various aspects of the Feldman-Mahalanobis model and its critiques. The Feldman-Mahalanobis model represented an alternative approach to the Harrod-Domar model of economic planning. Mahalanobis’s strategy for economic development evolved from a two-sector model, to a four-sector model, and, finally, to a multisectoral model. Mahalanobis underscored the importance of self-sufficiency, advocating for an economic framework that would gradually diminish its dependence on foreign machinery and equipment. This vision had materialized by 2025, when India evolved from a country reliant on machinery imports to one that exports considerable volumes of capital goods and foreign machinery, all generated through its indigenous manufacturing capabilities. The World Bank and proponents of neoliberal economics have consistently critiqued Mahalanobis’s model for its perceived pessimism regarding export potential and its disregard for the trade opportunities that East Asian nations embraced, but they disregarded the international political context wherein the combined West was against the industrial development of India.</jats:p>

title: What Temperament Can Tell Us About Language Development of Late-Talking Toddlers
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
63201448ae6a4db1089944a0f1b1c73797d901df.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The primary aim of this study was to compare temperamental traits in typically developing and late-talking toddlers. A secondary aim was to evaluate potential associations between language skills and temperament within each group.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Caregivers of typically developing (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                      = 21) and late-talking (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                      = 21) toddlers, aged 18–35 months, completed a brief measure of temperament (Early Childhood Behavior Questionnaire–Very Short Form) and expressive vocabulary (MacArthur–Bates Communicative Development Inventories: Words and Sentences). Toddlers' expressive and receptive language skills were also directly assessed using the Mullen Scales of Early Learning.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There were no significant group differences on the temperament measurement between general constructs; however, late talkers showed lower levels of sensory discomfort and positive anticipation compared to typical talkers. Associations between language and temperament differed between groups. For typical talkers, larger vocabularies were associated with higher levels of positive emotions and sociability. For late talkers, larger vocabularies were related to higher levels of attention and inhibitory control. Moreover, better developed receptive language in late talkers was associated with greater levels of negative emotion.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although only subtle differences were observed on temperament features, the divergent patterns of association between specific temperamental traits and language features between groups suggest unique ways in which temperament and language acquisition may interact in late talkers.</jats:p>

title: The Relationship Between Dynamic Assessment of Analogical Reasoning and Syntax in French-Speaking Children With and Without Developmental Language Disorder

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>According to usage-based theories of language development, typically developing (TD) children rely on analogical reasoning (AR) to learn syntactic structures. However, children with developmental language disorder (DLD) demonstrate difficulties in AR, which could contribute to explaining their difficulties in acquiring syntactic structures. While previous studies have reported no link between nonverbal AR and syntax using static assessment, we shifted focus onto dynamic assessment to explore the relationship between these two domains' learning potential in a French-speaking population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Ninety-seven TD children (25 bilingual) and 98 children with DLD (40 bilingual;
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">M</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>age</jats:sub>
                      = 8;8 [years;months]) were assessed by using (a) a static task of AR; (b) a static task of syntax; (c) a dynamic task of AR, with prompts assisting the learner to analyze the analogy required to complete the matrix; and (d) a dynamic task of syntax targeting six structures, with prompts based on syntactic priming.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Children with DLD scored lower than TD children on all our measures, except when considering the progression within the dynamic task of AR, where children improved similarly.
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Static</jats:italic>
                      syntactic skills were not linked to AR ones, unlike
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">dynamic</jats:italic>
                      syntactic skills that were predicted by AR, mainly in children with DLD. Only the production of the most complex syntactic structure was marginally impacted by AR in TD children.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Higher learning potential in AR predicts higher learning potential in syntax in children with DLD. Therefore, more preserved skills in AR could predict less severe difficulties in syntax in this population. These results could guide the design of future language interventions.</jats:p>

title: Resilience Through Language, Culture, and Community: A Qualitative Study of Multilingual and Multicultural Families
container-title: American Journal of Qualitative Research
6362416c59d28a6e9dc25c5239f91911c24dd31b.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en"><i>The purpose of this study was to explore how multilingual and multicultural immigrant families draw upon their cultural and linguistic assets to navigate challenges and foster resilience during the adaptation process. Using a strengths-based framework, a secondary qualitative analysis was conducted using narrative interview data from 15 multilingual immigrant mothers participating in a statewide early childhood evaluation. Data were analyzed using an inductive thematic analysis approach to examine how resilience emerged through participants’ lived experiences. Findings show how families used cultural practices, heritage language, and community engagement as tools for coping and adaptation. Three main themes of resilience were identified: (1) language as a link to cultural heritage, (2) cultural traditions as anchors of identity, and (3) community participation as access to social support and belonging. Results demonstrate that resilience operates as an everyday, culturally grounded process shaped through relational and community practices. These findings extend existing understandings of immigrant family resilience by highlighting how multiple forms of cultural wealth work together to support well-being. Implications for educational practice and policy include the importance of recognizing and supporting families’ cultural and linguistic assets.</i></jats:p>

title: A TOE–RBV–TBL Integrated Model of AI-Enabled Sustainable Food Logistics
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Food Logistics and Supply Chains
40d1fa5cdd6cd6c42b1d66704eea0c7b9caed768.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping food logistics by enhancing operational efficiency, reducing waste, and promoting sustainable supply chain practices. This study develops and validates an integrated Technology–Organisation–Environment (TOE), Resource-Based View (RBV), and Triple Bottom Line (TBL) framework to examine the determinants and outcomes of AI-enabled sustainable food logistics. Primary data were collected from 312 professionals in India's food supply chain and analysed using CB-SEM. The findings reveal that technological readiness, organisational capability, and environmental pressure significantly drive AI adoption, while AI capability positively influences environmental, economic, and social sustainability. The study offers a comprehensive theoretical framework and practical insights for policymakers and industry stakeholders seeking to build resilient, intelligent, and sustainable food supply chains.</jats:p>

title: Feasibility and Efficacy of a Hybrid Delivery Model of the Categorization Program for Individuals With Chronic Traumatic Brain Injury: A Pilot Study
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
10972d53bd51de47d10dc7556cbb4784b092c980.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The present study examined the feasibility and preliminary efficacy of a hybrid, telehealth-adapted delivery of the Categorization Program (CP), an evidence-based cognitive rehabilitation intervention, for adults with chronic moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury (msTBI) who were living in the community and not engaged in ongoing rehabilitation services. It was hypothesized that the telehealth-adapted CP would demonstrate high feasibility and lead to improvements in intervention-specific and standardized neuropsychological outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study employed a single-group, pre–post intervention design with follow-up assessments. Adults aged 18–65 years with msTBI sustained at least 1 year prior to enrollment were recruited from hospital and rehabilitation center databases. Participants completed a baseline neuropsychological assessment, followed by the eight-level, hierarchically structured CP intervention delivered primarily via telehealth. Neuropsychological measures were administered pre-intervention and post-intervention, while CP-specific measures were administered pre-intervention and post-intervention and at 4- and 8-week follow-ups. Feasibility was evaluated through recruitment, adherence, retention, and acceptability metrics. Effectiveness was measured by changes in cognitive performance using nonparametric Wilcoxon signed-ranks tests.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of 82 individuals screened, 21 enrolled, and 16 (76.2%) completed the full intervention. Retention rates for CP-specific assessments were 93.8% post-intervention, 68.8% at 4 weeks, and 75.0% at 8 weeks. Participants reported functional improvements, particularly in orientation, memory strategy use, and independence. Significant improvements were observed on CP-specific outcome measures and on certain neuropsychological outcomes. Gains were maintained at follow-up among participants.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings provide preliminary evidence that a telehealth-adapted CP is feasible, acceptable, and effective for individuals with chronic msTBI. Further clinical studies with larger samples are warranted.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Priorities and Fractures in DeafPlus Augmentative and Alternative Communication Decision-Making Teams
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
ea58048e5255213f2c21a83c9f3658a632559142.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Children who are DeafPlus often engage in multiple services across a range of settings. For children who are DeafPlus using augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), decisions require further distributed expertise when communication planning. However, the processes that these teams engage in when decision making for this cohort remains underexamined.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This qualitative study analyzed the transcripts of three focus groups to gain insight into how professionals perceive and experience aspects of multidisciplinary interaction such as negotiating roles, authority, and communication approaches specifically for students who are DeafPlus using AAC.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Within these teams and their decision-making processes, data revealed the presence of (a) unclear and overlapping roles, (b) conflicting perspectives on communication modalities, (c) gatekeeping and power in support team participation, (d) fragmented and inconsistent processes, and (e) system constraints shaping decisions. These themes, as well as their subsequent subthemes, were then discussed through the lenses of (a) roles, power, and access; (b) the negotiation of influence and voice; and (c) fragmentation and system constraints.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings suggest that decision making is shaped not only by interpersonal dynamics but also by institutional structures that DeafPlus students are situated within. In contexts where language modality, communication access, and additional disabilities intersect, fragmented or authority-driven processes may contribute to inconsistent implementation and reduced efficacy of supports. A conceptual roadmap was developed to support greater transparency and alignment during team-based AAC planning for this cohort.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Adolescents’ Perspectives on Uptake, Engagement, and Implementation to Inform the Development of a Preventive Transdiagnostic Digital Mental Health Intervention: Qualitative Interview Study
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
035d301ed77fce4e74ca0175c7cadf9839d24f1a.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adolescence is a critical period for mental health prevention; yet, many young people face barriers to help-seeking, including stigma, limited mental health literacy, and restricted access to services. Preventive digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) offer a scalable, low-threshold approach to early support, but uptake and sustained engagement remain limited. Existing research has predominantly relied on quantitative methods and has only partly captured adolescents’ perspectives. Qualitative research is therefore needed to inform the design and implementation of preventive DMHIs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to explore adolescents’ perspectives on factors influencing the anticipated uptake, expected engagement, and implementation of preventive transdiagnostic DMHIs across person, intervention, and system levels.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This qualitative study was conducted in Switzerland using a single-interview design in the predesign phase of the development of a transdiagnostic preventive DMHI. Adolescents aged 12‐21 years were recruited through voluntary response sampling via social media and the project website. Semistructured interviews explored experiences with online help-seeking, factors influencing DMHI anticipated uptake and expected engagement, and recommendations for implementation. Interviews were conducted in person or via video call between January and June 2022, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using a hybrid deductive-inductive qualitative content analysis. Intercoder agreement was assessed using Cohen κ (κ=0.72).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 48 adolescents (mean age 16.52, SD 2.67 years; 32/48, 72.9% female) participated. In total, 8 main topics and multiple subtopics were identified across person, intervention, system, and cross levels. Person-level factors highlighted the importance of mental health literacy, preuptake communication, and relevance of social networks. Intervention-level factors emphasized usability, personalization, and privacy, while system-level findings reflected expectations for adaptive, integrated, and low-threshold mental health services. Trust and support emerged as cross-level factors for engagement. In addition, participants described several discrepancies between desired intervention characteristics and practical implementation, particularly regarding personalization, anonymity, peer exchange, and human support.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adolescents’ perspectives highlight that successful implementation of preventive DMHIs requires attention beyond intervention design to preuptake communication strategies, mental health literacy promotion, and integration within adaptive care systems. The tension between adolescents’ desire for immediate human-delivered support and the self-guided nature of preventive DMHIs underscores the need for clear clinical boundaries and explicit escalation pathways.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Genomic and biological characterization of three lytic phages targeting Vibrio parahaemolyticus and their application in a raw salmon model
container-title: Microbiology Spectrum
d749f1e2ee58c91622bc2f2c3ab494e58910c19a.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title/>
                    <jats:p>
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Vibrio parahaemolyticus</jats:italic>
                      is a major seafood-borne pathogen that poses substantial threats to food safety and aquaculture. However, effective and food-compatible strategies for controlling this pathogen along the seafood supply chain remain limited. In this study, three novel lytic bacteriophages (Z5, Z44, and Z109) that infect
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">V. parahaemolyticus</jats:italic>
                      were isolated from seafood-market wastewater and characterized with respect to their biological properties, genomic features, and bactericidal activity under food-relevant conditions. All three phages exhibited siphovirus-like morphologies and short latent periods (~10 min), with Z5 and Z44 showing high burst sizes (267–688 plaque-forming units [PFU]/cell). The three phages showed stability across a wide range of temperatures (4°C–60°C) and pH values (4–10), supporting their compatibility with seafood processing and cold-chain storage. Phylogenetic analyses indicated that Z5 and Z44 represent novel species within the family
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Queuovirinae</jats:italic>
                      , whereas Z109 belongs to the genus
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Mardecavirus</jats:italic>
                      . Genomic analyses confirmed the absence of known antibiotic resistance genes or virulence factors, supporting their genetic safety for food applications. Predicted interactions between phage- and host-encoded anti-restriction and defense systems likely influence phage lytic efficacy and killing patterns. Specifically, Z5 and Z44 encode a putative 7-deazaguanine DNA modification pathway that may enhance resistance to host restriction-modification systems. Conversely, the presence of prophage-related regions in the host genome may contribute to the reduced killing efficacy of Z109 at high phage doses. In a salmon model, all three phages significantly reduced
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">V. parahaemolyticus</jats:italic>
                      at 25°C and 4°C, demonstrating effective biocontrol in a food matrix. In addition, the phages strongly inhibited biofilm formation, although their capacity to disrupt mature biofilms was limited. Collectively, these results indicate that Z5, Z44, and Z109 are promising candidates for the biocontrol of
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">V. parahaemolyticus</jats:italic>
                      contamination in seafood systems.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>IMPORTANCE</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Bacterial infections in aquaculture and seafood pose significant challenges to food safety, with
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Vibrio parahaemolyticus</jats:italic>
                      being a major seafood-borne pathogen. Bacteriophages are promising alternatives to antibiotics, but their effectiveness may be influenced by phage-encoded counter-defense strategies and host-encoded antiphage defense systems. In this study, we characterized three novel lytic phages and observed distinct killing patterns under different infection conditions. In a raw salmon model, these phages effectively reduced
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">V. parahaemolyticus</jats:italic>
                      , demonstrating their practical biocontrol potential. Genome analysis identified putative phage-encoded DNA modification genes and host prophage-associated defense genes that may help explain these differences. These findings highlight the importance of considering both phage and host genomic features when optimizing phage-based strategies for controlling
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">V. parahaemolyticus</jats:italic>
                      in aquaculture and seafood systems.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Multi-task Learning with Active Learning for Arabic Offensive Speech Detection
container-title: ACM Transactions on Asian and Low-Resource Language Information Processing
e788316b806502944a78e6f59c6c7305715445d0.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid growth of social media has amplified the spread of offensive, violent, and vulgar speech, which poses serious societal and cybersecurity concerns. Detecting such content in Arabic text is particularly complex due to limited labeled data, dialectal variations, and the language’s inherent complexity. This article proposes a novel framework that integrates multi-task learning (MTL) with active learning to enhance offensive speech detection in Arabic social media text. By jointly training on two auxiliary tasks, violent and vulgar speech, the model leverages shared representations to improve the detection accuracy of offensive speech. Our approach dynamically adjusts task weights during training to balance the contribution of each task and optimize performance. To address the scarcity of labeled data, we employ an active learning strategy through several uncertainty sampling techniques to iteratively select the most informative samples for model training. We also introduce weighted emoji handling to better capture semantic cues. Experimental results using the OSACT2022 dataset show that the proposed framework achieves a state-of-the-art macro F1-score of 85.42%, outperforming existing methods while using significantly fewer fine-tuning samples. The findings of this study highlight the potential of integrating MTL with active learning to efficiently and accurately detect offensive language in resource-constrained settings.</jats:p>

title: From Data–Model Fit to Model–World Fit: A Framework for Integrating Domain Knowledge into Artificial Intelligence
container-title: Information Systems Research
90b62a3119c6508d0cc057bd92609f5992407b47.abstract:
<jats:p>Machine learning (ML)–based artificial intelligence (AI) systems often perform well in controlled settings but fail when deployed in the real world. These failures stem from a fundamental problem: ML/AI models optimize data–model fit by increasing statistical performance on training data, whereas real-world deployment demands a new paradigm in ML/AI: model–world fit that preserves domain semantics and contextual understanding. We propose a machine learning model–world fit framework that provides both a conceptual structure for understanding how domain knowledge shapes ML/AI systems and a research road map for investigating these relationships. The framework identifies how domain knowledge can be integrated into the ML/AI development process via external knowledge representations, such as data, value, process models, or domain ontologies. Incorporating external knowledge representations can help overcome three types of knowledge deficiencies in AI: know-what, know-how, and know-why. To illustrate the framework, we apply it to a child welfare placement case, a domain in which contextual understanding is critical and statistical accuracy is an insufficient evaluation criterion. Our insights lead to several directions for scholars working at the intersection of machine learning, design science, and knowledge representation.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>History: Ahmed Abbasi, Senior Editor; Min Zhao, Associate Editor.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/isre.2023.0031 .</jats:p>

title: Variety Matters: Measuring Semantic Verb Types in Conversation Following ECoLoGiC Treatment for People With Moderate or Severe Aphasia
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
1c885b91cf69d71c1f2a85d2c78c1a9cc16b689f.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Expanding Communication and Language Opportunities Generated in Conversation Treatment (ECoLoGiC-Tx) is a conversation treatment designed to improve the everyday language abilities of people with moderate-to-severe aphasia. Previous research reported improved use of basic syntactic structures during posttreatment conversations. Although ECoLoGic-Tx does not specifically target verb use, it may change the frequency and/or types of verbs used during conversation. Semantic verb type analysis categorizes verbs by their intended meaning. Each of the five semantic verb types serves a unique function during discourse, and difficulty using verbs within and across semantic categories may limit what is shared during everyday interactions. Because verbs play an essential role in conversation, this study explores if ECoLoGiC-Tx changed the frequency and semantic categories of verbs used by people with aphasia (PWA).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ten PWA attended 60-min treatment sessions twice weekly for 10 weeks. Conversational discourse samples were collected three times at each assessment phase (pretreatment, posttreatment, and maintenance). Samples were analyzed for overall verb frequency and semantic verb types. Stability of pretreatment measures and intrarater and interrater reliability were calculated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Immediately following treatment, overall verb use increased for four participants with nonfluent aphasia and decreased for three participants with fluent aphasia. Semantic verb type use varied across participants, and no participant showed consistent increases across semantic categories. Several participants demonstrated continued gains at 6 weeks posttreatment, and increased verb diversity within semantic categories was also observed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>ECoLoGiC-Tx may change how PWA use verbs. This study provides additional evidence that ECoLoGiC-Tx may generalize to aspects of communication not explicitly targeted during treatment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: The Management of Swallowing Disorders in Children With Spinal Muscular Atrophy Type 1: A Scoping Review
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
ee60069e9a5c3d0dbb8e2b2202f4fdea5aea5418.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Spinal muscular atrophy Type 1 (SMA1) is a rare autosomal recessive neuromuscular disorder with progressive muscle weakness and atrophy. Dysphagia is common among children with SMA1, and its complications are frequently documented. This scoping review aimed to describe the management of swallowing disorders in this population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, four electronic databases were searched (PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and Cochrane Library) for studies on children with SMA1. We investigated the management of swallowing disorders in children with SMA1, including methods and protocols used to assess swallowing and feeding, and treatment option. The quality of included studies was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklists; two independent researchers conducted study selection and data extraction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thirty-eight studies with a total of 1,784 SMA1 patients were included. Swallowing was evaluated using instrumental methods (flexible endoscopic evaluation of swallowing and videofluoroscopic swallowing study) and clinical assessments, with one validated protocol identified for pediatric SMA (Oral and Swallowing Abilities Tool). Delayed initiation of swallowing, oral impairment, pharyngeal residues, and aspiration were frequently reported. Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy was used in cases of severe dysphagia, malnutrition, and failure to thrive. Few studies reported information on compensatory strategies and rehabilitative treatments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Further research is needed to standardize swallowing assessment approaches and to evaluate the effectiveness of rehabilitative and compensatory interventions in children with SMA1.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Large inversions in Lake Malawi cichlids are associated with habitat, lineage, and sex determination
container-title: eLife
cce4e72fed49b51c678d89766ba0271f7a3537de.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Chromosomal inversions are an important class of genetic variation that link multiple alleles together into a single inherited block that can have important effects on fitness. To study the role of large inversions in the massive evolutionary radiation of Lake Malawi cichlids, we used long-read technologies to identify four single and two tandem inversions that span half of each respective chromosome, and which together encompass over 10% of the genome. Each inversion is fixed in one of the two states within the seven major ecogroups, suggesting they played a role in the separation of the major lake lineages into specific lake habitats. One exception is within the
                    <jats:italic>benthic</jats:italic>
                    sub-radiation, where both inverted and non-inverted alleles continue to segregate within the group. The evolutionary histories of three of the six inversions suggest they transferred from the pelagic
                    <jats:italic>Diplotaxodon</jats:italic>
                    group into
                    <jats:italic>benthic</jats:italic>
                    ancestors at the time the
                    <jats:italic>benthic</jats:italic>
                    sub-radiation was seeded. The remaining three inversions are found in a subset of
                    <jats:italic>benthic</jats:italic>
                    species living in deep waters. We show that some of these inversions are linked to XY sex-determination systems but are also likely limited to a subset of total lake species. Our work suggests that inversions have been under both sexual and natural selection in Lake Malawi cichlids and that they will be important to understanding how this adaptive radiation evolved.
                  </jats:p>

title: Benchmarking the ladder dual fermion approach for the Falicov-Kimball model
container-title: Physical Review B
bf3019f5349c5ae89ab0f180f5752609dec75f0e.abstract: <jats:p>Strong electronic correlations generally require nonperturbative treatment. Local correlations are captured by dynamical mean-field theory, while nonlocal correlations can be treated with diagrammatic extensions such as the dual fermion approach. Dual fermion is built on physically motivated but in principle uncontrolled approximations, so careful benchmarking is needed to understand the strengths and limitations of the method. In this work, we benchmark ladder dual fermion and dynamical mean-field theory for the Falicov–Kimball model with the exact classical Monte Carlo solution. We focus on the thermodynamics, electronic structure, and susceptibility, especially on the combined frequency and momentum structure, and find that dual fermion clearly outperforms dynamical mean-field theory. Somewhat surprisingly, dual fermion is not as accurate for the relation between orbital density and chemical potential in the doped system. These results demonstrate the need for rigorous benchmarking of diagrammatic extensions of dynamical mean-field theory for models with inequivalent orbitals, a capability that is essential for modeling materials.</jats:p>

title: Bifurcation analysis in a discrete SIRS epidemic model with non-monotonic incidence rates
container-title: International Journal of Biomathematics
019b9adb703fbc657ecca6609a05fc11f6c06b0c.abstract: <jats:p>In this study, we investigate a discrete SIRS epidemic model with non-monotonic incidence rates. Employing bifurcation theory and critical normal form analysis, we study the existence of three codimension-two bifurcations, including 1:1 strong resonance, 1:2 strong resonance, and fold–flip bifurcation. To verify theoretical results, we provide a series of numerical simulations, including bifurcation diagrams, phase portraits, and maximum Lyapunov exponent diagrams. We further investigate the influence of initial conditions through two-parameter space plots.</jats:p>

title: A 3D robotic inspection framework for power quality monitoring in subterranean high-voltage transmission systems
container-title: International Journal of Modeling, Simulation, and Scientific Computing
92ac48b1a63451be6d4656aa7b5e50eabef9713a.abstract: <jats:p>The operation of underground power transmission systems is based on continuous monitoring to ensure reliable power transmission, maintain power quality, and avoid unexpected failures. However, most of the existing robotic inspection systems are mainly based on navigation and visual inspection, which have limited ability to integrate power quality monitoring and intelligent fault analysis. To overcome these drawbacks, this work proposes an intelligent robotic inspection framework that combines autonomous robotic monitoring, multimodal sensing, optimized deep learning and adaptive hyper-parameter optimization for power quality disturbance detection. The proposed framework uses a 101-layer Squeeze-and-Excitation Residual Network (SE-ResNet-101x) to classify pre-processed one-dimensional voltage signals into normal and fault classes and hyperparameters are optimized through the Self-Adaptive Sea Lion Optimization (SA-SLnO) algorithm. A set of data is generated based on simulation to mimic an actual underground inspection scenario, including the electrical, environmental, and robotic operational factors. The LiDAR data is used in isolation to provide three-dimensional localization for the robot, while the thermal and camera data provide additional inspection data. Experimental results show that fault detection performance is very good, with 99.10% accuracy, 99.97% precision, 98.94% recall, and 99.45% [Formula: see text]1-score. The proposed system has been able to successfully detect voltage sags, voltage swells, Harmonic distortions, Transient disturbances and Flicker events. Moreover, a high climbing efficiency of more than 89% is achieved on slopes of 30[Formula: see text]. Even in wireless mode, high communication reliability of 99.8% is achieved. The proposed framework is an effective way to monitor underground power automatically, which can achieve accurate early detection of faults and reliable underground power monitoring inspection by robots in complex underground power transmission scenarios.</jats:p>

title: Attention Trap? How Visual Motion Shapes Children’s Screen Time and Engagement on Video Platforms
container-title: Information Systems Research
3836bd62e72740b25fd59c7e03808cdae1f4dd40.abstract:
<jats:p>Children spend considerable time watching online video, yet we know relatively little about which features of video content shape their engagement. This research examines one measurable feature: visual motion. Analyzing more than 32,000 videos from popular children’s channels on YouTube, we find that videos with greater visual motion receive more views, even after accounting for other visual, audio, and content characteristics. A randomized YouTube advertising experiment using professionally produced educational videos confirms this relationship; adding motion to the background increased view rates by about 2% at essentially no additional cost.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>An eye-tracking study with children aged 6–10 helps explain why. Visual motion does not prevent children from looking away. Instead, it reduces the duration of longer attentional lapses by bringing their gaze back to the screen more quickly. The additional attention is directed primarily toward the moving background rather than the instructor. The findings show how a measurable design feature can shape children’s attention and provide creators and platforms with a way to assess and design children’s video content more systematically.</jats:p>

title: Reconnoitring Yogic Peace of Mind and Transient Happiness With Their Perceived Psychological Correlates
container-title: The Neuroscience of Happiness
2a08909a0d86148aae4b34a85733003e4a4fe6d2.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter discusses yogic peace of mind as a complex, self-reported psychological construct and looks into its linkages with perceived cognition, emotional regulation, meditative consciousness, and well-being. The empirical part of the research is a pilot cross-sectional study conducted only using data collected via questionnaires; it did not include measurements of brain activity, neurotransmitter levels, the autonomic nervous system, or any other biological parameters. Consequently, all neurological hypotheses are discussed as interpretations based on existing neuroscience literature and not on the findings of this particular research. Some preliminary findings of factor, regression, and structural modeling analyses will be used to evaluate the proposed theoretical links between the concepts. There is evidence of correlations between long-term yogic practice, reported peace of mind, and positive psychological outcomes; however, there is no proof of causation or physiological changes. Further large-scale longitudinal studies are required to verify the hypothesis.</jats:p>

title: Communication Difficulties and Management: The Lived Experience of Individuals With Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration Spectrum Disorders
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
1d522ff35f2664ebda12366ebfdad1028663284f.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) is the neuropathology that underlies a collection of progressive clinical syndromes typically classified by the initial/primary symptom. For example, individuals with loss of word meaning as a first manifestation are often diagnosed with the semantic variant of primary progressive aphasia. Growing evidence suggests that language and communication can be impacted in all clinical syndromes across the FTLD spectrum, but the functional relevance of these symptoms has yet to be explored.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The Frontotemporal Degeneration (FTD) Insights Survey is the largest community survey of individuals affected by FTLD. It was administered online and included questions related to demographics, symptoms, life participation, quality of life, and experiences with and hopes for treatment. Self-reported diagnoses of respondents included the nonfluent/agrammatic, semantic, and unspecified variants of primary progressive aphasia, semantic dementia, corticobasal syndrome, progressive supranuclear palsy, and behavioral variant FTD. Here, we grouped respondents according to whether they had a language-predominant (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                      = 43), motor-predominant (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                      = 43), or behavior-predominant (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                      = 90) variant of FTLD and used descriptive statistics to explore how they perceive their own communication difficulties and gauge their motivation for management.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Over 65% of respondents in each group identified changes to communication as a symptom; subsequent analyses focused on the responses of this cohort. Across groups, word finding and speaking were two of the most frequently endorsed difficulties. Over 50% of each group identified improved communication as a treatment priority, reflecting the impact that these symptoms have on their day-to-day life. Speech-language therapy is an important approach to manage these changes and minimize their impact. Whereas 76% of the language and motor groups had attended speech-language therapy, this was true for only 16% of the behavior group.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Individuals across the FTLD spectrum experience changes to communication that impact their social engagement and quality of life. Management needs to be tailored to the needs of each individual, but recommendations are provided based on the insights and group-level preferences reported here. Future research is needed to identify current referral practices and how to increase engagement in skilled communication interventions, especially for individuals with the behavioral variant of FTD.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Navigating Indeterminacy
container-title: Worldly Indeterminacy
a3587438b97f06a7797796214d3ad4f301d198e8.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter establishes the linguistic and logical dimensions of the theory of ontic indeterminacy by addressing how to understand the signifying nature of language and how to reason in the presence of worldly indeterminacy. It provides reasons to adopt a semantics that recommends understanding language as provisional, such that a linguistic expression does not predicate a determinate feature of its referent. This provisional understanding of language aligns well with the world’s indeterminate aspects. The chapter then elucidates a bivalent logic that is greatly, but not entirely, classical by retaining the laws of noncontradiction and excluded middle while rejecting the double negation elimination rule. It also addresses Dana Goswick’s challenges to the law of excluded middle, arguing that this logical principle can be maintained in the presence of indeterminate objects.</jats:p>

title: The application of an artificial intelligence–enhanced virtual reality cognitive behavioral therapy tool is feasible and acceptable in patients with inflammatory bowel disease: A multicenter mixed methods pilot study
container-title: Inflammatory Bowel Diseases
34e53c5af6594279fbcef7d176c277418b8c6c44.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) frequently experience anxiety, pain, and reduced quality of life. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is effective for anxiety, but access may be limited. We evaluated the feasibility and explored the potential clinical impact of an artificial intelligence–powered virtual reality CBT-based application (XAIA [eXtended Reality Artificially Intelligent Ally]) in patients with IBD.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This was a multicenter, mixed-methods pilot study recruiting adults with IBD from the University of Chicago and Cedars-Sinai medical centers. Participants completed a single 30-minute session with the XAIA conversational avatar. Pain and anxiety were measured before and after the session using a visual analog pain scale and State–Trait Anxiety Inventory, respectively. Semi-structured interviews were conducted after the session to assess acceptability. Quantitative analysis was completed using paired t tests, and interview transcripts underwent thematic analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thirty-four participants (median age 34 years, 71% women, 59% with Crohn’s disease) participated in this study. Qualitative analysis revealed high acceptability, with participants reporting feelings of safety, validation, and improved coping. Participants valued the immersive environment, conversational avatar, and ability to discuss sensitive topics without judgment. As an exploratory outcome, participants reported a statistically significant improvement in pain (−0.46; P = .011) and anxiety (−10.65; P &lt; .001) immediately following a single session.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A single artificial intelligence–driven virtual reality CBT-based session in patients with IBD was feasible and well accepted and demonstrated preliminary evidence for acute reductions in pain and anxiety scores. Immersive digital behavioral health interventions may represent a scalable adjunct to traditional mental health support among adults with IBD.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Investigating Variability and Malleability of Speech-Language Pathologists' Responsive Talk With Children: An Early-Efficacy Trial
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
787ca7fc74e150b12f0150dc580899969c52fcbd.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The purposes of this early-stage efficacy study were to examine speech-language pathologists' (SLPs') use of responsive talk with children and to determine the extent to which responsive talk can be modified through brief clinician education or an in situ, tablet-based feedback system, GENIE, that provided real-time prompts to use responsive talk.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Eleven SLPs (certified clinicians and graduate students) and 11 typically developing preschool-aged children participated in a quasi-experimental study. SLPs were paired with a randomly assigned child to complete two structured intervention sessions to assess responsive talk. In the first session, SLPs used their business-as-usual practices, whereas in the second session, SLPs were randomly assigned to receive clinician education or the in situ GENIE prompts, representing a planned variation in instructing SLPs to use responsive talk during intervention. SLP responsive talk was coded from video-recorded interactions to establish the frequency of use.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      SLPs demonstrated substantial variability in the baseline use of responsive talk. Responsive talk increased substantially from baseline for those receiving clinician education or the in situ GENIE prompts: Increases in responsive talk for the clinician education group represented a very large-sized effect (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">d</jats:italic>
                      = 2.1), whereas increases for the GENIE group represented a moderately sized effect (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">d</jats:italic>
                      = 0.6).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The primary conclusion to be drawn from this study is that SLPs' use of responsive talk during intervention is both variable and malleable
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">.</jats:italic>
                      Findings suggest that brief clinician education and in situ technological supports are promising strategies for increasing SLPs' use of responsive talk, and directions for future research are discussed.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Language Sample Analysis Practices in a Multilingual and Diglossic Context: A Survey of Speech-Language Pathologists in German-Speaking Switzerland
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
2bec9359c99e12a9e78b9a114f693e9e1c4b288a.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigated the frequency, purpose, target groups, and methods of language sample analysis (LSA) among speech-language pathologists (SLPs) in German-speaking Switzerland. LSA is particularly relevant in linguistically diverse and underresearched contexts such as diglossic settings, where everyday spoken language differs from standardized varieties.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A survey was conducted among 550 SLPs in German-speaking Switzerland. Descriptive statistics were used to analyze the data, focusing on reported use, target demographics, and analytical methods concerning LSA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Compared with previous research from English-speaking countries, LSA is used by a larger proportion of SLPs in Switzerland. Consistent with prior findings, Swiss SLPs primarily employ individualized approaches rather than established protocols. LSA is most frequently conducted in younger children, while the use of assistive tools remains low. Furthermore, SLPs mainly focus on microstructural parameters (e.g., morphology–syntax) rather than on macrostructural parameters during analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The LSA is a highly utilized method in German-speaking Switzerland, underscoring its clinical relevance in a diglossic context. However, the heavy reliance on individualized methods, the low adoption of assisting tools, and the narrow focus on microstructural parameters suggest a need for the standardization of the LSA process and the implementation of helpful, structured tools to better support LSA in diglossic and multilingual contexts in future practice and research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Effects of Naturalistic Developmental Behavioral Intervention Strategies and Visual Scene Displays on Autistic Children's Joint Engagement
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
79c50438a86c69cdc4a2560ab222319ad791d3ac.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Naturalistic developmental behavioral intervention (NDBI) and visual scene displays (VSDs), a type of augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), are research-supported practices focused on naturalistic instruction and increasing social communication skills in young autistic children. The purpose of our study was to extend previous research to understand the effects of embedding VSDs within a dynamic play-based NDBI for young autistic children.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We employed a randomized multiple-baseline single-case experimental design across three participants to evaluate the effects of (a) NDBI strategies and (b) NDBI strategies plus aided AAC modeling and just-in-time (JIT) programming of VSDs on joint engagement in young autistic children.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>When NDBI strategies were introduced, there was a large positive effect on child joint engagement and a corresponding large negative effect on child isolated attention. After aided AAC modeling and JIT programming were introduced, child joint engagement and isolated attention outcomes were mixed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings of the current study show promise to using VSDs within dynamic play-based NDBIs as a communication support. Limitations and implications are discussed.</jats:p>
