title: Immersive Virtual Reality Cognitive Stimulation for Delirium Prevention in Older Surgical Intensive Care Unit Patients With Cognitive Impairment: Protocol for a 3-Arm Randomized Pilot Trial
container-title: JMIR Research Protocols
6a0305024bfe7ca8c2a7ec25512ab1521c9d9887.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Postoperative delirium is common among older adults after major surgery, especially those with cognitive impairment, and is associated with prolonged hospitalization, functional decline, mortality, and subsequent cognitive deterioration. Nonpharmacologic delirium-prevention strategies are recommended but are difficult to deliver reliably in high-acuity environments because they require repeated staff-intensive interactions, consistent patient engagement, and integration into complex intensive care unit (ICU) workflows.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to evaluate the feasibility, usability, safety, acceptance, and adherence of ReCognitionVR 2.0, an immersive virtual reality (VR)–based cognitive stimulation intervention designed for older surgical ICU patients with mild-to-moderate cognitive impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This is a single-center, 3-arm, parallel-group randomized pilot trial. Ninety adults aged 65 years or older undergoing major surgery with expected postoperative ICU admission and Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores of 15 to 24 will be randomized in a 1:1:1 ratio to ReCognitionVR 2.0 cognitive stimulation, passive VR control exposure, or standard-of-care nurse-led reality orientation. VR sessions will be delivered once daily for up to 20 minutes on postoperative days 1 through 3 when participants are calm and alert. The primary outcomes are feasibility metrics, including recruitment, outcome completion, safety and tolerability, usability, acceptance, and adherence. Secondary outcomes estimate preliminary changes in attention and executive function using the Months Backward Test and NIH Toolbox Flanker Inhibitory Control and Attention Test. Postoperative delirium incidence is an exploratory clinical outcome.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study was funded in September 2025. Participant recruitment and data collection are currently ongoing. Preliminary data quality assessments and exploratory reviews of the collected data are underway. Formal statistical analyses of the trial outcomes will be conducted after participant enrollment is completed and the study database has been finalized and locked. As of July 29, 2026, we had enrolled 18 participants. Early operational experience informed the refinement of exploratory VR performance metrics and the documentation of protocol deviations. Following an oxygen-connection near miss, we added a preintervention oxygen/readiness checklist as an operational safety safeguard. Enrollment of 90 participants is projected to be completed in 2027 if the current recruitment pace is sustained. Results are expected to be published in winter 2027.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This protocol will generate data on feasibility, safety, usability, adherence, digital performance, cognitive assessment, and delirium measurement, all needed to optimize ReCognitionVR 2.0 and to design a future multicenter efficacy trial of VR-enabled delirium prevention in critical care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Microaggressions, Language Bias, and the Exclusion of Asian Faculty From Leadership in U.S. Higher Education
container-title: The Lack of Asian Leadership in Higher Education
9d567bb58b9b6fb50569c31be5f41af5718628bb.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how microaggressions and language-related bias contribute to the exclusion of Asian faculty from leadership opportunities in U.S. higher education. It shows how judgments about communication, clarity, and “cultural fit” can operate as neutral-sounding rationales for withholding authority, particularly for faculty whose speech, accent, or perceived nativeness is marked as different. The chapter traces how “forever guest” positioning limits institutional ownership, how supervisors and senior colleagues gatekeep networks and high-visibility roles, and how cumulative microaggressions produce emotional strain, narrowed opportunity, and reduced leadership self-efficacy. It concludes with practical recommendations to recognize linguistic bias, clarify selection criteria, strengthen sponsorship, and redesign evaluation and promotion practices to expand inclusive pathways to academic leadership.</jats:p>

title: Beyond binary AI text detection: Partial authorship, source-text similarity, and an integrated threshold model of detectability
container-title: International Review of Applied Sciences and Engineering
acc924b3d1c0e2463fe1a308d503fda2a23b1d77.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    This study investigates AI text detection under conditions that more closely reflect real-world writing practices than conventional binary human-versus-AI benchmarks. Rather than treating authorship as a dichotomy, detectability is examined as a function of partial AI authorship, source-text similarity, and generator heterogeneity. Ten pre-LLM, human-written English scientific abstracts were used as reference texts, from which four authorship states (H100, AI50, AI75, and AI100) were constructed through controlled rewriting and paragraph-level mixing. AI-generated content was produced using four large language models: ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and LLaMA. Detection outputs from Turnitin and GPTZero were evaluated using non-parametric statistics, correlation analysis, and logistic threshold modeling. The results demonstrate that fully human and fully AI-rewritten texts are statistically distinguishable: median AI scores increased from 0 in H100 to 53 in AI100 for Turnitin (
                    <jats:italic>U</jats:italic>
                    = 49.5,
                    <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                     < 0.001) and from 0 to 11 for GPTZero (
                    <jats:italic>U</jats:italic>
                    = 61.0,
                    <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                    < 0.001), although AI-generated texts did not constitute a homogeneous class. Detectability also varied significantly across the four nominal authorship states for both Turnitin (H = 30.39,
                    <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                    < 0.001) and GPTZero (H = 21.77,
                    <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                    < 0.001), and systematically with source-text similarity and the generating model. Turnitin showed greater sensitivity than GPTZero to changes in nominal AI proportion and transformation intensity, particularly under mixed-authorship conditions. Significant generator-dependent differences were also observed, with Gemini outputs generally receiving higher AI-detection scores than ChatGPT or LLaMA outputs. The main methodological contribution is the Integrated Detectability Threshold Model (IDTM), which represents detection probability as a joint function of nominal AI proportion and transformation intensity. Within the present sample, the model identified a similarity transition range of approximately 63–66%, below which Turnitin-based detection became more likely than non-detection. These findings support a shift from binary AI classification toward a threshold- and risk-sensitive interpretation of AI text detectability.
                  </jats:p>

title: Should quantum physics be approached with mathematical formalism in school? Effects of instructional approach on functional understanding under cognitive and affective controls
container-title: Physical Review Physics Education Research
6493f05b70eb976685bab6227f1a5b655fc3ff28.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Evidence from physics education research suggests that the introduction of mathematical formalism in quantum physics instruction can support the development of students’ conceptual understanding, particularly by promoting functional ways of reasoning about quantum phenomena. However, empirical findings on the effectiveness of such approaches at the secondary school level remain inconclusive, and little is known about the extent to which learning outcomes are shaped by instructional design as opposed to learners’ affective and cognitive characteristics. This study addresses this gap by investigating the relative influence of instructional approach on students’ understanding of single-photon states, while controlling for prior knowledge, cognitive load, situational interest, and physics self-concept. A quasiexperimental pre-post design was implemented with
                    <a:math xmlns:a="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <a:mi>N</a:mi>
                      <a:mo>=</a:mo>
                      <a:mn>172</a:mn>
                    </a:math>
                    upper secondary students, comparing a qualitative instructional condition with an approach supplemented by a reduced Dirac formalism. Learning outcomes were assessed using the framework of Functional Fidelity and Fidelity of Gestalt. A multivariate analysis of covariance, followed by univariate analyses of covariance, was conducted to examine the contributions of instructional and learner-related variables. The findings indicate that affective variables emerge as strong predictors of functional understanding and suggest that learning in quantum physics is driven less by instructional format than by learners’ affective and cognitive prerequisites. In particular, fostering interest appears to be a key mechanism for supporting the development of functional understanding. The results highlight the importance of integrating affective dimensions into instructional design and provide a basis for future research on the interaction between instructional approaches and learner characteristics in quantum physics education.
                  </jats:p>

title: Optimized Emergency Sign Language Recognition with Large-Kernel Attention Graph Convolutional Network for Accurate Gesture Classification
container-title: International Journal of Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence
3737bdb37c2afdac92e2c8a956436c9b57e10253.abstract: <jats:p>Sign Language Recognition (SLR) plays a significant role in improving communication accessibility for hearing-impaired individuals, particularly in emergency scenarios where fast and reliable gesture interpretation is required. However, emergency Indian Sign Language (ISL) recognition remains challenging due to rapid hand movements, visually similar gestures, and complex spatial–temporal relationships among hand components. This study proposes an SLR-HIE-LKAGCN framework that integrates topology-aware spatial representation, spatial–temporal feature learning, graph-based gesture modeling, and optimization-based parameter adaptation for emergency ISL recognition. Initially, input gesture frames are processed using a Simplicial Convolutional Filter (SCF) to preserve higher-order spatial relationships among hand regions and enhance gesture representation. The refined gesture sequences are then provided to a Spatial–Temporal Knowledge-Embedded Transformer (STKET) to capture temporal dependencies and contextual movement patterns. The extracted features are further analyzed employing a Large-Kernel Attention Graph Convolutional Network (LKAGCN), which models relationships among hand landmarks and learns discriminative gesture representations. In addition, the Secretary Bird Optimization Algorithm (SBOA) is employed to optimize critical network parameters and improve model convergence. The proposed framework is evaluated on emergency ISL gesture categories, including accident, call, doctor, help, hot, lose, pain, and thief. Experimental outcomes establish that the proposed technique achieves superior recognition performance with 98.82% accuracy, 98.57% precision, and 98.53% F1-score, outperforming existing approaches. The obtained results indicate that SLR-HIE-LKAGCN provides an effective and computationally efficient solution for real-time emergency ISL recognition.</jats:p>

title: ATT-SV2-ES Net: Hybrid Deep Learning Features and Lightweight Attention-Based Model for Early Glaucoma Detection
container-title: International Journal of Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence
bc275378bb5009d7f256155d09bb39b3c0bf9888.abstract: <jats:p>Glaucoma is one of the main causes of permanent blindness. Timely intervention is ensured by its early and precise identification. This paper proposes a new hybrid approach, integrating handcrafted features with Deep Learning (DL), for reliable glaucoma identification and prediction on the G1020 dataset. Initially, pre-processing is conducted, which includes data augmentation to increase the diversity of images, Gaussian filtering to reduce image noise, Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE) to enhance local retinal contrast and then grayscale conversion to simplify retinal image representation. After pre-processing, the enhanced images were given to Depthwise Dilated Spatial Attention Mechanism (DDSAM)-based Glau-SegNet for optic disk (OD) and optic cup (OC) segmentation. From the segmented images, handcrafted features, such as Local Binary Patterns (LBPs) and fractal analysis, which describe complementary texture and structural information, are extracted. In parallel, the segmented images are processed by the Attention ShuffleNet V2 with Echo State Network (Att-SV2-ES Net) to obtain high-level deep feature representations. Then these deep features and handcrafted features are concatenated and fed to a fully connected layer with sigmoid activation to classify into the class for the prediction of glaucoma. This combined approach achieves a balance between high accuracy and scalability, addressing the growing need for accessible and reliable glaucoma screening solutions. The experimental results demonstrate the proposed system’s superior performance in detecting and predicting glaucoma. Furthermore, the findings demonstrate that the proposed model, which integrates DL features, outperforms all other models in terms of key performance metrics, including achieving 99.32% specificity, 99.43% sensitivity, and 99.37% accuracy.</jats:p>

title: Engagement Patterns and Clinical Outcomes Among Adolescents and Young Adults Enrolled in the Somethings Digital Peer Support Platform: Retrospective Observational Study
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
953c4720688eb14be414f54a77f8999fcbb1a1a0.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adolescent mental health needs remain largely unmet, particularly among youth in geographically underserved communities. Digital peer support is a promising approach to expanding access to mental health support, yet real-world evidence on engagement patterns and clinical outcomes remains limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The purpose of this study was to characterize engagement patterns and real-world outcomes among adolescents and young adults enrolled in a commercially available, text-based peer support platform.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective observational study analyzed secondary data from 5673 adolescents and young adults enrolled in a commercially available digital peer support platform from January 29, 2023, through June 3, 2026. Engagement was operationalized as communication days per month. Standardized clinical outcome measures (Patient Health Questionnaire-9 [PHQ-9], Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 [GAD-7], and World Health Organization-Five Well-Being Index [WHO-5]) were administered as part of routine measurement-based care. Ordinary least squares regression was used to examine predictors of engagement, and complete-case pre-post change scores were evaluated across 4 assessment windows among participants with paired assessments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The sample was predominantly female (4600/5673, 81.1%) with a mean age of 16.4 (SD 2.1) years and moderate-to-severe symptom burden at baseline (PHQ-9: mean 12.6, SD 6.1; GAD-7: mean 10.7, SD 5.0; WHO-5: mean 44.8, SD 21.0). Of enrolled adolescents and young adults, 98.1% (5565/5673) had at least one recorded engagement with the platform, with a mean of 4.56 (SD 6.12) communication days per month. Female sex was a significant positive predictor of engagement intensity (β=.64, SE 0.22;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.004). Hispanic and Latino adolescents and young adults engaged significantly more frequently than White or non-Hispanic adolescents and young adults (β=.61, SE 0.26;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.02). Health Professional Shortage Area (HPSA) shortage score was significantly and positively associated with engagement intensity (β=.08, SE 0.02;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001). Baseline symptom severity was not associated with engagement intensity (β=.094, SE 0.23;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.68). Among participants with complete baseline and follow-up data (1437/5673, 25.3%), an exploratory complete-case analysis found within-measure paired scores improved significantly from baseline to follow-up across the PHQ-9, GAD-7, and WHO-5. At last assessment, 31.9% (237/742), 36.6% (222/606), and 37.8% (168/442) of adolescents and young adults met clinically meaningful improvement thresholds on the PHQ-9, GAD-7, and WHO-5, respectively.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Text-based peer support shows preliminary promise as a scalable approach to expanding mental health access for underserved adolescents, though clinical improvement estimates are based on the subpopulation exposed to the digital peer support platform and may not generalize to the full enrolled population. Prospective, controlled studies with more complete outcome ascertainment are needed to establish causal efficacy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Application of Digital Health Interventions for Cognitive Management in Children With Cancer: Scoping Review
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
488230a323f4a1db95fece744265b1e2765b04ec.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Advances in the diagnosis and treatment of childhood cancer have substantially improved survival, resulting in a growing population of survivors of childhood cancer who may experience long-term treatment-related sequelae. Cognitive late effects are an important long-term consequence of childhood cancer and can affect cognitive functioning, psychosocial well-being, and quality of life. Digital health interventions offer accessible and flexible approaches to managing cognitive difficulties among children with cancer. However, the existing evidence has not yet been comprehensively synthesized.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to map and synthesize the existing evidence on digital health interventions for cognitive management among children with cancer; characterize intervention modalities, delivery approaches, and functional components; and identify evidence gaps and priorities for future research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Arksey and O’Malley framework and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews) checklist. Six academic databases, including PubMed, Embase (Ovid), CINAHL, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library, were systematically searched for relevant studies published between January 2010 and August 2026. Eligibility criteria were developed using the population-concept-context framework. Two reviewers independently performed study screening and data extraction. The methodological quality of included studies was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Screening was performed independently at the title/abstract and full-text stages, with disagreements resolved through discussion and, when necessary, consultation with a third reviewer. Descriptive statistics and thematic content analysis were used to synthesize the findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 5371 records were identified through the literature search. Following screening, 19 publications representing 14 independent study samples and involving 566 children with cancer were included. Four digital health modalities were identified: computer-based interventions, internet-based interventions, mobile apps, and neurofeedback training. Computer-based interventions were the predominant modality. Across these modalities, working memory and attention were the most frequently targeted cognitive domains, while feasibility, acceptability, and adherence were the most commonly assessed implementation-related outcomes. However, relatively few interventions incorporated coach support, telephone-based communication, or educational components, and none evaluated economic outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although digital health interventions show promise for supporting cognitive function in children with cancer, substantial gaps remain in the current evidence. This scoping review mapped the field according to intervention modalities, delivery approaches, and functional components, rather than focusing solely on the efficacy of individual technologies. Future research should prioritize the development of multidimensional, personalized, and functionally integrated digital health interventions that combine cognitive training with supportive care, education, monitoring, and communication. Multicenter randomized controlled trials should subsequently evaluate these interventions using clinically meaningful outcomes, with comprehensive assessments of safety, adherence, implementation, and health economic outcomes to establish their effectiveness, feasibility, and sustainability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                    <jats:p>

                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Chlamydia muridarum</jats:italic>

                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">tc0066</jats:italic>

                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">C. muridarum</jats:italic>

                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">C. muridarum</jats:italic>

                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">tc0066</jats:italic>

                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">C. trachomatis</jats:italic>

                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">in vivo</jats:italic>

                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Chlamydia</jats:italic>
                      spp. are prevalent pathogens capable of infecting a wide range of hosts and tissues, yet the molecular determinants mediating differences in tropism remain incompletely defined.
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Chlamydia trachomatis</jats:italic>

                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">C. muridarum</jats:italic>

<jats:p>
                    Accurate and computationally efficient waveform models are required to infer the parameters of compact binaries from their gravitational-wave (GW) emission. Among these parameters, orbital eccentricity serves as a smoking gun for dynamical formation channels and must be accounted for to avoid systematic errors in GW analyses. Here, we present , a time domain, multipolar waveform model for binaries on generic planar orbits, calibrated to quasicircular (QC) numerical relativity (NR) simulations from SXS Collaboration. The model is built within the effective-one-body (EOB) framework, and it employs novel resummations of the radiation-reaction force and waveform modes. We validate its accuracy through comparisons against 592 QC, 319 eccentric, one dynamical capture, and two scattering SXS NR waveforms, and through scattering-angle comparisons against 61 SXS NR simulations. title: ESMA and the Evolution of the EU’s Supervisory Model for Financial Markets
container-title: The Anti-Money Laundering Authority and EU Financial Agencies
eaf69caea3e83f41b78349576cef3c7cee307ac1.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter considers the evolution of the EU’s institutional governance arrangements for the EU financial system by examining the supervisory role of the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA). The optimal institutional location for EU financial market supervision remains one of the most freighted questions in EU financial regulation law and policy, with the recent policy and political focus on the achievement of a Savings and Investments Union re-igniting the long-standing debate on the merits of a single supervisor.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This chapter considers how ESMA has evolved as regards direct supervision, and the factors which have shaped its incremental acquisition of supervisory powers and of a considerable related regulatory capacity. It suggests that persisting with this incremental and experimental strengthening of ESMA’s powers offers a more sustainable way forward than a material and punctuated expansion of ESMA’s current supervisory mandate.</jats:p>

title: The Current Model of European Financial Architecture
container-title: The Anti-Money Laundering Authority and EU Financial Agencies
40a15cc69d3b992efc1aea7ca8b76854316f6040.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter analyses the scope and structure of European financial architecture and questions the ex tent to which it can address effectively financial risks. Fifteen years after the creation of the European System of Financial Supervision in the wake of the Great Financial Crisis, the current architecture of financial supervision is being overstretched and exhibits its inadequacy to respond to long-standing and new challenges. The sectoral division in three European Supervisory Authorities is no longer suited for the rising transversal risks and challenges that the EU and its financial markets face, such as the continued growth of shadow banking and the need to accommodate the twin green and digital transition. The need for the creation of the Anti-Money Laundering Authority as a standalone authority outside of the existing sectoral division exemplifies the difficult solution to the current overstretching of European financial architecture in the absence of a more structural and radical overhaul.</jats:p>

title: Bridging Borders
container-title: The Anti-Money Laundering Authority and EU Financial Agencies
57af47e18fbfd0bfcdbd93458b0f5b7a19bed8e1.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter examines how third countries’ access to EU financial agencies is changing. These agencies increasingly work with non-EU countries because of global financial integration and rising regulatory interdependence across markets. Third-country involvement happens through association agreements, bilateral treaties, or administrative arrangements. The chapter highlights two types of participation: structured involvement, as European Economic Area (EEA) and European Free Trade Association (EFTA) States without voting rights, and flexible cooperation based on equivalence assessments and memoranda of understanding. Candidate countries, European Neighbourhood Policy partners, Switzerland, and the UK primarily rely on ad hoc arrangements and memoranda rather than negotiation-based sectoral agreements, reflecting different models of integration. The chapter highlights that cooperation improves regulatory consistency but also creates asymmetries by making third States non-voting rule-takers.</jats:p>

title: AMLA as a European Supervisory Pivot
container-title: The Anti-Money Laundering Authority and EU Financial Agencies
a94939306cc44850267d831d8ed7d60594581a9a.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The creation of the European Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) marks a watershed moment in the EU’s supervisory architecture. Triggered by systemic failures in national supervision and high-profile scandals, AMLA introduces a hybrid supervisory model: it directly oversees high-risk financial institutions while promoting convergence and capacity building across Member States. Legally rooted in Article 114 TFEU, AMLA reflects the evolving trend towards functional integration through EU agencies and tests the boundaries of the Meroni doctrine. It balances supranational oversight with national discretion. This chapter examines AMLA’s institutional design and how its hybrid model links supervision with convergence, capacity building, and data-driven governance. A comparison of AMLA with other EU financial agencies and bodies identifies key innovations in governance, supervisory technology, and legal doctrine. While AMLA promises coherence in Anti-Money Laundering/Countering the Financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT) enforcement, its success will depend on cultivating trust, legitimacy, and resilience within a multilevel governance framework.</jats:p>

title: Understanding the Concept of Fluency in Stuttering: A Grounded-Theory Study
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
a685aeb15db732ce2749502bfae71a1aa9e1c40a.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fluency is a widely used concept in stuttering research and clinical practice and has traditionally been approached through observable speech characteristics. Although theoretical and clinical perspectives have acknowledged internal aspects of fluency, the perspectives of people who stutter themselves remain largely unexplored. The purpose of this study was to examine how adults who stutter define fluency and experience it in their daily lives.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ten adults who stutter participated in individual interviews guided by an evolved grounded theory approach. Interviews began with the question, “What does fluency mean to you in the context of stuttering?” and follow-up questions were guided by participants' responses. Recruitment continued until saturation was reached. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analyzed using grounded-theory analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants described fluency as a dynamic construct shaped by the interaction between observable speech and internal experience, dimensions that are not always aligned. Fluent-sounding speech could involve substantial monitoring or tension and not feel fluent, whereas observable stuttering could be experienced as easy and comfortable and feel fluent. In that regard, observably disfluent speech can feel more fluent than observably fluent speech. This interaction was linked to different consequences, including changes in confidence, anxiety, relief, or happiness, and was influenced by emotional, cognitive, social, and therapy-related factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fluency in stuttering cannot be fully understood based only on external speech. Considering both observable and internal aspects of fluency, as well as their consequences, may support more person-centered research and clinical practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: The Role of Religion and Spirituality in Clinical Practice: Considerations for Speech-Language Pathologists
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
26368d7f8cec360a6fd02f46b2b14e50af2f76dd.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The purpose of this article is to review the potential role of religion and spirituality in the practice of speech-language pathology and to identify possible clinical resources and directions for future research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We reviewed the literature on health care providers' responses to the religious/spiritual practices of their patients, as well as existing tools for provider self-assessment in this domain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In a diverse and polarized country, it can be difficult for speech-language pathologists to address religious/spiritual practice with the patients and families they serve. These practices, however, may have significant implications for patients' needs and preferences in the domains of speech, language, and swallowing. Clinical tools for addressing these challenges appropriately can be viewed as a component of culturally responsive care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Health Dataspace Technology Acceptance Model (HDS-TAM): Development and Case Evaluation Study of Patient Acceptance of Germany’s Electronic Patient Record
container-title: JMIR Medical Informatics
59c5a2acb4b55cbaa40e50e1c7c0f7f58bade9eb.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The European Health Dataspace (EHDS) expands health data sharing beyond direct care and introduces governance, transparency, trust, and secondary-use considerations that are not fully captured by established technology acceptance models such as the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). To address this gap, we developed the health dataspace technology acceptance model (HDS-TAM) and evaluated it using the German electronic patient record (ePA) as an illustrative health dataspace (HDS) application.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed (1) to derive an HDS-oriented technology acceptance framework from the literature and (2) to assess its applicability in explaining acceptance of the ePA from a patient perspective.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A structured literature review screened 1788 records, reviewed 134 full-text papers, and retained 68 studies for model development. HDS-TAM was subsequently applied in a scenario-based online survey conducted between March and April 2025. Of 235 questionnaire accesses and 163 submitted responses, 149 valid responses were analyzed. Data were analyzed using multiple imputation, exploratory factor analysis, and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The association between behavioral intention and actual ePA use was examined using logistic regression.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The model explained 75.9% of the variance in behavioral intention to use (BI,
                      <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                      ²=0.759), 67% in perceived usefulness (PU,
                      <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                      ²=0.670), and 54% in perceived risk (PR,
                      <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                      ²=0.540). PU showed the strongest positive association with BI (
                      <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                      =.670,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001,
                      <jats:italic>f</jats:italic>
                      ²=0.457), whereas PR showed a small negative association (
                      <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                      =−.149,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.04,
                      <jats:italic>f</jats:italic>
                      ²=0.034). Transparency was positively associated with PU (
                      <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                      =.220,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.001) and perceived ease of use (PEOU;
                      <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                      =.454,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001) and negatively associated with PR (
                      <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                      =−.594,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001). Perceived need (PN) showed a strong positive association with PU (
                      <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                      =.567,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001) but no significant direct association with BI (

                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>

title: Engagement-Supportive Mechanisms in Stress-Focused Digital Mental Health Interventions With Adaptive, Conversational, and Context-Aware Systems: Narrative Review
container-title: JMIR Human Factors
7301e19c45feefeb630a365b5b8099fa710a891f.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Stress is a widespread public health concern associated with cardiovascular disease, depression, anxiety, and reduced quality of life. Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs), delivered through smartphones, web platforms, and wearables, offer scalable support for stress management but often struggle to sustain user engagement. Evidence describing how adaptive, conversational, and context-aware mechanisms function together within stress-focused DMHIs remains fragmented.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This review aims to synthesize evidence on engagement-supportive mechanisms in stress-focused DMHIs, with attention to personalization; biometric feedback; just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs); gamification; AI, including large language models (LLMs); and methodological approaches to studying engagement. It also examines methodological, motivational, and experiential dimensions of engagement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This narrative review was informed by a structured search of PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Scopus for peer-reviewed studies published between January 2018 and April 2025, followed by an evidence update through August 2026. Eligible studies described stress-focused DMHIs or related affective support interventions reporting at least 1 engagement-supportive mechanism. Randomized controlled trials, qualitative investigations, simulation or modeling studies, and implementation studies were included. Data were extracted using a structured form capturing study characteristics, engagement mechanisms, outcomes, and alignment with the review domains. Descriptive mapping summarized study types and mechanism frequencies, while a narrative synthesis integrated behavioral, experiential, methodological, and theory-informed findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thirty-two studies met the inclusion criteria. Randomized or microrandomized controlled trials were the most common design (n=17), followed by qualitative investigations (n=6), design or implementation studies (n=3), mixed methods studies (n=3), simulation or modeling studies (n=2), and a quasi-experimental study (n=1). Dynamic adaptation was identified in 14 studies, conversational support in 10, static tailoring in 9, social or co-design mechanisms in 9, context-aware prompting in 7, gamified reinforcement in 5, biometric-responsive adaptation in 4, and narrative immersion in 2. These mechanisms frequently overlapped within layered adaptive architectures rather than functioning as isolated engagement features. AI-enabled systems included conversational agents, LLM-supported systems, recommender systems, reinforcement learning, and computational modeling approaches. Outcomes included behavioral indicators such as adherence, retention, and prompt receptivity, alongside experiential indicators such as perceived relevance, trust, emotional support, and immersion. Evidence strength varied substantially; many AI-enabled systems contributed feasibility, acceptability, or optimization-oriented evidence rather than definitive comparative effectiveness evidence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Stress-focused DMHIs are increasingly adopting adaptive, conversational, and context-aware engagement-supportive mechanisms, but the evidence base remains heterogeneous and methodologically uneven. Dynamic adaptation, conversational support, and static tailoring were most frequently represented, whereas biometric-responsive adaptation, narrative immersion, and deeply integrated gamified systems were less common. AI-enabled systems may support contextual responsiveness and personalized interaction but require transparent adaptive logic, privacy safeguards, and human-centered evaluation. Future work should prioritize longitudinal, mixed methods research capable of distinguishing behavioral engagement, experiential engagement, feasibility, acceptability, and sustained stress-related outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Two-photon coupling via Josephson element. II. Interaction dressing, cross-Kerr coupling, and limits of the low-energy bosonic model
container-title: Physical Review A
ecdc199bde973ab92e412131dd894c14486804c5.abstract: <jats:p>We study the interactions mediated by a symmetric superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID), their renormalizations, and the applicability of the anharmonic oscillator (bosonic) model for a coupled phase qubit. The latter dwells in its metastable well holding a number of anharmonic energy states. The coupling SQUID can switch between the single- and two-photon interactions . We find that, in the bosonic two-photon regime, the cross-Kerr coupling never vanishes as it dresses due to asymmetry in the qubit potential and nonlinearity of the coupler. Our quantitative results also depend on the bosonic approximation. We approach determining its limits by finding the minimum number of coherent energy states required for a dressing. For that, we lay out diagrams of the dressing virtual processes that climb the qubit ladder as high as possible. Near the two-photon resonance with a coupled resonator, we systematically calculate other relevant renormalizations due to nonresonant interactions. We provide verifiable predictions for the coupling rates. Modified systems can be applied for two-photon detection and for quantum-nondemolition readout of a qubit with an asymmetrical potential.</jats:p>

title: Beyond the Acute Phase: Prevalence and Clinical Characteristics of Unreported Swallowing Impairments in Ambulatory Outpatient Stroke Survivors
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
b6ae26bb056e00088680cb59806440c4ecacfc7e.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Unreported dysphagia, imaging-identified swallowing impairment without symptom reporting, remains poorly characterized beyond the acute phase of stroke. This study aimed to (a) quantify the point prevalence of unreported dysphagia in ambulatory stroke survivors, (b) examine demographic and clinical factors associated with the presentation of this phenomenon, and (c) evaluate concordance between patient-reported symptoms and imaging-derived impairments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective secondary analysis included 45 ambulatory adults ≥ 3 months post–ischemic stroke who underwent videofluoroscopic swallow study and completed the Eating Assessment Tool-10 (EAT-10). Swallowing impairment was defined using the Dynamic Imaging Grade of Swallowing Toxicity (DIGEST Grade ≥ 1), and physiology was characterized using the Modified Barium Swallow Impairment Profile (MBSImP). Participants were classified as having no dysphagia (DIGEST = 0), overt dysphagia (DIGEST ≥ 1 and EAT-10 > 3), or unreported dysphagia (DIGEST ≥ 1 and EAT-10 ≤ 3). Group differences were examined using analysis of variance, Fisher's exact tests, and nonparametric analyses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Sixteen percent (7/45) of participants demonstrated unreported dysphagia, while 44% (20/45) exhibited some degree of swallowing impairment. Unreported and overt dysphagia groups had similar DIGEST grades, yet the unreported dysphagia group reported minimal symptom burden (EAT-10:
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Mdn</jats:italic>
                      = 2) compared to the overt group (EAT-10:
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Mdn</jats:italic>
                      = 9). Significant correlations were observed between the EAT-10 and the MBSImP oral total (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">r</jats:italic>
                      = .510,
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                      < .008), but not DIGEST (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">r</jats:italic>
                      = .21,
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                      = .163). Age, lesion characteristics, time since stroke, and admission stroke severity were not significantly associated with unreported dysphagia.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A clinically meaningful proportion of ambulatory, community-dwelling stroke survivors demonstrated persistent swallowing impairment without symptom reporting. Reliance on symptom-based referral pathways may fail to detect ongoing safety or efficiency deficits. These findings support the consideration of imaging-based surveillance strategies beyond the acute phase of stroke recovery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Quantum dynamical entropy and non-Markovianity: A collisional model perspective
container-title: Physical Review A
eae63fde0786eea53e125b6c41ac35a459b9602d.abstract: <jats:p>Accessing the physical mechanisms behind non-Markovian phenomena in open quantum dynamics requires the study of the full multitime statistical properties of the joint system-environment dynamics. This is impossible at the level of the reduced dynamics of the open system alone as the latter is obtained by suitably eliminating the environment. The task is instead made possible by considering multitime correlation functions involving observables of the open system, only: the open system-environment interactions turn them into global ones, thus building up correlations between the two systems. Multitime correlations form the basis of both the theory of quantum stochastic processes and of the Alicki-Lindblad-Fannes dynamical entropy (ALF entropy for short). This latter quantity provides for quantum systems a measure of the dynamical entropy production as the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy does for classical systems. Indeed, in the following we propose the open-system ALF entropy as a measure of non-Markovianity signaling deviations from the so-called quantum regression regime. In turn, the operational interpretation of the open-system ALF entropy makes it a suitable witness of backflow of information from the environment to the open system. In the case of a collisional model whereby the dissipative dynamics of a finite-level system is obtained by its coupling to an infinite classical spin chain, the ALF entropy can be explicitly computed. It turns out to depend on the parameters characterizing the statistical properties of the environment and can be related to the activation and superactivation of memory effects in the open quantum system.</jats:p>

title: Development and validation of a cefepime population pharmacokinetic model to guide treatment for patients with hospital-acquired pneumonia requiring renal replacement
container-title: Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy
8142bf6d16ad37819e29c243ea04a373ac32e381.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title/>
                    <jats:p>
                      Cefepime is used in critically ill pneumonia patients, but dosing in renal replacement therapy (RRT) is complicated by altered renal function, extracorporeal removal, and variability in pulmonary epithelial lining fluid (ELF) exposure. We sought to develop an integrated model linking systemic, extracorporeal, and pulmonary cefepime pharmacokinetics in RRT. Pharmacokinetic (PK) data from critically ill adults receiving cefepime and requiring RRT were included. In a dedicated continuous RRT (CRRT) cohort (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                      = 8), pre- and post-filter plasma and effluent PK data were collected. Additional patients (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                      = 43) requiring RRT also contributed plasma and ELF samples. A non-parametric population PK model was developed using an 80/20 subject-level development-validation split. Covariate models assessed the impact of residual renal function, effluent flow rate, body size, and fixed intradialytic hemodialysis (HD) clearance. Monte Carlo simulations evaluated plasma and ELF target attainment across dosing strategies, weight strata, and minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs). The final model jointly described systemic, extracorporeal, and pulmonary cefepime disposition using piecewise central volume, native clearance, linear effluent-flow-dependent CRRT clearance, fixed HD clearance, and ELF distribution. Simulations showed adequate plasma target attainment, whereas ELF attainment was sensitive to MIC, target, regimen, and body weight. Continuous infusions of 4 g/day provided adequate ELF attainment at MICs ≤4 mg/L. Plasma-based cefepime target attainment may overestimate pulmonary exposure during RRT, particularly at higher MICs, body weights, and
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">f</jats:italic>
                      T>MIC targets. External validation and prospective studies are needed to refine pulmonary target estimates and determine whether plasma-guided Bayesian dosing can reliably ensure site-of-infection exposure.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Prompt-Based Cognitive Scaffolding
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
bf7bc1447e7ed3caf087f04fb77606d4e98c71c2.abstract: <jats:p>While research on AI literacy, prompt engineering, and prompt literacy has expanded rapidly, an integrated framework explaining prompt-mediated learning remains underdeveloped. We introduce the Prompt-Based Cognitive Scaffolding (PBCS) model, which conceptualizes prompts as regulatory mechanisms that coordinate cognitive, epistemic, and metacognitive processes during human–AI interaction. Building on cognitive scaffolding, distributed cognition, epistemic cognition, and prompt literacy, PBCS explains learning as a recursive coordination process in which human reasoning and AI-generated outputs are continuously refined. The model is operationalized through three interacting scaffolding dimensions and a functional prompt typology. Its explanatory scope is demonstrated across seminar-based learning, academic writing, collaborative learning, and research-oriented inquiry. We provide a theoretical foundation for understanding recursive human–AI knowledge construction.</jats:p>

title: Prompt Engineering as Distributed Cognition and Epistemic Infrastructure in Higher Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
d3ce7c75e5f8d37877d734c90b6dc48c96bd1c5b.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter theorizes prompt literacy as epistemic infrastructure in higher education, conceptualizing prompting as distributed cognition across learners, generative systems, artifacts, and disciplinary genres. It models prompting as a regulated workflow of specification, constraint-synthesis, iterative diagnosis, triangulated verification, uncertainty labelling, and accountable disclosure, reframing authorship as auditable process rather than polished output. Integrating mediated action, activity-system contradictions, pragmatics, genre theory, and epistemic cognition, the chapter translates construct logic into scalable pedagogies, evidence-centred assessment architectures, and integrity-by-design governance. It foregrounds equity as a capability condition, embedding culturally responsive prompting, multilingual burden reduction, accessibility-by-design, and privacy-security postures within institutional quality assurance. The result is a tool-agnostic blueprint for future-ready universities that stabilizes validity, trust, and learning under platform volatility.</jats:p>

title: Prompt Literacy as a Pedagogical Resource
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
feb94f033fe2b7abcd2d34ab83cd576746ea93a7.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education is reshaping teaching, learning, and assessment practices. Within this evolving landscape, prompt literacy, the ability to design, refine, and critically evaluate prompts for AI systems, has emerged as a crucial yet underexplored competency. This chapter conceptualizes prompt literacy as a pedagogical resource within the Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) framework. It argues that while AI introduces new cognitive, pedagogical, and ethical demands, prompt literacy functions as a key resource that helps mitigate these challenges and enhances engagement, teaching effectiveness, and learning outcomes. Drawing on insights from digital literacy, AI literacy, and educational theory, the chapter develops a multidimensional understanding of prompt literacy. It also highlights implications for curriculum design, faculty development, and institutional policy, positioning prompt literacy as a strategic capability for fostering responsible and sustainable AI-enabled education.</jats:p>

title: Prompting for Academic Writing and Research
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
a33a6033f3bf398f73b26ab21bb6cfa211ed34c1.abstract: <jats:p>The chapter examines the role of prompt literacy as a structured academic competence in AI-supported writing and research within higher education. It develops and empirically tests a conceptual framework linking prompt quality to academic writing and research performance through the mediating role of cognitive engagement and the moderating influence of institutional academic integrity orientation. Drawing on cognitive, academic literacy, metacognitive, and socio-technical perspectives, the chapter demonstrates that effective prompting is not merely technical but central to scholarly practice. Findings indicate that high-quality prompts enhance analytical depth, coherence, and methodological clarity, particularly when users actively engage with AI outputs. Furthermore, institutional integrity environments strengthen responsible AI use and amplify performance outcomes. The chapter contributes theoretical, pedagogical, and policy insights by positioning prompt literacy as essential for sustaining academic rigor in AI-mediated scholarship.</jats:p>

title: Predicting Developmental Language Disorder in Bilinguals From Multiple Sources of Evidence: A Decision Tree Approach
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
9bd706b8952d03d5da9a6b4cf44b52056f17b88a.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Speech-language pathologists consider multiple pieces of assessment data when making diagnostic decisions for bilingual children. The current study explored the converging evidence framework by applying a decision tree model, a user-friendly prediction tool, to identify bilingual children with developmental language disorder (DLD) using multiple assessment data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>One hundred eighty-six Spanish–English bilingual children in kindergarten completed a bilingual language assessment battery, consisting of parents' and teachers' questionnaires, standardized language assessment, narrative sample analysis, and dynamic assessment. Decision tree models were constructed to identify DLD.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The decision tree models using (a) bilingual assessment data and (b) bilingual assessment data with parents' and teachers' data as fixed root achieved acceptable sensitivity and specificity. Decision tree models using English-only assessment achieved minimum sensitivity but not minimum specificity. Those using English-only assessment with parents' and teachers' data as fixed root did not achieve acceptable sensitivity or specificity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study suggests that decision tree models can help speech-language pathologists identify bilingual children with DLD using different evidence, aligning with the converging evidence framework. The feasibility of English-only assessment and the clinical use of decision tree models are discussed.</jats:p>

title: A Function-Led Tailored Speech-Language Intervention in Primary Progressive Aphasia: A Retrospective Observational Pre–Post Study From Routine Clinical Practice
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
39c30f8b9acd15f992f05055eb2c31c14ac31251.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Primary progressive aphasia (PPA) is a neurodegenerative disease that affects language abilities. Since no curative or pharmacological treatments are currently available, speech-language therapy represents one of the few clinical intervention options. Furthermore, evidence from routine clinical practice is needed to better characterize language changes associated with tailored, person-centered speech-language therapy approaches in PPA. The aim of this retrospective observational pre–post study was to explore baseline-to-follow-up changes associated with a function-led tailored speech-language intervention delivered in routine clinical practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A retrospective pre–post clinical study was conducted on data collected from individuals with a diagnosis of PPA who received weekly 45-min function-led, tailored speech-language therapy in routine clinical practice over 6–9 months. Patients within each PPA variant were treated using similar core intervention targets reflecting the predominant impaired language domains, while stimuli were personalized using ecologically relevant words and phrases derived from each patient's daily life and communicative needs. Home-based exercises reflecting the same task principles and stimuli used during therapy sessions were assigned and reviewed at each visit. The primary outcome was baseline-to-follow-up change in language performance measured using the Screening for Aphasia in NeuroDegeneration (SAND).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Seventeen individuals with a diagnosis of PPA completed the intervention. Across the whole cohort, pre–post comparisons showed statistically significant changes only in the naming of non-living items and a reduction in semantic errors during picture description. In exploratory subgroup analyses, statistically significant changes were observed in the logopenic variant for SAND overall word/nonword repetition and word repetition.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that function-led, tailored speech-language intervention delivered in routine practice may be associated with changes in selected language measures in individuals with PPA. These results should be considered preliminary and exploratory. Future prospective studies are warranted to further characterize and validate these real-world observations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Supplemental Material:</jats:title>

title: Two Measures, Same Outcome: Comparable Associations Between Exposure Measurements and Language Performance in Bilinguals With and Without Developmental Language Disorder
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
3f135c97ae008aeb5b79d854aabe770df9698d04.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Language exposure is associated with language performance in bilinguals. Two common ways of measuring language exposure are total hours of exposure and percentage of exposure. This study compared differences in these two methods and examined their associations with bilingual language performance. Differences between typically developing (TD) children and those with developmental language disorder (DLD) were also analyzed across exposure measures and language performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants were 1,397 Spanish–English bilingual preschool children (73 identified with DLD). Caregivers reported hour-by-hour language input and output for a typical weekday and a typical weekend. Children's bilingual language performance was measured using a standardized language screener. Correlation and effect size analyses were calculated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Percentage and total hours of exposure were strongly and significantly correlated for both Spanish and English. Both measures showed moderate, significant correlations with bilingual language performance, with minimal differences in effect sizes. Significant group differences emerged between TD and DLD children, with small-to-medium effect sizes. The DLD group showed significantly weaker correlations between language exposure measures and language performance compared to the TD group.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results indicate that both measurement methods are statistically comparable, suggesting that clinicians may use either method to assess language exposure in bilinguals. The weaker correlations observed in the DLD group imply that additional factors beyond exposure influence their bilingual language performance and should be considered in evaluation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>

title: Development of a Multimodal Assessment of Mastication Protocol
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
9f3922ff0973449ccd75d40ea41f9b0ef37cf8a2.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Within the field of speech-language pathology, the only validated noninstrumental assessment of mastication is the Test of Mastication and Swallowing Solids. This assessment protocol offers limited applicability and ecological validity, as it does not reflect typical meals, which involve greater volume and varied textures. Recognizing the need for a more comprehensive evaluation of mastication, this study aims to develop and evaluate a novel assessment protocol of the oral preparatory phase in healthy participants with typical chewing/swallowing. This protocol includes literature-based measures of masticatory parameters, a color-changing gum, and motion analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Using a within-subject design, 50 participants chewed a color-changing gum that was analyzed using Commission Internationale de l'Eclairage L*a*b* (CIELAB) values. Participants chewed a baby carrot, a shortbread cookie, and a Hi-Chew candy. The number of chews was manually counted and further measured using two-dimensional motion analysis. Participants completed a social validity questionnaire evaluating the assessment protocol. CIELAB values were correlated with masticatory parameters using Pearson's
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">r</jats:italic>
                      . Agreement between manually counted and motion analysis data was examined using intraclass correlation coefficients. Descriptive statistics were analyzed from Likert scale responses on the social validity questionnaire.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Mean CIELAB values reflected existing normative data; however, no significant correlation was observed between colorimetric data and masticatory parameters. The accuracy of two-dimensional motion analysis varied by texture. Chews for the carrot demonstrated the highest reliability, chews for the Hi-Chew candy had moderate reliability, and chews for the shortbread cookie had the lowest reliability. Participants rated the protocol favorably, emphasizing value in the assessment battery rather than individual components.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings provide preliminary evidence in support of a multidimensional evaluation of mastication. Nonsignificant correlations between masticatory parameters and gum outcomes suggest that each captures distinct aspects of mastication. Two-dimensional motion analysis shows promise for semi-automated chew counting, though further refinement is needed for broader texture applications. Overall, positive participant perceptions support continued exploration of the assessment protocol in clinical populations.</jats:p>

title: Dynamical large deviations, self-similarity, and criticality
container-title: Physical Review Research
44c3514b75caf9f02adc86e340b336120037f50d.abstract: <jats:p>Large-deviation theory describes the statistics of rare fluctuations, while self-similarity captures scale-invariant behavior. Both are central pillars of statistical physics, yet the extent of their overlap is not well understood. Here, we ask whether a stochastic process can simultaneously satisfy both. We show that, under a precise set of conditions—exact self-similarity governed by one Hurst exponent and a scaled cumulant-generating function that is analytic around the origin—compatibility holds only if the scaling distribution is Gaussian. We illustrate this result with a broad class of subordinated stochastic processes, including continuous-time random walks, diffusing-diffusivity models, and polymers in the grand-canonical ensemble. In non-Gaussian cases, a characteristic timescale separates regular large-deviation and self-similar regimes. At criticality, the divergence of the correlation time and the emergence of a singular cumulant generating function make a regular large-deviation description inappropriate and lead to a strong enhancement of extreme dynamical fluctuations.</jats:p>

title: Establishing perturbatively the Kostelecký conjecture in all massive sectors of the standard-model extension
container-title: Physical Review D
0d4ba67e9fdf1ba29dc498cdd824ae0770df27a9.abstract: <jats:p>Modified dispersion relations arising in Lorentz-violating effective field theories alter the propagation of free particles and lead to observable deviations from standard relativistic kinematics. We show that, under regularity and nondegeneracy conditions, such kinematical modifications naturally induce local pseudo-Finsler geometric structures governing the free-particle propagation. The pseudo-Finsler framework provides a geometric interpretation of Lorentz invariance violation effects, encoding them in branch-dependent structures on spacetime. The construction is illustrated in the massive sectors of the standard model extension, where modified dispersion relations define local pseudo-Finsler geometries determined by the particle species acting as a spacetime probe. In this setting, we therefore construct a perturbative proof of the Kostelecký conjecture in all the physical massive subsectors of the standard model extension.</jats:p>

title: Plasmonic lithography optical proximity correction method based on a decomposed machine-learning fast imaging model
container-title: Optics Express
f5a71eddc35cdf10aae1d107e6b06cf7c5d92b62.abstract: <jats:p>Strong near-field coupling in plasmonic lithography readily induces optical proximity effects such as line-end shortening, corner rounding, and local linewidth variation. In contrast, conventional model-driven optical proximity correction (OPC) requires repeated rigorous electromagnetic field calculations in each iteration, which severely limits computational efficiency. To address this issue, this paper proposes a plasmonic lithography OPC method based on decomposition-based machine-learning fast-imaging model. The method uses a pre-trained imaging transfer matrix to rapidly predict the photoresist image (PRI) of mask patterns. It embeds this prediction into a closed-loop optimization process driven by edge placement error (EPE) feedback. The signed EPE determines the movement direction of each edgex`, and an adaptive correction coefficient that varies with the overall EPE controls the movement distance, thereby enabling an iterative correction flow of fast imaging, threshold exposure, EPE calculation, edge movement, and mask update. Simulation results on seven complex two-dimensional patterns show that the proposed method converges stably under different illumination modes, pattern sizes, and polarization states, with the main errors decreasing rapidly within the first six iterations. After ten correction iterations, the average reductions in the sum of absolute EPE and pattern error are 75.03% and 63.54%, respectively, under TE polarization, and 73.77% and 63.02%, respectively, under TM polarization. Compared with OPC, which is based on a rigorous electromagnetic field imaging model on the same hardware platform, the overall computational efficiency, including the one-time training cost, is approximately 4 times higher. These results indicate that the proposed method can significantly reduce computational cost while maintaining correction accuracy and convergence stability, providing an effective route for fast plasmonic lithography OPC of complex two-dimensional patterns.</jats:p>

                    <jats:italic>Nucl. Mater. Energy</jats:italic>
                    <jats:bold>33</jats:bold>

                    <jats:italic>Contrib. Plasma Phys.</jats:italic>

New boundary condition types were implemented in the code to allow for multisine gas injection perturbations, as well as reservoir models for remote vessel regions without plasma. In steady state, it is possible to simulate plasmas ranging from attached to deeply detached using different gas injection rates. This allows for comparison between simulation and experimental results at similar levels of detachment. Comparison between simulation and experimental data in the frequency domain shows that the AFN SOLPS-ITER simulations predict faster response times to divertor fuelling perturbations than the experiments, likely in part due to the fluid approximation used for the neutrals.
