title: Can artificial intelligence align with Indigenous science?
container-title: Science
1909437f50640b985bc0294e2f2fafead20ae9e7.abstract: <jats:p>As the use of generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) increases, alarms are being raised about how the technology could replace human contribution, override human supervision, ignore ethical and technical guardrails, and cause increasingly irreparable harm to the environment. This creates potentially destructive outcomes for life on Earth. From a traditional Indigenous science perspective, such possibilities in themselves would be enough to immediately stop presently configured AI releases. In a Lakota context, science must ensure as little harm as possible is done to life. Therefore, AI as presently configured simply would not qualify to advance further from an ethical and scientific standpoint. Indigenous science asks something fundamentally different than what AI presently seeks to, or can, answer. But that does not mean that future forms of AI can never align with Indigenous science.</jats:p>

title: From business intelligence to conservation intelligence: Operationalizing adaptive pest control of crown‐of‐thorns starfish to protect the resilience of the Great Barrier Reef
container-title: Conservation Science and Practice
d67e5315f9d64bddc255d4a5f344e4956a169c64.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Resilience‐based management (RBM)—which focuses explicitly on preserving and actively enhancing an ecosystem's capacity to resist and recover from cumulative disturbances under climate change—is crucial for enhancing outcomes in conservation interventions as the climate changes. To be effective it requires continuous modeling, assessment, evaluation and adjustment. Here, we deploy enterprise Business Intelligence software for the purpose of conservation (i.e., Conservation Intelligence) to provide the near real‐time analytics and decision support system necessary for effective RBM. This approach is demonstrated using the Crown‐of‐Thorns Starfish Control Program on Australia's Great Barrier Reef where integrated visual dashboards were developed to assess outbreak severity, prioritize control actions, evaluate effectiveness and incorporate emerging research to close the research‐implementation gap. The flexibility of Business Intelligence software allows these Conservation Intelligence tools to be built and maintained “in‐house,” meeting the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority's (GBRMPA) explicit needs and reducing dependency on external developers or researchers. Conservation Intelligence tools can synthesize complex spatial–temporal data into flexible, user‐friendly platforms specifically targeting stages of the RBM cycle that enable rapid iterations as programs and ecosystems adapt to climate change. Importantly, this approach is platform‐agnostic and a methodological approach that leverages existing enterprise infrastructure to establish rapid, in‐house solutions. This approach is readily transferable to other conservation challenges, particularly in government‐led programs where enterprise software licenses may already exist and is particularly useful in ecologically complex but data rich environments.</jats:p>

title: Scanning Electron Microscopy Evaluation of the Protective Effects of Fluoridated Dental Materials on Enamel Surface Morphology under Artificial Demineralization
container-title: Materials Science
e7c34139f9de93719c2b33fb2b27226fbe328425.abstract: <jats:p>The primary aim of this in vitro study was to compare enamel surface morphology following standardized artificial demineralization among five protective dental materials and an untreated control. Specifically, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was used to characterize acid-exposed and wax-protected enamel regions and to compare five-point ordinal surface-preservation scores across the six experimental groups. Fifty-four human premolars extracted for orthodontic reasons provided 108 enamel surfaces. A 2 × 3 mm window was prepared on each surface, and specimens were randomly assigned to six groups (n = 18): control, APF gel containing 1.23 % fluoride ions, Enamel Pro Varnish containing 5 % sodium fluoride (NaF), Enamel Pro Prophy Paste with ACP, fluoride-releasing light-cured Pro Seal, and Duraphat containing 5 % sodium fluoride (NaF). Specimens were stored in artificial saliva and exposed to an artificial caries solution at pH 4.4 twice daily for 1 h over 30 days. After cycling, the surfaces were examined by SEM at ×500 and ×1500 magnifications. Images were morphologically classified and rated using a five-point ordinal surface-preservation scale, in which lower scores indicated better preservation. Data were analysed using the Kruskal–Wallis test followed by Holm-adjusted Dunn comparisons. Mean ordinal SEM scores were 5.00, 3.72, 2.06, 3.06, 3.50, and 3.56 for Groups A–F, respectively, with an overall group difference (H(5) = 68.32, p < 0.001). Enamel Pro Varnish had the lowest mean ordinal SEM score (2.06), although its difference from Group D was not statistically significant after Holm adjustment (p = 0.115). Although all treated groups had more favourable ordinal SEM scores than the control, none reproduced the SEM appearance of untreated sound enamel.</jats:p>

title: Prediction of Compressive Strength of Activated Binary Cement Mortars Using Response Surface Methodology and Artificial Neural Networks
container-title: Materials Science
a17df555f65a3730a334ba0b3ecd4e74df684b43.abstract: <jats:p>This study investigates the prediction of the compressive strength of activated binary cement mortars containing ground granulated blast-furnace slag (GGBFS) using two complementary modelling approaches: response surface methodology (RSM) and an artificial neural network (ANN). A database of 96 mix–curing combinations was assembled from the published literature on activated slag cement systems. Four input parameters were considered: slag replacement ratio (0–70 %), slag fineness (Blaine, 320–650 m²/kg), curing temperature (20–80 °C) and curing time (1–90 days). The output variable was the 1- to 90-day compressive strength (9–64 MPa). A second-order RSM polynomial was fitted and analysed by ANOVA, while a back-propagation feed-forward ANN with a 4–9–6–1 architecture and hyperbolic tangent activation was trained using the L-BFGS algorithm. The ANN reached R² = 0.996 and RMSE = 0.92 MPa over the whole dataset, clearly outperforming the RSM model (R² = 0.785, RMSE = 6.83 MPa). Sensitivity analysis showed that curing time was the dominant predictor (62 %), followed by slag fineness (22 %), curing temperature (8 %) and slag replacement ratio (8 %). The results confirm that ANN is a more reliable surrogate for the highly non-linear hydration kinetics of activated slag mortars and can be used to support mix-design decisions and reduce experimental effort.</jats:p>

title: Teaching UX Design to Engineers in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: The Double Diamond as a Framework for Reskilling
container-title: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology
883eb6d750049ed9ab384415097dc29d20dfa0bb.abstract: <jats:p>As generative artificial intelligence transforms software development and digital design practices, engineering education must address the interplay between technical expertise, an understanding of user needs, and critical judgment. This article examines the contribution of UX Design education to this evolution, using the Double Diamond model as a framework for structuring the design process. The research is based on a pedagogical experiment conducted at the École Supérieure Privée d’Ingénierie et de Technologies (ESPRIT) in Tunisia, as part of a 21-hour module for fourth-year students in web and mobile development during the 2025–2026 academic year. The methodological approach is based on the observation of teaching practices and the analysis of student work, including user interviews, personas, usage scenarios, and prototypes. The Double Diamond framework organizes the process into four phases: discover, define, develop, and deliver. It allows for an examination of how students explore usage scenarios, reframe problems, develop solutions, and subject their proposals to evaluation. The article also proposes a cross-cutting examination of the role of generative artificial intelligence in these phases, distinguishing between assisted production and the validation of design choices. It advances the hypothesis that teaching UX design can help broaden the skill set of future engineers, provided that technical mastery is integrated with human understanding, experimentation, and decision-making responsibility. This exploratory research proposes an analytical framework for studying this integration without presupposing the effects of the approach prior to the analysis of empirical data</jats:p>

title: Mapping Artificial Neural Networks on Minds and Brains—Problems and a Possible Solution
container-title: Boston Studies in the Philosophy and History of Science
Portuguese Studies in Philosophy of Science
66ae1b20a68a74b9e769c736ca13bbad8a091f0f.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In recent years, the advance of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) has been tremendous. Everyone got thrilled about what Large Language Models (LLMs) such as Chat GPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, etc. can do. Even though this excitement is largely justified, one may want to think about the deeper implications, i.e. whether sooner or later a grandchild of these systems will be intelligent and is even able to constitute some sort of mind. To give an answer is not easy, but there may be a way of trying to solve this incredibly complex question. It is often held that ANNs are inspired by what we know about the human mind and brain. Consequently, we should start by asking the question if ANNs are well equipped to simulate minds or emulate brains, or to put it differently, if ANNs can be mapped onto minds or brains. Traditional standard approaches in Cognitive Science suggest that either ANNs are potentially good models to—sooner or later—simulate minds and emulate brains, or they are not. The question of the specific correspondence criteria between ANNs and mind/brains, however, is often neglected. In what follows, we will think about what it means for an ANN to correspond to a mind or brain. We will conclude that the way traditional views think about ANNs and mind/brains is largely flawed. It is rather full of category mistakes. After analyzing the issue, we will finish by laying out a solution to this problem.</jats:p>

title:
Self‐Matting Waterborne Polyurethane for
                    <scp>PVC</scp>
                    Artificial Leather Finishing
container-title: Journal of Applied Polymer Science
c1270efcec05433f401803e38963107f816bacc7.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The development of low‐gloss waterborne polyurethane coatings for Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC) artificial leather finishing without external matting agents remains challenging. In this work, self‐matting waterborne polyurethane (SMWPU) dispersions were synthesized by the prepolymer method using Polytetramethylene ether glycol (PTMG‐2000), Isophorone diisocyanate (IPDI), Dimethylolpropionic acid (DMPA), and Trimethylolpropane (TMP). The effects of the isocyanate index (
                    <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                    value), DMPA content, and TMP content on particle size, Zeta potential, dispersion stability, thermal stability, surface morphology, and gloss were systematically investigated. Increasing the
                    <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                    value increased particle size and surface roughness, reducing gloss from 3.18 to 2.67. Increasing DMPA content enhanced surface charge density and dispersion stability, with the lowest gloss of 2.65 at 1.8 wt% DMPA. Increasing TMP content increased crosslinking density and particle size, with the lowest gloss of 2.66 at 1.2 wt% TMP, while improving thermal stability. SEM analysis showed that particle size and distribution strongly affected surface morphology, and a uniformly rough surface was essential for effective self‐matting. These findings provide practical guidance for developing low‐gloss SMWPU coatings for PVC artificial leather finishing.
                  </jats:p>

title: A Sequential Foresight–Delphi Protocol for Diagnosing Anticipatory Legitimacy: Futures Wheel, Causal Layered Analysis, and Delphi Applied to Artificial Intelligence‐Powered Digital Government in Vietnam
container-title: FUTURES & FORESIGHT SCIENCE
c4b5702331b837b56accac381f090571ee3bf850.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Futures and foresight research offers mature methods for generating consequences, interpreting their meaning, and converging expert judgment, but rarely integrates them into fully specified protocols that diagnose an emerging technology's legitimacy risks before they materialize. This study develops and applies a Sequential Foresight–Delphi Protocol linking Futures Wheel consequence mapping, Causal Layered Analysis (CLA), and Delphi appraisal through prespecified transition rules, ex ante consensus criteria, a stability‐based stopping rule, and retention of dissensus. The protocol diagnoses anticipatory legitimacy, the prospective justifiability of AI‐enabled public authority, across consequential visibility, institutional responsiveness, and narrative alignment. It was applied in Vietnam, a critical illustrative case of compressed digital transformation, with a Quadruple Helix panel (26 invited; 20 completing every round). The panel anticipated efficiency gains cascading into accountability gaps, profiling, exclusion, and faceless administration; CLA traced the risks to a technocratic worldview and participant‐supplied images condensed as the algorithmic mandarin. Across two original Delphi rounds (urgency, feasibility) and two supplementary rounds (legitimacy‐enhancing potential), the panel converged on impact assessment, public registers, human review, and sandboxes, whereas contestability‐by‐design and independent audit reached consensus on urgency and legitimacy‐enhancing potential (for audit, without meeting the stability criterion) yet did not converge on feasibility, retaining the portfolio's two lowest feasibility ratings. We advance this asymmetry as an open–closed proposition for comparative testing. All claims concern expert‐anticipated consequences and judgments; no causal, predictive, or statistically generalizable claims are made.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence in Solfeggio Teaching and Learning: Current Status, Needs, And Lecturer-Guided Priorities
container-title: Journal of Social Science and Human Research Studies
ee8e034db935c8130d1d88853d30058f3c3985c5.abstract: <jats:p>Background: Solfeggio requires repeated practice in listening, pitch production, rhythmic accuracy, and sight-singing, yet students may receive limited feedback during independent study. Objective: This study investigated teaching and self-practice difficulties, artificial intelligence (AI) readiness, and preferred support functions at Hong Duc University, Vietnam. Methods: A descriptive mixed-methods design used 12 valid lecturer questionnaires, 72 retained student questionnaires from 80 screened, and six semi-structured lecturer interviews collected during 1-7 September 2026. Frequencies, percentages, item-level means on five-point scales, and thematic summaries were examined without inferential testing. Results: Lecturers prioritized AI-assisted pitch practice and recognition (4.75/5) and listening, recording, and error identification (4.67/5). Students gave the strongest priority to exercises matched to individual errors (4.63/5) and recording with basic error detection (4.61/5). Readiness to try AI tools was 4.08/5 among lecturers; students’ readiness to use AI with lecturer guidance was 4.50/5. Concerns about feedback accuracy were substantial in both groups. Conclusion: The findings support a limited, lecturer-supervised role for AI in self-practice and formative feedback. They do not establish the effectiveness of any particular AI system.</jats:p>

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Sales Productivity: Field Experiments in Online Retail
container-title: Management Science
14d2d69361838d5ca6a668adfbdd71066da0222a.abstract:
<jats:p>We quantify the short-term impact of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) on sales performance through a series of large-scale randomized field experiments involving millions of users and products at a leading crossborder online retail platform. Over 2023–2024, the platform integrated GenAI into seven business workflows spanning customer service, consumer-product matching, advertising, and seller services. We find that GenAI adoption increases sales in most workflows, with effects ranging from no detectable impact to 16.3% depending on GenAI’s marginal contribution relative to baseline firm practices. Across the four GenAI applications with positive sales effects, the implied annual incremental value is roughly $5 per consumer—an economically meaningful impact given the retailer’s scale and the early stage of GenAI adoption. The gains operate primarily through higher conversion rates rather than larger cart values, consistent with GenAI improving the shopping experience by reducing search, information, communication, and personalization frictions. Importantly, these effects are not associated with worse postpurchase outcomes as product return rates and customer ratings do not deteriorate. Finally, we document substantial demand-side heterogeneity, with larger gains for less experienced consumers. Our findings provide novel, large-scale causal evidence on how GenAI shapes sales productivity in online retail, highlighting both its immediate value and broader potential.</jats:p>

title: Beyond the Cleft: Can Artificial Intelligence Redefine the Future of Cleft Care
container-title: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology
7353008bd6caa7c626928cb42aafa8d9a1eec7eb.abstract: <jats:p>Cleft lip and palate (CLP) represent a major group of congenital craniofacial conditions that require coordinated, long-term care involving multiple healthcare specialties. The increasing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in dentistry and orthodontics has opened new avenues for addressing the diagnostic and therapeutic complexities associated with cleft management. This narrative review examines the evolving applications of AI throughout the CLP treatment pathway, highlighting its potential contributions to clinical assessment, treatment planning, and outcome evaluation. The review considers seven key areas in which AI-based technologies may support cleft care. These include the identification of cleft anomalies from prenatal ultrasound and photographic images using deep learning algorithms; computer-assisted planning and digital fabrication of nasoalveolar molding appliances; automated localization of cephalometric landmarks in patients with atypical craniofacial structures; three-dimensional assessment and segmentation of alveolar bone grafts using conebeam computed tomography (CBCT); radiographic identification of dental abnormalities frequently associated with CLP; predictive modelling of orthognathic surgical requirements and postoperative facial soft-tissue changes; and computerized analysis of speech patterns associated with velopharyngeal dysfunction. Research in these areas suggests that AI may improve the efficiency and consistency of diagnostic procedures, facilitate quantitative analysis, and assist clinicians in complex treatment decisions. However, the translation of these technologies into routine clinical practice remains challenging. Important barriers include limited sample sizes, inadequate representation of patient populations, insufficient validation across independent clinical settings, the possibility of algorithmic bias, and ethical issues related to patient data protection and professional accountability. For orthodontists involved in cleft care, AI offers opportunities to enhance clinical decision-making and streamline selected aspects of treatment. Nevertheless, its outputs must be interpreted in conjunction with comprehensive clinical examination, patient-specific findings, and multidisciplinary expertise. Future research should prioritize larger and more diverse datasets, independent clinical validation, transparent reporting, and evaluation of real-world patient outcomes to establish the reliability and clinical value of AI-assisted approaches in CLP management.</jats:p>

title: Finlet AI: An Evidence-Driven Multi-Agent Financial Intelligence Platform Using Model Context Protocol and Deterministic Risk Governance
container-title: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
27dad0acee8d55eb44e2d11a6bed4fb2d73d8d08.abstract: <jats:p>Standalone conversational language models struggle to satisfy audit and compliance standards in institutional equity research. When an equity analyst prompts an ungrounded model to evaluate a listed company, three operational defects appear almost immediately: the model quotes outdated share prices from its pre-training cutoff, invents page or footnote numbers when summarizing regulatory filings, and produces inconsistent numerical risk ratings when executed repeatedly on identical inputs. This paper presents Finlet AI, a twelve-layer multi-agent financial intelligence platform that decouples quantitative market arithmetic and primary-source retrieval from neural text synthesis. Once an analytical query is submitted through our asynchronous FastAPI gateway, a stateful LangGraph supervisor triggers concurrent parallel fan-out across three specialized domain workers covering historical price series, live financial news feeds, and statutory annual reports isolated behind standardized Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool interfaces. Technical price action, 20-day volume momentum ratios, and 30-day annualized volatility (σ	) are computed directly from three-month 30d Open-High-Low-Close-Volume (OHLCV) series fetched via Yahoo Finance. Real-time news catalysts are gathered through Google News RSS syndication and sanitized of HTML markup, while balance-sheet debt and liquidity disclosures are extracted page by page from SEC Form 10-K and Indian annual reports indexed locally in ChromaDB using 384-dimensional all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings. Rather than delegating risk scoring to subjective prompt completion, our Risk & Governance module evaluates a bounded mathematical index weighting volatility (45% weight), news sentiment risk (35% weight), and filing flags (20% weight). Live validation on Reliance Industries (RELIANCE.NS) demonstrates real-time tracking at ₹1,184.50 (−2.03%), 23.1% annualized volatility, 1.0x volume momentum, and a deterministic risk score of 0.365 (LOW), while high-risk runs (≥ 0.65) pause at a persistent SQLite Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) checkpoint before compiling the final ReportLab PDF dossier..</jats:p>

title: Leveraging artificial intelligence for livestock genetics and breeding
container-title: Journal of Animal Science and Biotechnology
eba8a3caeb994d216fed8f4e16eb6eb3fc4c1161.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming modern society including animal genetics and breeding which is essential for meeting global nutritional needs in supplying milk, meat, and eggs among the most complete sources of protein and micronutrients. Although animal breeding has a long history of using data-driven prediction methods, the application of modern AI approaches remains at a relatively early stage and shows substantial potential for wide-ranging applications in animal genetics and breeding. This study aims to review the current use of AI tools in livestock species across three major applications of high interest: AI-assisted phenotyping, AI-enabled dissection of complex-trait biology (focusing on AI-assisted GWAS and AI-for-omics), and AI-assisted genomic prediction. In addition, we discussed emerging methods and tools developed in human genetics that are not yet widely adopted in farm animals but may offer translational potential for future livestock studies. Looking ahead, AI breakthroughs in livestock genetics and breeding are likely to be driven by increases in data scale and resolution, enhanced computational capacities, standardized data infrastructure and benchmarking, and systematic method development and validation. From a livestock genetic improvement perspective, the key value of AI will lie in integrating AI-generated inputs, including improved phenotyping and biological insights, into practical breeding decisions through statistical modeling.</jats:p>

title: MediDocker: An AI-Enabled Healthcare Intelligence Ecosystem Integrating Clinical Decision Support, Predictive Analytics, and Emergency Response
container-title: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
d04969a768c3b17a9f37083acda948b7e5571bb5.abstract: <jats:p>Patients keep their health information in places that do not talk to each other: handwritten prescriptions, PDF blood reports, appointment cards and paper bills, and in an emergency nobody can quickly see their blood group or allergies. This paper presents MediDocker, a web platform that keeps these records in one secure place and explains them in plain language. A vision-language model (Qwen2.5-VL, run locally) only copies what a prescription says; every medicine is then verified against RxNorm, an Indian brand dictionary and a hand-checked drug table, and its purpose and warnings come from verified sources, never from the model. Blood (CBC) reports are encrypted, read with a PDF text layer or PaddleOCR, checked by seven plausibility rules, and followed across reports with reference change values, a personal set point and Theil–Sen projection. A LightGBM model trained on 14,134 laboratory-confirmed NHANES participants screens for iron deficiency from the CBC alone and answers only when it is confident, otherwise advising a serum ferritin test. On 1,945 unseen participants from 2021 onwards it reached an AUROC of 0.836 (95% CI 0.816–0.857) and 94.2% accuracy on the 10.6% of cases it decides, with sensitivity 99.6% and specificity 99.3% at its two cut-offs. A record-aware assistant detects emergencies with rules before any language model is used, and an Ed25519-signed emergency QR code can be verified offline by anyone, without login</jats:p>

title: Agentic Artificial Intelligence for Decision-Making Augmentation in Higher Education Administration
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
4753ec1853130197948d90a206fa4f559f31bc1c.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid digital transformation of higher education has intensified the need for more adaptive, data-driven administrative decision-making systems. This chapter examines the emergence of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) as a transformative approach that extends beyond traditional analytics and generative models by enabling autonomous, goal-directed, and context-aware decision processes. It outlines the conceptual foundations of agentic AI through intelligent agent theory, decision intelligence, and socio-technical systems, and analyzes its core capabilities, including perception, reasoning, planning, and action. The chapter further explores its applications across key administrative domains and highlights its potential to enhance efficiency, predictive capacity, and institutional responsiveness. Despite these benefits, critical challenges related to governance, ethics, data fragmentation, and human-AI collaboration are emphasized, underscoring the need for balanced and responsible implementation.</jats:p>

title: Decision Intelligence for AI-Enabled University Governance and Data-Driven Administrative Transformation
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
1ea21bd12f81b110514bb8aff08dc36ff1204ee4.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming governance and administrative processes in higher education institutions. Traditional systems relying on manual operations and fragmented data are increasingly inadequate. This chapter proposes an AI-driven decision intelligence framework for efficient, data-driven, and policy-aligned governance. The framework integrates data collection, preprocessing, feature selection, and predictive analytics within a unified architecture, where institutional data from student, financial, and human resource systems are analyzed using machine learning models to generate insights. These are refined through policy-based decision mechanisms to ensure transparency and compliance. Results show improved decision accuracy, operational efficiency, and reduced processing time, supported by dashboards for real-time monitoring. Ethical concerns such as data privacy and bias are also addressed. A case study from Tamil Nadu demonstrates the framework's applicability as a scalable model for AI-enabled governance.</jats:p>

title: From Data–Model Fit to Model–World Fit: A Framework for Integrating Domain Knowledge into Artificial Intelligence
container-title: Information Systems Research
90b62a3119c6508d0cc057bd92609f5992407b47.abstract:
<jats:p>Machine learning (ML)–based artificial intelligence (AI) systems often perform well in controlled settings but fail when deployed in the real world. These failures stem from a fundamental problem: ML/AI models optimize data–model fit by increasing statistical performance on training data, whereas real-world deployment demands a new paradigm in ML/AI: model–world fit that preserves domain semantics and contextual understanding. We propose a machine learning model–world fit framework that provides both a conceptual structure for understanding how domain knowledge shapes ML/AI systems and a research road map for investigating these relationships. The framework identifies how domain knowledge can be integrated into the ML/AI development process via external knowledge representations, such as data, value, process models, or domain ontologies. Incorporating external knowledge representations can help overcome three types of knowledge deficiencies in AI: know-what, know-how, and know-why. To illustrate the framework, we apply it to a child welfare placement case, a domain in which contextual understanding is critical and statistical accuracy is an insufficient evaluation criterion. Our insights lead to several directions for scholars working at the intersection of machine learning, design science, and knowledge representation.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>History: Ahmed Abbasi, Senior Editor; Min Zhao, Associate Editor.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/isre.2023.0031 .</jats:p>

title: Multi-institutional Patient-Level Comparison of Decipher Genomic Classifier and Artera Multimodal Artificial Intelligence in Prostate Cancer
container-title: Clinical Cancer Research
d1076de8b8fd22d9d5f26b811c8b60d002ae17f0.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The Decipher Prostate Genomic Classifier (GC) and ArteraAI Multimodal Artificial Intelligence (MMAI) platform are widely used prognostic tools for localized prostate cancer, yet no direct comparison has been performed within the same patient cohort.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Experimental Design:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We sought to evaluate the concordance and prognostic value of GC and MMAI across multi-institutional cohorts totaling 688 patients with localized and oligometastatic prostate cancer. These included populations enriched for African American and East Asian patients. GC and MMAI scores were stratified into risk groups based on specimen type [biopsy or radical prostatectomy (RP)]. The primary endpoint was distant metastasis–free survival, measured from diagnosis to last follow-up or event.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GC and MMAI scores were significantly correlated across multiple cohorts. In Moffitt RP, biopsy, and National Cancer Centre Singapore cohorts, both MMAI and GC were prognostic alone and after adjusting for clinical variables. Multivariable analysis, including both biomarkers and clinical variables, showed that MMAI was significant even when accounting for GC in Moffitt RP and borderline in Moffitt biopsy. Analysis of concordant/discordant cases showed that patients who were high risk for both GC and MMAI did qualitatively worse. In pathway analysis, concordance with GC and MMAI was high for Moffitt RP and oligometastatic patients. Across both biopsy cohorts, although most biological pathways were concordant, there were consistent discordant signaling, metabolic, and DNA repair pathways.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In the first direct patient-level comparison of GC and MMAI in prostate cancer, these biomarkers were found to demonstrate moderate correlation, and both biomarkers demonstrated prognostic value across diverse populations and disease states.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Data Analytics for Smart Grid
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI Technologies for Renewable Energy Systems and Intelligent Grid Optimization
36115464283b4a94eb1013a154df03e7f1a1e053.abstract: <jats:p>As the earth's energy requires to grow, it is important to make sustainable power sources like sun, wind, and hydropower work as efficiently as possible. As power lines get more complicated and energy sources change, old ways of managing energy are not always up to the task. So, there is a greater need for new energy systems and methods to deal with issues like energy loss and waste. Big data and AI are transforming renewable energy and grid system worldwide. These technologies optimise renewable energy generation as demand for novel energy systems develops. AI-powered Smart Grid Technology improves real-time monitoring and matches energy flows to demand. Additionally, AI-driven energy optimization improves solar and wind resource allocation and operating efficiency. Predictive analytics improves renewable energy management by predicting output and consumption. This article shows how AI and big data are becoming crucial in renewable energy and grid management system. It addresses how improved forecasting and energy efficiency create a more robust and sustainable energy future.</jats:p>

title: The Synergy Between Smart Grids and Artificial Intelligence
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI Technologies for Renewable Energy Systems and Intelligent Grid Optimization
0cb2dc1ceaa5b8676d1cb89d0dc6729d797fa8dd.abstract: <jats:p>This study explores the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with smart grid systems to enhance renewable energy utilization and intelligent mobility. It highlights the transition from centralized power systems to decentralized, data-driven energy networks supported by IoT, big data, and advanced communication technologies. AI techniques such as machine learning and predictive analytics enable accurate demand forecasting, efficient energy management, and grid stability. The research also examines challenges in renewable integration, including intermittency and storage limitations, and presents AI-based solutions. Furthermore, it emphasizes the role of electric vehicles and vehicle-to-grid systems in achieving sustainable mobility, ultimately contributing to resilient, efficient, and environmentally friendly energy ecosystems.</jats:p>

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Practice: How Should Rheumatologists Evaluate and Monitor Emerging Tools?
container-title: Arthritis Care & Research
3f160ed41d422ffb9dd3b8b7e40c689996ef000c.abstract:
<jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in rheumatology practice, to assist with tasks such as documentation, record summarization, and clinical decision support. Rheumatologists need a practical approach to determining what evidence and oversight each application requires. This narrative review proposes a framework based on two dimensions: contextual complexity and influence on patient care. Greater contextual complexity can make errors harder to detect, whereas greater influence on care increases the potential consequences of an undetected error. We examine evidence for workflow benefits and clinical effectiveness within this framework and consider safety, equity, privacy, governance, and implementation. Existing evidence on the benefits, accuracy, and reliability of AI applications remains mixed. For example, studies of ambient AI scribes suggest reduced documentation burden, but evidence of improved patient outcomes from applications supporting clinical decisions is more limited. For applications with limited clinical influence, evaluation has initially focused on workflow, usability, and documentation quality. Tools that synthesize longitudinal information require additional assessment of completeness and source traceability. Those influencing diagnosis or treatment require prospective evaluation of clinical benefit and safety. Relevant vendor evidence should be assessed alongside proportionate local testing and ongoing monitoring. Safeguards should address risks such as hallucinations, automation bias, and propagating documentation errors, with attention to performance across patient groups. Changes in functionality or clinical use should prompt reassessment. The framework provides a structured basis for adoption decisions and identifies priorities for research on patient outcomes and feasible oversight in routine rheumatology care.</jats:p>

title: Using Artificial Intelligence in Qualitative Lupus Pregnancy Research: The Potential of Large Language Models and Prompting Strategies
container-title: Arthritis Care & Research
49af6cbea7d0a1475e89a3eeb0df446c8b67b9b6.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our objective was to evaluate the ability of different large language models (LLMs) to translate and analyze qualitative interviews describing pregnancy experiences among women with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). An additional objective was to compare themes identified by LLMs with those identified by human researchers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed 26 semistructured interviews originally conducted in Portuguese by Rodrigues et al among women with SLE exploring their perinatal care experiences. Three prompting strategies (zero‐shot, few‐shot, and chain‐of‐thought) were used on the transcripts across four state‐of‐the‐art LLMs (GPT‐4o, OpenAI; Claude Sonnet 4.5, Anthropic; Gemini 2.5 Flash, Google; and DeepSeek R, DeepSeek) to generate key themes. Model outputs were evaluated using an LLM‐as‐a‐judge framework assessing thematic coverage, thematic unity, and semantic similarity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Across models and prompting strategies, LLMs generated similar themes that closely aligned with those identified by human researchers. LLM‐as‐a‐judge evaluations demonstrated high thematic unity and semantic similarity. Claude Sonnet 4.5 showed the most consistent performance. Few‐shot prompting consistently outperformed zero‐shot and chain‐of‐thought approaches.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>LLMs show promise as supportive tools for analyzing qualitative research by preserving thematic coherence and capturing the complexity of pregnancy experiences in women with SLE. Although zero‐shot prompting is widely used, it produced lower thematic results in our study, whereas few‐shot prompting achieved the most comprehensive and coherent theme extraction. LLM‐assisted qualitative analysis may complement human interpretation and has the potential to support the inclusion of non–English language data and diverse patient perspectives in lupus research.</jats:p>

title: Accuracy and Efficiency of Articicial Intelligence Tools for Transcription in Qualitative Research
container-title: American Journal of Qualitative Research
3fb554ca1ea2ca5b9deafdc6db775bf91436427f.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en"><i>Verbatim transcription in qualitative research is hugely time consuming, yet critical for data validity. The rise in artificial intelligence tools for transcription provides new opportunities for researchers. We assessed the accuracy and efficiency of two widely accessible AI tools and human transcription to provide empirical guidance for researchers.&nbsp; We compared 10 verbatim transcripts generated via three transcription modes: human, Otter.ai and MAXQDA. We compared transcription time, cost, errors (volume and type), and correction time. Results show that the AI tools were highly time/cost efficient but had 2-3 times more errors than human transcription. Accounting for average correction time, AI tools generated a transcript in 1.25 - 2.5 hours for USD31-38 per transcript; thus 3–6 times faster and 3 times cheaper than human transcription. However, human review of AI transcription remains critical for data validity; thus, AI tools can assist in the transcription process versus generating the final product. We develop recommendations for each phase of the research process to maximize the benefits of using AI transcription tools.</i></jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence and Digital Health Policy for Reducing Global Health Inequalities
container-title: Innovation, Governance, and Resilience in Global Health Systems
a214df633cac73fcb7c72dbe04bdbf9a60400dd6.abstract: <jats:p>There are still high levels of inequality in healthcare access, quality of services and health outcomes between regions and populations in global health systems. Digital health technologies and Artificial Intelligence have already become the potential solution to close such disparities through better disease surveillance, increasing telemedicine service access, and assist in making health policy decisions based on the data. This chapter explores how AI-powered healthcare applications and digital health platforms can help to enhance healthcare access and health surveillance of populations as well as identify critical issues related to governance, ethical issues, data privacy, and the digital divide. The chapter, based on the conceptual analysis and the recent case studies, outlines the policy strategies that should be in place to ensure the responsible, inclusive, and equitable implementation of AI technologies in the healthcare systems across the world.</jats:p>

title: Digital Health and Artificial Intelligence in Global Health Policy
container-title: Innovation, Governance, and Resilience in Global Health Systems
9d2e274995dd8f32b7735b3232f10a964121b207.abstract: <jats:p>Digital health and artificial intelligence are becoming influential in shaping global health policy due to the opportunities they will offer in improving access, efficiency and health outcomes globally. At the same time, such technologies spark critical issues regarding inequality, ethics, and governance-especially in developing countries in low-income and middle-income countries. This chapter focuses on how digital health and AI are changing the global health systems and just how both these can have a positive effect or a threat towards those who might not have access to usable technology or AI. It examines policy issues concerning governance, regulation, and human rights and the role of international collaboration when working towards equitable and responsible adoption of health technologies using artificial intelligence.</jats:p>

title: Legal Challenges of Artificial Intelligence in Global Health Policy
container-title: Innovation, Governance, and Resilience in Global Health Systems
8e6a4d0442251e27ef2f25a2b827f4e9de5407b2.abstract: <jats:p>This article focuses on the legal challenges arising from the use of artificial intelligence in healthcare from the perspective of global health policy. While the active application of AI at various stages of healthcare demonstrates increasing efficiency, it also increases legal risks and highlights the necessity of an adapted legal framework. The article argues that the integration of artificial intelligence in healthcare is more challenging from a legal perspective than from a technological or ethical point of view, as it actively raises issues such as patient rights, the principle of informed consent, liability, and other related concerns, requiring coherent regulatory standards and coordinated policy responses. The authors propose a human-centered governance model that ensures the best possible balance, protects human rights and minimizes legal challenges arising from AI-related outcomes.</jats:p>

title: Interpretable Finger Vein Identification: Analysis of Fine-tuned Models with Explainable Artificial Intelligence
container-title: International Journal of Information Technology & Decision Making
28fb2182955c16ae0e2b0018164db6f7aebf61bf.abstract: <jats:p>Although convolutional neural networks report near-perfect accuracy in public finger vein datasets, their operational trustworthiness remains a critical, unevaluated blind spot. This study challenges the conventional reliance on accuracy as the primary metric for model viability. It is hypothesized that state-of-the-art models often achieve high scores not by learning robust vascular patterns, but by overfitting to spurious, nonbiometric cues in the dataset background. To expose this vulnerability, an explainability-driven audit is conducted using Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) on eight deep learning models across two benchmark datasets (SDUMLA and UTFVP). The results reveal a significant accuracy-reliability paradox. The highest-accuracy model, Densely Connected Convolutional Networks (DenseNet121-99.84%), is found to be functionally insecure, heavily relying on background artifacts for prediction. Conversely, Extreme Inception (Xception), despite lower raw accuracy, emerges as the most biometrically faithful architecture (Explainability Score: 89%), consistently targeting valid finger vein patterns. Unlike traditional performance-oriented studies, the primary novelty of this research lies in its explainability-driven audit approach, which systematically evaluates the trustworthiness of deep learning models in finger vein recognition, bridging the gap between high accuracy and model interpretability. This discovery demonstrates that high accuracy can mask significant security flaws, making models vulnerable to presentation attacks. Consequently, explainability is established not as a secondary feature, but as a mandatory security metric. It is proposed that future biometric evaluations must adopt interpretability analysis to ensure models characterize the biological trait rather than dataset noise.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence -Enabled Renewable Energy Management in Smart Cities
container-title: Renewable Energy Systems for Smart Cities and Urban Sustainability
4bffbc9d3ce152f4180027ae5d08a50dd6eca207.abstract: <jats:p>Urbanization and climate challenges are increasing pressure on cities to adopt sustainable energy solutions. Digital innovations such as artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and big data enable smart cities to optimize energy systems. This chapter examines AI-enabled renewable energy management in smart cities, focusing on governance, business models, and sustainability. It is grounded in key theories including Technology Acceptance Model, Diffusion of Innovation, Resource-Based View, Stakeholder Theory, and Sustainable Development Theory. The study highlights how AI enhances energy efficiency through demand forecasting, predictive maintenance, and real-time optimization, while governance and economic mechanisms support large-scale adoption. It also emphasizes community participation and social acceptance as critical factors. The chapter integrates technological, institutional, and socio-economic dimensions to provide insights for policy, research, and practice in sustainable urban energy transitions.</jats:p>

title: The end of the end, the beginning of the end: architecture, artificial intelligence and the exhaustion of the post-classical
container-title: Archnet-IJAR: International Journal of Architectural Research
e6c140b46fd10ab301c9925bbd907d7814e51f19.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This article examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is reconstituting the figure of the architect – not as an external disruption but as the latest instance of a recurring pattern in which mediating tools rewrite the discipline from within. Situating the present moment as the third in a sequence of paradigmatic “ends” diagnosed by Tafuri (1969/1973) and Eisenman (1984), the article traces a genealogy of the architect from Vitruvius through Alberti to the modern professional, and argues that generative AI has mechanically realized the post-classical project Eisenman announced as avant-garde provocation, thereby exhausting its critical force and demanding a fundamental redefinition of architectural labor.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The article employs a critical-theoretical methodology combining historical genealogy with contemporary empirical evidence. It constructs a genealogy of the architect-figure organized around successive mediating instruments (orthographic projection, notation, legal seal, computation, AI), drawing on Tafuri’s ideology critique, Eisenman’s post-classical theory and Carpo’s digital-turn thesis. This theoretical framework is grounded in recent empirical data, including RIBA’s 2024–2025 AI adoption surveys, Schneider et al.’s experimental study of client-AI co-design, Bernstein’s practice-based research and World Economic Forum labor projections.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The article finds that generative AI has industrialized the formal operations Eisenman theorized as avant-garde in 1984 – architecture without origin, without telos, without representational meaning – rendering the post-classical paradigm the default rather than the transgression. This exhaustion produces an asymmetric absorption: AI enters practice fastest where authorial labor concentrates (ideation, visualization) and is resisted where liability concentrates (documentation, certification), splitting the legal author from the substantive author. Five emergent functions of the architect are identified – dataset curator, question framer, output evaluator, liability bearer and system critic – collectively relocating architectural authority from form-giving to judgment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The article offers the first sustained reading of architectural AI through the combined lens of Tafuri’s ideology critique and Eisenman’s post-classical theory, demonstrating that the diffusion model mechanically performs the very operations Eisenman demanded as deliberate aesthetic transgression. This reframing moves the discourse beyond the prevailing optimism/dystopia binary toward a structural analysis of how tools historically constitute the architect-figure rather than merely assist it. By identifying five emergent functions that relocate architectural authority from authorship to judgment, the article provides a theoretically grounded framework for rethinking professional identity and disciplinary self-understanding in the age of AI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Artificial Intelligence in Paediatric Endocrinology: A Narrative Review from the Perspective of Early-career Clinicians and Researchers
container-title: Hormone Research in Paediatrics
dab59885d172cccf50ae39019c432da1441ba463.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) use by early-career paediatric endocrinologists has started without waiting for the training and governance structures to develop. Since early-career physicians and researchers of today hold no pre-AI performance baseline against which to appraise the AI outputs, career stage-specific concerns regarding rapid adoption of AI use in the field have emerged. The goal of this review was to examine AI use in paediatric endocrinology from the early-career perspective. Summary: A narrative, non-systematic literature review regarding the AI use in paediatric endocrinology across the four professional domains (curricular coverage, clinical practice, teaching, and research) was conducted in January 2026 and updated through July 2026. 57 relevant publications were identified, with level of evidence differing significantly between domains, and inversely with how freely the AI tools are used: from randomised-trials data regarding specific clinical applications like closed-loop insulin delivery and automated bone age assessment, to no published data regarding use of large language models in the research domain. Greatest benefit of automated bone age assessment in the early career stage was reported, while no published studies examining AI use by early-career paediatric endocrinologists were found. Key Messages: While being most exposed to unsupervised AI use, early-career physicians are also the least studied group. Having in mind the lack of pre-AI baseline in this population, findings of this review emphasize the potential career stage-dependent risks regarding the AI use, and the need for subspecialty-specific AI competency frameworks.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence in Spinal Diagnostics: Advances, Challenges and Future Directions
container-title: Journal of Orthopaedic Science and Research
228358c8fac2951f4dbb192b9ac4092ec5c41d96.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in spinal diagnostics, particularly through machine learning and deep learning applied to medical imaging and clinical data. These technologies may improve the detection and classification of spinal disorders, automate image interpretation and support clinical decision-making. This narrative review summarizes current applications of AI in spinal diagnostics, focusing on methods for detecting spinal cord injuries, spinal tumors, degenerative spine diseases and vertebral fractures, as well as predicting treatment outcomes and postoperative complications. It also examines convolutional and recurrent neural networks, automated image segmentation and other machine learning approaches for analyzing spinal images and clinical information. Available evidence suggests that AI models can perform comparably to conventional methods and expert assessments and may exceed them in some settings. However, implementation remains limited by challenges related to dataset quality and diversity, model generalizability and interpretability, data privacy and regulatory and ethical considerations. This review highlights both the clinical potential of AI and the major barriers to its integration into routine spinal diagnostic practice. Further prospective validation, external testing across diverse patient populations and interdisciplinary collaboration will be essential to establish the clinical utility and ensure the safe implementation of AI-based spinal diagnostic tools.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence and Youth Development: Assessing Negative Impacts in Cameroon
container-title: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology
d065024e3a7a3a4c848e7dd0b39abb55c8f7917f.abstract: <jats:p>This research evaluates the negative impacts of Artificial Intelligence dependency on the cognitive and academic development of students within the Cameroonian higher education landscape. Utilizing a multiple case study design to facilitate literal replication across diverse settings, this study analyzed data collected from students at the University of Yaoundé, the University of Bamenda, and Yaoundé International Business School. A total of 525 students were surveyed using a purposive sampling strategy to account for the unique dynamics of public university massification and private sector specialization in Cameroon. The findings indicate a high prevalence of AI utilization, with 85.3% of respondents reporting daily or weekly usage for academic tasks.</jats:p>

title: An Ecocentric Assessment Framework for Artificial Intelligence and Computational Design in Architecture
container-title: Research into Ecological Transformation in Architectural Sciences: From Anthropocentric Design to Ecology-Focused Design
9e7e6f7f02173ae504c123506aca35adbabc2089.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) supports environmental performance prediction and the evaluation of alternatives in architectural design. However, improvements in energy or carbon indicators alone do not demonstrate that non-human life holds independent value in design decisions. This chapter examines AI and related computational design approaches in architecture from an ecocentric perspective through a focused narrative review and conceptual synthesis supported by a structured database search. The 375 raw records retrieved from Scopus and Web of Science were reduced to 256 unique records; following title and abstract screening, a final purposive selection of 19 studies was established. Together with one supplementary publication, the 20 documents were examined under the themes of performance and decision-making, life cycle boundaries, the representation of non-human life, habitat geometry and materials, time and maintenance, and visual generation and ecological validation. The synthesis informs a preliminary ecocentric assessment framework comprising three dimensions: stakeholder scope, integration of environmental and ecological impacts into decision-making, and ecological responsibility. By distinguishing computational success from ecological outcomes, the framework provides an analytical basis for examining who benefits from design decisions, how environmental and ecological requirements influence those decisions, and how responsibility for their outcomes is addressed.</jats:p>

title: From Vernacular Ecological Intelligence to Planetary Design: Life Cycle Thinking as a Framework for Ecological Transformation in Architecture
container-title: Research into Ecological Transformation in Architectural Sciences: From Anthropocentric Design to Ecology-Focused Design
2fe3cfa7ebe20f96ad17653a7bea70674b592d24.abstract: <jats:p>The ecological transformation of architecture requires reconsidering how architectural knowledge is produced, environmental consequences are evaluated, and responsibility is addressed across spatial, temporal, and ecological scales. This chapter brings vernacular ecological knowledge into dialogue with Life Cycle Thinking and Planetary Design. Vernacular architecture is approached as a dynamic socio-ecological knowledge system shaped by culture, climate, materiality, and collective practices. Maintenance, repair, adaptability, and intergenerational learning are examined as forms of situated ecological intelligence rather than historical models to be replicated. Life Cycle Thinking provides a framework for integrating place-based knowledge into contemporary architectural decisions, extending environmental assessment beyond carbon to circularity, biodiversity, regeneration, cultural continuity, and resilience. The relationship with Planetary Design is understood as a scalar and epistemic connection through which local knowledge informs decisions affecting broader ecological and material systems. Rather than prescribing a universal method, Planetary Design is presented as a boundary-aware, sufficiency-led, regenerative, justice-oriented, and adaptive approach. The chapter argues that ecological transformation depends on combining quantitative assessment with local knowledge, social needs, interconnected system boundaries, and long-term stewardship.</jats:p>

title: Smart Democracy: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence to Combat Election  Misinformation in Nigeria
container-title: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology
f1d22cab6b57313eee0fba509858e3670f0893e5.abstract: <jats:p>The increasing use of digital communication technologies has transformed democratic participation in Nigeria, but it has also accelerated the spread of election misinformation through social media and other online platforms. False political information, manipulated digital content, and coordinated disinformation campaigns have continued to undermine electoral credibility, public trust, and informed voter decision-making. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool for detecting misinformation, verifying online content, identifying coordinated inauthentic behavior, and supporting evidence-based electoral communication. Despite these opportunities, there is limited empirical evidence on how AI can be effectively integrated into Nigeria's electoral communication system to strengthen democratic governance. This study examines the role of AI in combating election misinformation and promoting smart democracy in Nigeria. Specifically, it investigates the prevalence and patterns of election misinformation, assesses stakeholders' awareness and adoption of AI technologies for misinformation detection, examines the opportunities and challenges associated with AI deployment, and proposes communication strategies for responsible AI use during elections. The study adopts a mixed-methods research design, combining quantitative surveys with qualitative interviews involving electoral officials, journalists, fact-checkers, communication experts, and registered voters. Quantitative data will be analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, while qualitative data will be analyzed through thematic analysis. The findings are expected to provide practical recommendations for policymakers, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), media organizations, technology developers, and civil society organizations on leveraging AI to enhance electoral transparency, improve information integrity, strengthen public trust, and promote democratic participation in Nigeria. The study contributes to the growing literature on artificial intelligence, development communication, digital governance, and democratic innovation in Africa.</jats:p>

dc18be7938888a9e92c545bb24bcbfd1ebc30ece.abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents the roadmap and manufacturing challenges of electroabsorption-modulated lasers (EMLs) and continuous-wave (CW) lasers for 800G, 1.6T, and 3.2T super intelligence (SI) and artificial intelligence (AI) optical transmission and computing applications. We highlight the roadmap for EMLs and CW lasers across different generations of optical switching technologies and discuss key manufacturing challenges, including (1) technical complexity, (2) substrate constraints, and (3) process equipment requirements.</jats:p>

title: AI-Powered Global Expansion: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Adoption on Firms’ Outward Foreign Direct Investment
container-title: Journal of Academic Research and Advances
2a05bfef34581f00a29abb04125f82b362ae925e.abstract:
<jats:p>Against the backdrop of profound shifts in the global economic landscape and rapid advances in digital technologies, artificial intelligence (AI) offers firms new opportunities to expand into international markets and improve the allocation of resources across borders. Drawing on a sample of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2009 to 2024, this study empirically examines the relationship between AI adoption and outward foreign direct investment (OFDI), with particular attention to the mechanisms underlying this relationship.
The findings indicate that AI adoption is positively and significantly associated with firms’ OFDI activities. This result remains robust across a range of alternative specifications, including different measures of AI adoption, adjustments to fixed effects and standard-error clustering, and the exclusion of selected observations. Heterogeneity analyses suggest that the positive relationship is more pronounced among technology-intensive firms and larger enterprises. Further analysis identifies two potential channels through which AI adoption may facilitate OFDI: technological innovation and the alleviation of financial constraints. Together, these mechanisms may strengthen firms’ technological capabilities and improve their access to the financial resources required for international expansion.
By examining OFDI through the lens of firm-level AI adoption, this study extends the literature on the determinants of international investment and provides further insight into how AI may shape firms’ internationalization strategies. The findings also offer empirical evidence relevant to the integration of AI into the real economy, the enhancement of firms’ international competitiveness, and China’s efforts to pursue higher-standard economic opening-up.</jats:p>

title: DETERMINANTS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ADOPTION AMONG ACADEMIC AND NON-ACADEMIC STAFF OF AUCHI POLYTECHNIC, EDO STATE, NIGERIA
container-title: International Journal of African Innovation and Multidisciplinary Research
9607086033a46199229406ffe9c3b47558630420.abstract:
<jats:p>This study examined the determinants of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption among academic and non-academic staff of Auchi Polytechnic, Edo State, Nigeria. Specifically, it investigated the relationships between perceived usefulness, AI literacy, institutional support and AI adoption. The study adopted a descriptive survey research design. The population comprised 3,150 academic and non-academic staff, from which a sample of 354 respondents was determined using the Taro Yamane formula. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire and analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression analysis with SPSS Version 26. The hypotheses were tested at the 5% level of significance. The descriptive results showed that perceived usefulness had a mean score of 4.18, AI literacy recorded 3.65, institutional support had 2.84, while AI adoption recorded 3.92. The multiple regression results indicated that perceived usefulness (β = 0.396, p < 0.001), AI literacy (β = 0.339, p < 0.001) and institutional support (β = 0.246, p < 0.001) had significant positive relationships with AI adoption. The overall regression model was statistically significant (F = 150.29, p < 0.001), with an R² of 0.545, indicating that the three explanatory variables jointly accounted for 54.5% of the variation in AI adoption. Perceived usefulness was the strongest predictor, followed by AI literacy and institutional support. The study concluded that AI adoption among staff of Auchi Polytechnic is associated with perceived work-related benefits, employees’ AI competencies and the availability of institutional resources and support. It recommended that the Polytechnic promote practical AI applications in academic and administrative activities, strengthen staff AI literacy through regular training, and improve digital infrastructure, technical assistance and institutional guidelines for responsible AI use.
 </jats:p>

title: Mapping multidimensional artificial intelligence anxiety among academic librarians in the United Arab Emirates: An exploratory survey
container-title: Journal of Information Science
bd50d5aaa7dce3fb50374d1d4938e706264f0cda.abstract: <jats:p>This exploratory study examines artificial intelligence anxiety among academic librarians in the United Arab Emirates, a multilingual context undergoing rapid digital transformation. A cross-sectional online survey of 72 academic library professionals, recruited through purposive and snowball sampling, employed a newly developed 35-item instrument covering seven conceptually derived dimensions: job role evolution, ethical and bureaucratic concerns, patron resistance and social trust, governance and strategic alignment, infrastructure and digital divide, vendor and sustainability, and linguistic and cultural anxiety. Internal consistency ranged from acceptable to strong (α = 0.774–0.898). Overall, AI anxiety was moderate (M = 3.33 on a five-point scale), with ethical and bureaucratic concerns (M = 3.47), infrastructure and digital divide (M = 3.42), and vendor and sustainability concerns (M = 3.36) recording the highest means. However, the narrow range across construct means (0.23 points) warrants treating these differences as descriptive rather than substantive rankings. Concerns about storing patron data on foreign servers and shortages of skilled staff received the highest item-level ratings. Although women reported higher scores across all seven dimensions, no gender or other demographic differences remained statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. The findings highlight the institutional, infrastructural, ethical and governance conditions associated with AI anxiety in academic libraries. The proposed dimensions offer a context-specific framework for further investigation, subject to validation in larger samples. Practical implications include developing localized and multilingual AI tools, expanding inclusive professional development, and strengthening participatory governance of AI procurement and policy.</jats:p>

title: Assessment of Taraba Broadcast Journalists Knowledge, Adoption and Usage of Artificial Intelligence in Journalistic Practices
container-title: RESEARCH JOURNAL OF MASS COMMUNICATION AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY
3d595057b3e03ea8fa7b358699deebe39aca77a9.abstract:
<jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become an essential tool in various fields, including journalism.
However, the extent to which broadcast journalists in Taraba State, Nigeria embraced and utilized
AI in their practices remains a subject of debate. It is on the above premise that this research
examined Taraba State broadcast journalists' knowledge and usage of AI in journalistic practices.
The paper was built on the technology acceptance model, diffusion of innovation theory, and social
learning theory. The study adopted a qualitative approach where in-depth interviews were used.
The in-depth interviews were conducted until the results reached saturation point. Findings of the
study revealed that in journalists in Taraba State, Nigeria are slowly beginning to embrace AI for
journalistic practice. However, there knowledge of AI usage for journalistic practices is low hence
there is a significant knowledge gap that needs to be bridged. Therefore, the study recommends
among other things that journalists in Taraba State need to gain more knowledge about AI and its
potential applications in journalistic practices. The paper concludes that with proper training and
guidance, journalists in Taraba State can harness the power of this AI technology to improve their
reporting practices while ensuring ethical standards are upheld.</jats:p>

title: Where Do We Look? Visual Attention Competition Between Hyper-Salient Objects and AI-Generated Virtual Endorsers in Generative Artificial Intelligence Advertising
container-title: Journal of Eye Movement Research
498fcba14c2a3120971f1b6fed27c097dac981bd.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (AI) advertising, defined as advertising content created or substantially assisted by generative AI systems (AIGC), has introduced new visual features that combine algorithmically generated objects with human-like representations. Hyper-salient objects, defined by exaggerated perceptual prominence and semantic incongruity, and AI-generated virtual endorsers, represented by human-like AI-created figures, have become increasingly common in such advertisements. However, little is known about how these distinct visual cues compete for consumers’ limited attentional resources when presented together. Drawing on visual attention and scene perception perspectives, this study investigated how hyper-salient objects and AI-generated virtual endorsers influence visual attention allocation in AI-generated advertising. A 2 (hyper-salient object: present vs. absent) × 2 (AI endorser: present vs. absent) between-subjects eye-tracking experiment was conducted with 160 participants in a controlled laboratory setting using static AI-generated advertisements. Eye movements were recorded, and memory was assessed using signal detection measures (d′) from a recognition task involving target and distractor advertisements. Advertising attitude and product trust were measured using established scales. Results from linear and generalized linear mixed-effects models showed that hyper-salient objects increased early fixation probability and attracted a larger dwell time proportion, demonstrating strong attentional capture. AI-generated endorsers also attracted attention when presented alone, but their proportional attention share decreased when hyper-salient objects were simultaneously present. The effects of these visual elements on memory and product trust were conditional on their co-occurrence rather than uniform across conditions. Within the specific set of experimentally constructed stimuli and four sampled product categories, this research contributes to AIGC advertising literature by developing a visual competition perspective on how multiple AI-generated visual cues interact under limited attentional capacity, offering implications for designing effective generative AI advertisements.</jats:p>

title: Ethical Implications of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) Use Among Library and Information Science (LIS) Students: A Narrative Review
container-title: Education for Information
134409bd05e521d5a6bc11cc9a5957b37d242bf9.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly being used by students and is reshaping the way information is accessed, processed, and utilised for academic work and everyday purposes. As the use of AI technologies continues to expand, there is a growing need to discuss the ethical implications associated with the use of generative AI among LIS students. This study employed a narrative review method to analyse and synthesise evidence from existing scholarly literature obtained through various library resources and online databases on the Internet. The study identified several ethical implications regarding the use of generative AI among LIS students, which include breaches of academic integrity, plagiarism risks, misinformation, output bias, privacy and security concerns, reduced critical engagement with learning materials, overdependence on AI systems, fabricated references, and so on. The findings revealed that ethical use of generative AI requires LIS students to critically evaluate AI-generated content, acknowledge AI assistance where necessary, and maintain responsibility for the accuracy and originality of their academic work. The study showed areas for future research directions in ethical concerns of generative AI use among LIS students for responsible AI use in academic practices.</jats:p>
