title: Borrowed Grief Projection, Mourning, and the Artificial Screen in Kazuo Ishiguro's Klara and the Sun
container-title: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management
99cb999c074a0cf236435cb81f5b652a48ece6ad.abstract: <jats:p>Kazuo Ishiguro's Klara and the Sun (2021) has generally been read through the lens of posthumanism, with critics asking what the novel says about artificial minds, consciousness, and the ethical status of machines built to feel (Ajeesh and Rukmini; Sahu and Karmakar). Klara, the Artificial Friend (AF) who narrates the novel, is repeatedly framed by scholarship as a test case for whether a machine can possess genuine interiority, and whether human beings can ever truly know that interiority from the outside (Shang). This paper takes a different approach. Rather than asking what Klara is, it asks what Klara is used for. Read this way, Klara and the Sun is less a novel about artificial intelligence than a novel about human beings who cannot bear to look directly at loss, illness, and death, and who therefore route their most unbearable feelings through a listening, watching, uncomplaining object that will not look away, argue back, or die on its own schedule. Josie's mother, Chrissie, projects her anticipatory grief and her guilt over Josie's genetic "lifting" onto Klara by quietly preparing Klara to become a replacement daughter. Josie herself, isolated by illness from ordinary adolescent life, projects her need for an unthreatening companion onto Klara rather than risk further loss with human friends. Even Rick and the wider adult world around the Arthur family treat AFs as safe vessels for anxieties they will not name directly. Klara, in other words, functions across the novel as a screen: an entity human characters can fill with their own dread of mortality precisely because she seems not to have a mortality, or a claim, of her own.</jats:p>

title: Health Information-Seeking Behaviour Using Artificial Intelligence Applications in Mobile Phones Among University Undergraduates in Anambra State
container-title: RESEARCH JOURNAL OF MASS COMMUNICATION AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY
fd09e6681e6192c0ba32d60c1070cf2cc3b130b9.abstract:
<jats:p>Seeking health information is a common practice that helps individuals understand health
conditions and manage illnesses. Among young people, this behaviour has increased due to the
rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, improved mobile phone capabilities, and
widespread internet access. However, despite the speed and convenience AI applications provide,
there is a risk of inaccurate or misleading information, especially when users’ health conditions
differ from the data on which the AI systems were trained. This study assessed the use of AI
applications on mobile phones for health information-seeking among university undergraduates
in Anambra State. The main objective was to examine undergraduates’ health information-seeking
behaviour in relation to their utilization of AI mobile applications. The study was anchored on the
Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Diffusion of Innovation theory. A quantitative
survey design was adopted, using a structured Likert-scale questionnaire for data collection. From
a population of 60,903 students, a sample size of 358 was determined using the Krejcie and
Morgan formula. Data were analysed using mean scores, with 3.0 as the decision benchmark:
items with mean scores below 3.0 were rejected, while those above 3.0 were accepted. Findings
indicated that most respondents use AI applications on their mobile phones to seek health
information, largely due to accessibility, convenience, and ease of interaction. The study concludes
that although AI health information tools are useful, there is a need for greater caution and
guidance regarding the quality of information accessed. It recommends the development and
enforcement of stricter regulations on AI health information tools and the implementation of
institutional educational programmes to improve students’ understanding of responsible AI use.</jats:p>

title: Public Awareness of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Utilisation in Healthcare Institutions in Anambra State
container-title: RESEARCH JOURNAL OF MASS COMMUNICATION AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY
b95afc8cfcf288eee154d73cf330cab3e4fc70d8.abstract:
<jats:p>Given the growing adoption of AI-driven diagnostic and treatment tools across health systems,
understanding community awareness is crucial for effective integration and health
communication. Applying the survey design, data were collected from 384 adult residents selected
from across six Local Government Areas of Anambra State, Nigeria, using multistage and
proportionate sampling techniques. Findings revealed a moderately high level of awareness of AI
utilisation, with respondents expressing the strongest familiarity with AI-powered tools such as
automated diagnostics and virtual assistants. Social media emerged as the dominant source of AI
information, followed by traditional media, while healthcare providers contributed minimally to
public knowledge. Respondents also recognised significant benefits of AI, including improved
diagnostic accuracy, enhanced service delivery, and overall healthcare quality. However, concerns
were evident regarding potential medical errors, privacy concerns, and job displacement of
healthcare workers. These findings align with national and international studies showing high
exposure but limited depth of understanding among the public and health workers. Guided by the
Diffusion of Innovations and Agenda-Setting theories, the study concludes that public awareness
is largely media-driven and remains at an early diffusion stage, underscoring the need for
deliberate institutional communication, ethical safeguards, and structured public sensitisation.
The study recommends strengthening health communication strategies, promoting data protection
frameworks, and enhancing healthcare worker involvement in public AI education.</jats:p>

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR STRATEGIC DECISION-MAKING: IMPLICATIONS FOR THE TRANSFORMATION OF BUSINESS MANAGEMENT
container-title: International Journal of African Development and Sustainable Research
f38778fba2b7a2ee75337c994a2e5d698a95039b.abstract: <jats:p>In today’s rapidly evolving business environment, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a transformative technological capability with profound implications for strategic decision-making and modern business management. The growing ability of AI systems to analyse extensive volumes of structured and unstructured data, detect intricate patterns, produce predictive insights, and automate analytical activities is reshaping the processes through which organisations formulate and implement strategic decisions. Through the review of recent literature and real-world case studies, this paper critically argues that AI is fundamentally reshaping strategic decision-making and presents a reasoned perspective on how this shift is transforming business management practices and competitive strategies in contemporary organisations. This study also explores the challenges and risks of AI-driven strategic decision-making. The study concludes that the greatest value of AI lies in its capacity to augment rather than replace managerial intelligence. Hence, the study recommends that organisations should adopt hybrid decision-making by combining AI-generated insights with human expertise to enhance decision accuracy, critical thinking, and strategic judgement.</jats:p>

title: Emerging Artificial Intelligence Applications in Capture Fisheries Monitoring and Assessment: A Bibliometric and Synthesis Review
container-title: New Zealand Journal of Marine and Freshwater Research
ee25cebe3bc19dd162b38b33673a4ae1d6a88c30.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to monitor and assess capture fisheries, addressing persistent limitations of conventional observation systems that are labor‐intensive, costly, and difficult to scale. Despite rapid technological expansion, AI development in this field remains fragmented, limiting a comprehensive understanding of its structure and direction. This study aimed to map the development, intellectual structure, and thematic evolution of AI research in capture fisheries monitoring and assessment through a bibliometric and synthesis‐based review of Scopus‐indexed literature (2015–2026). Following a documented, large language model‐assisted screening protocol with human verification, a final corpus of 495 journal articles was analyzed using an integrated bibliometric and science‐mapping workflow. Results showed a marked, near‐exponential increase in publication output after 2020. Rather than confirming a pre‐defined three‐domain structure, keyword co‐occurrence analysis revealed that the field's thematic organization follows technical task type (detection, classification, and operational/vessel management) more closely than application domain, with acoustic AI failing to form an independent thematic cluster and representing the smallest share of the corpus (8.1%), behind visual AI (44.0%) and vessel monitoring (28.9%). For synthesis, we nonetheless compare the field across three functional categories visual AI for fish detection and measurement, vessel monitoring using AIS/VMS data, and acoustic survey support finding that the field is methodologically converging around a shared AI/ML toolkit while remaining largely siloed at the technical‐application level. Although research productivity remains heavily concentrated in China (85.9% of records) and international collaboration is limited (23.64%), the field is moving beyond isolated proof‐of‐concept studies toward more operational, management‐relevant applications. Overall, this study provides an evidence‐grounded, rather than assumed, understanding of how AI research in capture fisheries is thematically structured, and identifies acoustic AI and cross‐domain integration as priority areas for future development toward fisheries‐oriented, evidence‐based management.</jats:p>

title: Causal Geospatial Intelligence Framework for Identifying Environmental Drivers of Landslide Risk in Mountainous Regions
container-title: International Journal of Engineering, Science and Information Technology
49984f88f1fcb8aa17bf5b4a4f3b17e39097a693.abstract: <jats:p>Landslide susceptibility models can effectively predict areas prone to landslides but generally provide limited evidence on whether specific environmental exposures causally influence landslide occurrence. This research proposes an integrated causal-geospatial framework combining predictive modeling with causal effect estimation and spatial heterogeneity analysis for landslide occurrence in Desa Wih Pase, Bener Meriah, Indonesia. An analytical dataset comprising 18,450 30 m × 30 m grid cells from observations in 2025 was analyzed using Random Forest and Logistic Regression for occurrence probability modeling, followed by Causal Forest to derive average treatment effect estimates together with grid-level Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATE). The Random Forest model reached a discrimination performance of 0.91 in AUC-ROC, exceeding the 0.79 achieved by the Logistic Regression baseline, demonstrating stronger predictive discrimination under the imbalanced landslide dataset. Causal analysis estimated a positive effect of cumulative rainfall, with a 100 mm increase associated with a 0.142 increase in landslide occurrence probability (95% CI: 0.089–0.195). A 10° increase in slope produced an estimated effect of 0.218 (95% CI: 0.161–0.275). Spatial CATE analysis revealed substantial heterogeneity, with rainfall effects ranging from ?0.039 to 0.302 and slope effects from ?0.024 to 0.490 across valid 30 m grid cells. Sensitivity analyses showed that the positive causal effects remained stable across alternative confounder sets, rainfall accumulation windows, and spatial resolutions. The framework distinguishes predictive susceptibility from causal environmental effects and provides a basis for spatially targeted landslide risk reduction and environmental engineering interventions</jats:p>

title: REPOSITIONING NIGERIAN POLYTECHNIC CHEMISTRY PROGRAMMES FOR THE FOURTH INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION: A CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK FOR EMBEDDING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN THE CURRICULUM
container-title: Journal of Health Systems Research
be4c55d2d25341ccd62c22091c3fb35551b46df9.abstract: <jats:p>The emergence of the Fourth Industrial Revolution (Industry 4.0) is fundamentally altering the landscape of the global chemical sector through automation, cyber-physical infrastructures, machine learning, and data-intensive approaches to discovery. These shifts have generated an acute need for professionals who can function effectively at the convergence of chemistry, computation, and digital technologies. In contrast, Nigerian polytechnics (institutions constitutionally tasked with cultivating mid-level technical expertise) continue to operate largely conventional, content-saturated chemistry curricula that show little correspondence with these evolving workforce expectations. This conceptual study set out to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) could be systematically woven into the chemistry curricula of Nigerian polytechnics as a means of equipping graduates for Industry 4.0. By triangulating scholarship on AI in education, chemistry pedagogy, technical and vocational education and training (TVET), and Industry 4.0 workforce requirements, the paper constructed a conceptual architecture for curriculum integration and evaluated four distinct integration pathways: the supplementary, embedded, dual-track, and fully reformed models. The analysis also interrogated the structural, human-capital, infrastructural, ethical, and policy-related obstacles that impede AI uptake within Nigerian polytechnics, while delineating the Industry 4.0 capabilities that chemistry graduates must command—namely data literacy, computational reasoning, digitally mediated laboratory competence, and AI-supported problem resolution. The study concludes that a staged, context-attuned integration approach—anchored in purposeful policy reform, lecturer capacity building, industry collaboration, and deliberate investment in digital infrastructure—is indispensable for sustaining the relevance of Nigerian polytechnics. Concrete recommendations are advanced for curriculum authorities, institutional managers, and industry stakeholders.</jats:p>

title: Smart Leaf Identification and Analysis using Artificial Intelligence
container-title: Journal of ICT Research and Applications
27f2ffddee9d72a18a00007c73bc447b65a1247d.abstract: <jats:p>This paper describes a leaf classification framework based on machine learning methodologies. The dataset included 36 leaf species with 340 instances and 16 features. Decision Tree, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, XGBoost, AdaBoost, and Random Forest were applied initially on the raw dataset. It was found that Decision Tree, XGBoost and Random Forest performed well, with accuracy scores of 53%, 60% and 85% respectively. After feature reduction based on Information Gain and correlation matrix analysis, four highly correlated features were removed. This led to a marginal improvement in accuracy to 60% for Decision Tree and to 65% percentage for XG Boost, while the accuracy of Random Forest dropped to 74%. We also applied SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique) to balance the raw dataset. This enhanced the accuracy of Random Forest and XGBoost to 91% and 81% respectively. With Computer Vision, we achieved an accuracy of 66% for SVM, 61% for Random Forest, 43% for K-NN and 37% for the Decision Tree classifier on the image dataset. The pre-trained VGG16 model achieved an impressive 90.47% accuracy, outperforming the custom CNN model and conventional models like Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) and KNN with various K-values from the literature</jats:p>

title: Advanced artificial potential field for safe and efficient local path planning
container-title: Industrial Robot: the international journal of robotics research and application
dd532a404fcf9f7fceeb9a3f95dfb226f14fc588.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper addresses the problem of efficient and safe local path planning for mobile robots operating in environments with unknown and randomly distributed obstacles. The purpose of this study is to develop a computationally lightweight local path planner that is designed to support obstacle avoidance, smooth goal-reaching behaviour and reliable waypoint tracking in cluttered environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The proposed method is developed on the basis of the artificial potential field algorithm and extends the classical formulation by incorporating future position prediction, vortex potential, a single constrained quadratic optimization problem for control signal selection and a mechanism for maintaining a safe distance from obstacles. The algorithm is evaluated in Matlab using randomly generated obstacle configurations for both the standalone local path planning problem and the waypoint tracking problem. Its performance is compared with that of selected existing local path planning methods. In addition, the proposed approach is validated experimentally using a real mobile robot.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The obtained results indicate that the proposed local path planner achieves low goal-reaching time, short path length, satisfactory path smoothness and accurate waypoint tracking. The method maintained repeatable obstacle-distance behaviour in the evaluated scenarios while requiring relatively low computational effort. The AAPF guidance field is used to generate a predicted trajectory, which is then checked against the proposed safety-distance criterion.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The main contribution of this work is the development of an efficient local path planning algorithm that combines safety-distance-aware obstacle avoidance, prediction-based motion planning and constrained optimization-based control signal generation within a unified framework. The proposed method offers a favourable balance between navigation performance, safety and computational complexity, which makes it suitable for real-time implementation in mobile robotic systems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: A Study of Artificial Intelligence-Based Emotional Music Generation Systems
container-title: Communications in Humanities Research
f12acffd38082cbe1df40ae871eb13a861cf6c7d.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence-based affective music generation (AI-AMG) systems generate music automatically with the purpose of expressing or evoking particular feelings. This review examines studies published between 1990 and 2022 and organizes existing systems according to their main components and generation methods. A typical AI-AMG system includes target emotion identification, emotional music generation, and emotional evaluation. Rule-based, data-driven, optimization-based, and hybrid are the four categories of generation methodologies. Rule-based systems include connections between musical features and emotions, whereas data-driven systems identify structural patterns using Markov models or neural networks. Optimization methods use techniques such as genetic algorithms and graph or tree traversal, and hybrid systems combine multiple approaches. Evaluation is commonly performed through computational measures or human listener studies that assess perceived or induced emotion. Current systems can produce music associated with target emotional states, but important limitations remain, including dependence on labeled datasets, inconsistent evaluation procedures, limited measurement of induced emotion, and lower creativity than human composition. The review highlights the need for more reliable evaluation, improved emotional control, and systems that generate natural, diverse, and context-sensitive music.</jats:p>

title: Who Shapes AI? Technology, Institutions, and Power in the Development of Artificial Intelligence
container-title: Communications in Humanities Research
1c4f3b07d5aa2ed98414c236a298d3ddc1f04493.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is usually mainly explained through technological breakthroughs, such as larger models, improved algorithms, stronger computing power and expanded datasets. This article challenges this interpretation by viewing artificial intelligence as a sociotechnical system whose development and consequences are constantly influenced by social institutions. Based on research of the history of the Internet and human-computer interaction, institutional development, automated responsibility, and algorithmic labor, this paper compares early computing systems with contemporary artificial intelligence. Analysis shows that technical capabilities themselves cannot determine how a technology develops or how it affects society. Governments, universities, companies, markets, legal systems, workers and users all influence the way artificial intelligence is funded, deployed, regulated and understood. Meanwhile, these actors do not have equal power. Cases such as moral collapse zones and algorithmic wage discrimination demonstrate how automation unevenly redistributes responsibility, information and economic benefits. Therefore, this article holds that the future of artificial intelligence is not determined by the technology itself, but rather by the institutional structure and power relations in which the technology is developed and utilized.</jats:p>

title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on University-Level Professional Training
container-title: Palestine Technical University Research Journal
a1d822c71f8b94915792ca071ef8998080383933.abstract: <jats:p>The aim of the study was to assess the perceived effectiveness of implementing artificial intelligence tools into educational curricula and to evaluate the readiness of students, teachers, and graduates to apply artificial intelligence in the educational process and professional activities. The research methodology combined a content analysis of teaching and assessment forms integrated with artificial intelligence, a survey of 350 participants (students, graduates, and teachers) at the Industrial University of Ho Chi Minh City in May 2025 to evaluate their readiness and experience in using artificial intelligence, as well as the formulation of practical recommendations for enhancing the effectiveness of educational programmes using artificial intelligence tools. The results showed that after the implementation of the updated curriculum, 100% of students used AI tools for learning, 70% rated them as very useful, and 25% as high, indicating a high level of awareness of AI's benefits; all students expressed readiness to apply AI in learning and work and to attend dedicated courses or seminars. Among teachers, 30% rated the advantages of AI for teaching as very high, 60% as high, and 10% as moderate, while all teachers noted legal or ethical concerns. The practical significance of the work lies in the fact that the results and recommendations can be used by universities and teachers to update curricula with AI integration, by institutional administrations for planning digital infrastructure and pedagogical training</jats:p>

title: Prospects for Integrating Virtual Reality and Artificial Intelligence into University Learning: Approaches to Developing Interactive Educational Environments
container-title: Palestine Technical University Research Journal
6df12fe4bfdf3f69599dc9b1ea1b871b40089c02.abstract: <jats:p>The study aimed to identify key trends and define a conceptually coherent model for integrating virtual reality and artificial intelligence technologies into the university learning process. The methodology included a comparative method, document content analysis, expert verification, conceptual modelling, and scenario modelling. Three stages of expert verification produced a high level of consistency in evaluations across the criteria of necessity (mean – 4.8; median – 5), feasibility (mean – 4.4; median – 4) and innovation potential (mean – 4.8; median – 5), confirming the conceptual validity, practical feasibility and strong innovative capacity of the interactive educational environment model. This demonstrated the achievement of group consensus: 90% of experts assigned scores of 4-5 points in the second round and 96% in the third round, exceeding the 70% consensus threshold and confirming the model’s conceptual coherence and practical feasibility. The highest level of consistency was recorded in the pedagogical and cognitive-communicative components, which experts identified as essential for maintaining the didactic integrity of virtual reality and artificial intelligence as complementary technologies. The technological component received an average score of 4.4 points, confirming its flexibility but also indicating the need for further adaptation of university infrastructure. The managerial-analytical component had the lowest variability (interquartile range ≤1), reflecting stable expert agreement regarding its internal logic. The synthesis of the results made it possible to formulate three scenarios: an innovation-adaptive scenario, a technology-optimisation scenario and a transformation-forecasting scenario. These scenarios reflected varying levels of institutional readiness for digital transformation and made it possible to outline a gradual trajectory from local initiatives to a comprehensive interactive ecosystem. The practical value of the study lies in the fact that the proposed model can serve as a methodological basis for developing university digital strategies, designing educational programmes, and establishing systems for monitoring the quality of digital learning processes. It enables universities to develop their own strategies for implementing intelligent technologies in accordance with staff readiness, available infrastructure and pedagogical priorities</jats:p>

title: Development and application of artificial intelligence in the field of art education
container-title: Palestine Technical University Research Journal
1507f96315838409d3ee0b54869e74fb3a4a8b5f.abstract: <jats:p>This paper explores the specific features of artificial intelligence (AI) usage in the field of art education, with a focus on a comparative analysis of the experiences of China and Kyrgyzstan. The study employed a comparative analysis of academic discourse on AI, along with thematic analysis of interviews with lecturers from faculties of art and design in higher education institutions in China (n=2) and the Kyrgyz Republic (n=2). The primary emphasis was placed on the benefits, challenges, and prospects of AI use in the training of art designers. The research included an analysis of ten popular AI-based tools, such as DALL-E, MidJourney, Adobe Firefly, and Gradescope. The inclusion of interview methods enabled the identification of differences in approaches to AI use in the educational institutions of the two countries. The study’s findings confirm the significant potential of AI in personalising learning, optimising the educational process, and enhancing graduates' competitiveness in the labour market. At the same time, key obstacles were identified: limited awareness among lecturers, high costs of AI-based tools, as well as ethical and legal issues. Particular attention is paid to the differing levels of readiness in China and Kyrgyzstan for AI integration in their educational systems. The paper offers recommendations for effective implementation, including raising awareness, government support, and the development of international cooperation. The proposed four-step model of AI adoption was developed to support systematic implementation in higher education and may be adapted for use in other national contexts. The research highlights the importance of overcoming existing barriers in order to expand the application of AI in art education</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Women Entrepreneurship in the IT Sector: Emerging Opportunities and Entrepreneurial Challenges

57468ea9c09dfbf28e329fedbc923e46969e52db.abstract: <jats:p>The Information Technology (IT) industry is undergoing significant changes as Artificial Intelligence (AI) launches new areas for innovation, business expansion and entrepreneurship. Women entrepreneurs are increasingly embracing AI technologies to set up startups, to enhance their business operations. To increase productivity and take part more in domestic and international markets. In the present study, the role of Artificial Intelligence in the future of women entrepreneurship in the IT sector was discussed, with a special focus on emerging opportunities and challenges for the entrepreneurs. It brings to the forefront the potential of leveraging AI-powered tools, automation, machine learning, data analytics, and digital platforms for business planning, decision-making, customer relationship management, and resource optimization, particularly for women entrepreneurs. The research also pinpoints the major challenges such as limited access to finance, gender inequality, technical knowledge, digital skills gap, cyber security threats, and lack of institutional support. Particular emphasis is placed on the Indian context and how government’s initiatives, digital transformation and entrepreneurship development programmes are providing new opportunities for women entrepreneurs. The research method used in the study is descriptive and analytical descriptive method using secondary data or secondary sources of information. It seeks to grasp the potential of AI in fostering inclusive entrepreneurship, enhancing the role of women in the IT sector, and supporting sustainable economic growth.</jats:p>

title: Role Radar: An AI-Based Resume Intelligence and Skill Gap Analysis System
container-title: International Journal of Scientific Research in Engineering & Technology
9d2e83fdca6d967c999174c04ac4bc9c28b0e577.abstract: <jats:p>Job seekers face two linked problems: finding postings that are genuinely open and suitable, and presenting their experience to automated screening without exaggeration. General-purpose language-model resume writers aggravate the second problem because they can invent skills, metrics, and seniority. This paper presents RoleRadar, a full-stack career platform built on one rule: deterministic code decides what is true, and the language model only rephrases it. A geometry-based parser turns an uploaded resume into atomic, provenance-tagged evidence units. Job requirements are mapped to that evidence on an eight-level support scale, and a category-aware six-factor model yields an explainable match score and a readiness verdict. A rule-based Truth Guard compares every tailored bullet with its source and reverts fabricated technologies, unsupported metrics, inflated titles, and broken sentences before one-page export. Supporting modules provide a taxonomy of 119 roles, prerequisite-ordered learning roadmaps, verified job ingestion from direct employer feeds, and an assistant restricted to the signed-in user’s data. A regression suite of 1,268 test cases, internal validation harnesses, and an end-to-end acceptance run indicate that the pipeline is consistent and auditable. The system has not yet been evaluated with recruiters or in a controlled user study.</jats:p>

title: How Different Types of Artificial Intelligence Training Relate to Innovative Behavior Among Logistics Employees: A Cognitive–Affective Pathway Model
container-title: Systems
3626048d828e706fb3af96725f40054c01f03f1f.abstract: <jats:p>Despite substantial investments in artificial intelligence (AI) training, logistics organizations often struggle to translate these investments into measurable improvements in employee performance. Drawing on the extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Cognitive Load Theory, and Distributed Cognition Theory, this study examines how three AI-TPACK training dimensions—Strategic, Generative, and Optimization AI Training—are associated with employees’ innovative behavior through cognitive (Task–Technology Fit, AI Self-Efficacy) and affective (Perceived Technology Attractiveness, AI Usage Intention) mechanisms. Survey data from 245 logistics practitioners (cross-sectional, single-source) were analyzed using confirmatory factor analysis, competing structural models, and bootstrapped indirect effects in a final integrated model. The originally proposed dual-track structure was not supported; the data favored a cross-linked specification in which cognitive beliefs inform attitudes across tracks and attractiveness precedes usage intention. Strategic AI training was associated with innovative behavior indirectly, Generative AI training both directly and indirectly, and Optimization AI training showed no unique association once the other dimensions were controlled. Neither Training Environment Quality nor Supervisor Support Leadership moderated the hypothesized relationships in a robust way, although both showed direct associations with outcomes (Training Environment Quality with Task–Technology Fit, β = 0.288; Supervisor Support with innovative behavior, β = 0.141). These cross-sectional, single-source associations refine the technology acceptance literature for AI training and inform HRD strategies for digital transformation in logistics.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence Readiness among Public Elementary School Teachers in Mercedes District: A Descriptive – Comparative Study of Technology Self-Efficacy, Student Interaction, and Ethical Awareness
container-title: International Journal of Research on Multidisciplinary Studies
6512a551827963e2eb05329b5d1c43e122dea08b.abstract: <jats:p>This study assessed the artificial intelligence readiness of public elementary school teachers in Mercedes District, addressing the limited evidence on multidimensional readiness among elementary teachers in Philippine district settings. Specifically, it determined the overall level of readiness and the levels of technology self-efficacy, student interaction, and ethical awareness. It also examined whether readiness differed according to age, sex, highest educational attainment, and years of teaching experience. A quantitative descriptive-comparative research design was employed, involving 207 public elementary school teachers who completed the 19-item Readiness for Artificial Intelligence Applications Scale, consisting of six technology self-efficacy items, seven student interaction items, and six ethical awareness items. Mean and standard deviation were used to describe readiness levels, while the Mann–Whitney U test and Kruskal–Wallis H test examined differences between groups. The Holm correction was applied to the p-values of the 16 omnibus tests to account for multiple testing. The findings showed that respondents had an overall Agree level of readiness (mean = 4.10, standard deviation = 0.55). Ethical awareness obtained the highest rating and was interpreted as Strongly Agree (mean = 4.38, standard deviation = 0.50), while student interaction (mean = 3.99, standard deviation = 0.64) and technology self-efficacy (mean = 3.96, standard deviation = 0.72) were interpreted as Agree. After applying the Holm correction, no statistically significant differences were found according to age, sex, highest educational attainment, or years of teaching experience. Overall, the findings indicate positive readiness, with ethical awareness as the highest-rated dimension and opportunities to strengthen teachers’ technological confidence and student interaction. These findings may guide context-specific professional development initiatives to strengthen teachers’ technological confidence, pedagogical application, and responsible use of artificial intelligence in elementary education.</jats:p>

title:

f02f8dbc8f6c28288851ba300bc7e4badb233999.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Proteins are highly diverse functional polymers where the specific sequence of amino acids, selected from a standard genetically encoded alphabet of 20 (C20), determines the structure and ultimately the function of the resulting folded protein. This standard alphabet has been identified to be nonrandomly distributed in physicochemical properties crucial to both structure formation and function, often referred to as coverage theory. While machine learning models have drastically improved protein structure prediction, success of protein design models lags structure prediction, particularly for custom secondary structure motifs and amino acid alphabets. Here, we therefore bridge contemporary biological theory with recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) to develop and evaluate a generative AI protein design model, trained on hundreds of thousands of proteins within the RCSB PDB, for custom secondary structure motifs using reduced amino acid alphabets (RAAs). Results indicate an overall success in designing novel proteins with desired secondary structure motifs for a broad range of amino acid alphabets and complexity of designs. Interestingly, for a substantial fraction of designs, ESMFold predicts a fold close to that of the target structure despite training only on physicochemical sequence space and secondary structure information. The development of this model advances research across multiple disciplines, from general scientific AI architecture development to protein design for biotechnology, astrobiology, and early-Earth evolutionary biology.</jats:p>

3dce4b94762af4295ccc55331c5abd2af8b304b5.abstract: <jats:p>The purpose of this article is to discuss the construction of international sports communication curriculum system and the assessment of instructional effect with the assistance of artificial intelligence (AI). Under the background of globalization, the importance of international sports communication is increasingly prominent, and the rapid development of AI technology provides new opportunities for the optimization of curriculum system and the improvement of instructional effect. This article first defines the goal and orientation of the international sports communication course, and then designs a comprehensive curriculum system covering theoretical knowledge, practical skills and cultural literacy. On this basis, AI technology is introduced and intelligent learning support and services are provided. In order to scientifically assess the instructional effect, this article constructs a instructional effect assessment model based on deep learning (DL), and carries out experimental verification. The results show that the model has the advantages of fast convergence and small prediction error, and can accurately reflect the learning effect of students and the instructional effect of teachers. AI-assisted international sports communication course system construction and instructional effect assessment have obvious advantages, which provides new ideas for the innovation and development of international sports communication education.</jats:p>

title: Edge intelligence drives multiscale anomaly detection network for heterogeneous IoT traffic
container-title: International Conference on Wireless, Optical Communication, and Information Engineering (WOCIE 2026)
3fa3bcfb6aaffc7a22496a380913b0ef41e0ce25.abstract: <jats:p>When edge nodes undertake the task of near-source traffic monitoring in the Internet of Things (iot), limited computing resources and the difference of abnormal behavior time span are easy to cause local mutation and insufficient information representation of continuous attack. To solve this problem, this paper constructs a multi-scale anomaly detection network for heterogeneous traffic driven by edge intelligence. The traffic information is extracted at the edge side, and the communication changes of different persistence ranges are depicted through short, medium and long time scale coding, and the dynamic fusion is performed according to the scale contribution to realize the identification of normal communication and multi-class abnormal traffic. Experiments were carried out based on the CICIoT2023 dataset. The detection accuracy of DDoS, DoS, Recon, Web, Brute Force, Spoofing and Mirai traffic in our network reaches 99.2%, 98.9%, 97.8%, 96.4%, 96.9%, 98.1% and 99.0%, respectively. The accuracy is 97.88% when the traffic scale is 90000, and the average detection delay is 18.6 ms when the proportion of available computing resources of edge nodes is 20%. The results show that the constructed network can balance the accuracy of heterogeneous traffic anomaly detection, the stability of scale change and the real-time performance of edge deployment, which can provide technical support for the edge side anomaly communication monitoring of iot.</jats:p>

title: Prospects and challenges of artificial intelligence for food security sustainability in Africa: case of South Africa and Nigeria
container-title: Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems
1c0149e3d35a8ab308ed80bf5165b039ab5152b2.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly emerged as a transformative technology with the potential to reshape agricultural systems and strengthen food security sustainability in Africa. It is against this backdrop that this study examines the prospects and challenges of AI for food security sustainability in Nigeria and South Africa, adopting a qualitative comparative research design and drawing on secondary sources of data. The analysis is anchored in embedded liberalism theory and agro-ecological theory, which provide complementary perspectives for examining the institutional, socioeconomic, technological, and ecological conditions that shape the sustainable application of AI in agriculture. Findings indicate that large agricultural yield gaps and the predominance of smallholder farming in Nigeria, alongside South Africa’s relatively advanced digital infrastructure, commercial agricultural systems, and innovation ecosystem, present significant opportunities for AI-enabled improvements in agricultural productivity, resilience, and resource efficiency. However, these prospects are moderated by context-specific challenges. Nigeria faces persistent infrastructural, institutional, and technological constraints, while South Africa’s principal challenge lies in inequality-driven exclusion and uneven access to technological benefits. The study therefore argues that AI can contribute meaningfully to food security sustainability when embedded within inclusive institutional arrangements, sustainable agricultural practices, ecological conservation, and context-sensitive governance frameworks.</jats:p>

title: Joint Design of Beamforming and Artificial Noise for Dual Hybrid RIS-Assisted D2D Secure Communications
container-title: Engineering Research Express
9d1eb0410a6a7a3643c254a5eedffe8172c61b9a.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Hybrid reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (HRISs) alleviate cascaded attenuation by selectively activating reflecting elements. To improve secure multi-pair device-to-device (D2D) communications, this paper considers two cooperative HRISs and artificial noise (AN). The transmit beamforming and AN vectors, HRIS reflection coefficients, and binary active/passive configurations are jointly designed to minimize the modeled total system power subject to secrecy-rate and per-HRIS amplification-power constraints. The resulting mixed-integer nonconvex problem is addressed by a four-block alternating-optimization framework employing semidefinite relaxation, successive convex approximation, majorization–minimization, and a discrete mode-selection surrogate. The numerical comparisons in the revised manuscript illustrate the power-consumption trends of the dual-HRIS architecture, the role of adaptive element allocation, and the effect of AN for the studied nominal-CSI scenarios. A mathematical multiple-eavesdropper extension, an Eve-CSI-error sensitivity study using an explicit design margin, and a computational-complexity discussion are also provided. The CSI-error sensitivity study should not be interpreted as a certified worst-case robust-optimization solution.</jats:p>

title: DIGITAL INTELLIGENCE-DRIVEN AND INTEGRATED EVALUATION-CONSTRUCTION: PARADIGM RECONSTRUCTION AND PRACTICAL EXPLORATION OF "INTERCULTURAL COMMUNICATION" COURSES IN HIGHER EDUCATION
container-title: Educational Research and Human Development
e5f3fa300757ff446b423f5ec1ac55f55099e1b3.abstract: <jats:p>Addressing critical bottlenecks in traditional intercultural communication instruction—specifically, fabricated communicative contexts, the decoupling of teaching and assessment, and superficial technology integration—this study introduces a synergistic mechanism of "data-intelligence driving" and "evaluation–construction integration" to construct a data-driven precision teaching framework for college foreign language courses. Adopting a backward design approach, the study reconstructs a four-dimensional curricular objective matrix comprising language proficiency, digital-intelligence literacy, intercultural communicative competence, and comprehensive qualities. By deconstructing typical tasks in international professions, it develops a multimodal digital case repository and a three-phase, five-step virtual-real hybrid training chain ("Orient–Instruct–Practice–Explore–Evaluate"). Furthermore, a tripartite attainment assessment model integrating process evaluation, summative evaluation, and value-added evaluation is established. Drawing upon multiple rounds of pedagogical implementation at Zhejiang Yuexiu University, this paper summarizes the implementation pathways, core mechanisms, and preliminary observations of the proposed paradigm, while reflecting on its inherent constraints. This research aims to provide a transferable operational framework for the digital-intelligence transformation of tertiary foreign language courses, acknowledging that its empirical efficacy warrants validation through larger-sample and longer-term empirical testing.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence and Canada's Productivity Challenge: Bridging the Gap Between  Promise and Economic Reality
container-title: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology
c4addb4e1955a9162443e022cebd9559c404098a.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) offers considerable potential to improve productivity, yet its growing adoption has not necessarily translated into corresponding gains in aggregate labour productivity. This paper examines Canada's AI productivity challenge using evidence from Statistics Canada, Bank of Canada research, academic literature, and documented expert commentary. It considers the historical productivity paradox alongside business adoption patterns, projected productivity gains, sectoral differences, and emerging labour-market adjustments. Canadian evidence highlights a gap between the widespread personal use of AI by business leaders and its integration into core business operations. Conceptual illustrations demonstrate how implementation costs, organizational restructuring, complementary investment, and workforce skill development may influence the realization of AI's economic benefits. The analysis distinguishes planned adoption from actual implementation, projected gains from observed outcomes, and associations from causal effects. It argues that realizing AI's productivity potential requires effective organizational integration, workforce learning, and broader diffusion across businesses. The paper concludes with policy implications for Canada and emphasizes the importance of monitoring productivity and labour-market outcomes as AI adoption evolves.</jats:p>

title: Proactive early invisible spoilage-risk prediction through uncertainty-quantified temporal microbial growth intelligence
container-title: Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems
84b86375d5375960f6df8485ea7b6c42004d152f.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    The study addresses the need for proactive food safety monitoring because microbial growth can increase before visible spoilage becomes apparent. Existing microbial prediction methods mainly provide deterministic forecasts and often lack temporal interpretability, predictive uncertainty, and decision-oriented risk estimation. This study proposes the Bayesian Attention Temporal Microbial Growth Network (BAT-MG Net) to forecast microbial concentration and estimate early spoilage risk. The model is implemented using Python with GPU-accelerated deep-learning tools, using ComBase microbial growth time-series data. Missing values are handled using training-derived imputation, features are Min-Max normalized, and group-stratified 80:20 partitioning prevents experimental leakage. A 6-h temporal window and a 6-h-ahead forecasting horizon are used with LSTM and attention mechanisms, while Monte Carlo Dropout quantifies predictive uncertainty. The resulting D-PSRI combines microbial concentration and uncertainty to classify risk as low, moderate, or high. BAT-MG Net achieved 97.8% accuracy, 0.198 RMSE, 0.154 MAE, and 0.97
                    <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    , with 94.6% PICP and 0.021 calibration error. These results indicate effective microbial concentration forecasting and uncertainty-aware spoilage-risk estimation within the evaluated ComBase analytical subset. Previously reported studies are included as contextual references because differences in datasets, prediction endpoints, experimental conditions, and modeling tasks prevent direct head-to-head comparisons of performance.
                  </jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence in Dental Research: Innovation versus Integrity?
container-title: Journal of Dental Research
f9895b5bf02d68cbae01ff7ecbc1f562d233c7fa.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models and agentic pipelines, is reshaping dental research. This article examines the opportunities and risks of AI in knowledge production in oral health research. On one hand, AI accelerates literature synthesis, data analysis, and manuscript drafting; on the other, it introduces new risks, including fabricated findings and citations, overconfident inference, and homogenization of research focus. These shifts challenge the mechanisms that maintain scientific credibility such as peer review, reproducibility, and human judgment, especially in fields like dentistry, where small datasets and limited editorial capacity may amplify vulnerabilities. We here identify 3 structural asymmetries: 1) the growing gap between the rapid pace of AI-assisted production and slow human validation, 2) the divergence between AI-generated linguistic fluency and the true robustness of the generated evidence, and 3) unequal institutional capacity to govern AI and the incentives set by the research system for (mis)using AI for research. We conclude with a call for proportional and enforceable governance frameworks, including mandatory AI disclosure standards, provenance tracking, structured adversarial testing of research tools, and interdisciplinary oversight. Moreover, we suggest institutional reform, including revising incentive structures, fostering AI literacy, and enforcing auditability to safeguard research integrity. In the age of machine-assisted content, credibility becomes a scarce resource. Dental science must not merely adopt AI but actively govern it to ensure that its accelerated outputs remain trustworthy, equitable, and clinically meaningful.</jats:p>

title: Adoption de l'intelligence artificielle et performance perçue des missions d'audit : une étude empirique auprès des auditeurs marocains
Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Perceived Audit Engagement Performance: An Empirical Study of Moroccan Auditors
container-title: International Journal of Research in Economics and Finance
b91540671c49bf68590e60c8d9e2989354dfa9c6.abstract: <jats:p>L'intelligence artificielle (IA) transforme progressivement les pratiques d'audit, mais ses effets restent surtout documentés dans les économies avancées. Au Maroc, marché caractérisé par une maturité numérique intermédiaire et une forte fragmentation des cabinets, les travaux empiriques portent principalement sur l'intention ou la préparation à l'adoption de l'IA, et non sur son usage effectif dans les missions. Cette recherche examine la relation entre l'usage effectif des outils d'IA, les bénéfices perçus et le changement des pratiques, d'une part, et la performance perçue des missions d'audit, d'autre part. S'appuyant sur le Technology Acceptance Model, l'étude repose sur une enquête par questionnaire menée auprès d'un échantillon non probabiliste de 40 auditeurs exerçant au Maroc ; les données ont été analysées par régression linéaire multiple. Le modèle présente un pouvoir explicatif élevé (R² = 0,888 ; p < 0,001) et seul l'usage effectif des outils d'IA est significativement associé à la performance perçue (β = 0,937 ; p < 0,001). L'étude déplace l'analyse de l'intention d'adoption vers l'usage effectif et suggère que, dans un contexte émergent, la mise en œuvre concrète des outils compte davantage que les perceptions de leurs bénéfices. Le caractère non probabiliste et la taille réduite de l'échantillon limitent la généralisation des résultats ; la mesure perceptuelle de la performance, recueillie auprès des mêmes répondants, expose à un biais de méthode commune, et les associations observées ne permettent pas de conclure à une relation causale.</jats:p>

title: Capital immatériel, adoption de l’intelligence artificielle et performance des entreprises marocaines : proposition d’un modèle conceptuel et d’un protocole empirique
Intellectual Capital, Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Moroccan Firms’ Performance: A Proposed Conceptual Model and Empirical Protocol
container-title: International Journal of Research in Economics and Finance
3e9f3d77cbc2e91f6b992f3e95114c2f6ee72740.abstract: <jats:p>Cet article conceptuel et exploratoire propose un modèle reliant le capital immatériel à la performance des entreprises marocaines par l’intermédiaire de l’adoption de l’intelligence artificielle. Il mobilise la théorie des ressources et l’approche des capacités dynamiques, puis confronte le modèle proposé à des informations publiques sur les entreprises au Maroc. La démarche repose sur une analyse documentaire ciblée et sur des statistiques descriptives publiées par le Haut-Commissariat au Plan. La documentation de l’Enterprise Survey Maroc 2023 de la Banque mondiale est également examinée pour apprécier les possibilités d’une investigation ultérieure. Les données disponibles montrent des différences d’accès à Internet selon la taille des entreprises et un usage inégal des outils numériques. Elles ne mesurent cependant pas conjointement le capital immatériel, l’adoption effective de l’IA et la performance organisationnelle. L’article propose donc des hypothèses, un dispositif de mesure et un protocole de médiation, sans présenter cette relation comme statistiquement démontrée. Sa contribution est de préciser les conditions documentaires et méthodologiques d’une recherche empirique adaptée au contexte marocain.</jats:p>

title: Legal reconstruction of corporate digital responsibility in the context of artificial intelligence governance
container-title: Advances in Social Behavior Research
19b098549c72aee315e02925e7ab4287ff22b9c1.abstract: <jats:p>The emergence of artificial intelligence now influences corporate decision-making, information processing, automatic evaluations, and relationships with stakeholders, thus raising the question of corporate digital responsibility as the subject of corporate governance. Comparative analysis addresses the possibility of transforming corporate digital responsibility from voluntary ethical commitment into legally verifiable obligation via the algorithmic lifecycle approach. The corpus consists of 18 laws, regulations, and authoritative corporate governance guidelines released during 2021-2025 and 3-4 key documents of each of the 15 selected digital companies in the European Union, China, and the United States. Twenty indicators were coded in the following categories: data governance, fairness control, transparency, human oversight, and audit/ remedy. Every indicator includes absence of commitment, general commitment, and verifiable procedures, while legal requirement-responsibility indicator-scoring basis matrix provides the link between corporate data and normative requirement. The findings reveal that transparency, human oversight, and audit/ remedy are characterized by significant differences among jurisdictions, while data governance and fairness control are more alike. The median score for audit/remedy is 75.0 in the European Union and 50.0 in China and the United States. These findings support lifecycle-based legal reconstruction connecting corporate digital responsibility with identifiable duties of care, disclosure, oversight, auditing, correction, and compensation through a framework.</jats:p>

title: Examining artificial intelligence training as fair use: a comparative law reflection on Bartz v. Anthropic PBC
container-title: Advances in Social Behavior Research
32e18a7e1240838986393329daa6fd1721a1a1a9.abstract: <jats:p>Traditional legal doctrinal analysis easily regards the use of copyrighted works in artificial intelligence (AI) training as infringement; however, in substance this conclusion goes against the purpose of copyright law to balance interests. In Bartz v. Anthropic PBC , a U.S. federal district court held for the first time that the use of copyrighted books to train large language models is fair use, but did not accept fair use for the pirated copies acquired to build a permanent central library. Transformative use forms the core of this holding; training aims to build a technical tool, its results are transformative and differ in value from the original works, and no market substitution follows. The class action settlement reached later only concerned the acquisition of pirated copies; thus, the reasoning still stands. From the perspective of comparative law and legal interpretation, the decision offers a reference for China; Article 24 of the Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China lists fair use in a closed enumeration. It is better to give this provision a limited expansive interpretation. By means of teleological expansion, AI training can be included in the scope of "illustrating a point" under Article 24(1)(2) and treated by analogy as a special kind of illustrative use; its object is the linguistic patterns, statistical regularities, and knowledge structures in data, and three restrictive requirements apply. Then the degree of transformation serves as an auxiliary criterion and works inside the three-step test as a residual check.</jats:p>

title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into  Healthcare to Improve Quality of Care
container-title: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology
1c486bdd9210dac79d39533c3e32cf226f5892c9.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is transitioning from accuracy studies on historical data to prospective, real-world testing of performance in everyday care, but whether this will lead to better quality of care is debated. We review latest peerreviewed evidence (2023-26) by six quality domains-effectiveness, safety, efficiency, patient-centeredness, cost and equity across set of validated articles.</jats:p>

title: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence for Microbiome-Informed Precision Cardiovascular Medicine
container-title: Cardiac Research
8574bab53aff741fdc5e6b48133cb02164f20d7c.abstract: <jats:p>Microbial metabolism, intestinal barrier function, and immune signaling link the gut microbiota to vascular and cardiac disease. The clinical significance of these signals nevertheless varies across disease phenotypes and is influenced by host genetics, diet, medication, and kidney function. Multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) offers methods to examine these relationships by integrating microbial and host information. In this review, we synthesize the biological evidence and assess how multimodal analysis can support microbiome-informed precision cardiovascular medicine. We distinguish the gut–vascular and gut–heart axes and evaluate approaches that combine microbiome profiles, host genomics, and metabolomics with cardiovascular imaging and longitudinal clinical data to prioritize candidate mechanisms, identify disease endotypes and assess risk. We compare fusion strategies and examine AI applications in microbial functional prediction and disease classification, distinguishing these from mechanistic and statistical integration. Causal confidence and biomarker maturity are considered separately to clarify the evidence needed for mechanistic claims, risk prediction, and targeted intervention. Current evidence is stronger for biological discovery than for AI-guided cardiovascular care. Clinical translation requires control of confounding, comparison with clinical and unimodal models, external validation, and prospective assessment of clinical utility. The immediate priority is to identify reproducible cardiovascular endotypes and candidate microbial targets for intervention studies.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence‐Driven Extraction of Patient‐Reported Pain Outcomes in Osteoarthritis Using Large Language Models
container-title: Arthritis Care & Research
5b75f4a8210afea6004ad9767e55e992556bda4b.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Patient‐reported outcome measures (PROMs) are central to assessing symptom burden and treatment response in Osteoarthritis (OA) but are often embedded in unstructured clinical notes. We evaluated whether prompt‐engineered large language models (LLMs) could accurately extract or infer pain scores on a 0‐10 scale from routine OA clinical documentation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We retrospectively analyzed 163 paired internal medicine and orthopedic clinic notes from patients in a prospective OA registry. A trained abstractor extracted explicitly documented pain scores from notes. For notes lacking explicit pain scores, physicians estimated pain severity from narrative documentation. The Llama 3.2‐90B model, using Chain‐of‐Thought and Few‐Shot prompting, inferred pain scores. Registry‐collected pain scores served as a reference standard. Agreement was assessed using Kendall's Tau‐b.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Agreement between LLM‐extracted and abstracted scores was strong for IM notes (n =132, τ = 0.76, p < 0.0001) and excellent for orthopedic notes (n = 65, τ = 0.95, p < 0.0001). The LLM identified 15 EMR‐generated default zero scores in IM notes; after excluding them, agreement was perfect (τ = 1.0, p < 0.0001). For notes without explicit pain scores (31 IM and 98 orthopedic notes), LLM‐based pain inference showed weak correlation with registry scores (IM: τ = 0.17; orthopedic: τ = 0.11), but performed comparably to physician estimation. LLM–physician agreement ranged from 54.2%–88.0% within ±1 point and 66.7%–100% within ±2 points for IM notes, and from 54.8%–70.5% within ±1 point and 84.5%–97.7% within ±2 points for orthopedic notes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>LLMs accurately extract explicitly documented PROMs from clinical notes and reliably identify documentation artifacts. Inference from narrative documentation was less precise when notes lacked sufficient contextual information and detailed pain descriptions.</jats:p>

title: Deep Machine Learning-Driven Intelligence Architectures for Precision Surgical Strike Operations: A Multidimensional Analysis of Algorithmic Targeting, Predictive Threat Assessment, and Strategic Transformation in Contemporary Asymmetric Warfare
container-title: Kashmir Journal of Academic Research and Development
0042e0da026dbd20c3e93cb686c3ffa4f995c947.abstract: <jats:p>Purpose: This article asks what open-source evidence can and cannot tell us about the claim that deep machine learning (DML) has made surgical strike operations more precise. It treats an intelligence architecture as a socio-technical chain running from data, through models and human validation, to operational and strategic outcomes, and it examines the weakest link in that chain: the contested ground truth on which both algorithms and their evaluators depend. Design/methodology/approach: We assemble a sourced workbook covering US strikes in Pakistan (2004–2017; 409 strikes, 3,096 deaths), four cross-theatre campaigns, six competing Pakistan casualty estimates, Airwars evidential grades for Somalia, and reported throughput of algorithmic targeting systems. The estimation strategy combines negative binomial count models with exposure offsets and sandwich errors, a Quandt–Andrews sup-LR break test with parametric bootstrap, BIC-weighted break-date posteriors, Dirichlet-multinomial composition models, Manski partial identification with Imbens–Manski intervals, randomization inference, Paule–Mandel random-effects meta-analysis with Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman correction, and 100,000-draw Monte Carlo propagation of source ranges. Deep learning enters through a Poisson-loss deep neural ensemble, a long short-term memory (LSTM) forecaster and a label-noise variance decomposition; Erlang-C queueing models measure the human-review capacity implied by reported targeting throughput. Findings: Civilian deaths per strike fell by about 39 per cent a year, but the decline is a smooth trend rather than a datable regime break (sup-LR = 5.22, bootstrap p = 0.281), and it is not attributable to the 2013 Presidential Policy Guidance. Civilian deaths rose far less than proportionally with strike tempo (elasticity ≈ 0.25). Sources disagree so sharply that I² = 98.4 per cent and the 95 per cent prediction interval for the civilian share spans 0.1 to 93 per cent; label uncertainty accounts for 92.9 per cent of the deep ensemble's predictive variance. Deep models did not outperform parsimonious count models out of sample. At the reported rate of 1,000 recommendations an hour, a 20-person targeting cell can give each recommendation at most 1.2 minutes of review. Originality/value: The article is, to our knowledge, the first to combine partial identification, meta-analysis of competing casualty sources and deep-learning uncertainty decomposition in the study of algorithmic targeting, and to quantify the throughput–oversight constraint with queueing theory. Practical implications: Claims of algorithmic precision should be audited against bounded, multi-source ground truth, and review time per nomination should be treated as a measurable condition of meaningful human control.</jats:p>

title: P-161: Automated diabetic retinopathy detection in smartphone based fundus photography using artificial intelligence conducted at health camp in Assam
container-title: Hormone Research in Paediatrics
d56c5249e49c971e783cf739631e288c1e564930.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>1 in 3 diabetics is at risk of developing diabetic retinopathy (DR). 1 in 10 Diabetics suffers vision loss. 80% of all vision impairment globally is avoidable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study was conducted to assess the role of artificial intelligence (AI)-based automated software for detection of diabetic retinopathy (DR) and sight-threatening DR (STDR) by fundus photography taken using a smartphone-based device and validate it against ophthalmologist’s grading.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>1775 patients with type 2 diabetes underwent retinal photography with Remidio ‘Fundus on phone’ (FOP), a smartphone-based device, at health camp conducted at 5 places in the periphery of Lumding constituency of Assam. Out of 1775 patients, 501 patients were found to be having Diabetic Retinopathy of various grade. Grading of DR was performed by the ophthalmologists using International Clinical DR (ICDR) classification scale. STDR was defined by the presence of severe non-proliferative DR, proliferative DR or diabetic macular oedema (DME). The retinal photographs were graded using a validated AI DR screening software (EyeArtTM) designed to identify DR, referable DR (moderate non-proliferative DR or worse and/or DME) or STDR. The sensitivity and specificity of automated grading were assessed and validated against the ophthalmologists’ grading.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Retinal images of 501 patients were graded. DR was detected by the ophthalmologists in 323 (64.4%) and by the AI software in 343 (68.6%) patients while STDR was detected in 189 (37.8%) and 246 (49.3%) patients, respectively. The AI software showed 95.8% (95% CI 92.9–98.7) sensitivity and 80.2% (95% CI 72.6–87.8) specificity for detecting any DR and 99.1% (95% CI 95.1–99.9) sensitivity and 80.4% (95% CI 73.9–85.9) specificity in detecting STDR.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Automated AI analysis of FOP smartphone retinal imaging has very high sensitivity for detecting DR and STDR and thus can be an initial tool for mass retinal screening in people with diabetes for early detection and timely referral to ophthalmologist.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Librarians in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
container-title: Central European Library and Information Science Review Közép-európai Könyvtár- és Információtudományi Szemle
b4aafa45c108c0608892953dd42508752115d4ab.abstract: <jats:p>In the age of artificial intelligence, libraries and librarians are undergoing profound transformations in their missions, competencies, and professional roles. This conceptual paper examines how key 21st-century socio-technological trends – particularly the rise of artificial intelligence and changing labour market demands – are reshaping the ways in which libraries support education, research, and community engagement. Drawing on international policy documents and scholarly literature, complemented by illustrative examples of library practice, the paper analyses three interrelated dimensions: librarians’ professional attitudes towards technological change, the development of digital and AI-related competencies, and their emerging role as educational mediators. The analysis highlights the importance of librarians’ competencies, professional attitudes, and continuous professional development alongside technological infrastructure in shaping the integration of artificial intelligence into library services. The paper argues that libraries are emerging as human-centred, adaptive learning environments in which technological innovation is aligned with ethical, social, and educational values. By positioning librarians as key actors in mediating technological change, the study contributes to the ongoing redefinition of librarianship in an AI-driven world.</jats:p>

title: P-373: The role of emotional and spiritual intelligence in alleviating diabetes distress among young adults

                    <jats:p>The management of Type 1 Diabetes mellitus (T1D) poses significant challenges, as individuals with T1D face numerous psychological difficulties in their daily lives and adherence to treatment regimens.</jats:p>

                    <jats:p>The present study explores the role of cognitive (diabetes-related knowledge and locus of control), emotion-related (diabetes distress, trait emotional intelligence [EI], and satisfaction with life), and transcendental (spiritual intelligence and mindfulness) variables in self-management behaviors (SMB) and HbA1c (average blood sugar).</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The SEM results highlighted a positive mediation relationship that Trait EI had on Glucose Management through Meaning (β =0.25, p=.002) and the effect that Meaning had on HbA1c through Glucose Management (β =-0.32, p=.005). title: Inteligencia artificial y aprendizaje financiero
Artificial intelligence and financial learning
container-title: Accounting and Management Research
688dde4d25c7068b51d81398bdd92beb5fa4a467.abstract: <jats:p>El presente estudio tuvo como objetivo describir las percepciones asociadas al uso de inteligencia artificial (IA) generativa en el aprendizaje financiero y analizar los patrones de coincidencia y divergencia reportados al contrastar una resolución propia con otra apoyada en IA. Se realizó un estudio de métodos mixtos con integración interpretativa. El componente cuantitativo incluyó un cuestionario ad hoc aplicado a 121 estudiantes de dos instituciones de educación superior de Sahagún, Colombia, seleccionados por conveniencia. El componente documental comprendió 13 informes integradores de Análisis Financiero y Finanzas Corporativas, codificados por dos investigadoras mediante ocho categorías de presencia/ausencia; antes del consenso, el acuerdo global fue de 94,2 % y el AC1 de Gwet, de 0,915. En la encuesta, el 74,4 % consideró la IA útil o muy útil, el 36,7 % calificó sus respuestas como confiables o muy confiables y el 57,0 % declaró verificarlas siempre; el 55,4 % señaló como principal riesgo recibir resultados erróneos. En los informes, los 13 registraron coincidencia en al menos una tarea estructurada, 10 identificaron dependencia de datos o supuestos y 3 describieron desalineación estratégica en una resolución apoyada en IA. Los hallazgos no respaldan una mejora de la precisión técnica atribuible a la IA y deben interpretarse como exploratorios.</jats:p>

b9165e49d1055fe04d48829a571d4f75098f7c89.abstract: <jats:p>Este artículo analiza críticamente la relación entre inteligencia artificial, interoperabilidad de datos y fiscalización tributaria en Colombia. title: Accuracy and reliability of artificial intelligence-based automated measurement of hallux valgus-related angles on plain foot radiographs: a systematic review
container-title: Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research
3708baaaee3997c907d9331f7024a9a7ce189b0d.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This systematic review aims to evaluate the accuracy, reliability, and clinical utility of deep learning algorithms for automated hallux valgus measurements on weight-bearing radiographs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We searched Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane CENTRAL from inception to June 2026 for studies evaluating automated hallux valgus angle (HVA) and intermetatarsal angle (IMA) measurements by deep learning models. Reported measurement errors and reliability estimates were summarized descriptively. Risk of bias and applicability were assessed using an adapted QUADAS-2 framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>From 1080 initial records, 14 reports met the eligibility criteria. MAE was reported for HVA in 11 reports and IMA in 10, including one smartphone-based evaluation; six reports provided RMSE for both angles. For primary systems evaluated directly on radiographs, reported MAEs ranged from 0.69° to 4.14° for HVA and from 0.57° to 3.22° for IMA. Corresponding RMSEs ranged from 0.87° to 5.22° and from 0.92° to 3.76°, respectively. Seven reports provided numerical ICCs, which generally indicated high agreement, although differences in ICC definitions and reference measurements limited comparability. Differences in validation datasets, potentially overlapping cohorts, and insufficient reporting of metric-specific uncertainty precluded reliable pooling. Low average errors did not establish that all individual measurements were within clinically acceptable limits.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Deep learning algorithms showed promising accuracy and agreement with expert measurements of HVA and IMA on plain foot radiographs. However, methodological differences and limitations in the available validation evidence warrant cautious interpretation. Further independent validation, including assessment of individual measurement errors and performance in clinically challenging cases, is needed to establish their suitability for routine clinical use.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
