title: What Survives Technical Change? Artificial Identity and Persistence in Contemporary Cinema
container-title: Kashmir Journal of Academic Research and Development
c86a1e1ea636e55f21da3f7123a03ec400f54a2a.abstract: <jats:p>Contemporary science-fiction cinema keeps depicting artificial entities that develop, are technically modified, reconstructed, or copied, or stop operating while information about them stays accessible. These situations raise a narrower problem than whether artificial beings can think, feel, or count as persons: what makes an artificial individual the same individual across technical change? A system may keep its memories in a new body or preserve its organization while its components are replaced. It may produce a successor with an indistinguishable psychological profile or leave records behind after shutting down. Such cases usually get filed under “continuity,” but continuity takes different forms, none of which alone establishes “numerical identity.”I work through the problem with John Locke on personal identity, Derek Parfit on psychological continuity and branching, and Gilbert Simondon on individuation and technical objects. Locke separates information about past experience from the consciousness through which a person appropriates it. For Parfit, continuity can branch into several successors without making each numerically identical with its predecessor. Simondon explains how technical individuals emerge and change through their formation and associated milieus. He does not treat technical development as proof of personal identity or consciousness.The principal films are The Artifice Girl (Franklin Ritch, 2022), Archive (Gavin Rothery, 2020), and After Yang (Kogonada, 2021), with Moon (Duncan Jones, 2009) as a comparative reference for duplication and branching. Development, reconstruction, archival preservation, and duplication do not preserve the same thing. The Artifice Girl presents a developing technical system whose causal and operational history supports continuity across modification, while its distributed instances leave the unity of the system unresolved. Archive distinguishes the preservation or reconstruction of mental contents from the survival of the person they represent; its final revelation also changes the evidential status of the protagonist’s apparent experience. After Yang shows informational traces and social significance outlasting the operation of an artificial individual, without establishing that the individual himself continues. Moon shows distinct successors inheriting the same memories without becoming one individual. The comparison distinguishes six relations that may connect earlier and later states: causal, psychological, informational, organizational or technical, experiential, and social or narrative continuity. These are analytical distinctions, not an exhaustive taxonomy; numerical identity remains the question to be assessed, not another form of continuity. Memory, information, behavioral similarity, technical organization, and social remembrance are not interchangeable evidence of survival. Here, “artificial individual” is an analytical category, not an assumption that every represented system is a metaphysically unified subject. I propose no universal criterion of artificial identity.</jats:p>

title: A Systematic Review of Knowledge Management Practices as Antecedents of Artificial Intelligence Adoption in Nigerian SMEs
container-title: Journal of Business Development and Management Research
4b4b45b6ee2b8f853377a09c971f43a9dd5ebc3c.abstract: <jats:p>Research on artificial intelligence adoption among Nigerian small and medium enterprises is young and fragmented, and studies that pair knowledge management practices with an artificial intelligence adoption outcome are rare. This systematic review takes stock of that evidence and asks which knowledge management practices are plausible antecedents of artificial intelligence adoption in this setting. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines, Google Scholar, Scopus, Web of Science and ResearchGate were searched using database-specific Boolean strings, yielding 1,286 records. After removing 274 duplicates, screening 1,012 titles and abstracts and assessing 171 full texts against two-tier eligibility criteria, 21 studies were included: three from Nigeria, three from wider African settings and 15 international comparative studies. Study quality was appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool and Joanna Briggs Institute checklists. Thematic synthesis identified four themes: knowledge sharing culture, absorptive capacity, digital leadership and structural constraints. Only four studies examined knowledge management directly, while most measured proxy constructs such as digital leadership, human capital or dynamic capabilities, and no Nigerian study measured knowledge management and artificial intelligence adoption together. The review concludes with a conceptual framework and seven testable propositions, alongside low-cost knowledge management interventions for small firms and recommendations for national digital transformation agencies.</jats:p>

title: Engineering of the Future: Combining Big Data, Analytics and Artificial Intelligence to Develop Sustainable Technological Solutions
container-title: AFRICAN JOURNAL OF APPLIED RESEARCH
2895dbaf47a697111bde9750149eab43cc5bc5b0.abstract:
<jats:p>Purpose: This paper aims to critically review the integration of big data analytics and AI in engineering systems for addressing climate change, energy efficiency and resource optimisation, and to identify the key barriers to their wider adoption.
Design/Methodology/Approach: The study adopts a qualitative research methodology based on secondary data analysis of 17 peer-reviewed articles published between 2016 and 2026, using thematic analysis to identify key trends and patterns. 
Research Limitation: Challenges associated with implementing the described systems include high costs and data security concerns, indicating the need for further research on secure and cost-effective implementation. 
Findings: Big Data, Analytics, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) can enhance engineering decision-making by improving sustainability and efficiency. Data-driven methods are used to monitor and optimise industrial processes, with lower energy usage and waste. Predictive analysis reduces downtime and equipment failures using machine learning. 
Practical Implication: The combined use of digital technologies supports resource optimisation, environmental monitoring through carbon footprint tracking and climate modelling, and the transformation of traditional reactive engineering systems into proactive and autonomous systems. 
Social Implication: AI- and Big Data-related solutions improve smart cities, transportation systems, and buildings through traffic flow reduction, lower emissions, and more sustainable urban planning. 
Originality/Value: Unlike application-specific studies, this article contributes to knowledge by synthesising big data, analytics, and AI applications in engineering into five cross-cutting themes and outlining conditions for their sustainability effect, such as integration with cyber-physical systems.</jats:p>

title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Tourism Business
container-title: AFRICAN JOURNAL OF APPLIED RESEARCH
464c62499a892f47dabc549cf78483977c1cb430.abstract:
<jats:p>Purpose: To examine the use of artificial intelligence in the tourism industry and evaluate its impact on operational efficiency and service quality in the context of smart tourism. Design/Methodology/Approach: The study combines an analysis of 32 tourism enterprises operating in the European market with a survey of 124 consumers conducted in 2024–2025. Artificial intelligence adoption was assessed through the level of operational process automation, and content analysis of enterprise reports and platform analytics was used to measure performance before and after implementation. 
Research Limitation: The study is limited to European tourism enterprises and a relatively small consumer sample. Future research should include broader geographical coverage and longitudinal analysis. 
Findings: Artificial intelligence significantly improved operational performance. Average service time decreased from 18.6 to 11.2 minutes, automation increased from 27.4% to 61.8%, and customer interaction intensity rose from 1.8 to 2.6 contacts per user. Consumers reported high satisfaction with service quality and personalisation, although trust in intelligent systems remained moderate, indicating that behavioural barriers still constrain the full benefits of AI adoption. 
Practical Implication: The findings support the adoption of hybrid service models that combine artificial intelligence with human interaction. 
Social Implication: Effective AI implementation can improve service accessibility, customer satisfaction, and the sustainable development of smart tourism. 
Originality/Value: The novelty lies in an integrated model linking the share of AI-automated processes with operational variables (service time, customer contacts) and consumer variables (service quality, personalisation, trust).</jats:p>

title: Inteligência artificial e cuidado interprofissional na transição oncológica: Construindo decisões éticas compartilhadas em hematologia e oncologia
Artificial intelligence and interprofessional care in the oncology transition: Building shared ethical decisions in haematology and oncology
Inteligencia artificial y cuidado interprofesional en la transición oncológica: Construyendo decisiones éticas compartidas en hematología y oncologia
container-title: Research, Society and Development
a78f4c058787ec782742a74d849a042ac828e02b.abstract: <jats:p>A inteligência artificial (IA) chega às decisões oncológicas e hematológicas em um cuidado fragmentado nas transições entre diagnóstico, tratamento, sobrevivência e cuidados paliativos. Esta revisão integrativa, com dados públicos e abertos, sintetizou evidências de 2022 a 2026 sobre IA, cuidado interprofissional e decisões éticas compartilhadas e propôs um modelo operacional. Seguiram-se Whittemore e Knafl, Mendes et al., PICO e o relato PRISMA 2020. Foram executadas 18 buscas em 31/10/2026 em motor de busca acadêmico e páginas de periódicos (bases indexadas não consultadas). A apreciação usou listas de verificação do JBI e a escala SANRA, e o nível de evidência seguiu Melnyk e Fineout-Overholt. De 180 registros, 24 estudos foram incluídos (seis de nível V, 14 de nível VI e quatro de nível VII; 12 publicados em 2026). Emergiram sete categorias: percepções de profissionais e de pacientes, decisão multiprofissional, IA generativa, ética e governança, transições e panorama. Entre oncologistas, 84,8% exigiram explicabilidade para o próprio médico e 23,0% para o paciente; 82,9% dos pacientes aceitaram a IA se o médico mantiver a autoridade. Em 121 estudos de aprendizado de máquina em cuidados paliativos, a equidade foi tratada integralmente em cerca de 7%. Hematologia respondeu por três dos 24 estudos e nenhum testou a IA sobre a decisão compartilhada nas transições. Propõe-se o modelo PONTES (pactuar, oversight, narrar, transição, equidade e segurança) e um fluxograma para divergências entre a IA e a equipe, que não foram validados. Limitações: um revisor e oito relatórios não recuperados.</jats:p>

title: Assessing the Legal Challenges of Artificial Intelligence Use in Children’s Education in Tanzania
container-title: Advanced International Journal for Research
59099e662b654ef873ea427e5934e613eb9c44ba.abstract: <jats:p>This article examines the legal challenges related to the use of artificial intelligence in children’s education in Tanzania. It asks whether the existing legal framework protects children from risks arising from AI use in the learning process. The article invokes doctrinal methodology, while analysing the legal framework, international and regional instruments and scholarly literature relevant to the study. It finds that, although Tanzania has enacted laws on child protection, education and personal data protection and a National Guidelines for Artificial Intelligence in Education (2025), the law remains far from addressing AI-specific risks affecting children in education, which include personal data protection, consent, automated decision-making, algorithmic bias, transparency and accountability. The article recommends the adoption of clear, child-centred regulatory standards for AI use in education, supported by oversight and accountability mechanisms. It concludes that Tanzania’s emerging AI governance framework must expressly address children’s rights and educational contexts.</jats:p>

title: Teachers’ Trust in Artificial Intelligence and AI Dependency in Teaching and Learning Processes: Literacy and Responsible Use Plan
container-title: Advanced International Journal for Research
d4a37265846d2e8f96db9941fb57d4f577edcde7.abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to determine the relationship between teachers’ trust in artificial intelligence (AI) and AI dependency in teaching and learning processes in selected public elementary schools in Loon North District, Schools Division of Bohol, during School Year 2026–2027. Specifically, it examines teachers’ levels of trust in AI in terms of perceived reliability and accuracy, usefulness, confidence in AI-generated outputs, transparency, and perceived risks and concerns. It also assesses AI dependency in lesson planning, instructional material development, assessment preparation, instructional decision-making, professional tasks, and the exercise of independent professional judgment. The study will employ a descriptive-correlational research design involving 60 public elementary school teachers from Loon North Central Elementary School, Pondol Elementary School, and Lawis Elementary School, with 20 respondents from each school. Data will be gathered using a structured questionnaire and analyzed through appropriate descriptive and inferential statistical tools. Frequency counts, percentages, and weighted means will be used to describe respondents’ profiles and determine the levels of trust and dependency, while correlation analysis will establish whether significant relationships exist between the variables at the 0.05 level of significance. The findings are expected to provide an understanding of how teachers’ perceptions of AI relate to their reliance on AI-assisted educational tasks. The study will also identify trust dimensions that may be associated with AI dependency and inform the development of an AI Literacy and Responsible Use Plan. The proposed plan will focus on strengthening AI literacy, promoting ethical and appropriate AI integration, protecting data privacy, verifying AI-generated information, preserving teachers’ professional judgment, and establishing sustainable training, implementation, and evaluation mechanisms. Ultimately, the study seeks to support informed, responsible, and balanced AI use in elementary education while recognizing teachers’ central role in instructional planning and decision-making.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence Use and Critical Thinking in Nigerian Secondary Schools: Evidence from Students and Mathematics Teachers
container-title: Journal of Mathematics Instruction, Social Research and Opinion
341e3504a7366a94337468352d0ef739d615852b.abstract: <jats:p>The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in secondary education raises questions about its implications for students’ critical thinking. This study examined the relationship between AI use and critical thinking among secondary school students in Nigeria and explored students’ and teachers’ perceptions of AI’s influence on critical thinking. A mixed-methods design was adopted. Quantitative data were collected from 150 students randomly selected from five secondary schools in Ekiti State, Nigeria, using 10-item five-point scales measuring AI use and critical thinking skills. Qualitative data were obtained through interviews with selected students and teachers and analysed thematically. Pearson correlation was used to examine the relationship between AI use and critical thinking. The findings revealed a significant positive relationship between AI use and students’ critical thinking skills. Students perceived AI as useful for accessing alternative perspectives, obtaining detailed explanations, and deepening understanding, but also acknowledged that excessive reliance on AI-generated answers could reduce independent thinking. Teachers similarly perceived AI as a valuable learning aid while expressing concerns about dependence and reduced cognitive engagement. The findings indicate that AI can support critical thinking when students actively evaluate, verify, and reflect on AI-generated information rather than use it as a substitute for reasoning. The study recommends AI literacy and guided pedagogical practices that promote responsible, evaluative, and non-dependent AI use in secondary education.</jats:p>

title: Students’ Critical Thinking Disposition in Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Mathematics Learning
container-title: Journal of Mathematics Instruction, Social Research and Opinion
01311dffff56ef5b3fa25b6218e76dab727364c2.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) can be used by students to learn and solve math problems in seconds. However, the learning habits of Indonesian students tend to rarely involve the ability to think at a higher level. This study aims to analyze students’ critical thinking dispositions in AI-assisted learning based on factor structure and experience category mapping. This study involved students (N=99) at a junior high school in the city of Jambi, Indonesia, so the findings are exploratory and limited to the context of the school. Data were collected using a perception-scale questionnaire on AI-assisted math learning behavior, analyzed with Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) and Rasch analysis. The findings identified five factors as the basis of student response patterns associated with critical thinking dispositions in AI-assisted math learning—reflective monitoring, internalization of understanding, passive dependence on AI, critical evaluation, and cognitive load. The mapping results showed that most students rarely experienced cognitive overload or internal understanding. At the same time, only a small percentage routinely performed reflective monitoring and critical evaluation, accompanied by early indications of a tendency toward passive dependence on AI. However, these findings need to be interpreted conservatively given the relatively low reliability of these factors. Based on the difficulty level of item approval in Rasch’s analysis, student responses showed inconsistencies in several factors, which could indicate a risk of cognitive passivity; However, these findings reflect the overall difficulty level in item approval, not a direct classification of each student’s level of disposition. This is especially true of the passive dependency factor on AI, which has the lowest reliability among the five factors. Therefore, strengthening working memory in AI-assisted mathematics learning requires an emphasis on reflection, evaluation, and justification activities to support knowledge development through internalization.</jats:p>

title: The IMUNOPOLI Board Game: Effects on Students’ Self-Efficacy and Emotional Intelligence in Learning the Immune System<b></b>
container-title: Al Jahiz: Journal of Biology Education Research
ac495c9fcffce43337ffcd04c685315527a7d3f0.abstract: <jats:p>This study aimed to examine the effect of the IMUNOPOLI board game on students' self-efficacy and emotional intelligence in immune system learning, with concept mastery included as a supporting variable to contextualize learning outcomes. A quasi-experimental method with a Non-equivalent Control Group Design was used, involving 60 students, at a state senior high school in Bandung City, divided into an experimental and a control group (each with 30 students). Data were collected using a self-efficacy questionnaire (15 items), an emotional intelligence questionnaire (33 items), and a concept mastery multiple-choice test (25 items). Data were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney test, score categorization, effect size via rank biserial correlation, and Spearman correlation to explore the relationships among the variables. Descriptively, the experimental group showed a greater shift toward high self-efficacy than the control group, though this difference did not reach statistical significance. Emotional intelligence in the experimental group remained stable due to a baseline ceiling effect, whereas the control group showed a more noticeable increase, resulting in no statistically significant post-test differences between groups. Furthermore, no statistically significant correlations were found among self-efficacy, emotional intelligence, and concept mastery. These findings indicate that while IMUNOPOLI descriptively supported self-efficacy and maintained high emotional intelligence levels, it did not demonstrate statistically significant superiority over conventional instruction, highlighting the importance of initial student conditions in game-based learning interventions.</jats:p>

title: MediDocker: An AI-Enabled Healthcare Intelligence Ecosystem Integrating Clinical Decision Support, Predictive Analytics, and Emergency Response
container-title: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
d04969a768c3b17a9f37083acda948b7e5571bb5.abstract: <jats:p>Patients keep their health information in places that do not talk to each other: handwritten prescriptions, PDF blood reports, appointment cards and paper bills, and in an emergency nobody can quickly see their blood group or allergies. This paper presents MediDocker, a web platform that keeps these records in one secure place and explains them in plain language. A vision-language model (Qwen2.5-VL, run locally) only copies what a prescription says; every medicine is then verified against RxNorm, an Indian brand dictionary and a hand-checked drug table, and its purpose and warnings come from verified sources, never from the model. Blood (CBC) reports are encrypted, read with a PDF text layer or PaddleOCR, checked by seven plausibility rules, and followed across reports with reference change values, a personal set point and Theil–Sen projection. A LightGBM model trained on 14,134 laboratory-confirmed NHANES participants screens for iron deficiency from the CBC alone and answers only when it is confident, otherwise advising a serum ferritin test. On 1,945 unseen participants from 2021 onwards it reached an AUROC of 0.836 (95% CI 0.816–0.857) and 94.2% accuracy on the 10.6% of cases it decides, with sensitivity 99.6% and specificity 99.3% at its two cut-offs. A record-aware assistant detects emergencies with rules before any language model is used, and an Ed25519-signed emergency QR code can be verified offline by anyone, without login</jats:p>

title: Emotional Intelligence and Effectiveness of Non-Teaching Staff of Public Polytechnics in Southwestern Nigeria
container-title: DELSU Journal of Educational Research and Development
ff84c8781002255c5d37574898aa71a62de904c1.abstract: <jats:p>The study examined the impact of emotional intelligence on the effectiveness of non-teaching personnel in the Southwestern Nigerian polytechnics. Emotional intelligence is necessary to handle interpersonal relationships and improve workplace performance. Even though there have been a lot of emphasis on issues such as leadership, motivation and organisational commitment in previous studies as related staff effectiveness in higher education, there has been minimal focus on the problem of emotional intelligence. The study adopted a descriptive survey research design combining quantitative and qualitative (QUAN+qual) methods. and the data were analysed with descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and regression analysis with a level of significance of 0.05.  The results showed that emotional intelligence had a positive correlation with staff effectiveness and significantly contribute to effectiveness (β = 0.324). This suggests that the non-teaching personnel with a higher level of emotional intelligence perform better in discharging their responsibilities. It was concluded that emotional intelligence is an important aspect in improving the effectiveness of non-teaching employees in polytechnics. Therefore, the development of emotional intelligence should be a priority of the polytechnic management in terms of training and capacity-building programmes.</jats:p>

title: A Narrative Review of Artificial Intelligence Vulnerabilities in Cybersecurity
container-title: International Journal for Scientific Research
8156a43fdffdcf77ab879516dae581fd3b4a4349.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is used in malware classification traffic analysis software development and security decision support. Yet conventional accuracy metrics do not capture the attack surfaces introduced by these applications. This narrative review critically examines 35 purposively selected studies published between 2020 and 2026. Primary records were verified against publisher proceedings institutional and author sources. The corpus comprises 33 peer-reviewed publications and two identified preprints covering evasion poisoning privacy leakage model extraction language-model injection and evaluation assurance. The analysis distinguishes findings from security applications from mechanisms established in general machine -learning and agent benchmarks. Across these settings vulnerability depends on an attacker’s access whether manipulations are valid within the application domain, and whether an erroneous output can cross an authorization boundary. Malware attacks that preserve functionality and traffic attacks that respect domain constraints offer stronger evidence of feasibility than perturbations confined to feature space. Retrieval and persistent memory extend the scope for poisoning beyond training. Agent benchmarks, in turn, highlight the need to assess authorized task completion separately from unauthorized actions. Contrasting findings from developer studies also indicate that insecure model output is not a uniform measure of harm to users. The proposed lifecycle assurance framework brings together data provenance realistic adaptive evaluation restricted privileges and monitoring over time. The purposive sample and heterogeneous outcomes preclude pooled estimates of attack success or claim about prevalence. Deployment decisions therefore require evidence spanning the full decision and action pipeline and robustness claims must remain limited to the conditions evaluated.</jats:p>

title: Inteligência artificial no planejamento da alta hospitalar: Aplicações, desafios metodológicos e perspectivas para a reabilitação — revisão narrativa crítica
Artificial intelligence in hospital discharge planning: Applications, methodological challenges, and prospects for rehabilitation — a critical narrative review
Inteligencia artificial en la planificación del alta hospitalaria: Aplicaciones, desafíos metodológicos y perspectivas para la rehabilitación — revisión narrativa crítica
container-title: Research, Society and Development
26fb79b62cf3ca32ca646d57b761cef826538353.abstract: <jats:p>Objetivo: discutir criticamente as aplicações da inteligência artificial (IA) à previsão e ao planejamento da alta hospitalar, destacando desafios para a reabilitação e para o aproveitamento de registros multiprofissionais. Metodologia: revisão narrativa crítica fundamentada em publicações acadêmicas e documentos metodológicos selecionados por pertinência temática, incluindo revisões de alta hospitalar, estudos de modelagem preditiva e diretrizes de avaliação de IA em saúde. Resultados e discussão: a literatura distingue previsão do tempo, destino e volume de altas, mas esses resultados não equivalem automaticamente à prontidão clínica e funcional. Modelos preditivos podem apoiar decisões, embora enfrentem problemas de validade externa, qualidade dos prontuários, vazamento temporal e integração aos fluxos de cuidado. A IA generativa acrescenta possibilidades de interpretação de narrativas, mas requer avaliação específica de consistência, segurança e reprodutibilidade. Conclusão: a avaliação de modelos para alta em reabilitação deve adotar marcos temporais explícitos, comparadores multiprofissionais, desfechos definidos e governança clínica, sem pressupor benefícios assistenciais antes da validação.</jats:p>

title: When Artificial Intelligence Generates and Experts Validate: Specialist Allocation and the Aggregate Substitutability of Artificial Intelligence in Research
container-title: Systems
c490b1911e4bb3d7698e705e008e7ae1766f4a72.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly generates candidate hypotheses and designs, but candidates become usable knowledge only after specialists validate them. We study how this division of labor shapes the substitutability between AI and specialists in research as a whole. When generation and validation share a pool of specialists, the aggregate elasticity of substitution is a weighted average of the elasticities within generation and between the two tasks, with a weight equal to AI’s share in generation times the share of specialists in validation. Optimal staffing raises this weight as AI becomes abundant, so research is more complementary than its generation stage, and AI’s output elasticity in research rises only while the aggregate elasticity exceeds one. Gains confined to generation draw specialists into validation; sufficiently large gains in validation reverse the flow. In dynamic general equilibrium, the aggregate elasticity is a sufficient statistic for local aggregate dynamics, so these dynamics cannot reveal the task structure, but staffing data can. In an illustrative calibration to proxy evidence, the aggregate elasticity is 0.95 and ignoring validation overstates AI’s output elasticity by 25 percent. Whether that elasticity is already declining is not robust: the aggregate elasticity exceeds one in 22 percent of parameter draws.</jats:p>

Prospects for the methodological function of modern philosophy in the context of artificial intelligence development

5975d815ad3a6ec6a0a4e33bfea68cd8ef20ce1d.abstract: <jats:p>This article examines the methodological function of contemporary philosophy and its development prospects in the context of the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence from a philosophical perspective. In particular, it analyzes the transformations taking place in philosophical thought and methodological approaches under the influence of digitalization, the widespread adoption of intelligent technologies, and the integration of artificial intelligence into various spheres of human activity. Furthermore, the article explores the ontological, epistemological, axiological, and ethical foundations of artificial intelligence, the relationship between human and machine thinking, the limits of the cognitive process, and the correlation between human consciousness and the capabilities of artificial intelligence. It substantiates the significance of the methodological function of contemporary philosophy in critically understanding the nature of technological progress, safeguarding the interests of individuals and society, and establishing moral values and criteria for social responsibility. The study reveals that, in the context of artificial intelligence development, philosophy serves not only as a system of theoretical knowledge but also as a crucial methodological foundation for ensuring the humanistic orientation of technological development.</jats:p>

title: Patentability of Artificial Intelligence-Generated Inventions in India: Rethinking Inventorship and the Requirement of Human Contribution.
container-title: International Journal For Multidisciplinary Research
6a3328c6dc46c2029d8d1070aac93435dd1ac71d.abstract:
<jats:p>The growing use of AI in the innovation process includes the development of new technology with the various degrees of human interaction. It threatens the very basis of patent law, which is based on certain human elements such as inventorship, inventive step, and human intellect. As stated by the Patents Act, 1970 in India, “there should be a mention of the person who claims to be the true and first inventor in a patent application. The present examination process in India divides patents into inventions developed by AI and those with AI assistance. As per the new guidelines issued by India, inventions made solely by AI or by the AI with minimal human intervention are not patentable due to the fact that “the AI cannot be considered as a person claiming to be an inventor according to Section 6 of the Patents Act, 1970.
This study takes a critical look at whether the current requirement of human inventorship is still relevant in an age when AI systems could independently play a part in the conception and development of inventions. This paper discusses the interplay of AI-driven innovations and the current requirement of human contribution, paying attention especially to Sections 2(1)(j), 2(1)(ja), 3(k), 6 and 7 of the Patents Act, 1970 and the developing examination paradigm in case of inventions involving AI in India. Additionally, the paper will consider the implications of denial of patentability to inventions which are genuinely driven by AI in terms of their implications on innovation incentives, ownership and disclosure and commercialisation of the same. In this way, the paper demonstrates how insistence on traditional human inventorship creates a gap between technological reality and patent law.</jats:p>

title: Assessing the Quality of AI Explanations of Atrial Fibrillation: Comparative Analysis of ChatGPT and Google Gemini
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
598e2fa6d5c1d1ee8bb1eebc101a66353744cb13.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Atrial fibrillation (AF) is one of the most common arrhythmias and is associated with multiple risk factors, including stroke and heart failure. Therefore, it is important that accurate and comprehensive educational resources on AF are available. Artificial intelligence (AI) platforms such as Google Gemini and ChatGPT are emerging tools for medical education. To our knowledge, this is the first study to assess the quality of these platforms for AF education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This pilot study aimed to (1) assess the quality of ChatGPT and Google Gemini explanations of AF and its treatment, (2) compare responses from both platforms, and (3) analyze differences in interpretation between cardiologists and nonmedical professionals.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The prompt “Explain atrial fibrillation and how to treat it to a patient” was entered into both ChatGPT and Google Gemini. The responses, along with a survey created in Google Forms, were sent out to potential participants between September and October 2024. The survey questions were derived from the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials and DISCERN criteria. Each survey question was multiple choice and rated on a 5-point Likert scale, where 1 indicated strong disagreement and 5 indicated strong agreement. Averages of each answer from the survey were calculated and compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The survey was completed by 28 participants, including cardiologists and cardiology fellows and 17 nonmedical professionals (college graduates not employed in the medical field). No significant overall quality differences were observed between ChatGPT and Google Gemini. When comparing participant groups, cardiologists rated AI-generated responses higher than nonmedical professionals for perceived bias (mean 3.82 vs mean 4.33; P=.04) and for explaining consequences of no treatment (mean 2.85 vs mean 1.86; P=.005). In contrast, nonmedical professionals rated structural and organizational features more favorably than cardiologists, including visual cues (mean 3.97 vs mean 2.48; P<.001), informative headers (mean 4.77 vs mean 3.95; P=.001), concise sections (mean 4.71 vs mean 4.29; P=.04), identifiable patient actions (mean 4.21 vs mean 3.19; P=.04), and references to additional resources (mean 2.65 vs mean 1.71; P=.006).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The comparable quality of ChatGPT and Google Gemini suggests that both are viable for AF education. Differences in ratings of organizational features versus perceptions of bias and consequences of no treatment highlight a disconnect between cardiologists and nonmedical professionals. To optimize clinical application, cardiologists should evaluate both comprehensiveness and clarity of AI-generated responses. This serves as a pilot study, and future research should focus on longitudinal studies of AI-generated responses and their effects on clinical outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Expectation-driven gain modulation of preparatory spatial attention
container-title: eLife
42e0bff514a13e990dde6d5376170bcb87804ae4.abstract: <jats:p>The visual system can flexibly adjust attentional deployment to match task demands, but whether observers can proactively modulate the spatial scope of attention based on expectations about upcoming search difficulty remains unclear. According to the zoom lens model, attention can narrow or broaden its spatial extent, with narrower focus enhancing processing efficiency, a mechanism that would benefit target discrimination in crowded displays. We tested whether observers adjust attentional scope when expecting sparse versus dense search arrays by combining spatial cueing with block-wise manipulations of display density expectations. Participants performed a visual search task in which endogenous cues predicted target location, while blocks predominantly contained either sparse (1 target, 3 distractors) or dense (1 target, 7 distractors) displays. We applied inverted encoding models to broadband EEG data to reconstruct spatial channel tuning functions, enabling precise characterization of both the locus and breadth of attentional deployment. Behaviorally, expecting difficult searches selectively improved accuracy at cued locations without costs elsewhere. Consistent with this selective benefit, neural measurements revealed that expectancy enhanced the amplitude of spatially selective responses at the attended location but did not alter tuning width. These findings demonstrate that expectations about search difficulty modulate attention through gain-based signal enhancement rather than adjustments to spatial scope, revealing that preparatory attentional control operates via amplitude modulation within a stable spatial focus. This mechanism complements reactive attentional adjustments and provides an efficient means for the visual system to optimize processing under predictable task demands.</jats:p>

title: Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery, Endobariatrics, and AI - How AI is Contributing to Surgery and Endoscopy
Path Delay Faults Through Transition Faults with High Functional Switching Activities
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
d7c0604e26121ab930c68a14ad77f1a7756f99ac.abstract: <jats:p>Chip aging results in defects that are initially likely to appear as small delay defects. Path delay faults are used for detecting small delay defects. Because of the number of paths, path selection procedures are used for identifying a subset of path delay faults that are important to detect. A recent path selection procedure addresses small delay defects that are likely to occur because of chip aging. The procedure identifies a set of functionally possible path delay faults, from which it selects a subset based on an aging aware metric. This article studies this problem when the requirement for the path delay faults to be functionally possible is removed. The problem becomes that of selecting path delay faults through the largest numbers of transition faults with the highest susceptibilities to aging, and performing test generation for the selected path delay faults. Experimental results of path selection and test generation for benchmark circuits demonstrate the effectiveness of the procedures, and the differences from the case where the path delay faults are required to be functionally possible.</jats:p>

title: PCB-QA: A Task-Specific Question Answering Framework for Text-Centric Chip Datasheet Queries in PCB Design
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
1423d80f2f29ee75157e5dcd83cc4dfd6b7118eb.abstract: <jats:p>In PCB design, engineers often rely on datasheets to obtain crucial chip information, a process that is both time-consuming and labor-intensive. To streamline this workflow, we present PCB-QA, a task-specific Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based question-answering system that automatically addresses text-centric chip-related queries using the latest datasheets. Rather than aiming to replace broader commercial AI-assisted EDA platforms, this work focuses on a narrower and reproducible research problem: grounded datasheet question answering over a maintained corpus. While existing RAG technologies have made significant progress in document-based question answering, several challenges remain, primarily due to the erroneous segmentation of documents, the retrieval of inaccurate references, and under-specified user queries. To improve the accuracy of PCB-QA’s responses, our framework incorporates three key components. First, we propose a datasheet segmentation model that is specifically trained to divide the corpus into semantically coherent chunks. Second, we integrate a correlation estimation module to better assess the relevance of retrieved references and reduce the influence of distractors. Finally, recognizing that user inputs may lack critical details, we employ a query-rationalization mechanism to facilitate further reasoning and refine the query for under-specified technical and application-related questions. These task-specific customizations improve retrieval quality and support more accurate grounded answers for datasheet-centric QA. Experimental results on our customized ChipQuestion benchmark demonstrate that PCB-QA achieves consistent improvements over representative RAG baselines on text-grounded datasheet QA. We also clarify the current scope of PCB-QA: the present implementation is primarily text-centric and does not yet fully address image-only figures, waveform plots, complex visual tables, or other visuallygrounded datasheet content.</jats:p>

title: Towards Realistic Project-Level Code Generation via Multi-Agent Collaboration and Semantic Architecture Modeling
container-title: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
2e98affb75fe6b1c9fa0a80bf39cb6bb48af6b14.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in automated code generation. In real-world software engineering, the growing demand for rapid iteration and continuous delivery underscores the importance of project-level code generation, where LLMs are expected to generate complete software projects directly from complex user requirements. This task, however, presents greater challenges due to larger input scales, multi-modal information, and the need for holistic architectural reasoning. Although existing studies have made initial explorations, they still face key limitations, including unrealistic datasets and unreliable evaluation metrics that fail to reflect real-world complexity, the semantic gap between human-written requirements and machine-interpretable structures, and difficulties in managing hierarchical dependencies and maintaining quality throughout the generation process. To address these limitations, we first introduce
                    <jats:sc>CodeProjectEval</jats:sc>
                    , a project-level code generation dataset built from 18 real-world repositories with 12.7 files and 2,388.6 lines of code per task on average, supplemented with documentation and executable test cases for automatic evaluation. We further propose
                    <jats:sc>ProjectGen</jats:sc>
                    , a multi-agent framework that decomposes projects into architecture design, skeleton generation, and code filling stages with iterative refinement and memory-based context management. Within this framework, we introduce the Semantic Software Architecture Tree, a structured and semantically rich representation that effectively bridges user requirements and source code implementation. Experiments show that
                    <jats:sc>ProjectGen</jats:sc>
                    achieves state-of-the-art performance, passing 52/124 test cases on the small-scale project-level code generation dataset DevBench, a 57% improvement over the baseline approaches, and 310 test cases on
                    <jats:sc>CodeProjectEval</jats:sc>
                    , representing an improvement of roughly tenfold compared to the baselines.
                  </jats:p>

title: Beautiful Particulars
c6fe3d0377956ff06d423eb5e3d727284e365eac.abstract:
<jats:p>A fresh and eye-opening new explanation of AI—and how its focus on specifics is changing our ideas about ourselves and our world.From a Harvard researcher, philosopher, entrepreneur, former comedy writer, and bestselling author.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Amid the clamor about AI, Beautiful Particulars poses a unique question: Not how does our use of AI change what we do, but how is the idea of AI already subtly yet fundamentally reshaping how we think about ourselves and our world?</jats:p>
                  <jats:p/>
                  <jats:p>In clear, engaging, and even humorous prose, David Weinberger offers a new perspective on how machine learning works and how it may already be changing our basic and deepest ideas. Through lively examples, he shows that AI’s success—with all its risks and dangers—is taking us past our millennia of reliance on laws and principles by revealing what morality, free will, creativity, causality knowledge, and even reality itself look like now that we’re able to let the particulars speak their tiny truths.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p/>
                  <jats:p>The author poses questions not usually asked: What does a coin look like to AI? When AI gives you evidence that the earth is round, why are its own reasons for saying that so different? Why does an AI image generator create a “selfie” of ancient Aztec warriors with broad smiles that it “believes” are historically unlikely? If AI becomes conscious but bodiless, could it still make good moral decisions? Why is the world so much better at being causal than AI could ever “understand”? How does AI show us that genuine creativity is not about a “spark” but about moments that feel right? And how can you take the temperature of a joke?</jats:p>
                  <jats:p/>
                  <jats:p>Beautiful Particulars offers a new—and hopeful—perspective on how machine learning works, and how that’s already changing how we understand what it means to be human in the age of AI.</jats:p>

title: AI-Generated Exposure Hierarchies for Body Dysmorphic Disorder: Proof-of-Concept Study
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
475970c23de59b336f5f102fda0e80aa46b47e4e.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is a chronic, impairing condition for which cognitive behavioral therapy, including exposure and response prevention (ERP), is the first-line treatment, but few clinicians are trained in BDD-specific ERP. Constructing personalized exposure hierarchies is time-intensive and requires clinical expertise, particularly for patients with absent insight who may hold appearance beliefs with delusional conviction. Generative AI (GenAI)–powered chatbots, such as ChatGPT, have shown utility for clinical content, but their capacity to produce safe, appropriate ERP hierarchies for BDD has not been examined.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study evaluated the feasibility of using ChatGPT (GPT-5) to generate ERP hierarchies for BDD, assessed the influence of clinical and demographic characteristics on output quality, benchmarked AI-generated hierarchies against those created by doctoral-level BDD specialists, and tested whether blinded experts could distinguish AI-generated from expert-generated hierarchies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GPT-5 generated 10-item graded exposure hierarchies for 72 simulated vignettes that varied by body area, insight level (good, limited, or absent), symptom specificity, age, and gender. Expert clinicians independently generated hierarchies for a subset of 18 vignettes. Two researchers rated all GPT-5 hierarchies for task completion and information integration. Three BDD expert clinicians, blinded to the hierarchy source (expert vs GPT-5), rated all 90 hierarchies for relevance, specificity, variability, safety, and overall quality. After unblinding, raters attempted to identify the AI-generated hierarchy in the 18 matched pairs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      GPT-5 generated complete hierarchies for 69 of 72 (95.8%) vignettes. Blinded experts rated GPT-5 hierarchies highly across all dimensions (mean scores ranging from 4.39, SD 0.26 to 4.90, SD 0.16 out of 5), with no significant differences from expert-generated hierarchies except for variability, where experts scored modestly higher (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.02;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.24). After unblinding, raters correctly identified AI-generated hierarchies only 31.5% (17/54) of the time, significantly below chance (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.009); this below-chance result was mostly due to one rater, and no rater performed above chance. Insight level was the most consistent predictor of quality: absent-insight hierarchies received significantly lower safety (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.73) and overall quality ratings (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.01;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.43). This pattern was not unique to GPT-5; safety ratings for expert-generated hierarchies also declined significantly by insight level (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03). Miscalibration of exposure difficulty, particularly for low- and absent-insight cases, was the most common rater concern (30/43, 69.8% comments), disproportionately directed at GPT-5 hierarchies.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GPT-5 generated ERP hierarchies for BDD that blinded experts rated as comparable to clinician-created hierarchies and could not reliably distinguish them from clinician-created hierarchies. However, hierarchies for patients with absent insight received lower safety and quality ratings from both AI and expert sources, and qualitative comments suggested AI-generated hierarchies were less well calibrated to delusional-level presentations. GenAI thus shows promise as a clinician-facing aid for ERP hierarchy generation, but these findings underscore the need for clinician oversight, especially for patients with delusional conviction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: SAI: Virtualizing Shared Memory of GPU for AI workload acceleration
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
c8fa29b0323351e1659db262fc936958ed20d580.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    AI workloads increasingly demand high parallelism and efficient on-chip memory utilization on modern GPUs. However, the limited capacity of shared memory often constrains thread-level parallelism, while portions of the L2 cache remain underutilized. In this work, we propose
                    <jats:bold>SAI</jats:bold>
                    , a mechanism that virtualizes shared memory into the L2 cache to improve GPU performance for AI applications. SAI dynamically activates virtualization based on runtime resource usage, enabling additional CTAs with minimal architectural modifications. We further introduce an L2 cache management strategy that integrates associativity-based virtual page allocation and a replacement information table, reducing page-swapping overhead while preserving L2 cache performance. Experimental results demonstrate that SAI achieves an 18.6% performance improvement over the baseline design and outperforms SMILE-opt, our reproduced state-of-the-art baseline, by 8.8%. Moreover, SAI captures 60.2% of the performance gain delivered by the idealized Double SMEM design while reducing energy consumption to 87.7% of the baseline. These results highlight the effectiveness of SAI in enhancing thread-level parallelism and optimizing on-chip memory for AI workloads.
                  </jats:p>

title: AI-Enabled Early Detection of Epidemic Threats in a Resource-Constrained Health System: Implementation Research from Lebanon
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
94bf395e649f9c13344c021277ab854ad6c98be5.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Global South countries face heightened infectious disease risks compounded by fragmented surveillance systems and resource constraints. Lebanon’s health system crisis and recurrent outbreaks highlight the urgent need for new approaches to epidemic and pandemic preparedness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To describe the design, implementation process, and early implementation findings of an artificial intelligence (AI)–enabled early warning system (AI-EWS) that automates detection of epidemiologically relevant events using laboratory data in Lebanon, with emphasis on feasibility, workflow integration, stakeholder engagement, and implementation learnings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We applied an implementation research approach to co-design and validate an AI-EWS prototype integrated within a university hospital laboratory. The system incorporates a hybrid statistical and machine learning analytic pipeline and a real-time dashboard for detecting epidemic events across multiple pathogens using routine laboratory information systems (LIS) data. The system was developed in collaboration with the Ministry of Public Health (MoPH) to support future national adoption.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The project produced a structured framework for pathogen selection, rule development, dataset creation, and platform co-design with clinical and epidemiological experts, medical informatics professionals, MoPH experts, and technical specialists. Early implementation observations indicate operational feasibility within existing infrastructure, strong stakeholder engagement, and trust-building around AI-enabled surveillance through participatory design and responsible-AI governance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI-enabled laboratory surveillance is a viable and scalable approach to strengthening epidemic preparedness in low-resource health systems when grounded in implementation science and responsible AI, and when explicitly aligned with local workflows and national policy priorities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Bayesian Forecasting as the Analytical Core of an AI-Assisted Early Warning System for Dengue Outbreaks during the 2023 Epidemic: Implementation and Emergency Management in a Dominican Pediatric Hospital
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
056417fa3dbad64347775b6e5020ffb82cf01df1.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Dengue remains a major cause of pediatric morbidity in the Dominican Republic, with increasingly intense epidemic cycles. Advances in statistical modeling, probabilistic forecasting, and AI-assisted digital health systems offer new opportunities to enhance early warning capabilities and strengthen hospital preparedness. This study evaluated a Bayesian negative binomial regression forecasting model as the analytical core of an AI-assisted early warning system (EWS) for predicting weekly dengue cases nationwide, using strict out-of-sample validation during the 2023 epidemic and applying its outputs operationally in a high-demand pediatric hospital. National surveillance data (PLISA/PAHO), hospital records from the Dr. Hugo Mendoza Pediatric Hospital (HPHM), and climatic and satellite indicators (NOAA, MODIS) for 2014–2024 were integrated. The model incorporated climatically plausible lags, harmonic seasonality, two vegetation indices (NDVI_lag4 and EVI_lag4), a long-term spline trend, and weakly informative priors, achieving excellent convergence (Rhat = 1.00). Climatic and environmental predictors exhibited small and uncertain effects, whereas the temporal spline accounted for most long-term epidemic variability. In the 2023 national validation, the model captured the broad epidemic trajectory and improved RMSE and MAE compared with the historical seasonal baseline (RMSE = 783.3; MAE = 423.4; MAPE = 80.2%), although proportional accuracy remained limited during abrupt epidemic acceleration. The national model also captured ascending-phase signals that were temporally aligned with the HPHM hospital outbreak, including its sharp rise during epidemiological weeks 36–40. These outputs were used alongside routine surveillance and hospital indicators to support operational situational awareness, capacity planning, patient-flow reorganization, strengthened triage, and emergency preparedness during the epidemic. The model demonstrated temporal signal detection and operational relevance, positioning Bayesian probabilistic forecasting, embedded within an AI-assisted digital health workflow, as a useful analytical component for epidemic monitoring and hospital preparedness, subject to limitations in peak magnitude calibration and proportional accuracy.</jats:p>

title: Toward Human-Centered Pedagogy in the Age of Generative AI Among Higher Education Educators: Qualitative Phenomenological Study
container-title: JMIR Medical Education
46248c918f688c3c5f2cc8bb261f150c45f4e9cf.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Generative AI (GenAI) expands possibilities for content generation, feedback, personalization, and instructional support in higher education. Its growing use also challenges established assumptions about teaching, assessment, professional expertise, academic integrity, and educational responsibility. Although research has examined technology adoption and AI competencies, less is known about how educators experience and interpret the pedagogical transformation associated with GenAI in everyday teaching.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study explored how higher education educators experience GenAI-mediated pedagogical transformation, focusing on pedagogical practices, professional roles and expertise, educator agency, human-AI relationships, and associated opportunities and tensions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A qualitative phenomenological inquiry involved 23 educators from 3 Palestinian universities. Purposive maximum-variation sampling sought variation in academic rank, discipline, teaching experience, and experience with AI tools. Individual semistructured, in-depth interviews were conducted from March to April 2026, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and returned to participants for review. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis informed by phenomenology. Initial coding was inductive and grounded in participants’ accounts; human-centered AI and sociomateriality subsequently informed interpretation as sensitizing concepts. Themes were developed through iterative comparison of transcripts, analytic memos, and alternative interpretations. Informational sufficiency was observed after approximately 20 interviews, with 3 additional interviews used to examine the developing thematic structure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis generated 8 interconnected themes. Educators described a shift from content transmission toward mediation, inquiry, reflective learning, creative exploration, and process-oriented assessment. Professional expertise increasingly centered on facilitation, pedagogical design, contextual interpretation, ethical guidance, and evaluation of AI-generated content. Human-AI collaboration involved bounded and integrated configurations, with humans retaining responsibility for judgment and educational consequences. Educator agency appeared through decisions about AI participation, independent student reasoning, and the boundaries of human expertise. Credibility, bias, authorship, authenticity, and academic integrity became embedded as pedagogical concerns. Participants valued opportunities for creativity, personalization, flexibility, and instructional support while expressing concerns about dependence, reduced intellectual effort, and weakened human connection.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GenAI-mediated pedagogical transformation depends on educators’ alignment of AI use with learning purposes, the allocation of responsibilities, and the preservation of ethical accountability and meaningful relationships. The resulting human-centered pedagogy framework positions pedagogical intentionality, contextual judgment, negotiated agency, and relational presence as central to responsible integration. Universities should complement technical training and institutional policies with support for pedagogical design, critical evaluation, process-oriented assessment, and ethical reasoning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
