title: Known by the Machine: Building Relational Presence with AI NPCs for Stigma-Free Mental Health Literacy in Games
container-title: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
4c9c9964378a64482a43967764b54ff15bb6fa76.abstract: <jats:p>Mental Health (MH) remains a global priority, yet low literacy and stigma frequently limit open discussion and help-seeking behaviors. While game-based education has shown promise in supporting stigma reduction and literacy improvement, the potential for Large Language Models (LLMs) to support non-judgmental, playful exploration of sensitive topics remains underexplored, specifically, the role of conversational memory to support trust-building in MH discussions. We conducted a four-session, longitudinal mixed-methods study to evaluate how the relational presence of AI characters, powered by GPT-4o-mini with varied memory designs, relates to player experience and learning. Moving beyond an evaluation of learning, we examine how the perception of being known by an AI NPC is associated with engagement with stigmatized content. Results indicate that while participants achieved significant and sustained gains in Mental Health Literacy (MHL), these improvements did not differ by memory condition. Instead, memory appeared to operate as a relational design feature that shaped participants’ perceptions of social presence, with many describing conversational NPCs as supportive companions. We also identify interactional risks, such as algorithmic vagueness and privacy-induced hesitation, that participants described as reducing their comfort during conversations. We conclude by offering design recommendations for leveraging LLM memory to create more relational and stigma-sensitive environments for MH education.</jats:p>

title: Guards & Wards: The Creative Labour of GMs and Considerations for Designing with AI
container-title: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
97f59e27090381539a8186baf42b7de0cca1bb39.abstract: <jats:p>Tabletop role-playing games (TTRPGs) provide a complicated environment for creativity. Game masters (GMs) co-create a story along with their players and many choose to complete significant labour both prior to and during a gaming session. However, the boundaries that GMs may have about generative artificial intelligence (AI) being used in this creative hobby have not been examined. We examine the perceptions of GMs on the use of AI for creativity support in TTRPGs. We conducted a survey of GMs to discover the labour they completed in preparation for and play of TTRPG sessions, the existing creativity support tools (CSTs) that they use for this labour, and their opinions on the use of AI in TTRPGs. We performed both qualitative and quantitative analysis to examine survey data. We contrasted our results across two participant groups: those who have or have not been paid to GM a gaming session, and those who have or have not used AI as GMs. From our data, we created twelve distinct orientation groups encompassing the opinions of participants on AI for use in TTRPGs. We propose thirteen design considerations in the form of questions AI tool developers should ask when creating AI-based CSTs for TTRPG use.</jats:p>

title: Age Matters: Age-Differentiated Playtesting for AI Educational Games
container-title: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
51c2ffec725312491c89a2f2140899598712ae8b.abstract: <jats:p>Playtesting is widely employed in educational game design as a post-hoc method for game design validation within the age groups that the learning goals target. For domains such as AI literacy, age-targeted educational games testing may be limiting, as AI learning goals are relevant and frequently misunderstood by children, adolescents and young adults. Designing educational games that teach AI to a wider audience of ages requires playtesting with players of different ages to better interpret gameplay and narrative appropriateness of AI in AI educational games. In this study, we playtested four AI educational games with middle, high school, and college aged students, and analyzed playtesting data, including verbal discourse, in-game behaviors, and post-playtesting reflections. Our findings demonstrate that playtesting can serve as an asset-based practice which reveals how players of different age groups make sense of educational games during play. We provide critical reflections from multi-age playtesting of AI educational games that inform design, and recommendations for engaging AI educational game design.</jats:p>

title: Does Trust Spill Over?: Exploring Asymmetric Trust Dynamics Between Teammate AI and Guide AI in Cooperative Games
container-title: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
aa082ec48f7a3ea66734c5c6aa6b23a8c21c5b8a.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Cooperative games increasingly feature multiple AI agents serving distinct roles, yet how players form and transfer trust across such agents remains unclear. We investigated trust spillover between a task-executing Teammate AI and an advisory Guide AI in a web-based cooperative cooking game (within-subjects, N = 23). Teammate AI ability (high vs. low) and Guide AI accuracy (high vs. low/absent) were experimentally manipulated. Results revealed a directional asymmetry in trust spillover. Teammate AI ability significantly influenced trust in the Guide AI (
                    <jats:inline-formula content-type="math/tex">
                      <jats:tex-math notation="LaTeX" version="MathJax">\(\eta _p^2 =.220\)</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ), whereas Guide AI accuracy and presence had no effect on trust in the Teammate AI (
                    <jats:inline-formula content-type="math/tex">
                      <jats:tex-math notation="LaTeX" version="MathJax">\(\eta _p^2 =.002\)</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ). This suggests that, under cognitive constraints, trust propagates from high-salience task agents to lower-salience advisory agents, but not vice versa. Additionally, the presence of the Guide AI improved performance and perceived control independent of advice accuracy, suggesting an attentional cueing effect. Finally, congruent agent quality levels enhanced perceived relatedness, highlighting the importance of system-level coherence. These findings demonstrate asymmetric trust spillover in cooperative games with role-differentiated AI, where execution-focused agents anchor system-wide trust formation, with implications for multi-agent AI systems in which agents serve distinct functional roles.
                  </jats:p>

title: Player Perceptions of Generative AI in Games: A Steam Review Analysis
container-title: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
08911279f04c0994a25c0ab11145fcff09c60790.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid adoption of generative AI in game development has created large discussions among players, yet little empirical work has examined how players actually perceive AI-generated content. Employing quantitative methods, we study the adoption of generative AI in games in the Steam marketplace, using procedural content generation (PCG) as a baseline of a generative technology that was successfully integrated into games over several decades. Furthermore, using qualitative methods, we study player reception of generative AI by analyzing 508,192 English-language reviews. We found that games disclosing generative AI use receive lower recommendation rates and more negative overall sentiment than PCG games. Thematic analysis of 600 reviews shows that players perceive the use of generative AI in games as low developer investment in the game. Drawing on human-centered AI frameworks, we argue that successful generative AI adoption requires deploying generative AI for what players need, not for what makes development cheaper.</jats:p>

title: Meritocracy and generative AI in higher education: institutional pathways and use–response alignment across four systems
container-title: Advances in Social Behavior Research
1d18258e5287d5117654b68c5dc746e92d867f48.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines how higher education systems respond to the rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) under different institutional conditions, asking how meritocratic competition is translated into assessment and credential pressure and how student GenAI use aligns with institutional responses. Using a comparative qualitative case-study design, the study analyzes secondary evidence from China, the United Kingdom, the United States, and Germany through two a priori frozen indicator frameworks. The first framework traces how meritocratic competition is institutionalized through admissions, grading, and credential differentiation; the second maps student GenAI use patterns against institutional responses in teaching, assessment, and support. Strong credential differentiation and education–labour-market linkage emerge in all four systems, but through distinct pathways: state-coordinated in China, marketized in the United Kingdom, decentralized and market-oriented in the United States, and state–professional in Germany. Partial use–response alignment is the cross-system norm; systems differ mainly in pedagogical integration, regulatory adaptation, and institutional support. AI literacy and support provision lag behind student adoption in all four cases, making institutional capacity the most persistent source of misalignment, while limited comparable measurement of equity alignment and of guarded and compensatory use shows that monitoring capacity is itself part of governance. GenAI governance therefore converges less on common rules than on common capability gaps. The findings suggest that governing GenAI in meritocratic systems depends less on uniform rules than on sustained investment in institutional monitoring and support capacity.</jats:p>

title: Generative AI-enabled writing feedback in primary school English instruction: application landscape, practical dilemmas, and a teacher-led collaborative framework
container-title: Advances in Social Behavior Research
46a2a0e62e833b05feb28298ad275d5b27608889.abstract: <jats:p>Writing feedback is a pivotal yet chronically constrained component of primary school English writing instruction, squeezed by large class sizes, low marking frequency, and homogeneous comments. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), with its immediacy, personalization, and dialogic interaction, opens new possibilities for reconstructing writing feedback. Drawing on a narrative synthesis of 52 Chinese and international sources, and addressing a literature in which research on AI writing feedback concentrates on higher education and on the learner side, this paper maps the application landscape of GenAI-enabled writing feedback in primary school English, consolidates and examines five practical dilemmas concerning accuracy, appropriateness, teacher literacy, ethics, and evaluation orientation, and proposes a Teacher-led, AI-assisted, Student-centered Collaborative Feedback Framework (TAC-F). The framework assigns teachers responsibility for goal setting, affective support, and feedback verification, positions GenAI as an initial assessor and material provider, and treats students as reflective revisers within a pre-writing, while-writing, and post-writing closed loop, supported by prompt-template libraries, feedback-verification routines, school-based teacher AI literacy development, and ethical data norms. Preliminary multi-tool observations, together with a six-dimension observation framework and a same-prompt pilot protocol, are developed to help teachers screen AI-generated feedback; the observations suggest that current tools are reliable on explicit errors but unstable at the discourse level. Six implementation suggestions are advanced to inform the digital transformation of primary school English writing instruction.</jats:p>

title: Visual Sexual Health Communication Assisted by AI: The Case of Synthetic Menstruation Images
container-title: Archives of Sexual Behavior
08fb882f77177fa29f70584626a13ad9137367d1.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Public communication about sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) relies on both text and images. A recent development is the proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) image generators, which enable rapid, cost-effective, and highly customizable images with appealing aesthetics based on textual requests (prompts). To examine the opportunities and challenges of AI-generated images in SRHR communication, we used the topic of menstruation and developed six research questions (RQs) anchored in the current state of research on AI-supported visual health communication. These questions addressed key areas of concern, such as unsuccessful image creation (RQ1), objective image flaws (RQ2), lack of diversity of human representation (RQ3), stereotypical portrayals of women (RQ4), use of visual symbols (RQ5), and image valence (RQ6). Our study applied 15 AI image generators, 2 user accounts per generator, 5 menstruation-related prompts, 2 prompt languages, and 2 images per prompt, resulting in a sample of
                    <jats:italic>N</jats:italic>
                     = 600 AI outputs generated in Autumn 2025. All outputs were manually coded using a reliability-tested codebook developed through both deductive and inductive approaches. In 20.0% of cases, menstruation prompts did not produce the requested image but only text output (RQ1). When images were generated, they often (78.1%) exhibited visual and/or textual flaws (RQ2). The images showed a lack of diversity in some human attributes (e.g., body type) but not in others (e.g., skin tone; RQ3). Stereotypical depictions of women were observed but not predominant (RQ4). Common menstruation-related visual symbols (e.g., blood, pain) were identified (RQ5), but most images did not convey a negative portrayal and instead a neutral or positive portrayal of menstruation (RQ6). While results show that initial outputs from AI image generators are often not directly suitable for visual sexual health communication, they might work with targeted refinement. Further research is required to examine the production, characteristics, consumption, and effects of AI-generated images in SRHR communication.
                  </jats:p>

title: Exploring the user experience and improvement strategies of AI chatbots on China’s Meituan instant retail platform from the perspective of generation Z users
container-title: Scientific Reports
b0a46930437223a1f882cf0ac0bc1b7619c0f599.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is profoundly transforming traditional service models. In recent years, AI chatbots have gradually become a common smart service on instant retail platforms. However, existing research still lacks sufficient understanding of users’ actual experiences when using this type of AI service primarily based on intelligent interaction. This study focuses on the AI chatbots on Meituan’s instant retail platform, examines the experiences and conditions of Generation Z when using AI chatbots, and proposes strategies and recommendations for improving the user experience. The study examined the research questions by combining user interviews, the KANO model, and the Analytic Hierarchy Process. The main findings are as follows: Generation Z has the highest demand for the intelligent interaction experience provided by AI chatbots. At the same time, the degree of importance of needs such as personalized AI chatbot avatar, humanized AI interaction, AI personalized recommendations, and intelligent emotional perception interaction is relatively high. This indicates that Generation Z’s demands for AI chatbots have already expanded from simple needs such as consulting about products and orders to diversified online personalized consumption experiences. For example, inquiring about the usage rules of platform coupons, receiving intelligent recommendations based on personal dietary habits, and other diversified online lifestyles. Based on this, this study proposes experience enhancement strategies for optimizing the dialogue mechanism between users and AI chatbots, improving the anthropomorphic level of the interface dialogue mechanism, providing visualized presentation of intelligent service progress, and providing functional settings for user privacy protection. This study offers new insights into improving the user experience of AI chatbots on instant retail platforms.</jats:p>

title: Sycophancy and Extended Engagement with Publicly Accessible Generative AI: Aligning Deployment with Mental Health Needs
container-title: Current Psychiatry Reports
7de6b6683581dbeab2eb51390b3a0c61a1f2e780.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose of Review</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming a routine source of health information, emotional support, and companionship. As its use expands, the key public health question is not only whether these tools can support care, but whether their deployment is aligned with the mental health needs of the community. In this commentary, we argue that general-purpose AI systems pose distinct psychosocial risks, especially for young people and those experiencing loneliness or psychological distress.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Recent Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Emerging evidence suggests that sustained chatbot use may be associated with loneliness, reduced socialisation, emotional dependence, and problematic use, while sycophantic model behaviour may undermine users' capacity for self-correction and sustain a feedback loop of engagement. Current AI policy frameworks address governance and safety, but do not yet provide a coordinated response to these mental health risks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Summary</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Realising the benefits of AI without preventable community-level harm will require independent longitudinal research, psychosocial safety benchmarking, transparent post-deployment monitoring, and safety by design principles.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Evaluating Multi-Agent AI Systems for Decision Support in the Operational Readiness of Heavy Industrial Facilities
container-title: Journal of Engineering Research and Reports
660493abdd965d8a7c9e5ee350aab36e0d2a7930.abstract: <jats:p>This structured integrative review synthesizes evidence across five interconnected areas and develops an integrated framework for evaluating multi-agent AI in the operational readiness of heavy industrial facilities. The review examines multi-agent architectures and coordination, operational-readiness decision support, digital twins and virtual validation, safety and system assurance, and human–agent interaction and governance. From this synthesis, the study develops a reference architecture, a six-dimensional evaluation framework covering technical performance and reliability, coordination and context integrity, operational-readiness value, safety and assurance, human factors and governance, and implementation viability, scalability, and interoperability, together with a five-level maturity model. The framework considers both whether multi-agent AI can support assessment of facility readiness and whether the AI-supported decision system itself is sufficiently reliable, assured, governed, and mature for that role. Industrial evidence from Saudi Aramco and Bosch applications across Bosch and SICK manufacturing settings indicates practical value in maintenance planning, fault diagnosis, information synthesis, and production support. However, the available evidence is stronger for operational benefit and implementation feasibility than for coordination reliability, safety assurance, and lifecycle governance. Current systems are therefore best characterized as bounded, human-supervised decision-support tools rather than autonomous readiness authorities. Progress toward governed operational use will require stronger industrial benchmarks, traceable engineering evidence, reliable coordination, effective safeguards, lifecycle assurance, and clearly defined human decision authority.</jats:p>

title: Secure Edge-AI Sensing on an FPGA SoC: Lightweight ASCON Authentication of Model Updates and Interface-Bound Inference for Bearing-Fault Detection
container-title: Computers
303d4ba538744ba35fa73581feb18063f5c07d26.abstract: <jats:p>Vibration monitoring increasingly classifies on the sensing node. We ask where the cost of running and securely updating a small classifier on an FPGA system-on-chip node lies. One Q4.12 multilayer perceptron for bearing-fault detection, trained on 40 CWRU recordings over four loads and three severities, is deployed bit-exactly on an ESP32-S3, a Cortex-A53 and a custom AXI4-Lite accelerator of the same Zynq UltraScale+ device (Kria KV260), checked on all 2132 windows. The fabric computes one inference in 36 cycles (0.36 µs), yet the latency under the PYNQ driver is 133.2 µs; a native-C driver reduces it to 3.59 µs, placing 95–97% of the per-transaction cost in the host software stack. Moving the update decision into the fabric, with the ASCON-AEAD128 tag check, version freshness and staging enforced in hardware, rejects every tested forgery, replay and direct write, and cuts a 608-byte authenticated update from 148.7 to 66.0 µs in native C. The full chain runs in real time, with no deadline miss over 552 windows (worst case 1.8% of the 171 ms window), and feature extraction dominates its cost. The model reaches 98.2% on unseen segments but generalizes poorly to unseen fault severities and to real damage of unseen Paderborn bearings, which makes field updates a requirement.</jats:p>

title: Edge AI Imitation of Event-Triggered Model Predictive Control for an Inverted Pendulum
container-title: Computers
05938ee211a2e0d7b4b9a7b07cb4c17bb8bcfd63.abstract: <jats:p>Event-triggered model predictive control (MPC) updates the control input only when needed, but it still solves an optimization problem at every event, which on the studied cart–pole can exceed its 10 ms control period. We propose a compact multi-task neural network that replaces the whole scheme: it decides when to update the input and which value to apply, using only online measurements. It is trained on 500 physical recordings, adapted to a simulated teacher and refined with DAgger. Feeding it the held input produces a copycat policy that is accurate in open loop but sluggish in closed loop; in a matched comparison over four training seeds, removing that input raises full-episode success from three to 39 of 40 episodes. In simulation, at the default sensor noise, the final network completes all swing-up and tracking episodes, with time to upright and tracking error close to the teacher’s, whereas on the simulated teacher, tree ensembles have 1.4–1.6 times its open-loop error. In an open-loop replay on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller, a step takes under 40% of the period. In tracking and full episodes, it updates the input 33–39% more often than the teacher, mainly because it does not learn the rule’s sparsity.</jats:p>

title: Explainable Machine Learning for Analyzing AI Adoption and Teachers’ Professional Development Needs: Evidence from TALIS 2024 in Kazakhstan
container-title: Computers
d995276851023c13b6f90d18faa245a7956a09a2.abstract: <jats:p>The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in education highlights the need to distinguish teachers’ AI adoption from their professional development needs. This study examined these outcomes as separate predictive tasks using OECD TALIS 2024 data for 7360 teachers in Kazakhstan at ISCED level 2. After excluding invalid outcome records, the analytical samples comprised 2430 teachers for AI adoption and 4868 for professional development needs. Population estimates and confidence intervals were calculated using teacher weights and 100 Fay-BRR replicate weights, while predictive performance was assessed using out-of-fold predictions and school-grouped validation. The weighted prevalence of AI adoption was 59.0% (95% CI: 56.1–61.9). Logistic Regression and CatBoost demonstrated comparable discrimination (ROC-AUC = 0.754 and 0.753, respectively), with no clear performance advantage for CatBoost. SHAP analysis identified prior AI-related professional learning, uncertainty regarding AI attitudes, and perceived AI benefits as prominent predictive factors. Moderate or high professional development need was estimated at 80.3% (95% CI: 78.7–81.9). However, individual prediction was weak, with balanced accuracy of 0.268 and a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.082. These findings indicate that TALIS variables provide a moderate predictive signal for AI adoption but are insufficient for reliable, individualized professional development decisions.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer clinical questions, but comparisons by clinicians of general-purpose and knowledge-base-grounded systems remain limited. We conducted a non-blinded, paired evaluation at the 2026 congress of the German Society of Internal Medicine. Sixty-four physicians and medical students each assessed paired responses from LiSA, a knowledge-base-grounded clinical AI system developed by AMBOSS, and ChatGPT to one of 15 real-world internal medicine questions. Participants rated perceived quality, trust, and safety concerns. LiSA received higher ratings for overall quality (3.96 ± 1.20 vs. 3.48 ± 0.93;
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.002) and trust (5.11 ± 1.73 vs. 3.67 ± 1.39;
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     < 0.001). Safety concerns were reported in 15.6% of LiSA evaluations and 26.6% of ChatGPT evaluations (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.143). Clarity ratings did not differ significantly between systems, whereas LiSA was rated higher for completeness, actionability, and perceived medical accuracy, suggesting that the perceived advantage extended beyond linguistic clarity. In post hoc analyses, differences in quality and trust were greater among current than non-current AMBOSS users. These findings reflect perceived rather than objective performance, are susceptible to bias from non-blinding, question selection, and prior familiarity, and do not isolate the effect of knowledge-base grounding. Prospective, blinded studies are needed to determine clinical implications.

title: Hierarchical AI classification of benign laryngeal disorders using acoustic voice features
container-title: Scientific Reports
07f25b4a68de0c73d3d4a4f9eb49b34a491fa92b.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Benign laryngeal voice disorders affect nearly one in five individuals and often manifest as dysphonia, while also serving as non-invasive indicators of broader physiological dysfunction. We propose a clinically inspired hierarchical machine learning framework for automated classification of eight benign voice disorders alongside healthy controls using acoustic features extracted from short, sustained vowel phonations. Experiments were conducted on 15,132 recordings from 1,261 speakers in the Saarbrücken Voice Database, covering vowels /a/, /i/, and /u/ produced at neutral, high, low, and gliding pitches. Mimicking clinical triage workflows, the framework operates in three sequential stages: Stage 1 performs binary pathological screening by integrating convolutional neural network–derived mel-spectrogram representations with 21 interpretable acoustic features; Stage 2 groups voices into Healthy, Functional/Psychogenic, and Structural/Inflammatory categories; and Stage 3 performs fine-grained subtype classification by incorporating probabilistic outputs from preceding stages as auxiliary diagnostic features. The hierarchical framework demonstrated improved performance compared to flat multiclass classifiers and general-purpose self-supervised models (HuBERT, HeAR), suggesting the value of hierarchical decomposition for complex voice-disorder classification. A confidence-aware human-in-the-loop strategy further improved diagnostic performance by selectively referring low-confidence predictions for expert review while maintaining substantial automatic coverage, providing a practical pathway toward trustworthy clinical deployment and continual model refinement. But external validation on independent cohorts remains essential before clinical deployment. By combining deep spectral learning with interpretable voice features, the proposed framework demonstrates potential as a component of comprehensive diagnostic assessment pending clinical validation and external testing on diverse populations.</jats:p>

title: Generative AI in English Language Teaching: A Systematic Review of Its Impact on Teaching Practices and Learning Outcomes
container-title: International Journal of Social Science and Human Research
8fb433a0a2295e097a0eab7db1db828dcf5bf252.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are now common in English classrooms, but the research on them is spread thinly across different tools, settings and skills, and most of it records what people think rather than what learners actually gained. This review looks at how GenAI is changing the way English is taught and what learners gain from it. Using the PRISMA procedure, the review drew on Web of Science, Scopus, ScienceDirect and Springer, selecting peer-reviewed journal papers from 2024 to 2026; 28 studies were analysed in full. In most studies GenAI served as a helper for teachers in lesson planning, materials, feedback and classroom activities, but how far it was taken up varied with teachers’ own attitudes, self-assurance and preparation. Assessment was the area most challenged, prompting teachers to rethink task design and academic integrity. In terms of learning, GenAI is associated with perceived improvements in writing, grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation, motivation, confidence, and autonomy, but most evidence is perception-based rather than measured. The review concludes that GenAI is best used as a supplement to teacher-guided instruction, with teachers checking its output and guiding learners towards critical use. Future research should adopt longitudinal and controlled designs that measure language outcomes directly.</jats:p>

title: AI-generated medical advice is rated favourably but GP advice is more trusted in India
container-title: Scientific Reports
28285df99f5d6d0ddbe510dc63aa1c132dd2495f.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to provide health information and advice, yet its acceptance depends not only on how credible the information appears but also on whether individuals are willing to rely on it. Existing research has documented resistance to medical AI and source-labelling effects, but evidence from non-Western settings and factorial designs examining source, transparency, and clinical risk together remains comparatively limited. This study examined how individuals evaluate medical advice presented as AI-generated versus general practitioner (GP)-generated, whether source-related differences vary across transparency and clinical-risk conditions, and how these evaluations relate to stated willingness to follow the advice. We conducted a mixed-methods, partially within-subject 2 × 2 × 2 factorial experiment with 797 participants in Mumbai, India. Each participant evaluated four vignettes randomly drawn from eight conditions varying by source (AI or GP), transparency (high or low), and clinical risk (high or low), yielding 3,188 vignette observations. Following examination of the item structure, trustworthiness and a two-item uniqueness-recognition score (α = 0.944) were analysed as separate principal epistemically relevant outcomes. Perceived accuracy and binary behavioural intention were examined separately. The originally constructed three-item epistemic-value composite (α = 0.15) was retained only as an exploratory supplementary analysis. Data were analysed using linear and logistic mixed-effects models, participant-level paired comparisons, and equivalence testing using operational ± 0.20-SD bounds. Qualitative responses were analysed using inductive thematic analysis. Perceived recognition of individual uniqueness did not differ significantly between AI-generated and GP-generated advice, and equivalence was supported within the operational bounds. In contrast, GP-generated advice was rated as more trustworthy and more accurate than AI-generated advice and elicited greater stated willingness to follow. Nevertheless, willingness to follow remained high for both sources, with 86.5% of AI-generated advice responses and 97.3% of GP-generated advice responses indicating an intention to follow the advice. Transparency and clinical risk did not significantly influence the continuous evaluative outcomes. Qualitative findings indicated that AI-generated advice was valued particularly for accessibility and informational clarity, whereas GP-generated advice was more strongly associated with professional expertise, accountability, safety, and relational care. Favourable responses to AI-generated medical advice can coexist with a relative preference for advice attributed to a medical professional. Although AI- and GP-generated advice were comparable in perceived recognition of individual uniqueness within the operational equivalence bounds, GP-generated advice retained advantages in trustworthiness, perceived accuracy, and intended reliance. These findings suggest that responses to medical AI are multidimensional and support positioning AI as a complementary source of health information rather than as an interchangeable substitute for human medical expertise.</jats:p>

title: Mathematical spectrophotometric determination of ibuprofen and paracetamol in the presence of 4-aminophenol: AI-assisted comparative assessment
container-title: Scientific Reports
de01e4d0e6392defc9aad56492c71aa92c121d1e.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Simple mathematical filtration-based spectrophotometric methods were developed for the selective and accurate simultaneous determination of ibuprofen (IBU), paracetamol (PAR), along with the toxic impurity 4-aminophenol (4-AP) without prior separation. The procedures were implemented using built-in spectrophotometer software through a stepwise approach involving the removal of 4-AP by the ratio subtraction technique, followed by spectral processing of the resolved binary mixture of IBU and PAR. Three spectrophotometric strategies, namely ratio subtraction–constant multiplication (RS-CM), ratio difference (RD), and derivative ratio (DD¹), were established and validated for the quantitative determination of IBU and PAR. The concentration of 4-AP was also quantitatively determined and validated using the concentration-value method (conc. value), with wavelength selection optimized through Artificial Intelligence (AI). The proposed methods exhibited excellent linearity over concentration ranges of 4.0–40.0 µg/mL for IBU, 1.6–16.0 µg/mL for PAR and 1.0–10.0 µg/mL for 4-AP were successfully applied to laboratory prepared mixtures and pharmaceutical formulations. Statistical comparison with reference methods using Student’s
                    <jats:italic>t</jats:italic>
                    - and
                    <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                    -tests confirmed the accuracy and precision of the proposed procedures. The principal novelty of the study lies in the integrated comparative assessment of the three analytical strategies using the newly introduced Method Performance Score (MPS) and Method Performance Ranking (MPR) systems, which provide quantitative benchmarking of analytical performance. This framework was further complemented by an Environmental, Performance, and Practicality Index (EPPI) and an extended Sustainability of Analytical Methods Index (SAMI) mapped across all 17 United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), enabling a multidimensional assessment of analytical performance, practicality, environmental impact, and sustainability. The proposed integrated framework provides a comprehensive basis for selecting an appropriate analytical strategy for routine pharmaceutical quality control.
                  </jats:p>

title: A hybrid AI-IoT framework for predictive conservation of tropical heritage façades: empirical validation from a multi-site study in Indonesia
container-title: Scientific Reports
3c221cdccba61f5e5ee5bd48d31666769d212866.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Predictive conservation for tropical built heritage is hindered by the persistent separation of continuous environmental sensing from computational deterioration diagnostics. We address this gap through a fourteen-month hybrid AI-IoT deployment across three heritage sites in Semarang, Indonesia (Lawang Sewu, Pasar Johar, and Tawang Railway Station), integrating unsupervised HSV-space hierarchical clustering with Random Forest classification and a derived Humidity Stress Factor (HSF). The framework was evaluated using 48,686 expert-labelled pixels, achieving a macro-F1 of 0.87 (95% CI: 0.85–0.89) and pixel accuracy of 91.2% (95% CI: 89.4%–93.0%), with inclusion of the HSF producing a 9.2-percentage-point increase in macro-F1 (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     < 0.001). Cumulative exposure to RH > 85% showed a strong association with deterioration (Spearman’s ρ = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.71–0.89,
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     < 0.001), while leave-one-site-out cross-validation yielded F1 scores of 0.79–0.82 (95% CI: 0.76–0.84), providing evidence of spatial transferability within the study region. Retrospective testing detected 79% of impending high-risk events and yielded conditional technical lead-time estimates of 4.8, 9.2, and 16.7 h for the 6-, 12-, and 24-hour horizons, respectively (expected: 3.8, 7.3, and 13.2 h after accounting for missed events). These lead-time estimates are technical and require operational validation before integration into management practice. The study advances prior work through three methodological refinements: direct integration of environmental sensing as a predictive input, prevention of data leakage through training-set-only clustering, and quantitative estimation of early-warning lead times from retrospective analysis. The resulting workflow provides a reproducible basis for risk-prioritised intervention planning. However, generalisation beyond the tropical coastal context requires independent cross-site validation and operational piloting. The findings therefore provide an empirical basis for further development of anticipatory conservation approaches for tropical heritage façades.
                  </jats:p>

title: A Study on the Coupling Relationship Between AI Personalization and Long-Context Management
container-title: Computers and Artificial Intelligence
49889832b6f70b95f1a638c748d37b18136de351.abstract: <jats:p>With the large-scale deployment of large language models (LLMs) in various intelligent assistants and agent systems, homogenized outputs and the loss of user preferences across sessions have become key bottlenecks restricting improvements in user experience. Personalization technology aims to adapt LLMs to the language habits, thinking patterns, and subjective preferences of different users, while long-context and agent memory management addresses the underlying technical problems of storing, filtering, and reusing temporal information for LLMs. Current academic research mostly treats the two directions as independent fields, and systematic reviews of their internal coupling relationship are relatively scarce. This study first defines the core concepts of LLM personalization and long-context memory management and systematically reviews the technical principles, advantages, and existing limitations of four personalization paradigms: prompt-engineering personalization, lightweight parameter fine-tuning, user-preference alignment, and dynamic user profiling. It then divides long-context and agent-memory technologies into five routes: native-window expansion, context pruning and compression, adaptive context extraction, hierarchical memory architectures, and external retrieval-augmented memory, and analyzes the applicable scenarios and technical shortcomings of each route. On this basis, this study reviews progress in four intersecting directions: preference-aware memory updating, structured persona-memory representation, long-horizon personalization evaluation benchmarks, and training-free collaborative control at inference time. It further analyzes the internal coupling mechanism through which the two directions empower each other and summarizes three core conflicts: the capacity-accuracy trade-off, the conflict between general governance rules and personalized characteristics, and the conflict between computational cost and personalization stability. The study also summarizes five research challenges: difficulty in adapting to the dynamic evolution of user preferences, failure to recall implicit preferences, memory errors and preference drift, fragmented evaluation systems, and difficulty balancing engineering implementation costs. It proposes subsequent research paths in six dimensions: cognitively inspired memory architectures, preference-aware context compression algorithms, multimode hybrid indexing and retrieval, unified long-horizon personalization evaluation protocols, memory-error verification mechanisms, and multimodal long-term personalization. The findings indicate that long-term personalized intelligent systems cannot optimize the personalization module or memory module in isolation. Their coupling relationship should serve as the underlying design logic to promote the iterative upgrading of LLMs toward adaptation to individual user characteristics and to provide a reference for the theoretical research and engineering development of long-term agents and personalized dialogue assistants.</jats:p>

title: Budget-Aware Adaptive Test-Time Compute with Hierarchical Self-Verification for Semantic ID Generative Recommendation
container-title: Computers
ad812a7a10cc5144461b6cebf5c51d87590389d3.abstract: <jats:p>Semantic identifier (SID) generative recommenders cast retrieval as autoregressive decoding over short sequences of residual-quantized codewords. Most published SID recommenders decode all requests with one fixed beam width, which is optimal only if the marginal utility of compute is constant across requests. We find that it is not; additional search changes little for users with consistent histories, but improves accuracy substantially for cold start, interest-drifting, and long-tail users. The main methodological contribution of this paper is request-level allocation of decoding compute, in which a router predicts the accuracy gain of each configuration in a finite decoding menu over the cheapest configuration and selects the configuration with the largest gain net of a priced cost. The selection rule follows from standard Lagrangian arguments, which we use as tools; what is specific to this work is the use of this per-configuration gain as the routing target for SID decoding instead of a difficulty or uncertainty score. The resulting framework, called Bastion, combines the router with a hierarchical process verifier over the quantization levels, a listwise terminal verifier, codeword consistency voting, and budget-constrained group relative policy optimization. On five benchmarks built from Amazon Reviews 2023, MovieLens, and MicroLens, Bastion improves NDCG@10 by 5.7% to 8.7% over the strongest baseline. Its mean latency on Amazon-Beauty is 14.5 ms, against 14.6 ms for a beam-20 TIGER decoder, while its median and 99th-percentile latencies are higher by 0.9 ms and 7.0 ms. At every evaluated budget, its accuracy exceeds that of all baselines on the three datasets for which accuracy versus latency frontiers was measured.</jats:p>

title: Offloading Thoughts to the Bots: How Generative AI Access Influences Cognitive Reflection
container-title: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
89abf0f54d025ddf7e06b07b896cddba60561ff9.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly used to support reasoning and decision-making, raising questions about how AI influences reflective cognition and trust. This study examined how AI pedigree and reliability influenced cognitive reflection performance, cognitive load, trust, and performance overestimation during a verbal Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT-V). Participants (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">N</jats:italic>
                     = 148) were assigned to a no-AI control condition, a low-pedigree AI condition, or a high-pedigree AI condition. Participants in the high-pedigree AI condition demonstrated significantly greater trust and CRT performance than participants in both other conditions while also exhibiting lower performance overestimation. AI access did not significantly reduce perceived cognitive load, although greater cognitive load predicted poorer CRT performance overall. Importantly, trust interacted with AI condition such that greater trust predicted lower CRT performance in the low-pedigree AI condition but not in the high-pedigree AI condition. These findings support theories of calibrated reliance rather than indiscriminate cognitive offloading.
                  </jats:p>

title: Storying digital well-being and quality of life in Ghanaian adult learners’ use of generative AI
container-title: Scientific Reports
c634dad76c94b4e94f6f5c7d44b252ec2e09075d.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in higher education; however, little is known about what its use means for adult learners’ digital well-being (DWB) and quality of life (QoL). This mixed-methods study, which leaned towards a qualitative design (qualitative dominant), investigated these issues among adult learners at a university in Ghana. The quantitative phase involved 212 randomly selected respondents, while six (6) participants were purposively selected for the qualitative phase. The survey findings showed that overall DWB was above the midpoint of the 7-point Likert scale (M = 4.58, SD = 0.76). The mental (M = 4.09, SD = 1.12), emotional (M = 4.51, SD = 1.29), and reverse-coded physical (M = 5.14, SD = 1.45) subscales indicated generally positive perceptions of digital well-being. However, item-level responses showed that a notable minority of participants still reported physical challenges, including disturbed sleep, changes in eating habits, physical discomfort, and reduced physical exercise associated with GenAI use. QoL was measured using a 3-point substantive scale, with two non-substantive response options excluded from scoring. The QoL mean (M = 2.06, SD = 0.94) indicated modest gains in safety, control, activity engagement, and time efficiency. A digital storytelling analysis of the participants’ experiences revealed that the adults held ambivalent views about GenAI, reflecting both appreciation for its efficiency and anxiety over its encroachment on human creativity and authenticity. The coping strategies adopted included developing a critical distance and self-awareness, re-engaging human connection and support networks, mindful regulation and intentional use, and transforming frustration into learning. It is recommended that adult educators prioritise the digital safety of adult learners.</jats:p>

title: Material-dependent structure of roughness representation in generative AI-based texture analysis
container-title: Scientific Reports
99f1ede7a8a2589d8d22ae87299da11baf5b16a6.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Generative image models can produce visually different expressions of surface roughness depending on material context, but the structure of these variations remains unclear. Here, we systematically examined roughness-related image features in textures generated for six material categories at ten prompt-defined roughness levels. Three prompting conditions were compared: a Quantitative Model, a Generic Linguistic Model using common roughness descriptors across materials, and a Material-Specific Linguistic Model using category-specific descriptions. Nine interpretable image features comprising eight luminance-distribution statistics and the FFT spectral centroid were analyzed. Feature–roughness correlations varied substantially across materials, indicating that no single feature within the examined feature set consistently captured roughness-related variation across all categories. Hierarchical clustering revealed significant associations between material category and cluster assignment for both linguistic models but not for the Quantitative Model, with the strongest associations observed for the Material-Specific Linguistic Model. Silhouette scores in the full nine-dimensional feature space were −0.065, −0.001, and 0.271 for the Quantitative, Generic Linguistic, and Material-Specific Linguistic Models, respectively, indicating clearer category-dependent organization with material-specific linguistic conditioning. These findings demonstrate that roughness-related image-feature organization in the examined generative model depends on both material context and linguistic prompting. This framework provides testable hypotheses for future comparison with physically characterized surfaces and human perceptual judgments.</jats:p>

title: From Code-Centric to Intent-Centric Software Engineering: A Reflexive Thematic Analysis of Generative AI, Agentic Systems, and Engineering Accountability
container-title: Computers
b8b475504b37ed3bec01880f6991e5586b1ec8f1.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and agentic systems are shifting software engineering from code-centric production toward intent-centric human-agent work, in which natural language, repository context, tools, tests, and governance shape delivery. Prior studies examine code generation, AI pair programming, and software engineering agents, but less is known about how public technical discourse and peer-reviewed evidence jointly frame the profession’s near-term transition. This study addresses that gap through a reflexive thematic analysis (RTA) of public-discourse and document analysis. The corpus combines peer-reviewed software engineering and AI literature, technical benchmarks, public talks and interviews, essays, product-facing technical announcements, and X-originated discourse. The corpus contains 49 unique artifacts across three evidentiary layers: 28 peer-reviewed sources, 6 technical preprints/benchmarks, and 15 public discourse artifacts. Sources were organized using a corpus register, codebook, coding matrix, theme-to-source traceability table, DOI/reference audit, and reproducibility protocol. The analysis indicates that GenAI lowers the cost of producing plausible code while increasing the importance of intent specification, context curation, architecture knowledge, verification, security, provenance, governance, and accountable human judgment. Software engineering is consequently becoming less about isolated code authorship and more about supervising, validating, and governing socio-technical systems of humans, agents, tools, and evidence gates. Bounded autonomy can preserve quality, security, maintainability, and trust while limiting hidden technical debt and accountability gaps.</jats:p>

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Atrial fibrillation (AF) is one of the most common arrhythmias and is associated with multiple risk factors, including stroke and heart failure. Therefore, it is important that accurate and comprehensive educational resources on AF are available. Artificial intelligence (AI) platforms such as Google Gemini and ChatGPT are emerging tools for medical education. To our knowledge, this is the first study to assess the quality of these platforms for AF education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This pilot study aimed to (1) assess the quality of ChatGPT and Google Gemini explanations of AF and its treatment, (2) compare responses from both platforms, and (3) analyze differences in interpretation between cardiologists and nonmedical professionals.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The prompt “Explain atrial fibrillation and how to treat it to a patient” was entered into both ChatGPT and Google Gemini. The responses, along with a survey created in Google Forms, were sent out to potential participants between September and October 2024. The survey questions were derived from the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials and DISCERN criteria. Each survey question was multiple choice and rated on a 5-point Likert scale, where 1 indicated strong disagreement and 5 indicated strong agreement. Averages of each answer from the survey were calculated and compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The survey was completed by 28 participants, including cardiologists and cardiology fellows and 17 nonmedical professionals (college graduates not employed in the medical field). No significant overall quality differences were observed between ChatGPT and Google Gemini. When comparing participant groups, cardiologists rated AI-generated responses higher than nonmedical professionals for perceived bias (mean 3.82 vs mean 4.33; P=.04) and for explaining consequences of no treatment (mean 2.85 vs mean 1.86; P=.005). In contrast, nonmedical professionals rated structural and organizational features more favorably than cardiologists, including visual cues (mean 3.97 vs mean 2.48; P<.001), informative headers (mean 4.77 vs mean 3.95; P=.001), concise sections (mean 4.71 vs mean 4.29; P=.04), identifiable patient actions (mean 4.21 vs mean 3.19; P=.04), and references to additional resources (mean 2.65 vs mean 1.71; P=.006).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The comparable quality of ChatGPT and Google Gemini suggests that both are viable for AF education. Differences in ratings of organizational features versus perceptions of bias and consequences of no treatment highlight a disconnect between cardiologists and nonmedical professionals. To optimize clinical application, cardiologists should evaluate both comprehensiveness and clarity of AI-generated responses. This serves as a pilot study, and future research should focus on longitudinal studies of AI-generated responses and their effects on clinical outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery, Endobariatrics, and AI - How AI is Contributing to Surgery and Endoscopy
Towards Realistic Project-Level Code Generation via Multi-Agent Collaboration and Semantic Architecture Modeling
container-title: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
2e98affb75fe6b1c9fa0a80bf39cb6bb48af6b14.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in automated code generation. In real-world software engineering, the growing demand for rapid iteration and continuous delivery underscores the importance of project-level code generation, where LLMs are expected to generate complete software projects directly from complex user requirements. This task, however, presents greater challenges due to larger input scales, multi-modal information, and the need for holistic architectural reasoning. Although existing studies have made initial explorations, they still face key limitations, including unrealistic datasets and unreliable evaluation metrics that fail to reflect real-world complexity, the semantic gap between human-written requirements and machine-interpretable structures, and difficulties in managing hierarchical dependencies and maintaining quality throughout the generation process. To address these limitations, we first introduce
                    <jats:sc>CodeProjectEval</jats:sc>
                    , a project-level code generation dataset built from 18 real-world repositories with 12.7 files and 2,388.6 lines of code per task on average, supplemented with documentation and executable test cases for automatic evaluation. We further propose
                    <jats:sc>ProjectGen</jats:sc>
                    , a multi-agent framework that decomposes projects into architecture design, skeleton generation, and code filling stages with iterative refinement and memory-based context management. Within this framework, we introduce the Semantic Software Architecture Tree, a structured and semantically rich representation that effectively bridges user requirements and source code implementation. Experiments show that
                    <jats:sc>ProjectGen</jats:sc>
                    achieves state-of-the-art performance, passing 52/124 test cases on the small-scale project-level code generation dataset DevBench, a 57% improvement over the baseline approaches, and 310 test cases on
                    <jats:sc>CodeProjectEval</jats:sc>
                    , representing an improvement of roughly tenfold compared to the baselines.
                  </jats:p>

title: AI-Generated Exposure Hierarchies for Body Dysmorphic Disorder: Proof-of-Concept Study
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
475970c23de59b336f5f102fda0e80aa46b47e4e.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is a chronic, impairing condition for which cognitive behavioral therapy, including exposure and response prevention (ERP), is the first-line treatment, but few clinicians are trained in BDD-specific ERP. Constructing personalized exposure hierarchies is time-intensive and requires clinical expertise, particularly for patients with absent insight who may hold appearance beliefs with delusional conviction. Generative AI (GenAI)–powered chatbots, such as ChatGPT, have shown utility for clinical content, but their capacity to produce safe, appropriate ERP hierarchies for BDD has not been examined.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study evaluated the feasibility of using ChatGPT (GPT-5) to generate ERP hierarchies for BDD, assessed the influence of clinical and demographic characteristics on output quality, benchmarked AI-generated hierarchies against those created by doctoral-level BDD specialists, and tested whether blinded experts could distinguish AI-generated from expert-generated hierarchies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GPT-5 generated 10-item graded exposure hierarchies for 72 simulated vignettes that varied by body area, insight level (good, limited, or absent), symptom specificity, age, and gender. Expert clinicians independently generated hierarchies for a subset of 18 vignettes. Two researchers rated all GPT-5 hierarchies for task completion and information integration. Three BDD expert clinicians, blinded to the hierarchy source (expert vs GPT-5), rated all 90 hierarchies for relevance, specificity, variability, safety, and overall quality. After unblinding, raters attempted to identify the AI-generated hierarchy in the 18 matched pairs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      GPT-5 generated complete hierarchies for 69 of 72 (95.8%) vignettes. Blinded experts rated GPT-5 hierarchies highly across all dimensions (mean scores ranging from 4.39, SD 0.26 to 4.90, SD 0.16 out of 5), with no significant differences from expert-generated hierarchies except for variability, where experts scored modestly higher (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.02;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.24). After unblinding, raters correctly identified AI-generated hierarchies only 31.5% (17/54) of the time, significantly below chance (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.009); this below-chance result was mostly due to one rater, and no rater performed above chance. Insight level was the most consistent predictor of quality: absent-insight hierarchies received significantly lower safety (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.73) and overall quality ratings (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.01;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.43). This pattern was not unique to GPT-5; safety ratings for expert-generated hierarchies also declined significantly by insight level (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03). Miscalibration of exposure difficulty, particularly for low- and absent-insight cases, was the most common rater concern (30/43, 69.8% comments), disproportionately directed at GPT-5 hierarchies.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GPT-5 generated ERP hierarchies for BDD that blinded experts rated as comparable to clinician-created hierarchies and could not reliably distinguish them from clinician-created hierarchies. However, hierarchies for patients with absent insight received lower safety and quality ratings from both AI and expert sources, and qualitative comments suggested AI-generated hierarchies were less well calibrated to delusional-level presentations. GenAI thus shows promise as a clinician-facing aid for ERP hierarchy generation, but these findings underscore the need for clinician oversight, especially for patients with delusional conviction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: SAI: Virtualizing Shared Memory of GPU for AI workload acceleration
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
c8fa29b0323351e1659db262fc936958ed20d580.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    AI workloads increasingly demand high parallelism and efficient on-chip memory utilization on modern GPUs. However, the limited capacity of shared memory often constrains thread-level parallelism, while portions of the L2 cache remain underutilized. In this work, we propose
                    <jats:bold>SAI</jats:bold>
                    , a mechanism that virtualizes shared memory into the L2 cache to improve GPU performance for AI applications. SAI dynamically activates virtualization based on runtime resource usage, enabling additional CTAs with minimal architectural modifications. We further introduce an L2 cache management strategy that integrates associativity-based virtual page allocation and a replacement information table, reducing page-swapping overhead while preserving L2 cache performance. Experimental results demonstrate that SAI achieves an 18.6% performance improvement over the baseline design and outperforms SMILE-opt, our reproduced state-of-the-art baseline, by 8.8%. Moreover, SAI captures 60.2% of the performance gain delivered by the idealized Double SMEM design while reducing energy consumption to 87.7% of the baseline. These results highlight the effectiveness of SAI in enhancing thread-level parallelism and optimizing on-chip memory for AI workloads.
                  </jats:p>

title: AI-Enabled Early Detection of Epidemic Threats in a Resource-Constrained Health System: Implementation Research from Lebanon
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
94bf395e649f9c13344c021277ab854ad6c98be5.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Global South countries face heightened infectious disease risks compounded by fragmented surveillance systems and resource constraints. Lebanon’s health system crisis and recurrent outbreaks highlight the urgent need for new approaches to epidemic and pandemic preparedness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To describe the design, implementation process, and early implementation findings of an artificial intelligence (AI)–enabled early warning system (AI-EWS) that automates detection of epidemiologically relevant events using laboratory data in Lebanon, with emphasis on feasibility, workflow integration, stakeholder engagement, and implementation learnings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We applied an implementation research approach to co-design and validate an AI-EWS prototype integrated within a university hospital laboratory. The system incorporates a hybrid statistical and machine learning analytic pipeline and a real-time dashboard for detecting epidemic events across multiple pathogens using routine laboratory information systems (LIS) data. The system was developed in collaboration with the Ministry of Public Health (MoPH) to support future national adoption.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The project produced a structured framework for pathogen selection, rule development, dataset creation, and platform co-design with clinical and epidemiological experts, medical informatics professionals, MoPH experts, and technical specialists. Early implementation observations indicate operational feasibility within existing infrastructure, strong stakeholder engagement, and trust-building around AI-enabled surveillance through participatory design and responsible-AI governance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI-enabled laboratory surveillance is a viable and scalable approach to strengthening epidemic preparedness in low-resource health systems when grounded in implementation science and responsible AI, and when explicitly aligned with local workflows and national policy priorities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Bayesian Forecasting as the Analytical Core of an AI-Assisted Early Warning System for Dengue Outbreaks during the 2023 Epidemic: Implementation and Emergency Management in a Dominican Pediatric Hospital
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
056417fa3dbad64347775b6e5020ffb82cf01df1.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Dengue remains a major cause of pediatric morbidity in the Dominican Republic, with increasingly intense epidemic cycles. Advances in statistical modeling, probabilistic forecasting, and AI-assisted digital health systems offer new opportunities to enhance early warning capabilities and strengthen hospital preparedness. This study evaluated a Bayesian negative binomial regression forecasting model as the analytical core of an AI-assisted early warning system (EWS) for predicting weekly dengue cases nationwide, using strict out-of-sample validation during the 2023 epidemic and applying its outputs operationally in a high-demand pediatric hospital. National surveillance data (PLISA/PAHO), hospital records from the Dr. Hugo Mendoza Pediatric Hospital (HPHM), and climatic and satellite indicators (NOAA, MODIS) for 2014–2024 were integrated. The model incorporated climatically plausible lags, harmonic seasonality, two vegetation indices (NDVI_lag4 and EVI_lag4), a long-term spline trend, and weakly informative priors, achieving excellent convergence (Rhat = 1.00). Climatic and environmental predictors exhibited small and uncertain effects, whereas the temporal spline accounted for most long-term epidemic variability. In the 2023 national validation, the model captured the broad epidemic trajectory and improved RMSE and MAE compared with the historical seasonal baseline (RMSE = 783.3; MAE = 423.4; MAPE = 80.2%), although proportional accuracy remained limited during abrupt epidemic acceleration. The national model also captured ascending-phase signals that were temporally aligned with the HPHM hospital outbreak, including its sharp rise during epidemiological weeks 36–40. These outputs were used alongside routine surveillance and hospital indicators to support operational situational awareness, capacity planning, patient-flow reorganization, strengthened triage, and emergency preparedness during the epidemic. The model demonstrated temporal signal detection and operational relevance, positioning Bayesian probabilistic forecasting, embedded within an AI-assisted digital health workflow, as a useful analytical component for epidemic monitoring and hospital preparedness, subject to limitations in peak magnitude calibration and proportional accuracy.</jats:p>

title: Toward Human-Centered Pedagogy in the Age of Generative AI Among Higher Education Educators: Qualitative Phenomenological Study
container-title: JMIR Medical Education
46248c918f688c3c5f2cc8bb261f150c45f4e9cf.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Generative AI (GenAI) expands possibilities for content generation, feedback, personalization, and instructional support in higher education. Its growing use also challenges established assumptions about teaching, assessment, professional expertise, academic integrity, and educational responsibility. Although research has examined technology adoption and AI competencies, less is known about how educators experience and interpret the pedagogical transformation associated with GenAI in everyday teaching.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study explored how higher education educators experience GenAI-mediated pedagogical transformation, focusing on pedagogical practices, professional roles and expertise, educator agency, human-AI relationships, and associated opportunities and tensions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A qualitative phenomenological inquiry involved 23 educators from 3 Palestinian universities. Purposive maximum-variation sampling sought variation in academic rank, discipline, teaching experience, and experience with AI tools. Individual semistructured, in-depth interviews were conducted from March to April 2026, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and returned to participants for review. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis informed by phenomenology. Initial coding was inductive and grounded in participants’ accounts; human-centered AI and sociomateriality subsequently informed interpretation as sensitizing concepts. Themes were developed through iterative comparison of transcripts, analytic memos, and alternative interpretations. Informational sufficiency was observed after approximately 20 interviews, with 3 additional interviews used to examine the developing thematic structure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis generated 8 interconnected themes. Educators described a shift from content transmission toward mediation, inquiry, reflective learning, creative exploration, and process-oriented assessment. Professional expertise increasingly centered on facilitation, pedagogical design, contextual interpretation, ethical guidance, and evaluation of AI-generated content. Human-AI collaboration involved bounded and integrated configurations, with humans retaining responsibility for judgment and educational consequences. Educator agency appeared through decisions about AI participation, independent student reasoning, and the boundaries of human expertise. Credibility, bias, authorship, authenticity, and academic integrity became embedded as pedagogical concerns. Participants valued opportunities for creativity, personalization, flexibility, and instructional support while expressing concerns about dependence, reduced intellectual effort, and weakened human connection.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GenAI-mediated pedagogical transformation depends on educators’ alignment of AI use with learning purposes, the allocation of responsibilities, and the preservation of ethical accountability and meaningful relationships. The resulting human-centered pedagogy framework positions pedagogical intentionality, contextual judgment, negotiated agency, and relational presence as central to responsible integration. Universities should complement technical training and institutional policies with support for pedagogical design, critical evaluation, process-oriented assessment, and ethical reasoning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: AI and Machine Learning in Broadcast Media
