title: Polycentrism in the Digital Geoeconomic Order
container-title: Rethinking Authority and Legitimacy in Global Politics
711935f459dab859b4d3505b506126d69c84de7d.abstract: <jats:p>The twenty-first century is marked by the paradox of global interdependence alongside deepening fragmentation, as digital infrastructures and data regimes reshape economic and geopolitical dynamics. This chapter critiques the limits of monocentric governance models and advances polycentric governance as a more adaptive framework for a complex digital era. Drawing on Ostrom, it conceptualizes polycentrism as a multi-level, networked mode of governance suited to distributed authority and uncertainty. Through cases such as COVID-19 governance failures, data sovereignty disputes, and digital inequality in the Global South, it shows how overlapping governance systems can enhance resilience and legitimacy. Compared to hierarchical models, polycentric systems enable flexibility, innovation, and coordination across diverse actors. The chapter argues that polycentric governance is both theoretically robust and empirically necessary for sustaining cooperation in the evolving digital geoeconomic order.</jats:p>

title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
Digital Transformation of Accounting and Financial Management Through Emerging Technologies
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
072ee30c1139742aaee5825be31b3e984571eca4.abstract: <jats:p>Digital transformation has created an opportunity for accountants and financial managers to create new efficiencies, add transparency to their work, and develop better strategies for decision-making. This chapter looks at how artificial intelligence, automation, big data analytics, and cloud-based financial management are changing how accountants use technology, as well as how those technologies are changing the practices and processes that accountants follow when doing their jobs. It also describes how the digital transformation of Finance will cause a dramatic shift in the way financial services are delivered to customers from being reactive to value-driven. By integrating intelligent systems into forecasting, performance management, risk assessment, and real-time reporting functions, the ability to make informed decisions is enhanced. The chapter identifies the organizational, regulatory, and ethical challenges that digital finance poses, including data privacy, cybersecurity, and governance risks.</jats:p>

title: The Importance of the Mastering of Technological Skills and Profile of Professional Accounting
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
50dd51a7264e3966f834e8645c738ce22d306e48.abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to assess whether the importance given to information and communication technologies by accounting professionals is conditioned by age, gender, and the type of company where they work. It also intends to assess the relationship between the skills under study, determining which one is most important. The main results obtained allow us to affirm that the variables age and gender do not condition the importance given to information and communication technologies by accounting professionals, while for the type of company there are differences of opinion, constituting the main innovative contribution of this article to academic knowledge, given the scarcity of studies on this topic. We also conclude that “specific accounting technological skills” are the strongest manifestation in the construct of “technological skills”. This study aims to contribute to the reflection of Professional Orders and Higher Education Institutions on the importance of information and communication technologies for accounting professionals.</jats:p>

title: Preparing Finance Professionals for the Digital Age
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
a93fe9bb395867eb78859ec32fbdad9bef6d3cb5.abstract: <jats:p>Emerging digital technologies—AI, big data, RPA, blockchain, and cloud computing—are rapidly transforming the financial sector, shifting finance professionals from traditional record-keepers to strategic digital advisors. Using a qualitative approach grounded in academic literature and institutional reports, this study identifies critical technical competencies including data analytics, financial modeling, cybersecurity awareness, and digital literacy, alongside essential soft skills such as strategic thinking, communication, adaptability, and emotional intelligence. A significant gap is revealed between current educational and corporate training systems versus industry expectations. To bridge this divide, the study proposes a comprehensive competency model integrating digital proficiency, behavioral skills, and financial expertise. The findings underscore the necessity of continuous learning and digital resilience, ensuring sustained professional relevance in an increasingly technology-driven financial landscape.</jats:p>

title: Education and Curriculum Design for Future Finance Professionals
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
688a834c57266bfb9c64b3f458ee9b94b666529f.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid digital transformation of global financial systems has created an urgent need to redesign finance education and curriculum frameworks for future professionals. Traditional finance curricula remain largely theory-oriented and often fail to address emerging competencies related to artificial intelligence, FinTech, blockchain, data analytics, sustainability, and ethical governance. This chapter proposes the Future Finance Curriculum Framework (FFCF Model), an integrated and competency-based framework designed to bridge the gap between academic learning and evolving industry expectations. Drawing upon theories of competency-based education, outcome-based learning, and experiential learning, the study emphasizes interdisciplinary approaches, industry collaboration, technology integration, and continuous curriculum upgradation. The chapter also highlights the growing importance of analytical, digital ethical, and soft skills in preparing adaptive finance professionals for a globally connected financial environment and society too.</jats:p>

title: The Accounting Professional in the Fourth Industrial Revolution
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
09542450f279522e6869f1c9442864fdbc2fe620.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how the digital transformation of accounting is reflected in labour-market demand in Spain. Using a quantitative content analysis of 803 accounting-related job advertisements published on InfoJobs, the study identifies the digital competencies explicitly required by employers and analyses the factors associated with more digitally intensive vacancies. A Digital Demand Index is constructed from four technological dimensions: Excel and data processing, data visualisation and business intelligence, ERP and management systems, and artificial intelligence (AI). The results show that digital demand is mainly concentrated around established tools, particularly Excel and ERP systems, while business intelligence and AI remain much less visible in recruitment requirements. The regression analysis indicates that higher salaries, junior profiles, large firms, and higher education requirements are associated with stronger digital competence demand.</jats:p>

title: Digital Skills and Professional Judgment in AI-Driven Financial Decision-Making
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
fa94d39fbd808cc46e56a32eb78b60762c9d5124.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping financial decision-making by altering how information is analyzed, interpreted, and translated into professional judgment. This chapter examines the role of digital skills in determining whether AI strengthens or undermines the quality and accountability of financial decisions. Drawing on interdisciplinary literature, the chapter conceptualizes digital skills as cognitive–governance capabilities that extend beyond technical proficiency to include critical interpretation, calibrated reliance on AI, explainability, professional skepticism, and ethical judgment. Particular attention is given to automation bias, accountability risks, and the organizational conditions that shape human–AI interaction. The chapter concludes that responsible AI-enabled financial decision-making depends not on algorithmic capability alone, but on the alignment of digital competence, professional judgment, and effective governance.</jats:p>

title: Building Future-Ready Finance Professionals
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
9e847b36a842d0128695027264f9ae732156fa68.abstract: <jats:p>Digitalization is transforming the competency landscape for the modern finance professional, and this chapter explores the digital skills, technological tools, and strategic capabilities needed to navigate this rapidly changing environment, grounded in recent advancements in data analytics, cloud-based enterprise systems, artificial intelligence (AI), robotic process automation (RPA), and blockchain. Integrating scholarly literature, professional frameworks, and industry reports, the chapter shows that digital competencies are not simply technical skills but a combination of analytical, technological, ethical, and strategic skills. In this chapter, the authors introduce a multi-dimensional Digital Finance Competency Framework (DFCF). The results highlight that entities and educational establishments that allocate resources towards digital competencies enhancement will be most strategically equipped to adeptly manage the rapid evolution of the international financial landscape.</jats:p>

title: From Financial Accountant to Digital Finance Architect
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
301bb7a811700c54a3c8f72796dd343a397ed320.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter analyzes the digital transformation of the finance function as a structural reconfiguration of processes, decision-making logic, and governance. It demonstrates how automation, artificial intelligence, sustainability, and RegTech are shifting traditional job profiles from process execution to the architectural design of digital financial systems. On this basis, the Digital Finance Competency Architecture (DFCA) is developed, integrating technological, data-analytical, governance-related, and strategic-cognitive competencies. The analysis illustrates that effective performance in digital finance environments requires systemic competence, i.e., the ability to translate data, models, and regulatory requirements into coherent decision-making architectures. Finally, implications for education, organization, and governance are discussed, and the Digital Finance Architect is established as a new professional role model.</jats:p>

title: Fintech Frontiers
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
36d3f1be0785d18f51b68fb81cc99645251bd25a.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid progress of financial technology (Fintech) has profoundly changed financial services in terms of efficiency, accessibility and innovativeness across banking, insurance sectors and investment. This chapter will examine the effects of fintech on financial systems and the emerging competencies of finance professionals in a digitalized world. This chapter adopts a conceptual and integrative review used in this research, with the findings synthesized from academic and institutional sources to examine the significant technological changes, including blockchain, artificial intelligence and digital platforms. This chapter will also focus on the contribution of fintech to financial inclusion, customer satisfaction and sustainability. In addition, the challenges of regulation, workforce readiness and cybersecurity will be explored. The findings will focus on the importance of developing competencies and adapting strategically in navigating to the dynamic landscape of Fintech effectively.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Financial Decision-Making
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
9804e231d1b385dde790b1cf795ea7aaec80b1c1.abstract: <jats:p>Financial decision-making is being revolutionized by the use of artificial intelligence (AI). Whereas traditional statistical methods may be limited by the scope and complexity of contemporary financial datasets, AI technologies such as machine learning and natural language processing (NLP) permit companies to analyze not only structured but unstructured datasets efficiently. As such, there have been significant improvements in financial decision-making processes related to portfolio management, risk analysis, fraud detection, and algorithmic trading. However, the use of AI in the financial industry is also associated with issues such as lack of model transparency, algorithmic bias, and high reliance on past data, which create certain problems when it comes to transparency and reliability.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence in Financial Decision-Making
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
478d0167085f2f271218a60ba78cf0ed82a89eb2.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping financial decision-making by enhancing analytical accuracy, speed, and strategic insight across corporate finance and financial services. The primary objective of the study is to evaluate how AI applications support strategic and operational financial decisions, while also assessing associated risks related to transparency, accountability, and decision control. A qualitative case study methodology is adopted, drawing on secondary data sources including corporate reports, financial disclosures, technology implementation documents, and industry publications. The findings indicate that AI significantly improves forecasting accuracy, real-time financial monitoring, and scenario analysis, leading to more informed and timely financial decisions. The study offers original value by providing practical, case-based evidence on how AI transforms financial decision-making processes beyond theoretical models. The implications are relevant for stakeholders seeking to leverage sustainable financial performance.</jats:p>

title: AI-Driven Financial Decision Support for Handicraft Artisans
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
1d34157c42ec302960b797359d16b132c9fe0d28.abstract: <jats:p>Handicraft artists play an important role in conserving cultural and social history while also contributing to the growth of their respective economies. It contributes four to five percent to the world economy and creates a huge number of job opportunities in the neighbourhood. Handicraft workers contribute to societal innovation in the shape of innovative work methods, techniques, and so on. This area sheds light on the hidden talents and abilities of craft workers. However, their salary and economic situation do not allow for this. They are frequently confronted with issues and obstacles such as limited market access, intense rivalry from major companies, a lack of technology, and a communication gap. The article focuses on using Artificial Intelligence (AI) to solve difficulties for the handicraft industry. Primary data were acquired from 120 handicraft workers for the study using a structured questionnaire, including demographic information, production costs, profit from their company, and numerous problems they encounter.</jats:p>

title: FinTech Accounting in Financial Services Within Developing Countries
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
db8335e5a2deda558f8cb80d55476f5148e3b100.abstract: <jats:p>Fintech growth in developing nations revolutionized financial inclusion by bypassing banks, yet harmonizing accounting principles in low-infrastructure economies remains a challenge. This scoping review uses a PCC framework to map the intersection of fintech, corporate oversight, and accounting platforms to identify standard-setting frictions. Sourcing English literature up to 2026 from Scopus and Google Scholar, the study assessed fintech tools, disclosure quality, and regulations. Duplicate data extraction captured demographics, analytical models, and reporting contradictions across eleven studies spanning East Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, and the Middle East. Reflexive thematic analysis revealed four themes: corporate green reporting, infrastructure vulnerabilities, algorithmic controls, and small business viability. Stability requires adapting global reporting rules for high-velocity data. Transparent tools must replace static reporting to attract capital and prevent deep instability.</jats:p>

title: Meaning-based retrieval of Kannada Vachana literary works: a comparative analysis of retrieval techniques
container-title: Digital Scholarship in the Humanities
2aea2ebbfcfdf79834bc89c6acc4ea0799a733d5.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper examines the challenge of meaning-based verse retrieval for Kannada literary works, including Vachanas, Tripadis, and Kaggas, using Kannada queries. These literary verses are, in a sense, a form of poem-cum-prose. Given their philosophical depth and metaphorical nature, retrieval was performed using interpretations provided by Kannada scholars rather than direct text matching. We evaluated five retrieval approaches: TF–IDF, TF–IDF with Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI), KannadaSBERT-STS sentence embeddings, a cluster-based tree model of interpretations, and a proposed Hybrid Verse Retrieval (HVR) approach that fuses TF–IDF and KannadaSBERT-STS similarity scores. Experiments were conducted on a refined subset of the KannadaLit4NLP corpus comprising 5,158 verses with 17,930 scholarly interpretations, evenly split for training and testing. The results show that the proposed HVR approach performed best overall, achieving 82.40% exact-match accuracy at Top 20, an improvement over KannadaSBERT-STS embeddings alone (78.75%), which in turn outperformed the classical TF–IDF and LSI baselines. The cluster-based approach offered competitive early-rank accuracy and the added advantage of grouping related themes, though its performance plateaued at greater retrieval depths. Overall, the study demonstrates that combining statistical and transformer-based semantic signals through a simple, fixed-weight fusion can meaningfully improve verse retrieval, highlighting the promise of hybrid natural language processing approaches for the retrieval and exploration of Kannada’s literary heritage.</jats:p>

title: Attention Trap? How Visual Motion Shapes Children’s Screen Time and Engagement on Video Platforms
container-title: Information Systems Research
3836bd62e72740b25fd59c7e03808cdae1f4dd40.abstract:
<jats:p>Children spend considerable time watching online video, yet we know relatively little about which features of video content shape their engagement. This research examines one measurable feature: visual motion. Analyzing more than 32,000 videos from popular children’s channels on YouTube, we find that videos with greater visual motion receive more views, even after accounting for other visual, audio, and content characteristics. A randomized YouTube advertising experiment using professionally produced educational videos confirms this relationship; adding motion to the background increased view rates by about 2% at essentially no additional cost.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>An eye-tracking study with children aged 6–10 helps explain why. Visual motion does not prevent children from looking away. Instead, it reduces the duration of longer attentional lapses by bringing their gaze back to the screen more quickly. The additional attention is directed primarily toward the moving background rather than the instructor. The findings show how a measurable design feature can shape children’s attention and provide creators and platforms with a way to assess and design children’s video content more systematically.</jats:p>

title: Stakeholder Perspectives on Information About Digital Health Applications in German Outpatient Mental Health Care: Qualitative Interview Study
container-title: JMIR Human Factors
53786725fea7a172d562c7b958f00be3fc9858bc.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Digital health applications (digitale gesundheitsanwendungen; DiGA) were integrated into the German statutory health care system in 2020 and can be prescribed by physicians and psychotherapists. Nevertheless, their use within routine care, particularly in the treatment of mental disorders, remains limited. Previous research suggests that a lack of information and knowledge among health care providers and patients may contribute to these difficulties.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to explore the perspectives of stakeholders on the information-related aspects of DiGA implementation in outpatient mental health care in Germany. This included investigating the perceived information status, information needs, suitable information providers, and potential approaches to improve information provision.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted semistructured interviews with experts representing stakeholder groups relevant to DiGA in outpatient mental health care in Germany. Participants were recruited using purposive stakeholder sampling. Potential participants were identified through existing professional contacts and web-based searches and were subsequently approached by email. The web-based interviews were conducted via Microsoft Teams between September and November 2023. The transcripts were analyzed using qualitative content analysis based on the method described by Kuckartz, combining deductive and inductive category development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 13 interviews with 14 participants were conducted, comprising 5 health care provider representatives, 4 statutory health insurance representatives, 4 DiGA developer representatives, and 1 patient representative. The findings were grouped into 3 main themes: perceived information status, improvement of the information status, and information suppliers. Representatives of health care providers described a general awareness of DiGA but said they lacked more detailed knowledge required to assess and compare individual applications. They also perceived information gaps among patients. Participants distinguished between general information on aspects such as regulatory requirements and organizational processes and more detailed product-specific information. Different potential information suppliers were associated with different opportunities and problems, particularly regarding expertise, objectivity, available resources, and the ability to provide product-specific information.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings indicate that information-related challenges in the implementation of DiGA extend beyond general awareness. Health care providers may require accessible information with different levels of detail, while the source of information also appears relevant. Addressing these different information needs may support the integration of DiGA into outpatient mental health care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>International Registered Report Identifier (IRRID)</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>RR2-10.2196/56205</jats:p>
