AI and Machine Learning in Broadcast Media
45211ebcedbc6bad1d33a282df18d35a0dac1227.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines the digital transformation of television broadcasting through personalized broadcasting and algorithmic recommender systems. It aims to explain how television has evolved from a linear medium into a data driven, platform centered, and algorithmically organized environment. The study discusses the conceptual foundations of personalized broadcasting and the main types of recommender systems, including content based, collaborative, and hybrid models. The findings show that these systems are not merely technical tools for content discovery, but socio technical mechanisms that shape audience experience, engagement, content visibility, and cultural circulation. The Netflix case further demonstrates that algorithmic personalization has become a strategic force that restructures media economies, influences user preferences, and redefines contemporary broadcasting practices.</jats:p>

title: Watching What You Want
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Machine Learning in Broadcast Media
d1ff86b30e4ee238eb295d1fbf660002d7278fc2.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how algorithmic recommendation systems have become central to television broadcasting. Drawing on critical media theory, platform studies, and research, it argues artificial intelligence and machine learning reshaped relationships between broadcasters and audiences by shifting curation from human programmers to automated systems. It situates collaborative filtering, content-based filtering, and deep learning within debates on filter bubbles, cultural fragmentation, editorial responsibility, and the political economy of digital media. Treating recommendation as a categorical transformation, it addresses ethics, including transparency, bias, and viewer autonomy, reviews regulatory and self-governance frameworks, and outlines future trends such as emotion-aware AI and cross-platform personalization.</jats:p>

title: AI, Television News, and the Future of Democratic Gatekeeping
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Machine Learning in Broadcast Media
3ee3b8c7e6d4280704c4999714e0509349e034cd.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is increasingly shaping television news production by influencing how stories are selected, prioritized, and targeted to audiences. While AI offers efficiency and data-driven decision-making, it also raises concerns about democratic gatekeeping in broadcast journalism by challenging traditional ideas of editorial judgment, accountability, transparency, and pluralism. This chapter examines how AI reshapes gatekeeping in television news by shifting decisions from human editors to hybrid human-AI systems. Drawing on gatekeeping theory and journalism studies, it explores issues such as algorithmic opacity, automation bias, and reduced diversity in news coverage. The chapter argues that without proper governance, AI-assisted gatekeeping may weaken the democratic role of television news. To address these concerns, it proposes a framework for democratic gatekeeping in AI-assisted television news based on transparency, human oversight, editorial responsibility, and pluralism, offering guidance for integrating AI into news workflows.</jats:p>

title: The Transformation of News Discourse in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Machine Learning in Broadcast Media
8e94f02ed0fdcf254c98a1451e802610a07e5039.abstract: <jats:p>In the digital media ecosystem, AI-based text generation systems, particularly large language models, have become increasingly influential in news production processes. These systems are viewed not only as technical tools but also as new mechanisms of discourse production that reshape how news content is created. This development has made the comparative examination of human-produced and AI-generated news texts increasingly important. In this context, the study comparatively analyzes news texts selected from international news organizations such as Al Jazeera and Reuters alongside texts generated by ChatGPT. The research focuses on military interventions and violent incidents in Palestine. Using document analysis as a qualitative research method, the study evaluates the texts through Teun A. van Dijk's Critical Discourse Analysis approach and identifies major differences between human-produced and AI-generated news texts in terms of discourse structure, framing strategies, linguistic choices, and meaning production practices.</jats:p>

title: Opening Doors
container-title: Innovative Strategies for Well-Being and Motivation in Education
5757047efd1b486d86fd71fc4cf1233deb96ae21.abstract: <jats:p>Secondary education is often exclusionary, with teachers sometimes acting as barriers to inclusive practices. Educators need to embrace differences and ensure all students' rights are respected. A challenge in inclusive pedagogy is that secondary teachers, though experts in their subjects, often lack training in inclusive education. This chapter presents strategies for fostering inclusive classrooms, moving away from a medical model of support and instead promoting a more holistic and inclusive teaching approach. Teachers must consider the emotional dimensions of learning, creating supportive environments that avoid exclusionary adjustments. Inclusive assessment methods should also be implemented. By adopting these approaches, teachers can open doors to inclusive learning spaces, promoting social justice and equity. This chapter benefits both student teachers and practicing teachers, inspiring them to engage others in inclusive pedagogy, improve practices, and foster changes in institutional cultures, policies, and practices, creating a more inclusive environment for all students.</jats:p>

title: Advances in Machine Learning Paradigms for Reliable Swimming Pool Drowning Detection: Systematic Review of Methods and Implementations
container-title: JMIR Rehabilitation and Assistive Technologies
500b08b86cf4f906d0e8d252807f895639c6c37f.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drowning is a leading cause of unintentional injury-related mortality worldwide, particularly in swimming pool environments, where rapid detection is critical to prevent fatalities. Traditional monitoring approaches rely on lifeguards and rule-based systems, which are often limited by human error, delayed response, and environmental challenges such as occlusion, glare, and multiple swimmers. Machine learning (ML) and computer vision methods have emerged as promising alternatives for automated drowning detection; however, their methodological rigor, real-world applicability, and reliability remain unclear.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to systematically review advancements in ML-based drowning detection systems over the past 15 years. The review focused on detection methods, sensing modalities, evaluation metrics, and validation practices. It also examined how studies addressed real-world challenges such as occlusion, lighting variability, and multiswimmer environments, and identified key gaps related to generalizability, reliability, and privacy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic literature review was conducted using major electronic databases, including IEEE Xplore, Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, ACM Digital Library, and Google Scholar. A total of 4927 records were initially identified and screened by 2 independent reviewers using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. A final set of 30 studies was included for data extraction and synthesis. The methodological quality and risk of bias were assessed using the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST), while reporting transparency was evaluated using the TRIPOD (Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis) guidelines. Data analysis was conducted in R.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings indicate that drowning detection research is dominated by supervised, vision-based approaches (23/30, 76.7%), with convolutional neural networks (5/30, 16.7%) and You Only Look Once–based architectures (7/30, 23.3%) being the most commonly used methods. While reported performance is generally high, with mean accuracy exceeding 90.9%, evaluation practices are heavily centered on accuracy, with limited reporting of precision, recall, false alarm rate, and latency. One of 30 (3.3%) studies reported validation under real-world operational conditions, with an additional 5 (16.7%) studies using real-world data without formal real-world validation, and no studies conducted cross-dataset evaluation. In addition, critical real-world challenges such as occlusion, glare, and crowding were rarely addressed (<10% of studies), and all studies relied on private datasets. The PROBAST assessment further indicated a high risk of bias in 96.7% (29/30) of studies, primarily due to limited validation and nonrepresentative data sources.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>ML-based drowning detection systems have demonstrated substantial progress in algorithm development, particularly in vision-based models. However, this progress is not matched by equivalent advances in validation, robustness, and real-world applicability. The field is characterized by a significant gap between experimental performance and deployment readiness. Future research should prioritize standardized evaluation frameworks, external validation, comprehensive performance reporting, and the integration of multimodal and privacy-preserving approaches to enable reliable real-world implementation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: AI and Robotic Companions for Human Socialization

title: “Friendship” and “Love” With Companion Robots
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Robotic Companions for Human Socialization
022fceef735cce777f0d8dacf51096f466dfc905.abstract: <jats:p>The emergence of companion robots introduces profound questions about the nature of human relationships, specifically regarding friendship and love. Unlike conventional machines, these robots are designed to provide emotional support, social interaction, and even intimacy, blurring the boundaries between human and artificial companionship. This paper explores the psychological, ethical, and societal implications of forming such bonds. It investigates the drivers behind these attachments including loneliness, accessibility, and advances in AI realism and examines whether these relationships can be considered authentic. The study also assesses potential benefits, such as improved mental well-being, alongside challenges like dependency, ethical concerns, and broader societal acceptance. By analyzing theoretical frameworks, real-world applications, and future trajectories, this work offers a holistic understanding of how companion robots are reshaping fundamental human experiences like friendship and love in contemporary life.</jats:p>

title: Human Socialization (and Dis-Socialization) by AI and Robotic Companions in Educational Ecosystems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Robotic Companions for Human Socialization
21e354c94bb2573462d54359bd698db08de31a01.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter interrogates how AI chatbots, social robots, and ambient agents function as companion technologies that reconfigure human socialization and dis-socialization in educational ecosystems. Drawing on socialization theory, ecological systems, sociocultural mediation, sociomaterial assemblages, and posthuman subjectivity, it constructs a multi-level lens spanning micro interactional dynamics, meso institutional architectures, and macro political economies. The chapter develops typologies of companion configurations, maps learner needs to companion affordances, and analyses interactional quality through constructs such as social presence, parasociality, and epistemic justice. It then articulates normative, rights-based, and governance frameworks that distribute responsibilities across learners, educators, institutions, vendors, regulators, and civil society. The chapter positions humane companionable education as an agenda that seeks to harness machine companionship for inclusion and flourishing while resisting surveillance, stratification, and civic erosion.</jats:p>

title: Aesthetics of Robotic Digital Pets
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Robotic Companions for Human Socialization
7e635f747fbbe5476f902f978891bbe7c498f00f.abstract: <jats:p>Robots designed to replace pets are being developed to meet the emotional, social and cognitive needs of different age groups, from children to seniors. This chapter analyzes the factors that influence people's perception of robotic pets as companionable and socially present, focusing on shape aesthetics and motion quality, sound quality and textural effects and behavioral patterns. By examining the history of how humans have created and used artificial beings, it also becomes possible to understand how aesthetics has been viewed in the past and how it continues to shape expectations for the future. User expectations regarding the design of artificial pets, as well as the personalization of these products, are shown to influence acceptance and engagement. Understanding the role of aesthetics in the development of artificial pets therefore supports the creation of ethical and meaningful companions within contemporary and global society.</jats:p>

title: Emotional and Social Intelligence in AI Systems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Robotic Companions for Human Socialization
6a2e01dfa5708795013bf97dce0351890b7ec891.abstract: <jats:p>As artificial intelligence increasingly engages emotional and social dimensions of human life, its ability to recognize and respond to emotion raises important ethical and philosophical concerns. This chapter examines the development of emotional and social intelligence in AI, highlighting the shift from rational computation toward affective interaction. Drawing on cognitive psychology, affective computing, and moral philosophy, it explores whether machine empathy reflects genuine understanding or performative simulation. The discussion addresses risks such as emotional surveillance, manipulation, dependency, and cultural misrecognition, while acknowledging benefits of emotionally responsive AI in education, healthcare, and assistive contexts. To address ethical gaps, the chapter proposes a Computational Compassion Framework (CCF) integrating moral intentionality, transparency, human oversight, and contextual sensitivity into AI design. It argues that the future of emotional AI lies not in humanizing machines, but in embedding ethical responsibility within technological systems.</jats:p>

title: Iron Man or Tin Man?
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Robotic Companions for Human Socialization
739e5ce062b70ab12c4e4d9faa2f7e77bf9b8104.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence and robotics are no longer distant technologies but intimate infrastructures of everyday life, shaping how humans think, decide, feel, and relate to time, data, and one another.Drawing on cultural allegories (the Tin Man as the loss of emotional agency, Iron Man as the promise and peril of augmentation, In Time as a warning about the commodification of time, and the contemporary data economy where habit itself becomes a product) this chapter argues that the central challenge of AI is not technological capability, but human capacity. Through interdisciplinary perspectives from communication studies, psychology, and critical AI ethics, the analysis reveals how persuasion, efficiency, and optimization quietly reshape human behavior without overt coercion. Rather than asking whether machines can become more human, this chapter reframes the question: can humans remain reflective, empathetic, and morally responsible in systems designed for speed and prediction?</jats:p>

title: The Human Side of Robotic Warehousing
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Robotic Companions for Human Socialization
49ef72dbd7010ac0048e4e4ae894fc8d134c1a59.abstract: <jats:p>The chapter explores the perceptions of employees working in Amazon's Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS). We used a netnographic approach to uncover employees' perceptions related to the use of this technology, as well as the social and ethical considerations related to the topic. The results of the study show several advantages perceived by the employees in terms of flexibility, improved picking rates, and ergonomics at work. Nevertheless, numerous risks and challenges emerged from the qualitative analysis conducted specifically in relation to job security and human-machine interaction. The results and analyses offer us several perspectives regarding the automation and robotization of workspaces in relation to employees' perceptions and social considerations.</jats:p>

title: Integrating Emotion, Social Intelligence, and Culture in Robotic Companions
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Robotic Companions for Human Socialization
11b5a43f16d9978c902b26af103395a866acf26f.abstract: <jats:p>The chapter discusses how emotional, social and cultural intelligence can be integrated into the design of robotic companions and their importance in promoting authentic, empathetic and adaptive human-machine relationships. It explores theoretical assumptions, technology methods, and examples of the application of emotional recognition, social adaptability, and cultural sensitivity. The most notable challenges mentioned in the discussion include ethical dilemmas, trust, and cross-cultural differences, as well as determine the way forward as influenced by affective computing, cultural AI, and large language models. Finally, the chapter encourages an integrated system that incorporates human compassion and machine predictability to increase emotional resonance, inclusivity, and universal acceptance in human socialization with AI.</jats:p>

title: Ethical Dimensions of Companion Bots, Intelligent Devices, and Artificial Intelligence
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI and Robotic Companions for Human Socialization
3244f1bc2f7abb55a5b6321434f09e48bbe95961.abstract: <jats:p>Companion bots and emotionally responsive AI systems integrate deeply into daily life, managing social interactions, emotional support, learning, and care. Unlike standard computational tools, they maintain ongoing relationships and mimic empathy, transforming perceptions of companionship, autonomy, and moral responsibility. They deliver key benefits like alleviating loneliness, advancing healthcare, and customizing education, but raise ethical issues around authenticity, dependency, privacy, manipulation, and accountability. This chapter explores these ethics through philosophy, human-computer interaction (HCI), psychology, and policy lenses. It contends that evaluations must go beyond utility to examine effects on human dignity, moral agency, and social values. Principles for ethical design, governance, and deployment follow, emphasizing human well-being amid AI companionship's moral stakes .</jats:p>

title: AI-Enabled Quality Assurance in Higher Education
container-title: Harnessing Digital Platforms for Quality Assurance and Monitoring in Higher Education
fb5843c135ec13caf51a5f619643fd47db8d0fec.abstract: <jats:p>In today's dynamic landscape of higher education, institutions must prove to society the societal benefits of their teaching, learning, and research. Many organizations are embracing AI-enabled quality assurance (QA) to foster a mindset of constant growth and outstanding performance inside their institutions. This approach aims to enhance education, cater to the requirements of students and communities, and ultimately help them stay competitive. The complex quality assurance system is open to multiple interpretations and potential improvements due to the interconnected nature of technology in higher education. Excellence requires continuous institutional growth. It is common for stakeholders to see quality assurance as too bureaucratic. To prioritize institutional change and ongoing improvement, modern QA frameworks should use organic and dynamic operating methods.</jats:p>

title: AI-Enabled Digital Platforms for Learning-Centred Quality Assurance in Higher Education
container-title: Harnessing Digital Platforms for Quality Assurance and Monitoring in Higher Education
2e6b9dfed2d61a7b891e8850e05ec19839ab8002.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter theorises AI-enabled digital platforms as socio-technical quality infrastructures that orchestrate learning, accountability, and equity in higher education. It fuses constructs from quality theory, learning sciences, organisational studies, and critical datafication to recast quality as holistic capability formation rather than performance compliance. The chapter outlines competing quality lenses, sketches platform typologies and algorithmic logics, and shows how governance architectures and stakeholder attitudes co-produce datafied regimes of merit and risk. It then advances design principles for learning-centred, justice-responsive AI ecosystems that foreground equity-sensitive analytics, participatory governance, and reflexive professional judgment. The chapter contends that AI must be treated as pedagogical and civic infrastructure, with human actors retaining epistemic primacy in steering quality work toward rigorous, inclusive higher education.</jats:p>

title: Quality by Design
container-title: Harnessing Digital Platforms for Quality Assurance and Monitoring in Higher Education
99a02b8d40ae031ce9afe816538422b86464b6b0.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter focuses on how AI and digitalisation are affecting assurance and improvement activities within Higher Education and how the concept of Quality by Design (QbD) can help integrate AI technologies, automated governance, and advanced analytics into institutions' processes and workflows. It contends that the digital university must undergo both a technological and cultural transformation, moving away from a compliance-driven model of quality evaluation and moving toward a model focused on intelligent, seamless assurance. The AI-Enabled Quality Ecosystem Model is designed and offered as a means of accomplishing this aim as it integrates the appropriate data infrastructure, AI-augmented human supervision, and mechanisms for continuous improvement. The chapter draws on ethical, digital, participatory governance frameworks and on the role of AI as a complement to human judgment to advance the argument that AI enhances institutional quality and integrates the key institutional elements of leadership, inclusiveness, and collaborative, adaptive learning.</jats:p>

title: Digital Assurance Ecosystems
container-title: Harnessing Digital Platforms for Quality Assurance and Monitoring in Higher Education
ea5f0137283fa7bf65376788b0b0b8d6da893fc2.abstract: <jats:p>The high pace of digitalization of higher education has changed the quality assurance to a standard data-based institutional process instead of a long-term and compliance-based process. The chapter focuses on the digital assurance systems based on artificial intelligence, analytics, and integrated platforms as the means to facilitate the continuous quality improvement within the higher education sector. It discusses the role of AI-driven dashboards, learning analytics, predicting models, and feedback loops in the process of coming up with good decisions in the areas of teaching, learning, governance, and accreditation. Quality by Design is highlighted in which quality is actively incorporated by tracking on time, detection of risks at early stages, and remedies. It discusses the stakeholder involvement, institutional benefits, ethical issues, and case studies of AI-based quality monitoring and student success management in the near past, and hence digital platforms would be the solution providers of quality assurance systems in the future.</jats:p>

title: Next-Generation AI Architectures for ECG Arrhythmia Detection
container-title: Harnessing Digital Platforms for Quality Assurance and Monitoring in Higher Education
c06f20ff59b2a1a32fbb1574e77b84f20954089e.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) has revolutionized cardiac healthcare by enabling rapid, accurate, and automated arrhythmia detection using electrocardiogram (ECG) signals. This chapter explores advanced AI-driven arrhythmia classification techniques that integrate deep learning (DL), preprocessing, and explainable model interpretation. Emphasis is placed on convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent networks, and hybrid architectures capable of learning morphological and temporal ECG features. The proposed framework covers data acquisition, filtering, segmentation, feature extraction, model training, and validation. Ethical challenges, interpretability, and clinical deployment frameworks are discussed. By bridging computational intelligence with clinical expertise, AI systems have demonstrated near-cardiologist-level diagnostic accuracy, making them vital in next-generation cardiac care.</jats:p>

title: Governing AI-Driven Universities in Cambodia
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Responsible AI Governance in Higher Education Management for Creative Public Sector Innovation
1c876c30e971c0906955347a760678450910f5f3.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter focuses on Cambodian higher education institutions to explain the pillars of Trust-Centred AI Governance for responsible AI and how AI can support services and functions currently burdened by demand and under-resourced in the Cambodian higher education sector, which is rapidly growing and flexible in enrollment. Without governance, the Threats to Educational Equity caused by algorithmic bias, Data Breaches, Digital Exclusion, and Breaches of Trust will dangerously flourish. This chapter presents a Trust-Centred AI Governance Framework built around seven principles: ethical leadership, transparency, and data privacy. It is supported by core ideas such as algorithmic accountability, inclusive access, human oversight, and public-sector innovation, and guides partner institutions on fostering ethical innovation ecosystems. It presents, through analyses and the implementation of proposed strategies, case studies, and policy frameworks, a model that balances technological efficiency with human-centred principles, empowering global competence and leadership in the south.</jats:p>

title: From Knowledge Transmission to Democratic Transformation
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Responsible AI Governance in Higher Education Management for Creative Public Sector Innovation
14a3b3c15207f76fff58adce5bfb961062efee1c.abstract: <jats:p>The rapidly evolving context of digitalisation, democratic fragility, and educational inequality has highlighted the need to change conventional teacher education practices that focus on transmission of knowledge and skills. Although teacher identity is a key concept in contemporary educational reform discussions that focus on inclusion, digital innovation and democratic citizenship, the concept is still fractured in policy, curriculum and governance. This research faces this challenge and critically explores the changing landscape of teacher education in terms of reconstructing the teacher identity as a multidimensional and transformative professional construct to support democratic transformation. In this study, the doctrinal and analytical research methodology is used, which systematically reviews and synthesizes the current educational theories, international policy instruments, governance models, and scholarly debates on inclusive education, digital pedagogy, democratic citizenship and professional development.</jats:p>

title: Integrating Internet of Things and Artificial Intelligence for the Development of Sustainable, Intelligent, and Efficient Physical–Digital Learning
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Responsible AI Governance in Higher Education Management for Creative Public Sector Innovation
26c5b42ef86ad41f27f523603793d198bf2cb6ce.abstract: <jats:p>The application of the Internet of Things (IoT) and artificial intelligence (AI) is driving towards a new era of intelligent, adaptive, and sustainable smart campus ecosystems in higher education institutions. This research aims to examine the potential of IoT-powered physical–digital learning environments and AI systems in the fields of personalized learning, intelligent campus management, predictive analytics, and sustainable resource optimization. The study also explores the opportunities and challenges associated with the application of AIoT technologies for enhancing operational efficiency, learner participation, and environmental sustainability, as well as those of cybersecurity, data privacy, interoperability, and ethical governance. The results emphasize the need to implement human-centered, secure, and sustainable technological frameworks to empower future-ready universities and foster inclusive, efficient, and resilient educational ecosystems.</jats:p>

title: Shadows in the Lecture Hall
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Responsible AI Governance in Higher Education Management for Creative Public Sector Innovation
66561a07cf91a6cd744b035edb6f73babf583b22.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence has rapidly transitioned from a supporting tool to a central force in academic research, teaching, and institutional governance. Its capacity to process vast datasets, generate scholarly content, and enhance decision-making offers unprecedented opportunities for innovation. Universities now employ AI to streamline administrative operations, improve academic workflows, and enable personalized learning experiences. In research, advanced algorithms and large language models facilitate literature synthesis, data interpretation, and even hypothesis generation, thereby accelerating scholarly output. This chapter advances the argument that the future of academia depends on striking a careful equilibrium between embracing AI's transformative power and preserving the foundational principles of truth, fairness, and accountability. It proposes a framework for “Responsible AI in Academia” grounded in transparency, inclusivity, and continuous ethical evaluation.</jats:p>

title: Responsible AI Governance Frameworks for Intelligent Higher Education Management and Creative Public Sector Innovation
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Responsible AI Governance in Higher Education Management for Creative Public Sector Innovation
99d99fa7c05bdbaa0acde5b32467be06597babd5.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines responsible AI governance for intelligent higher education management and public-sector innovation. It highlights the importance of ethical AI, governance transparency, institutional readiness, stakeholder AI literacy, and sustainability-oriented governance in AI-enabled ecosystems. The study proposes a conceptual governance framework integrating ethical oversight, intelligent decision-support systems, governance interoperability, and adaptive governance mechanisms. The chapter also discusses governance challenges associated with generative AI, including algorithmic bias, explainability, misinformation, and compliance risks. The findings emphasize that responsible AI governance supports sustainable institutional transformation, public trust, accountability, and human-centred innovation across higher education and public-sector environments.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive Adaptation and Leadership in AI-Augmented Higher Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Responsible AI Governance in Higher Education Management for Creative Public Sector Innovation
a5612c037c0c5391ee895bba1a4fc5ae65f530b1.abstract: <jats:p>Generative AI poses pressing governance challenges regarding the future of human-AI interaction and how it enhances or diminishes the cognitive capabilities, professional role, and leadership of academic professionals. Three cognitive adaptation patterns emerge from the analysis of the qualitative data (retrieved from the interviews) and the quantitative data (PLS-SEM survey): AI Augmentation, AI Dependency, and AI Co-construction. The positive relationship between adaptation outcomes and AI trust is supported by PLS-SEM, with the cognitive load change as a mediator and the organisational learning orientation as a moderator, the most significant institutional factor influencing adaptation outcomes. The chapter suggests embedding metacognition and AI literacy in workforce governance, institutional reflection in HR and L&D processes, and complementarity guardrails. For practical governance tools for adopting responsible AI in higher education, a validated diagnostic instrument and a Human-AI Capability Convergence Model are provided.</jats:p>

title: Transforming Academic Governance in the AI Era
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Responsible AI Governance in Higher Education Management for Creative Public Sector Innovation
e49d653e589a416eb7de0e2ea2a3cdd823c5f09a.abstract: <jats:p>Generative AI (GAI) has rapidly become an integral part of higher education, significantly reshaping the teaching, learning, assessment, and research experiences of institutions around the globe, thereby creating unprecedented moral, legal, and governance dilemmas. Academic honesty and honour codes, which typically aimed to combat cheating and plagiarism in human-powered settings, are no longer adequate to deal with the challenges of AI-enabled environments. The study critically reviews the current paradigm of academic governance in the context of the emergence of generative AI and addresses the interplay of institutional honour codes, ethical responsibility, accountability systems, and regulatory compliance in higher education institutions. The research is done by a doctrinal, interdisciplinary and policy-oriented approach, analysing new institutional polices on AI, international ethical guidelines, university governance frameworks, data protection laws, and current academic discussions on responsible use of AI in academia.</jats:p>

title: AI Governance in Academia
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Responsible AI Governance in Higher Education Management for Creative Public Sector Innovation
82978771df486b7a50f02bfe7e3688784c7559c6.abstract: <jats:p>The ability to add artificial intelligence (AI) to higher education institutions in the entire public sector has opened up never-before opportunities to personalised learning, administrative efficiency and evidence-based policy-making. However, such opportunities are kept in company with serious governance issues that relate to transparency, fairness and institutional accountability. The chapter examines ethical strains that are inherent in utilisation of AI systems in the evaluation of students, collection of admission details, and distribution of resources, and argues that without the presence of robust governance architectures these systems have a risk of entrenching the existing inequalities and also eroding democratic educational values. The chapter is based on a multi-layered governance model which incorporates regulatory compliance, stakeholder participation, algorithmic auditing, and continuous ethics oversight.</jats:p>

title: Improving CommonGround, an Online Peer Support Intervention for People Living With Long-Term Physical Health Conditions and Subthreshold Depression: Theory of Change–Informed Qualitative Study
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
590525e4319b41b895c89aaf36dad4b53e1e076e.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>People living with long-term physical health conditions who are also experiencing subthreshold depression are at risk of developing major depression. In partnership with lived experience experts, clinicians, and software developers, we co-designed CommonGround, an online peer support and psychoeducation platform. CommonGround’s Theory of Change (ToC) was also conceptualized to outline the intermediate outcomes (and associated indicators of whether such outcomes are achieved) needed to improve the mental health of the target population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This qualitative study, informed by the ToC, aimed to examine the acceptability, usability, and intervention mechanisms of CommonGround and ultimately refine the ToC and corresponding intervention design ahead of definitive evaluation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A nested qualitative study was conducted within a remote, 12-week feasibility randomized controlled trial comparing CommonGround (intervention group) to signposting to National Health Service (NHS) web pages (control group). Thirty-nine participants were purposively sampled and interviewed within 6 weeks postintervention about their experiences of CommonGround and trial participation. The interview schedule and thematic framework analysis were rooted in a pretrial ToC while being responsive to emergent themes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Evaluating the assumptions and intermediate outcomes (via their indicators) refined our understanding of how CommonGround may support mental well-being. Overall, participants viewed CommonGround as an appropriate, safe space to access self-management information and support from others with a unique shared understanding of chronic illness. However, many participants felt more time was needed for genuine social relations to form and community culture to evolve. Anonymity helped foster a sense of safety but, for some participants, limited the formation of genuine connections. Other factors contributing to low engagement included personal circumstances (eg, limited time). Key suggestions for future development included creating a mobile app that would be easier and more intuitive to access and navigate.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>CommonGround was considered an acceptable and appropriate space to access peer support, with the potential to positively impact psychological well-being by fostering shared understanding, support, and knowledge exchange. Beyond informing the future evaluation of CommonGround in a definitive trial, the refined ToC identifies the key preconditions, intermediate outcomes, and associated indicators, and assumptions that may underpin the acceptability and usability of digital peer support interventions in achieving their intended outcomes. We also demonstrate how evaluating and refining components of the ToC after the intervention had been implemented in the trial enabled a more nuanced understanding of how and why the intervention may work, for whom, under what circumstances, and informed changes to improve the co-designed intervention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy–Based Digital Interventions for Illicit Substance Use Disorders: Scoping Review of Intervention Design, Efficacy Indicators, and Methodological Gaps
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
9d1858cff34c91ccfc45c7d996e799804ca90d99.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Illicit substance use disorders (SUDs) are escalating globally; yet, social stigma and legal barriers restrict access to conventional treatment, and existing research remains skewed toward alcohol and nicotine. Digital interventions incorporating cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) offer a discreet, scalable alternative.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This scoping review maps how CBT-based digital interventions for illicit SUDs are designed and delivered across platforms, identifying their theoretical frameworks, functional components, outcome indicators, and reported methodological limitations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) scoping review methodology and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews). Six databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, APA PsycINFO, Web of Science Core Collection, Cochrane Library, and CINAHL) were searched from inception to June 28, 2026, without language, date, or study design limits, supplemented by backward and forward citation searching (July 3, 2026). Eligible studies were empirical primary studies quantitatively evaluating digital interventions incorporating CBT for illicit or nonprescribed substance use; alcohol- or nicotine-only populations were excluded. Three reviewers independently screened and charted all studies, with disagreements resolved by consensus or adjudication. Data were synthesized narratively, with tables, figures, and an evidence gap map.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fifty-six studies published between 2008 and 2026, drawn from 47 distinct participant samples, met the eligibility criteria. Most were conducted in North America (40/56, 71.4%) and used randomized controlled designs (39/56, 69.6%). Polysubstance-using populations were most frequently targeted (32/56, 57.1%), followed by cannabis (13/56, 23.2%), opioids (6/56, 10.7%), and stimulants (5/56, 8.9%). Interventions were delivered mainly via web (24/56, 42.9%) or app (24/56, 42.9%) platforms, and most (49/56, 87.5%) were grounded in traditional CBT, most often combined with contingency management (18/56, 32.1%) or motivational interviewing (17/56, 30.4%). Core functional components included therapeutic intervention (55/56, 98.2%), self-tracking and notification (25/56, 44.6%), reward (24/56, 42.9%), and support and feedback (21/56, 37.5%). Primary outcomes focused on substance use and abstinence (41/56, 73.2%), retention/feasibility (16/56, 28.6%), and mental health status or coping skills (14/56, 25%). Author-reported limitations were predominantly participant-level (52/56, 92.9%), measurement-level (43/56, 76.8%), study-level (34/56, 60.7%), and intervention-level (25/56, 44.6%) domains.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Unlike previous reviews confined to a single substance or delivery platform, this review is innovative in mapping CBT-based digital interventions across the full spectrum of illicit substances, including polysubstance use, and in linking their functional components to intended therapeutic mechanisms. It thereby contributes to the development of these technologies and, by synthesizing author-reported limitations, proposes methodological improvements for their future evaluation. At present, CBT-based digital interventions are best positioned as adjuncts that extend the reach and continuity of existing addiction care rather than as stand-alone substitutes for it; substance-specific customization, objective outcome measures, and modular trial designs are needed to establish them as scalable clinical tools.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Calibrating Self-weighted Shear Estimation via Field Distortion
container-title: Research in Astronomy and Astrophysics
89f0ec410e91a4bff2779ec1d28215febe582909.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Accurate cosmic shear measurement is the key to fully realize the scientific potential of large scale galaxy surveys. The Fourier_Quad (FQ) shear measurement method has been significantly developed to avoid biases caused by various factors, including the point-spread function (PSF), photon noise, pixelation effect, selection effects, etc. Shear statistics have also been optimized using the PDF-SYM method (symmetrization of the Probability Distribution Function of the shear estimators) to achieve the minimal statistical error, without introducing systematic error. Nevertheless, the iterative nature of the PDF-SYM method makes it computationally expensive for massive datasets. To improve computational efficiency, we introduce the self-weighted shear estimation (SWSE) method, which employs a specific self-weighting scheme to naturally suppress the shape noise as well as to balance the contributions from the bright and faint galaxies. Because SWSE is intrinsically biased, the primary focus of this work is to robustly evaluate whether the field-distortion test (FD test, a way to calibrate the shear bias on real data) can accurately recover and correct these inherent multiplicative and additive biases. Using both simulated and real survey data, we demonstrate that the FD test can successfully calibrate SWSE for galaxy–galaxy lensing measurements, while computational benchmarks show a reduction in shear-estimation time by factors of approximately 40–200 relative to PDF-SYM. After calibration, SWSE achieves statistical precision consistent with that of PDF-SYM within the uncertainties examined in this work. Our results demonstrate the potential of combining the FD test with SWSE as a computationally efficient framework for forthcoming large-scale weak-lensing surveys.</jats:p>
