title: AI Tools for Students
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Cases on Fostering Critical Thinking and Competence in AI-Based STEM Programs
89bedececedb8d701eafe8c286aa09d05c376fc6.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become the indispensable element of the modern educational process that offers groundbreaking instruments to make the process more efficient, creative, and productive in terms of learning, creation, and academic achievements. Thoughtfully tutoring systems and customized learning guides are just but few examples of AI applications that are changing how students learn, collaborate and develop the requisite critical skills. Adaptive learning, automated testing and content development have become more effective with the use of AI in education, and has provided learners with an opportunity to engage with the learning content more interactively and meaningfully. Also, AI-based applications can be used to enhance time management, research assistance, and language translation to make the educational process more universal and globalized. The chapter analyses various AI tools that have been student specific and explain their functionality, advantages and its prospects on the learning environments.</jats:p>

title: Unlocking Profits in Generative AI: The Impact of AI Adaptive Learning on Freemium Strategy
container-title: Information Systems Research
1e71b78eb99b705782120789109bb4b568ed47eb.abstract: <jats:p>Generative AI firms increasingly rely on freemium strategies, offering a basic service at no charge while charging for a more capable version. Unlike conventional digital products, generative AI systems can improve through user interactions, making free users a potential source of valuable learning data. Using an analytical model, this study shows that freemium is not always the most profitable strategy. Free access can expand the user base and accelerate AI adaptive learning, but it can also cannibalize paid demand and create substantial service costs. More effective adaptive learning does not necessarily make freemium more attractive; under some conditions, the firm earns more by offering only a paid version at a lower price. When freemium is used, a moderate capability gap between free and premium versions can be more profitable than making the free tier either too limited or too close to the premium product. Managers should evaluate learning benefits alongside service costs, market coverage, and premium cannibalization. Policymakers should also avoid assuming that free access automatically improves consumer welfare, because capability gains may allow firms to raise premium prices.</jats:p>

title: Attention, Obligation, and the Rootedness of Human Identity in the AI Renaissance
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Reconfiguring Human Identity and Social Contracts in the AI Renaissance
e4417ce1339c12cc05dc70011ea7ae674c983fe8.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how the AI renaissance is reconfiguring fundamental anthropological conditions of human existence and how Simone Weil's ethics of attention, obligation, and rootedness can provide a normative framework for understanding these transformations. Methodologically, the analysis combines conceptual reconstruction, philosophical-hermeneutic updating, and critically reflected conceptual engineering to translate Weil's categories into contemporary AI contexts. The analysis identifies three interconnected transformations: AI-mediated environments can reshape the conditions for sustained attention; distributed human-machine agency can create responsibility and obligation gaps; and digital infrastructures can weaken the conditions for social, economic, and political rootedness. The chapter develops a Weilian governance framework that deepens human-centered AI by identifying the anthropological conditions that underlie rights, human oversight, accountability, and participation.</jats:p>

title: Reconfiguring Identity, Ownership, and Legal Framework in the Digital World
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Reconfiguring Human Identity and Social Contracts in the AI Renaissance
f0a6336edb0b64a20e417a3a4a4f176bb513d8c1.abstract: <jats:p>Humankind's lived reality of an experience heavily mediated by Generative AI and the digital realm calls for a critical reconfiguration of existing social modes of being as well as legal contracts and regulations. The chapter attempts to address significant challenges presented by AI and AI-generated content specifically within literary creation in terms of copyright and ownership as well as legal systems pertaining to digital personhood and identity. A reworking of the traditional understanding of authorship and creativity also traces the inadequacy of existing global legal frameworks, largely anthropocentric in nature, grappling with the dilemma of attributing ownership and accountability for AI-generated creative content and prosecution of AI entities. The chapter also explores digital personhood with specific focus on the idea of digital necromancy and sophisticated AI crime as a threat to the world at large. The aim is to raise questions that could foster dialogue and initiate some form of policy change in the aforementioned realms.</jats:p>

title: Cholera_Microscope: An intelligent mapping and predictive analysis of cholera disease in Ogun State
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
0f9c1a0e50db115929253bec0c6b87c60771acc1.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cholera remains a primary epidemic-prone disease in Nigeria, with Ogun State identified as a high-burden region. National surveillance data from the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) reported 10 353 suspected cases and 244 associated fatalities between January 1 and September 14, 2025, representing a significant public health challenge. Some of the factors that mitigate against effective control of cholera in Nigeria are poor hygiene, lack of basic infrastructure, inadequate surveillance structure and ineffective preparedness plan. This research work presents Cholera Microscope, an intelligent geospatial surveillance system for visualising and predicting cholera outbreaks. Variogram, a geospatial mapping technique, was used to generate insights into cholera outbreak dynamics. A hybridised model, which combines Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), was developed for effective prediction of cholera outbreaks. The hybrid model was based on the strength of CNN in efficient extraction of salient features and the capability of LSTM in capturing long-term sequential dependencies for training and prediction. The implementation was done on a Flutter-based platform integrated with geocoding and polygon mapping. The pre-processed data were also visualised using heat circle mapping, spatial pictograms, colour gradient and variogram analysis to dynamically identify outbreak hotspots and spatial dependencies. Experimental results show that the hybrid CNN-LSTM model outperformed individual CNN, LSTM, and traditional machine-learning classifiers. The model obtained 94.7% accuracy in hotspot detection and outbreak trend prediction, demonstrating its high reliability. These findings show that the cholera microscope is a very reliable hotspot detection and outbreak trend prediction.</jats:p>

title: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, gut microbiome composition, impulsivity, and attention covary in a human cohort
container-title: Microbiology Spectrum
4b2ea61ea8ae67962d02b43bdd0ca11c398c565c.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title/>
                    <jats:p>
                      Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are pervasive environmental pollutants linked to adverse neurobehavioral outcomes, yet the biological pathways coupling exposure to behavior are poorly defined. The gut microbiome is both sensitive to PAH exposure and a modulator of central nervous system function, suggesting it may mediate how PAH exposure influences neurobehavior. We tested whether PAH exposure, gut microbiome composition, and neurobehavioral function covary in a statewide sample of 34 adults stratified into high-impulsivity/poor-attention (HH) and low-impulsivity/fast-attention (LL) groups. Participants wore silicone wristbands for 30 days to passively sample PAH exposure and provided a single fecal sample for 16S rRNA profiling at the end of the wear period. Higher PAH exposure was associated with HH group membership in a sex-dependent manner, with the largest elevations among HH males. At the community level, PAH exposure profiles correlated with microbiome dissimilarity, and HH membership was associated with increased alpha-diversity and altered community composition relative to LL members. At the taxon level, 22 genera were significantly associated with 14 PAH compounds (FDR < 0.1). No individual genera were significantly associated with neurobehavioral group after multiple testing correction. Nevertheless, cross-referencing PAH-responsive genera (FDR < 0.1) against those with nominal neurobehavioral associations (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                      < 0.05) identified two candidate genera
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">—Hydrogenoanaerobacterium</jats:italic>
                      and
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Methanobrevibacter</jats:italic>
                      —whose abundance covaries with both PAH exposure and neurobehavioral phenotype. Both have been independently linked to cognitive or neurological outcomes in prior work. These findings support a three-way relationship among environmental chemical exposure, gut microbiome composition, and neurobehavioral function, establishing an empirical foundation for testing microbiome-mediated links between PAH exposure and neurobehavioral outcomes.
                    </jats:p>
                    <jats:sec>
                      <jats:title>IMPORTANCE</jats:title>
                      <jats:p>Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) exposure is widespread and is associated with impulsivity and attention problems, but how exposure translates into neurobehavioral risk is unclear. The gut microbiome is a plausible intermediary: gut microbes biotransform environmental chemicals and produce metabolites that influence brain function. In a statewide adult cohort, higher PAH exposure associated with with greater impulsivity and poorer attention in a sex-dependent manner, and both PAH exposure and neurobehavioral phenotype were associated with distinct gut microbiome features at the community and taxon levels. We identify candidate genera at the intersection of PAH exposure and neurobehavioral group whose biology independently implicates them in cognitive and neurological function. Because their associations with neurobehavioral phenotype are nominal, we present these genera as hypothesis-generating candidates for future study. By showing that all three domains covary within a single cohort, this work moves beyond pairwise associations toward testable microbiome-targeted and exposure-reduction strategies for PAH-related neurobehavioral risk.</jats:p>
                    </jats:sec>
                  </jats:sec>

title: The Digital Twin Paradigm in Head and Neck Cancer: Clinical Opportunities and Challenges
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
54c677b31783774112add4167610545c88129e39.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) represents a significant public health challenge. Its treatment is characterized by high anatomical complexity and a critical need for functional preservation of speech, swallowing, and respiration. While multimodality care, including surgery, radiotherapy, and systemic therapy, has substantially improved patient survival, there are still high rates of life-altering toxicities and low response rates to immunotherapy. Current clinical decision-making largely relies on “digital snapshots”—static representations derived from population-based statistics and time point–specific imaging—which usually fail to account for the rapid anatomical and biological change during the course of treatment. Digital twins hold great promise in accelerating scientific breakthroughs and transforming oncology treatment and precision medicine through the creation of high-fidelity virtual patient representations that integrate real-time biological, anatomical, and clinical data. In this viewpoint, we propose 3 interconnected digital twins to establish a conceptual framework for the HNSCC digital twin. These digital twins include the anatomical twin, using virtual surgical planning and augmented reality for geometric precision; the dosimetric twin, using daily imaging and synthetic computed tomography generation for automated adaptive radiotherapy; and the biological twin, integrating deep phenotyping, radiomics, and mechanistic omics to simulate individualized therapeutic trajectories. Beyond acute care, we explore the clinical utility of digital twins in navigating the “de-escalation dilemma” for human papillomavirus–associated disease and improving survivorship through digital phenotyping. With the advent of longitudinal data from medical-grade Internet-of-Things sensors and circulating tumor DNA kinetics, digital twins can serve as active sentinels, detecting functional decline or subclinical events months before clinical manifestation. Furthermore, the implementation of synthetic control arms via virtual populations offers an avenue to accelerate clinical trials and address ethical issues in rare molecular subtypes. Despite this potential, substantial barriers to implementation remain, including profound anatomical instability during treatment, the “black box” nature of deep learning algorithms, and the challenges of multiscale data integration. We provide a technical roadmap for the development of “morphing” digital twins—dynamic systems capable of continuous geometric and biological auditing. By bridging the gap between the macroscopic world of radiation physics and the microscopic world of cellular evolution, digital twins may help shift the management of HNSCC from population-based statistical probability toward more individualized, biologically informed decision-making, with the goal of optimizing HNSCC management while preserving essential patient functions.</jats:p>

title: Adolescents’ Perspectives on Uptake, Engagement, and Implementation to Inform the Development of a Preventive Transdiagnostic Digital Mental Health Intervention: Qualitative Interview Study
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
035d301ed77fce4e74ca0175c7cadf9839d24f1a.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adolescence is a critical period for mental health prevention; yet, many young people face barriers to help-seeking, including stigma, limited mental health literacy, and restricted access to services. Preventive digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) offer a scalable, low-threshold approach to early support, but uptake and sustained engagement remain limited. Existing research has predominantly relied on quantitative methods and has only partly captured adolescents’ perspectives. Qualitative research is therefore needed to inform the design and implementation of preventive DMHIs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to explore adolescents’ perspectives on factors influencing the anticipated uptake, expected engagement, and implementation of preventive transdiagnostic DMHIs across person, intervention, and system levels.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This qualitative study was conducted in Switzerland using a single-interview design in the predesign phase of the development of a transdiagnostic preventive DMHI. Adolescents aged 12‐21 years were recruited through voluntary response sampling via social media and the project website. Semistructured interviews explored experiences with online help-seeking, factors influencing DMHI anticipated uptake and expected engagement, and recommendations for implementation. Interviews were conducted in person or via video call between January and June 2022, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using a hybrid deductive-inductive qualitative content analysis. Intercoder agreement was assessed using Cohen κ (κ=0.72).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 48 adolescents (mean age 16.52, SD 2.67 years; 32/48, 72.9% female) participated. In total, 8 main topics and multiple subtopics were identified across person, intervention, system, and cross levels. Person-level factors highlighted the importance of mental health literacy, preuptake communication, and relevance of social networks. Intervention-level factors emphasized usability, personalization, and privacy, while system-level findings reflected expectations for adaptive, integrated, and low-threshold mental health services. Trust and support emerged as cross-level factors for engagement. In addition, participants described several discrepancies between desired intervention characteristics and practical implementation, particularly regarding personalization, anonymity, peer exchange, and human support.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adolescents’ perspectives highlight that successful implementation of preventive DMHIs requires attention beyond intervention design to preuptake communication strategies, mental health literacy promotion, and integration within adaptive care systems. The tension between adolescents’ desire for immediate human-delivered support and the self-guided nature of preventive DMHIs underscores the need for clear clinical boundaries and explicit escalation pathways.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Tenecteplase Before Thrombectomy at 4.5 to 24 Hours for Basilar Artery Occlusion
container-title: JAMA
ef60472e8a004149c416d5f14b5651c60704d5a8.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Importance</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Whether intravenous tenecteplase before endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) improves outcomes in patients with basilar artery occlusion presenting 4.5 to 24 hours after stroke onset remains uncertain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To evaluate the efficacy and safety of intravenous tenecteplase before EVT vs EVT alone in patients with moderate to severe basilar artery occlusion admitted within 4.5 to 24 hours from stroke onset.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design, Setting, and Participants</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This multicenter, open-label, blinded end point, randomized clinical trial was conducted at 40 stroke centers in China. Between March 16, 2023, and February 4, 2025, a total of 330 patients with moderate to severe basilar artery occlusion (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score ≥10) presenting within 4.5 to 24 hours from stroke onset to EVT-capable centers were enrolled. Final follow-up was completed on May 4, 2025.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Interventions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Patients were randomized 1:1 via a centralized web server using a minimization method to receive either intravenous tenecteplase (bolus injection, 0.25 mg/kg; maximum, 25 mg) followed by EVT (n = 166) or EVT alone (n = 164).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Main Outcomes and Measures</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The primary outcome was functional independence (modified Rankin Scale score, 0-2) at 90 days. Safety outcomes included symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage and 90-day mortality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 332 patients randomized, 2 withdrew consent. Of the remaining 330 patients (mean [SD] age, 66 [11] years; 241 males [73%]; 89 females [27%]), 329 completed 90-day follow-up. Of whom, 50 of 165 (30%) in the tenecteplase plus EVT group and 50 of 164 (30%) in the EVT alone group achieved functional independence (adjusted rate ratio, 0.92 [95% CI, 0.67 to 1.25]; risk difference, −0.18% [95% CI, −10.13% to 9.76%]). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 8 patients (5%) in the tenecteplase plus EVT group and 6 (4%) in the EVT alone group. Mortality at 90 days was similar between the groups (66 [40%] vs 70 [43%], respectively).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions and Relevance</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among patients with moderate to severe basilar artery occlusion admitted directly to EVT-capable centers who presented 4.5 to 24 hours after stroke onset, the addition of intravenous tenecteplase before EVT did not result in improved functional outcomes compared with EVT alone.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial Registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>

                    </jats:p>

title: Introduction
container-title: Environmental Justice in Digital Worlds
f2f52c38a7a73aa0cb5a9acdafbd209f152f4fe6.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter begins with examples of Mixed Reality technology currently in existence or soon likely to be. These examples motivate a description of what the book is and an argument for why it’s important: that society is on the cusp of widespread technological change which has radical implications for the world, and that it is important to think through what these technologies mean for our environment. It discusses the ways different audiences may engage with this book, and how by using these philosophical tools to look at emerging technologies, this book engages in a process of “technophilosophy” that will examine both the philosophical frameworks and the technologies. The introduction ends with a brief summary of each chapter.</jats:p>

title: Environmental Justice in More-Than-Physical Environments
container-title: Environmental Justice in Digital Worlds
30c810e4e34bf3d572d92380ff471cc35f8b53cf.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter introduces environmental philosophy, and particularly environmental justice, that will be an underlying framework for the book’s approach. The chapter argues that “the environment” ought to include the technologically shaped environments people actually live in, rather than only referring to wild places undamaged by humans. It further argues that environmental philosophy ought to also incorporate virtual entities in material surroundings or even wholly virtual environments. The chapter then introduces a framework for environmental justice, which looks at distributional, participatory, and recognition justice as well as self-determination for individuals and communities when thinking about environmental goods as well as bads, and opportunities as well as risks.</jats:p>

title: Mixing Reality
container-title: Environmental Justice in Digital Worlds
dbb8a9dd5cbe4b161c1a8a14adcfb4674776f777.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter looks in depth at what “Mixed Reality technology” is and which digital technologies will count for the book’s purposes. It defends the critical approach the book takes to looking at technology and the optimism that the roles it plays in society can be democratically shaped, as well as the more pessimistic treadmill path that these developing technologies will take absent just participation in their design and implementation by stakeholders. The chapter also includes a philosophical discussion of the ontological status of the virtual entities that are being mixed into our material world, as well as the partial and fully virtual places we are creating.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence in Mixed Reality
container-title: Environmental Justice in Digital Worlds
e04323502a4b153b2e9de555a487f931fc1a6812.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter looks at the ways in which Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Mixed Reality are inextricably linked. To do that, this chapter first looks at what is meant by current “Artificial Intelligence” and argues that in some ways it is best thought of as being neither artificial nor intelligent. The chapter then discusses the various ways in which Mixed Reality is the “eyes and ears” of AI, including using data collected via MR to train AI, using AI to create or improve MR elements in real time, and using AI to process MR data for users to allow a more minimally virtual mixed reality. Ultimately, the chapter argues that AI and MR work in concert to alter our experience of the environment and people’s roles in it.</jats:p>

title: Augmenting and Fragmenting the Public Square
container-title: Environmental Justice in Digital Worlds
441df7068f7f5364f436052650c0eb1bec9ace85.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter looks at the effects of Mixed Reality technologies on privacy. When people talk about privacy and digital technology, they typically mean personal information being viewable by others. While this is a serious concern which discussed more in Chapters 4 and 5, here privacy is being used in a second sense: the private worlds that people inhabit which are only partially shareable or connected with one another. This chapter argues that Mixed Reality technologies are likely to increase privacy in this sense, and in so doing degrade or supplant our shared, contested, public spaces that enable and require the messy conversations that are part of democratic deliberation. This is partly a process of privatization of public resources, a third sense of privacy.</jats:p>

title: Thinking Through Mixed Realities
container-title: Environmental Justice in Digital Worlds
7e2a004df4a83c1b92fd39dd0f7d5d36604859f2.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter explores knowledge of and in mixed realities and uses tools from epistemic justice discourses to think about ways our environment is made more intelligible or less so. As Mixed Reality technologies embed more knowledge into our environment in new ways, decisions must be made about what and whose knowledge is included and what interactions with the environment are made easier or harder. The chapter also looks at the ways in which Mixed Reality can be used by companies to gain knowledge about the world to train up AI agents, and the ways in which MR and AI tools can be used by those with the resources to employ them to understand the world, and the implications of both. Finally, the chapter looks at how forming knowledge of partially or fully virtual entities and worlds is different from a fully material environment.</jats:p>

title: Alienation in the Worlds We Create
container-title: Environmental Justice in Digital Worlds
9680c8ece9610c25416231a920ba1dcf5a7c2acb.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter addresses alienation. Mixed Reality technologies promise to find new ways of connecting people to each other and giving meaning to their environments. Like many other technologies making this promise before, however, there is a risk of them leaving people further isolated and hostile to one another, and more distracted and removed from the world around them. This chapter uses several different conceptions of alienation in philosophy to look at the ways in which MR might alienate people from themselves, from each other, and from their environment. It also looks at the aesthetic appreciation of the environment and what that looks like for mixed realities with virtual elements. The chapter concludes with a discussion of whether Mixed Reality technologies can reduce alienation, including a look at an app designed to engage people with their environment.</jats:p>

title: Conclusion
container-title: Environmental Justice in Digital Worlds
027dbf941663f3c5996004512e8c581c9d8d95b3.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The conclusion draws on the issues discussed in the main chapters of this book to look at ways to mitigate possible harms while promoting the potential benefits of these technologies. The conclusion looks at frameworks for incorporating epistemic justice into the design, development, and implementation of these technologies. These tools are useful both for understanding issues as they arise and for collaborative conversations and projects for all the audiences of this book. The conclusion argues that some harms and injustices may well be avoidable, while others might be inherent to the technologies themselves. Even in that case, however, harms can be mitigated or compensated.</jats:p>

title: Polycentrism in the Digital Geoeconomic Order
container-title: Rethinking Authority and Legitimacy in Global Politics
711935f459dab859b4d3505b506126d69c84de7d.abstract: <jats:p>The twenty-first century is marked by the paradox of global interdependence alongside deepening fragmentation, as digital infrastructures and data regimes reshape economic and geopolitical dynamics. This chapter critiques the limits of monocentric governance models and advances polycentric governance as a more adaptive framework for a complex digital era. Drawing on Ostrom, it conceptualizes polycentrism as a multi-level, networked mode of governance suited to distributed authority and uncertainty. Through cases such as COVID-19 governance failures, data sovereignty disputes, and digital inequality in the Global South, it shows how overlapping governance systems can enhance resilience and legitimacy. Compared to hierarchical models, polycentric systems enable flexibility, innovation, and coordination across diverse actors. The chapter argues that polycentric governance is both theoretically robust and empirically necessary for sustaining cooperation in the evolving digital geoeconomic order.</jats:p>

title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
Digital Transformation of Accounting and Financial Management Through Emerging Technologies
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
072ee30c1139742aaee5825be31b3e984571eca4.abstract: <jats:p>Digital transformation has created an opportunity for accountants and financial managers to create new efficiencies, add transparency to their work, and develop better strategies for decision-making. This chapter looks at how artificial intelligence, automation, big data analytics, and cloud-based financial management are changing how accountants use technology, as well as how those technologies are changing the practices and processes that accountants follow when doing their jobs. It also describes how the digital transformation of Finance will cause a dramatic shift in the way financial services are delivered to customers from being reactive to value-driven. By integrating intelligent systems into forecasting, performance management, risk assessment, and real-time reporting functions, the ability to make informed decisions is enhanced. The chapter identifies the organizational, regulatory, and ethical challenges that digital finance poses, including data privacy, cybersecurity, and governance risks.</jats:p>

title: The Importance of the Mastering of Technological Skills and Profile of Professional Accounting
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
50dd51a7264e3966f834e8645c738ce22d306e48.abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to assess whether the importance given to information and communication technologies by accounting professionals is conditioned by age, gender, and the type of company where they work. It also intends to assess the relationship between the skills under study, determining which one is most important. The main results obtained allow us to affirm that the variables age and gender do not condition the importance given to information and communication technologies by accounting professionals, while for the type of company there are differences of opinion, constituting the main innovative contribution of this article to academic knowledge, given the scarcity of studies on this topic. We also conclude that “specific accounting technological skills” are the strongest manifestation in the construct of “technological skills”. This study aims to contribute to the reflection of Professional Orders and Higher Education Institutions on the importance of information and communication technologies for accounting professionals.</jats:p>

title: Preparing Finance Professionals for the Digital Age
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
a93fe9bb395867eb78859ec32fbdad9bef6d3cb5.abstract: <jats:p>Emerging digital technologies—AI, big data, RPA, blockchain, and cloud computing—are rapidly transforming the financial sector, shifting finance professionals from traditional record-keepers to strategic digital advisors. Using a qualitative approach grounded in academic literature and institutional reports, this study identifies critical technical competencies including data analytics, financial modeling, cybersecurity awareness, and digital literacy, alongside essential soft skills such as strategic thinking, communication, adaptability, and emotional intelligence. A significant gap is revealed between current educational and corporate training systems versus industry expectations. To bridge this divide, the study proposes a comprehensive competency model integrating digital proficiency, behavioral skills, and financial expertise. The findings underscore the necessity of continuous learning and digital resilience, ensuring sustained professional relevance in an increasingly technology-driven financial landscape.</jats:p>

title: Education and Curriculum Design for Future Finance Professionals
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
688a834c57266bfb9c64b3f458ee9b94b666529f.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid digital transformation of global financial systems has created an urgent need to redesign finance education and curriculum frameworks for future professionals. Traditional finance curricula remain largely theory-oriented and often fail to address emerging competencies related to artificial intelligence, FinTech, blockchain, data analytics, sustainability, and ethical governance. This chapter proposes the Future Finance Curriculum Framework (FFCF Model), an integrated and competency-based framework designed to bridge the gap between academic learning and evolving industry expectations. Drawing upon theories of competency-based education, outcome-based learning, and experiential learning, the study emphasizes interdisciplinary approaches, industry collaboration, technology integration, and continuous curriculum upgradation. The chapter also highlights the growing importance of analytical, digital ethical, and soft skills in preparing adaptive finance professionals for a globally connected financial environment and society too.</jats:p>

title: The Accounting Professional in the Fourth Industrial Revolution
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
09542450f279522e6869f1c9442864fdbc2fe620.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how the digital transformation of accounting is reflected in labour-market demand in Spain. Using a quantitative content analysis of 803 accounting-related job advertisements published on InfoJobs, the study identifies the digital competencies explicitly required by employers and analyses the factors associated with more digitally intensive vacancies. A Digital Demand Index is constructed from four technological dimensions: Excel and data processing, data visualisation and business intelligence, ERP and management systems, and artificial intelligence (AI). The results show that digital demand is mainly concentrated around established tools, particularly Excel and ERP systems, while business intelligence and AI remain much less visible in recruitment requirements. The regression analysis indicates that higher salaries, junior profiles, large firms, and higher education requirements are associated with stronger digital competence demand.</jats:p>

title: Digital Skills and Professional Judgment in AI-Driven Financial Decision-Making
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
fa94d39fbd808cc46e56a32eb78b60762c9d5124.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping financial decision-making by altering how information is analyzed, interpreted, and translated into professional judgment. This chapter examines the role of digital skills in determining whether AI strengthens or undermines the quality and accountability of financial decisions. Drawing on interdisciplinary literature, the chapter conceptualizes digital skills as cognitive–governance capabilities that extend beyond technical proficiency to include critical interpretation, calibrated reliance on AI, explainability, professional skepticism, and ethical judgment. Particular attention is given to automation bias, accountability risks, and the organizational conditions that shape human–AI interaction. The chapter concludes that responsible AI-enabled financial decision-making depends not on algorithmic capability alone, but on the alignment of digital competence, professional judgment, and effective governance.</jats:p>

title: Building Future-Ready Finance Professionals
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
9e847b36a842d0128695027264f9ae732156fa68.abstract: <jats:p>Digitalization is transforming the competency landscape for the modern finance professional, and this chapter explores the digital skills, technological tools, and strategic capabilities needed to navigate this rapidly changing environment, grounded in recent advancements in data analytics, cloud-based enterprise systems, artificial intelligence (AI), robotic process automation (RPA), and blockchain. Integrating scholarly literature, professional frameworks, and industry reports, the chapter shows that digital competencies are not simply technical skills but a combination of analytical, technological, ethical, and strategic skills. In this chapter, the authors introduce a multi-dimensional Digital Finance Competency Framework (DFCF). The results highlight that entities and educational establishments that allocate resources towards digital competencies enhancement will be most strategically equipped to adeptly manage the rapid evolution of the international financial landscape.</jats:p>

title: From Financial Accountant to Digital Finance Architect
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
301bb7a811700c54a3c8f72796dd343a397ed320.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter analyzes the digital transformation of the finance function as a structural reconfiguration of processes, decision-making logic, and governance. It demonstrates how automation, artificial intelligence, sustainability, and RegTech are shifting traditional job profiles from process execution to the architectural design of digital financial systems. On this basis, the Digital Finance Competency Architecture (DFCA) is developed, integrating technological, data-analytical, governance-related, and strategic-cognitive competencies. The analysis illustrates that effective performance in digital finance environments requires systemic competence, i.e., the ability to translate data, models, and regulatory requirements into coherent decision-making architectures. Finally, implications for education, organization, and governance are discussed, and the Digital Finance Architect is established as a new professional role model.</jats:p>

title: Fintech Frontiers
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
36d3f1be0785d18f51b68fb81cc99645251bd25a.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid progress of financial technology (Fintech) has profoundly changed financial services in terms of efficiency, accessibility and innovativeness across banking, insurance sectors and investment. This chapter will examine the effects of fintech on financial systems and the emerging competencies of finance professionals in a digitalized world. This chapter adopts a conceptual and integrative review used in this research, with the findings synthesized from academic and institutional sources to examine the significant technological changes, including blockchain, artificial intelligence and digital platforms. This chapter will also focus on the contribution of fintech to financial inclusion, customer satisfaction and sustainability. In addition, the challenges of regulation, workforce readiness and cybersecurity will be explored. The findings will focus on the importance of developing competencies and adapting strategically in navigating to the dynamic landscape of Fintech effectively.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Financial Decision-Making
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
9804e231d1b385dde790b1cf795ea7aaec80b1c1.abstract: <jats:p>Financial decision-making is being revolutionized by the use of artificial intelligence (AI). Whereas traditional statistical methods may be limited by the scope and complexity of contemporary financial datasets, AI technologies such as machine learning and natural language processing (NLP) permit companies to analyze not only structured but unstructured datasets efficiently. As such, there have been significant improvements in financial decision-making processes related to portfolio management, risk analysis, fraud detection, and algorithmic trading. However, the use of AI in the financial industry is also associated with issues such as lack of model transparency, algorithmic bias, and high reliance on past data, which create certain problems when it comes to transparency and reliability.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence in Financial Decision-Making
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
478d0167085f2f271218a60ba78cf0ed82a89eb2.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping financial decision-making by enhancing analytical accuracy, speed, and strategic insight across corporate finance and financial services. The primary objective of the study is to evaluate how AI applications support strategic and operational financial decisions, while also assessing associated risks related to transparency, accountability, and decision control. A qualitative case study methodology is adopted, drawing on secondary data sources including corporate reports, financial disclosures, technology implementation documents, and industry publications. The findings indicate that AI significantly improves forecasting accuracy, real-time financial monitoring, and scenario analysis, leading to more informed and timely financial decisions. The study offers original value by providing practical, case-based evidence on how AI transforms financial decision-making processes beyond theoretical models. The implications are relevant for stakeholders seeking to leverage sustainable financial performance.</jats:p>

title: AI-Driven Financial Decision Support for Handicraft Artisans
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
1d34157c42ec302960b797359d16b132c9fe0d28.abstract: <jats:p>Handicraft artists play an important role in conserving cultural and social history while also contributing to the growth of their respective economies. It contributes four to five percent to the world economy and creates a huge number of job opportunities in the neighbourhood. Handicraft workers contribute to societal innovation in the shape of innovative work methods, techniques, and so on. This area sheds light on the hidden talents and abilities of craft workers. However, their salary and economic situation do not allow for this. They are frequently confronted with issues and obstacles such as limited market access, intense rivalry from major companies, a lack of technology, and a communication gap. The article focuses on using Artificial Intelligence (AI) to solve difficulties for the handicraft industry. Primary data were acquired from 120 handicraft workers for the study using a structured questionnaire, including demographic information, production costs, profit from their company, and numerous problems they encounter.</jats:p>

title: FinTech Accounting in Financial Services Within Developing Countries
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
db8335e5a2deda558f8cb80d55476f5148e3b100.abstract: <jats:p>Fintech growth in developing nations revolutionized financial inclusion by bypassing banks, yet harmonizing accounting principles in low-infrastructure economies remains a challenge. This scoping review uses a PCC framework to map the intersection of fintech, corporate oversight, and accounting platforms to identify standard-setting frictions. Sourcing English literature up to 2026 from Scopus and Google Scholar, the study assessed fintech tools, disclosure quality, and regulations. Duplicate data extraction captured demographics, analytical models, and reporting contradictions across eleven studies spanning East Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, and the Middle East. Reflexive thematic analysis revealed four themes: corporate green reporting, infrastructure vulnerabilities, algorithmic controls, and small business viability. Stability requires adapting global reporting rules for high-velocity data. Transparent tools must replace static reporting to attract capital and prevent deep instability.</jats:p>

title: Meaning-based retrieval of Kannada Vachana literary works: a comparative analysis of retrieval techniques
container-title: Digital Scholarship in the Humanities
2aea2ebbfcfdf79834bc89c6acc4ea0799a733d5.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper examines the challenge of meaning-based verse retrieval for Kannada literary works, including Vachanas, Tripadis, and Kaggas, using Kannada queries. These literary verses are, in a sense, a form of poem-cum-prose. Given their philosophical depth and metaphorical nature, retrieval was performed using interpretations provided by Kannada scholars rather than direct text matching. We evaluated five retrieval approaches: TF–IDF, TF–IDF with Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI), KannadaSBERT-STS sentence embeddings, a cluster-based tree model of interpretations, and a proposed Hybrid Verse Retrieval (HVR) approach that fuses TF–IDF and KannadaSBERT-STS similarity scores. Experiments were conducted on a refined subset of the KannadaLit4NLP corpus comprising 5,158 verses with 17,930 scholarly interpretations, evenly split for training and testing. The results show that the proposed HVR approach performed best overall, achieving 82.40% exact-match accuracy at Top 20, an improvement over KannadaSBERT-STS embeddings alone (78.75%), which in turn outperformed the classical TF–IDF and LSI baselines. The cluster-based approach offered competitive early-rank accuracy and the added advantage of grouping related themes, though its performance plateaued at greater retrieval depths. Overall, the study demonstrates that combining statistical and transformer-based semantic signals through a simple, fixed-weight fusion can meaningfully improve verse retrieval, highlighting the promise of hybrid natural language processing approaches for the retrieval and exploration of Kannada’s literary heritage.</jats:p>

title: Attention Trap? How Visual Motion Shapes Children’s Screen Time and Engagement on Video Platforms
container-title: Information Systems Research
3836bd62e72740b25fd59c7e03808cdae1f4dd40.abstract:
<jats:p>Children spend considerable time watching online video, yet we know relatively little about which features of video content shape their engagement. This research examines one measurable feature: visual motion. Analyzing more than 32,000 videos from popular children’s channels on YouTube, we find that videos with greater visual motion receive more views, even after accounting for other visual, audio, and content characteristics. A randomized YouTube advertising experiment using professionally produced educational videos confirms this relationship; adding motion to the background increased view rates by about 2% at essentially no additional cost.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>An eye-tracking study with children aged 6–10 helps explain why. Visual motion does not prevent children from looking away. Instead, it reduces the duration of longer attentional lapses by bringing their gaze back to the screen more quickly. The additional attention is directed primarily toward the moving background rather than the instructor. The findings show how a measurable design feature can shape children’s attention and provide creators and platforms with a way to assess and design children’s video content more systematically.</jats:p>

title: Stakeholder Perspectives on Information About Digital Health Applications in German Outpatient Mental Health Care: Qualitative Interview Study
container-title: JMIR Human Factors
53786725fea7a172d562c7b958f00be3fc9858bc.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Digital health applications (digitale gesundheitsanwendungen; DiGA) were integrated into the German statutory health care system in 2020 and can be prescribed by physicians and psychotherapists. Nevertheless, their use within routine care, particularly in the treatment of mental disorders, remains limited. Previous research suggests that a lack of information and knowledge among health care providers and patients may contribute to these difficulties.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to explore the perspectives of stakeholders on the information-related aspects of DiGA implementation in outpatient mental health care in Germany. This included investigating the perceived information status, information needs, suitable information providers, and potential approaches to improve information provision.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted semistructured interviews with experts representing stakeholder groups relevant to DiGA in outpatient mental health care in Germany. Participants were recruited using purposive stakeholder sampling. Potential participants were identified through existing professional contacts and web-based searches and were subsequently approached by email. The web-based interviews were conducted via Microsoft Teams between September and November 2023. The transcripts were analyzed using qualitative content analysis based on the method described by Kuckartz, combining deductive and inductive category development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 13 interviews with 14 participants were conducted, comprising 5 health care provider representatives, 4 statutory health insurance representatives, 4 DiGA developer representatives, and 1 patient representative. The findings were grouped into 3 main themes: perceived information status, improvement of the information status, and information suppliers. Representatives of health care providers described a general awareness of DiGA but said they lacked more detailed knowledge required to assess and compare individual applications. They also perceived information gaps among patients. Participants distinguished between general information on aspects such as regulatory requirements and organizational processes and more detailed product-specific information. Different potential information suppliers were associated with different opportunities and problems, particularly regarding expertise, objectivity, available resources, and the ability to provide product-specific information.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings indicate that information-related challenges in the implementation of DiGA extend beyond general awareness. Health care providers may require accessible information with different levels of detail, while the source of information also appears relevant. Addressing these different information needs may support the integration of DiGA into outpatient mental health care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                    <jats:title>International Registered Report Identifier (IRRID)</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>RR2-10.2196/56205</jats:p>
