title: The Neuroscience of Happiness
Neuropsychology of Happiness
container-title: The Neuroscience of Happiness
6becf76eb51a852f4802a4007d69c26fcabd8a96.abstract: <jats:p>Recent studies indicate that happiness and emotional balance are becoming major concerns in today's fast-paced world. In India, around 35% of people reported feeling negative emotions like stress, anger, sadness, or worry in 2023, compared to 33% the year before. At the same time, people who said they experienced positive emotions dropped from 70% to 67%. This chapter explores how the brain and mind together shape happiness, focusing on the role of emotions, mindfulness, and manifestation. A systematic review will be performed to collect and synthesize current research on mindfulness, manifestation, and happiness. A bibliometric analysis will subsequently be conducted to discern significant research patterns, leading authors, keywords, and emerging trends within global studies in this domain. By examining adaptive and maladaptive aspects, the study aims to create a balanced understanding of how the brain processes happiness through emotional and cognitive channels. The findings shows outcomes through manifestation that lead to happiness</jats:p>

title: The Role of Neuroplasticity in Well-Being
container-title: The Neuroscience of Happiness
8a621a948f334e54f813c4b638353c7756a40e46.abstract: <jats:p>The neuroplasticity, the natural ability of the brain to change its structure and its functioning based on experience has become a unifying concept of neuroscience, psychology and even clinical practise. This chapter discusses the potential of neuroplasticity in achieving psychological wellbeing through deliberate cognitive and behavioral activities, including mindfulness, positive thinking, and cognitive reappraisal. Basing on historical underpinnings, modern neuroimaging and molecular neuroscience, the discussion follows the restructuring of synaptic efficiency, neurological connectivity and gene expression through experiences through the lifespan. The evidence has shown that mindfulness meditation changes default mode network, improves prefrontal-limbic regulation, and increases cortical thickness of the areas related to attention and emotion regulation.</jats:p>

title: Happiness Cocktail
container-title: The Neuroscience of Happiness
9f70a444499d574c37522f8e51431d9396559006.abstract: <jats:p>Positive psychology defines happiness as an enduring state of well-being that includes satisfaction across the pleasant, good, and meaningful aspects of life. When examined through the lens of neuroscience, however, happiness emerges not as a single emotional state but as a coordinated neurochemical symphony shaped by multiple interacting systems. The limbic–striatal pathway forms the core of the brain's reward circuitry. Happiness unfolds dynamically through the interplay of neurotransmitters. These neurochemicals operate across cortical and subcortical regions, creating a convergent framework where motivation, emotional valence, social connection, and regulatory balance co-construct the experiences we identify as joy, serenity, or fulfillment.The orchestration of this neurobiological “cocktail” demonstrates that well-being is the result of precise temporal and functional coordination among systems that signal wanting, liking, social bonding, and emotional stabilization. Exploring individuals with SLD and the pursuit of sustained happiness.</jats:p>

title: The Dual Engine of Well-Being Dopamine Serotonin and the Neurobiology of Drive and Contentment
container-title: The Neuroscience of Happiness
050faeac98bf0370f9e4ee84361deb60cef808e5.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter provides a neuroscientific synthesis challenging the popular, simple view of dopamine and serotonin. It establishes the Dual Systems Framework to accurately define their roles in motivation and well-being. The Dopamine Pursuit System (VTA-NAcc-PFC) drives wanting, anticipation, and learning via the RPE signal. This drive system is contrasted with the Serotonin Stability System (raphe nuclei), which manages emotional resilience, impulse control, and contentment. The analysis shows how modern strong stimuli create a constant drive leading to the Hedonic Treadmill. The framework explains mood disorders as problems with the dynamic balance between these two systems (e.g., dopamine deficiency causes low drive; serotonin deficiency impairs control). The chapter concludes that lasting well-being requires managing the equilibrium between the motivating Pursuit Engine and the stabilizing Stability Engine. This study offers a vital brain-based foundation for improving emotional management and treating affective disorders.</jats:p>

title: A Conceptual Synthesis of Ancient Ethical Principles and the Modern Neuroscience of Well-Being
container-title: The Neuroscience of Happiness
152104867ecb67f85ad35e3d31136880a22e598b.abstract: <jats:p>The current theme works towards the Dharma-Dopamine Integrative Framework, and in this respect, it is the way to symbiosis of ancient ethical modes with the psychology of the modern man. It is through this manner of execution and practical implication that the study has been able to show that the direction of the moral compass and human discipline are the major support of a decrease in dopamine-related activity, reinforcement of the prefrontal-limbic convergence, and activation of intrinsic motivation. The all-in-one, combined way of thinking and acting makes a way of the future of well-being, and besides, it concentrates on the brain and moral redemption, which will open up a new area in psychology, for it includes the mental health aspects, psychological aspects, and classes in moral philosophy practice. The proposed concept of research, in the long run, seeks to validate by neuroimaging, to conduct a study that compares different cultures, and to establish a moral well-being program that is based on virtue-based neuropsychology interventions.</jats:p>

title: Reconnoitring Yogic Peace of Mind and Transient Happiness With Their Perceived Psychological Correlates
container-title: The Neuroscience of Happiness
2a08909a0d86148aae4b34a85733003e4a4fe6d2.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter discusses yogic peace of mind as a complex, self-reported psychological construct and looks into its linkages with perceived cognition, emotional regulation, meditative consciousness, and well-being. The empirical part of the research is a pilot cross-sectional study conducted only using data collected via questionnaires; it did not include measurements of brain activity, neurotransmitter levels, the autonomic nervous system, or any other biological parameters. Consequently, all neurological hypotheses are discussed as interpretations based on existing neuroscience literature and not on the findings of this particular research. Some preliminary findings of factor, regression, and structural modeling analyses will be used to evaluate the proposed theoretical links between the concepts. There is evidence of correlations between long-term yogic practice, reported peace of mind, and positive psychological outcomes; however, there is no proof of causation or physiological changes. Further large-scale longitudinal studies are required to verify the hypothesis.</jats:p>

title: ANANDA
container-title: The Neuroscience of Happiness
5c30e1813dfa2c5f51a10100dd9beaeb97f71c55.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the connection between gratitude, neuroscience, and ancient Indian wisdom to understand the nature of human happiness, or Ānanda. Drawing on cutting-edge research in neuroplasticity, emotional regulation, and brain-body communication, this chapter explains how gratitude reshapes neural pathways, reduces stress responses, and improves overall health. The article integrates Upanishad concepts, such as Pancha Kosha and the principle “Yad Bhāvam Tad Bhavati,” to demonstrate how gratitude affects physical, mental, and spiritual aspects of life. The chapter demonstrates how gratitude can be a transformative practice that awakens inner harmony and long-lasting happiness by examining convergences between contemporary scientific findings and classical teachings from texts such as the Bhagavad Gita.</jats:p>

title: Cross-Cultural Perspectives on Happiness
container-title: The Neuroscience of Happiness
202ea2ad1cf28bdfd7fd3337799f9885f6213148.abstract: <jats:p>Happiness is framed as a universal human goal, yet its definition and experience vary significantly across cultures. This chapter critically examines happiness through a cross-cultural neuroscientific lens, challenging Western views that equate well-being with personal achievements and hedonistic pleasure. While emotional experiences have a biological basis, cultural norms shape emotional expression and well-being pathways. By integrating cultural psychology, anthropology, and neuroscience, it explores how distinct cultural frameworks influence brain operations through neural plasticity. It contrasts Western individualism focused on dopaminergic reward systems with Eastern collectivism, where well-being emphasizes social harmony and mindfulness. Additionally, Indigenous perspectives link happiness to ecological connections. Ultimately, the chapter advocates for a culturally informed neuroscience of happiness that recognizes diverse, valid pathways to well-being, promoting respectful, culturally nuanced models over globalized approaches.</jats:p>

title: Neural Pathways to Happiness From a Cross-Cultural Neuroscience Perspective
container-title: The Neuroscience of Happiness
219a1f882091f166d8acf4c355d9e3f80a50de49.abstract: <jats:p>The chapter examines the neural, cultural, and developmental foundations of happiness by integrating evidence from neuroscience, cross-cultural psychology, and Indigenous studies. It discusses how reward pathways, emotion regulation systems, and neurotransmitter mechanisms interact with experience-dependent neuroplasticity to shape well-being. The chapter compares Western, Eastern, and Indigenous perspectives on happiness and explains how cultural practices such as meditation, social rituals, and community participation influence brain function. By synthesizing biological and cultural perspectives, the chapter presents happiness as both a universal and culturally grounded phenomenon, offering implications for mental health, psychological research, and culturally sensitive well-being interventions.</jats:p>

title: Psychological Pathways to Happiness
container-title: The Neuroscience of Happiness
efd3fed18eb7e59ebcfa84679681177ce6e2132c.abstract: <jats:p>This cross-sectional study explores the relationships among five self-report psychological constructs, including positive affect, life satisfaction, meaning and purpose, emotional regulation, and achievement satisfaction, and their relationship to overall happiness. Data from questionnaires completed by 232 participants were analysed using an exploratory structural equation model (SEM). This model explains 68% of the variance in overall happiness reported. Meaning and purpose demonstrated the greatest standardised relationship, followed by positive affect, life satisfaction, achievement satisfaction, and emotional regulation. The current study does not involve the measurement of brain function, neural networks, neurochemicals, hormones, or other biological markers. References to the default mode network, prefrontal-limbic systems, dopamine, serotonin, or oxytocin are theories based on previous literature and not data resulting from the SEM. Because the design is cross-sectional, the coefficients show associations consistent with the model but do not establish causality or time order.</jats:p>

title: Technology, Digital Life, and Happiness
container-title: The Neuroscience of Happiness
6cfac7f3569751479eaa16befe7281b6b4613f80.abstract: <jats:p>The booming use of digital technologies is changing human thoughts, emotions, and social behaviours, thus creating important questions about the role of the digital existence on the well-being. The chapter is interdisciplinary and incorporates research findings in neuroscience, psychology, behavioural science and digital sociology to examine how the digital environment and dopaminergic reward circuitry, stress response mediated by amygdala, prefrontal control of attentional and neuroplastic habit formation interact. Even though it predetermines many possible dangers, like clogging the imagination, being a good comparer, and having a fractured attention, the text also illustrates how carefully constructed technologies can strengthen personal connectivity, innovation, education, self-building, and emotional control. The authors introduce an integrated model that summarizes neurobiological, psychological, behavioural, sociocultural, and technological aspects of online well-being, therefore, providing recommendations to individuals who need to find the balance.</jats:p>

title: How Digital Life Shapes the Neuroscience of Happiness
container-title: The Neuroscience of Happiness
46c95d48febb96d6e135f4b9d09cac8a0a32344c.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter explores how digital technologies reshape the neural systems underlying happiness, motivation, and emotional regulation. It shows that dopamine-driven rewards from notifications and algorithmic feeds can create cycles of anticipation and compulsive use, while rapid stimuli and social comparison disrupt mood stability and attention. At the same time, digital tools such as mindfulness apps, supportive communities, and therapeutic platforms can strengthen prefrontal control, reduce stress, and enhance emotional resilience. The chapter argues that digital happiness is a neuro-cultural construct shaped by both neural plasticity and technological design. It proposes neuroscience-informed strategies—mindfulness, structured digital breaks, and intentional technology use—to restore balance, and presents a neuroethical framework emphasizing autonomy, transparency, and humane design to support well-being in a digitally mediated world.</jats:p>

title: Future Directions in the Neuroscience of Happiness
container-title: The Neuroscience of Happiness
03898f49602ddb6e7d7483909df639c270c581e6.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter questions the neuroscience of happiness as a contemporary interdisciplinary field connecting affective neuroscience, psychology and education. At the same time, it brings out its limited engagement with neurodiverse people, predominantly children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). Current happiness research has mainly advantaged neurotypical standards, emphasizing deficit-based interpretations of well-being in ASD. The chapter reimagines happiness for children with ASD by joining in perspectives from neuroscience, developmental psychology and educational practice, advocating for a wide-ranging, more inclusive conceptualisation of well-being. It focuses on a paradigmatic shift from deficit-oriented models to strength-based approaches that acknowledge alternative pathways to happiness, sensory satisfaction, focused interests and non-traditional systems of social connection. The chapter further situates this reconceptualisation within present-day gaps in happiness research and offers inclusive directions for future investigation, among them neuroimaging and longitudinal studies. It ends by identifying interventions that can nurture and sustain happiness among children with ASD.</jats:p>

title: Integration of Digital Technologies in Classroom Assessment Practices: Exploring Teachers’ Attitudes, Challenges, and Future Perspectives at Al-Madinah International School (A Field Study)
container-title: Arid International Journal of Educational and physcological sciences
0bb44354e3da33b5839adc96098976154dd8f08d.abstract: <jats:p>This study aimed to explore the attitudes of teachers at Al-Madina International School in Saudi Arabia towards integrating digital technologies into formative classroom assessment. It also sought to identify the types of technologies used, the enablers and barriers teachers encounter, and their future visions for development. The research adopted a mixed-methods approach, utilizing both a questionnaire and semi-structured interviews. The sample included 33 female teachers from various subjects and educational levels. Results revealed generally positive attitudes towards digital integration, although levels of use varied based on subject and experience. The most notable enablers were the availability of technical infrastructure and prior training, while the main barriers were lack of time and insufficient technical support. The study concluded with recommendations such as offering ongoing professional development, encouraging innovation in assessment practices, and refining school policies to better support the effective integration of digital tools in classroom assessment.</jats:p>

title: AI-Enabled Digital Health Tool Implementation in Clinical Practice Settings: Umbrella Review
container-title: JMIR AI
ed6b7c7bd88c542620745d58d7720ce6fb1ecaf8.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI has the potential to improve clinical decision-making, efficiency, and patient outcomes, yet adoption in routine clinical practice has been slower than anticipated. While prior studies have identified factors that influence AI implementation, a comprehensive synthesis grounded in implementation science frameworks is lacking.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to qualitatively and comprehensively describe barriers and facilitators to AI implementation in clinical care settings using an implementation science determinants framework, the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR), and to identify AI-specific determinants not fully captured by CFIR.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted an umbrella review of reviews examining determinants of AI implementation in clinical practice. In accordance with the PRIOR (Preferred Reporting Items for Overviews of Reviews) reporting guidance, we systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, and CINAHL for English-language reviews published between January 2013 and July 2025. Reviews were included if they addressed barriers to and facilitators of implementing AI-enabled digital health tools in clinical care settings. Determinants were deductively mapped to the updated CFIR and inductively analyzed to identify emergent AI-specific constructs. Review quality was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklist, and overlap among primary studies was evaluated using the GROOVE (Graphical Representation of Overlap for Overviews) tool.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twenty-two reviews published between 2021 and 2025 were included, encompassing studies conducted from 1990 to 2025. Reviews varied in design, including systematic, scoping, rapid, narrative, and literature reviews. Overall review quality was mixed, with 9 (41%) reviews rated at 100% quality and 4 (18%) at 50% or lower. Primary study overlap was slight, with a corrected covered area of 0.4%. Determinants of AI implementation were identified across all CFIR domains. Prominent barriers at the innovation level included limited evidence of clinical impact, poor interpretability, complexity, lack of adaptability, and insufficiently representative data. Facilitators included perceived relative advantage, co-design with clinicians, and evidence of local clinical benefit. At the implementer level, low AI literacy, limited confidence, time constraints, and concerns about professional displacement were common barriers, while training and technical support facilitated adoption. Inner setting barriers included inadequate infrastructure, limited resources, poor workflow compatibility, and weak governance structures. Outer setting barriers included unclear policies, laws, and liability frameworks, whereas partnerships and cross-sector collaboration were frequent facilitators. Inductively identified AI-specific determinants included transparency, trust, accountability, model bias, data governance, model maintenance, robustness, generalizability, existential threat, and concern about loss of the human element in care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI implementation in clinical settings is shaped by complex, multilevel, and AI-specific determinants that extend beyond traditional digital health considerations. Implementation science frameworks can be adapted to incorporate these constructs. Tailored, theory-informed strategies addressing technical, organizational, psychological, and regulatory factors are essential to support safe, equitable, and sustainable integration of AI into clinical care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Retracting Attention
container-title: Seeing and Subjectivity
3a0cc0cdb516ebbc09d01859d15f1425d1efc074.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Further insight is at hand in a text Bhattacharyya does not discuss, but might have, Manu’s Code Law. Here we find a description of the lived experience of the wandering ascetic (yati), depicted as consisting in a state of ambient perceptual awareness; the experience of the ascetic is one of full attentional retraction. When Kalidas Bhattacharyya writes that ‘negative attention [is] a sort of concentrated withdrawal from, rather than positive fixation of, the content whose truth is sought to be discovered’, it is negative attention as attentional retraction that he has in mind, rather than either as absential attention or apophatic attention. The ascetic’s ambient awareness consists of a field of purely marginal consciousness, and it is here alone, Gurwitsch insists, that the sense of self (the dative of presentation) is to be found.</jats:p>

title: Optimized Emergency Sign Language Recognition with Large-Kernel Attention Graph Convolutional Network for Accurate Gesture Classification
container-title: International Journal of Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence
3737bdb37c2afdac92e2c8a956436c9b57e10253.abstract: <jats:p>Sign Language Recognition (SLR) plays a significant role in improving communication accessibility for hearing-impaired individuals, particularly in emergency scenarios where fast and reliable gesture interpretation is required. However, emergency Indian Sign Language (ISL) recognition remains challenging due to rapid hand movements, visually similar gestures, and complex spatial–temporal relationships among hand components. This study proposes an SLR-HIE-LKAGCN framework that integrates topology-aware spatial representation, spatial–temporal feature learning, graph-based gesture modeling, and optimization-based parameter adaptation for emergency ISL recognition. Initially, input gesture frames are processed using a Simplicial Convolutional Filter (SCF) to preserve higher-order spatial relationships among hand regions and enhance gesture representation. The refined gesture sequences are then provided to a Spatial–Temporal Knowledge-Embedded Transformer (STKET) to capture temporal dependencies and contextual movement patterns. The extracted features are further analyzed employing a Large-Kernel Attention Graph Convolutional Network (LKAGCN), which models relationships among hand landmarks and learns discriminative gesture representations. In addition, the Secretary Bird Optimization Algorithm (SBOA) is employed to optimize critical network parameters and improve model convergence. The proposed framework is evaluated on emergency ISL gesture categories, including accident, call, doctor, help, hot, lose, pain, and thief. Experimental outcomes establish that the proposed technique achieves superior recognition performance with 98.82% accuracy, 98.57% precision, and 98.53% F1-score, outperforming existing approaches. The obtained results indicate that SLR-HIE-LKAGCN provides an effective and computationally efficient solution for real-time emergency ISL recognition.</jats:p>

title: ATT-SV2-ES Net: Hybrid Deep Learning Features and Lightweight Attention-Based Model for Early Glaucoma Detection
container-title: International Journal of Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence
bc275378bb5009d7f256155d09bb39b3c0bf9888.abstract: <jats:p>Glaucoma is one of the main causes of permanent blindness. Timely intervention is ensured by its early and precise identification. This paper proposes a new hybrid approach, integrating handcrafted features with Deep Learning (DL), for reliable glaucoma identification and prediction on the G1020 dataset. Initially, pre-processing is conducted, which includes data augmentation to increase the diversity of images, Gaussian filtering to reduce image noise, Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE) to enhance local retinal contrast and then grayscale conversion to simplify retinal image representation. After pre-processing, the enhanced images were given to Depthwise Dilated Spatial Attention Mechanism (DDSAM)-based Glau-SegNet for optic disk (OD) and optic cup (OC) segmentation. From the segmented images, handcrafted features, such as Local Binary Patterns (LBPs) and fractal analysis, which describe complementary texture and structural information, are extracted. In parallel, the segmented images are processed by the Attention ShuffleNet V2 with Echo State Network (Att-SV2-ES Net) to obtain high-level deep feature representations. Then these deep features and handcrafted features are concatenated and fed to a fully connected layer with sigmoid activation to classify into the class for the prediction of glaucoma. This combined approach achieves a balance between high accuracy and scalability, addressing the growing need for accessible and reliable glaucoma screening solutions. The experimental results demonstrate the proposed system’s superior performance in detecting and predicting glaucoma. Furthermore, the findings demonstrate that the proposed model, which integrates DL features, outperforms all other models in terms of key performance metrics, including achieving 99.32% specificity, 99.43% sensitivity, and 99.37% accuracy.</jats:p>

title: Engagement Patterns and Clinical Outcomes Among Adolescents and Young Adults Enrolled in the Somethings Digital Peer Support Platform: Retrospective Observational Study
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
953c4720688eb14be414f54a77f8999fcbb1a1a0.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adolescent mental health needs remain largely unmet, particularly among youth in geographically underserved communities. Digital peer support is a promising approach to expanding access to mental health support, yet real-world evidence on engagement patterns and clinical outcomes remains limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The purpose of this study was to characterize engagement patterns and real-world outcomes among adolescents and young adults enrolled in a commercially available, text-based peer support platform.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective observational study analyzed secondary data from 5673 adolescents and young adults enrolled in a commercially available digital peer support platform from January 29, 2023, through June 3, 2026. Engagement was operationalized as communication days per month. Standardized clinical outcome measures (Patient Health Questionnaire-9 [PHQ-9], Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 [GAD-7], and World Health Organization-Five Well-Being Index [WHO-5]) were administered as part of routine measurement-based care. Ordinary least squares regression was used to examine predictors of engagement, and complete-case pre-post change scores were evaluated across 4 assessment windows among participants with paired assessments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The sample was predominantly female (4600/5673, 81.1%) with a mean age of 16.4 (SD 2.1) years and moderate-to-severe symptom burden at baseline (PHQ-9: mean 12.6, SD 6.1; GAD-7: mean 10.7, SD 5.0; WHO-5: mean 44.8, SD 21.0). Of enrolled adolescents and young adults, 98.1% (5565/5673) had at least one recorded engagement with the platform, with a mean of 4.56 (SD 6.12) communication days per month. Female sex was a significant positive predictor of engagement intensity (β=.64, SE 0.22;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.004). Hispanic and Latino adolescents and young adults engaged significantly more frequently than White or non-Hispanic adolescents and young adults (β=.61, SE 0.26;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.02). Health Professional Shortage Area (HPSA) shortage score was significantly and positively associated with engagement intensity (β=.08, SE 0.02;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001). Baseline symptom severity was not associated with engagement intensity (β=.094, SE 0.23;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.68). Among participants with complete baseline and follow-up data (1437/5673, 25.3%), an exploratory complete-case analysis found within-measure paired scores improved significantly from baseline to follow-up across the PHQ-9, GAD-7, and WHO-5. At last assessment, 31.9% (237/742), 36.6% (222/606), and 37.8% (168/442) of adolescents and young adults met clinically meaningful improvement thresholds on the PHQ-9, GAD-7, and WHO-5, respectively.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Text-based peer support shows preliminary promise as a scalable approach to expanding mental health access for underserved adolescents, though clinical improvement estimates are based on the subpopulation exposed to the digital peer support platform and may not generalize to the full enrolled population. Prospective, controlled studies with more complete outcome ascertainment are needed to establish causal efficacy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Application of Digital Health Interventions for Cognitive Management in Children With Cancer: Scoping Review
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
488230a323f4a1db95fece744265b1e2765b04ec.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Advances in the diagnosis and treatment of childhood cancer have substantially improved survival, resulting in a growing population of survivors of childhood cancer who may experience long-term treatment-related sequelae. Cognitive late effects are an important long-term consequence of childhood cancer and can affect cognitive functioning, psychosocial well-being, and quality of life. Digital health interventions offer accessible and flexible approaches to managing cognitive difficulties among children with cancer. However, the existing evidence has not yet been comprehensively synthesized.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to map and synthesize the existing evidence on digital health interventions for cognitive management among children with cancer; characterize intervention modalities, delivery approaches, and functional components; and identify evidence gaps and priorities for future research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Arksey and O’Malley framework and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews) checklist. Six academic databases, including PubMed, Embase (Ovid), CINAHL, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library, were systematically searched for relevant studies published between January 2010 and August 2026. Eligibility criteria were developed using the population-concept-context framework. Two reviewers independently performed study screening and data extraction. The methodological quality of included studies was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Screening was performed independently at the title/abstract and full-text stages, with disagreements resolved through discussion and, when necessary, consultation with a third reviewer. Descriptive statistics and thematic content analysis were used to synthesize the findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 5371 records were identified through the literature search. Following screening, 19 publications representing 14 independent study samples and involving 566 children with cancer were included. Four digital health modalities were identified: computer-based interventions, internet-based interventions, mobile apps, and neurofeedback training. Computer-based interventions were the predominant modality. Across these modalities, working memory and attention were the most frequently targeted cognitive domains, while feasibility, acceptability, and adherence were the most commonly assessed implementation-related outcomes. However, relatively few interventions incorporated coach support, telephone-based communication, or educational components, and none evaluated economic outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although digital health interventions show promise for supporting cognitive function in children with cancer, substantial gaps remain in the current evidence. This scoping review mapped the field according to intervention modalities, delivery approaches, and functional components, rather than focusing solely on the efficacy of individual technologies. Future research should prioritize the development of multidimensional, personalized, and functionally integrated digital health interventions that combine cognitive training with supportive care, education, monitoring, and communication. Multicenter randomized controlled trials should subsequently evaluate these interventions using clinically meaningful outcomes, with comprehensive assessments of safety, adherence, implementation, and health economic outcomes to establish their effectiveness, feasibility, and sustainability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: A unified adaptive weighting framework for GNSS/visual/inertial odometry with deep-learned point-line features
container-title: Measurement Science and Technology
5ab074a05b2819f579a8e1c397749014530dbaa4.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Visual-inertial odometry often suffers from performance degradation in challenging environments due to the failure of handcrafted features and fixed-weight fusion schemes. This paper proposes a tightly-coupled global navigation satellite system (GNSS)/visual/inertial odometry system with two core advances: a deep learning-based point-line feature front-end and a geometry-aware adaptive weighting strategy that dynamically adjusts the contribution of visual and GNSS observations. The front-end employs SuperPoint with SuperGlue for robust point extraction and matching, and the Richer Convolutional Features network for enhanced edge detection to obtain reliable line segments. For the back-end, we derive analytically the sensitivity of point reprojection error to depth and of line reprojection error to the line’s orientation relative to the camera axis, and construct adaptive weight functions that replace the conventional fixed covariances. Crucially, this adaptive weighting strategy is extended to GNSS measurements by incorporating the dilution of precision, carrier-to-noise ratio, and multipath anomaly detection, thus enabling a unified framework where every observation is weighted according to its instantaneous geometric reliability. Extensive experiments on the EuRoC MAV dataset, and self-collected campus sequences demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior accuracy and robustness in most standard and moderately degraded scenarios compared to representative baseline methods. On the EuRoC MAV dataset, the proposed unified framework reduces the average Root-Mean-Square of the absolute trajectory error by 8.4% relative to fixed-weight PL-VINS, while the deep feature front-end further improves robustness and trajectory accuracy in low-light and low-texture environments. In GNSS-degraded urban canyons, the adaptive GNSS weighting mechanism suppresses the influence of unreliable satellite observations without manual tuning, leading to more stable and reliable localization.</jats:p>

title: Effectiveness of a Multicomponent Digital Therapeutic Program on Inhaled Medication Adherence in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
container-title: JMIR mHealth and uHealth
2bc33ab0b8ca8bbbac0cbbb8d8a5f79d36217054.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Poor medication adherence is a critical impediment to effective chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) management and remains challenging to track in routine care. Digital therapeutic interventions may improve chronic disease management through remote monitoring and patient education. However, most existing digital interventions focus on individual components of disease management, and evidence from longer-term pragmatic randomized controlled trials evaluating integrated digital therapeutics in routine clinical practice remains limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of a multicomponent digital therapeutic program combining electronic inhaler monitoring (EIM) with behavioral support in improving medication adherence and symptom-related outcomes among patients with COPD prescribed pressurized metered-dose inhalers, and to assess patient engagement and implementation in routine clinical practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this prospective, open-label, unblinded, randomized controlled trial, patients with COPD prescribed pressurized metered-dose inhalers were enrolled and randomized in a 2:1 ratio to either the intervention group or the control group. All participants received an EIM device to objectively record inhaler use throughout the 24-week study period. Patients in the intervention group also received personalized medication reminders from the EIM, adherence feedback, educational content, and clinician-supported follow-up through an integrated digital management platform based on EIM-derived data, whereas the control group received usual care. The primary outcome was medication adherence over 24 weeks. Secondary outcomes included exacerbations, COPD symptoms, quality of life, and lung function.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A total of 158 participants were randomized, including 106 in the intervention group and 52 in the control group. The median monitoring coverage was 161.5 (IQR 86.3‐168.0) days during the follow-up period. The self-reported adherence measured using the Test of Adherence to Inhalers showed no significant between-group differences at any follow-up time point. However, the electronically monitored adherence was significantly higher in the intervention group than in the control group (59.5% vs 33.1%,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.009). Adherence declined over time in both groups, decreasing from 85.3% during weeks 0 to 4 to 43.0% during weeks 12 to 24 in the intervention group and from 76.8% to 11.9% in the control group over the same intervals, resulting in a progressively larger between-group difference over follow-up. No significant differences were observed in exacerbations, health-related quality of life, symptom burden, lung function, or mental health outcomes. In an exploratory analysis, a significantly greater proportion of participants in the intervention group achieved the minimal clinically important difference in the COPD Assessment Test score than in the control group (odds ratio 2.21, 95% CI 1.11‐4.41;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.02).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The multicomponent digital therapeutic program significantly improved objective medication adherence in patients with COPD over 24 weeks. While most clinical outcomes did not differ significantly between groups, the higher proportion of participants achieving a clinically meaningful improvement in the COPD Assessment Test score warrants further investigation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Climate and Digital Transitions Among Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises in Africa: The Role of Development Finance Institutions
container-title: Frugal Innovations, Eco-Innovations, and AI Innovations in Modern Small Businesses
8b27d253570775e220ff4e8a070d64f9459a0838.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In this chapter, the authors examine the role of Development Finance Institutions (DFIs) in enhancing climate and digital transitions among micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs). The authors iterate the crucial role of these transitions in achieving resilience, competitiveness and sustainability among MSMEs’ amid evolving global challenges. Additionally, the authors explain the importance of DFIs in providing critical financial and technical assistance, enabling MSMEs to adopt climate-smart technologies and embrace digital transformation. The authors also highlight case studies illustrating successful DFI interventions. This chapter concludes by emphasising the need for DFIs to prioritise outreach to marginalised communities, balancing developmental goals with financial sustainability and capacity building to scale their impact.</jats:p>

title: Engagement-Supportive Mechanisms in Stress-Focused Digital Mental Health Interventions With Adaptive, Conversational, and Context-Aware Systems: Narrative Review
container-title: JMIR Human Factors
7301e19c45feefeb630a365b5b8099fa710a891f.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Stress is a widespread public health concern associated with cardiovascular disease, depression, anxiety, and reduced quality of life. Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs), delivered through smartphones, web platforms, and wearables, offer scalable support for stress management but often struggle to sustain user engagement. Evidence describing how adaptive, conversational, and context-aware mechanisms function together within stress-focused DMHIs remains fragmented.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This review aims to synthesize evidence on engagement-supportive mechanisms in stress-focused DMHIs, with attention to personalization; biometric feedback; just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs); gamification; AI, including large language models (LLMs); and methodological approaches to studying engagement. It also examines methodological, motivational, and experiential dimensions of engagement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This narrative review was informed by a structured search of PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Scopus for peer-reviewed studies published between January 2018 and April 2025, followed by an evidence update through August 2026. Eligible studies described stress-focused DMHIs or related affective support interventions reporting at least 1 engagement-supportive mechanism. Randomized controlled trials, qualitative investigations, simulation or modeling studies, and implementation studies were included. Data were extracted using a structured form capturing study characteristics, engagement mechanisms, outcomes, and alignment with the review domains. Descriptive mapping summarized study types and mechanism frequencies, while a narrative synthesis integrated behavioral, experiential, methodological, and theory-informed findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thirty-two studies met the inclusion criteria. Randomized or microrandomized controlled trials were the most common design (n=17), followed by qualitative investigations (n=6), design or implementation studies (n=3), mixed methods studies (n=3), simulation or modeling studies (n=2), and a quasi-experimental study (n=1). Dynamic adaptation was identified in 14 studies, conversational support in 10, static tailoring in 9, social or co-design mechanisms in 9, context-aware prompting in 7, gamified reinforcement in 5, biometric-responsive adaptation in 4, and narrative immersion in 2. These mechanisms frequently overlapped within layered adaptive architectures rather than functioning as isolated engagement features. AI-enabled systems included conversational agents, LLM-supported systems, recommender systems, reinforcement learning, and computational modeling approaches. Outcomes included behavioral indicators such as adherence, retention, and prompt receptivity, alongside experiential indicators such as perceived relevance, trust, emotional support, and immersion. Evidence strength varied substantially; many AI-enabled systems contributed feasibility, acceptability, or optimization-oriented evidence rather than definitive comparative effectiveness evidence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Stress-focused DMHIs are increasingly adopting adaptive, conversational, and context-aware engagement-supportive mechanisms, but the evidence base remains heterogeneous and methodologically uneven. Dynamic adaptation, conversational support, and static tailoring were most frequently represented, whereas biometric-responsive adaptation, narrative immersion, and deeply integrated gamified systems were less common. AI-enabled systems may support contextual responsiveness and personalized interaction but require transparent adaptive logic, privacy safeguards, and human-centered evaluation. Future work should prioritize longitudinal, mixed methods research capable of distinguishing behavioral engagement, experiential engagement, feasibility, acceptability, and sustained stress-related outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Robust Adaptive Control of Fractional-Order UAVs Using DNN Observer and Fractional Kalman Filters to Mitigate Simultaneous Sensor Noise and Actuator Faults
container-title: Unmanned Systems
8902c6962799979d1564c831d08bb1060153203a.abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a control strategy for quadrotor trajectory tracking, combining a barrier-function adaptive fractional-order sliding-mode controller with a deep neural network fault observer and a fractional Kalman filter. Fractional-order modeling captures memory effects, while the adaptive barrier keeps sliding variables within limits, reducing chattering. The deep neural network observer estimates additive actuator faults for compensation, and the fractional-order Kalman filter reduces sensor measurement noise. Simulations under simultaneous measurement noise and actuator faults show that, in the high-variance noise case, the proposed method improves the position-loop RMSE by 41.6% over adaptive fractional-order sliding mode control and 42.8% over adaptive sliding mode control.</jats:p>

title: Digital Twin Technologies for Plasma Reactor Modeling and Optimization
container-title: Theory, Applications, and Impacts of Advanced Plasma Engineering
3126707e07403a777025e8a7263a74fb5f1629d5.abstract: <jats:p>Technology based on the creation of a digital twin has been developed as an innovative solution to cope with increasing complexities of modern plasma engineering systems. Traditional approaches to modeling plasma reactors are focused on performing static simulations, empirical optimization, and inadequate experiments to obtain insights into their behavior. However, due to nonlinear dynamics of plasma reactors, these methods do not provide comprehensive understanding of their complex behavior. The use of edge computing, cloud computing, robotics, and autonomous control systems has enabled the application of digital twins in the areas of semiconductor processing, plasma medicine, advanced material synthesis, environmental remediation, aerospace propulsion systems, fusion energy, and plasma-assisted manufacturing. The current chapter offers an in-depth look at the principles, architectures, methods, applications, optimization techniques, limitations, and future possibilities associated with digital twins of plasma reactors.</jats:p>

title: Maternal Health Outcomes of Digital Health Interventions in Low- and Middle-Income Countries in Southeast Asia: Scoping Review
container-title: Asian/Pacific Island Nursing Journal
f49e7cd3356464d89b8b2c9eac76e9e3454f488d.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Digital health interventions (DHIs) have gained increasing attention as strategies to improve maternal health in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Previous reviews of DHIs have included studies from Southeast Asia (SEA) but have not examined maternal health outcomes in SEA LMICs as a distinct regional evidence base.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This scoping review aimed to map maternal health outcomes of DHIs in SEA LMICs using an adapted proximal-intermediate-distal (PID) framework, describe DHI characteristics, and summarize contextual factors related to target groups and intervention settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The review followed the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews) and the Joanna Briggs Institute guidance. PubMed, CINAHL, and Scopus were searched for English-language interventional studies evaluating DHIs that were published from January 2005 through May 2025. Google Scholar, reference lists, and the Index Medicus for the South-East Asia Region were searched as supplementary sources. Maternal health outcomes were mapped using an adapted PID framework, and all results were summarized descriptively.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twenty-five studies from 7 SEA LMICs were included. Mobile apps and SMS were the most commonly used technologies, reported in 22 (88%) studies. Fourteen (56%) studies reported maternal health outcomes across more than one PID domain. Intermediate outcomes were reported most frequently (n=23, 92%), followed by proximal knowledge outcomes (n=10, 40%) and distal biomedical and clinical outcomes (n=8, 32%). Findings related to proximal knowledge outcomes were predominantly significant, whereas intermediate and distal outcomes showed mixed results. All but one study (n=24, 96%) recruited participants through existing health care services, and most interventions were implemented in primary care settings (n=17, 68%).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Maternal health outcomes were represented across all 3 PID domains, with intermediate outcomes reported most frequently and distal biomedical and clinical outcomes least frequently. Future studies should give more attention to distal biomedical and clinical outcomes, as well as underrepresented SEA LMICs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
