While conventional activation function extraction methods rely on manual design or register-transfer level analysis, a gate-level alternative exists: deriving activation functions through the extraction of observability don’t care (ODC) conditions from the underlying netlist. This article presents
                    <jats:bold>ODCGate</jats:bold>
                    , a framework designed to automatically detect ODC conditions as the activation functions and safely block clock transitions for unused registers, thereby further reducing dynamic power consumption during clock gating. The computation begins with cut boundary enumeration and simulation. To further minimize additional PPA overhead, we apply hybrid simplification techniques to the extracted logic, and enable sharing among registers through clustering. Experimental results show that, beyond the clock gating optimization of a commercial logic synthesis tool, our method achieves an average 33.46% additional reduction in dynamic power, with minimal impact on other PPA metrics.
                  </jats:p>

title: EnVector: Encoding using Pattern based Vectors for Energy Efficient Non-Volatile Main Memories
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
5243326e813a5b6c6c744dd3b22a5532319d4f01.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Non-Volatile Memories (NVMs) provide new opportunities for scalable main memory due to their great scalability and other favorable attributes. However, considering their inherent write defects (long latency, high energy consumption), combined with their limited write endurance, their inclusion into the memory hierarchy requires careful handling. This not only shortens the lifespan of NVMs but also renders them as an expensive option. In this work, we propose a technique called
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">EnVector</jats:italic>
                    that exploits the intrinsic uniformity in memory data to encode the cacheline data before the memory write takes place. By using well-designed fixed vectors, it minimizes the variation between the incoming and the stored data. This saves a lot of possible bit flips, reducing the likelihood of any memory failure from an excessive number of writes. Consequently, improving performance and lowering latency and energy requirements. We empirically demonstrated that
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">EnVector</jats:italic>
                    upgrades the NVM lifetime by 37% and accelerates its performance by 15% over the baseline.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p/>

title: Design and Implementation of a Vision Integrated Autonomous Research Rover
2e019a77a34534cace9acae8857fa40918f60895.abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents the design and implementation of a low-cost, vision-integrated autonomous rover for automated soil data collection. Traditional soil sampling methods are labor-intensive, and existing robotic solutions frequently depend on costly hardware and Global Positioning System (GPS) navigation, which can easily degrade in obstructed environments. To address these issues, a GPS-denied rover was developed using a Raspberry Pi 4B for high-level computer vision and a Robot Operating System 2 (ROS2) framework, paired with an Arduino Nano for real-time hardware control. The platform utilizes a linear actuator to autonomously deploy sensing probes for localized soil analysis. For stable navigation, an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) is implemented to fuse wheel encoder odometry with inertial data. An OpenCV-based vision pipeline directs autonomous path following and marker detection. To mitigate tracking errors caused by processing and mechanical latency, a custom delay-compensation filter is introduced to actively reverse the rover and correct overshoot. This is paired with a history-dependent sweep prioritization algorithm that intelligently re-acquires lost paths based on prior trajectory data. The resulting system provides a reliable, accessible framework for independent environmental monitoring.</jats:p>

title: MLLM-Driven Autonomous Driving: Closed-Loop Decision-Making with Language-State Alignment and Human Instruction Integration
container-title: ACM Journal on Autonomous Transportation Systems
d800c7e114eb4db4826982c6e016151dc7d88ec1.abstract: <jats:p>The core challenge of autonomous driving is achieving real-time decision-making and safety control in complex, dynamic environments, especially in long-tail scenarios where conventional systems often fail due to limited adaptability, poor human-vehicle interaction, and low interpretability. This article introduces MLLM-CLAD, a closed-loop decision-making framework powered by a multimodal large language model, which addresses semantic gaps and feedback limitations through a co-optimization strategy that integrates behavior-state alignment and language instruction fusion. MLLM-CLAD integrates three core modules: (1) The Mapping-Enhanced Language-State Alignment Module employs a deterministic mapping pipeline from language instructions to control signals, which enables highly accurate mapping from LLM semantic outputs to executable control signals. (2) The Hierarchical Dynamic Instruction Integration Module robustly categorizes and dynamically prioritizes human language instructions into different semantic types. (3) The Multimodal Fusion Module leverages a lightweight spatiotemporal Q-Former to jointly encode images and LiDAR point clouds, aligned with language in latent space for improved temporal reasoning and cross-modal consistency. Evaluated in the CARLA Town05 Long, MLLM-CLAD achieves a 78.3% Driving Score and reduces collision rates by 35% in safety-critical scenarios. On the LangAuto benchmarks, MLLM-CLAD attains a 78.5% long-tail scenario pass rate. Furthermore, the end-to-end latency is reduced to 128 milliseconds. This work establishes a scalable path toward safe, low-latency, and interpretable autonomous driving in simulation, with a clear roadmap for real-world extension.</jats:p>

title: Study Design and Lessons Learned From Using Google Takeout Donations for Suicide Prevention Research: Prospective Cohort Study
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
6610fc8dba7dec763399be61f0e967f4f50c2399.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Social media and search engine tech companies, such as Google, use the wealth of data at their disposal to create algorithms to predict suicide risk and provide interventions based on company policies and outputs from these algorithms. Neither the details of these algorithms nor their accuracy in risk prediction are shared with the public; thus, research is needed to verify whether algorithms applied to search engine data can accurately predict suicide risk in a platform user. This paper provides new information about the methodological challenges in studying the value of search engine data for suicide prediction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper describes the study methods and experiences regarding recruiting and retaining participants in a year-long, fully remote prospective cohort study of suicide prediction in people with variable risk of suicide, using Google Search data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We aimed to recruit 1000 United States–dwelling and English-speaking adults with current suicidal ideation who fell into 1 of 3 categories: participants with a suicide attempt in the past year, participants with a lifetime suicide attempt but not one in the past year, and participants with no suicide attempt in their lifetime. Recruitment sources included online advertisements hosted on various websites, to differing levels of success. Participants completed online surveys and an interview via Zoom to enroll in the study and then were sent follow-up surveys every 2 weeks for the year following initial enrollment. Recruitment was conducted from March 2022 to January 2024, with follow-up data being collected through February 2025.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of 15,120 records created in our Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) survey system, 485 participants were eligible to participate in the prospective year of the study. Recruitment challenges were mainly due to participant dropout across all enrollment time points, with 63.7% (9636/15,120) of the prescreening sample dropping out or refusing. Other issues included the difficulty of downloading Google Search data (446/3277, 13.6%) and not having enough data to meet the inclusion criteria among those who were able to successfully donate (252/3277, 7.7%). Lastly, the study encountered fraudulent behavior, with 489 of 15,120 records (3.2%) being identified as fraudulent over the course of the study.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Despite past success with remote clinical research methods, we found that recruitment can be significantly hampered by fraudulent participation, despite the use of state-of-the-art methods to mitigate this problem. Further, the ability to acquire useful Google Search data is extremely challenging and necessitates the use of technical assistance and continuous monitoring of Google Takeout data structure to ensure accurate and complete data donations. The solutions we provide for this type of research should be helpful for future endeavors. However, research is still limited by the barriers to obtaining data from technology companies. These limitations have significant implications in detecting the accuracy and utility of suicide prediction from search engine data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Design optimization of Belleville washers made of shape memory alloys for advanced damping devices
container-title: International Review of Applied Sciences and Engineering
8b7bb47b9288de915570c928d3492949f6e6ceec.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Belleville washers made of Shape Memory Alloy (SMA) merge the unique properties of these materials with the advantages of conical disc spring geometry. Recent research has focused on characterizing these devices under cyclic compression. Key studies have involved numerical simulations and experimental testing. The findings confirm excellent recentering and energy dissipation capabilities of SMA Belleville washers, establishing them as prime candidates for next-generation seismic dampers for buildings and bridges. However, further investigation is required to optimize SMA Belleville washers by finding the cone angle and thickness that maximize energy dissipation. Considering damping devices fabricated by stacking Belleville washers, which rely on the pseudo-elastic effect, this work details an original methodology for systematic optimization of their design. This encompasses a preliminary elastic based sizing performed using adapted stress formulas, which is followed by a refinement stage employing Finite Element Analysis, via the 2020 R2 release of Ansys Mechanical solver. By generating a set of viable design alternatives, this novel methodology facilitates the efficient identification of the optimal configuration to maximize damping energy for given design constraints. The effectiveness of this approach was validated through case studies focused on optimizing SMA Belleville washers within advanced vibration suppression dampers.</jats:p>

title: CHARIOT: A Communication-Aware Exploration Framework for 2.5D/3D Silicon Interposer Design
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
fde248b576388e57d31ec8cfcc2323e389897a4a.abstract: <jats:p>Interposer design is crucial for optimizing inter-chiplet communication efficiency, performance, and energy consumption in 2.5D/3D integrated systems. To facilitate performance analysis and design space exploration (DSE) of interposers, this work presents CHARIOT, a fast, comprehensive exploration framework that establishes a systematic methodology for analyzing and exploring the design space of both passive and active interposers’ architecture. The design space of interposers is first developed to evaluate system performance. Then a roofline model-based methodology is introduced to analyze the bottleneck of performance. A multi-objective Bayesian optimization-based DSE framework, CHARIOT, is proposed, featuring a scheduling engine tailored to different interposer types and a communication-aware exploration engine for coordinated multi-objective exploration of the design space. Compared to the state-of-the-art (SOTA) chiplet system, the CHARIOT-generated optimal passive and active interposer designs achieve energy efficiency improvement up to 1.33× and 1.96×, as well as performance gains up to 1.49× and 1.75× speed-up. The Pareto frontiers of competitive design choices enable selecting the most suitable option based on the designers’ requirements.</jats:p>

title: SEC-CiM+: Selective and Reconfigurable Error Compensation for ReRAM-based Compute-in-Memory
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
11453691504ff8ab721724d52aa2fc6fce4b4ca2.abstract: <jats:p>ReRAM-based Compute-in-Memory (CiM) architectures provide a promising solution for accelerating Deep Neural Network (DNN) inference in edge computing environments. However, these architectures are susceptible to stuck-at faults (SAFs), including stuck-at intermediate states, which degrade inference accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose a reconfigurable error compensation (EC) mechanism that selectively mitigates errors while operating under memory constraints. By leveraging an indexed storage format, our approach efficiently compensates for errors without excessive overhead. We develop a theoretical framework to determine the minimum number of critical columns requiring compensation and analyze how EC transitions between three modes of operation across different models. The EC mechanism requires only 0.3874 mW of additional power for single operational-unit correction and introduces negligible latency overhead, while sustaining near-baseline accuracy for DenseNet121, VGG16, ResNet18, and SwinT under high fault densities (5–10%). Moreover, the overall energy overhead remains below 6% for ResNet18 and VGG16, and below 10% for DenseNet121.</jats:p>

title: DSETune: An Efficient Design Space Exploration Approach for Logic Synthesis
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
a855d3f0f9d5f837d27164f18752c0380dbbd423.abstract: <jats:p>As a critical step in the chip design flow, logic synthesis generates target circuits by iteratively applying various optimization algorithms. In practical applications, engineers must adjust the combination of optimization algorithms based on expert knowledge to meet diverse design requirements. However, existing approaches lack a multi-objective optimization perspective and exhibit poor solving efficiency. In light of this, we propose DSETune, the first synthesis flow search approach capable of thoroughly exploring the design space. First, a discrete particle swarm optimization algorithm incorporating genetic operators significantly improves search efficiency of design space. Second, a domain knowledge-driven initialization strategy of particles accelerates convergence and enhances solution quality. Finally, an update mechanism integrating a customized elite strategy enables more comprehensive solution space exploration, yielding superior Pareto-optimal solutions. Experimental results on the EPFL benchmark suite and four technology libraries demonstrate that DSETune outperforms existing methods: it reduces the area-delay product by 10.99%, improves the hypervolume metric by 109.80%, and achieves a 22.99% speedup, all on average.</jats:p>

title: Path Delay Faults Through Transition Faults with High Functional Switching Activities
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
d7c0604e26121ab930c68a14ad77f1a7756f99ac.abstract: <jats:p>Chip aging results in defects that are initially likely to appear as small delay defects. Path delay faults are used for detecting small delay defects. Because of the number of paths, path selection procedures are used for identifying a subset of path delay faults that are important to detect. A recent path selection procedure addresses small delay defects that are likely to occur because of chip aging. The procedure identifies a set of functionally possible path delay faults, from which it selects a subset based on an aging aware metric. This article studies this problem when the requirement for the path delay faults to be functionally possible is removed. The problem becomes that of selecting path delay faults through the largest numbers of transition faults with the highest susceptibilities to aging, and performing test generation for the selected path delay faults. Experimental results of path selection and test generation for benchmark circuits demonstrate the effectiveness of the procedures, and the differences from the case where the path delay faults are required to be functionally possible.</jats:p>

title: Quantifying Scalability-Performance Trade-offs: A Design Space Exploration of Compute-in-Memory based Ising Machines
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
314c1f4d98507cae1dbda9fa514e347fedc40048.abstract: <jats:p>Ising machines offer a promising paradigm for solving NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems (COPs). Among various approaches, Compute-in-Memory (CIM) based Ising machines show superior performance due to the reduced data transfer and efficient Multiply-and-Accumulate (MAC) operation. However, the scalability of CIM-based implementations remains limited due to challenges including restricted mapping size, circuit limitations and device non-idealities especially with emerging non-volatile memory (eNVM) technologies. This work presents a comprehensive design space exploration of three scalable CIM architectures for fully connected Ising models, analyzing their performance under constraints such as IR-drop, device variation, parasitic capacitance and analog to digital converter (ADC) precision loss across different memory technologies. According to our evaluation for randomized MAX-CUT benchmarks, the properly chosen design (Single array XNOR-based CIM mapping with Current Sense Amplifier) maintained over 95% solution quality while achieving nearly 2× higher energy efficiency and a 40% area reduction for 128-spins Ising model, while the optimal solution (Distributed subarray computation with 1-bit ADC precision loss) improves energy efficiency by 2.1× with small solution quality degradation (̴ 10%) for large-scale models (1,024 spins) compared to other designs options.</jats:p>

title: Toward Enhanced Hardware IP Security: Community Evaluation of Logic Locking, State Space Transformation, Redaction, and NoC Routing Table Configuration
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
274ba93baa637941a987ccfc15ebb7a42e0bfdac.abstract: <jats:p>As global hardware manufacturing expands and the need to meet time-to-market demands grows, companies increasingly depend on the zero-trust model to manage most of the design process for Integrated Circuits (ICs). Consequently, valuable hardware intellectual property (IP) becomes vulnerable to piracy, cloning, reverse engineering (RE), and unauthorized modifications throughout the global IC supply chain. Current security solutions are designed to safeguard the designs and protect sensitive information throughout the design flow. In this study, we present a thorough evaluation of various IP countermeasure techniques, including Logic Locking, State Space Transformation, Fine-grain Hardware Redaction, and NoC Routing Table Configuration, described in the existing literature. Inspired by cybersecurity competitions and community evaluation efforts, we designed a collaborative benchmarking initiative to evaluate these techniques on open-source benchmark designs, unveil the gaps and limitations of each technique, and discover crucial paths for future exploration. Through a retrospective analysis of this initiative, the insights we gained can significantly contribute to improving countermeasure techniques in the broad domain of hardware security and trust.</jats:p>

title: Fast TDDB Hotspot Detection of Large-Scale BEOL Circuits Using Physics-Informed Central Emphasized CNN
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
43ca2ee0c70088e2af9b1e91e0c2fd8f1b809f8c.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Time-Dependent Dielectric Breakdown (TDDB) has emerged as a critical reliability concern in Back-End-of-Line (BEOL) interconnects. In Electric Path Generation (EPG) based TDDB analysis, the evolution of metal ion concentration is governed by a Partial Differential Equation (PDE). Traditional numerical methods for solving this equation are time-consuming and demand considerable computational resources, making them impractical for large-scale circuits analysis. To address this challenge, we propose a physics-informed learning framework for fast prediction of ion concentration distributions in large BEOL layouts. The framework represents BEOL patterns as two-dimensional images, partitions large layouts into overlapping sub-graphs for encoding, and predicts transient concentration fields for each sub-graph. Based on the reconstructed full-layout concentration map, the method supports efficient TDDB hotspot analysis. The proposed Physics-Informed Central Emphasized Convolutional Neural Network (PICE-CNN) is applicable to diverse interconnect patterns and operating conditions, including different line widths, line spacings, and supply voltages. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves up to 357.1× speedup over conventional numerical solvers while maintaining high prediction accuracy, with the mean squared error below 1× 10
                    <jats:sup>-4</jats:sup>
                    in the emphasized central region.
                  </jats:p>

title: Multi-Scale Feature Refinement Network for Lithography Hotspot Detection
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
5fa622b91bc87aba9ec00699837e6f89ca6a5477.abstract: <jats:p>As semiconductor manufacturing advances toward smaller process nodes and more complex layouts, lithography hotspot detection faces increasing challenges. Traditional methods often struggle to capture subtle geometric variations in complex layouts, resulting in low recall and high False Alarm Rate (FA). To address this problem, we propose a Multi-Scale Feature Refinement Network (MSFRN). The key innovation lies in a collaborative “Extraction–Refinement–Decision” framework specifically designed for Hard-To-Classify samples: the Multi-Scale Feature Extraction module comprehensively captures rich information ranging from local geometric details to global layout context; the Feature Refinement Network enhances responses to critical geometric features through a lightweight gating mechanism; and finally, ConvNeXt serves as the decision module, integrating and classifying the refined features for final hotspot prediction. Experimental results show that on the most challenging ICCAD 2019-2 benchmark, MSFRN improves recall by up to 11.3%, with the FA varying from a 0.2% increase to a 5.8% reduction, demonstrating superior detection capability.</jats:p>

title: LE-Timing: Layout-Aware and Explainable Timing Prediction
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
a88b9c42bcbdbf6644f9ee04fd0b43f4f65e6fa0.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Accurate and fast timing prediction at early design stages is crucial for achieving timing closure in very-large-scale integration (VLSI) design. Machine learning (ML) based approaches have been widely adopted for timing prediction to pursue both accuracy and speed. Unfortunately, these approaches fail to fully exploit the layout features, which can significantly impact the timing metrics, thus leading to great accuracy degradation. In this article, we propose LE-Timing, an end-to-end layout-aware timing prediction approach that can achieve better accuracy by leveraging important layout information. The key insight is that crucial information about coupling capacitance between routing wires can significantly impact timing metrics, and fully exploiting this layout information in the timing prediction model can substantially improve its accuracy. However, efficiently leveraging layout features while maintaining accuracy poses three key challenges: node-level layout-graph integration, domain experience utilization and training efficiency. To address these, we further propose three key technologies specially designed for LE-Timing correspondingly, including a layout-encoding net model, an explainable cell model, and an explicit-message-passing scheme. Experimental results on 16 open-source designs with an advanced 7-nm technology node demonstrate that LE-Timing achieves
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">R</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    score 0.94 for arrival time prediction and lower error accumulation compared to the baselines.
                  </jats:p>

title: PCB-QA: A Task-Specific Question Answering Framework for Text-Centric Chip Datasheet Queries in PCB Design
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
1423d80f2f29ee75157e5dcd83cc4dfd6b7118eb.abstract: <jats:p>In PCB design, engineers often rely on datasheets to obtain crucial chip information, a process that is both time-consuming and labor-intensive. To streamline this workflow, we present PCB-QA, a task-specific Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based question-answering system that automatically addresses text-centric chip-related queries using the latest datasheets. Rather than aiming to replace broader commercial AI-assisted EDA platforms, this work focuses on a narrower and reproducible research problem: grounded datasheet question answering over a maintained corpus. While existing RAG technologies have made significant progress in document-based question answering, several challenges remain, primarily due to the erroneous segmentation of documents, the retrieval of inaccurate references, and under-specified user queries. To improve the accuracy of PCB-QA’s responses, our framework incorporates three key components. First, we propose a datasheet segmentation model that is specifically trained to divide the corpus into semantically coherent chunks. Second, we integrate a correlation estimation module to better assess the relevance of retrieved references and reduce the influence of distractors. Finally, recognizing that user inputs may lack critical details, we employ a query-rationalization mechanism to facilitate further reasoning and refine the query for under-specified technical and application-related questions. These task-specific customizations improve retrieval quality and support more accurate grounded answers for datasheet-centric QA. Experimental results on our customized ChipQuestion benchmark demonstrate that PCB-QA achieves consistent improvements over representative RAG baselines on text-grounded datasheet QA. We also clarify the current scope of PCB-QA: the present implementation is primarily text-centric and does not yet fully address image-only figures, waveform plots, complex visual tables, or other visuallygrounded datasheet content.</jats:p>

title: PRLBridge: A Legality-Aware Interface between Compilers and LLMs for Secure DNN Obfuscation
container-title: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
46be701001595abdaba5bc28cbeafbfa42646ab0.abstract: <jats:p>Deep learning compilers such as TVM generate highly optimized binaries, but these transformations also expose structural cues exploitable by reverse-engineering attacks. Existing defenses are difficult to control and offer limited support for balancing security and performance. Motivated by the symbolic reasoning ability of Large Language Models (LLMs), we ask whether LLMs can assist compiler-level obfuscation. However, because schedule obfuscation and kernel-family classification involve intertwined compiler semantics, legality constraints, and experience transfer across kernels, directly exposing raw programs to LLMs often leads to unreliable reasoning, legality violations, and poor generalization across kernels. We therefore design a language-model-friendly Program Representation Language (PRL) that links compiler-side information with LLMs and recasts kernel classification and obfuscation-experience inheritance as a constrained generation task. Our framework, PRLBridge, introduces two abstractions: a kernel-family intermediate that canonically captures legality and structural information, and PRL, a compact grammar-constrained language through which LLMs express candidate transformations. The compiler incrementally verifies generated outputs and deterministically replays legal sentences into schedules. Experiments across four models and ten LLMs show that PRL-based generation consistently improves defense effectiveness, maintains over 97% legality and 100% reproducibility, and substantially reduces compilation cost through verified and reusable schedules.</jats:p>

title: Interpretable Cross-Corner Timing Prediction Based on XGBoost-SHAP Solution
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
adf2d6f3d22de840eb2a60b9755ab2d123483171.abstract: <jats:p>With the continuous advancement of semiconductor technology, the explosive increase in the number of corners to be covered during chip design has imposed severe challenges on timing analysis resource and time cost. Recent studies on machine learning-based cross-corner timing prediction have emerged as a promising paradigm for accelerating multi-corner timing analysis. Those existing approaches predominantly rely on precomputed multi-corner timing analysis results or process technology parameters for model training, but suffer from limited industrial adoption due to the large number of training corners, the complex pre-training flow, and the opaque nature of the black-box architecture. In case of this, we propose an XGBoost-based cross-corner timing analysis framework that requires only a single-corner static timing analysis report as input to achieve high-precision timing prediction with an average mean absolute error of approximately 1.604 ps across corners. The proposed methodology has been validated through commercial projects based on different deep nanometer process nodes (7 nm and below), demonstrating robust performance stability. In the task of critical path identification and optimization, this proposed method achieves near-100% coverage with acceptable increase in additional STA overhead. Furthermore, we employ SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis to interpret the XGBoost model, quantifying key contributors to cross-corner timing variations. This not only enhances the explainability of the black-box model but also provides insights for design optimization and robustness improvement.</jats:p>

title: Exploring student activism as a pedagogical tool in human rights education
container-title: Journal of Human Rights Practice
bb54d056b46c83b7f6a1c8c579b95b8521f37124.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This article interrogates the role that activism can play in pedagogy by focusing on student-led activism within formal curricula. This article is written using a collaborative ethnographic approach by alumni and faculty on a human rights internship undergraduate module, which runs along three parallel strands: 1. students are trained to undertake advocacy and campaigning, 2. they learn about the political sociology of social movements, the psychology of persuasion and marketing, and the international law and politics of human rights, and 3. they design and run a campaign for a wrongfully imprisoned academic or student. Through the reflections of the alumni on the module, this article explores the features of student activism as a pedagogical tool for learning ‘about, through, and for’ human rights education. We identify three themes that encapsulate our experiences of student activism: in-group dynamics, mixed hierarchical structures, and learning through reflection. Based on these themes, we argue that using student activism as a pedagogical tool enables teachers to align the process of learning with the goal of learning. Integrating human rights education and student activism in the context of higher education can create dynamic learning environments for students that empower both students and faculty, develop critical and reflective thinking, enhance students’ ‘employability’ skills, and contribute to human rights change.</jats:p>

title: Immunometabolic drivers of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease in non-obese people living with human immunodeficiency virus
container-title: World Journal of Gastroenterology
62358354440e3fb41236a2c24cad5c43a44d10b1.abstract:
<jats:p>BACKGROUND</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is common in people living with human immunodeficiency virus (PLWH), but its drivers in non-obese individuals are unclear. A low cluster of differentiation (CD) 4/CD8 ratio marks immune senescence, yet the role of a normalized ratio in MASLD risk in non-obese PLWH remains unexplored.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>AIM</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>To investigate MASLD prevalence, risk factors, and short-term integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) impact on steatosis in non-obese PLWH.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>METHODS</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This prospective study enrolled virologically suppressed PLWH who had received antiretroviral therapy for ≥ 6 months. All participants underwent clinical assessments, biochemical tests, and vibration-controlled transient elastography. Multivariate logistic regression identified independent risk factors for MASLD. Changes in parameters across the INSTIs-based, non-INSTIs-based, and switching to the INSTIs-based regime groups in non-obese PLWH were compared using mixed-effects models from baseline to month 12.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>RESULTS</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Among 181 enrolled participants [median age, 40 years (interquartile range: 35-48); 5.0% female], the overall prevalence of MASLD was 46.4%. Notably, among all patients with MASLD (n  = 84), 28.6% (24/84) were non-obese. In the non-obese subgroup, higher body mass index [odds ratio (OR) = 2.14, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.32-3.47], alanine aminotransferase (ALT) (OR = 1.04, 95%CI: 1.003-1.069), triglyceride-glucose index (OR = 3.29, 95%CI: 1.04-10.40), CD4/CD8 ratio (OR = 8.55, 95%CI: 1.57-46.66) and lower high-density lipoprotein level (OR = 0.029, 95%CI: 0.001-0.688) were independently associated with increased MASLD risk. 12-month longitudinal analysis revealed no significant group-by-time interaction effects for ultrasound attenuation parameter, liver stiffness measurement, and ALT.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>CONCLUSION</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>MASLD is prevalent in non-obese PLWH. Higher CD4/CD8 ratio associates with MASLD, indicating that immune reconstitution does not ensure metabolic health. INSTIs were not associated with short-term hepatic steatosis progression.</jats:p>

title: Fast Electromigration Analysis of Multi-segment Interconnects Based on Recurrent Neural Networks
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
58684a324d90aaafa88519c8358acf193dec8657.abstract: <jats:p>Predicting electromigration (EM) stress is a critical reliability challenge in power delivery networks. Existing semi-analytical Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) models neglect the Markovian sequential dependencies of EM diffusion and suffer from severe scalability issues due to global topological evaluations. To address these architectural and computational bottlenecks, this article proposes a dynamic spatiotemporal stress forecasting framework. Specifically, a physics-aligned Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) is constructed to directly model the Markovian sequential evolution of EM stress. This is integrated with a tensor mapping-based dynamic local subgraph extraction strategy, effectively isolating spatial complexity from the global interconnect scale. At the numerical integration level, we develop a physics-driven adaptive hybrid convolution algorithm. Regulated by a stress relaxation time constant, this algorithm dynamically invokes discrete convolution during the early acceleration phase to strictly preserve the abrupt variations of the auxiliary function used for stress computation, and seamlessly switches to Gauss-Legendre quadrature during stable periods to maximize precision while eliminating smoothing artifacts. Furthermore, a simulation-time-based optimization strategy is incorporated to mitigate the prediction error gap between early and late simulation stages. Experimental results validate the efficiency of the proposed framework. Compared with the MLP baseline, our model achieves up to a 93.2% reduction in relative error and a 117.79× computational speedup. Against the Finite Element Method (FEM), it delivers up to 1335.6× acceleration while maintaining engineering-grade accuracy.</jats:p>

title: CGNet: A Lightweight Multimodal Framework for Congestion Prediction in VLSI Physical Design
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
ef87539cfd3f7abda9a4252462a8b9ac57e0188c.abstract: <jats:p>Early access to accurate congestion information can effectively optimize the physical design flow of modern very large scale integration (VLSI) circuits. Existing unimodal models suffer from limited feature utilization and insufficient prediction accuracy, while current multimodal approaches typically involve large parameter sizes, slow inference, and high computational complexity, making them difficult to apply in time-critical tasks. To address these limitations, we propose CGNet, a novel lightweight multimodal model for congestion prediction that simultaneously processes feature maps and heterogeneous graphs. To enable efficient feature fusion without significantly increasing model complexity, we incorporate a cross-stitch module. Furthermore, we propose a heterogeneous graph compression method that significantly simplifies the graph structure, thereby reducing the computational complexity of processing heterogeneous graphs and improving the prediction speed of the model. Additionally, we design a composite loss function that jointly captures global structures and local details. For a more comprehensive evaluation, we propose a localized metric, intersection over union (IOU), and integrate the predicted congestion maps into the downstream design rule check (DRC) violation prediction task. Experimental results in the CircuitNet-N28 dataset demonstrate that CGNet consistently outperforms the best-performing model in both prediction accuracy and prediction speed.</jats:p>

title: From Space to Place: A Review of Landscape Design and  Children's Health Research
container-title: The International Journal of Healthy Space
1939632f78e2d09bfcfdb00af563cd63d937f93b.abstract: <jats:p>Against the backdrop of rapid urbanization and the “indoor, sedentary” lifestyle of children, the role of the built environment in promoting children’s health has garnered increasing attention. This review systematically synthesizes research advances in the field of landscape design and children’s health, aiming to provide an academic reference for child-friendly city initiatives and evidence-based design. The article elucidates core theories such as environmental behavior, environmental affordance, place attachment, and play classification, establishing the foundation for understanding the chain mechanisms of “physical environment → psychological perception → behavioral response → health outcomes.” At the scales of public open spaces, playgrounds, neighborhoods, and school routes, the review synthesizes the multidimensional impacts of landscape spaces on children’s physical activity, cognitive development, and socio-emotional well-being. Methodologically, the review explores the converging trend of diverse techniques, including objective measurements (accelerometers, GPS, computer vision), systematic behavioral observations (SOPARC, behavioral mapping), subjective perception and participatory methods (perceptual mapping, photovoice, walking interviews), and spatial analysis. Current research remains limited, with a stronger emphasis on physiological indicators over psychological development, a predominance of cross-sectional designs, the lack of focus on children’s own perspectives, and insufficient exploration of the underlying mechanisms within China’s high-density urban contexts. Future research should develop interdisciplinary performance evaluation frameworks, extend to higher-order benefits such as cognition, emotion, and environmental ethics, promote participatory action research paradigms, and bridge the gap between policy and design through longitudinal studies and indigenous theoretical innovation, thereby translating “child-friendliness” into high-quality spatial realities.</jats:p>

title: Trading-Off Performance and Sustainability in Internet of Things: An Uncertainty-Aware Hierarchical Energy Management Approach
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
fd3d451e23529f6c37adeff5a792d90cc52faa50.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Internet of things (IoT) devices have been heralded as a key technology to enable several high-impact applications, such as healthcare, remote environmental monitoring, and digital agriculture. However, they suffer from energy sustainability challenges due to small form-factor and batteries. Recent research has proposed to integrate energy harvesting (EH) technologies into IoT devices. However, ambient sources are highly stochastic in nature, which introduces new challenges in IoT energy management (EM) since the decisions must account for the associated uncertainty. To this end, this article presents a multi-target conformal prediction algorithm to provide
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">provably correct uncertainty estimation</jats:italic>
                    of future energy prediction for multiple future time steps. Prediction of energy alone is not sufficient since we must use the predictions along with uncertainty estimates in an energy management algorithm to make energy consumption decisions. A common approach in IoT devices is to follow energy-neutral operation (ENO), whereby the energy consumed in a given period is equal to the harvested energy. However, this may lead to low performance in cases where the energy harvest is insufficient. To resolve this, we propose to design a suite of policies that can tradeoff performance and energy sustainability. Moreover, the proposed approach includes a charging management policy that aims to introduce additional energy into the system when the energy harvest is low to maintain system performance. Evaluations with two real-world datasets show that the proposed conformal prediction algorithm achieves the desired coverage level of 90% for all users. The energy management policies achieve performance that is within 10% of an optimal Oracle that has the knowledge of future energy harvest. Moreover, evaluation of the charging management policy shows that it provides additional energy only when EH values are low. Finally, measurements on an IoT device show that the proposed algorithms are light-weight and consume less than 10 mJ per decision.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p/>

title: Towards Realistic Project-Level Code Generation via Multi-Agent Collaboration and Semantic Architecture Modeling
container-title: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
2e98affb75fe6b1c9fa0a80bf39cb6bb48af6b14.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in automated code generation. In real-world software engineering, the growing demand for rapid iteration and continuous delivery underscores the importance of project-level code generation, where LLMs are expected to generate complete software projects directly from complex user requirements. This task, however, presents greater challenges due to larger input scales, multi-modal information, and the need for holistic architectural reasoning. Although existing studies have made initial explorations, they still face key limitations, including unrealistic datasets and unreliable evaluation metrics that fail to reflect real-world complexity, the semantic gap between human-written requirements and machine-interpretable structures, and difficulties in managing hierarchical dependencies and maintaining quality throughout the generation process. To address these limitations, we first introduce
                    <jats:sc>CodeProjectEval</jats:sc>
                    , a project-level code generation dataset built from 18 real-world repositories with 12.7 files and 2,388.6 lines of code per task on average, supplemented with documentation and executable test cases for automatic evaluation. We further propose
                    <jats:sc>ProjectGen</jats:sc>
                    , a multi-agent framework that decomposes projects into architecture design, skeleton generation, and code filling stages with iterative refinement and memory-based context management. Within this framework, we introduce the Semantic Software Architecture Tree, a structured and semantically rich representation that effectively bridges user requirements and source code implementation. Experiments show that
                    <jats:sc>ProjectGen</jats:sc>
                    achieves state-of-the-art performance, passing 52/124 test cases on the small-scale project-level code generation dataset DevBench, a 57% improvement over the baseline approaches, and 310 test cases on
                    <jats:sc>CodeProjectEval</jats:sc>
                    , representing an improvement of roughly tenfold compared to the baselines.
                  </jats:p>

title: Consensus on Core Competencies of Undergraduate Life Sciences Students for Entry-Level Participation in Clinical Trials: RAND-Modified Delphi Study
container-title: JMIR Human Factors
a76d448b9a2f4ee1a74acae6ea70f90e6c266c00.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The competencies required of life sciences graduates to participate in clinical trial research teams are poorly defined.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to establish a structured consensus on the core competencies that students must acquire during their degree programs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A RAND-modified Delphi procedure was conducted using 2 rounds of online questionnaires, a virtual meeting, and a final review. The process began with a questionnaire completed by experts from the University of Córdoba and the Maimonides Institute for Biomedical Research of Córdoba (3 principal investigators, 1 study coordinator, and 1 data manager). The 48 competencies initially proposed were reviewed by a panel of 18 experts representing 6 clinical research groups from universities and biomedical research institutes in Andalusia, Spain. The relevance of each proposed competency was rated on a 9-point Likert scale. Competencies were accepted if they achieved a mean score of 7 points or higher and at least 70% of ratings in the top tertile (scores of 7-9).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The 18 experts achieved 100% consensus on a panel of 48 competencies organized into 3 sections: fundamental concepts (n=23, 47.9% of the competencies), clinical trial development (n=23, 47.9% of the competencies), and certifications (n=2, 4.2% of the competencies).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This consensus defines the core competencies required of undergraduate life sciences students for entry-level participation in clinical trial research. It also provides a framework for designing training strategies in both undergraduate and graduate programs of study.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: ComCam preliminary software design: a systemic approach
container-title: Software and Cyberinfrastructure for Astronomy IX
e0e1f3afa173765c48ad599787996c650aaada86.abstract: <jats:p>ComCam is a medium-field visible imager conceived as a test camera – and likely a science instrument – for the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT). In terms of operation, the ComCam Device Control System (DCS) is responsible for all internal functionalities, responding to the Observatory Control System (OCS) at the top level, which orchestrates each DCS among ~30 controllable subsystems. The GMT adopts a domain engineering approach, in which a metamodel describes the observatory-wide architecture and a software development kit (SDK) is provided for DCS implementation. This work presents the systemic approach employed in developing the ComCam software design, suited to the compliance with GMT standards. A SysML model was developed using Visual Paradigm tool to capture the products from analysis to design, and to establish a partial representation of the ComCam DCS. Finally, the software components (e.g., controllers) and their properties could be transcribed into SDK specification files.</jats:p>

title: Beautiful Particulars
c6fe3d0377956ff06d423eb5e3d727284e365eac.abstract:
<jats:p>A fresh and eye-opening new explanation of AI—and how its focus on specifics is changing our ideas about ourselves and our world.From a Harvard researcher, philosopher, entrepreneur, former comedy writer, and bestselling author.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Amid the clamor about AI, Beautiful Particulars poses a unique question: Not how does our use of AI change what we do, but how is the idea of AI already subtly yet fundamentally reshaping how we think about ourselves and our world?</jats:p>
                  <jats:p/>
                  <jats:p>In clear, engaging, and even humorous prose, David Weinberger offers a new perspective on how machine learning works and how it may already be changing our basic and deepest ideas. Through lively examples, he shows that AI’s success—with all its risks and dangers—is taking us past our millennia of reliance on laws and principles by revealing what morality, free will, creativity, causality knowledge, and even reality itself look like now that we’re able to let the particulars speak their tiny truths.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p/>
                  <jats:p>The author poses questions not usually asked: What does a coin look like to AI? When AI gives you evidence that the earth is round, why are its own reasons for saying that so different? Why does an AI image generator create a “selfie” of ancient Aztec warriors with broad smiles that it “believes” are historically unlikely? If AI becomes conscious but bodiless, could it still make good moral decisions? Why is the world so much better at being causal than AI could ever “understand”? How does AI show us that genuine creativity is not about a “spark” but about moments that feel right? And how can you take the temperature of a joke?</jats:p>
                  <jats:p/>
                  <jats:p>Beautiful Particulars offers a new—and hopeful—perspective on how machine learning works, and how that’s already changing how we understand what it means to be human in the age of AI.</jats:p>

title: A CNN-Based Technique to Assist Layout-to-Generator Conversion for Analog Circuits
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
9d8d5f637e48e7f5f366eea75e35c8a6cbd65ae0.abstract: <jats:p>We propose a technique to assist in converting a reference layout of an analog circuit into the procedural layout generator by efficiently reusing available generators for sub-cell creation. The proposed convolutional neural network (CNN) model automatically detects sub-cells that can be generated by available generator scripts in the library, and suggests using them in the hierarchically correct places of the generator software. In experiments, the CNN model examined sub-cells of a high-speed wireline receiver that has a total of 4,885 sub-cell instances including 145 different sub-cell designs. The CNN model classified the sub-cell instances into 51 generatable and one not-generatable classes. One not-generatable class indicates that no available generator can generate the classified sub-cell. The CNN model achieved 99.3% precision in examining the 145 different sub-cell designs. The CNN model greatly reduced the examination time to 18 seconds from 88 minutes required in manual examination. Also, the proposed CNN model could correctly classify unfamiliar sub-cells that are very different from the training dataset.</jats:p>

title: Human mitochondrial DNA variants influence telomere length: evidence from a transmitochondrial cybrid model
4725b8e99f05ac13b837679013707693bcb6df16.abstract: <jats:p>Telomere shortening is a hallmark of aging, yet telomere length (TL) varies considerably among individuals and is strongly influenced by inheritance. In mice, efficient mitochondrial function-characterized by low reactive oxygen species (ROS) production-is critical for telomere elongation during early embryogenesis. Since mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) encodes several subunits of the electron transport chain, it may influence TL at birth by regulating mitochondrial function in utero. To explore the relationship between mtDNA and TL in human, we used a transmitochondrial cybrid approach, introducing mitochondria from donor platelets with varying telomere lengths into mtDNA-depleted cells. This revealed an inverse correlation between donor blood TL and mitochondrial ROS levels measured in the resulting cybrids, suggesting that specific mtDNA variants may contribute to the maintenance of long telomeres in humans by enhancing mitochondrial fitness. During in vitro cybrid formation, a transient phase of oxidative stress precedes cellular adaptation. In this specific window, mtDNA variants associated with reduced complex I (CI) activity induced rapid telomere shortening—an effect rescued by antioxidant and NAD⁺ precursor supplementation. While these variants occur naturally in certain individuals with long telomeres, our data suggest that, at least under in vitro conditions of acute oxidative stress, CI is critical to support PARP1 activity by maintaining the NAD⁺/NADH balance, thereby preserving telomere integrity. Collectively, these findings solidify the link between mtDNA variants and human TL regulation, highlighting potential therapeutic opportunities for mitochondrial replacement strategies.</jats:p>

title: More than a Judge: An Empirical Study of Agent–Human Interaction in Crowdsourced Testing Assessment
container-title: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
49975cd4125b898209e2142ed146e44a76b5602b.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Agentic AI is increasingly being integrated into software engineering workflows, and crowdsourced testing is no exception. In this setting, the large volume and uneven quality of submitted test reports still create a substantial review burden for developers. To help address this burden, we previously developed and validated a multi-agent assessment backbone based on the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm. The backbone, which assesses reports along the dimensions of textuality, adequacy, and competitiveness, was shown to align well with human consensus while substantially reducing assessment effort. Yet reliable automated judging does not by itself show whether agent outputs can improve human work when embedded into the workflow. This article studies that missing question in the context of crowdsourced testing. We investigate whether assessment-derived, actionable feedback can improve how testers revise reports, perform on later tasks, and transfer reporting practices across applications. To do so, we conducted a controlled four-stage human-subject study with 20 testers across three real-world applications. The results show that agent-generated feedback supports immediate improvements in revised reports, better first submissions on a new task after prior feedback exposure, and evidence of partial but meaningful transfer to a later application. A post-task questionnaire completed by 17 participants complements these artifact-based findings by suggesting that the feedback was generally understandable, acted upon in revision, and carried into later tasks, while also revealing remaining friction in specificity and execution. Overall, the study provides empirical evidence that, in the studied crowdsourced testing setting, assessment agents can serve not only as
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">post-hoc</jats:italic>
                    judges but also as workflow-integrated feedback providers that support upstream report-quality improvement.
                  </jats:p>

title: GTRCiM: Generic Temperature-Resilient Subthreshold-FeFET Based Compute-in-Memory
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
4deade109392dac2f175f8b26f4f54a125c17c60.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Compute-in-memory (CiM) offers a promising solution to the hardware challenges faced in artificial intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT), particularly in tackling the “memory wall” problem. By leveraging non-volatile memory (NVM) devices arranged in a crossbar structure, CiM efficiently accelerates multiply-accumulate (MAC) computations, which are essential for neural networks and various AI models. Emerging NVM, i.e., Ferroelectric FET (FeFET), is a particularly appealing choice for constructing ultra-low-power CiM arrays due to its CMOS compatibility, voltage-driven write/read mechanisms and high I
                    <jats:sub>
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">ON</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sub>
                    /I
                    <jats:sub>
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">OFF</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sub>
                    ratio. Operating FeFETs in the subthreshold region, i.e., subthreshold-FeFETs, further reduces power, but introduces vulnerability to temperature drift, leading to potential accuracy degradation. In this article, we present subthreshold-FeFET based temperature-resilient 2T-1FeFET and 2FeFET-1T CiM cell designs that address the temperature vulnerability. These two cells leverage feedback mechanisms to minimize the output current fluctuations caused by temperature drift. We further propose GTRCiM, a novel generic temperature-resilient CiM design that accommodates both our proposed CiM cells and other typical FeFET based cells while maintaining ultra-low-power consumption with subthreshold-FeFETs. By incorporating an additional column of the CiM array as a reference, and leveraging the temperature-resilient cell design, GTRCiM compensates for the effects of temperature drift, as temperature affects both arrays uniformly. We integrate the proposed GTRCiM array with typical 1FeFET-1R, and our proposed 2T-1FeFET, 2FeFET-1T cells and validate that GTRCiM enhances the temperature resilience with our proposed cells and even the temperature vulnerable 1FeFET-1R cell. Benchmarking results at system level using the NeuroSim framework show that our proposed GTRCiM array integrated with subthreshold-FeFET based 1FeFET-1R cells achieves 28.09 TOPS/W energy efficiency, surpassing existing CiM designs while maintaining sufficient temperature resilience.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p/>

title: Error analysis of a fully discrete structure-preserving finite element scheme for a diffuse-interface model of tumour growth
container-title: IMA Journal of Numerical Analysis
fe6b9e84bc72cca71001db7f4f92a365473b7b1e.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We develop a linear fully discrete structure-preserving finite element method for a diffuse-interface model of tumour growth. The system couples a Cahn–Hilliard-type equation with a nonlinear reaction–diffusion equation for nutrient concentration and admits a dissipative energy law at the continuous level. For the discretization we employ a scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) formulation together with a mixed finite element method for the Cahn–Hilliard part and standard conforming finite elements for the reaction–diffusion equation in space, combined with a first-order time-stepping scheme. The resulting method is unconditionally energy-stable, mass-preserving, and inherits a discrete energy dissipation law associated with the SAV-based approximate energy functional, while requiring the solution of only linear systems at each time step. Under suitable regularity assumptions on the exact solution we derive rigorous error estimates in the $L^{2}$, $H^{1}$ and $L^\infty $ norms, establishing first-order accuracy in time and optimal-order accuracy in space. A key step in this analysis is the proof of boundedness of the numerical solutions in $L^\infty $. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical convergence rates and demonstrate the robustness of the method in capturing characteristic phenomena such as aggregation and chemotactic tumour growth.</jats:p>

title: A physics-informed active learning framework for the inverse design of vacuum coatings
container-title: Friction
ae34ed81c5672e26d3d9a557c43e534317209d67.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The multiobjective optimization of physical vapor deposition (PVD), as a predominant modality of vacuum coating, is indispensable for surface engineering, yet its optimization is bottlenecked by the conflict between experimental efficiency and data scale. Traditional trial-and-error and purely data-driven machine learning (ML) suffer from low efficiency and severe overfitting under typical “small-sample” constraints, often recommending nonphysical or unsafe parameters. To address these challenges, this study proposes a closed-loop physics-informed active learning (PIAL) framework integrating three core modules: physics-enhanced feature engineering, a physics-regularized heteroscedastic neural network (PR-HNN), and a risk-aware dual-point batch acquisition strategy. By embedding fundamental sputtering kinetics into the PR-HNN via continuous partial derivative constraints, the model is softly regularized toward physically plausible monotonic and saturating trends within the investigated CoCrFeNiTi magnetron sputtering process window while effectively quantifying nonstationary experimental noise. Experimental results demonstrate that physics-based regularization reduces the generalization error of the PR-HNN by 41% compared to purely data-driven baselines, effectively eliminating nonphysical fluctuations in sparse data regions. Guided by the risk-aware acquisition function, the framework progressively expanded the initial Pareto front through three closed-loop iterations. The PIAL-optimized coatings achieved a peak hardness of approximately 13.4 GPa and a minimum wear depth of 0.25 μm while maintaining robust corrosion resistance. This methodology establishes a highly efficient, physically interpretable, and safe paradigm for artificial intelligence (AI)-driven surface engineering and high-performance coating development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: DECODE: Detecting Structural Obfuscation in HLS based DSP Designs using Machine Learning Framework
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
095f7ff7d24d9759b348b94a06c3ce25cdef85dd.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Structural obfuscation has been a widely used hardware security technique that is used to transform the internal structure of a high-level synthesis (HLS) digital signal processing (DSP) intellectual property (IP) design such that it becomes unobvious and obscure. The intent is to thwart deobfuscation/reverse-engineering (RE) attempts. These transformations in structurally obfuscated DSP designs are elusive and non-intuitive, making them arduous to identify and detect from an attacker's perspective. In this article, we for the first time, present a novel strategy for detecting structural obfuscation in HLS based DSP designs using machine learning (ML) frameworks. This article presents a novel technique called
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">‘DECODE’</jats:italic>
                    :
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">
                      <jats:underline>DE</jats:underline>
                      tecting Stru
                      <jats:underline>C</jats:underline>
                      tural
                      <jats:underline>O</jats:underline>
                      bfuscation in HLS based
                      <jats:underline>D</jats:underline>
                      SP Designs using Machine L
                      <jats:underline>E</jats:underline>
                      arning Framework
                    </jats:italic>
                    . The presented approach introduces a set of unique/distinct features that can successfully classify between structurally obfuscated HLS DSP designs and its non-obfuscated versions. The article also presents a novel ML database consisting of several instances of structurally obfuscated and un-obfuscated DSP HLS designs that can be fed into our ML framework (logistic regression and random forest classifier). Results of the proposed approach revealed successful detection of structurally obfuscated DSP designs with high accuracy.
                  </jats:p>

title: ModelAuflow: A Highly Scaffolded LLM-Orchestrated Framework for RF Passive Device Parameter Extraction
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
79f7352dad853b0722ee0d8cfd4d508a9af246c8.abstract: <jats:p>Accurate parameter extraction for RF passive devices is a critical step in semiconductor design because compact models directly determine the reliability of circuit simulation. Conventional extraction remains highly iterative and depends on substantial expert intervention for parameter grouping, optimizer selection, range adjustment, and curve-quality assessment. This article presents ModelAuflow, a highly scaffolded LLM-orchestrated framework for RF passive-device parameter extraction. The framework combines structured LLM reasoning with deterministic strategy conversion so that high-level optimization decisions are mapped into executable commands for commercial extraction tools. To improve convergence efficiency, the system integrates sensitivity-aware parameter filtering, historical self-reflection, and a classification knowledge base. Across the evaluated RF passive-device cases, the framework reduced the RMSE of a complex inductor below 3.5%, a capacitor below 2%, and a resistor below 1%. Under favorable initial conditions, the shortest successful extraction required 134 seconds and one optimization attempt. These results indicate that schema-constrained LLM orchestration can substantially reduce continuous manual intervention while maintaining accurate extraction for the evaluated RF passive-device workflows.</jats:p>

title: Introduction
container-title: Decolonial Human Rights Practice
e92fefb48b7236eac93f35b1b3c31ec89a7decff.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Human rights advocacy takes place within a deeply unequal world. As activists seek to protect rights, they struggle against the global economic and political power imbalances that drive violations. Movements for human rights are engaged in an internal struggle as well: against a human rights ecosystem that has long favored global north organizations at the expense of civil society in the global south. The Introduction provides a detailed summary of the findings of the coauthors’ novel global study of power relations among human rights organizations. The findings are based on over 150 interviews with activists from many countries, and the coauthors’ experiences as advocates. The Introduction provides an overview of the authors’ stakes and goals for this book and situates the book in the context of existing scholarship and critiques of human rights. It also explains the nature of contemporary human rights advocacy, and sets out the book’s research methods.</jats:p>

title: Everyday Practices and Effects
container-title: Decolonial Human Rights Practice
ce9edd330e9fc9c92d59434ac31fadb86f71daf0.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Chapter 2 argues that a common set of INGO advocacy practices reproduce and exacerbate inequities between NGOs in the global north and south. The chapter offers a framework to make visible these techniques of domination and their harmful effects. There are four interrelated elements of dominating advocacy practice: extraction, control, condescension, and recuperation. Extraction involves INGOs “mining” the expertise of global south advocates, in ways that produce INGOs as experts, and hoarding, where INGOs fail to report back or share information with south partners. Practices of control are INGO efforts to determine human rights agendas, strategy, representation, and finances. Condescension refers to INGO advocate beliefs, expressions, and practices of superiority that demean south advocates. Recuperation is a more recent and insidious development. As INGOs struggle to decolonize, colonial practices often coexist with reform efforts. Recuperation practices ostensibly respond to critiques of INGO domination, but with tokenism or other shallow approaches. Chapter 2 also examines in detail the harms caused when INGOs deploy these forms of advocacy practice.</jats:p>

title: Architecture
container-title: Decolonial Human Rights Practice
472ef3b09ecdb69e0e22527c247f338b69196fd3.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Chapter 3 explores structural and cultural aspects of the contemporary human rights ecosystem that enable or incentivize dominating advocacy practices, shape NGO power relations, and stymie decolonial and power-shifting reform efforts. Historical and ongoing inequities and injustices produce a human rights advocacy field that favors global north INGOs. The chapter examines the political economy of human rights advocacy, and systemic obstacles faced by south NGOs in accessing international advocacy opportunities and influencing advocacy targets, including English dominance, racism, nationality disadvantage, and distance from power centers. It examines “white savior” and “superstar” cultures, which have long persisted in dominant sectors of human rights, and directly link to colonial-era constructions of race, racial hierarchies, and ideas of Europeans “saving” victims. Finally, the chapter explores aspects of human rights violations—and how advocates commonly respond to and conceive of them—that shape NGO inequality and domination practices.</jats:p>

title: Build “Power Within” and Engage
container-title: Decolonial Human Rights Practice
379f5c034b4a4bc2f62a8b528e9c0c029289e4c6.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Chapter 4 examines resistance in partnership: how global south NGOs resist and/or empower when they also prioritize maintaining partnerships with INGOs. The chapter first analyzes “power within” or NGO conscientization (an organization’s understanding of oppression and of its own power), and sources of global south NGO power. South advocates’ assessment of power relations and of the NGO’s resources and capacities influences how they view the space available for resistance. The chapter then examines three common tactics south NGOs use to resist domination or build power while working with INGOs: strategic engagement, in which the global south NGO remains deliberately silent in the face of harmful practices; educate, to encourage INGOs to reflect and reform; and negotiate with INGOs to promote greater equality and condition partnerships on essential terms. The chapter analyzes what enables, restricts, or shapes these forms of resistance, and the kinds of effects they can have on power relations.</jats:p>

title: Condemn, Refuse, and Create
container-title: Decolonial Human Rights Practice
7c7ac8aa734354c69fe2e938778b359153480b6c.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Chapter 5 examines tactics in which south NGOs counter INGO domination, move away from INGO partnerships, and build their own agency. It explores three forms of tactics: condemn, refuse, and create. Where efforts to educate INGOs fail, south groups critique and call out INGO harms through condemnation, often applying a “name and shame” theory of change to INGO behavior. Global south NGOs use refuse tactics when they refuse to sign INGO documents, refuse information, or refuse funding; and in cases of strong domination, they may also refuse partnerships entirely. Build and create tactics grow south NGO agency, create new spaces and networks, and produce new knowledge or elevate alternative ideas—often independently of INGOs. The chapter explores numerous examples of these tactics, their interactions with other forms of resistance, INGO domination, and allyship, and what makes them possible, or ineffective. With these tactics, south NGOs endeavor to work outside spaces occupied by and the approaches used by INGOs, seeking to work in ways better aligned with their values and vision, and through constructive resistance that can contribute to decolonizing or transforming human rights methods and norms.</jats:p>

title: Unlearn Domination and Build “Power With”
container-title: Decolonial Human Rights Practice
89f6ca477292f187b5b2e7399f35e475ad731cb0.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Chapter 6 examines reforms internal to INGOs and global north advocates and related to beliefs, values, and priorities. Shifts at this level are important for ensuring that other changes in practice are rooted in principles of solidarity. The chapter focuses on the cultural, value, and attitudinal shifts foundational to shifting power relations in transnational advocacy partnerships. These shifts in the ideological dimension are important for ally practices to be meaningful, genuine, and transformative, rather than shallow or even counter-productive. The chapter examines the need for INGOs to engage in an (un)learning or challenging phase, and to also move toward the positive building up of a value-base centered on equality, solidarity, allyship, and building “power with.” The chapter explores obstacles to these internal shifts, and shares and challenges common frames around independence, efficiency, and capacity.</jats:p>

title: Build Equitable Partnerships
container-title: Decolonial Human Rights Practice
0e4954009d603c2e61fe44f2e83b106fcf0c0714.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Chapter 7 focuses on approaches to build equitable NGO partnerships. This chapter discusses two ally tactics for establishing interpersonal and organizational relations of trust, respect, and reciprocity. These tactics seek to counter the harmful impacts of colonization and global socioeconomic inequality on transnational NGO partnerships or coalitions. They are specific practices for equity and collaboration that enact within partnerships the value shifts from “power over” to “power with” discussed in Chapter 6. In the first tactic, Listen to Learn, INGOs listen to the expertise and priorities of south advocates. This involves a significant shift in orientation from INGO domination and is complex to implement in practice. The second tactic, Mutual Exchange, involves sharing knowledge and skills in a two-way flow. The chapter examines what incentivizes and supports these tactics, how they interact with global south resistance, and their limits, barriers, and effects.</jats:p>

title: Bend Privilege
container-title: Decolonial Human Rights Practice
504b01af6fc7dd88dd56f7ccd2efa2aa30e8e3c2.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Chapter 8 explores INGO tactics for supporting the power of global south NGOs in the human rights ecosystem. The chapter examines three privilege-bending tactics: Funding Equity, Recognition, and Amplification and Access. Funding Equity practices increase south NGO access to philanthropic networks and funds. The tactic is practiced directly between organizational partners, as well as outwardly to national or international levels in funder relations. Recognition aims to reverse the domination practice of extraction and to support global south power by crediting and foregrounding south NGO expertise and labor. This tactic is typically practiced outwardly and publicly, vis-à-vis actors such as the media, funders, and advocacy targets. Amplification and Access tactics work against inequality in voice in partnerships and structures by supporting global south advocates to participate and be heard in advocacy spaces. The chapter examines many examples of these tactics in practice, what supports or hinders them, their impacts and limitations, and the tensions inherent in INGOs using existing privileges to support global south partners and transform human rights practice.</jats:p>

title: Conclusions
container-title: Decolonial Human Rights Practice
fd74051d2076471877b6e9a5a416c2d3a70ce659.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Growing numbers of human rights organizations are seeking to break colonial-like relations between global north and global south groups. Many advocates push for change on a daily basis. Will the human rights field be able to institute the deep transformations of practice and structure required? Chapter 9 summarizes the main arguments and implications of the book, highlighting the urgent need for more concerted, collective, global efforts toward transformation. It argues that human rights movements constantly innovate and change, and that the human rights field is ripe for deeper reform.
