title: From Fragmented Adoption to Systematic Transformation: Curriculum Analysis and an Institutional Roadmap for AI Convergence Education at a Korean University
container-title: Education Sciences
d695ca21af7e3fbf7af2d4e2bf3eebdf2f836e3a.abstract: <jats:p>Higher education institutions are under mounting pressure to transform their curricula in response to artificial intelligence (AI), yet many universities—particularly teaching-focused private institutions facing demographic decline—struggle to move beyond fragmented, course-level adoption. This study examines how a mid-sized private university in South Korea diagnosed and redesigned its major curricula for AI convergence education, framing this transformation as an institutional survival and quality strategy amid a shrinking college-age population. The study combined four methods: analysis of national AI education policies and of domestic and international university cases; a complete census of all undergraduate major curricula (67 program units; 1646 courses across the 55 non-AI-specialist majors) using a four-type typology of AI-linkable courses; a needs survey of department heads and program chairs; and rapid prototyping of a staged curriculum framework. The curriculum analysis indicated an articulation gap: explicitly AI-articulated courses accounted for only 1.5% of the curriculum (25 courses in 13 of 55 majors), whereas courses provisionally identified as plausible candidates for AI integration were nearly eight times as numerous (193 courses, 11.7%) and present in 84% of majors, but were not connected to curriculum documentation, learning outcomes, or progression pathways; whether these courses already contain AI-related practice requires syllabus-level verification. Two-thirds of responding program leaders (66.7%) endorsed AI convergence education while prioritizing concerns about infrastructure, institutional support, and unverified learning effects. Based on these findings, the study proposes the CROSS AX competency model—crossing disciplinary expertise with AI application capability—operationalized through a three-stage curriculum structure (AX-Foundation, AX-Bridge, AX-Field Lab) and a five-phase institutional roadmap moving from shared infrastructure toward full curricular transformation with quality management; both were expert-reviewed and iteratively refined over two review rounds. The study offers a diagnostic typology and roadmap that may be adapted by universities seeking to institutionalize AI-driven curricular transformation rather than accumulate isolated initiatives.</jats:p>

title: Learning Chemistry with Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Phenomenological Study of Secondary School Students’ Experiences in Bayelsa State, Nigeria
container-title: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATION AND EVALUATION
2ef11c7527b21d3e626e9fdbc241643faa188b9f.abstract:
<jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence offers new opportunities for supporting Chemistry learning, but
accessible explanations may not translate into independent conceptual understanding. This
paper examined experiences of understanding Chemistry concepts, perceptions of usefulness and
challenges associated with generative artificial intelligence within a secondary school context in
Bayelsa State, Nigeria. A qualitative analysis informed by an interpretative phenomenological
approach was undertaken using ten participants. Analysis involved examining individual
accounts, identifying experiential meanings and comparing patterns across cases. The accounts
portrayed conceptual understanding as developing through manageable explanations,
recognition of errors, comparison with other resources, and independent practice. However,
apparent clarity sometimes coexisted with difficulties applying knowledge to unfamiliar
problems. Perceived usefulness centred on repeated clarification without embarrassment,
support outside classroom instruction, revision activities and alternative explanations.
Challenges included shared devices, data costs, unreliable connectivity, unfamiliar terminology,
uncertainty about response accuracy, difficulty formulating questions and the temptation to copy
solutions. The analysis suggests that generative artificial intelligence may serve as a
supplementary resource when combined with teacher guidance, textbooks, practical
demonstrations, and independent problem-solving. Faculty of Education, Niger Delta University,
Wilberforce Island, Bayelsa State</jats:p>

title: Effect of thermal sensation on cognitive performance
container-title: Pollack Periodica
53bc30e0ff67b9dc855c7d59c699c1fa64b7bd72.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Thermal sensation of the human body and cognitive performance are closely related. Extreme temperature conditions can significantly impair concentration, memory and mental state, leading to reduced productivity. It is therefore important to ensure appropriate climatic conditions to maintain productivity. This is particularly important in modern buildings, where thermal comfort can be ensured and guaranteed through building services engineering. It is uncertain, however, what the exact thermal satisfaction value is for people in terms of mental performance. There is both consensus and unresolved matters in the literature on the subject. The aim of this research is to investigate the optimal thermal comfort level with live subjects and by measuring thermal comfort parameters. It also aims to confirm or refute the results presented in the literature.</jats:p>

title: Compliance-by-Design in an AI-Enabled Platform for Early Crohn Disease Interception: A Viewpoint
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
51c3cf4682e1640bc274480c0925c7d09ca3e377.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>AI-enabled digital medicine platforms in Europe are developed within overlapping rules for personal data, medical devices, AI, clinical research, health data access, and health technology assessment. This viewpoint represents the authors’ experience and interpretation from the preimplementation phase of INTERCEPT, an Innovative Health Initiative consortium that plans to validate biomarkers and develop a blood-based risk score for early Crohn disease interception. It does not report original empirical research, a systematic regulatory review, a deployed platform, or a validated AI model. Our aim is to explain how compliance-by-design can be translated into an auditable governance architecture and to identify what still requires scientific evaluation. We advance 3 messages. First, governance must begin with intended purpose and boundary mapping: a digital platform may contain research, operational, and medical device software functions, and conformity of one module cannot be inferred for the platform as a whole. Second, overlapping obligations can be operationalized through 5 linked controls: modular responsibility and change control, federated data governance, traceable AI life cycle management, consent and participant rights orchestration, and a common cross-border governance core with local adaptations. Third, compliance is not a surrogate for model validity, clinical benefit, trust, scalability, or market access. Before clinical deployment, planned AI components require prespecified labels and cohorts, leakage prevention, missing data and imbalance strategies, calibration, subgroup assessment, external validation, human factors evaluation, and postdeployment algorithmovigilance. A hypothetical biomarker risk score update illustrates how the 5 controls interact. INTERCEPT is informative because it combines cross-border biomarker research, planned predictive analytics, and heterogeneous institutional settings while key design decisions remain modifiable. Its contribution is nevertheless conceptual: the proposed framework is a testable governance hypothesis, not evidence of implementation success. Prospective studies should compare it with alternative governance models and assess safety, workload, participant experience, evidence generation, and regulatory performance.</jats:p>

title: Association of eHealth Literacy With Cognitive Function, Frailty, and Functional Status in Hospitalized Geriatric Patients: Cross-Sectional Observational Study
container-title: JMIR Human Factors
ec5a1f530dd5164a01c8bee946e12a446e866836.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The rapid growth of digital health technologies has highlighted the importance of eHealth literacy, which is crucial for navigating health information and tools such as telemedicine and eHealth records. However, older adults often have reservations about digital technologies and face barriers due to cognitive, sensory, and motor impairments, which hinder their ability to effectively use digital health applications. Despite its relevance, research on eHealth literacy in older populations is limited, with a particular gap in understanding how self-assessments of eHealth literacy correlate with health characteristics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study seeks to explore eHealth literacy among hospitalized geriatric patients in Germany. The main objective is to evaluate the eHealth literacy level within this particular group and identify the clinical and sociodemographic factors that may influence it.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Data from this observational study were analyzed to explore characteristics influencing eHealth literacy in hospitalized geriatric patients. The study included patients aged 60 or older in the Department of Geriatric Medicine at Marien Hospital Herne and enrolled in the standardized early rehabilitation pathway. eHealth literacy was measured using the German version of the eHealth Literacy Scale (GR-eHEALS), a self-assessment tool. Sociodemographic and clinical data, including cognitive function (Montreal Cognitive Assessment [MoCA]), frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale [CFS]), and depression (Depression in Old Age Scale [DIA-S]), were collected. Statistical analyses involved descriptive statistics,
                      <jats:italic>t</jats:italic>
                      tests, chi-square tests, and regression analyses to examine the relationship between eHealth literacy and various factors. Sociodemographic and clinical data, including cognitive function (MoCA), frailty (CFS), and depression (DIA-S), were collected.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 244 participants (aged 60‐97, mean 77.2, SD 6.9 years) were included in the analysis. Participants generally reported an eHealth literacy, with higher scores in “information seeking” (mean 3.64, SD 0.84) compared to “information appraisal” (mean 3.32, SD 0.80). Significant differences in eHealth literacy were observed by age, with older participants scoring lower on both subscales. Frailty was significantly associated with critical appraisal of online health information (B=–1.372, 95% CI –2.554 to –0.189), suggesting that individuals who are frail struggle more with evaluating health information. No significant associations were found with other sociodemographic variables, including MoCA scores, education, or gender.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While the findings suggest a positive self-reported ability to engage with digital health tools, the selective sample and reliance on self-assessment limit the accuracy of these results. It also emphasizes the need for tailored interventions to support older adults in improving their eHealth literacy, particularly those with higher levels of frailty. Further research, including longitudinal studies and objective assessments, is essential to better understand and address the digital health needs of the geriatric population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Methods and Effectiveness of Auditory-Cognitive Training for Older Adults: Scoping Review and Meta-Analysis
container-title: JMIR Rehabilitation and Assistive Technologies
8c56aa534088f3531aa1721d2149a75ff1a11acc.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Auditory-cognitive training (ACT) combines auditory and cognitive exercises to improve listening and cognition in individuals with hearing difficulties; yet, it lacks standardized implementation and consistent evidence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This mixed-evidence synthesis aimed to map ACT’s implementation characteristics and summarize its reported short-term and maintenance effects on trained and nontrained cognitive and auditory outcomes, including hearing function in daily life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The review followed the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines and the Arksey and O’Malley scoping review framework. Databases searched included Embase, the Cochrane Library, PubMed, and APA PsycNet from inception to July 30, 2026. Articles were included or excluded based on specific criteria, and included articles were evaluated for risk of bias.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      ACT showed significant pooled effects on speech-in-noise performance (mean difference [MD]=−1.23 dB, 95% CI −2.35 to −0.10;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03), attention (standardized mean difference [SMD]=0.50, 95% CI 0.23-0.77;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001), memory (SMD=1.08, 95% CI 0.25-1.92;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.01), and global cognition (MD=3.27, 95% CI 0.27-6.26;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03). Effects on pure-tone audiometry, subjective hearing function, working memory, and executive function were limited and nonsignificant. Current evidence is limited by unstandardized training dosage/duration, limited linguistic generalizability across non-English languages, and insufficient assessment of patient-reported real-life listening outcomes.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>ACT may improve selected auditory and cognitive outcomes in older adults, particularly speech-in-noise perception, and attention. The evidence remains limited by substantial heterogeneity, a small number of studies, and low certainty for most outcomes. Standardized protocols, clinically meaningful outcome measures, and longer follow-up are needed to determine its clinical effectiveness and long-term benefits.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Bias in Medical AI in Relation to Patient Empowerment and Digital Equity: Scoping Review
container-title: Online Journal of Public Health Informatics
f32f1aabe6ae0bf9d4d8547544d818e333a71e0b.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI is increasingly embedded in health care and digital health applications, shaping clinical processes as well as how patients access information and participate in care. Research on bias in medical AI has largely focused on technical and performance-related disparities. Less attention has been paid to how such biases may affect patients’ access, understanding, trust, and opportunities for meaningful involvement in care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This scoping review aimed to map how studies of bias in medical AI describe patient-related consequences relevant to patient empowerment and the digital divide and to identify gaps across technical, social, structural, and patient-centered perspectives.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This scoping review followed JBI (Joanna Briggs Institute) methodology and PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) reporting guidance. PubMed/MEDLINE and EBSCOHost databases were searched in August 2025 and supplemented by Google Scholar searches. Peer-reviewed studies published from 2015 onward were included if they addressed bias in medical AI and described patient-related consequences relevant to patient empowerment or digital inequality. Data charting focused on AI application types, bias dimensions, patient empowerment domains, digital divide–related factors, intersectionality, and debiasing strategies. Findings were synthesized descriptively and thematically.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The search identified 497 records, of which 22 studies met the inclusion criteria. Bias was represented as a multidimensional sociotechnical phenomenon, with social bias identified most frequently (21/22 studies), followed by algorithmic bias (16/22 studies), structural bias (14/22 studies), and design-related bias (12/22 studies). Patient empowerment was most frequently addressed through involvement in care (n=13), followed by health literacy (n=9) and trust and assurance (n=7), whereas broader psychosocial and everyday-life domains were addressed less frequently. Digital divide–related factors were identified in 19 of the 22 studies, with digital literacy and usability barriers reported most frequently. Seven studies considered 2 or more social or structural dimensions of disadvantage. Although many studies discussed approaches that could mitigate bias-related barriers, explicit empirical evaluation of debiasing strategies in relation to patient empowerment or digital equity was largely absent.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Patient-related consequences of bias in medical AI extend beyond algorithmic performance and are reflected in access, understanding, trust, and involvement in care. Broader empowerment dimensions, multidimensional disadvantage, and empirically evaluated mitigation strategies remain comparatively underexplored.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Detecting Emotional Signals of Relationship Well-Being Using AI: A Cross-Sectional Comparison of Transformer-Based and Lexicon-Based Models for Couples Therapy Research

9a1dea4de03ecd7baadc72f963637ef4a595c7ee.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Natural language processing and AI models are increasingly used to extract emotional signals from textual data; however, systematic validation of different computational paradigms in emotionally complex relational contexts remains limited. Such approaches may contribute to digital health research, particularly in the fields of digital mental health and couples therapy, where understanding emotional expressions within romantic relationships is especially relevant.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to compare a lexicon-based approach (NRC Emotion Lexicon) and a transformer-based model (Pysentimiento) in detecting affective patterns within spontaneous romantic relationship narratives and to evaluate their criterion-related associations with a theory-driven measure of relational well-being.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this cross-sectional exploratory study, 112 Spanish adults completed the Couple Flourishing Measure (CFM) and provided an open-ended description of their romantic relationship. Narratives were analyzed using both computational approaches to generate emotion and sentiment indices. Pearson correlations were computed between model outputs and CFM scores. Steiger Z tests were conducted to compare dependent correlations across models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Both approaches showed significant associations with couple flourishing, although the transformer-based model yielded stronger correlations for several affective dimensions, particularly positive sentiment (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.66, 95% CI 0.54-0.76) and negative sentiment (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =−0.74, 95% CI −0.82 to −0.65). The lexicon-based approach showed smaller associations, primarily for negative emotions. Steiger Z tests identified significant between-model differences for disgust (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.04), joy (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.01), sadness (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.004), surprise (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03), and positive and negative sentiment (both
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001), but not for anger or fear.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this sample, Pysentimiento showed stronger associations with couple flourishing than the NRC Emotion Lexicon across several affective dimensions, although differences were not consistent across all categories. These findings support the value of theory-driven external criteria for evaluating computational emotion detection in relational narratives and underscore the importance of context-sensitive interpretation when applying AI tools in psychologically sensitive domains. These findings also highlight the potential relevance of computational emotion analysis for digital health research, particularly in digital mental health and couples therapy research, although further validation in clinical settings is needed before clinical implementation.</jats:p>

title: Minimizing classical resources in variational measurement-based quantum computation for generative modeling
container-title: Physical Review A
f6e3b076d2c8fe4a522ed55998ca8b61da435589.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC) is a framework for quantum information processing in which a computational task is carried out through one-qubit measurements on a highly entangled resource state. Due to the indeterminacy of the outcomes of a quantum measurement, the random outcomes of these operations, if not corrected, yield a variational quantum channel family. Traditionally, this randomness is corrected through classical processing in order to ensure deterministic unitary computations. Recently, variational measurement-based quantum computation (VMBQC) has been introduced to exploit this measurement-induced randomness to gain an advantage in generative modeling. A limitation of this approach is that the corresponding channel model has twice as many parameters compared with the unitary model, scaling as
                    <a:math xmlns:a="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <a:mrow>
                        <a:mi>N</a:mi>
                        <a:mo>×</a:mo>
                        <a:mi>D</a:mi>
                      </a:mrow>
                    </a:math>
                    , where
                    <b:math xmlns:b="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <b:mi>N</b:mi>
                    </b:math>
                    is the number of logical qubits (width) and
                    <c:math xmlns:c="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <c:mi>D</c:mi>
                    </c:math>
                    is the depth of the VMBQC model. This can often make optimization more difficult and may lead to poorly trainable models. In this paper, we present a restricted VMBQC model that extends the unitary setting to a channel-based one using only a single additional trainable parameter. We show, both numerically and algebraically, that this minimal extension is sufficient to generate probability distributions that cannot be represented by the corresponding unitary model.
                  </jats:p>

title: Micro-credentials in Comparative and International Education: Global Trends, Critical Success Factors, and Future Implications
container-title: Annual Review of Comparative and International Education 2025, Part B
ea66c902fc679a25c77368560a9d91c0fe2dd757.abstract: <jats:p>The rise of micro-credentials is a global response to shifting labour market demands, the growth of lifelong learning, and digital acceleration. Designed to be flexible, targeted, and competency-based recognitions of learning, micro-credentials challenge traditional higher education (HE) structures while offering opportunities for innovation, access, and global collaboration. This chapter explores the strategic implications of micro-credentials in HE, paying particular attention to leadership perspectives and institutional positioning. Through a thematic literature review of studies published between 2023 and 2025, it examines how micro-credentials are framed within educational ecosystems across diverse regions, where regulatory frameworks, funding mechanisms, and cultural norms influence their adoption and recognition. Central themes include the role of leadership in balancing technological progress with academic integrity, navigating challenges of quality assurance and equity, and managing tensions between institutional legitimacy, global rankings, and graduate employability. The findings contribute to the evolving discourse on micro-credentials by presenting a leadership decision-making framework that recognises the roles of leadership, policies, structures, stakeholders, and the internationalisation agenda at the macro-to-micro level. By highlighting leadership strategies and governance frameworks, this chapter provides insights into aligning micro-credentials with broader institutional and international agendas, with a particular focus on bridging the gap between the Global North and Global South.</jats:p>

title: Beyond Ethical Principles: A Comparative Review of National and Institutional AI Policies in Higher Education
container-title: Annual Review of Comparative and International Education 2025, Part B
8536db1c538358f24ed4b0c46d8e64444efc0c9d.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has produced a proliferation of ethical guidelines, national strategies, and institutional policies. Yet convergence around principles such as transparency, fairness, and accountability has not produced consistent governance outcomes across contexts. This chapter offers a comparative review of national and institutional AI policies in higher education, examining how ethical commitments are translated into regulatory frameworks and operational practice. Drawing on policy texts and institutional guidance from multiple regions, the analysis traces how governance logics shift as they move from ethical aspiration to national strategy and, ultimately, to institutional implementation. This chapter argues that national AI strategies consistently frame higher education instrumentally as part of workforce development and technological competitiveness agendas, while institutional responses remain shaped by organizational capacity, fiscal constraint, and fragmented governance. A cross-national comparison reveals that differences in regulatory philosophy matter less than variations in institutional design and resource distribution. This chapter concludes by identifying methodological implications for comparative education research and outlining a future agenda focused on policy translation, capacity building, and the uneven global distribution of educational risk associated with AI.</jats:p>

title: National AI Strategies and Higher Education in the Global South: Policy, Practice, and Power
container-title: Annual Review of Comparative and International Education 2025, Part B
aea880b7dde6be71ddcff68393b451b2c7d9de49.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how national artificial intelligence (AI) strategies are translated into higher education (HE) policy and practice across the Global South (GS), with particular attention to issues of equity, governance, and power. Drawing on cases from Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), and South Africa, this chapter explores how universities are positioned within national AI agendas and respond through fragmented policies, pedagogical experiments, administrative adoption, and partnerships. The analysis also highlights how structural constraints shape institutional responses and how Global North–developed AI intensifies concerns about autonomy, bias, and inequalities within and between HE systems. Situating these dynamics within the broader political economy of AI, this chapter shows how market concentration, industry influence, and North–South power relations shape both the possibilities and limits of AI integration in GS universities. It argues that meaningful, context-responsive AI adoption requires closer alignment between national strategies and institutional governance, sustained public investment, and equity-focused pedagogical frameworks that move beyond market-driven models of innovation.</jats:p>

title: Impact of ChatGPT on Academic Integrity among Youth: Mediating Role of Critical Thinking
container-title: Pakistan Journal of Positive Psychology
02fef5bdca9dd7afe51bf3058d7bfa0ea9412d04.abstract: <jats:p>The study aimed to check the association of ChatGPT use and critical thinking on academic integrity.  The research design is cross-sectional correlational study to collect data from university students aged from 18 to 23 years old. The sample size was 600 students taken via purposive sampling from the University of Gujrat, Pakistan. Standardized psychological scales of ChatGPT usage scale, critical thinking evaluation scale, and academic integrity scales were used. Our findings showed that ChatGPT has no significant effect on academic integrity but has positive effect on critical thinking. While critical thinking has positive effect on academic integrity. It showed that ChatGPT doesn’t directly change cheating behavior, but it can boost critical thinking for students, and that improved critical thinking is what increases academic integrity. Implications of the findings are discussed.</jats:p>

title: Refugee Stereotypes in Teacher Education: Towards a Critical Migration Literacy (CML)
container-title: Refugee Education in Canada
f88721fda78aa33a509d521f8a40110bd70762f1.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how teacher education programs can prepare future educators to critically examine and challenge stereotypes about refugees through a Critical Migration Literacy (CML) framework. Situated within the broader context of whiteness in teacher education, the study draws on critical pedagogy and service-learning theory to analyze the reflections of per-service teachers from an Ontario teacher-preparation course focused on teaching students from newcomer backgrounds. Discourse analysis of a classroom discussion on refugee stereotypes revealed three themes: the refugee as ‘other’, the ‘good refugee’ as ‘model minority’, and the privilege-disadvantage dichotomy. The findings highlight how dominant sociopolitical discourses and the racialized norms of a predominantly white teaching workforce shape perceptions of students with refugee status. The chapter argues that embedding CML in teacher education can foster critical consciousness and support more equitable engagement with refugee learners.</jats:p>

title: Newly Qualified Teachers Fostering Inclusive Education for Their Refugee Students: A Critical Children’s Rights Studies and Critical Multicultural Education Perspective
container-title: Refugee Education in Canada
7942a35ca64b12f8c58a9b1b57fd7132e1cc1e6e.abstract:
<jats:p>As Children’s Rights Studies (CRS) emerged alongside the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, there has been a predominant legal focus to the field. However, over time, Critical Children’s Rights Studies (CCRS) emerged to problematize normative legal assumptions and situate children in their life worlds to more holistically advance their rights.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Multicultural Education (ME) developed as demographics diversified, with aims to inform laws, norms, and values that reduce prejudice and promote equality for all students. While an important endeavour, it has importantly advanced through Critical Multicultural Education’s (CME) emergence; an equity-based approach that can address historical wrongs and support social justice through education.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Canada has a long-standing legal commitment to multiculturalism through the integration of newcomers, including refugee children, and the school is a uniquely situated community space within which multicultural principles can transpire. However, while refugee children may experience social inclusion, they may just as well experience social exclusion despite their right to a sustained sense of belonging.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This project sees CCRS and CME come together as a united analytical framework to explore the strategies and experiences that newly certified teachers and refugee students, respectively, encounter in relation to children’s rights, multiculturalism, and inclusive educational practices in their Toronto, Ontario schools. It is argued that this heightened commitment to theoretical analysis can offer insights into ensuring a safer, more inclusive, and equitable environment that may better advance refugee students’ right to social inclusion at school.</jats:p>

title: Applications and challenges of biocementation in ground improvement: a critical review
container-title: Geotechnical Aspects of Land Reclamation and Ground Improvement
62fdbc12eecc8a448ad693ec26a4f548cbe635da.abstract: <jats:p>Biocementation is a new sustainable and green technology in the area of geotechnical engineering. Biocementation enhances the strength of the soil and improvements in the engineering characteristics can also be observed. The most common biocementation technique is microbially induced calcite precipitation (MICP) which can be introduced into the soil by bioaugmenting or biostimulating ureolytic bacteria in the soil. These ureolytic bacteria help to fill the pore spaces of the soil and enhance its strength characteristics through the formation of calcite precipitate. This treatment can be used due to both its lesser impact on the environment and cost-effectiveness. However, the optimization of this technique needs more research for successful implementation in the field. This chapter aims to critically review applications of various biocementation techniques and their implementation in the area of geotechnical engineering.</jats:p>

title: Critical Pillars of Competitive Edge for Firms in the Digital Era
container-title: A Comparative Handbook of Redesigned Sales and Marketing Management in the Digital Era
09bbd5ba9b057e1dbb3d3c42c2df721c7869b840.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Today, one of the critical success factors of long-term profitable business in the highly competitive arena is the digital transformation by utilizing the benefits of technology, streamlining the workflow of operations, automating routine tasks to improve the business efficiency and productivity. On the other hand, the technologies are still not at the complete maturity stage including the cybersecurity concerns while the growth of digital technologies is very fast, setting expectations for overcoming the existing challenges by profiting from the data-based insights, real-time information, interactive communication without the geographical barriers as well as automation and optimization of processes impacting the operational excellency and faster decision mechanisms. Also, consumers have evolved into more conscious buyers profiting from digital platforms, social media, and real-time information encouraging them for personalized solutions matching their care abouts. This new phenomenon equally bridges the customer and the firm for co-creating value by faster innovations. In the interim, there are major criteria for impactful digital transformation, and this chapter underlines the essence of 11 parameters with an authentic scheme addressing the readiness for competitive edge. The firms are expected to have a cultural organizational change toward digitalization by investing in new technologies, in house IT with a focus of improving digital competencies of their employees, channel partners, and human resource management (HRM) stakeholders. The corporate governance digital transformation strategy with the set key performance indicators (KPIs) embracing compliance, digital ethics, cybersecurity infrastructures, and sustainability efforts are crucial for long-term profitable business.</jats:p>

title: Diminishing returns to calibrated reliance on AI: effects on deliverable quality and rework effort, moderated by task verifiability
container-title: Information Technology & People
18ace5ca3b42d9fb0b8f41f64d72dabeee644487.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) tools can function as both “performance accelerators” and “risk propagators” in organizations. This study investigates how AI-enabled work capability, particularly employees' decomposition and evaluation skills, is associated with deliverable quality and rework effort through the behavioral pathway of calibrated reliance on AI. Additionally, it examines task verifiability as a critical boundary condition that shapes the effectiveness of human-AI collaboration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Guided by appropriate reliance and automation trust theories, data from 380 workers were analyzed using SmartPLS 4 (partial least squares structural equation modeling) and hierarchical polynomial regression to test mediation, moderation, and quadratic effects. Procedural remedies and a latent method factor approach were employed to assess common method bias.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI-enabled work capability was positively associated with calibrated reliance on AI. Calibrated reliance on AI was associated with higher deliverable quality and lower rework effort. A double diminishing marginal pattern emerged: as reliance calibration increased, quality gains and rework reductions leveled off, indicating a “too-much-of-a-good-thing” pattern. Task verifiability strengthened the positive association between calibrated reliance and deliverable quality and also strengthened its negative association with rework effort.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study shifts the focus from reliance intensity to reliance calibration in explaining AI-enabled work outcomes. It documents a double diminishing marginal pattern, showing that the benefits of calibrated reliance are meaningful but not unlimited. It also identifies task verifiability as a boundary condition that helps explain when calibrated reliance is more strongly associated with improved deliverable quality and reduced rework effort. These findings provide focused guidance for capability development, reliance calibration, and task-specific AI governance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Newspapers Blocking AI Crawlers Expose Their Voters to a Partisan Flood
ff70f45920800194d1d03e1d4f840cbc01c7805f.abstract: Major newspapers block AI crawlers, while parties and partisan sites leave their text open. This paper builds a game-theoretic model of the hold-out and asks what voters hear while it lasts. In the model, an AI that cannot grade its sources pools the text it can read; two persuaders choose how much nearly free text to publish; and an AI lab may license a newspaper's reporting for its lost revenue. Neither the newspapers nor the lab has a political aim. Three results follow. First, the persuaders flood the AI, and the lab licenses each newspaper once a fixed share of the voters closest to it asks the AI, whatever the AI says. Second, newspapers whose voters dislike the AI's answers more hold out longer, and their voters hear the flood longer. Third, licensing bends the persuaders' contest by a small tilt from where the costs alone put it: patient persuaders tilt the AI's answers against the voters' average ideology, and impatient ones toward it. Business decisions with no political aim thus set how long each group hears the flood and which way the AI's answers tilt.

title: Disentangling fairness, accountability and transparency in AI travel recommendations: the role of algorithm trust across hedonic and utilitarian contexts
container-title: Journal of Hospitality and Tourism Technology
738b7c93882da5391370ebea7288b2d89b749fc4.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to examine how tourists’ perceptions of fairness, accountability and transparency (FAT) in artificial intelligence (AI) recommendation algorithms shape algorithm trust and how trust influences recommendation acceptance and resistance, with tourism product type as a moderator.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A scenario-based online survey of 355 Korean adult consumers was conducted via travel-related Naver cafés and KakaoTalk communities. Hypotheses were tested with structural equation modeling in AMOS 23.0, and the moderating role of tourism product type was assessed through multigroup analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>All three FAT dimensions positively predicted algorithm trust, with transparency showing the largest effect, followed by accountability and fairness. Algorithm trust positively predicted recommendation acceptance and reduced resistance. Indirect effects through trust were significant for accountability and transparency but not fairness; accountability influenced trust only in the utilitarian condition.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Self-reported, cross-sectional data from a Korean-only sample may limit causal inference and generalizability. Future research could use objective behavioral data, longitudinal designs and cross-cultural samples to extend the FAT–trust–behavior framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Tourism platforms should prioritize explainable AI features, adopt context-sensitive communication – emphasizing accountability cues for utilitarian services and transparency-based emotional appeal for hedonic ones – and focus on building trust at the first AI recommendation touchpoint.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings provide empirical grounding for tourism-specific AI governance. The dominant role of transparency suggests that policymakers should consider introducing recommendation rationale disclosure requirements for AI-powered tourism platforms, enabling consumers to understand why specific products are suggested. In addition, the finding that consumers cannot directly evaluate algorithmic fairness highlights the need for independent, third-party fairness audits of recommendation systems to protect consumers from potential algorithmic bias that may systematically favor certain destinations, accommodations or price segments over others.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study is one of the few to empirically apply the AI ethics FAT framework to tourism consumer behavior. The findings suggest that the three FAT dimensions may not contribute equally to algorithm trust – with transparency showing the strongest association regardless of context and accountability becoming relevant primarily in utilitarian service settings – which points to the limitations of treating FAT as a uniform construct in AI recommendation design. The resulting framework offers tourism platforms an empirical basis for tailoring AI trust strategies to specific product categories.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: Transformative Potential, Implementation Challenges, and Future Trajectories
container-title: Journal of Research in Engineering and Computer Sciences
4f57fb5aa53ffc9a9ad9de6e928127777efd4d6e.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into educational systems has accelerated dramatically, transitioning from experimental pilot programs to mainstream pedagogical practice by 2026. This paper examines the current landscape of AI in education through quantitative analysis of global adoption data, stakeholder perceptions, and performance outcomes. Drawing on surveys from over 3,800 students across 16 countries, institutional reports, and longitudinal studies, we find that 86% of higher education students now utilize AI tools. In contrast, 60% of teachers have integrated AI into their teaching practice. The global AI education market is projected to reach $112.03 billion by 2034, reflecting a compound annual growth rate of approximately 38%. However, significant challenges persist: 65% of educators’ express concern about plagiarism, 71% of K-12 teachers lack formal AI training, and only 7% of schools worldwide have established AI usage guidance. This paper synthesizes current evidence, identifies critical implementation barriers, and proposes a framework for responsible AI integration that preserves human-centric pedagogy while leveraging technological affordances.</jats:p>

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE APPS: ENEMY OR FRIEND IN ESP SEMINARS? A CASE STUDY WITH 1ST YEAR ECONOMICS UNDERGRADUATES
container-title: The International Conference Synergies in Communication
c2116a25db56f173319947a42953b784a6c2b53e.abstract:
<jats:p>This paper addresses the multifaceted impact of AI on ESP-based language learning environments.
Increasingly present in education through a wide array of tools – AI powered learning platforms,
virtual tutors, speaking tools, chatbots, customized feedback systems – AI technology is both prized
for enhancing foreign language learning, but also questioned for generating over-reliance on
technology, lack of equity and lack of students’ engagement. This paper researches and presents a
case study showing relevant data on students’ individual patterns of approaching and using AI tools
for academic ESP tasks. In assessing the popularity and influence of such tools on students’ training
process, the directions followed in this paper aim to reveal students’ understanding of AI tools
general usage, the frequency of use, its impact on learning, creativity and originality, as well as some
ethical considerations. The beneficiary target group consists of first-year Economics students from
the Bucharest University of Economic Studies, Romania, majoring in Business Administration and
Finance and Banking.</jats:p>

title: THE MISERABLE EMPATH. ABOUT THE DARK SIDE OF EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE
container-title: The International Conference Synergies in Communication
a52c35b5e775ef84a157326dcab7e9c4292a75a8.abstract:
<jats:p>This paper makes a short incursion into emotional intelligence and its potential implications with
regard to mental health issues and other negative effects. It was initially assumed that emotional
intelligence would have a good impact on health, overall wellbeing, interpersonal relations and
would be a predictor of success at the workplace. However, more recent studies have also explored
the darker sides of emotional intelligence and have shown that it might have downsides for the
individual as well. Aspects such as increased sensitivity, heightened affective states and overemphasis on emotions can represent drawbacks for emotionally intelligent people, making them more vulnerable, hindering their judgment, or impairing their social and professional performance.
Empathy is one of the core dimensions of emotional intelligence and we can argue that it is the most
likely to have destructive influence, to be emotionally draining and overwhelming for the person who
exhibits an empathetic mindset and behavior. The present paper includes a small experiment that
investigates the relationship between empathy and sadness, or depressive tendencies. The results
indicate that individuals who display a predisposition to depression or report a history of depression score higher in several components of emotional intelligence, particularly in empathy. Differences between men and women are also taken into consideration and prove to be relevant in the analysis.</jats:p>

title: Effect of thermal sensation on cognitive performance
container-title: Pollack Periodica
53bc30e0ff67b9dc855c7d59c699c1fa64b7bd72.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Thermal sensation of the human body and cognitive performance are closely related. Extreme temperature conditions can significantly impair concentration, memory and mental state, leading to reduced productivity. It is therefore important to ensure appropriate climatic conditions to maintain productivity. This is particularly important in modern buildings, where thermal comfort can be ensured and guaranteed through building services engineering. It is uncertain, however, what the exact thermal satisfaction value is for people in terms of mental performance. There is both consensus and unresolved matters in the literature on the subject. The aim of this research is to investigate the optimal thermal comfort level with live subjects and by measuring thermal comfort parameters. It also aims to confirm or refute the results presented in the literature.</jats:p>

title: Association of eHealth Literacy With Cognitive Function, Frailty, and Functional Status in Hospitalized Geriatric Patients: Cross-Sectional Observational Study
container-title: JMIR Human Factors
ec5a1f530dd5164a01c8bee946e12a446e866836.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The rapid growth of digital health technologies has highlighted the importance of eHealth literacy, which is crucial for navigating health information and tools such as telemedicine and eHealth records. However, older adults often have reservations about digital technologies and face barriers due to cognitive, sensory, and motor impairments, which hinder their ability to effectively use digital health applications. Despite its relevance, research on eHealth literacy in older populations is limited, with a particular gap in understanding how self-assessments of eHealth literacy correlate with health characteristics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study seeks to explore eHealth literacy among hospitalized geriatric patients in Germany. The main objective is to evaluate the eHealth literacy level within this particular group and identify the clinical and sociodemographic factors that may influence it.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Data from this observational study were analyzed to explore characteristics influencing eHealth literacy in hospitalized geriatric patients. The study included patients aged 60 or older in the Department of Geriatric Medicine at Marien Hospital Herne and enrolled in the standardized early rehabilitation pathway. eHealth literacy was measured using the German version of the eHealth Literacy Scale (GR-eHEALS), a self-assessment tool. Sociodemographic and clinical data, including cognitive function (Montreal Cognitive Assessment [MoCA]), frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale [CFS]), and depression (Depression in Old Age Scale [DIA-S]), were collected. Statistical analyses involved descriptive statistics,
                      <jats:italic>t</jats:italic>
                      tests, chi-square tests, and regression analyses to examine the relationship between eHealth literacy and various factors. Sociodemographic and clinical data, including cognitive function (MoCA), frailty (CFS), and depression (DIA-S), were collected.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 244 participants (aged 60‐97, mean 77.2, SD 6.9 years) were included in the analysis. Participants generally reported an eHealth literacy, with higher scores in “information seeking” (mean 3.64, SD 0.84) compared to “information appraisal” (mean 3.32, SD 0.80). Significant differences in eHealth literacy were observed by age, with older participants scoring lower on both subscales. Frailty was significantly associated with critical appraisal of online health information (B=–1.372, 95% CI –2.554 to –0.189), suggesting that individuals who are frail struggle more with evaluating health information. No significant associations were found with other sociodemographic variables, including MoCA scores, education, or gender.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While the findings suggest a positive self-reported ability to engage with digital health tools, the selective sample and reliance on self-assessment limit the accuracy of these results. It also emphasizes the need for tailored interventions to support older adults in improving their eHealth literacy, particularly those with higher levels of frailty. Further research, including longitudinal studies and objective assessments, is essential to better understand and address the digital health needs of the geriatric population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Methods and Effectiveness of Auditory-Cognitive Training for Older Adults: Scoping Review and Meta-Analysis
container-title: JMIR Rehabilitation and Assistive Technologies
8c56aa534088f3531aa1721d2149a75ff1a11acc.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Auditory-cognitive training (ACT) combines auditory and cognitive exercises to improve listening and cognition in individuals with hearing difficulties; yet, it lacks standardized implementation and consistent evidence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This mixed-evidence synthesis aimed to map ACT’s implementation characteristics and summarize its reported short-term and maintenance effects on trained and nontrained cognitive and auditory outcomes, including hearing function in daily life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The review followed the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines and the Arksey and O’Malley scoping review framework. Databases searched included Embase, the Cochrane Library, PubMed, and APA PsycNet from inception to July 30, 2026. Articles were included or excluded based on specific criteria, and included articles were evaluated for risk of bias.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      ACT showed significant pooled effects on speech-in-noise performance (mean difference [MD]=−1.23 dB, 95% CI −2.35 to −0.10;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03), attention (standardized mean difference [SMD]=0.50, 95% CI 0.23-0.77;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001), memory (SMD=1.08, 95% CI 0.25-1.92;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.01), and global cognition (MD=3.27, 95% CI 0.27-6.26;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03). Effects on pure-tone audiometry, subjective hearing function, working memory, and executive function were limited and nonsignificant. Current evidence is limited by unstandardized training dosage/duration, limited linguistic generalizability across non-English languages, and insufficient assessment of patient-reported real-life listening outcomes.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>ACT may improve selected auditory and cognitive outcomes in older adults, particularly speech-in-noise perception, and attention. The evidence remains limited by substantial heterogeneity, a small number of studies, and low certainty for most outcomes. Standardized protocols, clinically meaningful outcome measures, and longer follow-up are needed to determine its clinical effectiveness and long-term benefits.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Impact of ChatGPT on Academic Integrity among Youth: Mediating Role of Critical Thinking
container-title: Pakistan Journal of Positive Psychology
02fef5bdca9dd7afe51bf3058d7bfa0ea9412d04.abstract: <jats:p>The study aimed to check the association of ChatGPT use and critical thinking on academic integrity.  The research design is cross-sectional correlational study to collect data from university students aged from 18 to 23 years old. The sample size was 600 students taken via purposive sampling from the University of Gujrat, Pakistan. Standardized psychological scales of ChatGPT usage scale, critical thinking evaluation scale, and academic integrity scales were used. Our findings showed that ChatGPT has no significant effect on academic integrity but has positive effect on critical thinking. While critical thinking has positive effect on academic integrity. It showed that ChatGPT doesn’t directly change cheating behavior, but it can boost critical thinking for students, and that improved critical thinking is what increases academic integrity. Implications of the findings are discussed.</jats:p>

title: NBD-Net: a structured degradation memory and local-global bridging network for lithium-ion battery remaining useful life prediction
container-title: Measurement Science and Technology
8c03d2c97d56b1e68b27b736b5a2ab9dc505e5dd.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Remaining useful life (RUL) prediction of lithium-ion batteries from measured capacity is a core function of battery management, but public datasets contain few cells, a predictor must generalize to unseen cells, and training cells often miss the late-life regime. This paper proposes NBD-Net, a Nonstationary-Bridged Degradation Network for next-cycle capacity prediction, and examines which elements make it reliable on unseen cells. NBD-Net normalizes each input window (reversible instance normalization), encodes it with a local stabilization branch, a causal detrending followed by learned causal convolutions, in parallel with a recurrent trend encoder, and couples the two branches through an attention memory (SDMC) and a bidirectional cross-attention bridge (LGBI). Under a leave-one-battery-out protocol covering all eleven cells of the CALCE, NASA, and TJU datasets, NBD-Net has the lowest capacity root mean square error of nine models on every unseen cell, 9%–27% below the strongest baseline of each dataset, also after nested tuning of all models. When the training cells cover only the first half of life, it remains the most accurate model on every cell, and its error grows by 29% where that of PatchTST and TCN grows by 160% and 222%. Controlled experiments attribute these two results to different elements: with complete training data the per-window normalization carries the advantage, lowering the error by 22%–34% on every cell, so that a normalized recurrent predictor reaches comparable accuracy; with incomplete training data the local stabilization branch provides 84% of the gain over the recurrent backbone, whereas SDMC and LGBI add smaller gains at regeneration events and in late life. The results hold for next-cycle prediction under one cycling condition per dataset; its RUL relative error statistically matches that of the baselines, and its accuracy gain holds while input noise stays comparable to the scatter of the training data. The source code is publicly available at:
                    <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="https://github.com/luxing-just/NBDNet_open_source">https://github.com/luxing-just/NBDNet_open_source</jats:ext-link>
                    .
                  </jats:p>

title: Diminishing returns to calibrated reliance on AI: effects on deliverable quality and rework effort, moderated by task verifiability
container-title: Information Technology & People
18ace5ca3b42d9fb0b8f41f64d72dabeee644487.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) tools can function as both “performance accelerators” and “risk propagators” in organizations. This study investigates how AI-enabled work capability, particularly employees' decomposition and evaluation skills, is associated with deliverable quality and rework effort through the behavioral pathway of calibrated reliance on AI. Additionally, it examines task verifiability as a critical boundary condition that shapes the effectiveness of human-AI collaboration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Guided by appropriate reliance and automation trust theories, data from 380 workers were analyzed using SmartPLS 4 (partial least squares structural equation modeling) and hierarchical polynomial regression to test mediation, moderation, and quadratic effects. Procedural remedies and a latent method factor approach were employed to assess common method bias.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI-enabled work capability was positively associated with calibrated reliance on AI. Calibrated reliance on AI was associated with higher deliverable quality and lower rework effort. A double diminishing marginal pattern emerged: as reliance calibration increased, quality gains and rework reductions leveled off, indicating a “too-much-of-a-good-thing” pattern. Task verifiability strengthened the positive association between calibrated reliance and deliverable quality and also strengthened its negative association with rework effort.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study shifts the focus from reliance intensity to reliance calibration in explaining AI-enabled work outcomes. It documents a double diminishing marginal pattern, showing that the benefits of calibrated reliance are meaningful but not unlimited. It also identifies task verifiability as a boundary condition that helps explain when calibrated reliance is more strongly associated with improved deliverable quality and reduced rework effort. These findings provide focused guidance for capability development, reliance calibration, and task-specific AI governance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Talent analytics: a systematic review and topic modeling approach
container-title: Global Knowledge, Memory and Communication
3dad544bd8a12e3c5f0732d73366666724907d9b.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Talent analytics has emerged as a vital tool for enhancing organizational effectiveness by informing strategies for attracting, developing and retaining talent, as well as predicting employee turnover. In response to growing interest in data-driven decision-making, this study aims to explore recent developments in talent analytics, synthesizing key themes from the literature and proposing directions for future research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper presents a systematic literature review of 117 scholarly publications retrieved from the Scopus database. To uncover underlying thematic structures, this study uses Latent Dirichlet Allocation, a topic modeling technique that enables the identification of prominent research clusters within the field.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis identifies three themes: attraction in talent management, development and retention in talent management and applications of talent analytics in sports. Their configuration indicates that talent analytics is progressing from discrete analytical applications toward a broader organizational capability spanning the talent lifecycle. The findings of this study further show that the value of this capability depends on managerial translation, contextual applicability and the legitimacy and governance of data-driven talent decisions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study moves beyond descriptive mapping of talent analytics by combining topic modeling with qualitative interpretation to examine relationships among research streams across the talent lifecycle. The synthesis positions talent analytics as an emerging organizational capability whose value depends on strategic alignment, complementary organizational capabilities, contextual applicability and responsible governance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: AI-mediated teacher learning in Chinese lesson study: regulating cognitive demands in EFL pre-service teachers
container-title: International Journal for Lesson & Learning Studies
0e6125580ca1df6bbbbb713f6ce60254ae38faa1.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study, guided by the cognitive theory of multimedia learning (CTML), investigates how multimodal large language models (MLLMs) mediate the professional learning of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) pre-service teachers within Chinese lesson study (CLS). It aims to elucidate the cognitive and dialogic mechanisms through which AI-supported mediation shapes teacher learning processes and participation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A three-month intervention integrating MLLMs into CLS was conducted with 50 EFL pre-service teachers at a Chinese normal university. Adopting an interpretive qualitative design, data were collected from longitudinal reflective journals, MLLM interaction logs, field notes and two rounds of semi-structured interviews with 5 purposively selected focal participants. Data analysis combined deductive coding based on CTML (intrinsic, extraneous and germane cognitive load) with inductive thematic analysis to capture emergent patterns of AI-mediated learning and interaction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings reveal that MLLMs functioned as cognitive-dialogic mediators in three key ways: (1) reducing linguistic and organizational barriers, thereby lowering extraneous cognitive load; (2) redistributing cognitive resources to support meaning-making and pedagogical reasoning; and (3) enabling deeper engagement in collaborative knowledge construction and reflective inquiry within CLS. However, participants also reported tensions related to epistemic reliability and the risk of overreliance on AI-generated outputs, indicating a shift in cognitive demands from knowledge construction to evaluation and regulation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study advances the field by proposing a cognitive-dialogic framework that brings CTML into dialog with sociocultural perspectives on mediation, offering a nuanced account of how AI reshapes teacher learning in practice-based settings. It contributes empirical evidence on the role of MLLMs as mediating tools in CLS and provides design implications for cognitively and ethically informed AI integration in teacher education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Less effort, less meaning? Authorship ambiguity and impostor-like experiences in GenAI-mediated knowledge work
container-title: Journal of Enterprise Information Management
e6ba728929d70207fe480d161dff79d0ede6a1a0.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines how knowledge workers make sense of GenAI-enabled co-production, with particular attention to authorship ambiguity and its implications for competence attribution, self-evaluation and meaningful work.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study uses a qualitative approach based on in-depth interviews with 32 knowledge workers who work directly with GenAI tools, combining inductive coding with abductive interpretation. We used the Gioia methodology to analyze participants' reported experiences and interpretations of human–AI collaboration, with sensemaking informing the interpretation of emergent themes and aggregate dimensions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings identify authorship ambiguity as a central interpretive challenge in GenAI-mediated knowledge work. When GenAI contributes to ideation, analysis, drafting, coding or other knowledge-intensive outputs, workers may find it difficult to distinguish their own contribution from that of the technology. Participants responded to this ambiguity differently. Some reconstructed their expertise around judgment, validation and contextualization and experienced GenAI as extending their professional capability. Others struggled to internalize successful outputs as evidence of their own competence and reported impostor-like experiences and reduced meaningfulness. The findings suggest that experiences of GenAI-enabled co-production depend on whether workers interpret and reconstruct their contribution.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Managers in comparable knowledge-intensive settings may consider making human judgment visible, clarifying legitimate uses of GenAI and recognizing contributions beyond output speed and quality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study identifies authorship ambiguity as a central interpretive challenge in GenAI-mediated knowledge work. It shows how uncertainty regarding the respective contributions of the worker and GenAI can complicate competence attribution and initiate sensemaking about professional contribution. By explaining how workers' interpretations of authorship ambiguity are associated with divergent identity and meaning outcomes, including enhanced capability, impostor-like experiences and changing meaningfulness, the study extends research on human–AI collaboration beyond its predominant focus on performance and productivity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Enhanced Ferroelectric Performance of P(VDF-TrFE) Composites via MAPbI3-Mediated Crystallization for Flexible Memory Applications
container-title: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces
14a16671c5815a6f5a80d98022a3fe6eb3823e01.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We report a material-engineering strategy in which methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI3) perovskite is added to poly(vinylidene fluoride-trifluoroethylene) (P(VDF-TrFE)) composites to overcome intrinsic polarization and stability limitations. MAPbI3 incorporation enhances crystalline ordering and ferroelectric response in P(VDF-TrFE) composites, enhancing β-phase formation and strengthening dipole alignment through electrostatic interactions with –CF2– dipoles while simultaneously increasing dielectric permittivity and suppressing depolarization-field-driven polarization loss. With increasing MAPbI3 content, the composite films exhibit progressively improved ferroelectric performance and reach an optimum at 1.0 wt %, exhibiting a substantial increase in remanent polarization (2Pr from 13.7 to 18.4 μC/cm2), a 2.6-fold enhancement in the ferroelectric field-effect transistor (FeFET) on/off ratio, and a memory window expansion of 0.3 V. However, extremely high loadings and excessive MAPbI3 incorporation lead to aggregation and leakage-related degradation, resulting in reduced crystallinity and switching stability. Using P(VDF-TrFE) composites with optimized MAPbI3 composition, the composite FeFETs achieve extended retention up to 103 s, while the flexible ferroelectric capacitor (FeCAP) maintains stable ferroelectric switching after 10,000 mechanical bending cycles, demonstrating excellent mechanical resilience. These results demonstrate a practical material-engineering strategy for high-performance and mechanically reliable ferroelectric memory using a polymer–perovskite composite design.</jats:p>

During her childhood, she attended Liang-Jia-Ci Primary School from 1945 to 1950, and then continued her education at Chang-Chen Middle School from 1950 to 1956.
