1f3013f0f87b46219e5e47e632b8219c3eb30c4f.abstract: <jats:p>تهدف هذه الدراسة إلى تقديم مقاربة تحليلية نقدية لقصيدة "ديسان" للشاعر محمد بن عبد القادر الفطيسي التي كتبها حوالي سنة (ت 1252ه – 1836م)، بوصفها أنموذجاً لأدب الأوبئة في الذاكرة الليبية. ومع أن الدراسة تسعى إلى لفت انتباه الباحثين إلى أهمية هذه القصيدة في التأريخ الأدبي لأدب الكوارث والأوبئة والمجاعات، إلا أن الإشكالية الرئيسة التي تتمحور حولها الدراسة تتمثل في تساؤل جوهري حول الآليات التي اعتمد عليها الفطيسي لتجسيد الكارثة، وتشخيص المكان المتمثل في الجبل لكي يكون فاعلاً دلالياًّ قادراً على تعويض الفقد البشري الجماعي، حيث حوَّل الفطيسي جبل "ديسان" من معلم جغرافي صامت إلى مستودع ذكريات حفظت قيم المجتمع الذي أباده الطاعون. وتعتمد الدراسة منهجاً وصفياً تحليلياً يفيد من أبعاد سيميائية المكان وجماليات التلقي، مع إجراء موازنة نقدية معمقة مع نونية أبي البقاء الرندي في رثاء الأندلس باعتبارها نصاً معارَضاً. وقد كشفت الدراسة استراتيجية جمالية وظفها الشاعر تقوم على الإحياء بالصور، وأنسنة الجبل، وتشكيل فردوس لغوي يعوض فردوس المجتمع المفقود، وجعل من شخصية (سالمة) في النص معادلاً موضوعياً لمنظومة القيم الأخلاقية المنهارة. كما أكدت الدراسة سيرورة النص عبر المعارضة والتخميس الشعري، وعبر التدوين التاريخي على يد (الطاهر الزاوي وأحمد الصاري) اللذين أسهما في نقل القصيدة من سياقها المحلي الضيق إلى مركز الذاكرة الوطنية الليبية.</jats:p>

title: Relocation of the Fuel Fast Fill Unit on the Komatsu PC2000 from Beneath the Engine to the Unit Stairs as an Effort to Improve Safety, Refueling Efficiency, and Reduce Production Loss Time (Case Study of Quality Control Project Implementation in the AMM Pit Area, Mifa Jobsite, PT Putra Perkasa Abadi, 2025)
container-title: Journal Transnational Universal Studies
4a0e1f301d7e243304973f0270922ecdaf9a4709.abstract: <jats:p>The Komatsu PC2000 excavator operating in the AMM Pit Area at the Mifa Jobsite was equipped with a fast-fill fuel system positioned beneath the engine, exposing its components to potential damage from boulder impacts and creating accessibility challenges during refueling operations. Maintenance records from February 2024 to July 2025 documented nine system-related incidents resulting in at least 25 hours of equipment downtime, of which 16.7 hours (66.8%) were attributed to structural damage. This study evaluated the relocation of the fast-fill fuel connection point from beneath the engine to the excavator stairway area using the eight-step Quality Control Circle (QCC) methodology integrated with the Plan–Do–Check–Act (PDCA) cycle. Data were collected through maintenance records, field observations, cross-functional team discussions, Pareto analysis, Ishikawa cause-and-effect analysis, and solution-selection matrices to identify the primary causes of equipment downtime and determine appropriate corrective measures. Following the relocation, no additional fast-fill system disturbances were recorded during the specified monitoring period. For seven Komatsu PC2000 excavators, the projected operational benefits included annual savings of 638.5 equipment operating hours, a reduction in fuel consumption of approximately 76,620 liters, and a potential productivity gain of 447,125 bank cubic meters (BCM). However, these estimates were based on projected operational scenarios rather than independently verified annual performance measurements. The reported implementation cost was IDR 34,815,899 per excavator. Overall, the modification improved access to the refueling connection and potentially reduced component exposure to mechanical impacts, although its long-term reliability, safety performance, and economic benefits required further evaluation. These findings demonstrated the potential of evidence-based maintenance practices and multidisciplinary QCC methodologies to support targeted equipment modifications, improve refueling efficiency, and minimize production-related downtime in mining operations.</jats:p>

title: Speculative memory in Bora Chung’s Cursed Bunny: folklore, science fiction and the reconfiguration of cultural memory
container-title: The University of Danang - Journal of Science and Technology
2ba7b39b64208f9e93752f0cdc13ca98aaa01a29.abstract: <jats:p>This article examines how Bora Chung’s Cursed Bunny reconfigures cultural memory through the interaction of folklore and science fiction. Drawing on cultural memory studies and speculative fiction theory, it argues that these modes offer complementary ways of making memory. Curses, ghosts, and haunted objects bring suppressed histories into the present, while robots, posthuman bodies, and imagined worlds expose unresolved social contradictions. Memory thus moves across objects, bodies, spaces, and nonhuman subjects instead of remaining a stable archive. Adapting the concept of speculative memory, the article identifies three interrelated operations: haunting return, material displacement, and speculative projection. Together, these operations reveal how the collection critically reworks relations among past, present, and future, using speculative forms to interrogate history, technology, embodiment, and social transformation.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive Crutch or Cattellian Catapult? Technology Use and Human Capital Formation
a95e4dfbc1e7a89522cb303c6bb2bc5057481316.abstract: <jats:p>Technology can substitute for internal cognition, reducing investment through disuse of internal abilities, or complement it by amplifying learning capacity. This paper develops a dynamic model of human capital formation in which individuals allocate cognitive effort between internal reasoning and external technological support. It suggests that which mode predominates depends on the curvature of returns to human capital: diminishing returns induce cognitive offloading, while convex returns generate path-dependent amplification. The main implication is that technological change widens dispersion in cognitive outcomes across individuals and environments rather than simply shifting mean cognitive capacity.</jats:p>

title: Learning to remember: advances in memory mechanisms for large language models
container-title: Vicinagearth
28c6c3eb0320a8accc7d79af8785bb177dbc912f.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Memory has become a central mechanism for extending large language models (LLMs) beyond fixed context windows, stateless interaction, and static parametric knowledge. This survey organizes the literature around three complementary dimensions: the life cycle of memory, the storage substrate, and the system role that memory plays in LLM-based agents, while using cognitive-science-inspired memory concepts as a lightweight conceptual motivation rather than as a separate technical contribution or implementation family. On this basis, we distinguish three mechanism families: nonparametric memory, where information is stored outside model parameters in text, graph, multimodal, or database-like structures; parametric memory, where information is stored or accessed through activations, key-value caches, learned modules, adapter-based parameterizations, or model weights; and memory for agent evolution, where stored experiences support reinforcement learning, continual learning, procedural reuse, context engineering, and agent harness design. Evaluation is treated as a separate cross-cutting component rather than as a memory mechanism. Unlike surveys that focus primarily on retrieval-augmented generation or long-context modeling, this paper emphasizes the full memory life cycle: construction, maintenance, retrieval, consolidation, forgetting, governance, and evaluation. By aligning conceptual motivations, computational memory mechanisms, benchmarks, and deployment concerns, the survey provides a structured roadmap for designing memory-augmented LLM agents that are persistent, adaptive, auditable, and safe to update over time.</jats:p>

title: Folklore as Collective Moral Memory: Reactualizing Ethical and Moral Values in the Digital Era
container-title: Proceeding Bali-Bhuwana Waskita: Global Art Creativity Conference
d6a855ba8a6bd2b9b9689d5c59bad9a180ad6355.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines folklore as collective moral memory and explores the reactualization of ethical and moral values in the digital era. Although folklore, collective memory, and digital culture have been widely studied, their interrelationships in sustaining moral values require further conceptual integration. This study employs a qualitative-descriptive method using folkloristic, interpretive, collective memory, and digital culture approaches. Data are collected through observation, in-depth interviews, documentation, and literature review, and analyzed through data reduction, data presentation, and conclusion verification. The study conceptualizes folklore as a cultural medium that preserves collective experiences, transmits ethical values across generations, and enables their reinterpretation within contemporary contexts. Digital platforms expand access to folklore but may also simplify narratives, detach stories from their cultural contexts, and alter their moral meanings. Reactualization is therefore essential to connect traditional values, including honesty, responsibility, solidarity, respect for others, and environmental awareness, with contemporary social challenges. This study contributes a conceptual framework for understanding folklore as living moral memory and supporting culturally sensitive, ethically relevant cultural transmission.</jats:p>

title: Large language model agents in watershed environmental response: a hypothesis-and-theory framework for the cognitive orchestration layer
container-title: Frontiers in Environmental Science
823d869206d11e1de8c9c7db02759dea8c11971b.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Watershed environmental governance increasingly combines dense sensing infrastructure with institutions whose attention, authority, and coordination capacity remain limited. We develop the cognitive orchestration layer as a theory-building concept for examining how large language model (LLM)-based agents may connect sensing, assessment, decision advice, institutional response, and feedback without displacing domain models or public authority.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The Agentic Framework for Watershed Governance (AFWG) specifies three enabling pathways, three institutional interfaces, and four propositions. A purposively selected set of eight publicly documented cases is used to illustrate functional configurations, source limitations, and research gaps; it is not a systematic review or empirical evaluation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The cases document sensing, assessment, and decision-support functions, but do not establish improved decision quality, sustained institutional use, environmental outcomes, or agent-executed response closure. MAESTRO is retained as an adjacent-domain design illustration, not an existence proof of full-loop closure: human authorization remains necessary, and its reported performance has not been independently replicated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Transfer to watershed governance is plausible only where domain models remain authoritative, outputs carry provenance and uncertainty, named officials retain authority to authorize consequential actions, and institutional audit and failure handling are built into deployment. AFWG therefore offers a bounded conceptual framework and a falsifiable research agenda, rather than a claim that agents have already closed the watershed response loop.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Empirical dietary inflammatory pattern and cognitive-state transitions in older US adults: a multistate cohort study
container-title: Frontiers in Nutrition
418d4e32effc93fa5cb9fcab250ac8d8c4d3f623.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Dietary inflammatory potential may be associated with cognitive aging, but evidence on cognitive-state transitions is limited. We examined the association of the empirical dietary inflammatory pattern (EDIP) with transitions from normal cognition to survey-classified cognitive impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We linked 2013 Health Care and Nutrition Study dietary data to 2014–2022 Health and Retirement Study cognitive classifications and mortality records for 4,997 adults aged 60 years or older without dementia at baseline. A piecewise continuous-time Markov model represented normal cognition, cognitive impairment, and death. The primary model assigned EDIP only to the normal-to-impairment transition; a key sensitivity analysis allowed EDIP associations with all four transitions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Across 21,197 state observations, 1,615 observed normal-to-impairment transitions occurred. The primary hazard ratio (HR) per 1-SD higher EDIP was 1.074 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.014–1.138;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.014). With EDIP assigned to all transitions, the corresponding HR was 1.029 (95% CI, 0.963–1.099;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.401). Under the primary model, four-year standardized cognitive-impairment probabilities among 4,068 participants with normal cognition at baseline were 17.0% and 18.9% at EDIP values of −1 and +1 SD, respectively, a difference of 1.87 percentage points (95% CI, 0.48–3.42).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The modest positive association in the restricted primary model was not robust to allowing EDIP associations with all transitions. title: Chronic pain, memory, and adult hippocampal neurogenesis: Current advances, insights, and future directions
container-title: Chinese Medical Journal BioMed
bf5b100e278384876a320288adecf2b24c8fddac.abstract: <jats:p>Beyond the sensory dimension, chronic pain commonly disrupts cognitive function, with memory loss being a frequent and debilitating complaint that complicates treatment. Memory impairment has been observed in multiple animal models of chronic pain. This review summarizes the literature related to memory impairment induced by chronic pain across species. Increasing evidence suggests that chronic pain affects adult hippocampal neurogenesis by disrupting the proliferation and survival of newborn granular cells. Given that adult hippocampal neurogenesis is critical for learning and memory processing, we focused on recent preclinical studies on the role of adult hippocampal neurogenesis in memory impairment induced by chronic pain. Based on the collected evidence, we postulated that chronic pain reduces adult hippocampal neurogenesis, thereby contributing to memory impairments. We also considered the intrinsic and circuit mechanisms in the hippocampus by which chronic pain leads to adult hippocampal neurogenesis injury and memory impairment. In this review, we emphasize the role of brain-derived neurotrophic factor supplementation in the dentate gyrus and local inflammatory factors, including cytokine release and glial activation. Future research aimed at deciphering the precise mechanisms underlying impairments in adult hippocampal neurogenesis in chronic pain may help identify novel biomarkers for early diagnosis and inspire the development of non-invasive neuromodulation or pro-neurogenic therapies tailored for chronic pain patients with cognitive comorbidities.</jats:p>

title: An integrated role of cognitive and psychological mechanisms in shaping financial well-being: Evidence from Sri Lankan Public Sector Physicians
container-title: Asian Journal of Finance
efed5b140c4e31e66df60504378ff841befb7634.abstract: <jats:p>Financial literacy has become a national priority in Sri Lanka, particularly in light of the country’s persistent economic challenges. Despite decades of increased focus on financial education, the nationwide financial literacy survey conducted in 2021 reported that although Sri Lankans have a satisfactory level of financial knowledge, their financial attitudes and actual financial behaviour lag behind their financial knowledge. Hence, financial literacy can no longer be considered to be directly associated with financial well-being, and there is a need to examine mechanisms that convert financial literacy into positive financial behaviour and thereby improve financial well-being. Concerning the widely held belief in the significance of psychological processes in making behavioural changes, this study attempts to examine whether individuals’ psychological states, in particular financial self-efficacy and financial resilience, can help in explaining the gap between financial literacy and their financial well-being. The study is particularly concentrated among Sri Lankan public sector physicians, as they often lack formal financial education or training; however, they are expected to be financially secure due to their high-income status. Data collected from a sample of 101 government-employed physicians in Sri Lanka were analysed using regression analysis with the PROCESS macro available in the IBM SPSS software. The findings show that financial literacy influences financial well-being only when financial self-efficacy and financial resilience act as mediators. These results highlight the significant role of financial self-efficacy and financial resilience as psychological mechanisms in translating financial literacy cognitions into financial well-being of the public sector physicians. This study makes a theoretical contribution by extending the conceptualisation of financial capability as integrative of both cognitive and psychological mechanisms that guide financial behaviours, leading to financial well-being. From a practical standpoint, the findings highlight that financial literacy interventions should be designed beyond the dissemination of financial knowledge to strengthen individuals’ confidence in applying financial knowledge and their capacity to withstand financial shocks. Accordingly, these implications are especially pertinent to the execution of Sri Lanka’s National Financial Literacy Road-map.</jats:p>

title: Deciphering the correlation between virtual learning and Saudi EFL majors' affective-cognitive variables: a social cognitive-theoretic perspective
container-title: Frontiers in Psychology
3d09600f7c94ee248b778eb7922ab3d297d26514.abstract: <jats:p>With the rapid evolution of virtual learning, teaching and learning practices worldwide have greatly changed, and the correlation between virtual learning and affective-cognitive variables (ACVs) is context-bound. This study seeks to fulfill in part this research gap by offering insights into the extent to which virtual learning is associated with the ACVs of Saudi EFL majors at the university level in relation to four psychological learning constructs: learning autonomy (LA), self-efficacy (SE), willingness to communicate (WTC), and motivation (M). The study draws on social cognitive theory (SCT), which postulates that the ACVs of learners shift dynamically through intricate relationships between the virtual learning environment, learners' beliefs, and communicative interaction. Quantitative and qualitative methods are employed to gather data from 200 EFL university students and 12 EFL instructors from one Saudi university. This paper has four main findings pertaining to the Saudi EFL context. First, there is a significant relationship between virtual learning, learners' beliefs, and the ACVs among Saudi EFL majors. Second, there is a positive correlation between virtual learning and willingness to communicate in low-anxiety virtual settings, particularly in asynchronous and small-group communicative contexts. Third, motivation is positively correlated with the teacher's presence, interactivity, and feedback. Fourth, a significant relationship is found among virtual learning, learners' beliefs, and their communicative behavior. Because this study is Saudi EFL context-oriented, its findings cannot be generalized across different cultural, linguistic, and educational settings.</jats:p>

title: MDM-DDI: a drug–drug interaction prediction framework integrating multi-dimensional molecular features and memory-augmented networks
container-title: Frontiers in Pharmacology
c15750b3900fbf14e6711f80e2570b49c6315734.abstract: <jats:p>When patients take multiple medications concurrently, drug–drug interactions (DDIs) can induce severe adverse reactions, making accurate DDI prediction critical for ensuring medication safety. Existing deep learning approaches often struggle to comprehensively characterize the complex molecular structures and physicochemical properties of drug molecules. Meanwhile, related studies that directly incorporate pharmacological knowledge from large language models tend to introduce redundant noise, thereby limiting predictive performance. To address these issues, we propose MDM-DDI, a framework that integrates four dimensions of drug molecular features: one-dimensional sequences, two-dimensional topologies, three-dimensional conformations, and pharmacological prior knowledge. A bidirectional drug interaction module is designed to capture latent associations between drug pairs, and a memory network mechanism is innovatively introduced to filter and denoise the pharmacological priors generated by large language models. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including DrugBank demonstrate that MDM-DDI achieves small but consistent improvements over the evaluated baseline methods across multiple evaluation metrics, and also shows improvements over the evaluated baseline methods under cold-start scenarios. Case studies and interpretability analyses further provide preliminary evidence for the rationality of the model predictions.</jats:p>

title: Perceptual versus memory-guided affordances: training-related adaptations in a spatial computer game
container-title: Frontiers in Neuroscience
c23a2656dc197bb30a38af46c59760159b07ac22.abstract: <jats:p>Traditional sequence learning research relies on discrete button-press paradigms where pauses segment responses. We developed a continuous game-based adaptation of the Serial Reaction Time task and tracked neural changes in 25 participants using fMRI before and after 1–3 weeks of training. Participants learned to control an avatar’s position and follow fixed and random sequences in the game. Behaviourally, fixed sequences showed robust learning with shorter response times and increased number of perfect playthroughs between Scan1 and Scan2. Random sequence performance unexpectedly declined, with fewer perfect playthroughs, consistent with negative transfer from consolidated sequence representations. For fixed sequences at Scan2 relative to Scan1, we identified the expected cerebellar and occipital decreases alongside unexpected increases in bilateral superior temporal regions. Random sequences showed increased insular activity, consistent with conflict monitoring when consolidated predictions fail. The temporal recruitment suggests continuous sequences consolidated through integrative mechanisms, potentially grammatical encoding, verbal mediation, or spatiotemporal binding, not typically reported in discrete tasks. Critically, training produced no premotor or superior parietal decrease within the fixed sequence, the automatisation signature discrete paradigms report. Our results suggest that discrete sequence learning principles may not fully generalise to continuous environments and highlight the need for paradigms that capture the spatiotemporal demands of real-world skill acquisition.</jats:p>

title: Empowering Digital Twins with Generative AI: Applications, Case Studies, and Limitations
container-title: Cognitive Computation
e5355fcc9bb2dc8a8d8c7eaa39ce0f9e18361378.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The rise of the Generative Pre-Trained Transformer(GPT) language model, more commonly used as ChatGPT, has brought a spotlight on the ever-developing field of Generative AI (GAI). With current advancements in graphics processing units (GPUs), training and using deep generative models have become easier. Similarly, the developments in edge computing have made it possible to make the most of GAI’s potential for numerous use cases. One such use case involves its integration with Digital Twin technology, offering new possibilities for enhanced simulations, predictive analytics, and real-time decision-making. This paper explores the prospects of combining GAI with Digital Twin technology to create innovative solutions for applications like healthcare, manufacturing, agriculture, cybersecurity, etc. It also discusses how GAI can train Digital Twins by simulating various scenarios and providing different data sets, enabling predictive maintenance. It also delves into the real-world scenarios in which the technology has been implemented. The paper concludes with the limitations of GAI technology for Digital Twin applications, which can be worked upon in the future.</jats:p>

title: A Governed Computational Architecture for Predictive Process Monitoring with Policy-Constrained Orchestration and Auditable Decision Making
container-title: Cognitive Computation
d8a18ce6a430c3ba0e9dde46da56ceff8a2e9d7b.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Predictive process monitoring enables organizations to anticipate process outcomes from event logs, although deployment in real operational environments remains challenging due to temporal drift, heterogeneous traces, and limited interpretability of deep predictive models. This work presents an integrated framework combining Transformer-based predictive monitoring with governed operational orchestration for business-process automation. The predictive layer jointly estimates case outcome, next activity, and remaining decision time, while the orchestration layer manages routing, escalation, explanation triggering, and execution logging under explicit policy constraints. Integrated Gradients provide event-level attribution evidence, while calibration and confidence signals support conservative decision regulation under uncertainty. Experiments were conducted on the BPI Challenge 2017 and BPI Challenge 2012 datasets under leakage-aware and drift-sensitive conditions. The evaluation includes comparisons with neural and tree-based predictive-process-monitoring baselines, selected ablation analyses, policy-sweep experiments, and a structured expert-agent proxy assessment of the audit layer across six selected case studies. In the main BPI Challenge 2017 evaluation, the predictive model achieved PR-AUC = 0.6963 for outcome prediction, Top-3 Accuracy = 0.9986 and NDCG@3 = 0.9698 for next-activity prediction, and MAE = 183.45 hours for remaining-decision-time estimation. The audit-layer assessment showed improved post-hoc inspection support and reduced duplicate explanatory evidence after meta-XAI consolidation. The results indicate the technical feasibility of integrating predictive monitoring, policy-constrained routing, explanation support, and audit traceability under drift-affected process conditions.</jats:p>

title: How Finite Brains Generalize Without Bound: Spatial Memory as a Universal Computer
828a64c00c3c43bf68206dc2431a91e4916f7ba8.abstract: <jats:p>A child who has learned to add small numbers adds numbers of any length. LSTMs and Transformers trained on short sequences fail on longer ones. We trace the difference to what a learner reads when it decides. A position, a count or a time keeps taking new values as the input grows: it is a coordinate, and a learner that reads one meets in every long input values its experience never covered. Whether two things are the same has the same two answers at every size: it is a coincidence, and a learner that reads only coincidences finds in a long input nothing that short inputs lacked, so finite experience fixes its rule for every size. The memory carries the size of the input and the rule stays finite, and this determines the memory a generalizing brain can have: a memory that grows while what the learner reads of it stays finite has to look the same from every place, so it is made of cycles, and the past is reached by asking what happened when the cycles last stood where they stand now. The cycles are the grid modules, the cells that detect their return the place cells, the records the hippocampal index; a prefrontal controller moves the cycles and never sees them. Reading only coincidences costs no power: what finite experience fixes in such a learner is what Turing machines compute in step with their input, which is why a circuit that evolved to find the way home can learn arithmetic and grammar. In a network of neurons this machine of cycles is the dynamics seen through its symmetry, and symbols are its invariants. Trained on strings of up to 40 symbols, the machine solves five benchmark tasks that no LSTM or Transformer solves, among them duplication and binary addition, and beyond the reach of its cycles it fails on the curve the theory predicts. Given larger cycles after training, a machine that has seen no string longer than five symbols reverses a string of a million without error. Its controllers run unchanged on neurons.</jats:p>

d586dc4b41856454441f6fb9173458d2655434ec.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In this article, I describe how I came to read my Armenian grandmother’s Jerusalem pilgrimage tattoos as maps. These tattoo maps linked the now disconnected routes and geographies of Armenian life across Cilicia, Beirut and Palestine. Her stories about the pilgrimage tattoos centered her childhood memories of Beirut, a city whose urban form was deeply shaped by ongoing displacement, violence and dispossession. To read my grandmother’s tattoos as maps is to read against the grain of existing political boundaries in a time of accumulating catastrophes and ongoing erasures that cannot be framed as past events.</jats:p>

title: Assessment of Hydroclimatic Lag and Memory Across Major European Basins Using GRACE and MERRA
container-title: Applied Sciences
385edfbe101aa3a1d7aae78708817cb5b7e94d63.abstract: <jats:p>Large basins show substantial variation in the timing and persistence of hydrological responses to climatic forcing. Quantifying hydroclimatic lags and basin memory is important for understanding hydrological response dynamics, assessing drought persistence, and informing future research on drought prediction and water-resource management. This study presents a harmonised comparison of hydroclimatic response delays and hydrological memory across ten major European basins. Basin-scale Water Budgets (WBs) were derived from precipitation, evapotranspiration, and runoff components, while hydroclimatic forcing was represented by the Combined Climatologic Deviation Index (CCDI), based on precipitation anomalies and Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) total water storage anomalies (TWSAs). Cross-correlation (CCF), autocorrelation (ACF), partial autocorrelation (PACF), and autocorrelation decay time (e-folding) were used to quantify response timing and persistence. The results show basin-specific differences in lag relationships and autocorrelation-based persistence. Estimated memory durations depend on the diagnostic used, highlighting the need to distinguish e-folding time, zero-crossing lag, and significance-decay lag. Because WB and CCDI share precipitation-related information, the observed cross-correlations are interpreted as statistical associations rather than direct evidence of causality. The findings provide a comparative assessment of hydroclimatic lag and persistence characteristics for the selected basins and study period; their predictive value requires separate validation.</jats:p>

title: Resistant starch and diabetes-associated cognitive dysfunction: structure-dependent fermentation and gut-brain framework
container-title: Frontiers in Nutrition
392a963c07f6139ec12b9146d52b805385fd7e96.abstract: <jats:p>Diabetes-associated cognitive dysfunction (DACD) affects memory, executive function, attention, and processing speed through interacting metabolic, vascular, inflammatory, and neural disturbances. Human observational studies show heterogeneous microbial profiles and associations between circulating short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), particularly acetate, and cognitive status, although causal relationships remain unestablished. Resistant starch (RS) escapes small-intestinal digestion and is fermented in the colon. Differences among RS1–RS5 in physical accessibility, crystallinity, retrogradation, chemical modification, and lipid complexation determine microbial access and fermentation kinetics. Fermentation produces an integrated acetate–propionate–butyrate response: acetate supports cross-feeding, propionate contributes to FFAR2/FFAR3 and hepatic signaling, and butyrate links colonocyte energetics with epithelial, immune, and histone deacetylase-dependent pathways. This narrative Mini Review integrates human DACD observations, controlled RS feeding studies, and mechanistic animal evidence within a structure-dependent microbiota-gut-brain framework. The available evidence indicates that RS responses are conditioned by substrate structure, food matrix, and baseline degraders and cross-feeders, providing a basis for responder stratification. We therefore propose a proof-of-concept design using a chemically and physically specified RS, longitudinal microbiome and fecal/circulating SCFA profiling, separate intestinal and cerebrovascular measures, and multidomain cognitive outcomes. RS efficacy for cognitive outcomes in DACD remains unestablished, but RS offers a food-compatible and experimentally controllable platform for determining whether a reproducible microbial-metabolite response can modify cognition-relevant pathways in diabetes.</jats:p>

title: RECONSTRUCTING REALITY IN INCEPTION (2010): A COGNITIVE-CULTURAL ANALYSIS THROUGH PIAGET
MEREKONSTRUKSI REALITAS DALAM FILM INCEPTION (2010): SEBUAH ANALISIS KOGNITIF-BUDAYA MELALUI PIAGET
container-title: Serat
855c165aa9c3cf459fd1b83c7264c18d7a7ce24d.abstract: <jats:p>This study investigates how Inception (2010) dramatizes memory distortion, perception instability, and the construction of reality through the lens of Jean Piaget’s cognitive developmental theory. The film’s protagonist, Cobb, experiences internal dissonance and psychological fragmentation as unresolved emotional trauma warps his cognitive schema. Using Piagetian concepts such as assimilation, accommodation, and equilibrium, the analysis reveals how Inception visualizes the mind's struggle to maintain stability in the face of repressed memory and external manipulation. Beyond individual psychology, the film engages with contemporary cultural anxieties surrounding the fluidity of truth, the unreliability of memory, and the mediated construction of reality in a post-digital age. The layered dream architecture becomes a metaphor for modern cognitive confusion, where the boundaries between fact and fabrication collapse. This paper contributes to interdisciplinary discussions on how film can serve as a cultural lens for examining psychological dissonance and epistemological uncertainty. In bridging cognitive theory with narrative cinema, the study positions Inception as a reflection of collective memory crises in 21st-century cultural consciousness.</jats:p>

title: Archival and palaeoenvironmental documentation of extreme climate events reveals generational amnesia in collective memory
container-title: Nature Communications
8f05a4df469d9606228ab2edf16c49a9e1849314.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Collective memory shapes how societies respond to extreme climate events, yet long-term evidence on how the collective memory of such events becomes perceptually biased over time is lacking. Here, we utilise four centuries (1470–1900) of climatic archives from northern China, along with tree–ring–based hydroclimate reconstructions, which are validated against instrumental observations of Wet/Dry Index (1901–2000) to fill the gap. We find that historical records reveal systematic, non-random mismatches, where severity assessments are often biased toward recent experience rather than absolute climatic anomalies. Correlations between historical and natural records increase when the natural series is re-standardised using 20–40-year sliding windows, reflecting a generational offset. A heuristic agent-based model reproduces this pattern, suggesting that generational amnesia is sufficient to explain the offsets in perception of environmental change. We argue that historical archives carry a generational imprint of perceptual bias, in which the severity of climate extremes is judged against recent lived experience rather than long-term climate variability. This has implications for bias-aware corrections for risk assessment, adaptation, and paleoclimate reconstruction.</jats:p>

title: Long-term development of a motor memory
container-title: Nature Human Behaviour
bf1b1d4d3da22a4ccb854da0ccc44c41189d0313.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Human behaviour is developed through continuous adaptation to our environment over a range of timescales. Extensive studies have investigated the mechanisms and computations underlying this process of sensorimotor adaptation using several hundred trials. However, most of our motor skills have had countless hours of practice. Here we study a simple motor adaptation task using thousands of training trials over multiple weeks to study the long-term development of a motor memory, and examine changes in adaptation, retention, interlimb transfer, decay, spontaneous recovery and generalization. Unlike previous studies, participants showed near complete compensation to the novel dynamics, along with long-term increases in retention and spontaneous recovery. Moreover, we find narrowing in the angular generalization, suggesting continual tuning of the motor memory to the task. This demonstrates the extensive changes occurring with longer training of motor tasks, highlighting their importance in studies of sensorimotor control, rehabilitation and training.</jats:p>

title: HSR-APR: A Hybrid Secure Reflective Automated Program Repair Framework with Adaptive Reflection Memory
83f851516021bde25a11e919dd076916e5dc43da.abstract: Automated Program Repair (APR) has benefited from the rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs), but existing approaches still rely heavily on functional testing, provide limited security validation, insufficient integration of traditional program analysis, and have limited ability to learn from failed repair attempts. This research proposes HSR-APR (Hybrid Secure Reflective Automated Program Repair), a hybrid framework that integrates static analysis, fault localization, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), LLM-based patch generation, functional and security validation, self-reflection, and Adaptive Reflection Memory (ARM). The framework iteratively evaluates generated patches, analyzes failed attempts, stores repair experiences in ARM, and retrieves relevant knowledge to improve subsequent repair prompts. HSR-APR is evaluated on 300 SWE-Bench Lite instances using four configurations: Baseline LLM, Hybrid APR, Hybrid APR with Security Validation, and HSR-APR. Results show that HSR-APR achieves an 85% Repair Success Rate (255/300), compared with 63% for the Baseline LLM, while increasing the Test Pass Rate from 72% to 92% and Security Warning Reduction from 8% to 87%. It also reduces average repair iterations from 5.8 to 2.9 and execution time from 18 to 13 minutes, demonstrating that combining hybrid analysis, security validation, self-reflection, and adaptive memory improves the effectiveness, security, and efficiency of LLM-based APR.

title: An Analysis of the Cognitive Motivations of English Idioms Containing the Verb “Break”
container-title: Advances in Social Sciences and Management
6c2fee24008418f9ac288a985e1a11bb8bc51d0a.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines the cognitive motivations underlying English idioms containing the verb break, drawing on Conceptual Metaphor Theory (CMT) and conceptual metonymy. It investigates the semantic domains represented by these idioms, their figurative mechanisms and grammatical patterns, and the conceptual mappings that motivate their figurative meanings. Adopting a corpus-based descriptive and analytical design, the study examines 20 idioms identified through cross-referencing three established idiom dictionaries and screening them according to criteria of semantic non-compositionality, conventionality, and usage frequency. Qualitative cognitive-linguistic analysis is supplemented by frequency data from the Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA). The findings classify the idioms into nine semantic categories. Conceptual metaphor accounts for 18 expressions, whereas two are analyzed primarily in terms of metonymic relationships. The analysis identifies recurring conceptual patterns linking physical disruption to abstract experiences, including social interaction, emotional states, institutional norms, and achievement. The idiom break a leg represents a distinctive case whose conventional meaning is not readily explained by the principal mappings identified in the dataset. The findings suggest that many break idioms can be understood through systematic conceptual relationships grounded in physical experience, although conventional usage and cultural knowledge also contribute to their interpretation. The study provides a structured account of this verb-based idiom set and discusses how cognitive-linguistic analysis may inform idiom instruction in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) contexts.</jats:p>

title: Extracellular vesicle miRNAs, NOS/NO homeostasis, and NLRP3 inflammasome signaling in schizophrenia-related cognitive impairment: a mechanistic review and testable hypothesis
container-title: Frontiers in Psychiatry
cd27b8b5185c578943b8f1256aa5cfce6226c8c9.abstract: <jats:p>Cognitive impairment is a major determinant of poor functional recovery in schizophrenia, but the molecular events connecting neuroimmune disturbance, redox imbalance, and synaptic dysfunction remain incompletely understood. Studies in patients have reported altered extracellular vesicle microRNA (EV-miRNA) profiles, abnormalities in nitric oxide synthase/nitric oxide (NOS/NO)-related markers, and altered or increased microglial expression of NLRP3 inflammasome-associated proteins. These findings point to possible convergence among EV-mediated signaling, redox regulation, and inflammasome activity, yet they do not define a continuous causal pathway. This review examines evidence from patient studies, patient-derived and schizophrenia-related models, and mechanistic work in other disease contexts to assess a putative EV-miRNA–inflammatory transcriptional network–NOS/NO–NLRP3–synaptic/cognitive impairment framework. We emphasize several evidentiary boundaries: EV-miRNA expression changes should be distinguished from functional intercellular delivery, predicted targets should not be treated as validated mechanisms, and peripheral molecular associations cannot by themselves establish pyroptosis in the brain. The framework also highlights the context dependence of NO-related effects, particularly their reliance on the redox microenvironment, and separates cytokine maturation and release, GSDMD-mediated pore formation, and pyroptotic cell death as related but distinct downstream events. Future studies should determine whether source-defined EV-miRNAs directly regulate NOS/NLRP3 signaling, whether these molecular changes precede longitudinal cognitive decline, and whether intervention or rescue experiments can demonstrate causal links across the pathway. Integrating source-resolved EV profiling, multi-omics analysis, and clinical follow-up may clarify whether combined molecular indicators can support cognitive stratification and risk prediction in schizophrenia.</jats:p>

title: He ʻUpena No Ka ʻIke: Indigenous Pedagogy as Method, Memory and Creative Practice
container-title: AlterNative: An International Journal of Indigenous Peoples
055f64020bb039b356483be5b50f25e19e21682e.abstract: <jats:p>This paper offers a reimagined literature review grounded in Kānaka Maoli (Indigenous Hawaiian) pedagogical practices, with a focus on decolonizing art and design education. Drawing on moʻolelo (story), lived experience, and Indigenous scholarship, it explores relationality, place-based learning, storytelling, and the role of challenge in creative practice. Rather than centering written texts alone, the paper engages knowledge held in the body, in land, in silence, and in breath. Written from the perspective of a Kānaka Maoli artist-educator, it affirms Indigenous ways of knowing as complete, self-determined systems that carry their own integrity and their own genealogy. The paper also acknowledges the tension of presenting Indigenous knowledge within written academic form, positioning writing as a partial and situated translation rather than a complete representation. It critiques institutional structures that marginalize Indigenous epistemologies and advocates for pedagogical approaches rooted in relationship, responsibility, and cultural continuity. Through the metaphor of the ʻupena (net), knowledge is framed as something woven through story and practice. This work contributes to ongoing efforts to decolonize design education by advancing embodied, accountable, and ancestral approaches to teaching, where creativity is inseparable from land, identity, and collective liberation.</jats:p>

title: An Integrated Metacognition, Phenomenon-Based, and Inquiry Model for Critical Problem-solving and Self-Awareness
container-title: Higher Education Studies
92a4de6d1b8355ec9bda21967656e004b4ba6e90.abstract: <jats:p>This research-and-development study developed and evaluated the content and structural suitability of an instructional model integrating metacognition, phenomenon-based learning, and inquiry for undergraduate students&#39; critical problem-solving competency and self-awareness. In Phase 1, interviews with two instructors and nine students and observations of three general biology course sections at one Thai university identified a need for more explicit justification of alternative solutions and monitoring of thinking. These findings informed a six-component model with a five-step learning process. In Phase 2, five experts appraised the model and its assessment instruments. All 10 critical problem-solving items received an item-objective congruence (IOC) index of 1.00; the 18 self-awareness items received IOC indices of 0.60-1.00 (mean = 0.91). IOC-derived estimates of scale-level positive agreement (S-CVI/Ave proxies) were 1.000 and 0.956, respectively, under the reported distribution of expert judgments. The overall mean suitability rating for the model was 4.62 out of 5.00. The model positions evidence-based decision-making and metacognitive reflection particularly within Steps 4 and 5. The findings support the model&#39;s content and structural suitability in the studied context; learning-outcome effectiveness requires evaluation in implementation research.</jats:p>

title: Benchmarking foundation models for resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging time series in cognitive aging research
d3f0fc01a9d45d242643894850fd7ef5b86006ab.abstract: <jats:p>Foundation models trained on large neuroimaging datasets could help smaller studies investigate cognition from brain recordings. However, whether the foundation model-derived representations improve assessment of current cognition, prediction of follow-up cognition, or characterization of cognitive change remains unclear. We evaluated nine configurations from five model families that process regional resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging time series, using 3,103 scans from 1,653 participants across two observational and five intervention aging cohorts. Primary frozen representations showed no consistent superiority over conventional functional connectivity for concurrent cognitive associations or diagnostic classification. Changing the readout improved selected concurrent cognitive associations without updating model weights, indicating that performance depended partly on how representations were extracted. Additional post-training and embedding alignment yielded gains in selected settings but did not consistently improve performance across outcomes. In the primary longitudinal analyses, imaging representations did not establish added value beyond baseline clinical measures. These findings show that readout choice influences concurrent cognitive associations, while the added value of these representations for longitudinal outcomes remains unestablished.</jats:p>

title: Disentanglement of persistent and dynamic neural substrates of working memory
2a827b69f171ca8375b1ee603318ec871f4373fb.abstract: <jats:p>Competing theories of working memory have alternatively emphasized the importance of persistent and dynamic substrates of this cognitive function. Here, we directly tested these theories by computationally isolating the contributions of persistent and dynamic activity to working memory. We analyzed neuronal population activity recordings in macaques doing match/non-match working memory tasks. We first extracted signatures of persistent and dynamic activity through cue-specific temporal means, temporal principal components, and correlations of activity patterns across task epochs. We then generated synthetic data constrained by these signatures, and decoded cue stimuli from these data, separately from persistent and non-persistent neurons. We found that high decoding performance arose from a nuanced interplay of persistent and dynamic activity. Specifically, we could decode stimuli at empirical or above-chance levels across all tasks only from persistent neurons, but only after constraining correlations of activity patterns across epochs. In this way, we showed distinct roles for persistent and dynamic neuronal activity that help to unify two competing theories of working memory. More broadly, we also advanced computational controlled experiments as a principled framework for adjudicating between competing models of neuronal population activity.</jats:p>

title: Gait disorders in patients with sporadic age-depended cerebral small vessel disease: relationship with neuropsychological profile and severity of cognitive impairment
container-title: Russian Journal of Preventive Medicine
5fd57690ee807c36a3a9010669595517ee0aed7a.abstract: <jats:p>Cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD) is a major medical and social problem, with cognitive impairment (CI) and abnormal gait as its main clinical manifestations. Recent studies have examined the relationship between these symptoms and their contribution to disability in older adults. Objective. To assess the association between non-hemiparetic gait disorders, neuropsychological profiles, and the severity of CI in patients with cSVD. Materials and methods. The study enrolled 124 patients with cSVD (mean age 62±8 years) with Fazekas stage 2—3 white matter hyperintensity, and 30 control volunteers without gait disorders or MRI abnormalities. Groups were matched for age and sex. Cognitive function was evaluated, as well as severity and type of CI. Gait was assessed using the Tinetti test (with «balance» and «gait» subscales and a total score indicating fall risk), the 6-meter walk test, and the Clinical Scale for Assessing Gait Disorders in patients with cSVD. Results. All patients presented with CI of varying severity; 68.5% had gait disorders, and 41.8% were at risk of falls. Patients with gait disturbances had significantly more severe CI (dementia in 36.5% versus 5.1%) and poorer neuropsychological test performance compared with those without abnormal gait. Gait parameters showed the strongest association with overall cognitive function, particularly executive control (‘inhibition’ component) and memory. Conclusions. Gait disorders is closely associated with executive dysfunction, memory impairment, and deterioration of integrative brain activity. Early identification of gait impairment in patients with cSVD can indicate disease progression, CI, and an increased risk of falls.</jats:p>

title: Features of cognitive status in patients over 65 years of age after high-risk cardiac surgery
container-title: Russian Journal of Preventive Medicine
01e142902a1e9f6ec2b4ea0b29ffa08498f741d5.abstract: <jats:p>Objective. To evaluate early postoperative cognitive changes in patients older than 65 years following cardiac surgery and to identify factors associated with cognitive impairment. Materials and methods. The study included 76 patients with coronary artery disease, significant coronary artery involvement, or heart valve defects. The mean age was 68.5 years (range: 66.2—72.0). Cognitive function was assessed using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) before surgery and at discharge. Intraoperative cerebral oxygenation (rSO2, %) was monitored. Regression analysis was performed to identify factors associated with postoperative cognitive decline. Results. Cognitive impairment was generally mild both before surgery and in the early postoperative period, with MMSE scores of 28.2 (25.5—29.0) and 28.5 (24.2—29.0), respectively. Before surgery, 50% of patients exhibited no or mild cognitive impairment, 38.2% had moderate impairment, and 11.8% had mild dementia. By the seventh postoperative day, the proportion of patients with moderate cognitive impairment increased. A decline in cognitive function was observed in 40.7% of patients. Deterioration in cognitive function was associated with intraoperative rSO2 levels below 40% during cardiopulmonary bypass (OR 2.14; 1.65—4.63, p=0.03), chronic kidney disease stage C3a or higher (OR 2.11; 1.17—6.42, p=0.02), and atrial fibrillation or ventricular extrasystole (OR 1.96; 1.23–5.71, p=0.01). Conclusions. Postoperative cognitive decline occurred in 40.7% of patients and was associated with cerebral desaturation during bypass, chronic kidney disease stage C3a or higher, and life-threatening arrhythmias. Intraoperative monitoring of cerebral oxygenation is recommended for high-risk cardiac surgery patients to prevent cognitive impairment.</jats:p>

title: Selected Effect Theories of Representation and Representational Explanations in Cognitive Science
container-title: Philosophy of Science
6e8527cc0b89049b53ef09cdcbcf651667a0ba14.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>A widely held approach characterizes the concept of representation in cognitive science in terms of a selected effect notion of biological function. I argue that these theories of representation have trouble saying that there are representations where cognitive scientists say there are in at least some, and likely many, cases. I spell out the difficulties this raises for selected effect theories.</jats:p>

title: Mapping the brain-web morphology to characterise ageing and cognitive impairment
0687a4b3745ce7102fd13cf6b6299b2c1776216c.abstract: <jats:p>Ageing reshapes human brain anatomy across spatial scales, yet its geometrical organisation remains difficult to quantify. Here we introduce SHARP (Spectral Hierarchy Analysis, Reconstruction and Prediction), which transfers hierarchical cosmic-web classification to structural MRI, identifying knots, filaments, sheets and voids at four spectral levels and combining their morphology with higher-order spatial statistics and anatomical measurements. In CamCAN, selected filament- and sheet-associated features show opposing correlations with age and distinct associations with subcortical and ventricular volumes. To quantify their contribution, we compare SHARP with a neural-network baseline combining 36 regional anatomical measurements, total brain volume and sex. Adding cosmologically motivated descriptors reduces the mean absolute error of MRI-only age prediction from 6.04 to 4.71 years (22%) in CamCAN and from 4.57 to 4.07 years (11%) in OASIS-3 under participant-independent validation. Brain-web morphology with only brain volume and sex already achieves 5.12 years in CamCAN. For cognitive-status classification in OASIS-3, SHARP identifies 85% of Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR)-positive observations at 86% specificity, compared with 78% sensitivity for the anatomical baseline at matched empirical specificity. These results demonstrate that cosmological methods provide complementary geometrical information and measurable gains in characterising brain ageing and cognitive impairment.</jats:p>

title: Understanding Students’ Learning Processes in an Inclusive Mathematics Classroom: A Metacognition-Based Instructional Approach
container-title: Education Sciences
95e3f68c11b96c21bc614ee6ab1906d64ffe9be7.abstract: <jats:p>The study aims to develop an in-depth understanding of how metacognitive processes, mathematical knowledge construction and use, collaborative learning processes, and technology use unfold and are shaped in the experiences of a student with a Special Educational Needs profile and their peer group during the implementation of the USPİDMAT instructional approach in an inclusive mathematics classroom. In the study, metacognition-based instruction was conducted in a classroom in western Turkey with 22 students, one of whom had an intellectual disability. Using a case study model, interviews were conducted with nine students in this classroom, and the worksheets from the implementation process were examined. The data of the study were analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings indicate that, within the context of metacognition-based instruction, students were aware of their learning objectives prior to engaging in learning activities and established meaningful connections between mathematics and daily life.</jats:p>

title: Immediate, delayed, or intermittent workload-matched postprandial cycling and cardiometabolic and cognitive responses during sedentary behavior: a randomized controlled crossover study
container-title: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
b02f6a976cc4b7788618137959dcd8f48716261c.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Postprandial sedentary behavior is associated with negative health effects and constitutes a large part of daily life in modern society. This study compared the acute effects of immediate continuous, delayed continuous, and intermittent postprandial cycling on glucose levels, cerebral and muscle oxygenation, cognitive performance, and well-being during subsequent sitting.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In a four-armed randomized crossover trial, healthy adults consumed four standardized meals separated by 48-hour washout periods. Each meal was followed by 2 h of sitting combined, in random order, with one of four interventions: (1) sitting only, (2) 15 min of moderate intensity cycling immediately after eating, (3) 15 min of cycling 20 min after eating, or (4) three workload-matched five-minute cycling bouts during sitting. Interstitial glucose was the primary outcome and was assessed using continuous glucose monitoring (CGM). Cerebral and muscle oxygenation (Functional near infrared spectroscopy), cognitive performance (Stroop test), heart rate, blood pressure, and subjective ratings were assessed throughout the two-hour postprandial period at predefined measurement intervals. Data were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA, with ANCOVA applied to NIRS-derived outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Twenty participants (mean age 27.1 ± 10.3 years, 12 females) completed the study. Cycling immediately after eating was associated with significantly lower mean postprandial glucose compared with the control condition [relative change [RC] = −7.1%, 95% confidence interval [95%CI]: −14.03 to −3.43 mg/dL, t = −3.449,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.003]. Cerebral
                      <jats:italic>Δ</jats:italic>
                      HbO₂ was higher following immediate cycling (RC =  + 44.8%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.046) and delayed cycling (RC =  + 46.9%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.01). Muscle ΔHbO₂ was higher following immediate cycling (RC =  + 71.4%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.003), delayed cycling (RC =  + 49.2%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.047), and intermittent activity breaks (RC =  + 47.5%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.01). Heart rate and perceived arousal were higher following delayed cycling and intermittent activity breaks. No significant differences were observed for blood pressure, cognitive performance, focus, or well-being.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A short bout of moderate-intensity cycling immediately after eating is associated with reduction of postprandial hyperglycemia and higher cerebral oxygenation during prolonged sitting, whereas delayed cycling and intermittent cycling bouts increased physiological activation. None of the intervention conditions had a significant effect on cognitive performance. These findings highlight the potential relevance of postprandial cycling strategies, including differences in timing and bout structure, for acute metabolic and oxygenation responses during prolonged sitting.</jats:p>

title: From Archives to Public Memory: Collaborative Construction of Local History in Galeri Bumi Parawira, Indonesia

e84870997483682042d9d58240474ec626139296.abstract: <jats:p>Purpose: This research examines the transformation of static historical archives into dynamic public collective memory through collaborative curatorial and artistic practices at Galeri Bumi Parawira in Bogor, Indonesia. It explores how government agencies, archivists, librarians, local history communities, and artists negotiate authority to co-construct local historical knowledge.Method/approach: Utilizing a qualitative case study design, the research applies reflexive thematic analysis to data collected from institutional documents, semi-structured interviews, and participant observations across multi-stakeholder groups, including government agencies, librarians, archivists, local history communities, and artists.Results: The findings demonstrate that public memory within the gallery is not a passive reproduction of raw administrative records, but an interpretive narrative of local leadership history. This narrative is co-constructed through multi-stakeholder negotiations, field and historical validation, visual artistic representations, and active community participation.Conclusions/findings: The exhibition functions beyond a static archival repository, serving as a living center for public knowledge creation. These results validate the paradigm of “doing history with the public” and reinforce the conceptualization of heritage as an ongoing, dynamic social process.</jats:p>

title: AI-Generated Situated Storytelling for Sustainable Tourism: Cognitive and Affective Pathways to Local Heritage Exploration Intention
container-title: Sustainability
4b6ccb091434ecdde46110fdc1c35fb6f1693176.abstract: <jats:p>Heritage interpretation shapes which places enter public view and with what meanings, linking heritage protection under Sustainable Development Goal 11.4 (SDG 11.4) with public engagement. Yet visitors in historic urban districts concentrate on a few prominent sites, while historical buildings, remains and places dispersed through everyday streets are seldom recognized as heritage. This study draws on the stimulus–organism–response (SOR) framework and cognitive appraisal theory to examine how six perceived attributes of AI-generated situated storytelling relate to historical place meaning (HPM), place affect (PA) and local heritage exploration intention (LHEI). Data from 548 on-site walking experiences in Nanjing were analyzed using structural equation modeling and artificial neural networks. Place contextualization and perceived personalization were associated with both cognitive and affective pathways; historical contextualization and narrative coherence were associated only with HPM, whereas narrative vividness was associated only with PA. HPM and PA showed comparable direct associations with LHEI, and the model-implied indirect association via PA accounted for 22.1% of the total association between HPM and LHEI. In neural-network models, narrative vividness ranked higher in predicting PA than HPM. These findings support attribute–pathway matching and inform the design of AI interpretation intended to encourage willingness to explore dispersed, low-visibility heritage.</jats:p>

title: Compliance-by-Design in an AI-Enabled Platform for Early Crohn Disease Interception: A Viewpoint
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
51c3cf4682e1640bc274480c0925c7d09ca3e377.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>AI-enabled digital medicine platforms in Europe are developed within overlapping rules for personal data, medical devices, AI, clinical research, health data access, and health technology assessment. This viewpoint represents the authors’ experience and interpretation from the preimplementation phase of INTERCEPT, an Innovative Health Initiative consortium that plans to validate biomarkers and develop a blood-based risk score for early Crohn disease interception. It does not report original empirical research, a systematic regulatory review, a deployed platform, or a validated AI model. Our aim is to explain how compliance-by-design can be translated into an auditable governance architecture and to identify what still requires scientific evaluation. We advance 3 messages. First, governance must begin with intended purpose and boundary mapping: a digital platform may contain research, operational, and medical device software functions, and conformity of one module cannot be inferred for the platform as a whole. Second, overlapping obligations can be operationalized through 5 linked controls: modular responsibility and change control, federated data governance, traceable AI life cycle management, consent and participant rights orchestration, and a common cross-border governance core with local adaptations. Third, compliance is not a surrogate for model validity, clinical benefit, trust, scalability, or market access. Before clinical deployment, planned AI components require prespecified labels and cohorts, leakage prevention, missing data and imbalance strategies, calibration, subgroup assessment, external validation, human factors evaluation, and postdeployment algorithmovigilance. A hypothetical biomarker risk score update illustrates how the 5 controls interact. INTERCEPT is informative because it combines cross-border biomarker research, planned predictive analytics, and heterogeneous institutional settings while key design decisions remain modifiable. Its contribution is nevertheless conceptual: the proposed framework is a testable governance hypothesis, not evidence of implementation success. Prospective studies should compare it with alternative governance models and assess safety, workload, participant experience, evidence generation, and regulatory performance.</jats:p>

title: The AI trust paradox: how disclosure, brand authenticity and consumer mindset shape communication effectiveness
container-title: Internet Research
59dbcc5384193484dc87a5169d18eda65dfa1998.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigates the trust paradox in artificial intelligence (AI)-generated content, where efficiency conflicts with perceived inauthenticity. Integrating source credibility theory and congruity theory, it examines how the interplay between ad genesis (AI vs. genuine), strategic context (disclosure, brand authenticity) and consumer mindset (construal level) determines communication effectiveness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A three-study experimental design was employed to isolate specific contingencies. Study 1 manipulated ad genesis and AI disclosure to test engagement. Study 2 examined the moderating role of brand authenticity on purchase intentions. Study 3 tested the congruity between AI message focus (hedonic vs. utilitarian) and consumer construal levels.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Genuine imagery generally outperforms AI-generated imagery; however, effectiveness is contingent on strategic fit. Disclosure boosts engagement for genuine ads but reduces it for AI content. AI ads enhance purchase intentions for low-authenticity brands but damage high-authenticity ones. Furthermore, hedonic AI appeals align with high-construal mindsets, whereas utilitarian appeals suit low-construal consumers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The experiments used static images in controlled online settings. Future research should test dynamic and multimodal AI content and validate the effects with real-world behavioral metrics, such as click-through and conversion rates.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI use should fit the context. Heritage brands should avoid AI imagery, whereas challenger brands can benefit from it. Disclosure helps genuine-image ads but hurts AI-generated ads. Hedonic AI appeals suit abstract mindsets, whereas utilitarian appeals suit concrete mindsets.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research advances advertising theory by applying a split-credibility lens to AI-generated advertising, demonstrating that effectiveness depends on source-context congruence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: AI-driven knowledge management: a new frontier for innovation and collaboration in higher education
container-title: Journal of Applied Research in Higher Education
9f9f245e5f07161e21092c92b0d8f5dc4f48b0fa.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examined how artificial intelligence (AI) tools can be integrated into knowledge management (KM) systems in higher education institutions and assessed their impact on key KM objectives and learning-related outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In terms of purpose, the research was applied and developmental. Methodologically, a qualitative approach was adopted. The study participants consisted of faculty members from Iranian universities. Sampling was conducted using the snowball technique. A total of 11 faculty members participated in the study. The primary data collection instrument was the semi-structured interview. Using a fuzzy cognitive mapping (FCM) approach, the study modeled the relationships between AI technologies, KM variables, and KM functions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results indicated that AI tools have a significant positive effect on KM outcomes in higher education. Natural language processing (NLP) showed the strongest influence on personalized learning, while intelligent assistants and chatbots had the greatest impact on real-time feedback, decision-making, and pattern recognition. Overall, AI-driven KM systems enhanced collaboration, learning outcomes, and knowledge sharing, while improving the efficiency of decision-making processes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study contributes to the higher education literature by offering a systemic, AI-driven KM framework based on FCM. It provides practical insights for university leaders and policymakers on utilizing AI to strengthen KM practices, foster innovation, and support collaborative and data-informed decision-making in academic institutions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
