title: Awareness, Perceived Benefits, and Skill-Erosion Concerns Regarding Generative AI Among Higher Education Students
container-title: Research and Advances in Education
2f32211bef981f72ec3c5ea5163580c623b349d8.abstract: <jats:p>This research aimed to assess awareness of generative AI limitations, highlight its advantages, and identify potential threats from misuse, focusing on differences in opinions between future educators and students from non-education fields. The data were collected through surveying 931 undergraduate students of a private university in the Philippines. The researchers used a comparative-correlational research design with a qualitative strand. The study found moderate awareness of generative AI’s limitations (M = 3.31, SD = 0.94) and a moderate-to-cautious attitude toward its implementation (M = 3.15, SD = 0.87). Education students showed higher awareness than students from other majors (d = 0.40), while differences in usage, perception, and fear of skills deteriorating were negligible (d = 0.14–0.25) and, to some extent, neutralized in robustness checks. Differences between genders and years of study in perceptions were minor. The findings suggest that future teachers’ curricula should include a course on AI literacy and emphasize developing critical thinking skills to prepare students for implementing generative AI solutions in teaching practices.</jats:p>

title: Foresight and governance of complexity in the era of AI
container-title: European Journal of Futures Research
5ef0e2feab6bdfa6e88affebd46853032c0a25c9.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Today’s challenges address a multitude of interconnected agents, resulting in complex systems whose evolution is difficult to predict. Policy makers are asking scientists to identify future scenarios and provide different solutions. The European Union has recognised in foresight a strategic process to support decisions. We show that foresight, governance and lobby are intertwined, and we assign an increased relevance to foresight when dealing with the uncertainty of the evolution of the socio-economic systems. To tackle the complexity in governance and decision processes, we describe an operational methodology named CLEVER to facilitate the problem setting and identification of the most appropriate mode of governance. It can be also adopted to analyse scenarios and their dynamics. CLEVER is based on a logical scheme, thus not dependent on the rapid evolution of tools empowering the information retrieval and future orienteering. We also reflect on the role of AI as an emergent technology, already having an impact on many of the involved processes.</jats:p>

title: AI-Based Voice to Form Filling System: A Review of Speech Recognition, Information Extraction and Intelligent Form Automation
container-title: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management
93f339d87d3e241890bd2e17a2af7f7fe1ccfef7.abstract:
<jats:p>Digital forms support registrations, applications, service requests, surveys, and institutional processes, but completing them can remain difficult for people who face typing barriers, limited digital literacy, language differences, or accessibility challenges. An AI-based voice-to-form filling system aims to make data entry more natural by allowing a user to speak information and converting it into correctly structured form values. This review examines the technologies relevant to the project: automatic speech recognition (ASR), speech-to-text conversion, natural-language processing (NLP), information extraction, semantic field mapping, validation, multilingual interaction, and user confirmation. It considers how voice-driven form automation can coordinate these components and how optical character recognition (OCR) may support document-assisted entry. The discussion emphasizes that transcription accuracy alone does not guarantee successful form completion. Correct extraction, normalization, mapping, correction, privacy, and usability must also be addressed. The review identifies research and implementation priorities for the project, including handling accents and noisy environments, reducing errors that propagate between stages, supporting multiple languages, and providing a secure human-in-the-loop workflow.

Keywords— Artificial Intelligence, Voice-Based Form Filling, Speech Recognition, Speech-to-Text, NLP, Information Extraction, Accessibility, Form Automation, OCR</jats:p>

title: AI-Driven sustainable operations management in manufacturing supply chains: A systematic review, research gap analysis, and strategic framework for future directions
container-title: Supply Chain Research
fca03fbadeec5687818a95144d091938667a754b.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming manufacturing supply chains by enabling intelligent decision-making, adaptive operations, and more efficient resource utilization. Its potential to advance sustainable operations management, however, extends beyond technological adoption to the organizational integration of AI capabilities into operational processes and sustainability-oriented strategies. Despite growing scholarly attention, research in this field remains fragmented across technological applications, manufacturing functions, organizational conditions, and sustainability dimensions. In particular, limited conceptual integration exists regarding how AI capabilities are translated into operational transformation and under what organizational and technological conditions such transformation generates sustainable value. To address these limitations, this study conducts a systematic literature review and structured research gap analysis of peer-reviewed studies published between 2016 and 1 June 2026. The review examines the intellectual evolution of the field, synthesizes dominant research themes, evaluates AI applications across manufacturing and supply chain operations, and critically assesses their implications for operational, environmental, economic, and social sustainability. The synthesis highlights an emerging shift from isolated, function-specific AI applications towards interconnected and increasingly autonomous operational ecosystems, supported by the convergence of AI with the Internet of Things (IoT), digital twins, cyber-physical systems, and advanced analytics. These developments create opportunities for predictive and prescriptive decision-making, intelligent production planning, predictive maintenance, quality optimization, resource efficiency, supply chain visibility, and disruption management. Nevertheless, the realization of these benefits remains contingent upon organizational readiness, digital infrastructure maturity, data quality, workforce capabilities, effective governance, and the alignment of technological investments with sustainability priorities. The review further identifies persistent theoretical, methodological, technological, organizational, and empirical gaps, particularly concerning human–AI collaboration, implementation scalability, algorithmic accountability, sustainability trade-offs, and the assessment of long-term performance outcomes. Building on these insights, the study develops an AI-Driven Sustainable Operations Management Strategic Framework that integrates AI technological capabilities, organizational and digital enablers, AI-enabled operational transformation mechanisms, sustainability-oriented governance, and multidimensional performance outcomes. By connecting technological potential with organizational transformation and sustainability performance, the proposed framework provides an integrative conceptual foundation for understanding AI-enabled sustainable value creation across manufacturing supply chains. It also establishes a structured agenda for future research and offers strategic implications for manufacturing organizations and policymakers seeking to advance responsible AI adoption, strengthen operational resilience, and achieve sustainable long-term competitiveness.</jats:p>

title: AI-Powered Tutoring Quality and Perceived Mathematics Learning Outcomes among Higher Secondary School Students
container-title: American Journal of Interdisciplinary Research and Innovation
8a6673a0fd4602dc04348b3b4dd9ea259dc466f5.abstract: <jats:p>AI Tutoring has the potential to facilitate learning in mathematics, including through the quality of instruction, perceived usefulness, engagement, and confidence. This paper analyses these associations on the basis of provided partial least squares structural equation modelling result of 470 records. Perceived AI tutoring quality, perceived usefulness, mathematics learning engagement, mathematics self-efficacy and perceived mathematics learning outcomes are reflected in five reflective constructs and twenty-five indicators. The analysis records 5,000 bootstrap samples and tenfold repeated prediction. The suggested seven direct relationships are all positive with confidence intervals not equal to zero. The quality of tutoring is linked with usefulness, engagement and self-efficacy. The engagement is linked to self-efficacy and perceived outcomes and self-efficacy is linked to perceived outcomes independent of engagement. The model is used to explain 39.5 percent of the perceived outcomes. The indicators loading, internal consistency, convergent, and discriminant validity are reported to fulfill the assessment criteria as stated in the workbook. However, prediction is above the linear standard of nineteen of twenty endogenous indicators, but the differences are minor. These results set engagement and self-efficacy as complementary explanatory paths. Nevertheless, an empirical sample cannot be verified due to hypothetical platform labels and missing fieldwork documentation. The results thus detail the provided records of analysis and are not able to determine causal achievement gains. Substantive educational conclusions will still require independent evaluation and validated recruitment documentation.</jats:p>

title: The Lived Experiences of English Teachers in Assessing Essays with Suspected or Disclosed AI Involvement: Toward an AI-Informed Assessment Framework
container-title: QualiSearch Journal of Educational Research and Practice
aac36fe9340b95b608c20887d434129731324273.abstract:
<jats:p>This descriptive phenomenological study examined how eight purposively selected English teachers at a public secondary school in Manila assessed essays with suspected or disclosed generative AI involvement. Semi-structured interview data were analyzed using Colaizzi’s method.
Five themes emerged: recognizing AI through discrepancies in students’ writing, employing verification strategies before assessment decisions, negotiating assessment fairness and validity in AI-mediated writing, constructing authenticity through student ownership and personal expression, and adapting to the reality of AI while seeking support and guidance. Teachers compared submitted essays with students’ demonstrated abilities and sought clarification through student dialogue, comparison with earlier work, and, when needed, supervised writing. Teachers questioned whether grades represented student learning and sought clearer criteria. Authenticity involved independent performance, lived experience, personal voice, and student contribution. The experience was characterized by continuing negotiation of uncertainty while protecting authenticity, fairness, assessment validity, and academic integrity. Interpreted through Messick’s Unified Theory of Validity, the findings informed an AI-Informed Assessment Framework for English Writing Assessment that connects recognition, verification, authenticity evaluation, assessment decisionmaking, and professional adaptation.</jats:p>

title: Who Regulates AI Better? Exploring AI Self-Regulated Learning Among Novice and Experienced Vietnamese EFL Teachers
container-title: Journal of Language Teaching and Research
e0813688da54b059f9c552dfef12ec39314e9417.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly transformed teacher professional learning in English as a foreign language (EFL) education. However, relatively limited research has examined how teachers strategically regulate and sustain their AI-related learning processes, particularly across different stages of professional experience. This study investigated AI self-regulated learning (AI-SRL) among novice and experienced Vietnamese in-service EFL teachers. An explanatory sequential mixed methods design was employed. Quantitative data were collected from 1,108 Vietnamese in-service EFL teachers using the AI-SRL Scale, followed by semi-structured interviews with 10 teachers. The quantitative findings revealed that novice teachers demonstrated significantly higher levels of AI-SRL than experienced teachers, particularly in task planning, self-monitoring, and self-evaluation. Notably, no statistically significant differences were identified in help seeking and institutional support. Interestingly, the qualitative findings showed that teachers’ AI-SRL was shaped not only by technological factors, but also by professional identity, emotional responses toward AI learning, and contextual conditions surrounding AI integration. Novice teachers demonstrated remarkably stronger exploratory orientations toward AI learning, whereas experienced teachers expressed greater concerns regarding pedagogical stability and professional accountability. Overall, the study extends previous AI-related educational research by offering a more process-oriented and psychologically nuanced understanding of teacher professional learning in AI-mediated educational environments. The findings also provide valuable pedagogical implications for AI-related teacher professional development in EFL contexts.</jats:p>

title: Conceptualizing Responsible AI Governance Structures for Automated Decision Systems in Regulated Industries
container-title: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SOCIAL SCIENCES AND MANAGEMENT RESEARCH
58aa3ac0067124cce29224f7ff9a4fc00909aa90.abstract:
<jats:p>Automated decision systems (ADS) are increasingly embedded in the core operations of regulated
industries such as banking, insurance, healthcare, and utilities, where their outputs can affect
creditworthiness, medical treatment, employment, and access to essential services. This paper
conceptualizes a governance structure for responsible artificial intelligence (AI) that regulated
organizations can adopt to manage the risks associated with ADS while preserving their capacity
to innovate. Drawing on the regulatory landscape that had taken shape by 2023, including the
European Union's proposed AI Act, the United States National Institute of Standards and
Technology AI Risk Management Framework, sector-specific supervisory guidance in banking
and insurance, and long-standing model risk management practice, the paper proposes a sevenlayer governance architecture spanning board oversight, cross-functional coordination, model
validation, technical assurance, compliance mapping, independent audit, and stakeholder redress.
Each layer is examined in detail, and a worked scenario illustrates the structure applied to a
consumer credit model across its full lifecycle. The framework is then applied to six regulated
sectors, including energy and telecommunications alongside financial services, healthcare,
insurance, and employment, to illustrate how the same structural logic adapts to different statutory
obligations and risk profiles. The paper closes with a discussion of practical tensions and crosscutting themes, recommendations with an implementation roadmap, and directions for future
research.</jats:p>

title: THE IMPACT OF GENERATIVE AI ON TERTIARY EDUCATION
container-title: The International Conference Synergies in Communication
1cc9c8a3f27c42d3d2fcbde39a2b1cbad8aaff6d.abstract:
<jats:p>The rapid rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI), with tools like ChatGPT, has profoundly
reshaped tertiary education, prompting a critical re-evaluation of pedagogical practices, assessment
methods, and institutional policies. This article aims to examine some of the generative AI’s
multifaceted impact, exploring its potential to enhance personalized learning and discipline-specific
instruction, while addressing ethical challenges related to academic integrity, equity, and cultural
bias. Drawing on global research, including multinational studies and institutional case studies, the
analysis highlights how AI disrupts traditional assessments, requiring innovative redesigns that
balance authenticity with technological integration. By looking into empirical evidence and
theoretical insights, the article argues that generative AI’s transformative potential depends on
evidence-based, inclusive strategies that respect educational values. Educational institutions using
these approaches can optimally deal with AI’s challenges in order to create reliable learning
environments, even redefining higher education for the 21st century.</jats:p>

title: AI-Integrated Learning Across Four Generative AI-Supported Classrooms: Students’ Perceptions, Digital Confidence, Critical Digital Literacy, and Information Evaluation
container-title: European Journal of Educational Research
a65f35267c717a41f66b5f06fba65fb6537cc809.abstract: <jats:p>Generative AI is increasingly used in higher education, but evidence remains limited on how students report multiple digital-learning outcomes across classrooms using different platforms within a common instructional framework. This exploratory posttest-only study describes four intact classrooms using ChatGPT (n = 29), Gemini (n = 29), DeepSeek (n = 28), and Perplexity AI (n = 32) during an eight-session AI-integrated learning program. Because each platform was represented by only one classroom, platform and classroom effects could not be separated; therefore, the study reports descriptive classroom profiles rather than platform-level causal or inferential effects. The four classrooms showed distinct descriptive patterns across the outcomes. The DeepSeek-supported classroom had the highest observed means for AITBLM perception (4.10), Digital Confidence (4.06), and Critical Digital Literacy (4.07), whereas the Perplexity AI-supported classroom had the highest observed Technology Information Evaluation mean (4.21). Across classrooms, AITBLM perception ranged from 3.86 to 4.10, Digital Confidence from 3.84 to 4.06, Critical Digital Literacy from 3.90 to 4.07, and Technology Information Evaluation from 3.89 to 4.21. ChatGPT and Gemini showed nearly identical AITBLM perception means (3.91 and 3.90), while Gemini and Perplexity AI showed comparatively higher TIE means (4.08 and 4.21). These contrasts indicate different classroom response profiles rather than a consistent ranking across all outcomes. The findings are exploratory and should not be interpreted as evidence that one AI platform is more effective than another.</jats:p>

title: Revising Terminology and Phenotype Definitions for AI-Based Decision Support in Fluid Therapy: Call for Consensus
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
f329cbb522067f1529d3d23dce94d184d954dacd.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Intravenous fluid therapy is a cornerstone of optimizing body hydration, circulation, and perfusion, yet its rational implementation is limited by inconsistent clinical terminology. As fluid therapy moves toward AI-empowered clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS), there is a critical need for high-quality, verified training data. The reliability of these systems is currently threatened by misleading data resulting from ambiguous definitions and the interchangeable use of nonsynonymous terms, such as “dehydration” and “hypovolemia.” This multidisciplinary panel-of-experts opinion article intends to start a discussion by identifying the key drawbacks in current terminology and proposes solutions, including a shift toward adequacy-based phenotypes and categorizing blood and water volumes as “insufficient,” “optimal,” or “excessive” rather than relying on context-sensitive quantitative measures such as “low,” “normal,” or “high.” Illustrative scenarios are used to show how inconsistent terminology and static quantitative labels could mislead an AI-CDSS. The proposed phenotype matrix is designed to provide a structured, systematic description of fluid requirements for specific clinical objectives that can be integrated into clinical algorithms and machine learning databases. An example of a fluid requirement assessment algorithm is used for exploring its applicability in AI training. The proposed terminology and phenotype matrix are provisional: they represent the opinion of a multidisciplinary expert panel and have not undergone formal consensus, clinical validation, or testing within an AI system. Broad consensus-building initiatives will follow.</jats:p>

title: Pengaruh Pemahaman AI Dan Inovasi Digital Serta Literasi Pasar Modal Terhadap Niat Berwirausaha Digital Dengan Efikasi Diri Sebagai Variabel Mediasi
container-title: Zentrum Economic, Business, Management, Accounting Research
3c5ac900d590200206b0b61f4df5706a0f814fcb.abstract: <jats:p>The development of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital capital markets creates new business opportunities, yet little is known about how students' understanding of both domains shapes their digital entrepreneurial intention. This study examines the effect of understanding of AI and digital innovation and of capital market literacy on digital entrepreneurial intention, with self-efficacy as a mediating variable. A quantitative survey of 153 students attending a public lecture was analysed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4 with 5,000 bootstrap subsamples. The measurement model met the criteria for convergent validity, reliability, and discriminant validity. Understanding of AI and digital innovation (β = 0.480) and capital market literacy (β = 0.325) had positive and significant effects on self-efficacy. Self-efficacy had the strongest effect on digital entrepreneurial intention (β = 0.526) and mediated the effects of both independent variables. Capital market literacy also had a significant direct effect (β = 0.286), whereas understanding of AI and digital innovation had no direct effect (β = 0.099; p = 0.238), so its influence operates fully through self-efficacy. The model explains 69.8% of the variance in digital entrepreneurial intention. The findings imply that public lectures and entrepreneurship education should build students' self-belief rather than only transfer knowledge.</jats:p>

title: Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) in Nigeria: Empirical Analysis of Personality traits, Emotional intelligence and Gender as Determinants.
container-title: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SOCIAL SCIENCES AND MANAGEMENT RESEARCH
db22bd6539e265ed987f56bbb1d5839a2ce7ffa4.abstract:
<jats:p>This study investigated the Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) in Nigeria: Empirical Analysis of
Personality traits, Emotional intelligence and Gender as Determinants. The current study
adopted a cross-sectional survey research design and a random sampling technique to select
eighty-five (85) consisting 43 (50.58%) female and 42 (49.41%) male married adolescents.
Their age ranges from 21-41 years, as well as an estimated 56.4% from polygamous family,
and 44.6% from monogamous family. On their educational qualification, 7(8.4%) of the
respondents had SSCE, 46 (55.4%) had ND/NCE, 25(29.4%) had BSC, while 7(8.2%) had
postgraduate qualification. Participants completed the intimate partner violence, emotional
intelligence, and personality traits scales as study’s means of data collection. Three hypotheses
are tested at 0.05 level of significance, and results following multiple regression analysis
showed that personality traits jointly (R2 = .483; F (5, 58) = 10.824; p< .000) predicted
intimate partner violence. On the independent basis, agreeableness (β = -.356, t = -2.864; p<
.006), neuroticism (β = .245, t = 2.393; p< .020), openness to experience (β = -.010, t = -
3.012; p<.008) and extraversion (β = -.524, t = -5.604; p< .001) independently predicted
intimate partner (IPV) violence. While, conscientiousness (β = -.162, t = 1.271; p > .209) did
not significantly predict IPV. In addition, emotional intelligence did not significantly predict (β
= -.289, t = -2.374; p > .021) IPV. Lastly, result revealed a significant gender difference [t (65)
= 1.260; p < .212] in intimate partner (IPV) among Married Adolescents in Lagos, Nigeria.
The study recommended that developing and expanding counseling programs for individuals
with personality traits associated with IPV to help them manage their emotional intelligence,
and gender characteristics more constructively.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: Transformative Potential, Implementation Challenges, and Future Trajectories
container-title: Journal of Research in Engineering and Computer Sciences
4f57fb5aa53ffc9a9ad9de6e928127777efd4d6e.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into educational systems has accelerated dramatically, transitioning from experimental pilot programs to mainstream pedagogical practice by 2026. This paper examines the current landscape of AI in education through quantitative analysis of global adoption data, stakeholder perceptions, and performance outcomes. Drawing on surveys from over 3,800 students across 16 countries, institutional reports, and longitudinal studies, we find that 86% of higher education students now utilize AI tools. In contrast, 60% of teachers have integrated AI into their teaching practice. The global AI education market is projected to reach $112.03 billion by 2034, reflecting a compound annual growth rate of approximately 38%. However, significant challenges persist: 65% of educators’ express concern about plagiarism, 71% of K-12 teachers lack formal AI training, and only 7% of schools worldwide have established AI usage guidance. This paper synthesizes current evidence, identifies critical implementation barriers, and proposes a framework for responsible AI integration that preserves human-centric pedagogy while leveraging technological affordances.</jats:p>

title: EARLY LITERACY AND SOCIAL LITERACY IN CONTEMPORARY TIMES: MAGDA SOARES'S CONTRIBUTIONS FACING THE CHALLENGES OF POST-PANDEMIC AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
container-title: Rethinking Education: Knowledge, Learning, and Social Transformation
65b940967c749abb8a6f8fe3c48dc93d9171a021.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) has changed reading, writing, and knowledge-production practices, creating opportunities and challenges for early literacy and social literacy practices. This article examines the relationships between acting in discourse, the facets of written language proposed by Magda Soares, and literacy in the age of AI. It is a qualitative, interpretative bibliographic and documentary study based on classical works, recent research, and documents from Brazilian education authorities, UNICEF, and UNESCO. The diagnosis identifies persistent inequalities in learning and access to technology, intensified during the COVID-19 pandemic, without attributing these outcomes to AI. The analysis shows that Soares’s contributions connect learning the alphabetic writing system with text production and social participation. AI may support teachers in planning and reviewing educational materials, but it also raises concerns about authorship, reliability, bias, and technological dependence. Proposed pedagogical pathways include assessment of learning needs, teacher mediation, active student participation, source verification, and accessible alternatives. AI should therefore remain a complementary, ethically guided educational resource that does not replace children’s own development of reading and writing.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Professional Practice of Post-Secondary Teachers in Quebec: A Mixed-Methods Study of Gaps and Training Priorities
container-title: Education Sciences
78e0184830c977cb445ccbfbc2637b8f5ed87c32.abstract: <jats:p>In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly pervasive, and the field of education is no exception. However, ensuring that AI brings a positive and productive impact to teaching practices requires that AI training for instructors addresses their actual teaching needs. In the present study, the AI training needs post-secondary teachers in Quebec have been identified by simultaneously monitoring their AI usage, AI literacy, and training expectations. Data were collected between October 2024 and October 2025 for 345 teachers in 27 first-level postsecondary institutions (CEGEPS) using an online questionnaire. In-depth interviews were performed for 27 teachers in 10 CEGEPS. An integrated quantitative and qualitative approach was used to analyze the data. The largest majority of responses (94.7%) reveals the utilization of AI in a professional context, with time-saving being the main reason for use among participants. AI literacy exhibits statistically significant differences across gender and discipline groups, suggesting the need for multilevel training courses. While technical understanding is the lowest performing dimension of AI literacy (with an average score of 2.7 out of five points), participating teachers prioritize learning about practical applications, specifically in their own discipline field. Instead of abandoning the teaching of first principles, which are essential for unlocking advanced functionalities that users cannot yet foresee, future research should examine whether multilevel training courses, which embed these concepts within the practical tools that users desire, can foster meaningful professional development.</jats:p>

title: Artificial intelligence analysis of oral mucosal lesions in white‐light clinical photographs: A systematic review of visual features and validation
container-title: European Journal of Oral Sciences
faf03cc1755fb84b301613a3dafafc5968d5b24a.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to conventional oral photographs for recognition, classification, localization, segmentation, and risk assessment of oral mucosal lesions. This systematic review evaluated how clinically relevant visual information—including color, texture, morphology, borders, and spatial patterns—is represented by AI systems and assessed performance, validation, explainability, human comparison, and clinical translation. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched for studies directly analyzing conventional white‐light clinical photographs. Risk of bias was assessed with PROBAST + AI, and certainty with Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation‐based approaches. Fifty‐three studies were included, 30 published in 2025–2026. Forty‐six used implicit deep‐learning visual representations, three multimodal vision‐language models, two explicit color analyses, and two explicit texture analyses. Thirty‐one studies primarily addressed image‐level diagnostic classification/recognition, 15 spatial detection/localization or lesion delineation, six screening/triage/referral or biopsy‐oriented decision support, and one longitudinal malignant‐transformation prediction. Six used independent external cohorts and five compared AI with human readers. Methodological concerns were frequent, no sufficiently coherent group supported meta‐analysis, and certainty remained limited across evidence bodies. Current evidence therefore supports technical feasibility rather than established clinical effectiveness, with translation requiring stronger patient‐level independence, external validation, prospective multicenter evaluation, and evidence of clinical benefit.</jats:p>

title: Graph tree fusion model for efficient real-time data processing
container-title: Pollack Periodica
258d7c3f08bdf802054c852f339b2378e52ea54f.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>An innovative hybrid data model that integrates hierarchical tree structures with network-based graph representations to effectively manage dynamic, time-sensitive information. Developed using Python libraries for network analysis and discrete-event simulation, the model were evaluated using publicly available academic and social network datasets. It demonstrates efficient data traversal with logarithmic time complexity and minimal update overhead through techniques. Experimental analysis reveals significant improvements in update latency, memory efficiency, and system adaptability when compared to traditional data structures like graph-based trees. Statistical methods, including hypothesis testing and confirm the model's effectiveness for applications requiring real-time data processing.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>This study aims to develop a Digital Twin-based framework to address these challenges, with a practical application to heavy vehicle components. The proposed approach is characterized by the integration of planning data, operational parameters, and mathematical models into a unified digital platform that enables real-time monitoring and prediction. The results showed that the proposed system improved process performance prediction accuracy by 12.6%, reduced material waste by 9.4%, and reduced processing time by 7.8%, while achieving a significant improvement in the quality of the final surface. These indicators confirm that integrating Digital Twins into computer-aided manufacturing not only increases operational efficiency but also expands the potential for smart manufacturing by enhancing the reliability of digital modeling and supporting informed decision in complex industrial environments.</jats:p>

title: Evaluating large language models for generating programming questions from code
container-title: Pollack Periodica
60af7e8ea6e557b694e95e3ab555eec6e4683e39.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>E-learning platforms demand effective question-generation methods, and large language models have made this easier. While recent studies focused on generating questions from text, no prior research has evaluated their ability to generate questions from code. This work presents a framework to evaluate the models in question generation from code using average scores, win rates, and Elo ratings. Python, C++, and Java code were used to prompt models. The evaluation includes automatic metrics and human evaluators. Findings show GPT-4-0314, GPT-4-0613, and GPT-3.5-turbo-0613 outperform others, with GPT-4-0314 leading in score (8.86), win rate (1.000), and Elo rating, 2616.</jats:p>

title: Effect of thermal sensation on cognitive performance
container-title: Pollack Periodica
53bc30e0ff67b9dc855c7d59c699c1fa64b7bd72.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Thermal sensation of the human body and cognitive performance are closely related. Extreme temperature conditions can significantly impair concentration, memory and mental state, leading to reduced productivity. It is therefore important to ensure appropriate climatic conditions to maintain productivity. This is particularly important in modern buildings, where thermal comfort can be ensured and guaranteed through building services engineering. It is uncertain, however, what the exact thermal satisfaction value is for people in terms of mental performance. There is both consensus and unresolved matters in the literature on the subject. The aim of this research is to investigate the optimal thermal comfort level with live subjects and by measuring thermal comfort parameters. It also aims to confirm or refute the results presented in the literature.</jats:p>

title: Engagement, Feasibility, and Perceived Alliance With a Large Language Model–Enabled Mental Health Voice and Chatbot: Exploratory Longitudinal Observational Study
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
eea4be47b904228bd29f30f3e159f5966ee27e3b.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Conversational AI systems are increasingly used for web-based mental health support, yet evidence on sustained engagement, therapeutic alliance, and longitudinal outcomes remains limited. Baseline data from 527 self-referred users of the large language model–enabled chatbot Clare indicated high psychological distress and early development of a subjective working alliance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This exploratory study examined the feasibility and descriptive outcome patterns associated with the use of the multimodal conversational agent Clare over 4 and 8 weeks in a real-world setting, focusing on engagement, perceived working alliance, and mental health measures.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We conducted a naturalistic, single-arm, repeated-measures observational study of self-referred, English-speaking adults recruited online via social media and search advertisements. Participants interacted with Clare over 8 weeks. Two analytic samples were defined by engagement and assessment completion: a 4-week sample (active engagement plus completed 4-week assessment) and an 8-week sample (additionally requiring continued engagement and completed 8-week assessment). Outcomes were assessed at baseline, 4, and 8 weeks: engagement metrics (calls, messages, and call duration), alliance measures (Working Alliance Inventory–Short Revised and Mobile Agnew Relationship Measure), and mental health measures (Patient Health Questionnaire–4, Patient Health Questionnaire–Distress, Mini–Social Phobia Inventory, UCLA Loneliness Scale, and Satisfaction With Life Scale). Changes were evaluated using 2-tailed paired-samples
                      <jats:italic>t</jats:italic>
                      tests with effect sizes; given substantial attrition and reliance on complete-case analyses, linear mixed-effects models were run as sensitivity analyses, and findings warrant cautious interpretation.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of 527 baseline participants, 369 enrolled and 348 actively engaged with Clare; 53 out of 348 (15.2%) met the 4-week criteria and 21 out of 348 (6.0%) met the 8-week criteria. Engagement peaked in week 1 (calls: mean 1.77, SD 1.52; messages: mean 10.02, SD 16.68) and declined thereafter. Among T1-T2 complete pairs (n=52), mean Patient Health Questionnaire–Distress scores decreased by 1.13 (95% CI 0.25 to 2.02) points, Patient Health Questionnaire–4 scores decreased by 0.69 (95% CI −0.01 to 1.40) points, Mini–Social Phobia Inventory scores decreased by 1.73 (95% CI 0.88 to 2.58) points, Satisfaction With Life Scale scores increased by 6.23 (95% CI 4.70 to 7.76) points, and UCLA scores increased by 0.48 (95% CI 0.00 to 0.96) points. Among participants with Working Alliance Inventory–Short Revised data (n=53), total scores increased by 0.20 points from T1b to T2 (95% CI −0.01 to 0.42); among the 8-week retained subgroup (n=21), Mobile Agnew Relationship Measure scores increased by 0.22 points from T2 to T3 (95% CI 0.03 to 0.42).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sustained engagement was limited, and outcome estimates were obtained from small, highly selected follow-up samples. The observed changes cannot be attributed to Clare because the study had no control group and substantial, nonrandom attrition.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: A cU-Net-based surrogate model for predicting rough surface contact parameters in line-contact friction
container-title: Friction
8a747f75cef0183f664b30a4a602a4f164fb293e.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Accurate and efficient prediction of contact parameters on rough surfaces is critical for the tribological design, condition monitoring, and failure analysis of line-contact components. Although physics-based models offer high prediction fidelity, their multifield-coupled iterative solvers are computationally expensive and complex, limiting practical engineering deployment. This work proposes a digital surrogate model based on conditional U-Net (cU-Net) for predicting the spatial distributions of contact parameters, including contact temperature, pressure, and heat flux, on rough surfaces in line-contact friction. Real surface topographies are augmented via the generative patch nearest neighbor (GPNN) model, and a wide-ranging training dataset is constructed through batch computation using a boundary lubrication physics-based model. The cU-Net incorporates an operating-condition embedding mechanism to enable unified prediction across multiple operating conditions. Multiscale spatial and channel attention modules are further integrated to enhance cross-scale feature extraction. A four-component progressive composite loss, assembled from established loss terms and tailored to the sparse extreme-value characteristics of rough surface contact parameters, is combined with Bayesian hyperparameter optimization and a three-stage progressive training strategy. On completely unseen rough surfaces, the model achieves mean relative errors (MREs) of 3.53%, 12.32%, and 13.66% for the temperature, pressure, and heat flux fields, respectively, with peak and top-5% errors that are lower still, and it is approximately 105 times faster than the physics-based model on the same workstation. Out-of-distribution (OOD) tests quantify the degradation of accuracy under extrapolated operating conditions. Retraining with datasets generated from the corresponding physics-based models is expected to extend the framework to other lubrication regimes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Association of eHealth Literacy With Cognitive Function, Frailty, and Functional Status in Hospitalized Geriatric Patients: Cross-Sectional Observational Study
container-title: JMIR Human Factors
ec5a1f530dd5164a01c8bee946e12a446e866836.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The rapid growth of digital health technologies has highlighted the importance of eHealth literacy, which is crucial for navigating health information and tools such as telemedicine and eHealth records. However, older adults often have reservations about digital technologies and face barriers due to cognitive, sensory, and motor impairments, which hinder their ability to effectively use digital health applications. Despite its relevance, research on eHealth literacy in older populations is limited, with a particular gap in understanding how self-assessments of eHealth literacy correlate with health characteristics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study seeks to explore eHealth literacy among hospitalized geriatric patients in Germany. The main objective is to evaluate the eHealth literacy level within this particular group and identify the clinical and sociodemographic factors that may influence it.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Data from this observational study were analyzed to explore characteristics influencing eHealth literacy in hospitalized geriatric patients. The study included patients aged 60 or older in the Department of Geriatric Medicine at Marien Hospital Herne and enrolled in the standardized early rehabilitation pathway. eHealth literacy was measured using the German version of the eHealth Literacy Scale (GR-eHEALS), a self-assessment tool. Sociodemographic and clinical data, including cognitive function (Montreal Cognitive Assessment [MoCA]), frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale [CFS]), and depression (Depression in Old Age Scale [DIA-S]), were collected. Statistical analyses involved descriptive statistics,
                      <jats:italic>t</jats:italic>
                      tests, chi-square tests, and regression analyses to examine the relationship between eHealth literacy and various factors. Sociodemographic and clinical data, including cognitive function (MoCA), frailty (CFS), and depression (DIA-S), were collected.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 244 participants (aged 60‐97, mean 77.2, SD 6.9 years) were included in the analysis. Participants generally reported an eHealth literacy, with higher scores in “information seeking” (mean 3.64, SD 0.84) compared to “information appraisal” (mean 3.32, SD 0.80). Significant differences in eHealth literacy were observed by age, with older participants scoring lower on both subscales. Frailty was significantly associated with critical appraisal of online health information (B=–1.372, 95% CI –2.554 to –0.189), suggesting that individuals who are frail struggle more with evaluating health information. No significant associations were found with other sociodemographic variables, including MoCA scores, education, or gender.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While the findings suggest a positive self-reported ability to engage with digital health tools, the selective sample and reliance on self-assessment limit the accuracy of these results. It also emphasizes the need for tailored interventions to support older adults in improving their eHealth literacy, particularly those with higher levels of frailty. Further research, including longitudinal studies and objective assessments, is essential to better understand and address the digital health needs of the geriatric population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Anesthesia Teleconsultation for Pediatric Preoperative Assessment: A Large National Prospective Multicentric Study in Children (TeleCCCAP)
container-title: Anesthesiology
38453708e93d236221ed268d660a922a600af194.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While interest in pediatric anesthesia teleconsultation is growing, published data remain scarce. This study evaluated the feasibility of anesthesia teleconsultation in children, providing a comprehensive analysis of failure, quality, dedicated time, and satisfaction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      This prospective observational study was performed in 11 major French hospitals. The primary outcome was anesthesia teleconsultation feasibility. Feasibility was defined as the rate of successful anesthesia teleconsultations,
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">i.e</jats:italic>
                      ., those performed in the presence of both child and parent, exclusively
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">via</jats:italic>
                      the dedicated secure audiovisual platform, and not requiring a complementary in-person appointment. Secondary outcomes included causes and consequences of failure, factors associated with failure, quality of anesthetic preparation, medical time dedicated to preoperative assessment, analysis of parents, and anesthetist satisfaction.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A total of 830 children aged 6.7 [25th, 75th percentiles, 3.5,12.2] yr were included. Feasibility of anesthesia teleconsultation was 73%. Failure was due to technical (91%), organizational (9%), and medical (1%) issues. Three anesthesia teleconsultations (0.4%) were converted to in-person consultations. Factors associated with technical failure included the use of tablets or smartphones rather than computers (odds ratio, 2.44; 95% CI, 1.40 to 4.26;
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.002), the absence of a preconnection test (odds ratio, 6.21; 95% CI, 3.05 to 12.66;
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                      < 0.001), and several sociodemographic characteristics. On the day of surgery, no procedure was canceled, one was postponed, and one anesthetic strategy was modified. Medical time dedicated to preoperative evaluation was 28 [18,33] min. Parental satisfaction was high: 93% would choose teleconsultation for a future procedure. Anesthetists’ satisfaction was high: 96% with medical aspects, 90% with the suitability for the case, and 72% with the quality of information delivered. Technical failure consistently impacted all components of anesthetist satisfaction.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This national audit highlights that addressing technical and organizational issues appears essential to transform anesthesia teleconsultations from a mere tool into a robust clinical process, ensuring its reliability and clinical utility in pediatric anesthesia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Methods and Effectiveness of Auditory-Cognitive Training for Older Adults: Scoping Review and Meta-Analysis
container-title: JMIR Rehabilitation and Assistive Technologies
8c56aa534088f3531aa1721d2149a75ff1a11acc.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Auditory-cognitive training (ACT) combines auditory and cognitive exercises to improve listening and cognition in individuals with hearing difficulties; yet, it lacks standardized implementation and consistent evidence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This mixed-evidence synthesis aimed to map ACT’s implementation characteristics and summarize its reported short-term and maintenance effects on trained and nontrained cognitive and auditory outcomes, including hearing function in daily life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The review followed the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines and the Arksey and O’Malley scoping review framework. Databases searched included Embase, the Cochrane Library, PubMed, and APA PsycNet from inception to July 30, 2026. Articles were included or excluded based on specific criteria, and included articles were evaluated for risk of bias.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      ACT showed significant pooled effects on speech-in-noise performance (mean difference [MD]=−1.23 dB, 95% CI −2.35 to −0.10;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03), attention (standardized mean difference [SMD]=0.50, 95% CI 0.23-0.77;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001), memory (SMD=1.08, 95% CI 0.25-1.92;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.01), and global cognition (MD=3.27, 95% CI 0.27-6.26;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03). Effects on pure-tone audiometry, subjective hearing function, working memory, and executive function were limited and nonsignificant. Current evidence is limited by unstandardized training dosage/duration, limited linguistic generalizability across non-English languages, and insufficient assessment of patient-reported real-life listening outcomes.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>ACT may improve selected auditory and cognitive outcomes in older adults, particularly speech-in-noise perception, and attention. The evidence remains limited by substantial heterogeneity, a small number of studies, and low certainty for most outcomes. Standardized protocols, clinically meaningful outcome measures, and longer follow-up are needed to determine its clinical effectiveness and long-term benefits.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Large Language Model Risk of Bias Assessment for Studies in Environmental Health: Proof-of-Concept Study
container-title: JMIR Bioinformatics and Biotechnology
9c8dd83fe163e4250f0d674e01bdfc2647f6403f.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The assessment of the risk of bias (RoB) of each study is a necessary but labor-intensive step in conducting a systematic review (SR). There is a potential for AI to reduce the time and effort needed for RoB assessment and improve consistency between reviewers, but little is known about the accuracy of AI-based RoB assessments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this study, we aim to evaluate the performance of a large language model (LLM) when given the questions from the RoB tool and the relevant passages from the full-text papers in assessing RoB in observational studies of environmental exposures and health outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We evaluated the performance of GPT-5-mini on 128 observational studies from a SR of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances and health outcomes conducted by the National Academies of Sciences. The navigation guide (NavGuide), a domain-based RoB tool designed for environmental studies, was used. For each paper-domain pair, the LLM was provided with the questions and guidance from the NavGuide and the human-identified text passages addressing that domain. The LLM returned a structured RoB rating, which was compared to the human-adjudicated ratings to quantify agreement and identify patterns of discrepancy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      GPT-5-mini RoB assessments for exact matches (64.5%; κ=0.199, Gwet AC2=0.882,
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score=0.311) remained lower than the concordance between humans and the reference standard (87.5%-91.4%). Performance improved substantially for partial matches, reflecting agreement in direction but not necessarily in magnitude (eg, “low” and “probably low”), with percent concordance of 91.9% (κ=0.241, Gwet AC2=0.910,
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score=0.614; for humans, 97.9%-98.6% concordance). Performance varied across the NavGuide domains, with the worst performance in domain 1 (selection bias) and the best in domain 4 (outcome assessment). The models tended to be more stringent than humans, often assigning higher RoB ratings (eg, “probably low” when humans assigned “low”).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our results suggest that although concordance was moderate and inconsistent across domains, LLMs may be sufficiently accurate for use with human oversight. LLMs can flag cases for human adjudication or consistency checking but are not ready for use as an independent second reviewer without human oversight.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Quantum scattering model of dual-parallel Mach–Zehnder electro-optic modulators: general formalism, impairments, and applications to frequency-bin photonic quantum states
container-title: Journal of the Optical Society of America B
8ab824032059a1c7a6bdf3b81558a979e96e16f8.abstract: <jats:p>We present a quantum-mechanical model of dual-parallel Mach–Zehnder electro-optic modulators (DP-MZMs), derived using the quantum scattering formalism. We obtain the complete, unrestricted transformation of single-photon and coherent input states through the DP-MZM architecture, including independent radio-frequency (RF) drive conditions on each internal modulator, and recover the symmetric push-pull operating point as an exact special case. We numerically evaluate the resulting frequency-comb structure, quantify the device sensitivity to bias error, modulation-index imbalance, and RF noise, and use the model to design a DP-MZM-based frequency-bin qubit source, reporting its fidelity as a function of these impairments.</jats:p>

title: High-resolution parallel-translation CT reconstruction based on a patch-based adaptive-regularization-guided diffusion model
container-title: Optics Express
9f629735095f90d7829194ffafe5b6307a6f68fa.abstract: <jats:p>Computed tomography (CT) is an effective technique for industrial non-destructive testing (NDT). However, conventional rotational CT is difficult to apply to the scanning and reconstruction of large plate-like objects, while its mechanical system is also relatively complex. In response to these limitations, parallel translation CT (PTCT) has been introduced. Nevertheless, due to its limited scanning range, PTCT acquires incomplete projection data, which leads to aliasing artifacts and makes accurate reconstruction challenging. To address these issues and achieve high-resolution PTCT reconstruction, this paper proposes a patch-based adaptive-regularization-guided diffusion model. Specifically, an initial estimate obtained by the Simultaneous Iterative Reconstruction Technique (SIRT) is first employed, introducing structural prior information into the reconstruction process. Based on this, a split-and-reassemble denoising module (SRDM) is designed to perform patch-wise reconstruction, where positional encoding is incorporated as conditional guidance to enhance the representation of local structural details. Furthermore, an adaptive-regularization-based correction module (ARCM) is introduced, in which seam-based and mask-based regularization terms are adaptively adjusted according to the denoising stage to support global structural recovery and improve local structural continuity. To evaluate the proposed method, a PCB dataset containing samples with defect structures is constructed. The results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves reliable performance in global reconstruction while effectively recovering fine structural details within defect regions.</jats:p>

title: A novel inversion framework for gravity and magnetic field data: Geophysical model construction, forward modeling, and inversion
container-title: Geophysics
a31740b42e5920ded850e2170020139f22487483.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Deep learning-based 3D inversion of gravity and magnetic field data can directly predict the spatial distribution and physical property parameters of subsurface source bodies from observed data, offering high resolution and efficiency. However, in practical applications, its generalization capability is constrained by two factors: the extent to which the training data set approximates real geologic conditions and the network’s capacity to extract data features. Previous model construction, forward modeling, and inversion methods were reviewed and compared. First, to tackle the problem that existing modeling methods cannot simulate rock bodies with gradational morphologies and physical properties, the continuous smoothness characteristics of Perlin noise were introduced for 3D geophysical model construction, enabling the simulation of realistic geometric shapes and physical properties of source bodies. Second, to address the data set construction efficiency issue, a fast surrogate network was proposed, significantly accelerating batch forward modeling while maintaining precision. Third, a novel network integrating convolutional neural networks and Transformers was designed, combined with a dynamic noise-adding strategy, effectively enhancing the resolution of inversion results. In addition, to better quantify and evaluate inversion reliability, a new evaluation metric was proposed that characterizes spatial and physical property consistency between the predicted model and the true model. Subsequently, a deep learning inversion framework was proposed by integrating the above methods, aiming to enhance the generalization ability and practicality of deep learning-based 3D inversion of gravity and magnetic data. Tests on synthetic data demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed methods. Finally, the generalization capability of the inversion method and the effectiveness of the evaluation metric were discussed, and the method was validated on real data from the San Nicolas deposit in Mexico, yielding a subsurface 3D density model that was consistent with available geologic and borehole information and confirming the effectiveness and feasibility of the method.</jats:p>

title: Simulating the Haldane model in ultraclean GaAs heterostructures
container-title: Physical Review B
3195bd87e54931f8bdd6f6f8a03bc5e4e40b0900.abstract: <jats:p>The Haldane model represents the minimal lattice-based realization of a Chern insulator, exhibiting a quantized Hall conductance in the absence of Landau levels. Despite its conceptual elegance, the implementation in crystalline solids of the requisite pattern of Peierls phases breaking time-reversal symmetry remains experimentally demanding. In this work, we theoretically investigate the possibility to simulate the Haldane model in ultraclean GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures. Our proposal relies on recent experiments in which a high-mobility two-dimensional electron gas is subject to a gate-defined honeycomb electrostatic potential and a laterally periodic magnetic field generated by patterned ferromagnetic structures. The combined electrostatic and magnetic superlattices furnish a viable route to emulate the topological properties of the Haldane model.</jats:p>

title: Toward Teacher Agency for Quality Education for All: Reflections and Future Directions
container-title: Annual Review of Comparative and International Education 2025, Part A
ede007cabf2d49e6575f829fb1131d2162a04622.abstract: <jats:p>The quality of education, extending beyond mere accessibility, has become an indispensable means for addressing academic performance disparities and fostering social inclusion among students from diverse backgrounds within the realm of fee-free education. In this regard, teachers are often seen as pivotal social agents who can exercise their agency to mitigate academic discrepancies, ultimately alleviating social inequalities. Despite this consensus, however, scholarly discourse on teacher agency remains central to ongoing intellectual debates, presenting further opportunities for theoretical exploration and empirical contribution. This study, therefore, aims to survey the literature on teacher agency in addressing academic performance among all public-school students. To achieve this objective, the study builds on an ecological framework of teacher agency and conducts a literature review to elucidate this nuanced framework and outline future research trajectories. The study employs a systematic review to identify relevant studies in the SCOPUS database and selects a total of 18 articles. The analysis reveals a connection between individual teachers and their social contexts in shaping their agency, while also identifying potential areas that require further scholarly elaboration. The study calls for more diverse scientific approaches and geographical contexts to obtain stronger evidence that can enhance theoretical development and inform policy discussions regarding the pursuit of quality education for every child.</jats:p>

title: The Impact of Race, Wealth, and Language on the Decolonization of Education: Experiences Within the USA and South Africa
container-title: Annual Review of Comparative and International Education 2025, Part B
23513732c6f32f2d8475741d84f2d219df8797bf.abstract: <jats:p>This study begins by focusing on general perceptions regarding colonization, decolonization, and post-colonialism and their meaning, potential, and actual impact upon education globally. It then turns to a more specific discussion on decolonization legacies and their impact upon education in South Africa and the USA Specifically, the study addresses the continuing effects of coloniality through attempts to dismantle enduring structure of colonialism and imperialism that continue to oppress marginalized groups globally. The study also emphasizes the importance of indigenous knowledge systems and non-Western ways of knowing, by emphasizing the need to reconceptualize power dynamics and knowledge production processes through an analysis of decolonization of education within South Africa and the USA. The study then discusses the impact of post-colonialism on education within these two countries. It also discusses how post-colonial legacies within South Africa and the USA might have led to differing systems of education. The study then focuses on the impact of race/ethnicity, wealth, and economic inequalities, including the potential role of South Africa’s “no Fee” schools on providing more equitable educational opportunities and the educational and economic rewards based on student socioeconomic status (SES) in the USA and the potential impact of decolonizing wealth on the enhancement of equitable education opportunities. This chapter concludes with a discussion and comparison of unresolved colonial and post-colonial legacies that continue to impact access to equitable educational opportunities in both countries.</jats:p>

title: School Leadership and Community Engagement: Scholarly Explorations, Theoretical Contributions, and Future Directions
container-title: Annual Review of Comparative and International Education 2025, Part B
6f49f6351db55539c095c3307d56c24e220b0519.abstract: <jats:p>School–community engagement (SCE) fundamentally contributes to establishing a safe and effective learning environment for students. Its significance has become increasingly evident in both global–local education policies and empirical studies. Existing evidence suggests that school principals are key agents in engaging and sustaining families in school activities, although collaboration practices differ across contexts. Currently, although some studies have attempted to examine SCE in various settings, there is a limited understanding of overall trends in the literature, as well as the theoretical contributions and methodological approaches used in previous studies. This study aims to expand our understanding of the dynamic role of school leadership in SCE, focusing on geographical distributions, adopted research methods, and theoretical developments, by employing Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) guidelines to identify publications in the Scopus database. Initially, 422 papers were identified, and 15 papers that met the evaluative criteria were selected for analysis. The results indicated that most papers, particularly 14 studies, used qualitative methods, suggesting limited variation in scholarly approaches. In addition, inadequate empirical concentrations, along with geographical disparities, have created ambiguity regarding leadership practices in SCE in various educational settings. The adopted theoretical frameworks typically focus on two patterns: school leadership and social theories. This study, therefore, offers a comprehensive review of SCE and calls for stronger scientific contributions in different contexts, as well as diverse methodological adaptations and theoretical advancements.</jats:p>

title: A Cross-Comparison of Public and Private Universities Perceived University Fairness, Resilience and Academic Engagement among University Students of Karachi
container-title: Pakistan Journal of Positive Psychology
7ffb6e7e28d42e77fa4cd3621883ebd78ba9942a.abstract: <jats:p>The main aim of this study was to find the connection between perceived university fairness, resilience and academic engagement among university students in Karachi, Pakistan. The cross-sectional correlational design was used, 500 young adults (males = 121, female = 376, other = 3) aged 18 to 26 and above were selected from public, private and federally chartered universities through convenience sampling. The participants answered the University Fairness Questionnaire, Brief Resilience scale and Academic Engagement scale having 3 sub-scales including behavioral, cognitive and anxious engagement. The results via statistical analysis demonstrated that perceived university fairness has a significant negative correlation with behavioral engagement, and cognitive engagement, whereas it positively correlates with anxious engagement. Resilience showed positive correlation with cognitive engagement, a significant negative correlation with anxious engagement and no significant relationship with behavioral engagement. A significant negative correlation was found between perceived university fairness and resilience. The outcomes suggest that higher perceptions of university unfairness are linked to lower resilience and academic engagement, also increasing anxious engagement among higher education students. The research highlights the value of encouraging fairness, boosting resilience and improving student engagement alongside psychological well-being in university settings.</jats:p>

title: From Margin to Model: Reframing Inclusion in Adult and Post-secondary ESL Through ASFM Educator Narratives
container-title: Refugee Education in Canada
32f07a78357b05f64778421e9fc919222c3104af.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter critically examines systemic exclusion facing Arabic-speaking female Muslim (ASFM) educators in Ontario’s adult and post-secondary ESL sector, highlighting how Islamophobia, anti-Palestinian racism, linguicism, and sexism intersect within credentialing, hiring, and pedagogical practice. Using narrative case-study methodology, the chapter synthesizes structural critique and lived experience, drawing on intersectionality and critical hermeneutics. The RRAAV model – Representation, Recognition, Acceptance, Acknowledgement, and Value – guides equity-focused reform. Comparative analysis bridges adult and post-secondary ESL with K-12 refugee education and incorporates the post-7 October 2023 context. Policy recommendations are grounded in equity audits, funding-linked metrics, and recognition of compensated equity labour. By framing ASFM ESL educators and refugee students as differently positioned within the same educational system, the chapter argues that the marginalization of ASFM ESL educators also weakens the supports available to refugee and newcomer students, particularly where multilingualism, migration histories, and community-rooted knowledge are institutionally devalued.</jats:p>

title: Supporting Refugee-background Students’ Engagement with Difficult Knowledge Through Picturebooks
container-title: Refugee Education in Canada
bfde1e5cdc1793af831a7dcedb3a22779d8d8ed0.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter explores how educators can use refugee-themed literature to respond to difficult classroom conversations arising from students with refugee backgrounds. It draws on autobiographical reflections on one teacher’s experience introducing refugee-themed picturebooks in a Grade 6 English as a Second Language classroom in Canada to address students’ difficult questions related to conflict, war, violence, and racism. The findings demonstrate that relationship building between teachers and students was critical in supporting students’ engagement with their Funds of (difficult) Knowledge, defined as the emotionally difficult chapters of one’s cultural heritage, migration, and post-migration story. Informed by Critical Refugee Studies, the findings show that when picturebooks depicting refugee experiences are thoughtfully selected and responsively taught, they can validate students’ lived experiences and support inclusion and belonging.</jats:p>

title: Numerical study of large deformation and buoyancy effects on consolidation settlement in embankment construction
container-title: Geotechnical Aspects of Land Reclamation and Ground Improvement
8be5c1601313a350aed7c378874751aba5213c9d.abstract: <jats:p>Prediction of consolidation settlement in soft soils is a challenge for practising engineers. The use of simple modelling techniques without considering the large deformation and buoyancy effects results in the overprediction of settlement. This chapter presents a comparison study between small deformation analysis and large deformation analysis with and without buoyancy effect. A two-dimensional plane strain model was used to simulate an embankment constructed over soft deposits. The numerical results showed a maximum of 44% overprediction could happen if neither effect was taken into account. The study also examined the effects of key parameters such as compression ratio, soft soil thickness and fill height on the settlement performance when large strain and buoyancy are considered. Generally, the greater the value of parameters, the greater the effect of large deformation compared to the small deformation analysis. The numerical results were compared with 1D consolidation theory for small deformation and existing solutions for the buoyancy effect. The numerical results matched well with the 1D consolidation theory for small deformation analyses, while reasonable agreements were obtained for cases with buoyancy effects being considered.</jats:p>

title: 3D model to study the immunomodulatory functions of adipocyte/T lymphocytes paracrine crosstalk
container-title: Biofabrication
fa949b8870e09324a424da22e9e6d9f81317f3b1.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Adipose tissue (AT) dysfunction in obesity involves complex interactions among adipocytes, immune cells, endothelial cells and extracellular matrix components. However, most
                    <jats:italic>in vitro</jats:italic>
                    studies investigating adipocyte–immune interactions rely on simplified two-dimensional systems that incompletely recapitulate human AT physiology. Here, we developed a patient-derived three-dimensional (3D) human adiposphere model to investigate adipocyte-T-cell crosstalk under controlled metabolic conditions. Adipospheres were generated from the stromal vascular fraction of human subcutaneous AT obtained from donors with clinically distinct metabolic profile. Following 3D adipogenic maturation under normogenic or obesogenic conditions, adipospheres retained donor-specific adipogenic and metabolic characteristics during long-term culture, as demonstrated by differential expression of adipogenic markers, insulin-responsive AKT signaling and lipolytic activity. Compared with normogenic maturation condition, obesogenic maturation induced marked alterations in adiposphere morphology, cytokine secretion and metabolic function. In a second step, mature adipospheres were co-cultured with activated blood-derived T cells using a Transwell-based paracrine system. T-cells co-culture further modulated adiposphere inflammatory and metabolic- related responses. Transcriptomic analyses revealed coordinated regulation of immune- and metabolism related pathways, indicating extensive transcriptional remodeling during adipocyte–T-cell crosstalk. Overall, this modular 3D adiposphere platform reproduces key features of human AT immunometabolic interactions while preserving donor-specific responses. The system provides a flexible framework for integrating additional cellular components and may facilitate future mechanistic studies and therapeutic screening approaches targeting obesity-associated metabolic and inflammatory disorders.
                  </jats:p>

title: Fractional-Order Model-Based State-of-Charge and State-of-Power Estimation with Available-Capacity Feedback for Lithium-ion Batteries
container-title: Journal of The Electrochemical Society
04b47449708c7bfe6849b77320dc9927000aea45.abstract: <jats:p>Accurate state-of-charge (SOC) and state-of-power (SOP) estimation requires consistent treatment of voltage dynamics and available-capacity uncertainty. This study couples a fractional-order equivalent circuit model, a fast multi-innovation unscented Kalman filter SOC observer, and a slow capacity estimator. Self-adaptive learning particle swarm optimization (SLPSO) identifies the model parameters. Capacity feedback links SOC correction to voltage prediction and multi-constraint SOP calculation, with constant-power discharge verification. Compared with a second-order resistor-capacitor model, the fractional-order model reduces voltage root-mean-square error (RMSE) and mean absolute error by 3.45% and 5.82%, respectively. SLPSO reduces the mean final voltage RMSE from 2.215 to 1.561 mV. Across two dynamic profiles and initial SOC values of 0.90–1.05, the proposed method yields SOC RMSE values of 0.844%–0.966%. The fixed-capacity baseline yields 4.9%–9.8% under initial-SOC mismatch. The maximum capacity-related state-of-health indicator deviation remains below 0.279 percentage points. The maximum discharge-power error is 2.20% for 10 s and below 5% for all 30 s cases. It reaches 8.34% at 30% SOC for 60 s, indicating the need for caution under low-SOC, long-duration operation. These results are limited to fresh-cell tests at 25 °C.</jats:p>
