0be299f951d1b79cbaa07fe326f62bfe4ff28cc4.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In this chapter, the authors discuss six key elements to healthy and safe work, namely, leadership, autonomy, belonging, fairness, growth, and meaningfulness. They discuss research on the presence as well as the absence of each element in relation to occupational health and safety. The focus of this chapter is on creating workplaces in which employees can flourish and thrive without experiencing negative health and safety consequences. The chapter concludes with seven topics to consider moving forward: (1) where organizations should start, (2) interdependence of the elements, (3) workplace versus individual difference factors, (4) psychological safety, (5) remote and hybrid work, (6) the climate crisis, and (7) why the authors excluded compensation from the list of topics. New research should build upon and extend the authors’ model of healthy and safe work and encourage organizational decision-makers to realize that they can make a difference in healthy and safe work in their own organizations.</jats:p>

title: Integrating the Technology Acceptance Model and the Theory of Planned Behavior to Explain Electric Vehicle Purchase Intention Through Willingness to Pay
container-title: Jurnal Ilmiah Accusi
25ad4823ce65223c53f9590555b64b4c486f16d8.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines the determinants of electric vehicle (EV) purchase intention in Indonesia by integrating the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) through attitude and willingness to pay (WTP) as sequential mediating mechanisms. Addressing inconsistent empirical findings in prior literature regarding ease of use, infrastructure, and green lifestyle, this research offers novelty by combining psychological evaluations and financial commitments into a unified framework. A quantitative approach was applied using purposive sampling, collecting primary data via an online survey targeting Indonesian individuals aged 17 and older who are familiar with EVs and possess potential purchase interest. Data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling–Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS) via SmartPLS 4. The model demonstrates strong predictive power, explaining variance in attitude (R2 = 0.631), WTP (R2 = 0.628), and purchase intention (R2 = 0.707) The main findings reveal that attitude and WTP significantly drive purchase intention. Subjective norm, perceived usefulness, and battery warranty positively shape attitude, while price perception and perceived behavioral control enhance WTP. Conversely, perceived ease of use and charging infrastructure show no significant direct impacts, whereas green lifestyle and battery warranty negatively affect WTP. Theoretically, this study extends TAM and TPB by framing WTP as an economic bridge transforming attitudes into purchase decisions in emerging markets. Practically, it guides policymakers to maintain targeted fiscal incentives and assists automotive manufacturers in aligning pricing with perceived value.</jats:p>

title: Effectiveness of the PEKA-Pesisir Model for Financial Recording among Coastal Microbusinesses: A Pre-Experimental Study

1a6a7711cf9868f1eed8ec8b44272858de179d66.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines whether the PEKA-Pesisir model is associated with changes in financial-recording competence and self-reported practices among coastal microbusinesses. The model combines concise accounting instruction, coastal-transaction examples, guided worksheet practice, and structured feedback. A pre-experimental one-group pre-test–post-test design was used with 23 business actors in Medan Belawan who completed both measurements. The 25-item instrument covered basic recording knowledge, recording habits, separation of business and personal funds, simple financial-report preparation, and readiness to continue recording. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, Shapiro–Wilk, Wilcoxon signed-rank, and effect-size statistics. The mean score increased from 2.87 to 4.79; the paired difference was statistically significant (p < 0.001), with a large effect size (r = 0.875). The study contributes an applied, context-sensitive model that connects familiar coastal transactions with a basic recording-to-reporting sequence. The results provide initial empirical evidence of short-term improvement associated with implementation, although the one-group design and small sample limit causal inference and generalizability</jats:p>

                    <jats:italic>Objective</jats:italic>
                    . In the context of radiological accidents, retrospective dosimetry methods such as electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy and Monte Carlo simulation are used for dose reconstruction. EPR analysis of bone biopsies allows experimental assessment of absorbed dose. However, several factors may affect EPR dose estimation. The time delay between irradiation and sampling can lead to underestimation of absorbed dose to bone, and the influence of beam quality needs investigation. Therefore, this study aims to evaluate the influence of x-ray beam quality on bone EPR signal kinetics and the absorbed dose distribution in bone.
                    <jats:italic>Approach</jats:italic>
                    . A murine model of localized hind limb irradiation was developed using three beam qualities (50 kVp, 220 kVp, 10 MV). EPR measurements were performed to characterize radio-induced free radical kinetics in bone collected at different time points, from irradiation day to six months post-irradiation. A computational model of the irradiation setup was implemented in GEANT4 to study the dose distribution and complement the experimental observations.
                    <jats:italic>Main results</jats:italic>
                    . High-energy x-rays (10 MV) led to a rapid decrease in EPR signal, with 75% signal loss after 21 d and no detectable signal under our conditions after 42 d. For low-energy x-rays, the signal decreased more rapidly at 220 kVp than at 50 kVp, with signal loss of 51% and 31% respectively at 21 d, and a residual EPR signal remains at later time points (70%–80% signal loss at six months). Monte Carlo simulations highlighted heterogeneous dose deposition between tissues with low-energy x-rays, as well as significant beam attenuation within mouse tibia for 50 kVp x-rays, leading to inhomogeneous dose deposition in bone.
                    <jats:italic>Significance</jats:italic>
                    . Using a preclinical model, we have demonstrated that x-ray beam quality and time affect bone dose estimation. These findings improve our understanding of how radiation quality and bone physiology affect outcomes over time after irradiation.
                  </jats:p>

title: A Conceptual Model for Enhancing Sustainable Performance: The Synergy Of Green Innovation Based on Green Skills and Green Creative Self-Efficacy in Metalcraft MSMES
container-title: Jurnal Ilmiah Accusi
f99eb621daf129f9676e3fb6404a939ab3f389c7.abstract: <jats:p>Metalcraft micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in Bali contribute to the island’s craft economy, yet their transition to environmentally responsible production may be constrained by limited technical resources and uneven environmental capabilities. Although recent MSME studies associate green innovation with business performance, findings concerning environmental performance remain mixed, and previous studies rarely examine owners’ green skills and green creative self-efficacy together in traditional metalcraft enterprises. This study tests the effects of Green Skill and Green Creative Self-Efficacy on Sustainable Performance, with Green Innovation as a mediator, and identifies managerial priorities through Importance-Performance Map Analysis (IPMA). Survey data were obtained from 259 owners of metalcraft MSMEs in Bali Province using proportionate stratified random sampling and analyzed with PLS-SEM in SmartPLS 4. The estimated relationships are positive and statistically significant, and Green Innovation partially mediates the relationships between both capability constructs and Sustainable Performance. Green Creative Self-Efficacy has numerically larger path coefficients than Green Skill for Green Innovation and Sustainable Performance; this coefficient ordering is interpreted descriptively because a formal between-coefficient difference test was not reported. IPMA identifies environmental awareness and pollution-control facility deployment as specific improvement priorities. The study extends MSME sustainability research by linking an individual-level cognitive capability with operational innovation in a traditional craft setting. For practice, the results support combining practical green-skills training with confidence-building problem-solving activities and affordable, context-appropriate pollution-control and waste-management measures.</jats:p>

title: The Cuci Masks of Brănești between Social Biography and Cultural Revitalization: Reflections on Object Agency
container-title: Martor. The Museum of the Romanian Peasant Anthropology Review
bc1f6cfabaa7527f8d4cd931f6b67a728d1b9c66.abstract:
<jats:p>This article, based on ethnographic fieldwork conducted between 2015 and 2019, analyses the social agency of the Cucii ritual masks of Brănești, Romania. The study posits that these masks act as dynamic agents of cultural revitalization whose power lies in their shifting materiality. By examining the transition from organic materials to industrial wire and plastic, the paper explores how masks configure contemporary ritual and social worlds. 
Drawing on Alfred Gell’s theory of agency, the analysis demonstrates how the technical complexity of wire masks (the Chip) imposes a specific discipline on the maker and a hierarchy of prestige within the community. Conversely, the adoption of industrial polymers by younger generations facilitates a democratization of the ritual, ensuring its survival through a pragmatic “culture in transit.” The article also examines the “migration” of these masks to European festivals, where their morphology is recalibrated for global visibility, transforming them into material ambassadors of local identity. The study concludes that the hybridity of contemporary masks — where the handcrafted “aura” meets the pragmatism of industrial series — is a strategic negotiation that secures the continuity of the tradition in both local and global contexts, rather than a sign of decay.</jats:p>

title: AI-Enabled Talent Management: Transforming Recruitment, Performance and Employee Engagement
container-title: AI-Driven Transformation in Education and Business
ae74557c2bb6838779534a55f3892de085a328d8.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the way organizations recruit, assess, engage and retain employees by transforming the way they do these in the organization. Although existing literature has deeply explored various AI-based tools and applications in the field of human resource management, there is a strong need for a theoretical understanding of how AI alters the basic principles of talent management as a practice. Addressing the need, in this chapter, a theoretical and integrative approach has been applied, applying various established theories in the realms of organization, human resource and behaviours as a way of reinterpreting talent management in the AI era. Counter to conventional thinking that regards AI as a mere technological advancement, in this analysis, AI-based talent management has been identified as a social, technical and strategic phenomenon that alters the way organizations recruit members, manage their performance and encourage them to work. This analysis has applied classical concepts such as Person–Job Fit Theory, Signalling Theory, Human Capital Theory, Goal Setting Theory, Expectancy Theory, Agency Theory, Job Demands–Resources Theory, Social Exchange Theory, Self-Determination Theory, Resource-Based View and Institutional Theory. This chapter develops these new viewpoints and constructs a conceptual framework for AI-enabled talent management. The framework describes how talent outcomes are impacted by AI capabilities via hiring, performance and engagement processes.</jats:p>

title: An uncertainty-aware deep learning-based registration model for adaptive lung cancer radiotherapy
container-title: Physics in Medicine & Biology
e70e2ea6f4f27afb6e7298d00a0173ed4d1e93bc.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Objective</jats:italic>
                    . To develop a deep learning (DL) based probabilistic 3D deformable image registration framework for uncertainty-aware dose accumulation in magnetic resonance imaging-guided radiotherapy of lung cancer.
                    <jats:italic>Approach</jats:italic>
                    . We propose TransMorph-prob (TM-prob), a variational Bayesian model that predicts the voxel-wise mean and variance of dense displacement fields (DDFs). Two TM-prob models were trained on an internal computed tomography dataset (725 patients) and a low-field MR-linac dataset (102 patients), and benchmarked against Monte Carlo dropout TransMorph (TM-MCD) and DIRUncertainty with B-spline initialization (ASDIR) on the deformable image registration laboratory (DIRLAB) 4DCT dataset (10 patients, 3000 landmarks), and an annotated MR-linac dataset (16 patients, 107 image pairs, 227 landmarks) with target and seven organ-at-risk contours. Both datasets contained an additional 1239/13 289 algorithm-generated landmarks. Performance was evaluated using target registration error (TRE), Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), landmark- and voxel-wise expected calibration errors (LECE/ECE), and dose distributions derived from 2000 DDF samples per patient.
                    <jats:italic>Main results</jats:italic>
                    . On the DIRLAB dataset, TM-prob achieved a median TRE of 1.8 mm/2.8 mm on manual/algorithm-generated landmarks, versus 1.3 mm/2.4 mm for ASDIR and 2.1 mm/3.0 mm for TM-MCD. On the MRI dataset, TM-prob achieved the median TRE of 3.9 mm/2.6 mm and a mean DSC of 0.87, matching ASDIR (3.3 mm/2.7 mm, and DSC of 0.87) while outperforming TM-MCD (4.4 mm/2.9 mm, and 0.84). In uncertainty calibration, TM-prob achieved a LECE of 1.74 mm/0.30 mm on MRI manual/algorithm-generated landmarks versus 2.41 mm/0.56 mm for ASDIR and 6.65 mm/3.92 mm for TM-MCD, and an average contour ECE of 5.8% versus 7.0% and 21.2%. Two patients with indistinct gross tumor volume boundaries exhibited substantially wider target D95 distributions, demonstrating that calibrated DDF uncertainty translates into clinically relevant dose-coverage uncertainty.
                    <jats:italic>Significance</jats:italic>
                    . TM-prob is an end-to-end DL model, achieving fast, well-calibrated, uncertainty-aware registration for lung cancer patients, enabling reliable DDF uncertainty propagation into dose accumulation for clinical decision-making in online adaptive radiotherapy.
                  </jats:p>

title: Components of Language Proficiency
b1703374ee122e65e142ffba96259e95c498039b.abstract: <jats:p>Filling a significant gap in SLA research in highly instructed settings, this book explores language proficiency in learners of French and Spanish in English schools. This detailed study investigates aspects of linguistic knowledge and proficiency, and the relationships between them, to offer insights into language learning, teaching and testing.</jats:p>

title: Introduction
container-title: Components of Language Proficiency
f3cc7c321b6c182b53e7b3cd2757cec489308671.abstract: <jats:p>This book presents the key findings from Components of Language Proficiency (ComLaP), a project that sought to provide insight into the linguistic knowledge and proficiency of 15–16-year-old learners of French and Spanish in England, just after they had taken their high-stakes General Certificate of Secondary Education (GCSE) national exams, following about 450 hours of classroom instruction in secondary schools. Every year, approximately one quarter of a million adolescents take GCSE exams in these languages. Yet we know little about what they know and can do with the language at this stage.</jats:p>

title: Conceptualising Language Proficiency
container-title: Components of Language Proficiency
b24bbff02554fbfd54ce6ea561874935bb12b8fb.abstract: <jats:p>The main purpose of the current chapter is to provide a broad theoretical background and rationale for some of the analyses conducted in this book. In this chapter, we explain how our findings could provide insight into the nature of linguistic knowledge and different proficiencies and discuss theories about how those proficiencies might have developed. Research investigating these topics may inform educators and policymakers when considering which areas of language to prioritise through curriculum and pedagogy, by indicating the extent to which different kinds of linguistic knowledge or variables such as motivation or skill-specific self-efficacy might be associated with different proficiencies among the population investigated.</jats:p>

title: The ComLaP Study: The Participants, Their Attitudes, Motivations and Experiences, and the Design of the Study
container-title: Components of Language Proficiency
247efd76aa54e4b52869ec23fc4470f00907f63a.abstract: <jats:p>As described in Chapter 1, the ComLaP study expanded L2 proficiency research into a new population of learners to examine: (a) the nature of their knowledge and proficiency skills and (b) the relations between the two. In this chapter, we introduce readers to the participants in our study and the research design and methods.</jats:p>

title: Vocabulary Knowledge
container-title: Components of Language Proficiency
ff38a39facf17e52fbbb7bc22835ed1594118a65.abstract: <jats:p>Vocabulary knowledge is a strong predictor of L2 reading, listening, writing and speaking (see Chapters 7–11). It is thus critical for learners to build a breadth and depth of vocabulary knowledge and learn how to apply that knowledge when using language in real time. Vocabulary breadth (size) refers to how many and which words a learner knows. It is typically measured using receptive tests of written form(-meaning) recognition (Schmitt, 2014). Vocabulary depth, on the other hand, refers to ‘the quality or depth of understanding’ (Anderson & Freebody, 1981: 93), that is, the extent to which a person knows a word (Qian, 2002). For instance, a learner may recognise a word form (form-recognition) but may not recognise its meaning when presented with several definitions or translations (meaning-recognition). Similarly, a learner may recall (remember) a word’s meaning (meaning-recall) but may not recall the form of the word when presented with its meaning in their first (or dominant) language (form-recall).</jats:p>

title: Grammar Knowledge
container-title: Components of Language Proficiency
baac60e38a5553a3fb0813795aad32c3728f9420.abstract:
<jats:p>In this chapter, we provide insight into the grammar knowledge of GCSE French and Spanish learners. Specifically, we explore the extent to which grammar knowledge depends on the feature being tested (direct object pronouns, negation, noun–adjective agreement, subject–verb agreement and tense) and/or test (elicited imitation, grammaticality judgement and error
correction and identification). In the proficiency chapters, we then explore how this knowledge might help to explain proficiency in the four skills.</jats:p>

title: Knowledge of Sound–Symbol Correspondences
container-title: Components of Language Proficiency
a1b1348be5557975ef9dfdaa7ed7675a5225846e.abstract: <jats:p>Phonological decoding – the ability to apply one’s knowledge of the relations between symbols (letters) and sounds to read written words – is a strong, universal predictor of L1 reading development in alphabetic languages (Bradley & Bryant, 1983; Ziegler & Goswami, 2005). The orthographic depth of writing systems – that is, the systematicity and predictability with which languages map sounds to symbols and symbols to sounds – can also affect the rate and success of reading development (Ellis et al., 2004; Ziegler et al., 2010). For instance, L1 reading development typically progresses at a much faster rate in orthographically transparent languages (e.g. Spanish), where there are often one-to-one relationships between sounds and symbols (letters), than in orthographically deep languages (e.g. French or English), where one-to-many or many-to-many relationships (respectively) exist (e.g. Carrillo et al., 2013). The teaching of phonics – systematic and explicit instruction about the sound–symbol correspondences (SSCs) of the language – has been shown to improve children’s ability to read and write in their L1, particularly in orthographically deep languages, such as English (Ehri, 2020; Torgerson et al., 2019). Informed by this evidence base, phonics instruction has become firmly embedded in the curriculum for early L1 literacy development as part of several British policy initiatives (DfE, 2014).</jats:p>

title: Reading Proficiency
container-title: Components of Language Proficiency
b916f582d045e836a3e092200d7ac62a83bed280.abstract: <jats:p>In this chapter, we examine three sets of variables that have been associated with reading proficiency: (a) linguistic knowledge (receptive and productive vocabulary and grammar and phonics knowledge, described in Chapters 4–6); (b) affective factors (motivation and self-efficacy, described in Chapter 3) and (c) related skills (listening and writing, described in Chapters 9 and 10, respectively). First, we briefly review research into how linguistic knowledge, affective variables and related skills can be associated with reading proficiency. We then lay out our research questions and the methods and analyses we used to assess the relative importance of each variable in predicting reading proficiency. Finally, we present our findings and discuss some implications for teaching, learning and assessment, particularly for secondary FL education in England.</jats:p>

title: Lexical Inferencing in Reading
container-title: Components of Language Proficiency
84e96f8e1b8eae22ec61e23444a66ffaf632f83a.abstract: <jats:p>Lexical inferencing is one of the many subskills of reading and listening comprehension. It involves ‘making informed guesses as to the meaning of a word in the light of all available linguistic cues in combination with the learner’s general knowledge of the world, her awareness of the co-text, and her relevant linguistic knowledge’ (Haastrup, 1991: 40). It sits within a broader range of types of inferencing, such as pragmatic or semantic inferencing. Lexical inferencing happens throughout our lives when we encounter new words in both reading and listening. In this chapter, we focus specifically on lexical inferencing during reading, a critical part of reading comprehension and language development more generally. We provide this special focus on lexical inferencing both for (a) theoretical reasons, as it allows us to further probe strategy- and linguistic-related components from the models of proficiency presented in Chapter 2 and reading models in Chapter 7, and (b) practical reasons, as it is of timely relevance to recent assessment policy changes in our educational context.</jats:p>

title: Listening Proficiency
container-title: Components of Language Proficiency
e9fba6656147b4dd258a03f19931fce51f8e00f5.abstract: <jats:p>In this chapter, we investigate the extent to which listening proficiency relates to three sets of variables: (a) linguistic (phonics and receptive and productive vocabulary and grammar) knowledge; (b) motivation and listening self-efficacy and (c) the related skills of reading and speaking proficiency. We first review previous research into how these three sets of variables might contribute to explaining listening proficiency. Next, we outline the methods used in our study, including correlational analyses, regression modelling and dominance analyses, to investigate the relative importance of each variable in predicting listening proficiency. Finally, we present our findings from these analyses and discuss several implications for learning, teaching and testing.</jats:p>

title: Writing Proficiency
container-title: Components of Language Proficiency
d12afbf9df64eef487bc3b85b1a406bf566db8d7.abstract: <jats:p>In this chapter, we investigate L2 writing proficiency among beginner-to-low-intermediate learners of French and Spanish from two perspectives. In Study 1, we focus on what it means to be a proficient writer, exploring how writing proficiency can be conceptualised and measured via an analytic rating scale. In Study 2, we present similar content to that found in the previous three chapters: we examine the extent to which linguistic knowledge, affective variables (motivation and self-efficacy) and other skills (reading and speaking) relate to L2 writing proficiency.</jats:p>

title: Speaking Proficiency
container-title: Components of Language Proficiency
a08e01ed7a78f1ac378cc28eeddd9445b6999394.abstract: <jats:p>In this chapter, we explore the L2 speaking proficiency of our learners from two angles. In Study 1, we investigate what it means to be a proficient speaker by looking at how speaking proficiency can be conceptualised and measured in terms of listener judgements of speech quality. In Study 2, we examine the extent to which linguistic knowledge, motivation, speaking self-efficacy and other skills (listening and writing) contribute to speaking proficiency, as we have done in the previous chapters.</jats:p>

title: Conclusion: Summary of Findings, Key Implications and Final Remarks
container-title: Components of Language Proficiency
61c3b46179558598d1f2c0b376f5d25944f5f682.abstract: <jats:p>The ComLaP project was, in many ways, born out of changes to modern language education policy and practice in England and the discourse, debates and controversies that emerged around the role of language knowledge in relation to those changes. We believe our findings can inform some of that discourse (e.g. Woore et al., 2022). Our findings also add to a wider international research agenda about the nature of language proficiency (e.g. Jeon & In’nami, 2022) and knowledge development (e.g. Suzuki, 2023), by focusing on a neglected population of learners. Instructed, adolescent learners, with limited exposure to the language outside the classroom, represent large numbers of young people throughout the world, and we hope that more attention can be given to these individuals and their language learning. The findings of such research can enhance our understanding about the initial stages of instructed language development as well as inform policy and practice.</jats:p>

title: A multimode radiobiological model for advanced radiation therapy
container-title: Biomedical Physics & Engineering Express
403bafea77a58ad61d7a67103b4e9f88b5d74ac8.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Reliable radiobiological modeling is essential to the consistent dosimetric analysis and outcome comparison between conventionally fractionated radiation therapy (CFRT) that employs small daily doses (1.8–4 Gy) and stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) that employs large daily doses (> 5 Gy). This work investigates a new radiobiological model, the multimode (MM) model, for both CFRT and SBRT. The MM model assumes the existence of different modes of cell killing because of unsuccessfully repaired radiation damage to the cell deoxyribonucleic acid by any number of ionization events (or radiation tracks). The validity of the MM model was tested using previously published survival fractions of various cell lines. A comparison of the goodness-of-fit of the linear quadratic (LQ), multitarget (MT), universal survival curve (USC) and MM models was made to the survival curve of 12 non–small-cell lung cancer cell line. The same agreement was obtained between the USC and MM models with the survival data, which was significantly better than that with the LQ and MT models. The MM model is a comprehensive model that may offer a superior description of the mammalian cell survival curve in both conventional and ablative dose ranges, which can be used for designing new fractionation schemes and predicting and understanding treatment outcomes for both CFRT and SBRT.</jats:p>

title: Gendered Dimensions of Shadow Education: Examining Teacher's Role in Large - Scale Private Tutoring
container-title: Adhyapana Prathibha
76cc2c5a94724f12232a9880b3061f0c74c25530.abstract: <jats:p>The topic of gender has become a significant focus in political science literature. Numerous aspects have been explored, and this study investigates the gender imbalance in the professional role of teachers within large-scale tuition, an area that has received limited attention in the research literature in the Sri Lankan social context. As Wedikandage (2015) points out, unlike in the past, the teaching profession in Sri Lanka has become feminized, with social stereotypes playing a prominent role in this transformation. These stereotypes have fostered an environment where the role of the teacher in large-scale tuition classes, beyond the traditional government teaching profession, is predominantly filled by males. This research, which employed a quantitative dominant mixed method throughout the study, was conducted through a semi-structured questionnaire administered to 50 teachers involved in large-scale tuition in the Chilaw Municipal Council area of Puttalam District in the North-Western Province, reveals the gender division of labor, social stereotypes, and the marginalization of women within the household.</jats:p>

title: The Autonomous Learner; Decoding Cognitive Logic of Generation Z in the Sri Lankan Advanced Level Classroom
container-title: Adhyapana Prathibha
66c36a7cdf6e51d9fdecfc4ac37f940042bdf340.abstract: <jats:p>The Advanced Level (AL) classroom in the modern era is no longer a site of passive reception but a dynamic ecosystem of negotiation and cognitive autonomy. This paper explores the behavioral and cognitive shifts within Generation Z (Gen Z) individuals born between 1997 and 2012, who currently occupy the 17-to-19-year-old cohort in Sri Lanka (Dimock, 2019). Despite geographical, cultural & subject streamwise specificities, Sri Lankan Advance level students are increasingly bridging cultural disparities through digitalization, adopting a globalized "digital-native" logic. This article analyzes the "Authenticity Filter," the "Fast Brain" paradox, and the transition from instruction-following to instruction-making, arguing that modern pedagogy must direct toward relationship-based facilitation.</jats:p>

title: Promoting Foreign Language Learner Autonomy through Digital Resources

title: Speed profile optimisation for a semi-trailer truck based on a hybrid fuel consumption model with automatic calibration based on CAN bus data
container-title: Mining Industry Journal (Gornaya Promyshlennost)
39550c0136d55280b4c9147da58e332f9cdd4929.abstract: <jats:p>The paper proposes a method for optimising the speed profile of a long-haul semi-trailer truck that combines a physical fuel consumption model with a machine-learning correction with automatic calibration using on-board CAN bus data. The physical component is built on the tractive balance equation, which parameters, i.e. the power transmission efficiency, rolling resistance coefficient, brake-specific fuel consumption and lumped mechanical losses, are identified without bench testing by minimising the difference between the computed and the measured instantaneous fuel rate using the Powell's method; calibration is verified against the cumulative fuel counter (SAE J1939). The correction is implemented with the LightGBM algorithm that approximates the rest of the physical model; for the first time the current gear signal extracted directly from the CAN bus is used as an additional feature. The optimal speed profile is obtained by dynamic programming subject to a constraint on the travel-time increase; the speed range is lumped into 13 values within 60–80 km/h. The method was verified using a field trial with a Mercedes-Benz Actros 1845 truck on the M-11 «Neva» motorway (Moscow – Saint Petersburg, 672.5 km; about 14 million CAN records processed in under two minutes). The calibration error was 3.6%; introduction of the gear feature reduced the prediction root-mean-square error from 13.7 to 11.5 L/100 km (by 16%) and the cumulative-consumption deviation down to 1.4%. The computed fuel saving reached 9.3% at the travel time increased by less than 0.6%. Numerical simulation using the Moscow – Kazan route (809.1 km) confirmed the scalability: a 10.4% saving at a 2.8% time increase without model re-calibration.</jats:p>

title: Rethinking English Language Learning: A Needs Analysis in Fisheries and Marine Science Education
container-title: International Journal of Science Education and Cultural Studies
e067f741e009a09065d011ca90d6b79a4a78ce35.abstract: <jats:p>This study seeks to analyze the needs of Fisheries and Marine Science students in learning English to be a basis in developing a contextually relevant English for Specific Purposes (ESP) curriculum. The study used a descriptive qualitative design and included 23 participants: 20 undergraduate students in the third to fifth semesters, two English lecturers, and one Marine Science lecturer. Data were collected using semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, classroom observations and document analysis and analysed thematically using the concepts of necessities, lacks and wants. The results identified five major themes: academic English proficiency, professional communication, technical vocabulary, speaking confidence, and contextualized learning activities. Students faced difficulties in understanding scientific articles in international journals, writing academic texts and understanding terminology specific to fisheries and marine science disciplines. They also lacked confidence in speaking English that influenced their participation in English communication activities. Students also said they would like to have lessons about words used in the marine industry, workshops on how to read scientific journals, practice making presentations and learning through simulations. The results of the study suggest the need for an ESP curriculum that incorporates academic literacy, subject specific vocabulary and practical communication activities. The study offers an empirical foundation for synchronizing English teaching to the academic requirements and anticipated professional communication skills of Fisheries and Marine Science students.</jats:p>

title: Gendered entrepreneurial ecosystems and entrepreneurial agency: women's artisanal microenterprises in Chinchero, Cusco, Peru
container-title: International Journal of Gender and Entrepreneurship
c3f134d2f31134fc74b5cd01af50a965031d10fa.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines how gendered constraints shape women's entrepreneurial agency within artisanal microenterprises in the textile handicraft sector in Peru, challenging dominant assumptions that position entrepreneurship as a direct pathway to empowerment. Drawing on the perspective of gendered entrepreneurial ecosystems, the study analyses how institutional arrangements, social norms and power relations influence women's entrepreneurial processes, stakeholder interactions and access to opportunities. By situating these dynamics within broader social, cultural, economic and institutional contexts, the study explains how gendered structures produce differentiated and contextually constrained forms of entrepreneurial agency.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study adopts a non-experimental qualitative design with a descriptive and exploratory approach, suitable for understanding the complexity of women's artisanal microentrepreneurship within gendered contexts. Fieldwork included 13 in-depth interviews with key actors of the microenterprise ecosystem and two focus groups with 10 women textile microentrepreneurs. In addition, participant observation was conducted in the district of Chinchero, Cusco, Peru, enabling a contextualized understanding of social practices, gendered dynamics and lived experiences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study provides insights into the ecosystem of women-led artisanal microenterprises in a Latin American developing context and identifies three distinct types of artisan microentrepreneurs. The findings demonstrate how gendered constraints shape differences in autonomy, access to resources and sustainability across these types, producing differentiated entrepreneurial trajectories and forms of entrepreneurial agency. The study also highlights the role of organizational forms and stakeholder interactions in mediating access to opportunities and shaping sustainability outcomes and develops a conceptual framework derived from the empirical findings that explains the relationships between entrepreneurial typologies, contextual conditions, stakeholder interactions and sustainability outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study contributes to the literature on gender and entrepreneurship by advancing a process-oriented and gendered understanding of artisanal microentrepreneurship in a culturally embedded context. Focusing on women-led textile microenterprises in rural Peru, it demonstrates how gendered constraints and institutional conditions shape differentiated entrepreneurial trajectories and forms of entrepreneurial agency. By linking artisan typologies, contextual factors and stakeholder dynamics within a gendered entrepreneurial ecosystem perspective, the study challenges dominant assumptions of empowerment and reconceptualizes entrepreneurial agency as a relational and context-dependent process in developing economies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Employee agency in small and medium-sized enterprises: a qualitative analysis of psychosocial and organisational drivers of professional initiative
container-title: International Journal of Organizational Analysis
b50e468a6a1ed4b85dd9382713c7fb0bdd7295f9.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to examine how psychological, relational, experiential and organisational conditions shape employee agency and professional initiative among young professionals working in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Casablanca, Morocco.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An abductive qualitative design was used across 50 data-collection sessions involving 135 employees: 30 individual semi-structured interviews and 20 focus-group discussions. The material was complemented by more than 200 h of workplace observation and approximately 50 organisational documents. Analysis combined iterative thematic coding, triangulation and systematic examination of contrasting and disconfirming evidence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Four interrelated configurations were identified: capability without permission, relationally authorised agency, the translation of experience and training into situated practical judgement and organisational gatekeeping. Relational authorisation was the most recurrent configuration (39/50 sessions), followed by capability without permission (35/50), organisational gatekeeping (31/50), situated practical judgement (28/50) and training-to-work translation (20/50). Individual resources did not independently generate initiative; their effects depended on organisational permission, relational validation, discretion and workplace fit.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The Casablanca-based sample supports analytical rather than statistical generalisation. Transferability should be examined across other regional and national SME contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>SMEs can strengthen agency by clarifying decision boundaries, supporting peer mentoring, reducing fear of blame and aligning training with workplace realities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By promoting employee agency and professional initiative, organisations can contribute to improving job satisfaction, professional development and workplace engagement. Encouraging supportive social environments within SMEs may also enhance employees’ capacity to adapt to changing professional contexts and strengthen organisational resilience in dynamic economic environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study conceptualises employee agency as situated practical action produced through the conversion of individual capability into socially legitimate and organisationally permitted initiative.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Fan engagement beyond game outcomes: evidence from collective rituals and athlete-idolizing fandom in the digital sportscape
container-title: International Journal of Sports Marketing and Sponsorship
53c696c96a24c594ea8921888259c1d2b3573564.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Match outcomes are inherently uncertain and largely beyond the control of sport organizations; yet, defeats can negatively affect spectators’ emotions and subsequent behavioral intentions. This highlights the need to understand how sport organizations can sustain fan engagement through experiences that are not contingent on game outcomes. This study examines how outcome-independent forms of fan engagement – collective fan rituals and athlete-idolizing fandom activities – are associated with spectators’ word-of-mouth (WOM) and revisit intentions following match defeats in professional sport. Drawing on emotion regulation theory, the study focuses on experiential mechanisms that may sustain behavioral intentions beyond game outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were collected from 405 spectators who had recently attended a Korea Baseball Organization League match in which their supported team was defeated. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was used to test the proposed relationships. Multi-group analysis (MGA) compared spectators experiencing high versus low levels of post-match negative emotion. The model also includes team identification and objective team standing as control variables.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Satisfaction with collective fan rituals was positively associated with both WOM and revisit intention. Enjoyment of fandom activities positively influenced WOM but had no direct effect on revisit intention, indicating a fully mediated pathway through WOM. WOM was a significant predictor of revisit intention. MGA showed no significant differences between high- and low-negative-emotion groups, suggesting that the structural relationships are stable across emotional conditions. Objective team standing was not significantly related to WOM or revisit intention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings indicate that participatory fan engagement can contribute to behavioral intentions following defeat through outcome-independent experiential pathways. Rather than being driven primarily by game results or season-level performance, fan behavioral continuity appears to be shaped by ritualized stadium experiences and digitally extended fandom activities, which operate through social diffusion via WOM. The study extends sport consumer behavior research by highlighting the role of experiential engagement and communication processes in sustaining attendance intentions in performance-volatile contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Innateness is (still) an orienting principle for language development
febc013acf1b09ccab1c43b0a96aad083d5e8052.abstract: How humans come to acquire language has been a persistent object of philosophical and scientific inquiry, in part because it bears on fundamental questions about the nature of human cognition.Classically, this field of inquiry has centered innateness as a critical component of language acquisition, traditionally characterizing innate capability in terms of richly specified, biologically endowed linguistic structure, such as Universal Grammar. Contemporary theories have evolved considerably from these earlier formulations and now present several differing candidates for innateness in language. Throughout this evolution, though, questions of innateness have remained central to theories of language acquisition, even as the nature of those questions has shifted in response to new sources of evidence. In this Perspective, we consider evidence from three complementary sources of evidence—linguistic diversity, human social interaction, and language models (LMs)—that together inform the question of what children must bring to the task of language learning. We conclude by identifying desiderata for theories of language acquisition that seek to specify the nature, scope, and explanatory role of innate contributions to language development.

title: Private sustainability engagement in an emerging economy
container-title: Journal of Accounting in Emerging Economies
69bc8a82cee1bc8437fefa5f09a52a3b7f0c548c.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study critically examines how private sustainability engagement functions as a form of dialogic accountability when Nordic institutional investors interact with publicly listed companies in a state-dominated emerging economy, challenging the implicit universalism of consensus-seeking engagement models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study employs qualitative content analysis of Nordic investor engagement reports documenting extended interactions with Egyptian financial and telecommunication companies. Legitimacy theory, neo-institutional theory and dialogic accountability provide an integrated lens for examining information exchange and corporate answerability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Private engagements centre on political connections and human rights risks, with documented response patterns consistent with a prioritisation of political licence to operate over substantive answerability to international investors. The documented engagements record evidential burdens preventing independent verification. The response patterns across both cases constitute dialogic deadlock – a structural ceiling where genuine accountability exchange is foreclosed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Empirically, the study provides an in-depth qualitative content analysis of investor-side engagement reports, documenting the sustainability information Nordic investors seek in two Egyptian private engagements and the patterns of corporate response. Theoretically, it proposes political licence and audience primacy as concepts for interpreting the documented exchanges and specifies the contextual conditions under which audience hierarchy may shift toward audience primacy. Conceptually, it theorises dialogic deadlock as a structural outcome arising where legitimacy incentives prove insufficient and the preconditions for genuine dialogic accountability are constitutively absent.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Decision pathways in mobile-app shopping: a Throughput Model study of online consumers
container-title: Journal of Consumer Marketing
068f246007928de25bf9addd0f665c1f215ba121.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Mobile shopping environments increasingly rely on artificial intelligence (AI) to personalise recommendations, curate product information and support purchase decisions. Yet, existing consumer decision-making models maintain a linear, stage-based logic that fails to capture how AI-enabled interfaces compress, extend or reconfigure the pathways consumers actually follow. This study aims to use the Throughput Model (TPM) to conceptualise and empirically validate distinct algorithmic decision pathways through which perception, information search and evaluative judgement interact to shape purchase intentions in mobile-app shopping contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Survey data were collected from Gen Z consumers with recent mobile-app shopping experience. The study applies partial least squares structural equation modelling and mediation analysis to test the TPM and estimate one-step, two-step and three-step decision pathways in AI-enabled mobile commerce.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Perception, information search and judgement each exert significant effects within the model, with judgement emerging as the central integrative mechanism linking upstream inputs to purchase intention. These results demonstrate that AI-enabled mobile interfaces simultaneously support impulsive, efficiency-driven and deliberative decision architectures.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study provides the first empirical operationalisation of the TPM in mobile-app commerce, reconceptualising purchase decisions as coexisting algorithmic pathways rather than a single sequential route. It offers marketers a diagnostic framework for segmenting consumers by decision architecture and designing adaptive AI-enabled shopping experiences accordingly.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: When AI signalling backfires: a threshold model of perceived firm innovativeness
container-title: Journal of Services Marketing
756ffe6f906e26c28ec21cab27a632588e7de924.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to interrogate the implicit monotonicity assumption in service-dominant logic by examining whether AI signalling intensity uniformly enhances perceived firm innovativeness (PFI) or exhibits threshold-dependent fragility. The study empirically validates relational coherence as a perception-level mediating state, thereby confirming its role as the integrator of AI-enabled capability inference, and specifies structural and demographic boundary conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A two-study archival design tests the proposed threshold model. Study 1 exploits discrete AI capability announcements among 1,012 Asian service firms (2012–2024) using event-study difference-in-differences to identify dynamic shifts in customer text-based PFI. Study 2 estimates a dynamic panel system generalised method of moments model incorporating lagged PFI, non-linear AI intensity and relational coherence, addressing reverse causality and omitted capability shocks while computing turning points and moderated curvature.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI signalling exhibits an inverted-U relationship with PFI: moderate intensity strengthens capability perception, whereas high intensity attenuates and reverses effects. Relational coherence mediates this relationship, with the indirect pathway weakening and becoming negative beyond a calculable threshold. The curvature steepens and the threshold occurs earlier in high-contact services and firms serving older customer segments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study advances service-dominant logic by introducing threshold-fragility into its resource-integration premise, repositioning technological operant resources as legitimacy-constrained rather than uniformly accretive. It conceptualises relational coherence as the perception-level integrator governing AI-enabled capability inference and embeds demographic and structural heterogeneity within a formally identified non-linear, dynamic analytical model structure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Prior Authorization Outcomes for Advanced Dermatologic Therapies in a Centralized Coordination Model: A Postimplementation Descriptive Analysis
container-title: American Journal of Medical Quality
002e77964a354a9e7d4a537f1fe74cafe7691ba3.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Advanced systemic dermatologic therapies (ASDTs) have transformed dermatologic care but remain subject to prior authorization (PA) requirements that delay treatment initiation and impose administrative burdens. To address these barriers, the Mount Sinai Health System established the Biologics Treatment Center (BTC) in 2018 to centralize PA management and patient education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Assess PA approval rates, turnaround times, and patterns across medications and therapeutic categories within the BTC.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Following Standards for Quality Improvement Reporting Excellence guidelines, we conducted a quality improvement analysis of PA requests for ASDTs managed by the BTC. Using de-identified specialty pharmacy data from Shields Health Solutions, we examined PA submissions between June 2020 and December 2021. Descriptive statistics summarized PA status and turnaround time (mean, median, and interquartile range) overall and by medication and therapeutic category.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of 2,183 PA requests, 73.0% were initially approved, increasing to 87.3% after appeals. The median PA turnaround time was 1 day (interquartile range [IQR]: 0–3) overall. Median turnaround times were 1 day (IQR: 0–3) for approved requests, 2 days (IQR: 0–4.25) for appealed and overturned cases, 1 day (IQR: 0–4) for appealed and upheld cases, and 2 days (IQR: 0–6) for denials without appeal. Approval rates varied substantially by medication, ranging from 97.4% for adalimumab to 30.8% for tildrakizumab.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This analysis describes PA outcomes for ASDTs within a centralized coordination model, including approval rates, turnaround times, and variability across medications. These findings provide insight into operational performance and highlight areas for further investigation into factors influencing PA outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Racial identity and Chinese language learning among Asian American students
container-title: Journal for Multicultural Education
994467c4da045e35ad051f068e870962ded155f6.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to examine Asian American students’ racial identity and Chinese learning at two Midwestern suburban high schools.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Qualitative methodology is used in this study. Through in-depth interviews with student participants, this study explores how Asian American students interpret their racial identity and Chinese language learning experience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study finds that students’ racial/ethnic identity is shaped by dominant ideologies and power relations. Racism and stereotypical images toward Asian American students are visible and have negatively affected their schooling. Students validate their learning in Chinese and perform their racial/ethnic identity as capital to be invested. However, they barely experience and reflect on racial and cultural diversity at schools.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings of this study have implications for both research and practice at suburban schools. This study suggests school leaders and teachers work with students toward antiracism and create inclusive and equitable learning spaces.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study will contribute to an in-depth understanding of Asian American students’ racial/ethnic identity, knowledge and experience in Chinese language classrooms. It will enrich the current literature on Asian American education and identity in second language learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Energy-saving optimized parameters for 3D selective laser melting using dimensionless model and ANN surrogate mapping
container-title: Rapid Prototyping Journal
adb724e710250db3be204722b8458e9520b2ad3a.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to identify energy-efficient selective laser melting (SLM) parameters that achieve high relative density and mechanical performance while reducing trial-and-error experiments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The proposed workflow integrates dimensionless process mapping, an analytical melt-pool geometry model, specific energy consumption (SEC, Es) evaluation, and an artificial neural network (ANN) surrogate map. For Ti6Al4V, the selected parameter set was further evaluated by increasing hatch spacing based on powder-entrainment and melt-pool-width considerations, followed by density and tensile tests. The same SEC-guided screening strategy was also applied to an IN718 dataset to check cross-material applicability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>For Ti6Al4V at 80 µm hatch spacing, the optimized condition achieved 99.98% relative density, 1201 MPa tensile strength and 8.2% elongation. The experimentally assessed 120 µm energy-efficient hatch-spacing extension reduced model-estimated SEC by 36.2% while maintaining 99.95% relative density. Tensile strength increased to 1299 MPa, whereas elongation decreased to 6.22%, indicating a strength–ductility tradeoff.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This work proposes a physics-informed and data-assisted optimization workflow linking dimensionless modeling, melt-pool geometry screening, SEC-based energy evaluation, ANN surrogate mapping and experimental testing. Unlike approaches that apply dimensionless analysis or machine learning separately, the proposed method selects low-Es parameter sets within a physically constrained process window and assesses their density and tensile performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: A cost-aware intermittent demand forecasting method combining temporally attenuated discrete gray model with reward-guided adjustment
container-title: Grey Systems: Theory and Application
e842979279c7caffbc0488999f436aea15310bf8.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intermittent demand in distribution-center operations is difficult to forecast because long zero-demand periods are often interrupted by irregular demand bursts. This study develops TADGM–RGPL, a cost-aware gray forecasting framework that combines a temporally attenuated discrete gray model (TADGM) with reward-guided parameter learning (RGPL), to account for both statistical calibration deviation and the asymmetric inventory consequences of underforecasting and overforecasting.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>TADGM introduces a bounded recency-sensitive driver directly into the DGM state-transition equation, while RGPL learns a scalar decision-calibration factor from pre-origin inventory-cost feedback. The framework is evaluated on 701 intermittent and lumpy DC-SKU series using 4,206 rolling-origin windows. Conventional intermittent-demand methods, gray models, XGBoost and LightGBM are included as benchmarks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>TADGM does not dominate the benchmark methods in point-forecast accuracy. Standard TADGM–RGPL significantly reduces inventory cost relative to the conventional intermittent-demand and gray benchmarks under the stockout-sensitive p/h = 10 setting, whereas XGBoost and LightGBM achieve lower overall cost when all series are pooled. ADI-stratified analysis shows that TADGM–RGPL attains the lowest average cost in the highest-intermittency quartile, although its advantage over the machine-learning benchmarks is not statistically significant within that subset.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study differs from residual reweighting by introducing recency sensitivity as a time-varying gray input in the DGM state-transition equation and by separating statistical forecasting from downstream cost-aware decision calibration. The empirical analysis further identifies the demand conditions under which the proposed forecasting-decision framework is relatively more competitive.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Remaining useful life estimation of bearings using trend–detail decomposition and extended 1D-LBP features with a hybrid deep learning model
container-title: Engineering Computations
26618182a2845a1575e0f6072487c228bab97724.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to develop a robust and accurate remaining useful life (RUL) prediction framework for rolling bearings by overcoming the limitations of conventional health indicator construction under noisy and nonlinear degradation conditions. To achieve this, a unified end-to-end framework integrating trend–detail decomposition, cumulative damage modeling, extended one-dimensional local binary pattern (1D-LBP) encoding and a hybrid Convolutional Neural Network–Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory–Gated Recurrent Unit (CNN–BiLSTM–GRU) architecture is proposed. The objective is to improve degradation representation, prediction accuracy, robustness and interpretability for intelligent predictive maintenance under varying operating conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Raw vibration signals are first standardized on a bearing-wise basis and decomposed into trend and detail components. An extended 1D-LBP operator and a cumulative damage indicator are then employed to extract complementary degradation information and construct a four-channel health indicator. These features are processed by a hybrid CNN–BiLSTM–GRU network within a multi-task learning framework that jointly predicts health indicators, RUL percentage, degradation rate and degradation phase. The proposed framework is validated on the PRONOSTIA benchmark using 11 bearing prediction scenarios, supplemented by ablation studies and multi-seed experiments to evaluate robustness and model stability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The proposed framework consistently achieved accurate and robust RUL prediction across 11 PRONOSTIA bearing prediction scenarios, yielding average values of MAE = 0.0884, RMSE = 0.1225, RA = 0.855, and Score = 0.537. Ablation experiments and three independent random-seed evaluations demonstrated that each architectural component contributes to the overall performance, with the extended 1D-LBP encoding providing the largest improvement. The results also confirmed the framework's stability, robustness against noisy degradation signals and strong generalization capability under different operating conditions, highlighting its effectiveness for intelligent predictive maintenance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The proposed framework was validated using the PRONOSTIA benchmark under controlled laboratory conditions. Although the results demonstrate strong predictive performance and robustness, further validation on additional bearing datasets and real industrial environments is required to confirm its generalization capability. Future research will focus on domain adaptation, self-supervised learning, uncertainty-aware prognostics and multi-sensor fusion to improve adaptability under varying operating conditions and reduce dependence on labeled run-to-failure data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The proposed framework provides a practical solution for intelligent predictive maintenance by enabling accurate and stable RUL estimation under varying operating conditions. Its robust degradation representation supports timely maintenance scheduling, reduces unexpected machine failures, minimizes maintenance costs and improves equipment availability. The framework can be readily integrated into condition monitoring systems for rotating machinery and has the potential to support Industry 4.0 and smart manufacturing applications by enhancing maintenance decision-making and operational reliability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study presents a unified prognostic framework that integrates trend–detail decomposition, cumulative damage modeling, 1D-LBP encoding and hybrid CNN–BiLSTM–GRU learning within a multi-task architecture. Unlike existing approaches that employ these techniques separately, the proposed framework jointly exploits complementary degradation representations to improve RUL prediction. Comprehensive ablation studies, multi-seed stability analyses and a monotonicity constraint further validate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed methodology, providing an accurate, interpretable and reproducible solution for intelligent bearing prognostics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Understanding merchants' continued use of food delivery platforms: an investment model-based perspective on relationship commitment
container-title: British Food Journal
22f93112c411a7534f4a70461537727289d38e6a.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The rapid expansion of food delivery platforms has reshaped the foodservice industry, yet prior research has largely emphasized consumer behavior while overlooking merchants' relational decisions. This study examines the key factors influencing foodservice merchants' relationship commitment toward food delivery platforms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Grounded in the investment model of commitment, this study develops a relationship-based framework incorporating relational competence, brand image and perceived benefits as antecedents, with satisfaction, relationship investment and quality of alternatives as predictors of relationship commitment. The COVID-19 pandemic is examined as a contextual moderator. Survey data were collected between May and August 2023 from 253 foodservice merchants in Taiwan and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results show that relational competence positively affects satisfaction, brand image strongly enhances relationship investment and perceived benefits significantly reduce the perceived quality of alternatives. <jats:p>Workplace flexibility has become an important feature of contemporary employment, influencing how employees organize work and manage professional responsibilities. However, flexibility does not automatically produce stronger commitment or improved performance. This conceptual paper examines how workplace flexibility may shape employee commitment and performance through perceived autonomy, work-life balance, and job satisfaction. Drawing on Social Exchange Theory, Self-Determination Theory, the Job Demands-Resources Model, and Conservation of Resources Theory, it develops an integrated framework identifying organizational support and managerial trust as important contextual conditions. title: A differential model for coupled heat conduction in highly porous polymer networks
container-title: Transport Phenomena
6480039add46a02ccb99e1280be649544d5a95c1.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Highly porous polymer networks combine a continuous solid skeleton with a gas-filled pore space and may exhibit effective thermal conductivities close to, or below, that of the unconfined gas. Predicting this conductivity from independently measurable material properties remains difficult because heat is transported through the polymer skeleton, the confined gas, and thermal radiation, while each contribution depends differently on density and microstructure. A differential framework is developed in which the nonporous polymer or multicomponent solid is taken as the initial material and gas-filled pores are introduced incrementally. This construction preserves the connected character of the solid skeleton and couples solid and gas conduction within a single effective-medium equation. Unlike conventional decompositions that add separately estimated solid and gas contributions, the confined gas is homogenized directly into the evolving connected skeleton. In addition, the commonly fitted density exponent is predicted from the pore depolarization factors and can be evaluated from a measured pore-shape distribution. The conductivity of the pore gas is allowed to depend on temperature, pressure, and pore size through Knudsen suppression, while pore shape is represented by the depolarization factors of randomly oriented spheroids. Thermal radiation is added through an independently measurable infrared extinction coefficient. For spherical nonconducting pores, the model recovers the density scaling with exponent 3/2 associated with the classical differential effective-medium result; for nonspherical pores, the corresponding exponent follows directly from pore geometry. Multicomponent polymer, cross-linker, and particulate skeletons are incorporated through a fixed-composition differential homogenization at the solid-skeleton scale. The resulting model requires bulk constituent conductivities, skeletal and apparent densities, gas properties, an effective pore size or pore-size distribution, and at most a small number of microstructural parameters. It therefore provides a practical basis for comparing different polymer aerogels and for predicting the effects of composition, porosity, pore geometry, gas pressure, and temperature.</jats:p>

title: Digital Marketing Acceleration of Shopee for Lapeo Marlin Shredded Fish Products as a Catalyst for Economic Resilience and Independence of Local Communities

f509968e13f4d62f9a6b3caf51811dfe5da854fa.abstract: <jats:p>Lapeo Village, Campalagian District, Polewali Mandar Regency holds significant fishery potential, notably the processing of marlin fish into shredded fish (abon) by the Rezky Kuliner Lapeo Business Group. However, this potential is hindered by conventional marketing, simple packaging, and the absence of a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP). This partnership-based community service program aims to accelerate digital marketing via the Shopee platform, redesign product packaging, create a QRIS account for non-cash transactions, and compile operational SOPs to build resilience and economic independence for both productive partners (Rezky Kuliner Lapeo) and non-productive partners (PKK Pokja III Lapeo Village). The implementation methods included socialization, intensive training, daily technical assistance, and data-driven evaluation based on data analytics. The results indicated a significant increase in partners' capacity: the creation of a competitive new visual identity with marketable standing pouch variations, implementation of payments via QRIS barcode scans, the formulation of SOP documents implemented in up to 80% of business activities, and the operation of an official store on Shopee. The most accelerated result was demonstrated by the performance of the Shopee store, which recorded its first sale within one week after the Shopee account was verified and declared active. The active involvement of PKK Pokja III as a digital promotion support team further reinforces the sustainable self-reliance of the village economy.</jats:p>

title: Implementation of a Sharia-Based Waste Bank as  a Community Empowerment Model for Managing Economically Valuable Waste
container-title: MOVE: Journal of Community Service and Engagement
c1a917237b3f3ea89ebd285bf1ed71bac2141316.abstract: <jats:p>Waste management requires a community-based approach that addresses environmental cleanliness while increasing the economic value of recyclable materials. This community service activity aimed to implement a Sharia Waste Bank as a community empowerment model for managing economically valuable waste. The program applied a participatory approach through socialization, customer registration, waste sorting and collection, weighing, transaction recording, and community assistance, with students involved as facilitators. The results showed the establishment of a more structured waste management mechanism involving paper, plastic bottles, and glass bottles, supported by weighing and value-recording procedures. Community participation in depositing recyclable materials indicated that the waste bank could function as both an environmental education platform and an economic empowerment instrument. The implementation of the Sharia Waste Bank strengthened community involvement by transforming waste from discarded material into a resource with measurable economic and value.</jats:p>

e5333a54d45a54d46a27ac447b9b95c37ad75e7d.abstract: <jats:p>Taxation is primary source of state revenue and plays a strategic role in supporting national development. title: Transforming Kitchen Waste into Biogas through Community Empowerment in Petamburan
container-title: MOVE: Journal of Community Service and Engagement
e0e96309875a780ac6f5429eb4d540ab3a621035.abstract: <jats:p>Dense urban settlements face limited organic-waste treatment capacity, inconsistent household waste sorting, and insufficient skills in operating biogas technology. This community engagement program aimed to strengthen the capacity of residents of Neighborhood Unit 009, Petamburan, Central Jakarta, to convert kitchen waste into energy and organic fertilizer. The program involved community outreach, hands-on training, technology deployment, mentoring and evaluation, and sustainability strengthening. Twenty-three residents participated, and five were appointed as local operators. A 1,400-L digester was installed and initially charged with 200 kg of fresh cow manure as the microbial inoculum, followed by the gradual addition of sorted kitchen waste. The mean waste-sorting knowledge score increased from 72.61 to 100.00, while the biogas-technology score increased from 71.88 to 93.62. Slurry was first collected during the second week, and methane-containing biogas was detected during the fourth week. Integrating appropriate technology, practical training, standard operating procedures, an operational logbook, and resident-led management improved community knowledge and operational readiness.</jats:p>
